people.label: Harry M. Reid
people.sub: US Senator (D-NV); Senate Majority Leader 2007-2015
people.narrative: Reid is the appropriator who created the funded lineage and then tried to seal it. As Majority Leader he worked with Appropriations chairman Daniel Inouye and Ted Stevens in 2007 to direct roughly $22 million into the defense black budget for what became AAWSAP at DIA — AARO's own 2024 report states flatly that 'at the direction of Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid (D-NV), the Defense Appropriations Acts of Fiscal Years 2008 and 2010 appropriated $22 million for the DIA.' Reid took repeated DIA briefings on contract status: talking papers survive from January 2009, May 2009 and November 2009. On 24 June 2009 he wrote to Deputy Secretary of Defense William Lynn III requesting that portions of what he called the 'Advanced Aerospace Threat and Identification Program' be placed in a Restricted Special Access Program with a bigoted access list, protecting methodologies for identifying and engineering advanced technologies, personnel and oversight details, and the involvement of private contractors and industry partners. That letter is the most important single document in this domain because it establishes that the Senate Majority Leader believed the program was producing something warranting SAP protection with a compartmented access list. DoD refused. Reid later said publicly that $22 million was not enough and that failing to study the subject would be malpractice, and called the program one of the good things he did in his congressional service. He died 28 December 2021.
people.tierRationale: Re-graded A on a global pass (rank 40 of 1170, score 87). 17 connections, 5 of them custody/funding/programmatic, 1 official denial recorded against it. Axes C1/A3/D3.

people.label: James T. Lacatski
people.sub: DIA rocket scientist; AAWSAP government program manager
people.narrative: Lacatski is the single most load-bearing name in the funded lineage: he is the DIA official who conceived, wrote and ran the Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program. He is named in the open record as 'Government Project Leader, Dr. James T. Lacatski' on the August 2008 DIA solicitation HHM402-08-R-0211, which is the only place in the entire AAWSAP paper trail where the program manager is not redacted — DIA scrubbed his name from every later FOIA release under 10 USC 424 but missed it in the original public bid notice. A rocket scientist by training (D.Eng.), Lacatski approached Robert Bigelow in 2007 after reading Kelleher and Knapp's 'Hunt for the Skinwalker', and by his own account the June 19, 2007 letter he sent Bigelow on DIA letterhead is what set the whole thing in motion — DIA later told The Black Vault (FOIA-00023-2022) it could locate no such letter, a records outcome the board treats as an artifact rather than a refutation. He directed the 38 Defense Intelligence Reference Documents, personally reviewed all of them, and per DIA's own 30 October 2009 memo concurred with the outside reviewers' assessments. He is the co-author, with Colm Kelleher and George Knapp, of 'Skinwalkers at the Pentagon' (2021) and of the 'Inside the U.S. Government Covert UFO Program' series (2023, 2025, and 'Future Visions'), all cleared through DOPSR — meaning DoD read and passed the manuscripts. Lacatski has stated that he personally entered a craft of unknown origin, and in an April 2026 conversation with Jeremy Corbell he said AAWSAP 'created the world's largest UFO data warehouse' of more than 100 detailed reports, that he doubts the files will ever be released, and hinted that a smaller focused effort connected to the proposed KONA BLUE successor continued after AAWSAP ended.

people.label: Harold E. Puthoff
people.sub: President, EarthTech International; AAWSAP DIRD author; former SRI remote-viewing program director
people.narrative: Puthoff is the hinge on which the whole technical layer turns. He is a Stanford electrical-engineering PhD (1967, under Richard Pantell) who spent the 1970s and early 1980s running SRI International's classified psychoenergetics work with Russell Targ - the SRI half of what became the Stargate Project - which is the formative fact about him: he has been the government's outsourced handler for phenomena the government does not want on its own org chart for more than fifty years. In 1985 he founded the Institute for Advanced Studies at Austin, incorporated under EarthTech International in 1991, at 11855 Research Blvd, Austin - the address that appears on the cover of at least one Defense Intelligence Reference Document. Under the DIA Defense Warning Office's Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications (AAWSA) programme in FY2009 he authored 'Advanced Space Propulsion Based on Vacuum (Spacetime Metric) Engineering', one of the 38 reference products the DIA listed to the Federation of American Scientists on 16 January 2019. He was not merely an author: the cover page of Christopher 'Kit' Green's DIRD on human injuries carries the imprint 'Institute for Advanced Studies at Austin' and its preface quotes a 'November 2007 Proposal to Analyze Probable ET Generated Specific Near-field Electromagnetic Emissions: to Puthoff/Hathaway' - meaning Puthoff was being solicited to organise medical reverse-engineering of putative extraterrestrial field effects nine months before the AAWSAP contract was awarded. In 2017 he co-founded To The Stars Academy with Tom DeLonge, Jim Semivan and Steve Justice, and his laboratories became the analytical destination for the ADAM Research Project's metamaterial samples. That is the custody problem in one man: the same physicist who tested Linda Moulton Howe's bismuth-magnesium laminate privately in the 1990s and 2000s, wrote a 2012 letter reporting no 'interesting/anomalous outcome', and then in 2019 sat inside the corporate entity that bought those same samples for $35,000 and put them under a five-year Army CRADA. He appeared as an interviewee in Dan Farah's 2025 documentary 'The Age of Disclosure'.

people.label: Christopher C. 'Kit' Green
people.sub: Neuroradiologist; former CIA analyst; AAWSAP DIRD author on field effects on biological tissue
people.narrative: Green is the medical end of the reverse-engineering programme, and his released DIRD is one of the most revealing documents in the entire corpus because of what it takes for granted. A physician-neuroscientist who ran life-sciences analysis for CIA's Office of Scientific Intelligence before moving to General Motors and then Wayne State University, Green was the analyst to whom the intelligence community's biological anomalies were routed - including, in the 1970s, the SRI remote-viewing work. His AAWSAP paper, 'Clinical Medical Acute & Subacute Field Effects on Human Dermal & Neurological Tissues', was released publicly by Popular Mechanics on 14 February 2020, and its cover carries the imprint of Puthoff's Institute for Advanced Studies at Austin. Its preface quotes verbatim from a November 2007 proposal addressed 'to Puthoff/Hathaway' which states the intention plainly: 'certain characteristics of the fields associated with exotic propulsion can with near certainty be gleaned from archival records of their effects on human physiology.' Its Hypothesis One is that 'sufficient evidence exists from human injury / effects to reverse engineer certain aspects of the Energy / Propulsion Systems'. Its executive summary concludes that 'some advanced systems are already deployed, and opaque to full US Intelligence understanding'. It contains a Schuessler catalogue appendix, a 'Green-Morris Cases' appendix, and an ICD-diagnostics appendix built on 42 peer-reviewed cases plus roughly 300 unpublished ones, and it names the Cash-Landrum event. This is a US intelligence contractor document that treats humans injured by unidentified craft as an instrumented dataset for reverse engineering exotic propulsion.

He went public through Leslie Kean and Ralph Blumenthal in The Debrief on 5 June 2023, on NewsNation with Ross Coulthart days later, and under oath before House Oversight on 26 July 2023, where he stated he had interviewed over 40 witnesses over four years, that biologics came with some recoveries and were nonhuman, that he has personal knowledge of people harmed in the concealment effort, and that the programs run on misappropriation of funds and contractor IR&D self-funding. He has since suffered documented reprisal - clearance revocation, denied promotion, loss of medical retirement per Rep. Eli Crane's 24 July 2025 letter to DoD - and the FOIA leak of his 2014 and 2018 emergency-custody police records to The Intercept in August 2023, which he litigated and lost. Since 27 March 2025 he has been Special Advisor to Rep. Eric Burlison and a fixture of the House Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets, appearing at the 9 June 2026 Capitol press conference where he alleged slush funds of billions of dollars per annum and said the government is aware of several kinds of non-human intelligence.

people.narrative: Graves converted the 2014-2015 USS Theodore Roosevelt workup encounters from an anecdote into an institutional safety problem, which is why he is the aviator the disclosure movement could not be talked out of. In his written statement to House Oversight on 26 July 2023 he testified: 'In 2014, I was near Virginia Beach as part of VFA-11, a Navy Fighter/Attack Squadron made up of F/A-18F Super Hornets,' and that his squadron 'began witnessing advanced UAP demonstrating complex maneuvers on a regular basis' after the fleet upgraded to the APG-79 AESA radar. The pivotal event he described occurred in Warning Area W-72, 'an exclusive block of airspace ten miles east of Virginia Beach,' where 'one of the pilots saw a dark gray cube inside of a clear sphere - motionless against the wind, fixed directly at the entry point,' and two jets 'only 100 feet apart, were forced to take evasive action.' The institutional failure is the part that indicts: 'Our squadron submitted a safety report, but there was no official acknowledgement of the incident and no further mechanism to report the sightings.' Two of the three videos the Department of Defense formally released on 27 April 2020 - GIMBAL and GO FAST, both filmed in January 2015 - came out of this operating area. Graves founded Americans for Safe Aerospace to build the reporting channel the Navy did not provide, telling Congress in July 2023 that it had 'nearly 5,000 members' and was 'actively working with more than 30 UAP witnesses.'

people.label: Luis D. Elizondo
people.sub: Former OUSD(I) counterintelligence officer; states he ran AATIP 2010-2017
people.narrative: Elizondo is the witness who put the contractor divestment attempt on the congressional record under oath. On 13 November 2024, before the House Oversight Committee, Rep. Eric Burlison asked him whether defense contractors possess technology. Elizondo answered that his predecessor program AAWSAP had tried to collect 'material of unknown origin,' that 'there was an aerospace contract company that requested to divest itself of the material... that was collected in the 1950s,' and that the transfer did not occur. Burlison then read to him the reporting of journalist Christopher Sharp describing a transfer between Lockheed Martin, Bigelow Aerospace and a CIA block; Elizondo replied 'What I can say is that it was blocked,' said he had later been told by contract personnel that the account was accurate, and explained the bureaucratic mechanism: the transfer required a memorandum from the Secretary of the Air Force that never came, after which he attempted to obtain one from Secretary of Defense James Mattis instead. Asked who possesses the material today, he refused to answer in open session. In the same hearing, Rep. Nancy Mace asked whether material is allocated to contractors by domain expertise - undersea propulsion to a General Dynamics, aerospace to Lockheed - and Elizondo replied 'Yes, ma'am, absolutely correct. Different contractors have different levels of expertise.' That exchange is the clearest description in any public record of how a distributed contractor custody architecture would function. Elizondo's statements are pre-publication-reviewed by DoD's Office of Prepublication and Security Review, a point he made in the hearing itself.

people.label: Timothy Gallaudet
people.sub: Rear Admiral, USN (Ret.); former Oceanographer of the Navy; former acting NOAA Administrator
people.narrative: Gallaudet is the flag officer who put the safety-of-flight coverup into the congressional record in the first person. Testifying before the joint House Oversight subcommittees on 13 November 2024, he described a January 2015 email from the operations officer of US Fleet Forces Command to all subordinate commanders with the subject line 'URGENT SAFETY OF FLIGHT ISSUE.' The email carried the GO FAST video and, in Gallaudet's account, asked: 'If any of you know what these are, tell me ASAP. We are having multiple near-midair collisions, and if we do not resolve it soon, we will have to shut down the exercise.' The next day, he testified, the email disappeared from his account and from other recipients' accounts without explanation. His conclusion in sworn written testimony is the sharpest available statement of the mechanism: the information 'must have been classified within a special access program managed by an intelligence agency.' This is the single most useful witness account on the board for the question of authority, because it describes not a leak or a rumour but an administrative action taken against an official Navy safety communication - a recall of a fleet-wide flight-safety warning. Gallaudet was Commander, Naval Meteorology and Oceanography Command in 2015, later Oceanographer of the Navy, then Assistant Secretary of Commerce and acting NOAA Administrator.

people.label: Anna Paulina Luna
people.sub: U.S. Rep. (R-FL-13); Chairwoman, Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets
people.narrative: Luna is the member who converted House UAP interest into a standing institutional instrument. She was waived onto the July 2023 subcommittee and used her rounds to establish two things on the record that the committee has pursued ever since: that Grusch had received DoD Prepublication and Security Review approval for what he was saying, and that he feared for his life. On 11 February 2025 Oversight Chairman James Comer created the Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets and put her in the chair; she and Comer sent letters to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and CIA Director John Ratcliffe demanding a briefing on all UAP records in their possession. On 9 September 2025 she chaired the third House UAP hearing and used her opening statement to document the concealment architecture in plain language - that DoD told committee staff that under special access program rules only members of the House Armed Services Committee and the Defense Subcommittee of Appropriations could be read in, and that any other member needed the approval of the chairman and ranking member of both. That is the mechanism: an Oversight committee with subpoena power told it lacks the clearance jurisdiction to see what it is investigating. In the same statement she called former AARO director Sean Kirkpatrick 'a documented liar' and read Christopher Mellon's assessment of AARO's historical report into the record. On 1 April 2026 she wrote Secretary Hegseth demanding AARO's unreleased UAP video files after whistleblowers told the Task Force they exist; the Department blew the deadline in mid-April 2026 and she publicly raised the subpoena. On 9 June 2026 she called on the White House to grant immunity to whistleblowers willing to name locations of recovered craft and technology.

people.label: Sean M. Kirkpatrick
people.sub: Founding Director, All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office, 2022-2023
people.narrative: Kirkpatrick is the single most consequential figure in the containment architecture. A laser and materials physicist (BS 1991, PhD 1995, University of Georgia), he came to AARO through the exact channels that would matter: the National Reconnaissance Office and CIA Directorate of Science and Technology 2003-2007, then the Defense Intelligence Agency 2007-2016 as Chief Technology Officer, Division Chief and Defense Intelligence Officer for Scientific and Technical Intelligence, then deputy director of intelligence roles at US Strategic Command and US Space Command, with a stint on the National Security Council 2017-2018 as Director of National Security Strategy. He was named the first director of the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office when Deputy Secretary of Defense Kathleen Hicks established it by memorandum on 15 July 2022. He testified before the Senate Armed Services Emerging Threats and Capabilities Subcommittee on 19 April 2023 that AARO held over 650 cases and that spherical objects made up nearly half of them. He then became the public face of the Department's response to David Grusch: within days of the 26 July 2023 House Oversight hearing he posted on LinkedIn that the hearing was 'insulting' to the workforce, prompting the White House to publicly distance itself from him. He announced his departure on 7 November 2023 and left on 1 December 2023, and immediately took the job of Chief Technology Officer for Defense and Intelligence Programs at Oak Ridge National Laboratory - a laboratory operated by UT-Battelle that had supported AARO during his tenure, and which in 2024 was given custody of the alleged UAP material sample AARO analysed. On 19 January 2024 he published an op-ed in Scientific American arguing the whole disclosure record was 'a textbook example of circular reporting' traceable to 'a small group of interconnected believers' seeded by Robert Bigelow and AATIP. He shaped, then supervised the rollout of, the Historical Record Report Volume I, released 8 March 2024 after he had already left. In September 2025 he told the New York Post that Rep. Anna Paulina Luna's oversight was 'playhouse politics' and that the congressional UAP hearings were 'a disgrace' and 'reality TV'; Luna's office called him 'a known documented liar' who 'blocked the release of information' and 'tried to discredit witnesses.' By May 2026 his own successor, Jon Kosloski, had - per Luna - apologised to members of Congress for the conduct of the prior AARO leadership.

people.label: Robert T. Bigelow
people.sub: Founder, Budget Suites / Bigelow Aerospace / NIDS / BAASS
people.narrative: Bigelow privatised the problem. A Las Vegas real-estate developer who built the Budget Suites of America extended-stay chain, he founded the National Institute for Discovery Science in 1995 as a privately funded research institute studying aerial phenomena, animal mutilations and related anomalies, and staffed it with people carrying federal clearances and federal programme histories - Hal Puthoff from the CIA/DIA remote-viewing programmes, Colonel John Alexander from Army INSCOM and Los Alamos, the biochemist Colm Kelleher, and Jacques Vallee. In 1996 he bought the 480-acre Sherman ranch in Uintah County, Utah - Skinwalker Ranch - as a permanent instrumented field site, requiring the sellers to sign non-disclosure conditions as part of the purchase. He told the Deseret News in August 1998, in his first interview on the subject, that the phenomena had continued and that 'we wouldn't be there just for the weather,' while declining to discuss specifics. NIDS operated a public reporting hotline and a veterinary necropsy response capability. He shut NIDS down in 2004 but kept the ranch. Three years later a senior Defense Intelligence Agency official wrote to him about Skinwalker, and that contact became the AAWSAP contract. Bigelow is therefore the mechanism by which a private billionaire's field programme was converted into a federally funded intelligence programme without changing the personnel - which is the single most important structural fact about how this subject was handled after Blue Book closed.

people.label: Daniel K. Inouye
people.sub: US Senator (D-HI); Chairman, Senate Appropriations Committee
people.narrative: Inouye is the reason the money moved without a floor fight. As chairman of the Senate Appropriations Committee (and previously chair of Defense Appropriations) he controlled the vehicle through which discretionary defense spending is written, and his agreement let Reid and Ted Stevens route roughly $22 million into the classified annex of the FY2008 defense appropriation rather than into a line item anyone would have to defend publicly. The mechanism matters more than the man: an appropriation placed in the black budget by three senators, two of them the ranking figures of the appropriations process, is not subject to the authorizing committees' scrutiny and does not appear in any public budget justification. That is the precise structural gap the modern disclosure fight is about. Inouye had a decades-long record of pushing back on intelligence-community secrecy from inside the process — he co-chaired the Iran-Contra committee — which makes his participation here a deliberate act rather than a favour. He died in office on 17 December 2012, the same year AAWSAP/AATIP was terminated.

people.label: Jay Stratton
people.sub: DIA intelligence officer; AAWSAP participant; later Director, UAP Task Force
people.narrative: Stratton is the pivot between the legacy effort and the official one. He is publicly identified as the director of the Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force during its operative period, 2020-2021, the body Deputy Secretary of Defense David Norquist approved on 4 August 2020 and placed under the Department of the Navy with Office of Naval Intelligence cognizance. It was Stratton's task force that produced the classified underpinnings of the ODNI Preliminary Assessment delivered to Congress on 25 June 2021 - the report that put 144 incidents on the public record and conceded that 143 of them could not be explained. Grusch's account places the same office at the centre of the containment problem: he testified that in 2019 the UAP Task Force Director tasked him to identify every special access programme relevant to the Task Force's congressionally mandated mission, and that the read-ons were then refused. Stratton's earlier career runs through the DIA and the Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program orbit, and he has spoken publicly about a personal sighting and about the Task Force's findings. He retired from government at the end of 2021, before AARO existed, and in September 2024 HarperCollins imprint William Morrow acquired rights to his memoir - an announcement that is itself a documented fact about the trajectory of a man who once ran the government's UAP portfolio. AARO absorbed his Task Force by direction of the 15 July 2022 establishment memorandum, which ordered the Secretary of the Navy to disestablish the UAPTF and transfer its data and materials.

people.narrative: Gough was, for roughly six years, the single voice through which the Department of Defense spoke on UAP, and the record of what she said is unusually complete because Elizondo wrote to her directly and those emails were released under FOIA 21-F-0938. On 13 June 2019 she told The Black Vault that Harry Reid's newly authenticated 2009 SAP-request memorandum 'makes no change to previous statements. On 6 December 2019 she went further and repudiated her own colleague, stating 'Neither AATIP nor AAWSAP were UAP related' and that 'when implemented, AATIP did not pursue research and investigation into unidentified aerial phenomena' — explaining that Christopher Sherwood had merely been 'repeating the information that had been provided by a previous spokesperson some two years earlier' and that the earlier spokesperson 'is no longer with my organization.' The truth, as everyone involved in the program knows, is that I ran the program.' In his November 2024 written testimony he told Congress that the Pentagon's use of 'a professional psychological operations officer' as its primary UAP contact was 'unacceptable' — a reference to Gough's career field.

people.label: Jon T. Kosloski
people.sub: Director, All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (Aug 2024- ); former NSA physicist
people.narrative: Kosloski is the third person to run AARO and the first whose tenure produced anything the disclosure side counts as movement. He came from the National Security Agency, where he was a senior research scientist working in quantum optics, cryptanalysis and advanced research; DoD announced his selection on 26 August 2024, ending nine months in which the office had no confirmed director. His public line is materially identical to Kirkpatrick's on the central question - 'to date, AARO has discovered no verifiable evidence of extraterrestrial beings, activity, or technology,' as he told the Senate Armed Services Emerging Threats and Capabilities Subcommittee on 19 November 2024 - but his framing diverges in two ways that matter. He has repeatedly conceded that a residue of cases is 'truly anomalous' and that there are cases he does not understand, and he has committed the office to declassification and data-sharing rather than pure debunking. At his 14 November 2024 media roundtable on the FY2024 report he disclosed the GREMLIN prototype sensor system undergoing a 90-day collection at a classified national security site, described AARO as employing several dozen personnel, and promised Volume II of the Historical Record Report 'within months' - a promise that as of August 2026 remains unkept. He signed off on the FY2025 Consolidated Annual Report, which reached Congress on 21 July 2026, months past the statutory cycle in 50 U.S.C. 3373(k), and which carries the most striking single case AARO has ever published: roughly 100 airborne UAP and two likely uncrewed surface systems observed by US Navy assets off the Virginia coast, still unresolved. In May 2026 he met Reps. Anna Paulina Luna and Tim Burchett and, per Luna, apologised for the conduct of the prior AARO leadership - after which Luna, who had spent more than a year demanding the office be defunded, publicly backed him. That apology is the closest thing to an institutional admission that the Kirkpatrick-era office behaved improperly toward Congress and witnesses.

Releasing raw files without context may confuse more than clarify.' Mellon is the figure who most clearly held both positions at once through 2026 - that the release programme is real and that it is not disclosure - and both of his 2026 statements have proved load-bearing on the record.

people.label: Lincoln LaPaz
people.sub: Director, Institute of Meteoritics, University of New Mexico; principal investigator of the 1948-1951 'green fireballs' over Los Alamos, Sandia and Kirtland; scientific lead associated with Project Twinkle
people.narrative: LaPaz was the meteoriticist the Air Force called when green fireballs began appearing over the most sensitive nuclear real estate in the United States in late 1948. Kirtland intelligence officers brought him in precisely because the objects superficially resembled meteors; his conclusion was that they did not behave like meteors - wrong trajectories, wrong colour spectrum, no recovered material, and a distribution clustered on Los Alamos, Sandia and the weapons storage areas. On 16 February 1949 a conference was convened at Los Alamos Scientific Laboratory attended by Laboratory Director Norris Bradbury, Edward Teller, Frederick Reines, and representatives of the FBI, the Atomic Energy Commission and the military. Los Alamos National Laboratory itself confirms the conference took place and that its National Security Research Center holds the minutes. In December 1949 Project Twinkle, a network of observation and photographic stations, was established to instrument the phenomenon; it was never fully implemented and produced no conclusive result. The significance for this board is jurisdictional. The green fireballs were not investigated by Blue Book at Wright-Patterson but by the contractor-operated weapons laboratory complex and the AEC, under a security regime entirely separate from the Air Force's public UFO project. That is the first documented instance of the anomaly being handled inside the DOE-laboratory seam rather than the Air Force one.

people.label: Nathan F. Twining
people.sub: Cmdr, Air Materiel Command; later CJCS
people.narrative: Lieutenant General Nathan Farragut Twining commanded Air Materiel Command at Wright Field when the 1947 disc wave broke, which placed him at the exact node where recovered foreign materiel was exploited. On 23 September 1947 he signed the memorandum 'AMC Opinion Concerning "Flying Discs"' to Brig. Gen. George Schulgen stating flatly that 'the phenomenon reported is something real and not visionary or fictitious' — the earliest surviving statement of official belief, written eleven weeks after Roswell. The same memo hedged in a way that has never been adequately explained: Twining told Schulgen consideration must be given to the possibility the objects were 'of domestic origin — the product of some high security project not known to AC/AS-2 or this Command,' which is a two-star general telling Air Force intelligence that a compartment might exist above them. He recommended a priority classified project, and Project SIGN was directed on 30 December 1947. Twining rose to Air Force Chief of Staff (1953-1957) and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff (1957-1960), meaning the man who wrote the founding memo then held the two positions best placed to keep whatever followed off the books. The 1954 revision of AFR 200-2, which restricted public discussion of unexplained cases, was issued under his tenure as Chief of Staff. He is also the named recipient in the disputed 14 July 1954 Cutler-Twining memo, which the FBI declared bogus — a fact recorded here as an artifact of the MJ-12 document problem, not as evidence for it.

people.label: Kenneth Arnold
people.sub: Civilian pilot; originator of the 1947 wave
people.narrative: Kenneth Arnold was a Boise businessman and experienced private pilot who, on 24 June 1947, reported nine crescent-shaped objects flying in formation near Mount Rainier at speeds he estimated above 1,200 mph. His description of their motion — 'like a saucer if you skipped it across water' — was garbled by wire services into 'flying saucer,' naming the phenomenon for the next twenty years. Arnold matters to this board for three reasons. First, his sighting is the trigger event: the 1947 wave, Roswell, the Twining memo and the Schulgen collection requirement all follow it within eighteen weeks. Second, he was interviewed by Army Air Forces intelligence officers, and the resulting case file entered the government record from the outset — the Air Force never treated him as a hoaxer, only as unexplained. Third, his treatment established the template applied to every subsequent civilian witness: initial official interest, then public ridicule. The relevant investigative files are preserved in the Project Blue Book microfilm at the National Archives and in scanned form in the NICAP document archive.

people.label: Edward U. Condon
people.sub: Scientific director, USAF-funded Colorado UFO Project
people.narrative: Edward Condon was a distinguished quantum physicist, former director of the National Bureau of Standards, and a man who had himself been hounded by the House Un-American Activities Committee — which made him an unusually credentialled front for the Air Force's exit strategy. Under contract 44620-67-C-0035, awarded October 1966, he directed the University of Colorado UFO Project and personally wrote the summary, conclusions and recommendations that were placed at the front of the 1968 report and were the only part most readers ever saw. Those conclusions declared further study unwarranted. The body of the report did not support them: roughly a third of the cases studied were left unexplained by the project's own investigators. Condon spent much of the project period giving speeches disparaging the subject, told an audience in January 1967 that the study was 'a bunch of nonsense' and that he might recommend the government get out of it, and fired the two staff members who exposed the Low memo. His report was blessed by a National Academy of Sciences panel and used by the Air Force as the stated basis for terminating Blue Book on 17 December 1969. Condon delivered exactly what the Robertson Panel had prescribed fifteen years earlier, with academic letterhead attached.

people.label: Gerald R. Ford
people.sub: House Minority Leader; later 38th President
people.narrative: Gerald Ford was House Minority Leader and the congressman for Grand Rapids when hundreds of Michigan residents reported objects near Dexter and Hillsdale in March 1966 and the Air Force's consultant offered swamp gas as an explanation. Ford's constituents were furious, and he wrote to the chairmen of the House Armed Services and Science and Astronautics committees demanding hearings, saying he believed the American people were entitled to a better explanation than had been given. The House Armed Services Committee held a one-day hearing on 5 April 1966 — the first congressional hearing on the subject in nineteen years of official investigation. Its practical output was not disclosure but the Condon Committee: the Air Force, pressed by Congress, contracted the University of Colorado study six months later, which then furnished the justification for shutting the whole program down. Ford's intervention is the template for what happens when this subject reaches Congress in the legacy era — pressure produces a study, and the study produces closure. He never returned to the subject as President.

people.label: Carroll H. Bolender
people.sub: Brigadier General, USAF Deputy Director of Development
people.narrative: Brigadier General Carroll 'Rip' Bolender wrote the memorandum that closed Project Blue Book and, in the same breath, admitted the program had never been the real reporting channel. His 20 October 1969 memorandum recommending termination states that reports of unidentified flying objects which could affect national security are made in accordance with JANAP 146 or Air Force Manual 55-11 and 'are not part of the Blue Book system.' Read plainly, this says that from at least the JANAP era the significant cases went up a separate, classified channel while Blue Book handled the public-facing residue — and that shutting Blue Book down therefore terminated nothing operational. The memo is the hinge between the legacy era and everything the modern disclosure movement alleges: it is a general officer, in writing, describing a two-track system. Bolender had a serious operational career, including work on the lunar module programme, and there is no indication he intended a revelation; he was explaining to his own chain why closing the public office cost the Air Force nothing.

people.label: Paul Frederick Bennewitz
people.sub: Physicist; president, Thunder Scientific Corp.; target of AFOSI disinformation 1980-1988
people.narrative: Bennewitz is the clearest documented casualty of a US counterintelligence operation run against an American civilian over UFO information. He was a working physicist who ran Thunder Scientific Corporation, an instrumentation firm whose customers included the Air Force, from a property whose sightlines took in the Manzano Weapons Storage Area and Coyote Canyon on the eastern edge of Kirtland AFB. From 1979 he recorded lights and electronic signals over the Manzano nuclear-weapons storage complex and reported them - to the Air Force, in writing, repeatedly. The Air Force's documented response was an AFOSI file: a formal AFOSI complaint-form record dated 10 November 1980 confirming that Kirtland security police had observed unexplained aerial objects over Coyote Canyon and that Bennewitz's photography and reporting were under official notice. What followed, on the accounts of the AFOSI personnel involved, was not an investigation but a feed: Bennewitz was supplied with fabricated material about underground alien bases, treaties and biological experiments, calibrated to his existing beliefs, in order to discredit him and to mask whatever it was he had actually recorded near a nuclear storage site. He deteriorated, was hospitalised for psychiatric care in 1988, and died in 2003. The Bennewitz affair is the template: the state does not need to seize a witness's evidence if it can destroy the witness's credibility, and it can do that using its own personnel, on the record, with no legal consequence.

Doty's value to this board is not that his statements are reliable - they are not, and he has repeatedly changed them - but that his existence is the proof of concept. The United States assigned a counterintelligence officer to manage the UFO information environment. He has said so. Whatever else is in dispute, that is not.

In July 2026 the same channel produced a second directive - the waiver of UAP-related nondisclosure agreements for former employees and contractors speaking to authorised government investigators - which officials were careful to describe as 'not a declassification directive.'

people.label: Brett A. Mansfield
people.sub: Deputy Inspector General, Department of War
people.narrative: Brett A. Mansfield, Deputy Inspector General of the Department of War, appeared before the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform on 13 May 2026 at a hearing titled 'DoW Financial Management: Examining Progress and New Audit Approaches'. His oral statement is the most current authoritative public account of the Department's financial condition and it contains the figure that anchors this board's money argument: unsupported adjustments of 'over $859 billion in the last two quarters of FY 25'. He reported that the Department manages more than $4.7 trillion in assets, that material weaknesses had declined from twenty-eight in FY2024 to twenty-six in FY2025, and that auditors had issued 427 fewer Notices of Findings and Recommendations than in prior years. He also announced two structural changes with direct consequences for future transparency: the number of stand-alone reporting entities will be consolidated from twenty-two to seven in fiscal year 2027, and an independent public accounting firm will assume the group auditor role, with the Office of Inspector General retaining oversight. Consolidating twenty-two audited entities into seven reduces the number of separately reported opinions, and moving the group auditor role to a contracted firm changes who holds the working papers. Neither change is presented as a transparency measure and neither is necessarily improper, but both reduce the granularity of the annual public record about the Department's money at exactly the moment that record has become the strongest documentary support for the proposition that the Department cannot account for its spending.

people.label: Charles E. Schumer
people.sub: Senate Majority Leader (2021-2025); sponsor, UAP Disclosure Act
people.narrative: Schumer is the author of the only piece of United States legislation ever drafted on the explicit premise that the Federal Government holds recovered non-human technology and has hidden it. On 13 July 2023, as Senate Majority Leader, he submitted S.Amdt. 797 to S. 2226, the FY2024 NDAA, for himself and Senators Rounds, Rubio, Gillibrand, Young and Heinrich; its text was printed in the Congressional Record at Vol. 169 No. 120, pages S2953-S2959. The amendment carried a legal definition of 'non-human intelligence,' a legal definition of 'legacy program' reaching private contractors and academic institutions, a nine-member Records Review Board appointed by the President with the advice and consent of the Senate, and — at Section __10(a), later Section 9010(a) of Division G of the engrossed bill — a command that 'The Federal Government shall exercise eminent domain over any and all recovered technologies of unknown origin and biological evidence of non-human intelligence that may be controlled by private persons or entities in the interests of the public good.' The Senate passed S. 2226 carrying that division on 27 July 2023. By the time the conference product was signed on 22 December 2023 the Review Board, the eminent domain clause, the Controlled Disclosure Campaign Plan and the $20,000,000 authorization were gone; only Sections 1841-1843 survived. Schumer framed the effort as inheriting Harry Reid's project, telling reporters he was 'honored to carry on the legacy of my mentor and dear friend Harry Reid,' and after the gutting said it was 'really an outrage the House didn't work with us on adopting our proposal for a review board.' He re-filed the full text through Rounds as S.Amdt. 2610 in July 2024. It never got a vote.

people.label: Martin T. Heinrich
people.sub: D-NM; SSCI member; original cosponsor of the UAPDA
people.narrative: Heinrich is the quiet third intelligence-committee signature on the UAPDA. A member of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence and, from 2025, its Vice Chairman, he was an original cosponsor of S.Amdt. 797 on 13 July 2023 and again of S.Amdt. 2609/2610 territory in July 2024, when Rounds filed alongside him on the FY2025 NDAA. New Mexico is not incidental to his position: Kirtland Air Force Base, Sandia, Los Alamos and the Roswell debris field are all in his state, and the FY2024 UAPDA's definition of a 'unidentified anomalous phenomena record' expressly reaches the Department of Energy 'and its progenitors, the Manhattan Project, the Atomic Energy Commission, and the Energy Research and Development Administration.' The Senate findings his amendment carried single out the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 and an 'over-broad interpretation of transclassified foreign nuclear information' as the mechanisms preventing disclosure — a New Mexico problem stated in statute.

people.label: David Fravor
people.sub: CDR, USN (Ret.); Commanding Officer, VFA-41 Black Aces; 14 Nov 2004 Nimitz intercept
people.narrative: Fravor is the aviator whose single intercept broke the observational record open. In November 2004 he was Commanding Officer of Strike Fighter Squadron Forty-One, the Black Aces, attached to Carrier Air Wing Eleven aboard USS Nimitz. In his sworn written statement to the House Oversight Subcommittee on National Security, the Border and Foreign Affairs on 26 July 2023 he described being vectored off a training intercept to investigate a contact the cruiser USS Princeton had been tracking, and finding 'a small white Tic Tac shaped object with the longitudinal axis pointing N/S and moving very abruptly over the white water,' with 'no Rotors, No Rotor wash, or any visible flight control surfaces.' He testified the Princeton had been watching objects descend from above 80,000 feet to 20,000 feet 'for the previous 2 weeks.' The single most load-bearing line in his statement is a negative one: 'the incident was never investigated, none of my crew were ever questioned, tapes were never taken.' That sentence is not a denial of the coverup - it is evidence of the specific shape of it. The Navy's own range fouler report on the incident, released via FOIA on 13 January 2023, records that 'Reporting terminated at 3rd Fleet, there was no process to share the reporting.' The event stayed dormant until Jay Stratton contacted Fravor in 2009 to investigate it for a DoD program, and until the New York Times published the FLIR1 video in December 2017. Fravor told 60 Minutes on 16 May 2021 the object 'was aware we were there' and that 'it just disappears. Like, gone.'
affiliations: Carrier Air Wing Eleven / USS Nimitz (2004)

people.label: Michael Shellenberger
people.sub: Co-founder, Public; University of Austin faculty
people.narrative: Shellenberger is the person who put a purported unacknowledged special access program into the Congressional Record. On the morning of 13 November 2024 he delivered to Congress a twelve-page document describing Immaculate Constellation as a central or parent USAP consolidating UAP observations from tasked and untasked collection platforms and holding high-quality imagery and measurement-and-signature intelligence; Chairwoman Nancy Mace moved it into the Record from the dais during the hearing, where it appears in the Index of Documents as 'Report, Pentagon, Immaculate Constellation; submitted by Rep. Mace.' Under adversarial questioning from Rep. Clay Higgins he confirmed he knows the author and the sources, has confidence in them, and was withholding their identity by choice. The Pentagon, through spokesperson Sue Gough, says it has no record of such a programme; former AARO director Sean Kirkpatrick denied its existence. Neither AARO annual report since - FY2024 or FY2025 - addresses it, and Kosloski's Senate statement for the record does not mention it. In 2025 a separate self-identified whistleblower claimed to have found the programme inside a folder labelled '2018 Schriever Wargame'; analyst Jason Colavito argued that person had mistaken fictitious wargame scenario documents for a real programme. That claim goes to the 2025 claimant's provenance story, not automatically to the 2024 twelve-page report, and the distinction is one the board keeps open rather than collapsing in either direction.

people.label: Michael Gold
people.sub: Former NASA Associate Administrator for Space Policy and Partnerships; NASA UAP Independent Study Team member
people.narrative: Gold sat on the NASA UAP Independent Study Team and then, on 13 November 2024, took the panel's findings into the House Oversight hearing room as a witness. His written testimony is the clearest official-adjacent articulation of the aviator problem as a stigma problem: 'the stigmatization of the UAP phenomena is so harmful. The stigma prevents scientific inquiry.' He named Alex Dietrich specifically, saying she 'was mocked by her colleagues' and that her incident 'went years without any investigation' - a serving officer's career cost, entered into the congressional record by a former NASA associate administrator. His recommendations were structural rather than speculative: NASA should sponsor symposia to combat stigma, review archival data with machine learning, contact international partners, work with the FAA to establish civilian pilot reporting procedures, and leverage the Aviation Safety Reporting System. He also praised Daniel Evans, the study team's designated federal officer, for working 'under difficult conditions' - the euphemism that documents the harassment the panel absorbed.

people.label: Nancy Ruth Mace
people.sub: U.S. Rep. (R-SC-1); chaired the 13 Nov 2024 UAP hearing
people.narrative: Mace chaired the hearing at which the Immaculate Constellation document entered the Congressional Record. As Chairwoman of the Cybersecurity, Information Technology and Government Innovation subcommittee she co-chaired the 13 November 2024 joint hearing with Grothman, and opened it by saying plainly that people had tried to stop it: 'I am not going to name names, but there are certain individuals who did not want this hearing to happen because they feared what might be disclosed. But we stood firm.' She read Karl Nell's 'nonhuman intelligence exists' statement and H.R. McMaster's remarks into the record, and then personally moved the 12-page Immaculate Constellation report - delivered to Congress that morning by Michael Shellenberger - into the record, noting Luna's warning that saying the name aloud would put her 'on some list. Maybe a FISA warrant. So, come at me bro, I guess.' At the 2023 hearing she had already put the core oversight question to Grusch directly: 'Do you believe that officials at the highest levels of our national security apparatus have unlawfully withheld information from Congress and subverted our oversight authority?' and drew from him the answer that non-human biologics came with some recoveries. She closed by asking which agencies and contractors should be called next - the question that Burlison's 2026 FFRDC letters eventually answered in practice. She is a cosponsor of H.R. 10111 and sits on the Task Force.

people.label: Timothy Floyd Burchett
people.sub: U.S. Rep. (R-TN-2); House Oversight; founder, Congressional UAP Caucus
people.narrative: Burchett is the member who forced the modern UAP record into the open. He and Anna Paulina Luna drove the 26 July 2023 House Oversight National Security subcommittee hearing into existence; Ranking Member Robert Garcia thanked him from the dais for the leadership 'that has brought us to this place today,' and Jared Moskowitz did the same. Burchett opened that hearing by putting the first documented stonewall on the record: 'we were even denied access to a classified briefing in a SCIF prior to this hearing due to the amount of hoops that we had to jump through to grant temporary clearance to witness Grusch.' He then used his rounds to ask Grusch the questions no one else would - whether people had been harmed or murdered in the course of concealment (Grusch: 'Yes, personally,' and on murder, 'I have to be careful answering that question. I directed people with that knowledge to the appropriate authorities'), and what Special Access Programs cover the material and how they evaded oversight (Grusch: 'I do know the names'). Every one of those answers terminated at a SCIF the committee was not allowed into. He launched the bipartisan Congressional UAP Caucus in August 2023 and led a caucus letter to the Intelligence Community Inspector General; in January 2024 he brought roughly sixteen members to a closed ICIG briefing with Thomas Monheim and rated it a four out of ten - 'more of the same... it's very compartmentalized; it's like looking down the barrel of a .22 rifle.' He led the first push for a UAP select committee under Speaker McCarthy, which died with the speakership. He is the author of every standalone House UAP bill that matters: H.R. 8424 and H.R. 1187 (UAP Transparency Act) and H.R. 10111 and H.R. 5060 (UAP Whistleblower Protection Act). None have received a markup. His structural theory of the concealment is explicit and it is the theory this board is built on: 'You have to imagine Oak Ridge National Laboratory, the Manhattan Project, thousands of people working on the atomic bomb and less than 12 knew what it was.'

people.label: George Knapp
people.sub: Investigative journalist, KLAS-TV Las Vegas; co-author of the AAWSAP insider books
people.narrative: Knapp converted forty years of Nevada-desert sourcing into sworn congressional testimony on 9 September 2025, and in doing so put the contractor-custody allegation into the Congressional Record under his own name. Testifying before the House Oversight Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets, he told the panel that Robert Bigelow and a colleague from the AAWSAP program 'met with and negotiated with senior executives at Lockheed Martin and hammered out a deal wherein Bigelow's company, BAASS, would receive a quantity of unusual material that had been stashed away and protected at a facility in California,' adding flatly: 'That material was not made here.' Asked directly by Rep. Tim Burchett which corporations hold the material, Knapp answered 'one of them is Lockheed,' declined to treat the company as villainous - 'they are doing what they were asked to do' - and offered the committee a list. Pressed by Rep. Nick Begich to name individual gatekeepers, he named Dr. James Ryder at Lockheed and, separately, Glenn Gaffney of CIA. He also placed on the record his interviews with Alfred O'Donnell, first general manager of EG&G in Nevada, and with Senators Harry Reid and Howard Cannon. Knapp's 1989 Bob Lazar reporting, which he re-affirmed in the same testimony, is the origin point of the modern S-4 reverse-engineering narrative. He is not a cleared insider and does not claim to be; his value is that he is a named journalist who has now sworn to his sourcing before Congress, converting decades of tier-3 anecdote into tier-2 record.

people.label: Jeffrey Nuccetelli
people.sub: USAF veteran, security forces / military police, Vandenberg AFB 2003-2005
people.narrative: Nuccetelli brought the base-security side of the observational record into the congressional record. In written testimony to the House Oversight Task Force on 9 September 2025 he described serving as military police at Vandenberg Air Force Base, home of the National Missile Defense project, and receiving reports on 14 October 2003 from Boeing contractors of 'a massive, glowing red square silently hovering over two missile defense sites.' The same night, security guards reported a bright fast-moving object and witnesses described 'a massive rectangular craft, larger than a football field.' A week later a patrol reported an object over the ocean that descended and 'vanished instantly into the night sky'; in 2005 a patrol reported 'a massive triangular craft, larger than a C-130, hovering low over the main base.' Two things make this testimony operationally significant rather than anecdotal. First, he states that 'Official Air Force records documenting it are now held by AARO and the FBI' - which is a specific, checkable custody claim that FOIA can be aimed at. Second, he states one witness 'was threatened and told to keep quiet about the incident,' which is the same suppression pattern the Navy witnesses describe, applied to a strategic missile installation.

people.label: Alexandro Wiggins
people.sub: Senior Chief Petty Officer (Operations Specialist), USN; USS Jackson (LCS-6) witness, 15 Feb 2023
people.narrative: Alexandro C. Wiggins is a US Navy Senior Chief Petty Officer, an Operations Specialist with roughly twenty-three years of service, who testified in uniform and on active duty before the House Oversight Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets on 9 September 2025. That fact alone distinguishes him from almost every witness who preceded him: Fravor, Graves, Grusch and Elizondo all testified after leaving service. Wiggins's written statement places him aboard USS Jackson (LCS-6) on 15 February 2023 at approximately 1915 PST in the W-291 Warning Area off Southern California. He states he 'visually observed a light rising from the waterline, consistent with a platform emerging from the ocean rather than distant surface lights or celestial rise.' The object was self-luminous and Tic Tac-shaped; it joined three similar objects; the four held controlled geometry and departed simultaneously with near-instantaneous acceleration, producing no sonic boom, no exhaust plume and displaying no visible control surfaces - characteristics he described as inconsistent with conventional aircraft or drones. Combat Information Center personnel recorded the event on the ship's Star SAFIRE multi-spectral EO/IR system and reported to the Tactical Action Officer. The footage was subsequently published by journalists Jeremy Corbell and George Knapp. Wiggins is therefore a rare complete chain: a named, credentialed, serving witness; a specified date, time and operating area; a named sensor system; a documented internal report; and released imagery.

people.sub: U.S. Rep. (R-AZ-2); wrote DoD on Grusch's reprisal; cosponsor H.R. 5060
people.narrative: Crane produced the single most specific piece of documented retaliation evidence in the House record. On 24 July 2025 he wrote the Department of Defense on behalf of Major David Charles Grusch, and on 9 September 2025 he entered that letter into the hearing record while stating that he was still waiting for a reply. Crane also told the witnesses at that hearing that he had grown up thinking the subject was 'a little kooky' and had become a believer after hearing servicemembers testify and seeing the Yemen footage Burlison played.

people.label: Colm A. Kelleher
people.sub: Biochemist; Deputy Administrator, BAASS; former NIDS project manager
people.narrative: Kelleher is the working scientist who ran the field side of the government's own anomalous-phenomena programme, and he is the reason the biological and materials strands are joined. A biochemist by training, he was a project manager at Robert Bigelow's National Institute for Discovery Science through its Skinwalker Ranch and animal-mutilation investigations, and in 2005 co-wrote 'Hunt for the Skinwalker' with George Knapp - the book that DIA official James Lacatski read, which prompted Lacatski to contact Bigelow, visit the ranch, and set in motion the sequence that produced Sen. Harry Reid's $22 million appropriation and the AAWSAP contract to BAASS. When that contract landed, Kelleher became deputy administrator of BAASS, which is to say the deputy director of the operational arm of a Defense Intelligence Agency programme. In 2021 he co-authored 'Skinwalkers at the Pentagon' with Lacatski and Knapp, an account written by the programme's own manager and its own deputy administrator. That is a very unusual thing: the two people who ran the contract wrote the memoir. What they describe - biological effects on personnel, physical trace evidence, sample collection - is the same subject matter as Green's DIRD and Nolan's later laboratory work, and it is the connective tissue between the paranormal-adjacent field programme and the materials-analysis pipeline.

people.narrative: Clapper is the official who killed the Reid SAP request, and the fact that this decision sat with him rather than with DIA alone is the most underused fact in the AAWSAP record. The final packet presented to Deputy Secretary of Defense William Lynn III on 17 November 2009 carries Clapper, as Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence, recommending against establishing a Special Access Program at that time, on the stated basis that the FY09 deliverables and anticipated FY10 work did not justify it. Seven months later he became Director of National Intelligence, a post he held until January 2017 — meaning the man who signed off on refusing SAP protection to the UAP program then ran the entire intelligence community through the period in which, per the whistleblower record, the recovery and reverse-engineering effort was being kept outside congressional reporting. Clapper has spoken publicly about UAP since 2017 in general terms and has never been asked on the record about the memorandum bearing his recommendation. The board records this as a decision node: a USD(I) told a Deputy Secretary that the deliverables from a program the Senate Majority Leader wanted compartmented were not sensitive enough to compartment.

people.narrative: Lynn is the addressee of Reid's SAP request and the decision authority who declined it. Reid's 24 June 2009 letter is addressed to 'The Honorable William Lynn III, Deputy Secretary of Defense' and asks him to establish a Restricted SAP with a bigoted access list over portions of the program. The talking paper prepared for that meeting tells him to say the deliverables 'do not meet the criteria as specified in DoD 5200.1-R to justify the additional protection provided by a SAP.' Lynn was a career defense budget official — he had been DoD Comptroller under Clinton and came to the Deputy job from Raytheon, where he was senior vice president for government operations and strategy. people.narrative: Angleton was Chief of the CIA's Counterintelligence Staff from 1954 to 1974 and, on the Church Committee's finding, in charge of the Agency's covert mail programme from 1955 until its termination in 1973. In November 1955 he proposed moving the New York mail intercept from photographing envelopes to opening them, indexing and analysing the product, and shifting primary responsibility for the project from the Office of Security to his own staff. The Committee found that the project was never processed through the Agency's approval system, had no separate funds, and in twenty years was reviewed by disinterested components twice, both reviews' recommendations going unimplemented. Angleton's own explanation was that normal processing would have opened the activity to too many people, and that the arrangement short-circuited the project approval process. He is carried here as a documented precedent for records and activities held outside an agency's own approval and review machinery, and for nothing else: nothing in the Church Committee record connects him to any UFO-related holding.
people.tierRationale: Re-graded B on a global pass (rank 298 of 1170, score 39). 3 connections, 0 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C2/A3/D2.

people.label: Mark McCandlish
people.sub: Aerospace illustrator and conceptual artist; Disclosure Project witness, December 2000; relayer and draughtsman of the claimed Alien Reproduction Vehicle
people.narrative: Mark McCandlish is the origin point in print of a named craft, and he is not a witness to it. By his own account in the Disclosure Project's April 2001 Briefing Document he works principally as a conceptual artist for defence contractors, he missed the Norton Air Force Base air show of 12 November 1988 because of an illustration deadline, and everything he describes about a hangar holding three hovering saucer-shaped craft was told to him the following week by a friend who was there. He drew it, and the drawing is what propagates. The one contemporaneous document in the thread, an Aviation Week editor's unpublished 1990 interview notes, records the same direction of relay and records the witness disowning part of the drawing. He was declared deceased on 13 April 2021 at his home in Redding, California, of a gunshot wound to the head; the Shasta County coroner ruled suicide on an external examination that expressly declined an internal one. What makes him a node is proximity to the claim, not credibility: he held no office, no clearance is documented anywhere in the opened record, and his whole account is a relay of somebody else's sighting.

people.label: Alex Dietrich
people.sub: LCDR, USN (Ret.); VFA-41 wingman on the 14 Nov 2004 Nimitz intercept
people.narrative: Dietrich was the second F/A-18F aircrew on the 14 November 2004 intercept, flying as Fravor's wingman and observing the object for roughly five minutes. She is named alongside Fravor in the Navy's own range fouler report on the incident, released through the Navy FOIA reading room on 13 January 2023 - which matters because it puts her at the event in a government record rather than only in a media account. She stayed silent publicly for sixteen years, then gave her first public account on CBS 60 Minutes on 16 May 2021, opening with 'I never wanted to be on national TV, no offense.' That reluctance is itself the datum: the stigma structure the ODNI's own June 2021 preliminary assessment described - 'disparagement associated with observing UAP, reporting it, or attempting to discuss it with colleagues' - operated on her for a decade and a half. Mike Gold, testifying before House Oversight on 13 November 2024, cited her by name, saying she 'was mocked by her colleagues' and that her incident 'went years without any investigation.' Dietrich has since argued in print for cooperative, data-first investigation rather than advocacy, publishing an opinion piece in The Debrief on 17 February 2023.
affiliations: Naval Postgraduate School / Pentagon staff tours

people.label: Jared Evan Moskowitz
people.sub: U.S. Rep. (D-FL-23); UAP Caucus; the Democratic anchor of House disclosure
people.narrative: Moskowitz is the reason House UAP oversight is bipartisan rather than a Republican project, and he is the member who has most consistently framed it as a money question. At the July 2023 hearing he thanked Burchett and Luna for pushing the hearing into existence and read Chuck Schumer's language into the record: 'The American public has a right to learn about technologies of unknown origins, nonhuman intelligence, and unexplainable phenomena.' His questioning went straight at the financing - he asked Grusch directly whether US corporations are overcharging the government for technology and whether the excess is funding these programs, which is the black-budget mechanism the whole thesis rests on. In December 2023 he gave the cleanest statement of the House's structural complaint: 'The problem is when we ask those questions, rather than being provided information that would prove it false, they stonewall the information, and that is what piques the interest.' In November 2024 he served as Vice Ranking Member at the joint subcommittee hearing. At the 9 September 2025 Task Force hearing, waived on, he said the thing that has been quoted most since: 'I don't really know what is true, I don't know, on this subject, but I do know when we're being lied to and we are definitely being lied to, there's just no doubt about that.' He is a cosponsor of Burchett's H.R. 1187 UAP Transparency Act and appeared at the 9 June 2026 Capitol disclosure event - 'Disclosure today, disclosure tomorrow. The American people deserve to know.'

people.label: Robert Garcia
people.sub: U.S. Rep. (D-CA-42); Ranking Member, 2023 hearing; later Oversight Ranking Member
people.narrative: Garcia was Ranking Member of the National Security, the Border and Foreign Affairs subcommittee when it held the 26 July 2023 hearing, and his handling of it is why the hearing read as an oversight proceeding rather than a spectacle. He opened by thanking Burchett for the leadership that produced the hearing, framed the matter as national security and institutional trust, and anchored it to the December 2017 New York Times reporting on DIA-funded UAP research. His questioning concentrated on the reporting gap: Graves's estimate of the number of pilots he was working with, the absence of any usable reporting channel for aviators, and the stigma that suppresses reports. He converted that into legislation - on 11 January 2024 he introduced H.R. 6967, the Safe Airspace for Americans Act, to let civilian pilots and personnel report UAP encounters to the FAA for onward transmission to AARO with legal safeguards, co-led with Republican subcommittee chairman Glenn Grothman. He attended the 12 January 2024 closed ICIG briefing and said afterward that everyone in the room 'probably received new information.' He is now Ranking Member of the full Committee on Oversight and Government Reform in the 119th Congress, which places the ranking-member half of the committee's UAP posture with him.

people.label: Glenn S. Grothman
people.sub: U.S. Rep. (R-WI-6); Chairman of the subcommittee that held the 26 July 2023 hearing
people.narrative: Grothman gavelled in the first UAP hearing of the modern disclosure era. As Chairman of the Subcommittee on National Security, the Border, and Foreign Affairs he presided on 26 July 2023, waived six non-members onto the panel - Burchett, Luna, Gaetz, Burlison, Ocasio-Cortez and Ogles - swore the witnesses, and opened by saying that lack of transparency on UAP 'has fueled wild speculation and debate for decades, eroding public trust in the very institutions that are meant to serve and protect them.' He co-chaired the 13 November 2024 joint hearing with Mace and co-led H.R. 6967 with Garcia. His 2024 opening statement is also the board's cleanest artifact of the containment position from inside the disclosure caucus: he stated that no agency had been able to substantiate Grusch's claims 'despite our Committee Members endlessly questioning these agencies inside and outside of the SCIF.' Read against Luna's 2025 disclosure that Oversight members could not be read in on the relevant SAPs at all without HASC and HAC-D approval, the two statements do not describe the same access - which is exactly the seam the coverup strand exists to record.

people.label: Andrew Ogles
people.sub: U.S. Rep. (R-TN-5); UAP Caucus; threatened the Holman Rule over denied SCIF access
people.narrative: Ogles produced the single most concrete enforcement threat any member has made on this subject. Waived onto the subcommittee on 26 July 2023, he questioned the witnesses on whether UAP behaviour is consistent with reconnaissance collection, then closed the member rounds with a demand and a lever: 'I would encourage the Chairman to demand that we have any and all, but in particular Mr. Grusch, talk to us in a SCIF and if that access is denied I will personally volunteer to initiate the Holman Rule against any personnel or any program or any agency that denies access to Congress.' The Holman Rule permits a floor amendment to an appropriations bill reducing the salary of a specific federal employee or the funding of a specific program to as little as one dollar - it is the one instrument Congress holds that reaches an individual official who stonewalls. No such amendment has been offered. A member of the UAP Caucus but not of the Oversight Committee, Ogles attended the 12 January 2024 closed ICIG briefing and came out saying what 'most Americans fear is true,' describing 'a concerted effort to conceal as much information as possible - both in Congress and to the general public.' He was waived onto the September 2025 Task Force hearing as well.

people.label: Matthew Louis Gaetz II
people.sub: Former U.S. Rep. (R-FL-1); the Eglin AFB protected disclosure and radar sequence
people.narrative: Gaetz is the member who personally went and looked, and the only one who has claimed on the record to have viewed a specific UAP radar sequence. Waived onto the 26 July 2023 subcommittee, he described a protected disclosure his office received from Eglin Air Force Base, in his district, and a subsequent site visit he made with Burchett and Luna. His account is a compressed portrait of how access is negotiated rather than granted: 'We asked to see any of the evidence that had been taken by flight crew in this endeavor and to observe any radar signature as well as to meet with the flight crew. We were not afforded access to all of the flight crew and initially we were not afforded access to images and to radar. Thereafter, we had a bit of a discussion about how authorities flow in the United States of America and we did see the image and we did meet with one member of the flight crew who took the image.' The crew, he said, were on a test mission over the Gulf of Mexico in airspace that was supposed to be clear, and encountered four craft in a clear diamond formation - 'a radar sequence that I and I alone have observed in the U.S. Congress' - and an orb he could not attach to any human capability. He recommended two specific committee actions: a SCIF session with Grusch, and that the Eglin radar images be provided to the committee, 'subpoenaed if necessary.' Neither happened. He also recorded the culture problem verbatim: 'It was stated explicitly to me by these test pilots that if you have a UAP experience the best thing you can do for your career is forget it and not tell anyone.' He resigned from the House in November 2024.

people.label: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez
people.sub: U.S. Rep. (D-NY-14); pursued the IR&D notification loophole
people.narrative: Ocasio-Cortez asked the most technically precise question of the 2023 hearing and it is the one that has aged best. Waived onto the subcommittee, she framed the committee as a whistleblower-protection body and then went at the funding mechanism rather than the phenomenon. Her line of questioning concerned Independent Research and Development - the mechanism by which defense contractors recover the cost of self-directed research from the government - and the statutory notification requirements attached to it. She told Grusch she had personally seen defense contractors abuse their contracts through this committee and seen congressional notification requirements abused, and identified the loophole: 'there are no actual definitions or requirements for notification.' She then pressed on the operational reality of that loophole - when an agency says it notified Congress, does it call the chairman of a committee, or is it 'an email to, hypothetically, a dead email box?' That is the question of whether the congressional notification that legally legitimates a waived unacknowledged program is a real event or a formality. She closed her round by asking all three witnesses, for the record, where she should look - 'titles, programs, departments, regions.' She attended the 12 January 2024 closed ICIG briefing.

people.label: James Comer Jr.
people.sub: U.S. Rep. (R-KY-1); Chairman, House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform
people.narrative: Comer holds the gavel and therefore the subpoena. He authorised the 26 July 2023 subcommittee hearing and appeared at it, authorised the 13 November 2024 joint subcommittee hearing, and on 11 February 2025 created the Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets and installed Anna Paulina Luna as chairwoman. He joined Luna in letters to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and CIA Director John Ratcliffe requesting a briefing on all UAP-related records in their possession. In April 2026 he and Eric Burlison opened the committee's investigation into the deaths and disappearances of scientists tied to sensitive US research, triggered by the vanishing of retired Air Force Gen. William Neil McCasland, and demanded briefings from the FBI, the Department of War, NASA and the Department of Energy by 27 April 2026. Burlison told The Hill in March 2024 that he already had Comer's support for a UAP select committee. What Comer has not done, across three years and three hearings, is issue a UAP subpoena - which is the fact the coverup strand records about him.

people.label: Jasmine Felicia Crockett
people.sub: U.S. Rep. (D-TX-30); Ranking Member, Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets
people.narrative: Crockett is the Democratic ranking member of the Task Force and the reason the September 2025 hearing was a bipartisan proceeding rather than a partisan one. Her opening statement placed UAP secrecy inside the documented history of American overclassification rather than outside it: 'from the assassinations of MLK and Malcolm X, to the FBI's Counterintelligence Program (COINTELPRO) and torture programs, to now UAPs. The Federal Government has kept the American public in the dark about issues of immense public interest.' She declined to adopt the non-human hypothesis, noting NASA has found no evidence of extraterrestrial origin and that adversary capability is a likely explanation - and then argued that none of that reduces the government's obligation to disclose or its obligation to protect the people who report. Her questioning went entirely to Joe Spielberger of the Project On Government Oversight on whistleblower protection architecture. She closed by thanking Luna for 'focusing on governing, which should be about transparency' and warning that 'we cause more harm than good when we allow a lack of transparency to fester.'

people.label: Lauren Opal Boebert
people.sub: U.S. Rep. (R-CO-4); Task Force member; asked about non-human genetic material
people.narrative: Boebert sits on the Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets and questioned witnesses at both the November 2024 and September 2025 hearings. Her 2024 round is worth preserving for two reasons. First, she answered Luna's 'you'll be on a list' warning by daring the surveillance apparatus outright before proceeding to name the program. Second, she asked all four witnesses, on the record, whether they were familiar with 'a secretive project within the Department of Defense involving the manipulation of human genetics with what is described as nonhuman genetic material potentially for the enhancement of human capabilities - hybrids.' All four - Gallaudet, Elizondo, Shellenberger and Gold - said no. That is a documented member-level rumour reaching the Hill and being tested under oath and coming back negative, which is exactly how the unverified layer should be handled. She also drew from Shellenberger the affirmative answer that Immaculate Constellation covers oceanic as well as terrestrial cases, and a flat 'Yes' to whether there is a concerted Pentagon effort to keep Congress out of the loop on UAP activity in US waters.

people.label: Glen Clay Higgins
people.sub: U.S. Rep. (R-LA-3); pressed Shellenberger on his Immaculate Constellation sourcing
people.narrative: Higgins performed the most rigorous adversarial questioning of the November 2024 hearing, and it improves rather than damages the record. A former law enforcement officer, he took Shellenberger through the Immaculate Constellation sourcing methodically: whether a non-public version of the author's report exists and where it might be found, whether the author's sources are known to him, whether they are inside the Department of Defense. Shellenberger confirmed he knows the author and knows the sources, expressed confidence in them, and declined to say whether they sit inside DoD - answering 'I cannot say' and then declining to distinguish cannot from will not. That exchange is the reason the 12-page document entered the Congressional Record as a sourced claim rather than an anonymous leak: a hostile questioner established that the journalist knew and could identify his sources and was withholding their identity by choice, not because they did not exist.

people.label: Thomas A. Monheim
people.sub: Inspector General of the Intelligence Community (2021-2025); briefed the House on UAP
people.narrative: Monheim is the official who stood between the Grusch complaint and Congress. As Inspector General of the Intelligence Community his office received Grusch's PPD-19 urgent-concern complaint through counsel in May 2022 and found it credible and urgent in July 2022, which triggered mandatory notification to the congressional intelligence committees. On 12 January 2024, at the Capitol, he gave a roughly ninety-minute closed briefing to House Oversight members - the House's first and only formal encounter with the watchdog who validated the complaint that started all of this. The result is documented and it is a null. Krishnamoorthi said he did not get the answers he hoped for. Burchett rated it four out of ten and said it was 'more of the same' and 'very compartmentalized.' Ogles said he asked very specific questions and was unable to get specific answers. Burlison and Garcia said it gave direction and probably new information. The most important structural fact is that a credible-and-urgent finding by the IC's own inspector general produced, eighteen months later, a briefing from which a bipartisan group of members emerged reporting they had learned essentially nothing about the substance.
