people.label: William Neil McCasland
people.sub: Maj. Gen., USAF (ret.); former AFRL commander; disappeared February 2026
people.narrative: McCasland is the point where this board and The Vanishing become the same board. A retired Air Force major general who commanded the Air Force Research Laboratory at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, he vanished from his Albuquerque home in February 2026, leaving behind his phone, prescription glasses, hiking boots, wallet and a .38-calibre revolver. Rep. Eric Burlison revealed on 21 April 2026 that his staff had been trying to reach McCasland in connection with a separate congressional investigation before he disappeared, and that his disappearance is what triggered the House Oversight probe that Chairman Comer and Burlison opened into eleven people in nuclear or rocket-adjacent work who have died or vanished since 2022. Burlison's stated reasoning is the reasoning of an investigator: 'How many people walk out their front door without their phone, their wallet, their keys, or anything?' The committees demanded briefings from the FBI, the Department of War, NASA and the Department of Energy by 27 April 2026. McCasland's institutional position is the reason his name carries the nickname the press has given him: AFRL at Wright-Patterson is the single installation most persistently named in the legacy recovery literature, and he commanded it.

people.label: Michael R. Turner
people.sub: R-OH; Chairman, House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence (2023-2025)
people.narrative: Turner is the name most consistently attached to the killing of the UAP Disclosure Act. As Chairman of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence through the FY2024 NDAA conference he held one of the four corner positions on the intelligence side of the negotiation, and the two provisions reported to have been his targets — the eminent domain clause and the Review Board's subpoena power — are precisely the two the enacted statute does not contain. Attorney Daniel Sheehan, who lobbied the conference directly, has stated on the record that 'Mike Turner first attacked those two elements,' demanding the eminent domain provision and the subpoena power be taken out. Turner had already positioned himself against the underlying testimony: after the 26 July 2023 House Oversight hearing he said the striking thing was that 'repeatedly over and over again, the whistleblowers had to say, actually, I don't have any knowledge.' The documentary result is not in dispute even if the attribution is journalistic: the Senate passed Sections 9001-9015 on 27 July 2023; the conference product signed 22 December 2023 contains Sections 1841, 1842 and 1843 only. Sections 9007 through 9011 — Review Board, Board personnel, review of records, eminent domain, court-sealed materials — have no enacted counterpart. Under the board's premise this is the single most consequential act of concealment in the modern legislative record, and it was performed by a committee chairman with access to the underlying compartments.

people.label: Mike D. Rogers
people.sub: R-AL; Chairman, House Armed Services Committee (2023- )
people.narrative: Rogers chaired the House Armed Services Committee through the FY2024 NDAA conference and, as chairman of the committee of primary jurisdiction over the bill, was one of the four principals whose sign-off the conference report required. He is named alongside Turner as leading the effort to eliminate or significantly alter the UAP Disclosure Act. His institutional interest is structural rather than personal: the UAPDA as passed by the Senate would have created an independent agency outside the Armed Services Committee's oversight, with authority to compel production from the Department of Defense and from its contractors, and to seize material from those contractors by eminent domain. Every enforcement mechanism in the Senate text that would have operated outside the armed services and intelligence committee structure was removed; the mechanisms that survived — a records collection at the National Archives, a review by agency heads, and postponement decisions made by the original classification authority — leave the existing committee architecture untouched. The FY2024 NDAA also confirms this in a second place: Sec. 1687, which Rogers's committee produced, disciplines unreported UAP special access programs by cutting off funds, but routes the remedy to 'the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership' rather than to any outside board.

people.label: Mark R. Warner
people.sub: D-VA; SSCI Chairman 2021-2025; author of the IAA contractor turn-in
people.narrative: Warner is the author of the provision that goes furthest of anything Congress has ever passed toward acknowledging privately held recovered material. On 13 July 2023 he submitted S.Amdt. 666 to S. 2226, the Intelligence Authorization Act for FY2024, which became Division M of the engrossed bill. Its Section 1102 does three things no other enacted or passed text does. It cuts off all funds for UAP activity 'protected under any form of special access or restricted access limitations' that has not been 'formally, officially, explicitly, and specifically described, explained, and justified' to Congress, and then enumerates exactly what it means: recruiting and securing personnel whose mission is 'capturing, recovering, and securing unidentified anomalous phenomena craft or pieces and components of such craft'; analysing such craft to determine 'material composition, method of manufacture, origin'; 'reverse engineering or replicating unidentified anomalous phenomena technology'; and 'any aerospace craft that uses propulsion technology other than chemical propellants, solar power, or electric ion thrust.' Second, it orders any person under contract with the Government holding such material to notify the Director of AARO within 60 days and to hand over within 180 days 'a comprehensive list of all non-earth origin or exotic unidentified anomalous phenomena material,' with civil and criminal immunity for those who comply. Third, it disallows independent research and development funding on such material as an indirect expense unless it is surrendered. The Senate passed all of it on 27 July 2023. The enacted version, Section 7343 of P.L. 118-31, kept the funding limitation in generic form and deleted the enumerated activities, the contractor turn-in, the comprehensive list, and the immunity.

people.label: John F. Reed
people.sub: D-RI; SASC Chairman 2021-2025; sponsor of S. 2226
people.narrative: Reed is the single most continuously entitled person on this board. He has held a 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) seat on the Senate Armed Services Committee across every one of the load-bearing moments the board tracks after 2009: he was ranking member in 2020 when the Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force was stood up, chairman in 2023 when David Grusch testified, and ranking member again in August 2026. In each configuration he was entitled to receive waived special access program information and the Secretary's justification for the waiver, jointly with his opposite number. He also sits on the Senate Appropriations Committee and its Defense Subcommittee, though membership on those bodies confers nothing under section 119 - only the chair and ranking seats do. Reed's importance to the board is that he is the continuity: where chairmanships rotated with party control, Reed occupied one of the two Senate armed services seats without interruption. If a waived DoD special access program concerning recovered non-human technology existed and was notified under 119(e)(2) at any point between 2015 and 2026, Reed is the person most likely to have received that notification. He has made no public statement to that effect, and no public statement denying it. That silence is the expected behaviour of someone lawfully constrained by the statute, and it is not evidence either way - but it does mean the board should treat him as a node of known entitlement rather than known knowledge.

people.narrative: Wicker holds the senior of the twelve seats that 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) designates. His continuity across both configurations, ranking member then chairman, makes him the longest-serving current occupant of a 119(e)(2) seat on the Senate armed services side.

people.narrative: The president who signed the founding instruments of the structure this board maps has had no node on it, because the board's prose says 'Truman' and never 'Harry'. Two records settle the office and the instruments. The directive of 22 January 1946 creates the National Intelligence Authority and the Central Intelligence Group and the post of Director of Central Intelligence, and carries his signature. The National Security Act of 1947, approved 26 July 1947, creates the National Security Council, the Central Intelligence Agency, the National Military Establishment and a Research and Development Board, and requires the Secretary of Defense to come from civilian life. people.label: John Callahan
people.sub: Federal Aviation Administration manager at Washington headquarters in the mid-1980s; the FAA official who in 2000 and 2001 publicly described the agency's handling of the Japan Air Lines 1628 case of 17 November 1986
people.narrative: John Callahan is the most useful witness the Disclosure Project produced and the reason is not him. The event he describes is one of the very few claims in this cluster with a large federal record that owes nothing whatever to Steven Greer: over 1,500 pages at the National Archives in Record Group 237, archival identifier 733667, containing the air traffic control transcript, the FAA's own forms, dated January 1987 interviews with all three Japan Air Lines crew members, Captain Terauchi's written statement in Japanese and in translation, and the FAA Alaskan Region's press release of 5 March 1987. That record exists whether or not Callahan ever spoke, and it was recovered only because John Greenewald kept asking for seventeen years after the FAA wrote to him on 27 June 2001 that the documents would be destroyed in thirty days. The asymmetry is the whole point of this node. The case is documented to an unusual depth; the man's claimed office is not. He says, in the Briefing Document and at the National Press Club, that he was Division Chief of the Accidents and Investigations Branch at FAA headquarters for about six years. The researcher who set out in 2015 specifically to confirm that found, in his own words, that only four references to a John Callahan at the FAA came up and that none of them matched the claimed area; what the public record showed was a Quality Control Branch Manager on the Quality Assurance Staff under the Associate Administrator for Air Traffic. The document eventually published in support of the claimed title is an OMB Form 171, a Personal Qualifications Statement, which Callahan handed the researcher himself in 2015. Its dates are consistent with the incident falling inside his tenure and they reconcile the researcher's negative finding with Callahan's account, so it is a point in his favour, but a form supplied by its own subject is not an agency release and this board does not score it as one. Nothing about that weakens the FAA file. It is why the case node beside this one matters more than the person node.
people.tierRationale: Re-graded B on a global pass (rank 480 of 1170, score 31). 4 connections, 0 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C0/A0/D3.

I stayed there for about six years and then retired.' THIS CLAIM IS TIER 1 FOR THE FACT THAT HE GAVE THAT TESTIMONY UNDER THAT HEADING AND DATE, AND FOR NOTHING ELSE. people.label: Clifford E. Stone
people.sub: US Army sergeant, 1968 to 1990, whose documented assignments were clerical and administrative; claimant from the 1990s of service on Army crash-retrieval teams recovering craft and occupants
people.narrative: Clifford Stone is on this board because the evidence against his extraordinary account is unusually good, not because the account is. His ordinary career is a federal record and it was obtained: Philip J. Klass requested it from the National Personnel Records Center in St. Louis and printed the assignments in the summer of 2001, and they run clerk/typist from basic training, clerk/typist in Vietnam from February 1970 to August 1972, administration specialist from March 1975, seven years in Germany, detachment sergeant, and from May 1985 chief administrative clerk at the New Mexico Military Institute. Kevin Randle, who is already a node on this board, who met Stone in February 1989 and visited his home many times, independently records the same shape: four claimed Vietnam tours against a record showing thirty-seven months overseas and not all of it in Vietnam, and nothing in the record supporting the story of slipping out at night to hunt the enemy. Those are two genuinely independent methods, a records request and a thirty-year acquaintance, and one of the two men spent his career arguing that other UFO cases are real. But the item that matters most is not an absence at all. It is something Stone did. He told the Disclosure Project that an Army team took him to Bentwaters in England in late December 1980 to investigate the incident there. On 23 December 1983, three years later, he filed a Freedom of Information Act request with the United States Air Force asking for information about that same incident, from his home address, without indicating that he was a serving Army sergeant. A man who had been there officially does not write in as a member of the public for the file. The record also contains something in his favour and it belongs here: after he was relieved for administrative inefficiency in January 1988, an Army investigation cleared him and he was later awarded the Meritorious Service Medal for the work he had been criticised over.

people.narrative: Robert Jacobs is the one witness in this cluster whose claimed role is confirmed by an independent named participant, and the confirmation comes from the man who spent a published article demolishing his interpretation. He published his own account twelve years before the Disclosure Project existed, in the MUFON UFO Journal of January 1989, giving his post as Officer-in-Charge of Photo-optical Instrumentation in the 1369th Photographic Squadron at Vandenberg Air Force Base from May 1963 to May 1966. In 1993 Kingston A. George, who identifies himself in his opening line as the project engineer for the experiment, answered him in the Skeptical Inquirer, and in the course of doing so confirmed that Jacobs was named on-site commander by the 1369th Photo Squadron and managed the logistics at the Big Sur location, published photographs of the team and captioned Jacobs into and out of them, named the launch and gave its date, and cited a contemporaneous internal Air Force staff study by title and date. That is the rarest evidentiary shape on this board: two first-person published accounts by two people who were both there, agreeing about who was present and disagreeing about what the film showed. George's counter-explanation is that the imagery was decoy and chaff deployment, that the alarm which followed was about a classified weapons vulnerability rather than anything extraterrestrial, and that Jacobs was not cleared to interpret what he had seen. Jacobs's own dating is uncertain in his own article, which gives 2, 3 or 15 September 1964, while George fixes the event at dawn on 22 September 1964. The board should build this node on the 1989 publication and not on the Briefing Document, which arrived last and adds nothing but a date.

people.label: Kingston A. George
people.sub: Air Force project engineer for the 1964 Big Sur image-orthicon telescope deployment; author of the published rebuttal of Robert Jacobs's account and of a contemporaneous 1964 staff study on the same imagery
people.narrative: Kingston George is the reason the Big Sur case is worth carrying at all. He identifies himself in the opening paragraph of his 1993 article as the project engineer for the experiments, and everything that makes the case checkable comes from him: the deployment's dates and location, the borrowed Boston University 24-inch telescope on a modified five-inch gun mount owned by the Range Measurements Laboratory of the Air Force Eastern Test Range, the photographs of the team, the name and date of the launch, the sequence of the security reaction, the disposal of the film, and a contemporaneous internal document cited by title and date. He is an interested party against the UFO reading, and he is also the only person in this cluster who both held the access at issue and published about it under his own name. He is careful where a polemicist would not be: he concedes the point about lasers to Jacobs, he describes the classified matter as a weapons-system vulnerability rather than anything exotic, and he records that he himself was questioned along with everyone else. That combination, documented access plus a published concession, is why he is a node and not a footnote.

people.label: Larry Warren
people.sub: USAF security specialist who says he was assigned to the 81st Tactical Fighter Wing at RAF Bentwaters in December 1980; co-author of Left at East Gate, a book his co-author repudiated and his publisher withdrew
people.narrative: Larry Warren is carried here for the dispute rather than for the claim, because the dispute is documented and the claim is not. What is not in dispute is his assignment: his own co-author, after repudiating almost everything else, still accepts as authentic the handwritten letter Warren sent his mother in January 1981 and says explicitly that its authenticity does not carry the rest. What is in dispute is his presence at the events and the documentary evidence he produced for it. The case against him was not assembled by sceptics. Peter Robbins wrote Left at East Gate with him and defended it for twenty-nine years before publishing a statement on 13 June 2017 alleging, among other things, that a USAF Form 490 in the book's evidence carries an ophthalmic notation attributed to a physician Robbins found to be an orthopaedic surgeon, that a photograph purporting to show Warren with John Lennon is fabricated, that signatures on an in-processing sheet do not match, and that testimonial letters attributed to two named fellow airmen were never sent. Four months later the publisher, Cosimo, Inc., announced it was suspending distribution of the book because some of the experiences described in it 'may be inaccurate or embellished'. The senior officer on the record, Col. Charles Halt, is reported as saying Warren was not there; that strand reaches this board only through summaries and is graded Tier 3 until something Halt wrote is opened. The Briefing Document's own editorial header asserts that Warren is corroborated by Nick Pope, Lord Hill-Norton and Clifford Stone, but two of those three are witnesses inside the same document and one of them is Stone, whose service record is on this board.

people.label: Peter Robbins
people.sub: Co-author of Left at East Gate with Larry Warren; author of the June 2017 statement repudiating his own co-author's account after twenty-nine years
people.narrative: Peter Robbins is a node because the strongest evidence against one of this cluster's witnesses is a document he wrote, and a claim of that weight should not hang off an unattributed note. He spent twenty-nine years as Larry Warren's co-author and public defender, and then on 13 June 2017 published a statement setting out, item by item, why he no longer believed what he had defended: an allegedly fabricated photograph, an allegedly altered USAF medical form, signatures that do not match, letters that were never sent. What makes the statement usable rather than merely dramatic is that it concedes: he accepts the authenticity of Warren's January 1981 letter home and says so, and he notes that the paperwork he examined came to him from Warren and was mostly photocopies. people.label: Steven M. Greer
people.sub: Emergency physician; founder of CSETI (1990) and the Disclosure Project (1993); National Press Club event 9 May 2001
people.narrative: Greer built the first mass witness-aggregation project and demonstrated both its power and its limits. A practising emergency physician, he founded the Center for the Study of Extraterrestrial Intelligence in 1990 and the Disclosure Project in 1993 with the explicit aim of assembling former military and government personnel willing to testify to Congress. On 9 May 2001 he convened roughly twenty of them at the National Press Club in Washington - radar operators, missile launch officers, air traffic controllers, FAA personnel - and announced that more than four hundred had given testimony, demanding congressional hearings with subpoena power and amnesty for witnesses. The event drew heavy international coverage and produced no hearing. Its consequence for the record is twofold. First, it created a large videotaped corpus of named former personnel making specific, dated, on-the-record claims, some of which - notably the missile-facility shutdown accounts - align with the FOIA-released overflight documents from 1975. Second, Greer's subsequent trajectory into claims that outran his evidence gave the institutions he was pressuring a durable reason to treat the whole category as unserious. The Clinton White House's own UFO FOIA collection (2006-0474-F) consists in the majority of documents Greer sent it, which is a precise measure of how the material was received: filed as correspondence.

people.label: Charles I. Halt
people.sub: Lt Col USAF (later Col); Deputy Base Commander, RAF Bentwaters/Woodbridge 1980-81
people.narrative: Halt wrote the single most consequential UFO document ever produced by a serving US officer inside a NATO nuclear-capable installation. On 13 January 1981, as Deputy Base Commander of the 81st Combat Support Group at RAF Bentwaters/Woodbridge, he sent a one-page memorandum captioned 'Unexplained Lights' to the RAF station commander describing events of 26-28 December 1980: security patrolmen encountering a 'strange glowing object' that was 'metalic in appearance and triangular in shape, approximately two to three meters across the base'; three ground depressions 1.5 inches deep and 7 inches in diameter; and radiation readings of 0.1 milliroentgens beta/gamma peaking in the depressions. The memo is not a UFO buff's account - it is an official USAF memorandum, released to the public through the Office of the Assistant Secretary of Defense FOIA office and re-released under DoD FOIA case 97-F-1677 in September 1997. Halt personally led the 28 December patrol and tape-recorded it. He remained in the Air Force for another decade, retiring as a full colonel, and only after retirement began stating publicly that he believed the objects were under intelligent control and that base personnel had been debriefed under pressure. In 2010 he executed a notarized affidavit asserting that the objects were not of terrestrial origin and that USAF and UK authorities had worked to suppress the incident; he has since stated that airmen were subjected to what he characterized as drugged and hypnotic debriefings. The 45-year documentary life of the Halt memo is a case study in the board's central thesis: the record exists, it was written by the responsible officer at the time, and the institutional response has been to route it into a category ('unexplained lights') that requires no follow-up.

people.label: Kevin D. Randle
people.sub: Lt Col (ret.), USAF/Army/Iowa NG intelligence officer; Roswell author
people.narrative: Kevin Douglas Randle (born 4 June 1949) is the closest thing the retrieval literature has to an internal auditor with a security background. He flew UH-1s with the 116th and 187th Assault Helicopter Companies in Vietnam, served in the Air Force as a public affairs officer, general's aide and intelligence officer, completed Air Force Reserve service as a captain and director of intelligence for an airlift group, then joined the Iowa National Guard as an intelligence officer after 11 September 2001, deploying with the 234th Signal Battalion to Baghdad International Airport in June 2003 and retiring as a lieutenant colonel in 2009. Schmitt he wrote 'UFO Crash at Roswell' (1991) and 'The Truth About the UFO Crash at Roswell' (1994), the two books that drove Roswell into congressional attention and produced the Air Force counter-reports. Randle is important to this board precisely because he moved against the current: he demolished the Majestic 12 documents in 'Conclusions on Operation Majestic Twelve' (1994) and 'Case MJ-12' (2002) while Friedman defended them, he withdrew his and Schmitt's support for witnesses who did not hold up, and he later told Skeptical Inquirer's Robert Sheaffer that he sets a very high bar for evidence, that most abductees are describing sleep paralysis, and eventually that he was 'no longer sure what actually happened' at Roswell and that the case for extraterrestrial involvement 'is no longer robust.' He also wrote 'Project Moon Dust' (1999), 'A History of UFO Crashes' (1995) and 'Crash: When UFOs Fall From the Sky' (2010), which is the field's most systematic case-by-case survey.

people.label: John Greenewald Jr.
people.sub: Founder, The Black Vault; FOIA requester of record on AATIP and Elizondo
people.narrative: Greenewald is the private citizen who has done more than any institution to build the documentary base this board runs on. He began filing FOIA requests as a teenager in 1996 and has since obtained and published well over two million pages. Two of his releases are load-bearing for the 1970s-2000s era: DoD FOIA case 97-F-1677, processed by the Office of the Assistant Secretary of Defense in September 1997, which produced the Halt memorandum on Rendlesham and the November 1975 Malmstrom AFB overflight records; and his 2013 Mandatory Declassification Review of the entire NSA UFO holding, which forced further release of documents NSA had previously produced with only a few words visible per page. In 2025 he became the principal test of the Pentagon's own honesty about disinformation: after the Wall Street Journal reported that the Secretary of Defense's office had issued a spring 2023 memo ordering an end to an Air Force practice of falsely telling personnel they were on a reverse-engineering programme, Greenewald filed for the memo. OSD responded in September 2025 that no such record existed; AFOSI said it had no records of any such investigation; the Pentagon spokesperson said in October 2025 she could not confirm the memo existed. In December 2025 an OSD appellate authority granted his appeal and remanded for a new search. That sequence - press claim, government no-records finding, appeal, remand - is the mechanism by which this board's evidence is actually produced.

people.label: Thomas Edwin Castello (fabricated)
people.sub: The claimed Dulce security officer. Confessed as an invention by the man who says he invented him
people.narrative: THE NAME WAS CONFESSED AS AN INVENTION BY THE MAN WHO SAYS HE INVENTED IT. Thomas Edwin Castello is presented in the Dulce literature as a security technician who worked inside the alleged facility, stole a set of photographs and papers, and vanished with his family. In November 2015 Tal Levesque, who wrote under the name Jason Bishop III and who authored the two original Dulce Base articles, told the researcher Adam Gorightly by email: 'You still do not get it. TEC (Thomas Edwin Castello) is a creation. A MYTH.' He named his ingredients in the same message and described mailing a hundred large packets of supporting material to authors and lecturers who then folded it into their own talks, articles and books. That last sentence is the important one, because it describes the deliberate manufacture of the appearance of independent corroboration: the many later sources that agree about Castello agree because they were seeded from one envelope. This node is therefore not an absence-of-record node and should never be rebuilt as one. Absence of record is what a board writes when it has looked and found nothing; here the author has spoken. The separate checks that were made are consistent with the confession and add nothing to it: John Greenewald, publishing on 1 April 2016, states 'There is no evidence that I have found, that shows that Thomas Costello even exists', and demonstrates that the single most-circulated piece of physical evidence attached to the name, a photograph of bodies in a chamber, is a frame from the 2000 film The 6th Day. One point of honesty about the sourcing: the confession reaches this board at second hand. It was read as reproduced on Norio Hayakawa's site, quoting Gorightly's book, and neither the email nor the book was opened. That is why the confession claim is graded Tier 2 rather than Tier 1, and it is the single item in this cluster most worth upgrading. A further negative recorded by Hayakawa in 2016, that an 'alleged' retired Air Force colonel told him no such person was ever employed at Dulce, is anonymous, is bracketed in quotation marks by Hayakawa himself, and is carried at Tier 3 so that nobody later mistakes it for a check. people.narrative: Philip Schneider supplied every specific number in the modern Dulce claim and none of them can be traced past him. In a lecture at Post Falls, Idaho on 8 May 1995 he said he had been 'involved in building an addition to the deep underground military base at Dulce', that his job was 'to go down the holes and check the rock samples, and recommend the explosive[s]', that the base 'goes down seven levels and over 2.5 miles deep', and that in a cavern there he shot two aliens, after which the thirty people already underground and about forty more who came down were killed. He arrived late: Norio Hayakawa's chronology places him outside the initial rumours entirely and dates his emergence to 1995, when the Dulce story was already about fifteen years old. WHAT COULD NOT BE ESTABLISHED IS RECORDED HERE AND NOT ONLY IN THE GAPS. No employment of Philip Schneider by anybody, ever, was documented by this board: no employer record, no contract, no clearance record, no payroll. The attribution to Morrison Knudsen, the Corps of Engineers and the Navy rests on a contributor-written biography attached to his Find a Grave memorial and on his own lectures, and a contributor-written memorial biography is not a record of employment. His death is likewise unresolved: the memorial record gives 11 January 1996 in Clackamas County, Oregon, while the date in circulation, tied to the discovery of the body, is 17 January 1996, and NO DEATH CERTIFICATE, MEDICAL EXAMINER'S REPORT OR POLICE REPORT WAS OPENED. The suicide ruling, the ligature and his former wife's letter contesting the finding are all in circulation and none of it is carried as a claim here. The one genuinely documented element of the Schneider story is his father: Captain Otto Oscar Schneider, US Navy, 22 January 1906 to 13 May 1993, on a Find a Grave memorial originally created by the US Veterans Affairs Office. The rank and the dates are real; the narrative attached to the same page, a captured U-boat commander repatriated into US Naval Intelligence, Operation Crossroads and the Philadelphia Experiment, is contributor prose and none of it is asserted. It matters only because Philip Schneider's own claim leaned on his father's standing, and the standing is real while the stories about it are not documented by anything opened here.

people.label: Milton William Cooper

people.narrative: Milton William Cooper is a propagation node and the board should be precise about what he propagated, because the usual account overstates it. His paper 'The Secret Government', dated on its own first page 23 May 1989 and updated 21 November 1990, delivered at the MUFON symposium in Las Vegas on 2 July 1989 and later absorbed into his 1991 book Behold a Pale Horse, was extracted and searched in full for this cluster. It contains the frame: 'It was agreed that bases would be constructed underground for the use of the alien nation and that two bases would be constructed for the joint use of the alien nation and the United States Government...These alien bases would be constructed under Indian reservations in the Four Corners area of Utah, Colorado, New Mexico and Arizona, and one would be constructed in an area known as Dreamland.' IT DOES NOT CONTAIN THE WORD DULCE. The string occurs zero times in forty-nine pages. A count is checkable and an adjective is not, which is why the number is carried in the claim rather than a characterisation. Cooper's edge to the hub is therefore Tier 3 frame-propagation and nothing stronger. Two further things belong on the node. First, he graded his own document: after describing his sources as top secret material seen between 1970 and 1973 as a member of the Intelligence Briefing Team of the Commander in Chief of the Pacific Fleet, plus sources he could not divulge and 'published sources which I cannot vouch for', he writes that 'this chapter must be termed a hypothesis'. The board should use the author's own grade. Second, the same document independently corroborates one element of the Kirtland affair: Cooper writes that Linda Moulton Howe 'confided to me that Sgt. Richard Doty of the Counterintelligence Division of the Air Force Office of Special Investigations had taken her into the Intelligence office at Kirtland Air Force Base in New Mexico and showed her the exact same documents that I had seen'. That corroborates that Howe was telling the story by 1989 to a third party. It corroborates nothing about the documents themselves.

people.label: William L. Moore
people.sub: Co-author, 'The Roswell Incident' (1980); first recipient of the MJ-12 film; self-confessed conduit for AFOSI disinformation
people.narrative: William L. Moore wrote the book that made Roswell a public case and then, nine years later, told a room full of ufologists that he had been working with Air Force counterintelligence. With Charles Berlitz he published 'The Roswell Incident' (Grosset & Dunlap, 1980), built on Stanton Friedman's 1978 contact with Jesse Marcel Sr. and on the second-hand Barney Barnett material, and it established the modern case. In December 1984 he and Jaime Shandera received in the post a roll of undeveloped 35mm film containing the Eisenhower Briefing Document and the Truman-Forrestal memorandum - the origin of the entire MJ-12 corpus that Friedman then spent a decade defending and Randle a decade attacking. At the 1989 MUFON symposium in Las Vegas, Moore stated publicly that from about 1980 he had cooperated with personnel of the Air Force Office of Special Investigations, and that he had knowingly passed disinformation to the Albuquerque physicist and businessman Paul Bennewitz, whose mental health collapsed under it. That admission is the single most consequential statement ever made by a researcher in this field, and this board treats it structurally rather than moralistically: it establishes, on the admission of the participant, that a US counterintelligence element used a civilian UFO researcher as a delivery channel for fabricated material into the UFO community. Any document, witness or claim entering the record through that channel between roughly 1980 and 1989 - and the MJ-12 papers arrived in the middle of it - carries a provenance problem that cannot be argued away.

people.sub: Documentary producer (HBO, KMGH-TV Denver); shown the 'Project Aquarius' paper at Kirtland AFB, 1983
people.narrative: Howe was an Emmy-winning Denver television producer whose 1980 documentary on cattle mutilations brought her to the attention of AFOSI. In April 1983, while developing an HBO documentary, she was invited to Kirtland AFB and met Richard Doty, who showed her a typed paper he described as a government briefing on retrieved craft and occupants - the material that entered the literature as the 'Project Aquarius' teletype. She was permitted to read it and take notes but not to copy it, and she was told a film of the subject would be made available for her documentary. It never was; the HBO project collapsed. Howe's account is important precisely because of its shape: an American journalist was shown a purported classified document by a serving counterintelligence agent on a military installation, and then the promised material evaporated. Whether the paper was authentic or fabricated, the operation is the same one that was run on Bennewitz, applied to a broadcaster instead of a physicist. Howe has told the story consistently for over forty years and her contemporaneous notes are the only surviving record of the document's text.

people.label: Leslie Kean
people.sub: Investigative journalist; co-author of the 5 June 2023 Debrief story
people.narrative: Leslie Kean is the person in this domain who took the government to court and won a search. On 31 January 2003 she filed a FOIA request with NASA for records referring to Kecksburg, the incident of 9 December 1965, the 'Fragology Files' for 1962-1967, Richard M. Schulherr, Project Moon Dust and Cosmos 96. NASA answered 'no records' on 11 April 2003. She appealed; NASA's Associate Deputy Administrator James Jennings granted the appeal on 18 June 2003 and promised an expedited agency-wide search; NASA then failed to act on its own letter, a failure the court later attributed to poor tracking and the relocation of the FOIA office. On 15 October 2003 she notified NASA she intended to sue, and on 9 December 2003 - thirty-eight years to the day after Kecksburg - she filed Kean v. National Aeronautics and Space Administration, Civil Action No. 03-2509 (EGS), in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia, represented by Lobel, Novins & Lamont. Judge Emmet G. Sullivan held a hearing on 20 March 2007 and on 27 March 2007 issued a memorandum opinion finding that NASA had not met its burden of showing its searches were adequate, denying the agency summary judgment on the search question and ordering the parties to propose search and documentation procedures that would create a proper record. NASA settled in part on 16 October 2007 and searched under court supervision, filing joint status reports every sixty days until the case was dismissed on 24 August 2009. Kean went on to write 'UFOs: Generals, Pilots and Government Officials Go on the Record' (2010) and, with Ralph Blumenthal and Helene Cooper, the 16 December 2017 New York Times story that revealed AATIP.

people.label: George F. Schulgen
people.sub: Chief, Air Intelligence Requirements Division
people.narrative: Brigadier General George F. Schulgen ran the Air Intelligence Requirements Division at Air Force headquarters in 1947 and was the addressee of the Twining memo. Five weeks later, on 28 October 1947, he signed the draft collection memorandum 'Intelligence Requirements on Flying Saucer Type Aircraft' — distributed 30 October — which is the moment the phenomenon became a formal worldwide intelligence collection target. The document is remarkable for what it asks collectors to look for: a plan form 'approximating that of an oval or disc with a dome shape,' a 'relatively flat bottom with extreme light-reflecting ability,' 'extreme maneuverability and apparent ability to almost hover,' composite and sandwich construction achieving 'extreme light weight,' and — listed among the propulsion options — 'Nuclear propulsion (atomic energy).' Schulgen framed the target as possible Soviet exploitation of German Horten brothers designs, and asked collectors to establish the Hortens' whereabouts. That framing is the standard cover story of the era, but the collection requirements themselves describe performance no 1947 airframe possessed. Schulgen also worked the FBI channel, and the resulting Bureau correspondence is the reason a parallel FBI file series on flying discs exists at all.

people.label: Hoyt S. Vandenberg
people.sub: Air Force Chief of Staff (1948-1953); former DCI
people.narrative: General Hoyt Vandenberg is the first documented destroyer of an inconvenient UAP record. He had been Director of Central Intelligence in 1946-1947 before becoming Air Force Chief of Staff in April 1948, so he arrived at the top of the Air Force already fluent in compartmentation. In mid-1948 the Project SIGN staff at Wright Field produced a Top Secret 'Estimate of the Situation' concluding the objects were interplanetary. Vandenberg rejected it for lack of proof and ordered it destroyed. This is not a fringe claim: it is stated in the Air Force's own contractor study, the Condon Report, which records that the estimate was prepared, that Vandenberg rejected it, and that copies were destroyed. The consequence was immediate and structural — SIGN was reorganised into Project GRUDGE on 11 February 1949 with an explicitly debunking posture, and the institutional lesson taught to every subsequent analyst was that the extraterrestrial conclusion was career-ending. Vandenberg's action set the template that the Robertson Panel formalised in 1953 and the Condon Committee executed in 1968.

people.label: Walter Haut
people.sub: Public information officer, 509th Bomb Group, RAAF
people.narrative: Walter G. Haut (3 June 1922 - 15 December 2005) wrote the sentence that started all of it. A bombardier who flew thirty-five missions against Japan and dropped instrument packages at the Bikini tests in 1946, he became public information officer for the 509th Bomb Group at Roswell Army Air Field, and on 8 July 1947 base commander Col. Haut's own testimony evolved in a documented, dateable sequence that this board records in full because the sequence is the evidence. In 1980's 'The Roswell Incident' he is explicitly 'not a witness.' In 1979 and again in a March 1989 interview he said he knew nothing of what was recovered and had been refused when he asked to see it. In a sworn affidavit signed 14 May 1993 he added that Blanchard must have seen the material himself and that neither Blanchard nor Marcel could have mistaken it for a weather balloon. Haut died in 2005 and the document was published by Carey and Schmitt in 'Witness to Roswell' (2007). A witness whose claims escalate monotonically over twenty-two years, with the largest escalation drafted by his interviewer and embargoed until he could not be cross-examined, is a specific kind of evidence, and this board grades it as such.

people.narrative: Robert Low was assistant dean of the graduate school at the University of Colorado and became project coordinator of the UFO study. people.label: James E. McDonald
people.sub: Senior physicist, Institute of Atmospheric Physics, University of Arizona
people.narrative: James E. McDonald was a senior atmospheric physicist at the University of Arizona and the most aggressive scientific critic the Air Force UFO program ever faced. He obtained access to Blue Book files, re-investigated cases himself, and concluded the program was not an investigation at all. On 29 July 1968 he testified to the House Committee on Science and Astronautics, telling Congress that 'credible observers are observing relatively incredible objects' and that the phenomenon warranted serious scientific attention rather than dismissal by ridicule. He was the conduit through which the Low memo reached the press, and he attacked the Condon Report publicly after its release. McDonald was subsequently humiliated in a 1971 congressional hearing on the SST — an unrelated subject on which he was a technical critic — when a member used his UFO interest to discredit him from the dais. He shot himself in the Arizona desert on 13 June 1971. His death is the earliest entry in the pattern this board tracks of scientific and official careers destroyed on this subject, and it is recorded here as such without any implication beyond the documented sequence.

people.label: James W. Penniston
people.sub: USAF SSgt, 81st Security Police Squadron; first responder, Rendlesham 26 Dec 1980
people.narrative: Penniston was the senior security police NCO who went outside the RAF Woodbridge east gate in the early hours of 26 December 1980. He has stated on the record that he approached the object, walked around it, and physically touched a warm, glass-smooth surface bearing raised symbols, and that he and John Burroughs were subsequently subjected to lengthy debriefings by personnel he could not identify. Penniston's later claims - including a binary-code download experienced during the encounter - have made him easier to dismiss, which is itself a familiar pattern in this record: the most exposed witnesses accumulate the most discrediting material.

people.label: John Burroughs

people.narrative: Burroughs matters less for what he saw than for what happened when he tried to get his own medical file. He was one of the airmen at the east gate on 26 December 1980. Missing records with no destruction authority is the same signature GAO found in the Roswell files in 1995.

people.label: Jaime H. Shandera

people.label: Eugene F. Yeates
people.sub: NSA Chief, Office of Policy; declarant of the in camera affidavit in CAUS v. NSA
people.narrative: Yeates is the man who signed the piece of paper that told a federal judge the United States could not talk about its UFO signals intelligence. In Civil Action No. 80-1562, Citizens Against Unidentified Flying Objects Secrecy v. National Security Agency, NSA located UFO-related records, withheld them, and supported the withholding with a lengthy classified affidavit executed by Yeates as the Agency's Chief of Policy. The district court reviewed it in camera - the judge was cleared to read the explanation the plaintiffs never saw - and ruled for NSA; the D.C. Circuit affirmed on 3 November 1981 and the Supreme Court denied certiorari on 8 March 1982. Years later NSA released the Yeates affidavit itself in redacted form, and it is now in the public UFO release. That document is the single most important artefact of the concealment in this era, because it is an official, sworn, judicially accepted statement that the National Security Agency holds UFO-related communications intelligence whose disclosure would damage national security. The government's position has never been that the records do not exist. Its position has been that they cannot be shown.

people.label: Laurance S. Rockefeller
people.sub: Financier and philanthropist; funder of the 1993-1996 Rockefeller UFO Disclosure Initiative
people.narrative: Rockefeller ran the only serious private attempt to force UFO declassification from inside the American establishment, and he did it with money, access and a written brief rather than a press conference. The Roswell file the White House did assemble (2006-0476-F) contains the 1995 GAO report and public correspondence - the residue of a request that was routed to the unclassified surface.

A Special Forces officer turned Los Alamos National Laboratory programme manager for non-lethal weapons, and previously involved in the Army's INSCOM psychoenergetics work, he convened in the 1980s an interagency group he called the Advanced Theoretical Physics working group, drawing senior people from CIA, DIA, the services and the national laboratories to determine whether a compartmented UFO effort existed. His conclusion, stated repeatedly since, is that he found no such programme - a finding that cuts against this board's premise and is recorded here in full for exactly that reason. What his account does establish is that the search happened, that it was conducted by cleared senior people, and that the answer they got was the same answer David Grusch got in 2019: the programme, if it exists, does not answer to people who ask through channels. Alexander then joined NIDS as a board member from 1995, working alongside Puthoff, Kelleher and Vallee on Bigelow's private version of the same inquiry.

people.label: Jacques F. Vallee
people.sub: Computer scientist and venture capitalist; ARPANET engineer; NIDS advisory board; materials-analysis researcher
people.narrative: Vallee is the provenance chain. Where Nolan brought the instruments, Vallee brought the samples and, crucially, the fifty-year paper trail attached to them. Trained in mathematics at Paris (1959) and astrophysics at Lille (1961), with a Northwestern PhD (1967), he joined Douglas Engelbart's Augmentation Research Center at SRI International in 1971 - the same institution and period as Puthoff's psychoenergetics work - and succeeded Paul Baran as principal investigator on the NSF computer-networking project, building PLANET, one of the first ARPANET conferencing systems. He then spent 1987-2010 as a Silicon Valley general partner. Across all of it he assembled a physical collection of alleged UAP-associated materials with documented case files: the 1957 Ubatuba magnesium fragments, the 1977 Council Bluffs molten mass, and the 1945 San Antonio, New Mexico 'Trinity' case material he wrote up with Paola Harris in 2021. He was a consultant to Robert Bigelow's National Institute for Discovery Science and a member of the Bigelow Aerospace scientific advisory board, which puts him inside the same Bigelow ecosystem that produced BAASS and the AAWSAP contract. His 2022 collaboration with Nolan is the moment the collection met modern instrumentation. The custody problem here is honest and stated: Vallee's samples come with newspaper reporting, police photographs, fire-department accounts and witness interviews - a civil chain, not a federal one - and that is exactly why the government-held material remains the missing term. His lifetime archive went to the Archives of the Impossible at Rice University, with embargoes running to 2028-2031: a dark segment with a published end date.

people.label: Robert "Bob" Lazar
people.sub: Los Alamos contract technician, 1982; claimant from 1989 of work on alien propulsion at a facility he calls S-4 near Papoose Lake; convicted Nevada felon, 1990
people.narrative: Bob Lazar is the origin point of the best-known claim in the field and, on the opened record, he is a contract electronics technician rather than the physicist the claim requires. In 1982 he worked at Los Alamos, and the Los Alamos Monitor of 27 June 1982 described him on its front page as 'a physicist at the Los Alamos Meson Physics Facility'. That description is the strongest documentary thread in his favour and it carries its own qualification: the Los Alamos telephone directory page that also lists his name states on its face that it covers Department of Energy employees and the outside contractor Kirk-Mayer, and a Los Alamos colleague interviewed on tape in 1996 said Lazar 'was a contractor' under Kirk Mayer. In 1989 he told KLAS-TV in Las Vegas, first silhouetted under the pseudonym 'Dennis' and then under his own name, that between December 1988 and April 1989 he had worked at a facility called S-4, about fifteen miles south of Groom Lake, back-engineering the propulsion of nine disc-shaped craft fuelled by a stable isotope of element 115. In 1991 he fixed that account in datable form by narrating it himself on a forty-minute videotape produced with his friend Gene Huff. The credential half of his account has been checked by named people and does not survive: no institutional record of the MIT or Caltech degrees exists, and the professor he named as a Caltech instructor turned out to teach at Pierce Junior College, where Lazar had taken at least one of his classes. The credential question is Tier 1 rather than gossip because Lazar's own reported education, listing a 1978 Pacifica University BS alongside the MIT and Caltech degrees, is printed in his Pre-Sentence Report of 27 July 1990, a Clark County court document produced after he pleaded guilty to felony pandering. What makes him a node is proximity to the claim, not credibility: no clearance is documented anywhere in the opened record, no office, and no physical trace of anything he describes.
people.tierRationale: Re-graded A on a global pass (rank 54 of 1170, score 77). 14 connections, 2 of them custody/funding/programmatic, 3 official denials recorded against it. Axes C0/A0/D3.

people.narrative: Gene Huff has two distinct roles in this cluster and the board should carry both, because the second is the structural one. He is a Las Vegas real-estate appraiser who met Lazar in 1985 and was socialising with him by 1988, and he is the named witness to the three Wednesday-night desert viewings of March and April 1989, the third of which ended with the group detained by the Lincoln County Sheriff. His first-hand claim is about lights seen from Tikaboo Valley and nothing more: he does not claim to have been inside any facility. His second role is that he wrote and co-produced the 1991 videotape, The Lazar Tape and Excerpts from the Government Bible, which is the artefact in which Lazar's whole account is fixed in datable form and which is the strongest opened source in this cluster. That makes him the publisher of the cluster's primary document, and the board treats publication as a structural fact. He is also the source of the $958.11 figure that circulates as the amount on Lazar's W-2: it is his recollection, in his own 1995 synopsis, of a cheque he says he saw.

people.label: Tom Mahood

people.narrative: Tom Mahood is the custody and analysis point for most of the documentary record in this cluster, and without a node for him the board's case-against edges have nothing to originate from. He describes himself on his own site as a former civil engineer and traffic engineer for Orange County, California, with a Master's degree in physics from Cal State Fullerton. His otherhand.org investigation reprints the Los Alamos Monitor front page of 27 June 1982, both Las Vegas Review-Journal reports of 1990, Mark Farmer's 1996 taped interview with an anonymised Los Alamos colleague, and David L. Morgan's physics critique, and it quotes Lazar's 1990 Pre-Sentence Report. His conclusion on the credentials is flat: 'Lazar never attended either CalTech or MIT. Of this I am certain of beyond a reasonable doubt.' His 2018 retrospective is the single best case-against document in the cluster precisely because it concedes what is true, granting that Lazar is 'amazingly believable', that Mahood himself initially found the story plausible, and that Lazar showed genuine technical cleverness. His counter-explanation is that there is nothing at Papoose Lake, that S-4 is a designator attaching to a Tonopah Test Range radar facility, and that the account began as a cover story after security caught Lazar bringing friends to watch classified tests in April 1989.

people.label: Stanton T. Friedman
people.sub: Nuclear physicist; first civilian Roswell investigator; MJ-12 researcher
people.narrative: Stanton Terry Friedman (29 July 1934 - 13 May 2019) was a nuclear physicist who spent fourteen years on classified nuclear propulsion programmes at General Electric, Aerojet General Nucleonics, General Motors, Westinghouse, TRW and McDonnell Douglas before leaving full-time physics in 1970 to investigate UFOs professionally. That industrial background matters to this board: Friedman had held clearances on compartmented nuclear aircraft and fission and fusion rocket work, and he argued from direct experience that a programme could be run for decades without leaking, because he had worked inside ones that did not. In February 1978 in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, he was put in touch with Major Jesse A. Marcel Sr., the 509th Bomb Group intelligence officer who had handled the Roswell debris - the single act that restarted the Roswell case after thirty years of silence and made him, as he put it, the first civilian to document the site. He fed Marcel to William Moore and Charles Berlitz, whose 1980 'The Roswell Incident' made the case public. From 1984 he was the principal defender of the Majestic 12 documents received by Moore and Jaime Shandera, publishing 'Top Secret/Majic' in 1996 and maintaining that no substantive grounds existed for dismissing the authenticity of the core documents - a position that split him permanently from Randle, Klass and much of the field. He was also the first to demonstrate that some MJ-12 papers were provably faked, showing that a purported 17 February 1948 Hillenkoetter-to-Truman memo was an emulation of a Marshall-to-Roosevelt letter reproduced in 'The American MAGIC'. He testified in writing to a House committee in 1968, appeared twice at the United Nations, and donated his research files to the Provincial Archives of New Brunswick shortly before his death.

people.narrative: Jeremy Corbell is the movement's primary conduit for leaked military imagery, and that role - not his filmmaking - is what makes him structurally significant. Beginning in 2019 he released a sequence of US Navy materials including the USS Omaha 'transmedium' footage and the pyramid-shaped object video, several of which the Pentagon subsequently confirmed as genuine Navy recordings. The confirmation pattern is the interesting datum: material leaks to Corbell, Corbell publishes, the Department authenticates the provenance while contesting the interpretation. He directed Bob Lazar: Area 51 & Flying Saucers, which premiered on Netflix in 2019 and returned Lazar to public attention, and Hunt for the Skinwalker, based on the George Knapp and Colm Kelleher book. He co-hosts Weaponized with Knapp. He has been criticised within the field for showmanship and for imagery later explained by lens artefacts, and both things are true at once: he is an unreliable narrator and a reliable pipe.

people.label: Thomas Townsend Brown
people.sub: Electrostatic-propulsion inventor; five patents; subject of a 1953 FBI fraud inquiry
people.narrative:
Thomas Townsend Brown is the technical origin point on which the entire electrogravitics thread hangs, and the useful thing this board can do with him is separate what he patented from what was later written about him. The patents are real and were read off the USPTO's own image server: US 1,974,483 ELECTROSTATIC MOTOR (1934), US 2,207,576 (1940), US 2,417,347 VIBRATION DAMPER (1947, assigned by mesne assignments to Lockheed Aircraft Corporation), US 2,949,550 ELECTROKINETIC APPARATUS (1960) and US 3,187,206 ELECTROKINETIC APPARATUS (1965). None of them claims gravity control. The 1934 patent claims 'a method of producing force or motion by applying and maintaining high potential electro-static charges'; the 1965 patent opens 'This invention relates to an electrical device for producing thrust by the direct operation of electrical fields' and is explicit that the reaction appears in the surrounding medium and, in vacuum, on the walls of the chamber. That is an electrostatic-thrust claim. The word 'electrogravitics' appears in none of them.

Project Winterhaven is real and does not say what the secondary literature says it says. The 66-page proposal, 'A PROPOSAL FOR JOINT SERVICES RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT CONTRACT, THE TOWNSEND BROWN FOUNDATION', does propose research on 'the control of gravitation' and lists 'electrified disc airfoils' among results to date. But the words 'saucer', 'interceptor', 'Mach' and 'Air Force' appear in it zero times. The saucer-as-USAF-interceptor framing belongs to the 1956 Aviation Studies (International) report 'Electrogravitics Systems', not to Winterhaven, and that report has no catalogue record anywhere WorldCat indexes.

The provenance that matters most is the one the enthusiast literature omits. Brown's own FBI file records the Winterhaven pitch inside a Fraud Against the Government inquiry: the LEADS section directs the Washington Field Office to 'ascertain from appropriate defense agencies the nature of any overtures made by BROWN' and to 'determine any possible violation of the [F]AG Statute'. The same file carries named informants describing the apparatus as a relabelled stock-market predicting machine, one of them 'confident this flying saucer thing is a phony'. A node on Brown that carries the patents without that is not an honest node.

people.label: Philip J. Corso
people.sub: Lt. Col., US Army; Chief, Foreign Technology Division, OCRD, 18 Apr - 18 Jul 1962
people.narrative:
Corso is the case where the primary record is both stronger and weaker than the claim made for him, and a node is the only place a reader sees both halves. His own DA Form 66, released by US Army Reserve Personnel Command in April 1998, puts the Army's Foreign Technology Division in his service record: staff officer in the division from 20 July 1961, then 'Chief Foreign Technology Div, OCRD USA' from 18 April to 18 July 1962 -- three months. The same form places him at Fort Riley, Kansas from 21 April 1947, which covers the alleged 6 July 1947 observation, and records him as an Intelligence Staff Officer on the Operations Coordinating Board in Washington from 24 February 1954 to 1957.

His 322-page FBI release is the other half. Searched in full, the words UFO, flying saucer, unidentified, Roswell, extraterrestrial and saucer appear zero times. What the file does contain is independent corroboration of the OCB posting from a source that is not Corso: in 1955 Gen. Arthur S. Trudeau told the FBI that 'Colonel Philip Corso, then assigned to the Operations Coordinating Board, would be in a position to elaborate' on a list of alleged Fabian Socialists, 'as he, Corso, had actually accumulated the information'. It also contains a 1964 episode in which Corso was found to be the source of a rumour that Oswald had been a paid FBI informant, and in which he 'emphasized the fact that his allegations had been strictly deductions and had no basis in fact'.

One line in his sworn statement does not survive his own service record. The affidavit says he 'was a member of President Eisenhower's National Security Council'. The DA Form 66 records the Operations Coordinating Board, which reported to the NSC and was not the NSC. That is a documentable overstatement in a sworn document, and this board carries it because the same record that supplies his strongest corroboration supplies it.
people.tierRationale: Re-graded A on a global pass (rank 167 of 1170, score 49). 2 connections, 0 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C2/A2/D2.

people.label: Roscoe H. Hillenkoetter
people.sub: First Director of Central Intelligence, May 1947 - October 1950; NICAP board member 1960
people.narrative:
The first Director of Central Intelligence went on the public record in 1960 saying that the objects were 'operating under intelligent control' and asking Congress to investigate, and the documents that establish it are held by the Central Intelligence Agency itself. A Worcester Gazette clipping of 1 June 1960, filed in CIA records and released in 2014, reports him declaring: 'The unknown objects are operating under intelligent control. It is imperative that we learn where the UFO's (unidentified flying objects) come from and what their purpose is.' The same clipping gives his tenure as DCI, May 1947 to October 1950, and reports that he wanted a congressional investigation. A second CIA-held clipping, an Enquirer editorial of 4 March 1960, independently records him as a board member of NICAP who 'has referred his conclusions to the Senate Space Committee, requesting an investigation' -- while itself disagreeing with him.

None of that requires MJ-12, and this board does not route him through it. The purported 1948 Hillenkoetter-to-Truman memo shown to be an emulation of a Marshall-to-Roosevelt letter is a claim about a document, not about the man, and nothing above depends on it. A negative finding points the same way as the Corso file: the National Security Archive's mirror of the FBI files on Hillenkoetter contains, across the sections searched, zero occurrences of NICAP, flying saucer, unidentified flying, Keyhoe, or the year 1960. His FBI file is not a UFO file.

The structural point is the ordering. A former DCI publicly contradicting the Air Force's public position, while sitting on the board of the organisation pressing for hearings, is a fact about the disclosure apparatus that the board should reach directly rather than through somebody else's narrative about a forgery.
people.tierRationale: Re-graded A on a global pass (rank 168 of 1170, score 49). 6 connections, 0 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C3/A2/D3.

Knowledge of this project should be restricted to the absolute minimum number of persons.' It asks him for approval and for an allocation of $65,515.

people.label: Robert I. Sarbacher
people.sub: Microwave engineer; Dean of the Graduate Division, Georgia Tech; author of the 1983 Steinman letter
people.narrative:
The board already leans on Sarbacher second-hand, through Wilbert Smith, and a node is the only place the distinction that matters can be put where a reader sees it: he says in his own signed letter that he was invited to the meetings and did not attend them. The letter is real. Two typed pages on Washington Institute of Technology letterhead, dated 29 November 1983, addressed to William Steinman, signed, with Steinman's handwritten receipt note 'Received 12-5-83'. In it Sarbacher says John von Neumann and Vannevar Bush 'definitely' were involved and 'I think Dr. Robert Oppenheimer also'; that 'I could not personally attend the meetings'; that materials 'reported to have come from flying saucer crashes were extremely light and very tough'; and that he 'got the impression these aliens were constructed like certain insects we have observed on earth.' Everything about a Wright Field meeting, and everything Eric Walker is said to have said, is not in this letter.

Two problems are visible on the document's own face. Sarbacher writes of 'My association with the Research and Development Board under Doctor Compton during the Eisenhower administration' -- the RDB was a Truman-era body abolished in June 1953, five months into Eisenhower's first term, and Karl T. Compton chaired it in the late 1940s. At about 76 he is conflating administrations in the most-quoted paragraph of the document. And his postscript, asking Steinman to check the spelling of Bush's name, is omitted from the typed transcript bound into the same PDF, so anyone quoting the transcript is quoting an abridged letter.

His credentials are not in doubt: the title page of his 1943 Wiley textbook names him 'Robert I. Sarbacher, Sc.D., Associate Professor of Electrical Engineering, Illinois Institute of Technology'. What is in doubt is the RDB consultancy the secondary literature attaches to him, for which no primary record was found, and the provenance of the letter itself, which reaches this board through an advocacy publisher's scan rather than an institutional archive.
people.tierRationale: Re-graded B on a global pass (rank 201 of 1170, score 45). 1 connections, 0 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C2/A1/D2.

people.label: Louis Witten
people.sub: General relativist; first researcher hired by RIAS, Inc., the Glenn L. Martin Company's research institute
people.narrative:
Louis Witten is on this board for one documented fact and its context: in January 1957 he attended the Chapel Hill conference on the role of gravitation in physics as a representative of RIAS, Inc., Baltimore. The participants list of the conference report prints it plainly -- 'Witten, L. | RIAS, Inc., Baltimore' -- immediately above 'Bass, R.W. | RIAS, Inc., Baltimore'. His contribution, with R. W. Bass, was 'Some Remarks on Cosmological Models'. The report's own designation is WADC Technical Report 57-216 and it exists because of a conference funding agreement with the Wright Air Development Center, which is to say an Air Force body paid for the meeting at which an aerospace prime's research institute discussed gravitation.

What is documented about his work is classical general relativity, not gravity control. The conference participants themselves recorded a concern about 'the absolute necessity to avoid identification with so-called anti-gravity research', and nothing read in this pass shows RIAS producing gravity-control results. The board carries him as the hire that establishes what RIAS actually was, and it does not carry the claim that George Trimble recruited him -- the one source that could be opened says Witten approached Bryce DeWitt to recruit DeWitt, and the oral history that would settle the direction refuses this environment.

The Foreword gives the reason the report exists at all: 'The present report was undertaken as a necessary requirement to obtain conference funds.' people.label: George S. Trimble
people.sub: Glenn L. Martin Company executive; proposed RIAS as an industrial institute for advanced study
people.narrative:
RIAS was Trimble's idea and gravity was explicitly its subject, and both facts come off his own dated letter. Writing to Bryce DeWitt on 10 June 1955 he opens: 'During a recent conversation with Mr. George Rideout, president of Roger Babson's Gravity Research Foundation, we were commiserating on the unfortunate state of the affairs that knowledgable folks do not wish to get mixed up in the field of gravity research.' He continues: 'It occurred to us some time ago that our industry was vitally concerned with gravity ... At least one category of the things one must study, when he desires to bring space flight to reality, is the laws of nature surrounding the force of gravity.' He described the proposed body as an 'industrial version of the Institute for Advanced Study'.

That is an aerospace prime's executive, in 1955, in writing, saying his industry needed gravity research and that respectable people would not touch it -- which is a documented statement of exactly the reputational mechanism this board maps elsewhere. Martin money also reached the university side: Trimble and the Glenn L. Martin Company bought a Founder's Membership in the Institute of Field Physics for $5,000 and offered to help solicit more.

The industrial and academic halves were deliberately kept apart, and the source says why. The Martin company's institute was 'industry-sponsored, and not ensconced in a university', while the Institute of Field Physics was placed inside UNC 'so as to avoid the conflict that physicists felt working in an industrial setting.' Note what is not carried here: no document read states that Trimble recruited Louis Witten, and this board draws no such edge.

people.narrative: Jesse Michels is the single most consequential independent interviewer in the modern disclosure movement and the reason this domain exists as a structural rather than anecdotal problem. Michels had already run the same researcher a year earlier (21 February 2025, 'The New Area51 Is HERE in Utah!', 450,091 views), which toured Air Force bases, deep underground facilities and 'Federally Funded Research Organizations' associated with reverse engineering. He broke Jake Barber's crash-retrieval account on 30 January 2025 to over a million viewers, sat with Michael Shellenberger on 14 November 2024 the day after Shellenberger delivered the Immaculate Constellation report to Congress, and on 8 March 2026 put Eric Davis in a room with Eric Weinstein for a four-hour session that worked through the Wilson-Davis memo. people.narrative: Bryce Zabel matters to this board for one specific reason: he is the person who systematically worked through what happens after disclosure, rather than whether it will occur. With Richard Dolan he co-authored A.D. That is the question the legislative strand keeps colliding with and never answers. Zabel's professional background is unusual for the field: a University of Oregon broadcast journalism graduate and former CNN correspondent who became a television showrunner, created the UFO-conspiracy series Dark Skies in 1996, and in 2001 was elected chairman and CEO of the Academy of Television Arts and Sciences. people.label: Walter Bedell Smith

people.narrative: Walter Bedell Smith is the Director of Central Intelligence whose own instruction, on 20 August 1952, turned unidentified flying objects from an Air Force nuisance into an intelligence-community problem with a draft National Security Council directive behind it. Chadwell's memoranda run to him, name him as the approving authority on the recommendation that the DCI take the subject to the Psychological Strategy Board, and attach a memorandum to the NSC Executive Secretary over his signature block proposing a coordinated research programme. The Agency's own later correspondence states plainly that the Robertson Panel 'was convened at the direction of General Smith'. The board carries the Robertson Panel at 112 occurrences and has one occurrence of his name; he is the office from which it issued. The Michels corpus describes a 1953 Bedell Smith letter proposing psychological warfare; the psychological-warfare document is Chadwell's, dated 2 October 1952, the approval line over Smith's name on the released copy is blank, and Smith's own 2 December 1952 draft proposes research rather than exploitation.

people.label: Allen W. Dulles

people.narrative: Allen W. Dulles signed the three letters that closed the Agency's 1952 flying-saucer file. On 13 March 1953, over his name and on Office of the Director paper classified SECRET, the CIA sent the Robertson Panel report to the Secretary of Defense, to the Federal Civil Defense Administration and to the National Security Resources Board, told each that the conclusions pointed to 'certain potential dangers to national security', and then said in the same letter that the Agency did not consider the subject primarily its concern. Those three letters do two things the board needs: they attribute the panel to Bedell Smith in the Agency's own words, and they are a dated, signed instance of the Agency stepping back from a subject it had itself convened a panel on ten weeks earlier. Dulles also has an OSS personnel file, named by the National Archives among the notable files opened in 2008; the board carries no Office of Strategic Services node, so no edge is drawn for it.

people.label: Robert J. Kaminski

people.narrative: Robert Kaminski is the one witness in the Malmstrom cluster who was close to the hardware rather than to the story, and his account is in direct and checkable tension with the Air Force's own paper. He is described as a Boeing engineer on the team sent to Malmstrom after the Echo Flight shutdown. In a 1997 letter to researcher Jim Klotz he wrote that the investigation team found nothing that would explain ten missiles dropping off alert, no significant failures and no engineering data that accounted for it, and that the inquiry was ordered ended mid-stream with no report to be filed. The first half of that is corroborated by the 341st Strategic Missile Wing history, which records in the engineering report's own words that the teams at Malmstrom were unable to determine a logical cause. The second half is contradicted by the same history, which records the investigation continuing at the contractor's facility through 1967, Boeing bench tests in its Network Resolution Area reproducing the fault signature, and three engineering change proposals submitted by Boeing as a result. Both cannot be wholly right, and the board records the tension rather than resolving it, because one of them is a document and the other is a letter thirty years after the fact.

people.label: Tim Hebert
people.sub: Former USAF Minuteman missile crew member, 490th SMS, Malmstrom AFB 1981-85, and Wing Codes Division, Grand Forks AFB 1985-88; later an Air Force Systems Command programme manager; sceptical analyst of the Echo Flight case
people.narrative: Tim Hebert is the most useful sceptic in this cluster because he argues from the released paper rather than from assertion, and because he held the job. By his own account he was a Minuteman crew member with the 490th Strategic Missile Squadron at Malmstrom from 1981 to 1985, then in the Wing Codes Division at Grand Forks from 1985 to 1988, and later a programme manager with Air Force Systems Command who handled engineering change proposals daily. His two load-bearing arguments are checkable and this board checked them. The first is that the 341st Strategic Missile Wing history details the capsule crew's debriefing but never mentions the maintenance teams whose presence the UFO account requires. The second is that Engineering Change Proposal 1221, an electromagnetic pulse suppression modification, shows what the Air Force actually concluded and actually bought; this board verified ECP 1221 independently against the release, where it appears with its own exhibit citation. His central move, an argument from a unit history's silence, has one documented counterexample inside this same cluster: at Wurtsmith in January 1979 the wing historian checked his own October to December 1975 Wing History for an event that other Air Force paper records, found no reference to it, and wrote that down.

people.label: Robert L. Hastings
people.sub: Researcher, UFO incursions at US nuclear weapons sites; author, 'UFOs and Nukes'
people.narrative: Robert Hastings has spent more than forty years doing one thing: locating and interviewing US Air Force personnel who were present at nuclear weapons sites during unexplained aerial incursions, and pairing their testimony with declassified documents obtained under FOIA. He states he has interviewed over 150 military veterans involved in such incidents at missile sites, weapons storage facilities and bomb test ranges, and he has published the underlying paper - FBI memoranda on Los Alamos in December 1948 and on Los Alamos and Sandia in August 1950, F. E. Warren AFB documents from 1 August 1965, Minot AFB material from 1966, the 17 March 1967 Air Force teletype reporting loss of strategic alert at Malmstrom, and 1975 Malmstrom documents - alongside signed witness affidavits. On 27 September 2010 he hosted the UFO-Nukes Connection press conference at the National Press Club in Washington DC, at which seven US Air Force veterans described incursions at nuclear weapons sites; CNN streamed the event live. That event is the single most important item in this section of the board, because it converted a body of anonymous or semi-anonymous claims into named, on-the-record testimony from identifiable former officers with signed affidavits on file - which is the difference between tier 3 and tier 2. His book 'UFOs and Nukes: Extraordinary Encounters at Nuclear Weapons Sites' is in a revised second edition of 580 pages, and his documentary 'UFOs and Nukes: The Secret Link Revealed' followed. He has lectured at more than 500 colleges and universities since 1981 and continues publishing, most recently on Grusch-era material in June 2026.
