people.label: Capt. Robert L. Salas
people.sub: USAF Academy graduate; Minuteman missile launch officer, 341st SMW, Malmstrom AFB, March 1967
people.narrative: Robert L. Salas is the named officer at the centre of the Malmstrom March 1967 missile shutdown claim. A US Air Force Academy graduate with a master's in aerospace engineering from the Air Force Institute of Technology, he served seven years on active duty as an ICBM launch controller and missile propulsion engineer, resigned his commission in 1971, worked at Martin Marietta and Rockwell International, then spent two decades at the Federal Aviation Administration to about 1995. He first went on the record in a 1996 interview with the Great Falls Tribune: while on duty in a launch control capsule at Malmstrom he took a call from a topside Air Force security police officer reporting a glowing red object hovering over the front gate, and within moments the missiles in his flight went off alert status one after another. He has repeated the account in a signed affidavit held by Robert Hastings, in his books 'Faded Giant' (2005, with James Klotz) and 'Unidentified' (2014), at the 27 September 2010 National Press Club event, and in the 2025 documentary 'The Age of Disclosure'. His most important corroboration is a letter from his commander, Col. Frederick Meiwald, dated 1 October 1996, published in facsimile by Hastings. Salas is also the case where this board's grading discipline bites hardest in both directions: the underlying fact that a Malmstrom flight of ten Minuteman missiles went off alert in March 1967 is documented in Air Force paper, while the causal attribution to an aerial object is testimony, and a competing engineering explanation - a nearby electromagnetic pulse simulator test - has been advanced against it.

people.sub: Aerospace engineer, NAWCAD, NAS Patuxent River (to 2019); named inventor on five Navy-assigned patent filings 2015-2019; later US Navy Strategic Systems Programs, then US Air Force
people.narrative:
Pais is the only person in the open record who has put a description of a craft with the reported UAP flight characteristics into the United States patent system, with the United States Navy as assignee and his own name on the front. That is the entire reason he belongs on this board, and it is a documentary fact independent of whether anything he described works.

Between July 2015 and March 2018 he filed five applications from NAWCAD at NAS Patuxent River, every one of them assigned to 'The United States of America as represented by the Secretary of the Navy': an electromagnetic field generator, a craft using an inertial mass reduction device, a high frequency gravitational wave generator, a piezoelectricity-induced room temperature superconductor, and a plasma compression fusion device. Three were granted. Two published as applications.

The Navy's own invention-disclosure briefing for the inertial mass reduction device, Navy Case PAX 205, was released under FOIA and is the most useful document in the set because Pais wrote it for an internal audience rather than for an examiner. It describes a 'hybrid aerospace / undersea craft (HAUC)' that would 'move with great ease through the air / space / water mediums' enclosed in a 'Vacuum plasma bubble/sheath', achieving 'extreme aerial and underwater speeds (lack of air/water-skin friction) and enhanced stealth capabilities (non-linear scattering of RF and sonar signals)'. Set that description beside the flight characteristics the Navy's own aviators reported in the same decade and the overlap is not subtle: transmedium travel, extreme acceleration, and low observability, itemised in a Navy invention disclosure.

The same briefing is equally explicit about what did not exist. Pais states, twice, that this 'is a theoretical concept - no prototype in existence, as yet', gives the invention original date as 6 March 2015, and proposes Section 219 NISE funding of 250,000 dollars in labour and 250,000 dollars in NAWCAD facility cost to investigate it experimentally. A slide header reads 'EXPERIMENT TRUMPS THEORY EVERYTIME!'. Whatever else the documents are, on their face they are a proposal to test an idea, written by someone asking for money to test it.

That is where the record turns against the strong reading. NAWCAD did fund the work, and reporting based on documents released under FOIA says it spent roughly half a million dollars between 2016 and 2019 and concluded that the effect could not be demonstrated, with no further research conducted. The figure matches the two 250,000 dollar lines Pais proposed. A board that leaves that out is not making the case stronger, it is making it dismissible.

What remains genuinely unusual, and is not disposed of by the negative test result, is the institutional behaviour around the filings. A patent examiner's job is to reject a claim that is not enabled, and the record as reported is that one was rejected on exactly that ground and then granted after the Naval Aviation Enterprise's chief technology officer wrote to the USPTO asserting operability and warning that China was pursuing the same capability. Agencies do not usually spend senior technical credibility forcing through a patent they believe describes nothing. Either the Navy believed the physics, or it wanted the priority date on the public record for reasons it has not stated. Both readings are live, and neither is established.
affiliations: Naval Air Warfare Center Aircraft Division (NAWCAD), NAS Patuxent River, Maryland
people.tierRationale: Re-graded A on a global pass (rank 43 of 1170, score 84). 8 connections, 6 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C2/A1/D1.

claims.text: Five patent filings between July 2015 and March 2018 name Pais as inventor and are assigned to the United States as represented by the Secretary of the Navy: applications 14/807943, 15/141270, 15/431823, 15/678672 and 15/928703. Three issued as US 10,135,366, US 10,144,532 and US 10,322,827.
claims.source: Patent bibliographic records for US10135366, US10144532, US10322827, US20190058105 and US20190295733 (FreePatentsOnline mirror of the USPTO full-text record), read 28 August 2026

claims.text: Reporting based on records released under FOIA states that NAWCAD funded testing of the claimed effect between 2016 and 2019 at a cost of roughly 500,000 USD and determined that it could not be demonstrated, with no further research conducted. The figure corresponds to the two 250,000 USD lines proposed in the PAX 205 briefing.
claims.source: Secondary reporting summarised at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salvatore_Pais citing FOIA-released NAWCAD records; the underlying release has not been obtained for this board

claims.text: The Sheehy intervention is a real document and it is not what the secondary reporting describes. On 15 December 2017 the Chief Technology Officer of the Naval Aviation Enterprise wrote to the examiner by name on NAVAIR letterhead (Ser 40T/33, from AIR 4.0T, to 'Mr. Philip J. Bonzell, Primary Patent Examiner'). Rather than asserting the invention was operable, Sheehy opened by CONCEDING the examiner's point: 'Dr Pais has shared your review of his patent disclosure and I agree with your main point that this mode of acceleration/movement is beyond the state of the possible, at least at present.' He praised the examiner's work: 'It is clear from your review that you did invest the time and did follow the theory.'
claims.source: USPTO file wrapper, application 15/141,270 (PAX 205), retrieved from USPTO Patent Center 28 August 2026; document image JCTFAFUKPXXIFW1.pdf, NAVAIR Ser 40T/33 dated 15 December 2017; transcript at research/patents/wrapper/sheehy-letter-2017-12-15.txt

claims.text: The PAX 205 description of a single craft combining transmedium air/space/water travel, extreme speed without skin friction, and low observability through non-linear scattering of RF and sonar tracks the flight characteristics reported by Navy aircrew in the same period more closely than any other document in the federal patent record. Reasoning: direct comparison of the briefing's own capability list against the reported characteristics; the correspondence is a matter of textual overlap and does not establish a causal direction in either direction.
claims.source: NAVAIR FOIA release 2021-003244, PAX 205 briefing, slides 4-5, compared against the reported characteristics on this board

claims.text: The intervention is better read as an argument about TIMING and about ownership than as an assertion that the device works. Sheehy's own analogy is the ruby laser: the theory preceded the device, and 'the Army at Picatinny Arsenal had built the first ruby laser in 1958 but never sought a patent much to DoD's loss.' His stated conclusion is procurement economics, not physics: 'China is already investing significantly in this area and I would prefer we hold the patent as opposed to paying forever more to use this revolutionary technology.' Reasoning: stated inference from the letter's own structure, which spends four paragraphs on why a not-yet-possible thing should be patented anyway and none on why it is possible now. The competing reading, that this is ordinary agency advocacy for a favoured research line, is equally available and is not excluded.
claims.source: USPTO file wrapper, application 15/141,270 (PAX 205), retrieved from USPTO Patent Center 28 August 2026; document image JCTFAFUKPXXIFW1.pdf, NAVAIR Ser 40T/33 dated 15 December 2017; transcript at research/patents/wrapper/sheehy-letter-2017-12-15.txt

claims.text: The argument that a cleared federal employee cannot confirm a working article, and so a denial from one carries little evidentiary weight, does not reach the 'no prototype in existence' statement in its strongest form, because that statement was not made to the public. It appears on an internal NAVAIR invention-disclosure slide addressed to the officials deciding whether to grant the author roughly 500,000 dollars to build an experiment. The incentive in that room runs the other way: an applicant who already possessed a working article would not gain by telling his own funding authority he had nothing. Reasoning: stated inference from the document's audience and purpose, which are visible on its face.
claims.source: NAVAIR FOIA release 2021-003244, PAX 205 briefing, slides 4 and 6

claims.text: The clearance argument does survive against a narrower and more defensible claim: classification constrains what a cleared person may say about the ORIGIN of a concept, not about whether hardware sits on his bench. A person read into a compartment could write 'no prototype in existence' truthfully while being unable to state that he knew the effect to be real from data he was not free to cite. Nothing in the released record establishes that this is what happened, and nothing in it excludes the possibility. Reasoning: stated inference distinguishing two different questions the same sentence is often taken to answer.
claims.source: Stated inference; no primary record bears on the origin question either way

claims.text: US 10,144,532 is EXPIRED. USPTO application data gives application status 'Patent Expired Due to NonPayment of Maintenance Fees Under 37 CFR 1.362' with a status date of 9 January 2023, following a maintenance fee reminder mailed 25 July 2022. The Navy prosecuted the application through a formal appeal to obtain the grant in December 2018 and then did not pay the first maintenance fee, so the invention passed into the public domain.
claims.source: USPTO application data for 15/141270 (product PTGRXML, data.uspto.gov), retrieved from the file wrapper 28 August 2026

claims.text: The application was pulled for security screening at filing. USPTO events record 'Referred to Level 2 (LARS) by OIPE CSR' and 'Referred by L&R for Third-Level Security Review. Agency Referral Letter Generated', both dated 2 May 2016, with 'Waiting LR clearance' on 12 May 2016. It cleared; no secrecy order issued.
claims.source: USPTO application data for 15/141270 (product PTGRXML, data.uspto.gov), retrieved from the file wrapper 28 August 2026

claims.text: The grant was obtained through a formal appeal, not a letter. The recorded sequence is: non-final rejection 22 November 2017; applicant-initiated telephonic examiner interview 17 January 2018 at which 'no agreement was reached'; final rejection 27 March 2018; response after final 24 May 2018 carrying a declaration under 37 C.F.R. 1.132 signed by Dr James Sheehy on 11 May 2018; Notice of Appeal filed 21 June 2018; Advisory Action 11 July 2018 refusing to allow; Appeal Brief filed 21 August 2018, re-filing the SAME 11 May declaration in its Evidence Appendix rather than a second one; Appeal Brief Review Complete 5 September 2018; Reasons for Allowance 24 October 2018; Notice of Allowance 31 October 2018; granted 4 December 2018. The examiner allowed the application before the Patent Trial and Appeal Board ever ruled.
claims.source: USPTO application data for 15/141270 (product PTGRXML, data.uspto.gov), retrieved from the file wrapper 28 August 2026

claims.text: The examiner of record was Philip J. Bonzell, Group Art Unit 3642. The attorneys of record were Mark Glut (USPTO registration 38,161), Robert S. Gorman (41,790) and Rohit K. Dewan (74,007), all of the Department of the Navy, Naval Air Warfare Center Aircraft Division, Office of Counsel, 47076 Liljencrantz Road, Building 435, Patuxent River, Maryland.
claims.source: USPTO application data for 15/141270 (product PTGRXML, data.uspto.gov), retrieved from the file wrapper 28 August 2026

claims.text: The assignment of record is reel 38412, frame 0760: assignor PAIS, SALVATORE, execution date 27 April 2016, recorded 28 April 2016, assignee DEPARTMENT OF THE NAVY, attorney docket number PAX 205. This is the documentary link between the granted patent and the NAVAIR invention-disclosure briefing released under FOIA, which carries the same Navy case number.
claims.source: USPTO application data for 15/141270 (product PTGRXML, data.uspto.gov), retrieved from the file wrapper 28 August 2026

claims.text: Paragraph [0020] of the application as filed credits the mechanism to a named figure already on this board: 'it is feasible to remove energy-mass from the system by enabling vacuum polarization, as discussed by Harold Puthoff; in that diminution of inertial (and thus gravitational) mass can be achieved via manipulation of quantum field fluctuations in the vacuum.'
claims.source: Application 15/141,270 as filed, 'A Craft Using an Inertial Mass Reduction Device', Navy Case PAX 205

claims.text: Paragraph [0037] of the application as filed states that the preferred electromagnetic generator for the craft is the one described in US application 14/807,943, 'incorporated by reference, and has the same inventor'. The inertial mass reduction craft and the electromagnetic field generator are therefore linked as components of one design by the filings themselves rather than by inference.
claims.source: Application 15/141,270 as filed, 'A Craft Using an Inertial Mass Reduction Device', Navy Case PAX 205

claims.text: The application as filed states the craft 'can be, but without limitation, a cone or lenticular triangle / delta wing configuration', and its two figures show a triangular craft and a diamond craft, each enclosed in the polarized vacuum boundary. The published drawings are the only depiction of the intended craft geometry in the federal record.
claims.source: Application 15/141,270 as filed, 'A Craft Using an Inertial Mass Reduction Device', Navy Case PAX 205

claims.text: The combination of a two-year fight for the grant and a refusal to pay the first maintenance fee is consistent with the Navy wanting the examining authority's FINDING rather than the property right. The reason this now bites harder is that Sheehy stated the opposite rationale in writing: he wanted to 'hold the patent as opposed to paying forever more to use this revolutionary technology', which is a freedom-to-operate argument. But publication in November 2017 had already created permanent prior art, and prior art alone prevents anyone else from patenting the idea and charging the Navy for it. The granted claims added nothing to that protection; what they added was the reversal of an enablement rejection, which is the Patent Office ceasing to say the invention does not work. A maintenance fee buys only the right to exclude an infringer, which the Navy would never exercise. Reasoning: stated inference from the prosecution record and the letter; the alternative reading, that the docket simply lapsed after its inventor transferred out of NAWCAD in 2019, is equally available and is not excluded.
claims.source: USPTO application data for 15/141270 (product PTGRXML, data.uspto.gov), retrieved from the file wrapper 28 August 2026

claims.text: The December 2017 letter places the NAWCAD experimental programme on the record and dates it. Sheehy wrote that 'Dr. Pais is currently funded by NAWCAD to design a test article and instrumentation to demonstrate the experimental feasibility of achieving high electromagnetic (EM) field-energy and flux values', and that 'He is currently one year into the project and has already begun a series of experiments'. That places the start of funded experimental work in about December 2016 and corroborates, from a primary document, the secondary reporting that NAWCAD funded testing from 2016.
claims.source: USPTO file wrapper, application 15/141,270 (PAX 205), retrieved from USPTO Patent Center 28 August 2026; document image JCTFAFUKPXXIFW1.pdf, NAVAIR Ser 40T/33 dated 15 December 2017; transcript at research/patents/wrapper/sheehy-letter-2017-12-15.txt

claims.text: The letter describes the actual test rig in specific terms: 'tests using a battery to charge a 10 cm test sample spinning at up to 100,000 RPM and is able maintain charge on these batteries for dwell times of more than 25 minutes (at max RPM) without loss of load', with a fallback to 'a super-capacitor as the spinning test asset' and a test asset surface charge density 'on the order of one Coulomb/meter 2'. This is the only description of the apparatus located on this board that comes from a government document rather than from reporting.
claims.source: USPTO file wrapper, application 15/141,270 (PAX 205), retrieved from USPTO Patent Center 28 August 2026; document image JCTFAFUKPXXIFW1.pdf, NAVAIR Ser 40T/33 dated 15 December 2017; transcript at research/patents/wrapper/sheehy-letter-2017-12-15.txt

claims.text: Sheehy's declaration of 11 May 2018 states his credentials: a PhD in physiological optics from Pennsylvania State University, a master's in Human Factors Engineering from Rensselaer, a bachelor's from Kean University; a civilian Navy employee since 1985; formerly Chief Scientist of the Naval Air Systems Command; Chief Technology Officer of the Naval Aviation Enterprise for the preceding eleven years; promoted to the Senior Executive Service in November 2001; awarded the Presidential Rank Award in 2007. It is sworn under 18 U.S.C. 1001.
claims.source: USPTO file wrapper, application 15/141,270 (PAX 205), retrieved from USPTO Patent Center 28 August 2026; document image JHRQ6JRIRXEAPX0.pdf, declaration under 37 C.F.R. 1.132 signed 11 May 2018, faxed 24 May 2018; transcript at research/patents/wrapper/sheehy-declaration-2018-05-11.txt

claims.text: The declaration's operative assertion is narrow and rests on citation rather than on test data. Sheehy declares that he 'can be considered a person of ordinary skill in the art' and that 'the invention described in the above referenced patent application is enabled via the physics described in the patent application and the peer reviewed papers described in the Inventor Amendment dated January 23, 2018'. He does not state that a device was built or that any effect was measured, and the experiments described in his own December 2017 letter are not mentioned.
claims.source: USPTO file wrapper, application 15/141,270 (PAX 205), retrieved from USPTO Patent Center 28 August 2026; document image JHRQ6JRIRXEAPX0.pdf, declaration under 37 C.F.R. 1.132 signed 11 May 2018, faxed 24 May 2018; transcript at research/patents/wrapper/sheehy-declaration-2018-05-11.txt

claims.text: Two of the five papers the enablement argument rests on are Pais's own conference papers: 'A Hybrid Craft using an Inertial Mass Modification Device', AIAA SPACE Forum, Orlando, 12-14 September 2017, and 'High Frequency Gravitational Waves - Induced Propulsion', SAE International 2017-01-2040, 19 September 2017. The other three are third-party technical papers on piezoelectric materials, Q-factor estimation and plasma channels, none of which concerns inertial mass reduction. The corroboration invoked is therefore in part the inventor citing himself.
claims.source: USPTO file wrapper, application 15/141,270 (PAX 205), retrieved from USPTO Patent Center 28 August 2026; document images JLZJWBOMRXEAPX0.pdf and JLZJWBOORXEAPX0.pdf, Appeal Brief under 37 C.F.R. 41.37 faxed 20 August 2018; notes at research/patents/wrapper/appeal-brief-2018-08-20.txt

claims.text: The examiner conceded the theory and still refused the claims. The Advisory Action of 11 July 2018 says of the Sheehy declaration: 'While the Examiner agrees that the math and physics are sound in this application, the Examiner holds that the claims are still not enabled.' The distinction is the whole case: enablement asks whether a person skilled in the art could BUILD the thing, not whether the equations are consistent.
claims.source: USPTO file wrapper, application 15/141,270 (PAX 205), retrieved from USPTO Patent Center 28 August 2026; document image JJEEPSU2RXEAPX0.pdf, Advisory Action mailed 11 July 2018; transcript at research/patents/wrapper/advisory-action-2018-07-11.txt

claims.text: The examiner set an explicit condition for allowance and it was experimental. Rejecting the argument that microwave excitation of a copper resonant cavity makes the required fields feasible, he wrote: 'While obtaining high vibrational frequencies are possible this does not mean that the E-fields and B-fields that are required to polarize the quantum vacuum can be created. If this is so then the Examiner asks that the Applicant demonstrate these high vibrational frequencies to create a local polarized vacuum.' No such demonstration appears in the file wrapper as uploaded, and the application was nonetheless allowed on 31 October 2018.
claims.source: USPTO file wrapper, application 15/141,270 (PAX 205), retrieved from USPTO Patent Center 28 August 2026; document image JJEEPSU2RXEAPX0.pdf, Advisory Action mailed 11 July 2018; transcript at research/patents/wrapper/advisory-action-2018-07-11.txt

claims.text: The specific physical quantities in dispute are on the record. The applicant argued that vibrational frequencies above 10 GHz in a copper resonant cavity enable electromagnetic flux values of 10^33 Watts per square metre, 'equivalent to the generation of E-fields on the order of 10^18 V/m and B-fields on the order of 10^9 Tesla'. The examiner's rejection was that those field levels are not feasible with current technology.
claims.source: USPTO file wrapper, application 15/141,270 (PAX 205), retrieved from USPTO Patent Center 28 August 2026; document image JJEEPSU2RXEAPX0.pdf, Advisory Action mailed 11 July 2018; transcript at research/patents/wrapper/advisory-action-2018-07-11.txt

claims.text: The 17 January 2018 examiner interview was telephonic, attended by examiner Philip J. Bonzell, attorney Mark Glut and Salvatore Pais personally. The summary records that no exhibit was shown and no demonstration conducted, and that 'The Examiner pointed out that he still felt that there were enablement issues. The Applicant to submit arguments to the contrary. No agreement was reached.'
claims.source: USPTO file wrapper, application 15/141,270 (PAX 205), retrieved from USPTO Patent Center 28 August 2026; document image JCKKXW5GRXEAPX4.pdf, Applicant-Initiated Interview Summary mailed 22 January 2018; transcript at research/patents/wrapper/interview-summary-2018-01-17.txt

claims.text: The Appeal Brief states the ownership position without qualification: 'The real party in interested is the United States Government represented by the Secretary of the Navy (The Department of the Navy). The inventor is a U.S.government employee who invented the invention during the course of his employment. As a result, Federal law provides all rights to this invention belong to the United States of America under 37 C.F.R. 501.6.' This is the Navy's own characterisation, in a filing signed by its Office of Counsel.
claims.source: USPTO file wrapper, application 15/141,270 (PAX 205), retrieved from USPTO Patent Center 28 August 2026; document images JLZJWBOMRXEAPX0.pdf and JLZJWBOORXEAPX0.pdf, Appeal Brief under 37 C.F.R. 41.37 faxed 20 August 2018; notes at research/patents/wrapper/appeal-brief-2018-08-20.txt

claims.text: The appeal was argued on burden of proof rather than on evidence of operability. The brief cites In re Rijckaert, 9 F.3d 1531 (Fed. Cir. 1993) and In re Oetiker, 977 F.2d 1443 (Fed. Cir. 1992) for the proposition that the burden of showing unpatentability rests on the Office and remains there even after a prima facie case. The Navy's legal position was that the examiner had not carried it, not that the device had been shown to work.
claims.source: USPTO file wrapper, application 15/141,270 (PAX 205), retrieved from USPTO Patent Center 28 August 2026; document images JLZJWBOMRXEAPX0.pdf and JLZJWBOORXEAPX0.pdf, Appeal Brief under 37 C.F.R. 41.37 faxed 20 August 2018; notes at research/patents/wrapper/appeal-brief-2018-08-20.txt

claims.text: A patent assigned to a federal agency owes maintenance fees on the ordinary schedule, which closes the question the expiry finding rested on. 37 CFR 1.362(a) requires them 'in all patents based on applications filed on or after December 12, 1980, except as noted in paragraph (b) of this section, to maintain a patent in force beyond 4, 8 and 12 years after the date of grant', and paragraph (b) gives the exemptions in full: 'Maintenance fees are not required for any plant patents or for any design patents.' Both Pais grants are utility patents from applications filed long after 1980. Neither was in an exempt class, and both owed the fee.
claims.source: 37 CFR 1.362, Time for payment of maintenance fees (CFR 2024, title 37, vol. 1) || https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2024-title37-vol1/xml/CFR-2024-title37-vol1-sec1-362.xml

claims.text: Both granted Pais patents lapsed at the first maintenance fee, five weeks apart. US 10,135,366, granted 20 November 2018, is recorded expired for non-payment on 26 December 2022; US 10,144,532, granted 4 December 2018, is recorded expired for non-payment on 9 January 2023. USPTO mailed a maintenance fee reminder for each in the preceding July.
claims.source: USPTO application data for 14/807943 and 15/141270 (product PTGRXML, data.uspto.gov), retrieved from the file wrappers 28 August 2026

claims.text: That both grants lapsed the same way weakens the reading that either was an isolated docketing slip, and it also weakens the sharper reading that the Navy specifically wanted the finding on the craft and not the property right. An office that files, prosecutes and then renews nothing across a family is exhibiting a maintenance practice, and a practice is as consistent with routine cost control on patents the Navy would never sue to enforce as it is with a judgement about these particular inventions. What can be said without inference is that the Navy paid to obtain both patents, fought a two-year appeal for one of them, and then let both go.
claims.source: Stated inference from the two USPTO application-data records, with the competing readings recorded alongside it

claims.text: The two applications were treated very differently by the Office, and the comparison is the strongest thing this cluster now has. The electromagnetic field generator, filed 24 July 2015, drew one non-final rejection and was allowed by Thomas M. Dougherty in Art Unit 2837 because 'the prior art fails to show' the claimed generator, with enablement never raised. The craft, filed nine months later on 28 April 2016 and expressly incorporating that generator by reference, was rejected twice by Philip J. Bonzell in Art Units 3644 and 3642 as not enabled and impossible, and reached allowance only after a Notice of Appeal and an Appeal Brief. The same physics, the same inventor and the same office of counsel produced opposite results depending on whether the claim was to the component or to the craft.

people.label: Ben R. Rich
people.sub: Director, Lockheed Advanced Development Projects (Skunk Works), 1975-1991
people.narrative: Rich is the single most-cited contractor figure in the custody allegation, and the most poorly sourced - which is exactly why he needs a disciplined entry. His documented record is not in dispute: he succeeded Kelly Johnson as head of Lockheed's Advanced Development Projects in 1975, ran the F-117 stealth fighter program to operational capability, held the deepest black-program access available to a private citizen in the United States, and retired in 1991. His 1994 memoir with Leo Janos, written after retirement and cleared for publication, is a first-person account of how unacknowledged special access programs were actually run at Burbank and Palmdale - the physical security, the compartmented staffing, the funding lines invisible to the aircraft's own users. That book is the primary document; it is also the reason his later remarks carry weight with researchers. The remarks themselves - the reported 1993 UCLA alumni-association talk in which he is said to have stated that 'we already have the means to travel among the stars, but these technologies are locked up in black projects,' and the reported private letters to model-maker John Andrews - survive only through secondhand recollection by attendees and correspondents. No recording, transcript, or letter facsimile has been produced in a verifiable archive. The board records the attribution as an attribution, not as a fact: what Rich unquestionably represents is that the man with the most complete inventory of American black aerospace in the twentieth century spent his last years being asked this question, and that Lockheed has never released his program records. He died of cancer on 5 January 1995.

people.label: Alfred 'Al' O'Donnell
people.sub: Senior manager and first general manager, EG&G in Nevada; nuclear test firing engineer
people.narrative: O'Donnell is the highest-placed contractor executive ever alleged to have described recovered material directly to a journalist. He was an EG&G man from the Manhattan Project era forward - the firing-circuit engineer who triggered US atmospheric nuclear tests, and, per George Knapp, the first general manager of EG&G's Nevada operations, the company that ran the classified support infrastructure at the Nevada Test Site and the Groom Lake facility. Knapp interviewed him repeatedly beginning in the early 1990s and reported that O'Donnell told him 'they did have a flying saucer that had been recovered from New Mexico' and, separately, a 'live being': 'We didn't know what it was... To tell you the truth, we couldn't communicate with it. In the beginning, we didn't know what it was, we didn't know where it was from. And we didn't know what to do with it.' Knapp reported that O'Donnell compared the being's appearance to Ross Perot rather than to the conventional grey. With the blessing of EG&G co-founder Herbert Grier, Knapp arranged a meeting between O'Donnell and Senate Appropriations investigator Richard D'Amato - and O'Donnell told D'Amato nothing. Knapp says O'Donnell was subsequently warned off, but agreed to record a deathbed statement to be released after his death. No such recording has ever surfaced. O'Donnell is the test case for the entire contractor-custody thesis: a man with unimpeachable access, an account given privately and repeatedly, and a total absence of artifact.

people.label: Richard D'Amato
people.sub: Senate Appropriations Committee counsel/investigator for Sen. Robert C. Byrd, 1980s-1990s
people.narrative: D'Amato is the first documented attempt by the legislative branch to audit the contractor-custody allegation, and the template for every failure since. As a staffer to Senate Democratic Leader Robert C. Byrd - chairman of the Appropriations Committee - his portfolio covered the DoD budget and the National Foreign Intelligence Program, which meant special access program oversight. In the early 1990s a senior committee chairman asked him to conduct a preliminary inquiry into allegations of unidentified aerial crashes in 1940s New Mexico. He interviewed witnesses, visited the Nevada facility, and reported back that the basis for the allegations did not merit further Senate investigation. His public statement is terse and closed: 'I have no personal opinion on the matter and consider the inquiry to have been closed for over 20 years.' But according to George Knapp, D'Amato privately concluded it was 'entirely feasible, that this UFO cover-up exists within a private company' - naming Lockheed Martin, EG&G or Northrop Grumman as the kind of company he meant. The structural lesson is the one that recurs: an investigator with appropriations jurisdiction, sent to look, found that the relevant knowledge sat with a corporation rather than an agency, and that his subpoena power over an agency did not reach it. The witness he most needed - Al O'Donnell - said nothing when they met.

people.label: Dr. James Ryder
people.sub: Lockheed Martin executive named in sworn congressional testimony as a program gatekeeper
people.narrative: Ryder exists on this board for one reason: on 9 September 2025 Rep. Nick Begich asked George Knapp to name specific gatekeepers 'within the root cell of the UAP SAP federation,' and Knapp answered, under oath, 'Well, one of them was named Dr. James Ryder at Lockheed.' That single sentence is the only time a private individual inside a prime contractor has been named to a congressional committee as a custodian of the alleged program. Knapp immediately qualified it - 'I do not fault these contractors for doing what they were asked to do by our government. They are supposed to lie if people ask about it' - and attributed the original tasking to the intelligence agencies, CIA primarily. The board records the naming precisely because it is on the record and because it is testable: Lockheed Martin's research organisation is a matter of public corporate record, and a Congress that wanted to resolve this could resolve it with a letter. What the board does not do is assert anything about Ryder beyond the fact of the naming. There is no released document, contract, complaint or corporate statement connecting him to recovered material, and no response from him or from Lockheed Martin has been published. This entry is a placeholder for an investigative thread, not a finding.

people.narrative:
George Hathaway is the author the DIA list names for "Role of Superconductors in Gravity Research," and separately for "Maverick Inventor Versus Corporate Inventor" (item 16). Two DIRDs, and they are an odd pair: one a technical review of the most contested claim in gravity-modification research, the other an essay on where breakthrough invention actually comes from. Both are consistent with what Hathaway has done for fifty years.

Hathaway graduated in electrical engineering from the University of Toronto in 1974 and is a registered professional engineer. He runs a private laboratory near Toronto International Airport, first as Hathaway Consulting Services, the affiliation the DIA letter records, and latterly as Hathaway Research International. The laboratory's stated function is to test claims of anomalous energy production and unconventional propulsion and gravity modification, which in practice means being the person who replicates other people's extraordinary claims and reports honestly when they fail. Between 1996 and 2003 he ran the Podkletnov rotating-superconductor gravity-shielding experiment for a prospective investor and obtained null results. He co-authored with Reiss a 2005 paper on correct laboratory practice in experiments designed to detect gravity-like forces.

That record is why his DIRD is more interesting than its title suggests. The superconductor paper, DIA-08-1003-013, dated 23 March 2010 in the Acquisition Threat Support series, reviews the Soviet-lineage gravity claims of Evgeny Podkletnov and the work of Ning Li. DIA commissioned a review of gravity modification from the one person in the field with a documented history of failing to replicate it. That is not the commissioning behaviour of a programme buying a predetermined conclusion, and it is a fact that cuts against the standard reading of the DIRD set in both directions.

Hathaway's disclosure role is scored above the other subject-matter authors because his laboratory is a standing independent node in the anomalous-physics network, referenced alongside EarthTech International as one of the few places where such claims get instrumented rather than argued.

His assessment of Release 01: 'Although there is a lot of information here, there is little context. Case summaries without coordinates, sensor parameters, or altitude data make independent analysis very difficult.' His critique and Gallaudet's converge from different directions on the same finding: the release preserved the imagery and stripped the physics.

Harvard astronomy faculty since 1993, tenured three years later, chair of the astronomy department 2011-2020, Baird Professor since 2012, and director of the Institute for Theory and Computation at the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics since 2007, he founded The Galileo Project on 26 July 2021 - four weeks after the ODNI preliminary assessment - on the explicit premise that the way out of a classified impasse is to build unclassified instruments and publish. He is Vice President of UAPx, a research affiliate of the Galileo Project, and co-author of the 2025 UAPx field-expedition paper. The editorship of Entropy is worth noting plainly: a journal editor publishing in his own journal invites the obvious criticism, and the paper's critics have made it.

people.label: Beatriz Villarroel
people.sub: Astronomer, Nordita / Stockholm University and Instituto de Astrofisica de Canarias; principal investigator, VASCO (Vanishing and Appearing Sources during a Century of Observations)
people.narrative: Villarroel is running the one line of investigation that could produce hard evidence about the 1940s-1950s period without any cooperation from the US government at all, because her dataset predates the government's ability to classify it. VASCO compares the Palomar Observatory Sky Survey plates - exposed between 1949 and 1957, before any artificial satellite existed - against modern sky surveys, looking for point sources that appear in the old plates and are absent now. Anything genuinely transient and star-like on a pre-Sputnik plate cannot be a satellite glint, which makes the archive a clean natural experiment. Her group published the VASCO methodology in The Astronomical Journal in December 2019, then in June 2021 reported in Scientific Reports nine simultaneous transients on a single plate from 12 April 1950, and in 2022 published the 'glint in the eye' analysis in Acta Astronautica arguing photographic plate archives are a viable search space for non-terrestrial artefacts. Then, on 20 October 2025, she and Stephen Bruehl published in Scientific Reports the result that matters most for this board: transients in POSS-I 'may be associated with nuclear testing and reports of unidentified anomalous phenomena'. That is a peer-reviewed, Nature-portfolio paper drawing a statistical association between above-ground nuclear tests, contemporaneous UAP reports, and anomalous point sources on astronomical plates from the exact period this board treats as the programme's origin. The Sol Foundation made it the subject of its first policy briefing in January 2026.

people.label: Edgar Fouche
people.sub: USAF master sergeant and avionics maintenance NCO, later a DoD contractor engineering manager; originating claimant of the TR-3B in an August 1998 presentation
people.narrative: Edgar Albert Fouche is the single named origin of the TR-3B account, and what makes him a node is that origin and not any documented authority. The ordinary facts of his life are settled at Tier 1: born 22 February 1948 in Americus, Georgia, died 11 May 2017 aged 69, buried at Coffey Cemetery in Mason County, Texas, and independently fixed at 1948 by the Library of Congress name authority attached to his own book. The career the opened records document is a twenty year enlisted avionics maintenance career: F-15 and F-16 manual test stations, the TEWS-TITE electronic warfare bay, a Strategic Air Command liaison post at Kelly AFB, a Community College of the Air Force associate degree in avionics systems technology, and three Meritorious Service Medals whose citations describe exactly that work. It is an honourable record and an entirely ordinary one, and nothing in it touches aerospace design, propulsion or physics. Everything extraordinary rests on his own word in documents he wrote and copyrighted himself: the Top Secret and 'Q' clearances, the descent from Napoleon's minister of police, the helicopter flights to Groom Lake, and the TR-3B. One document is a real counterweight and the node must carry it: an AF Form 77a of 24 August 1979 records him assigned temporary duty to AFFTC Detachment 3 on the Nellis range for ten weeks, and Peter Merlin, the historian whose analysis demolishes most of the rest of the account, is the source that identifies Detachment 3 AFFTC as the unit operating Groom Lake. That form also says its own limit out loud: his duties there 'have been verified via a separate report', and that separate report is not in the file. In July 1998 he published a novel with Brad Steiger; the Library of Congress catalogues it as science fiction. In August 1998 he gave the presentation that put the TR-3B into the world.
people.tierRationale: Re-graded B on a global pass (rank 216 of 1170, score 44). 8 connections, 1 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C0/A1/D3.

people.label: Peter W. Merlin
people.sub: Aerospace historian and aerospace archaeologist; author of nine books including three published by NASA and AIAA; the substantive named sceptic on Fouche's documents and photographs
people.narrative: Peter W. Merlin is on this board because he is the rare thing this subject almost never produces: a named, credentialed, checkable analyst who has gone through a claimant's own documents item by item. He holds a Bachelor of Science in Aeronautical Studies from Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, has researched Area 51 since 1984, co-founded the X-Hunters Aerospace Archeology Team, and has written or co-written nine books, three of them published by NASA and the American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics. His four findings against Fouche are not opinion: each is a falsifiable specific about something outside Fouche's own testimony. He says the 'SAC-DARPA' letter carries no classification marking, which the page image corroborates. He says the aircraft Fouche captioned 'Have Blue' is the first YF-117A SENIOR TREND prototype. He says no person called Steve Stenson was ever commander of the Air Force Flight Test Center. He says the KGB props are fakes sold in surplus stores. He has not, so far as any opened record shows, been checked and found wrong. The reason he earns a node rather than a footnote is that he is on both sides of the same file: his own published reference work on Groom Lake is what identifies Detachment 3 of the Air Force Flight Test Center as the unit operating the airfield, and that identification is the only thing that makes Fouche's single best document mean anything at all.

people.label: John M. McHugh
people.sub: Ranking Member, House Armed Services Committee, January 2009 to June 2009; thereafter Secretary of the Army, 21 September 2009 to 1 November 2015
people.narrative: McHugh held one of the twelve 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) seats for roughly the first half of 2009, the year the board treats as load-bearing because of the Reid special access program request. As ranking minority member of the House Armed Services Committee he was entitled, jointly with Chairman Ike Skelton, to receive whatever the Secretary of Defense withheld from a section 119 report under the waiver authority together with the written justification for withholding it, and to the 119(f) notification that must precede the initiation of any special access program by thirty days. His tenure in the seat is short and precisely bracketed by two dated statements from the committee's own chairman. On 2 June 2009 Skelton described him as 'House Armed Services Committee Ranking Member John M. McHugh (R-NY)' and recorded that McHugh 'took the reins as Ranking Member of the House Armed Services Committee in January.' On 16 June 2009 Skelton congratulated Buck McKeon as the new ranking member. McHugh therefore held a 119(e)(2) seat from January 2009 until some point between 2 and 16 June 2009, and not thereafter, even though he remained a member of the House until 21 September 2009. That distinction matters for date-specific claims: a waived-SAP notification made in the spring of 2009 reached McHugh, and one made in the autumn of 2009 reached McKeon. McHugh's later trajectory is the reason this node is worth keeping rather than folding into a footnote. He moved from a seat entitled to receive waived DoD special access program information directly into the office of Secretary of the Army, the service secretariat that runs its own SAP portfolio. There is no public record of any UAP-specific statement by him in either capacity, and none would be expected: section 119 supplies no disclosure route on the congressional side and Army SAP holdings are not publicly enumerated.

people.label: Howard P. "Buck" McKeon
people.sub: Ranking Member, House Armed Services Committee, from 16 June 2009; Chairman of the same committee in the 112th and 113th Congresses, January 2011 to January 2015
people.narrative: McKeon succeeded John McHugh in the House Armed Services ranking seat in June 2009 and thereby entered the twelve-member group designated by 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2). The date is fixed by the committee's own record: Chairman Ike Skelton issued a statement dated 16 June 2009 congratulating McKeon 'on his election as the Ranking Member of the House Armed Services Committee' following his selection by the House Republican Conference, and noted that the full committee was marking up the annual defense authorization bill that same day. This closes the board's open question about the 2009 House Armed Services succession, and it closes it in a direction that matters: the handover happened in June 2009, not in September when McHugh resigned his seat to become Secretary of the Army. Any claim tied to a specific 2009 date should use McHugh for the first half of the year and McKeon for the second. McKeon's entitlement did not end there. He chaired the House Armed Services Committee across the 112th and 113th Congresses, so he occupied a 119(e)(2) seat from June 2009 continuously into January 2015 - first as ranking member, then as chairman. That is a five-and-a-half-year sight line into whatever waived DoD special access program material the Secretary of Defense chose to route through the section 119 channel, spanning the entire period between the Reid SAP request and the establishment of the Advanced Aerospace Threat Identification Program's successor arrangements. McKeon has no publicly documented UAP-specific record, and the absence is structurally expected rather than exculpatory. Section 119 gives the twelve recipients no staff-sharing right in the statute, no route to brief colleagues, and no sunset that would eventually force the material into wider committee view. On this board McKeon is best treated as a long-duration entitlement node covering the 2009-2015 window that the current-holder roster does not reach.

people.label: Thad Cochran
people.sub: Ranking Member, Defense Subcommittee of the Senate Appropriations Committee, and Ranking Member of the full Senate Appropriations Committee, 111th Congress including 2009
people.narrative: Cochran held two of the twelve 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) seats simultaneously in 2009: ranking minority member of the Senate Appropriations Committee and ranking minority member of that committee's Defense Subcommittee, both named expressly as 'defense committees' by 10 U.S.C. 119(g)(1). His opposite number in both seats was Daniel K. Inouye, who chaired the full committee and the Defense Subcommittee. The Senate side of the group in 2009 therefore comprised four distinct individuals - Levin, McCain, Inouye and Cochran - filling six statutory seats, the same double-occupancy pattern the board records for Susan Collins in the 118th Congress. The board previously carried Cochran's Defense Subcommittee ranking role as an inference drawn from list order in a committee assignment publication that marks chairmen but not ranking members. That inference is now confirmed from a primary source that states the designation in terms. The bound Senate hearing volume for Department of Defense Appropriations for Fiscal Year 2010, the Subcommittee on Defense hearings of the 111th Congress running from 18 March 2009, contains a witness statement addressed 'Chairman Inouye, Ranking Member Cochran.' A witness formally addressing the subcommittee's two presiding officers by title, printed in the Government Publishing Office record of the proceeding, is a direct statement of who held the ranking seat rather than a reading of seniority order. What Cochran's seats entitled him to receive is the same as every other member of the group: whatever the Secretary of Defense withheld from a section 119 report under the waiver authority, plus the justification, delivered jointly with the chairman. What makes the appropriations pair distinctive is that it is the money side of the entitlement. Cochran has no publicly documented UAP-specific record. He is on this board because 2009 is a load-bearing year and because the Defense Subcommittee ranking seat is the single hardest of the twelve to source correctly for any historical date.

people.label: Tom Cole
people.sub: Chairman, House Appropriations Committee, from 10 April 2024 (ratified by the House Republican Conference), continuing through August 2026
people.narrative: This record supersedes the board's earlier, undated entry for Cole. His tenure in the 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) group now has a fixed start: a statement issued from his own congressional office on 10 April 2024 records that 'the full House Republican Conference ratified him as Chairman of the House Appropriations Committee,' following the House Republican Steering Committee's selection the previous day. He succeeded Kay Granger, who had announced in March 2024 that she would step down from the chair. The correction matters for how the board dates his node. Cole entered the group in the middle of the 118th Congress, not at the start of the 119th. That places him inside the twelve for roughly nine months longer than the earlier record implied, but still after all three of the board's load-bearing moments - the 2009 Reid special access program request, the 2020 establishment of the Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force, and the July 2023 Grusch testimony. Granger, not Cole, held the House Appropriations chair on the date of that testimony. As chairman of the House Appropriations Committee, Cole is entitled jointly with Ranking Member Rosa DeLauro to receive whatever the Secretary of Defense withholds from a section 119 report under the waiver authority, together with the justification, and to the 119(f) notification that must precede the initiation of any special access program by thirty days. His committee is also the one that writes the classified annex through which a waived programme is funded. There is no public record of any UAP-specific statement by Cole. As with every other holder, the statute supplies the entitlement and supplies no route to speak about it.

people.label: Cecilia Levy
people.sub: Associate Professor of Physics, University at Albany (SUNY); LZ dark-matter physicist; third UAlbany author on the 2025 UAPx field-expedition paper
people.narrative: Cecilia Levy is the third University at Albany physicist on the only peer-reviewed UAP field-expedition paper published to date, and she is on this board for a narrow and checkable reason: the University named her, in its own press release, as one of three 'UAlbany authors' on Szydagis, Knuth, Kugielsky & Levy (2025). Her career is otherwise entirely conventional astroparticle physics. She took a BSc at the Universite de Montreal, an MSc at Queen's University on the PICASSO dark matter experiment, a PhD at the University of Muenster on XENON100, a postdoc at RPI on XENON1T, and a postdoc at Albany on LUX/LZ, and she is now an Associate Professor in the same department as Szydagis and Knuth. Her stated research is the direct detection of dark matter: she works on the seven-tonne LZ detector at the Sanford Underground Research Facility, where her group handled detector cleanliness and the 206Pb wall background, and she co-develops the Snowball Chamber, a supercooled-water low-mass dark matter detector she describes as 'a research topic completely unique to the UAlbany dark matter group'. She co-authored the founding Snowball Chamber paper with Szydagis in 2018. That shared instrument work is the mechanism by which rare-event detection practice reached the UAP field campaign: the University's release explains that Szydagis's C-TAP frame-differencing software applies an approach 'used by physicists like him and Levy to look for direct evidence of dark matter'. One honest qualification belongs on the record. Unlike Szydagis, whose departmental page lists Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena among his research interests, Levy's faculty page makes no mention of UAP at all. Her involvement is visible in the publication and in the press office, not in her declared research profile - which is a reasonable description of how most working scientists have touched this subject.

people.label: Gerald Anderson
people.sub: Claimed first-hand child witness, Plains of San Agustin, 1947
people.narrative: Gerald Anderson came forward in 1990, after a television broadcast, claiming that as a five-year-old he had been rockhounding with his family on the Plains of San Agustin in July 1947 and had walked up to a crashed disc with dead and one living occupant. He was the only claimed first-hand witness to the San Agustin site and was accordingly promoted hard by Stanton Friedman and Don Berliner in 'Crash at Corona' (1992). The case against him was made not by the Air Force but by other ufologists: Mark Rodeghier of CUFOS and Fred Whiting of the Fund for UFO Research produced a joint report, 'The Plains of San Agustin Controversy', which established among other things that a telephone bill Anderson submitted as corroboration had been altered. His own quoted words in the Air Force's 1997 report - 'I thought they were plastic dolls' - and his descriptions of the recovery procedures were read by the Air Force as accurate reporting of an anthropomorphic dummy balloon launch and recovery, of which numerous examples were flown and recovered in the region. Anderson matters to this board as the field's most instructive self-correction: two civilian research organisations audited their own star witness and published the result against interest.

people.label: James Ragsdale
people.sub: Claimed civilian eyewitness to a crash site north of Roswell
people.narrative: James Ragsdale came forward in the 1990s claiming that he and a companion had been camping north of Roswell in July 1947 and had seen a crashed craft and bodies, with a military recovery arriving afterwards. He gave a sworn statement and a videotaped deathbed account, and Randle and Schmitt used him to anchor the impact site in 'The Truth About the UFO Crash at Roswell' (1994). Two things about Ragsdale are load-bearing and both cut against the case. First, his account moved: the location he gave shifted materially between tellings, in a way that tracked which impact site the researchers then favoured. Second, and more usefully, the Air Force's 1997 report quotes him saying of the objects at the site, 'They were using dummies in those damned things' - the witness himself volunteering the anthropomorphic dummy reading that the Air Force went on to adopt as its explanation. The Air Force notes he lived and worked around Roswell, Artesia and Carlsbad in the period when Alderson Laboratories anthropomorphic dummies were being dropped by high-altitude balloon and recovered by uniformed teams, and concludes he probably described one or more of nine documented dummy recoveries near there.

people.label: Général Bernard Norlain
people.sub: Former Director, Institut des Hautes Études de Défense Nationale; COMETA preface author
people.narrative: Bernard Norlain is the former director of the Institut des Hautes Études de Défense Nationale, the French state's own senior strategic-studies institute reporting to the Prime Minister, and later a prominent figure in nuclear-disarmament advocacy. His preface to the COMETA report is the reason COMETA cannot be dismissed as a hobbyist product: it places the report inside the IHEDN lineage. Norlain records that Denis Letty came to his IHEDN office in March 1995, that he referred Letty to the IHEDN Auditors Association which supported the project, and that the Association had itself produced a preliminary UFO report in its bulletin some twenty years earlier - the 1976 committee chaired by General Blanchard of the Gendarmerie Nationale whose recommendations produced GEPAN. His preface is titled 'Concrete problems are raised that call for a response in terms of action', and it ends with an explicit political demand: 'I express the wish that the recommendations of COMETA, which are inspired by good sense, will be examined and implemented by the authorities of our country ... May this new report, which is much more in-depth, give new impetus to our national efforts and to indispensable international cooperation. IHEDN will then have well served the nation and, perhaps, humanity.'

people.label: Professeur André Lebeau
people.sub: Former President/Chairman of CNES; COMETA forward author
people.narrative: André Lebeau, a former chairman of the Centre National d'Études Spatiales - the French national space agency, and therefore of the parent body of GEPAN, SEPRA and GEIPAN - wrote the opening forward to the COMETA report under the title 'Stripping the UFO phenomenon of its irrational layer'. Denis Letty states in his own foreword that without Lebeau and Norlain 'COMETA would not have been born'. Lebeau's contribution matters because it is the head of the agency that actually holds France's official UAP case file lending his name to the argument that the subject is a legitimate object of science, and his forward opens by conceding the professional cost: 'It is not looked on highly in certain scientific circles to be preoccupied with phenomena that are deemed to come under the heading of popular mythology', and drawing the analogy to stones falling from the sky - meteorites - which science rejected for centuries before accepting. That analogy is picked up in the report's own conclusion.

people.label: Senador Eduardo Girão
people.sub: Brazilian Senator for Ceará; led the 2022 Brazilian Senate UAP hearing
people.narrative: Eduardo Girão, a Brazilian Senator representing the coastal state of Ceará, led a Brazilian Senate hearing on unidentified aerial phenomena in 2022 - the first legislative engagement with the question in Brazil since the Air Force transferred its files to the National Archives. In January 2026 he travelled to Washington in a private capacity, not representing the Brazilian Senate, to meet members of the United States Congress and to attend the National Press Club press conference on the thirtieth anniversary of the Varginha events. He spoke from the podium commending the three Brazilian witnesses for their courage. During a break he met Representative Eric Burlison of Missouri for the first time; Burlison asked whether he could obtain videos or other material evidence, and Girão answered 'I'm going to try'. The two discussed a joint Brazilian-American effort to acquire tangible evidence. He is the point of contact through which the Brazilian legislature and the United States Congress could formalise a bilateral evidence-seeking arrangement, and his movement is worth watching.

people.label: Richard J. Genik II
people.sub: Wayne State University School of Medicine; author of three DIRDs including 'Cognitive Limits on Simultaneous Control of Multiple Unmanned Spacecraft' (DIA-08-1101-001)
people.narrative:
Richard Genik wrote three of the thirty-eight DIRDs, more than anyone except Eric Davis, and all three are human-factors papers rather than physics papers. The DIA list credits him with "Technological Applications to Controlling External Devices in the Absence of Limb-Operated Interfaces" (item 20, released as "Technological Approaches to..."), "Cognitive Limits on Simultaneous Control of Multiple Unmanned Spacecraft" (item 28), and "Quantum Computing and Utilizing Organic Molecules in Automation Technology" (item 33). His affiliation on the list is Wayne State University, which is where the human-effects strand of AAWSAP concentrated.

That concentration is the reason he matters to this board. Wayne State is also the institution the DIA list gives for Christopher "Kit" Green, author of the field-effects-on-biological-tissues DIRD. Two of the thirty-eight papers, and three counting Genik's second and third, were written inside one medical school, and the human-effects line of AAWSAP inquiry runs through it. He directs Wayne State's Emergent Technology Research Division. people.label: Mark Skidmore
people.sub: Morris Chair in State and Local Government Finance and Policy, Professor of Economics, Michigan State University
people.narrative: Mark Skidmore holds the Morris Chair in State and Local Government Finance and Policy at Michigan State University, where he is a Professor of Economics working in public finance, regional economics and the economics of natural disasters. In 2017, after hearing Catherine Austin Fitts assert that the Department of Housing and Urban Development had recorded $6.5 billion in undocumented adjustments, and initially assuming she had misspoken, Skidmore set his students to compiling the unsupported adjustment figures that federal Inspectors General and the Government Accountability Office had themselves published. The exercise ran from fiscal year 1998 to fiscal year 2015 and produced a summary report, co-authored with Fitts and dated September 2017, arriving at roughly $21 trillion in unsupported journal voucher adjustments at the Department of Defense and roughly $350 billion at HUD. He then co-wrote three Forbes columns with the Boston University economist Laurence Kotlikoff - December 2017, July 2018 and January 2019 - putting the number in front of a financial-markets readership. Skidmore's own methodological caution is the most valuable thing about him for this board: the report states plainly that the public Inspector General reports 'only provide summary information; thus it is impossible for us to conduct a detailed assessment of the nature of these unsupported adjustments and errors', and that data could not be recovered for several years in the series. He has never claimed that $21 trillion is missing money, and the popular restatement of his work in those terms is the single most common way the black-budget argument gets destroyed in public. Used correctly - as an eighteen-year aggregate index of documentation failure at two cabinet departments, drawn entirely from the government's own audit reports - his work is the quantitative backbone of the argument that the federal ledger cannot answer the question this board asks.

Three months after that interview he was found dead at his home, apparently having hanged himself with the belt of his bathrobe. He is the closest thing the Brazilian record has to a custody-adjacent officer who spoke and then died, and the sequence - operation, official denial, twenty years of silence, interview, death - is the reason the case has never settled.

people.label: Wilbert Brockhouse Smith
people.sub: Senior Radio Engineer, Canadian Department of Transport; head of Project Magnet 1950-1962
people.narrative: Wilbert Brockhouse Smith (1910 - 27 December 1962) is the earliest named government official anywhere on record to have been told, and to have written down, that the American flying saucer question was classified above the hydrogen bomb and was being run by Vannevar Bush. Smith joined the Canadian Department of Transport in 1939, built Canada's far north ionospheric monitoring system in 1947, and was Canada's chief delegate to the North American Regional Broadcasting Agreement conferences of 1949 and 1950; by 1952 he was Senior Radio Engineer of the DOT's Broadcast and Measurements section, and in 1957 became Superintendent of Radio Regulations Engineering. At the 1950 NARBA conference in Washington he made enquiries of the American scientist Dr Robert Sarbacher and came away with four assertions which he set down in a memorandum, 'Geo-Magnetics', addressed to the Controller of Telecommunications and dated 21 November 1950: that the matter was the most highly classified subject in the United States government, rating higher even than the H-bomb; that flying saucers exist; that their modus operandi was unknown but that a concentrated effort was being made by a small group headed by Doctor Vannevar Bush; and that the entire matter was considered by US authorities to be of tremendous significance. That memorandum was classified Top Secret and was not downgraded to Confidential until 1969. Library and Archives Canada quotes the same memorandum in its own online exhibition: 'the existence of a different technology is borne out by the investigations which are being carried on at the present time in relation to flying saucers ... I feel that the correlation between our basic theory and the available information on saucers checks too closely to be mere coincidence.' The memorandum was the successful request that produced Project Magnet.

people.label: Dr Mona Nemer

people.narrative: As Chief Science Advisor of Canada, Mona Nemer's office initiated and published the Sky Canada Project, the first Canadian federal review of UAP reporting since the National Research Council stopped collecting reports in 1995. A preliminary report appeared in January 2025 and the full report, 'Management of Public Reporting of Unidentified Aerial Phenomena in Canada', in June 2025, running to fifty-nine pages. The report is careful about what it is not - it disclaims any intention to prove or disprove extraterrestrial life or visitors, or to make the Office the point of contact for Canadians reporting sightings - and it is blunt about what it found. Canadians report an estimated 600 to 1,000 UAP sightings a year; a commissioned Earnscliffe Strategies survey found one in four Canadians say they have witnessed a UAP, only ten per cent reported it, and forty per cent would not know whom to contact. Federal departments receive reports but mostly do not compile them, so the government cannot even state how many it receives. The report's recommendations are structural: identify a lead department, establish a dedicated service that collects testimony, investigates and publishes its analyses, get Transport Canada and NAV CANADA to encourage pilots and controllers to report without stigma, open the data, and establish partnerships with AARO and NASA in the United States, GEIPAN in France and SEFAA in Chile. It is the clearest statement by any allied government that the American, French and Chilean models are the ones worth copying.

people.label: Leonard H. Stringfield
people.sub: Founder, CRIFO; MUFON director of public relations; author, UFO Crash/Retrieval Status Reports I-VII
people.narrative: Leonard H. Stringfield (1920-1994) is the origin point of the crash-retrieval literature as a body of work rather than a rumour. A former Army Air Forces intelligence officer in the Pacific in World War II, he founded CRIFO (Civilian Research, Interplanetary Flying Objects) in Cincinnati in the 1950s and served 1967-1969 as an Early Warning Coordinator feeding sighting reports to the Condon Committee, which put him inside the official investigative loop before he turned on it. After references to crashes and recovered bodies in his 1977 Doubleday book 'Situation Red, The UFO Siege' produced an unexpected flow of new informants, he delivered 'Retrievals of the Third Kind: A Case Study of Alleged UFOs and Occupants in Military Custody' at the ninth annual MUFON Symposium in Dayton, Ohio, on 29 July 1978. That paper opened the modern retrieval literature and he then produced six further Status Reports between January 1980 and February 1994, each a numbered, dated, case-coded compilation of testimony from sources he anonymised behind letter-number codes. His method is the load-bearing weakness and the load-bearing strength of the whole field: he protected sources absolutely, which is why they talked to him, and which is also why almost nothing he published can be independently audited. Stringfield himself said so, opening Status Report IV with a section titled 'The Burden of Proof' in which he wrote that 'we, in the domain of public research, do not have that exalted proof' and that affidavits, leaked documents and photographs do not constitute proof. He worked with the Fund for UFO Research, MUFON, CUFOS and the Mid-Ohio Research Associates, and Richard Hall edited Status Report VI. He died of lung cancer on 18 December 1994, ten months after the last report.

people.label: Grady L. 'Barney' Barnett
people.sub: Soil Conservation Service engineer; original claimed Plains of San Agustin eyewitness
people.narrative: Grady L. 'Barney' Barnett was a soil conservation engineer who travelled widely in New Mexico and who, according to friends, described coming upon a crashed disc and small bodies in open country, with an archaeological field party present, before military personnel arrived and cleared everyone out. Barnett died in 1969, years before anyone thought to record him, and every version of his account reaching the literature is second-hand, given by Vern Maltais and Alice Knight decades later - Knight on camera saying flatly, 'I don't recall the date.' The account entered the record through Berlitz and Moore's 'The Roswell Incident' (1980) and became the load-bearing support for a second, separate 1947 crash on the Plains of San Agustin, 175 miles northwest of Roswell. The Air Force's 1997 report offers a specific and testable alternative: that Maltais and Knight, thirty-plus years on, confused the Plains of San Agustin with San Agustin Pass or San Agustin Peak in the San Agustin Mountains, immediately outside White Sands Missile Range and the Jornada Test Range, where numerous anthropomorphic dummy balloon flights terminated and were recovered by military teams. Barnett is the clearest case in the whole domain of an account that cannot be graded above tier 3 by construction: the only first-hand witness died before being interviewed.

people.label: Frank Scully
people.sub: Variety columnist; author, 'Behind the Flying Saucers' (1950)
people.narrative: Francis Joseph Xavier Scully (28 April 1892 - 23 June 1964), a Variety columnist and humorist, wrote the first crashed-saucer book. Two 1949 Variety columns and then 'Behind the Flying Saucers' (Henry Holt, 1950) told readers that in March 1948 a 99-foot disc containing sixteen small humanoid bodies had come down in Hart Canyon twelve miles northeast of Aztec, New Mexico, had been taken by the military for secret research, ran on magnetic principles, came from Venus, and had every dimension divisible by nine. Scully's named sources were Silas M. Newton and a scientist he described as having 'more degrees than a thermometer' - later identified as Leo A. Gebauer. The book was a bestseller and it set the template: crash, bodies, immediate military cordon, exotic material, total official silence. San Francisco Chronicle reporter J. P. Cahn published exposures in True magazine in 1952 and 1956 showing Newton and Gebauer were confidence men selling 'doodlebug' oil-finding devices they claimed were built on recovered alien technology; a metal sample they supplied Cahn was ordinary aluminium; and in 1953 both were convicted of fraud after millionaire Herman Flader pressed charges. Scully is on this board as the origin of the crash-retrieval genre and as the reason the genre carried a fraud provenance from its first page - a provenance that Leonard Stringfield, Ryan Wood and the Aztec revivalists have each had to argue around rather than through.

The book is the direct methodological descendant of Stringfield's Status Reports and of Kevin Randle's 'A History of UFO Crashes', but where Stringfield presented anonymised narratives and Randle presented case essays, Wood presented rows in a table with a scoring column - which is what makes it usable and what makes it attackable. Wood also co-runs The Majestic Documents archive with his father Robert M. Wood and organises the annual UFO Crash Retrieval Conference series, which functioned through the 2000s as the field's clearing house for new retrieval claims. For this board, 'Majic Eyes Only' is best treated as the field's index rather than as its evidence: it is where you go to find out that a claim exists and who first made it, not to find out whether it is true.

people.narrative: Richard M. Dolan is the field's historian rather than its investigator, and that distinction is the point. Trained in history - he studied at Alfred University and Oxford and was a Rhodes Scholar finalist, with graduate work at the University of Rochester on Cold War strategy and the national security state - he wrote 'UFOs and the National Security State: Chronology of a Cover-Up, 1941-1973' (2002) and 'UFOs and the National Security State: The Cover-Up Exposed, 1973-1991' (2009). Dolan coined and popularised the 'breakaway civilisation' formulation for a technologically self-sustaining compartment operating outside public accountability. He hosts The Richard Dolan Show, has published on the Wilson-Davis memorandum and on the 2020-2023 disclosure sequence, and is one of the small number of researchers whose framing survived the transition from the 1990s literature to the post-2017 congressional era intact - because it was built on the secrecy architecture, which is documented, rather than on witness testimony, which is not.

people.label: Col. Richard L. Weaver
people.sub: Director, Security and Special Program Oversight, Office of the Secretary of the Air Force
people.narrative: Col. Richard L. Weaver ran the Air Force's official answer to Roswell, and his job title is the most interesting fact about him. He was Director of Security and Special Program Oversight in the Office of the Secretary of the Air Force - that is, the officer responsible for oversight of Air Force special access programmes - and it was that office, not a historical or public affairs office, that the Secretary tasked to respond to the General Accounting Office inquiry initiated by Rep. Steven H. Schiff. Weaver and 1st Lt. James McAndrew produced the July 1994 report to the Secretary of the Air Force, published in 1995 by the Government Printing Office as 'The Roswell Report: Fact Versus Fiction in the New Mexico Desert'. Its conclusion was Project Mogul: the classified balloon-borne acoustic programme flown from Alamogordo Army Air Field to detect Soviet nuclear tests, whose flight from 4 June 1947 was lost within seventeen miles of the Foster ranch. Weaver's report also states something operationally significant that is rarely quoted: at the express written direction of the Secretary of the Air Force, former and retired Air Force members and civilian contract scientists were released from any nondisclosure obligations they might have entered into on the relevant past classified activities, so that they could speak freely. This board records Weaver as an oversight-cluster node with A=3 not because he asserts access to a recovery programme - he denies one exists - but because the Secretary routed the inquiry to the SAP oversight directorate, which is a fact about where the Air Force believed the answer would have to be looked for.

people.label: Stan Gordon
people.sub: Pennsylvania field researcher; principal investigator of the 1965 Kecksburg incident
people.narrative: Stan Gordon is the field researcher who kept Kecksburg alive for four decades until it reached a federal courtroom. A western Pennsylvania investigator who was a teenager in Greensburg when the fireball came down on 9 December 1965, he spent the following decades locating and interviewing local witnesses - residents who described a military and state police cordon thrown around the woods, a flatbed truck leaving the site carrying something acorn-shaped and about the size of a Volkswagen, and men in unmarked vehicles - while the official position remained that searchers found absolutely nothing. His witness pool supplied the 1990 Unsolved Mysteries episode, the 2003 Sci Fi Channel documentary 'The New Roswell: Kecksburg Exposed', and, indirectly, the evidentiary basis for Leslie Kean's 2003 FOIA request and lawsuit against NASA. Gordon's work is the standard illustration of the retrieval literature's characteristic profile: a large, internally consistent body of local first-hand testimony describing a recovery operation, and no document. The Kean litigation was the attempt to close that gap by force of law, and it produced a federal finding that NASA's searches were inadequate and sworn testimony that two boxes of records from the period were missing - not the object, but the paper trail of its absence.
