people.label: Friedwardt Winterberg
people.sub: Theoretical physicist, Research Professor, University of Nevada, Reno; author of two AAWSAP DIRDs
people.narrative:
Friedwardt Winterberg is a German-American theoretical physicist and research professor at the University of Nevada, Reno, with a long publication record spanning general relativity, Planck-scale physics, nuclear fusion and plasma physics. He appears twice on the DIA list of AATIP/AAWSAP products transmitted to the Senate Armed Services Committee: as author of item 2, 'Advanced Nuclear Propulsion for Manned Deep Space Missions', and as author of 'Negative Mass Propulsion', both with the affiliation University of Nevada, Reno.

His geographic placement matters to the shape of the programme. AAWSAP funding was directed by Senator Harry Reid toward a Nevada constituent, and the DIRD author list carries an unusually heavy Nevada concentration — Winterberg at UNR, and separate deliverables credited to the University of Nevada, Las Vegas. Winterberg is the only author on the list credited with two Nevada-institution papers, and both of his are propulsion physics rather than the anomalous-phenomena material that dominates the EarthTech contributions.

'Negative Mass Propulsion' carries DIA document number DIA-08-1101-023, published 3 January 2011 with an Intelligence Cut-Off Date of 30 August 2010, in the 'Defense Futures' series, and its cover page identifies it as one of a series of advanced technology reports produced in FY 2010 under the AAWSA Program. The subject is the classic Bondi problem of runaway motion between positive and negative gravitational mass, considered as a propulsion concept: a vehicle accelerating without expelling reaction mass. Winterberg published closely related work in the peer-reviewed literature, which distinguishes his DIRD from several others on the list that have no independent scholarly footprint. The document was released by DIA under FOIA and posted to the DIA FOIA Electronic Reading Room; the author name is redacted on the released cover page under (b)(6), so the attribution rests on the congressional list rather than on the document itself.

people.label: Wil McCarthy
people.sub: Engineer and science-fiction novelist; President, The Programmable Matter Corporation, Lakewood, Colorado
people.narrative:
Wil McCarthy is the least conventional author in this batch and the one whose selection says the most about how AAWSAP sourced its expertise. He is an aerospace engineer and patent agent who began as a flight controller on Lockheed Martin space launch systems, moved to Omnitech Robotics as an engineering manager, served as chief technology officer of the aerospace research laboratory Galileo Shipyards, and is president of The Programmable Matter Corporation in Lakewood, Colorado. He is simultaneously a working science-fiction novelist, and it was in fiction that he first popularised the idea he was later paid by the Defense Intelligence Agency to survey. His "Queendom of Sol" novels, notably The Wellstone, are built around a substance he called wellstone: a programmable material whose effective atoms can be reconfigured on command so that a bounded but effectively unlimited range of material properties can be summoned or dismissed at will. He set the same idea out for a general readership in the non-fiction book Hacking Matter.

AAWSAP's statement of work included materials, structures and signature reduction. Programmable matter, quantum dots and reconfigurable metamaterial surfaces sit squarely in that space, and the pool of people who had written a book-length synthesis of the field in 2009 was tiny. McCarthy had both the engineering background to write to a defence-warning audience and a commercial vehicle, The Programmable Matter Corporation, through which the work could be contracted. His DIRD, "Aerospace Applications of Programmable Matter", is a twenty-page survey and carries the earliest publication date of the eight documents in this batch, 14 December 2009. He has no documented UAP-programme role beyond authorship of this single deliverable.

people.label: Claudio Maccone
people.sub: Italian SETI astronomer and mathematician; International Academy of Astronautics (Chair, SETI Permanent Committee; Director for Scientific Space Exploration). 1948-2025
people.narrative:
Claudio Maccone was an Italian space scientist, SETI astronomer and mathematician, and the only DIRD author in this batch whose deliverable is about the prevalence of extraterrestrial civilisations rather than about hardware. His central contribution, and the subject of his DIRD, was the Statistical Drake Equation: he replaced the seven fixed factors of Frank Drake's 1961 formula with seven positive random variables and showed that, by the central limit theorem applied multiplicatively, the resulting number of communicating civilisations must follow a lognormal distribution. That turns the Drake Equation from a rhetorical device into something with an error bar, and lets a mean and variance be propagated rather than a single indefensible point estimate. He later extended the machinery into what he called Evo-SETI, applying the same lognormal statistics to the evolution of life on Earth.

He was appointed Director for Scientific Space Exploration by the International Academy of Astronautics in Paris in 2010, and from 2012 chaired the IAA's SETI Permanent Committee. He died in 2025.

His presence on the AAWSAP author list is the clearest evidence that the contract's remit was not confined to foreign adversary hardware. A programme chartered to assess far-term aerospace threats commissioned a paper on how many technological civilisations the galaxy may hold, which only makes sense if the sponsor considered non-terrestrial technology a live category of "advanced aerospace threat". Maccone had also previously co-authored with Hal Puthoff and Eric Davis on the Levi-Civita effect in the polarizable-vacuum representation of general relativity, a paper cited in Puthoff's own DIRD, which places him inside the same small citation network as the EarthTech authors.

people.label: Vincent L. Teofilo
people.sub: Physicist; 28 years at Lockheed Martin Space Systems; DIRD author on aneutronic fusion propulsion. 1944-2026
people.narrative:
Vincent Louis Teofilo was a career industrial physicist whose path ran through almost every institution that has ever tried to build a fusion reactor in the United States. He took a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering at Manhattan College and a master's in nuclear engineering and a PhD in physics at New York University. He taught at Princeton and operated the university's nuclear reactor, then worked on fusion reactor development at Westinghouse, Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, Physics International and Bechtel. He then spent twenty-eight years at Lockheed Martin Space Systems, contributing to programmes including the Hubble Space Telescope and the Space-Based Infrared System. He died on 10 January 2026 at the age of 81.

That combination, deep fusion plasma physics plus long service inside a prime contractor's space division, is exactly the profile AAWSAP needed for a propulsion deliverable that had to be credible to a defence-warning audience rather than to a physics journal. Three of the 38 DIRDs went to Lockheed Martin staff, Teofilo on aneutronic fusion, S. Macheret on MHD air-breathing propulsion and J. Golightly on ultracapacitors, which makes Lockheed Martin the single most heavily represented corporate institution on the DIRD author list.

Teofilo's DIRD is not a physics monograph. It runs from confinement schemes through Hall thrusters to a roadmap figure, surveys the funding levels of privately backed fusion start-ups, and closes by arguing that the physicists who pioneered the reactor technology must now work alongside the space systems companies. It reads as an industrial technology-transition assessment, which is what a Lockheed Martin space-systems physicist would be expected to produce. He is also recorded as a co-author of "Review of Experimental Concepts for Studying the Quantum Vacuum Field", placing him adjacent to the EarthTech vacuum-energy literature.

people.label: William Culbreth
people.sub: Professor of Mechanical/Nuclear Engineering (ret.), University of Nevada, Las Vegas; founder of the UNLV Nuclear Engineering Lab; author of two AAWSAP DIRDs
people.narrative:
William Culbreth is a now-retired professor of mechanical engineering at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, and the founder of the UNLV Nuclear Engineering Lab, a facility since led by Alexander Barzilov and embedded in UNLV's national-security engineering research area. UNLV sits about sixty-five miles from the Nevada National Security Site, and Culbreth's academic career was built on that adjacency: reactor physics, radiation detection and transport, and the nuclear engineering pipeline that feeds the Department of Energy's Nevada operations.

The geography matters for how he ended up on a DIA contract. AAWSAP was executed by Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies out of Las Vegas, and BAASS drew on subcontracted subject-matter experts. Culbreth was a credentialed nuclear engineer at the city's own research university, and he is credited on the DIA list with two of the 38 deliverables, more than any author outside EarthTech: item 29, "Detection and High Resolution Tracking of Vehicles at Hypersonic Velocities", and item 30, "Aneutronic Fusion Propulsion II". The pairing is telling. One paper is about seeing something moving very fast, the other about what might make it move, which are the two halves of the question AAWSAP was chartered to ask.

The released aneutronic paper attributed to him reads like a nuclear engineering course text extended into speculation: chapters on fission rocket history at the Nevada Test Site and Project Rover, radiation shielding, muon-catalysed and cavitation fusion, antimatter annihilation, and an appendix containing a relativistic rocket worksheet. It cites standard nuclear engineering textbooks rather than primary plasma-physics literature. Culbreth has no documented role in AAWSAP's UAP casework or in the paranormal lines of effort later described by AARO.

people.label: George H. Miley
people.sub: Nuclear/plasma engineer, University of Illinois; author, DIRD 'Inertial Electrostatic Confinement Fusion' (DIA-08-1003-006)
people.narrative: Miley is the author the DIA list places first: entry 1 on both the July 2018 KLAS list and the 9 January 2018 letter to the Senate Armed Services Committee reads 'Inertial Electrostatics Confinement Fusion, Dr George Miley, Univ. of Illinois.' The released DIRD carries DIA document number DIA-08-1003-006, publication date 10 March 2010 and an Intelligence Cut-Off Date of 1 December 2009. At 72 pages it is the longest of the thirty-seven released deliverables. Miley is a genuine subject-matter figure rather than a fringe recruit: he is the co-author, with S. Krupakar Murali, of the Springer monograph 'Inertial Electrostatic Confinement (IEC) Fusion: Fundamentals and Applications', and IEC has been his declared research line for decades. That matters for how the DIRD set should be read. Hal Puthoff's own account of the commissioning, given at the Society for Scientific Exploration conference in June 2018, is that he acted as a surrogate buyer precisely so that DIA would not have to expose why it wanted the answers: 'it's difficult for contractors to obtain expert opinions on advanced technologies because they would expose why they are interested. So, I acted as a surrogate.' Miley is what that procurement posture produces at the credible end - an established university engineer asked, without being told the reason, where his own compact-fusion field would stand by 2050. IEC fusion is one of the few AAWSAP topics with a plausible aerospace power-source reading rather than an exotic-physics one: a compact, non-tokamak fusion device is the sort of thing that would be needed if a small craft were producing the observed energy budget. people.label: Robert M. L. Baker, Jr.
people.sub: GravWave LLC; author, DIRD 'High-Frequency Gravitational Wave Communications' (DIA-08-1004-005) - commissioned after a JASON review rejected the underlying physics
people.narrative: Baker is the single most consequential author in this batch, not for what his DIRD says but for what its existence demonstrates about AAWSAP's quality control. Entry 9 on the DIA list to the Senate Armed Services Committee reads 'High Frequency Gravitational Wave Communications, Dr Robert Baker, GravWave.' The released document carries DIA-08-1004-005, publication date 6 April 2010 and an Intelligence Cut-Off Date of 1 December 2009. Baker's company, GravWave LLC, had spent years promoting high-frequency gravitational waves as an enabling technology for communications, surveillance, propulsion and the remote initiation of nuclear events, and Baker had done HFGW work for the Office of the Director of National Intelligence. In 2008 the JASON advisory group - the standing panel of outside scientists convened to adjudicate exactly this class of question for the US government - reviewed that ODNI work and rejected it at the root. As quoted in The War Zone's audit of the AATIP list: 'The proposed applications of the science of HFGW are fundamentally wrong,' and 'No foreign threat in HFGW is credible.' DIA then published Baker's HFGW paper as an official Defense Intelligence Reference Document roughly eighteen months later. That sequence is the finding. It is not that a government programme funded speculative physics - that was the stated purpose of the survey, which asked authors to project to 2050. It is that the programme published, on a JWICS-hosted reference series carrying DIA's imprimatur, a paper on a topic that the government's own senior scientific review body had already assessed as not merely unproven but wrong, and whose threat premise it had already declared not credible. Baker is separately linked into the AAWSAP author network through Eric Davis: the two co-authored a 2005 STAIF paper with R. C. Woods on HFGW radiation patterns and aerospace applications, and Davis himself presented at a DIA and National Security Space Office HFGW working group at MITRE in 2003. The commission was therefore not a blind buy from a stranger.

people.label: Sergey O. Macheret
people.sub: Plasma physicist; senior staff engineer, Lockheed Martin Skunk Works 2006-2014; author, MHD Air Breathing Propulsion DIRD
people.narrative:
Sergey O. Macheret is a Ukrainian-American plasma physicist and aerospace engineer, and he is the single clearest example on the DIRD list of a mainstream, credentialled defence-industry scientist being drawn into the AAWSAP deliverable stream. He took an M.S. in physics from the Moscow Institute of Physics and Technology and a Ph.D. in plasma physics and plasma chemistry from the Kurchatov Institute, emigrated to the United States in 1991, and held research posts at Ohio State and Princeton before joining Lockheed Martin Aeronautics.

The DIA list transmitted to the Senate Armed Services Committee credits him as author of 'Magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) Air Breathing Propulsion and Power for Aerospace Applications' with the affiliation Lockheed Martin. That affiliation is exact for the period: he was a senior staff engineer at Lockheed Martin Skunk Works from 2006 to 2014, which brackets the document's 21 November 2010 publication date and its 20 July 2010 Intelligence Cut-Off Date. He left for Purdue University in 2014 as a professor of aeronautics and astronautics, added a professorship in electrical and computer engineering in 2022, was elected an AIAA Fellow, received the AIAA Plasmadynamics and Lasers Award in 2022, and founded US Plasma Engineering LLC in 2023.

His DIRD is one of three Lockheed Martin products on the DIA list and reads as ordinary hypersonics work rather than fringe physics: MHD control of ionised flow around an air-breathing vehicle, with explicit reference to Soviet work on the Ajax (Ayaks) hypersonic concept associated with the Leninets Design Bureau in St. Petersburg. That is squarely within the stated AAWSAP purpose of assessing foreign advanced aerospace weapon threats out to forty years, and it is the strongest available counterweight to the assumption that the DIRD series was uniformly speculative. Macheret has no public association with UAP research, with Bigelow's organisations, or with the anomalous-physics network that produced the EarthTech deliverables; his presence on the list is best read as a contracted subject-matter survey by a working plasma dynamicist.

people.label: Gerald A. Smith
people.sub: Experimental particle physicist; Professor Emeritus, Penn State; founder, Positronics Research LLC (New Mexico)
people.narrative:
Gerald A. Smith is an experimental high-energy physicist with an unusually deep institutional pedigree who ended his career building antimatter storage hardware for NASA and then selling antimatter propulsion concepts through a small New Mexico company. He is credited on the DIA list of AATIP/AAWSAP products transmitted to the Senate Armed Services Committee as author of 'Positron Aerospace Propulsion', affiliation Positronics Research.

His background: B.A. in physics from Miami University (Ohio) in 1957, M.S. (1958) and Ph.D. (1961) in physics from Yale, a second-generation graduate student of Enrico Fermi, and post-doctoral years from 1961 to 1966 as an assistant professor under Luis Alvarez at Berkeley. He built a high-energy physics programme at Michigan State from 1968, served as Associate Laboratory Director for High Energy Physics at Argonne in 1978, and in 1983 became Director of the Laboratory for Elementary Particle Science and Physics Department Head at Penn State. He was spokesperson for international collaborations at Brookhaven, CERN, Fermilab and SLAC, has more than 300 refereed publications, and is a Fellow of the American Physical Society. At Penn State he oversaw the ICAN-II and AIMStar antimatter-catalysed designs and the development of two antiproton traps: the Mark I portable trap for JPL and the High Performance Antimatter Trap (HiPAT) for NASA Marshall. He became Professor Emeritus in 2000 and founded Positronics Research LLC in 2001.

His DIRD is therefore a case where AAWSAP bought a survey from a genuine domain authority, and it aligns with work he was already doing publicly: his positron-propelled vehicle concept was a NASA Institute for Advanced Concepts Phase I study and was written up by NASA in 2006. The AAWSAP deliverable carries DIA document number DIA-08-1003-002, published 2 March 2010 with an ICOD of 1 December 2009, in the 'Acquisition Threat Support' series. It is one of the DIRDs released by DIA in redacted form; the author line on the released cover page is blanked.

people.label: James Wells
people.sub: Author, Pulsed High-Power Microwave Source Technology DIRD; affiliation given as J W Enterprises on the DIA list
people.narrative:
James Wells is credited on the DIA list of AATIP/AAWSAP products transmitted to the Senate Armed Services Committee as author of 'Pulsed High-Power Microwave Technology'. He is one of the least publicly traceable names on the list, and he is also the one clear instance in this batch where the two circulating versions of the DIRD roster disagree on affiliation.

The DIA list released to the Federation of American Scientists in January 2019 gives his affiliation as 'J W Enterprises'. The earlier list published by George Knapp and Matt Adams of KLAS-TV on 25 July 2018 — a near-complete roster whose authenticity was confirmed by former programme manager Luis Elizondo, but whose source was never disclosed — gives his affiliation as 'Northrop Grumman'. The DIA list is the authoritative document because it was prepared by the agency and transmitted to Congress; 'J W Enterprises' is therefore recorded here as the affiliation of record, with the Northrop Grumman variant preserved as a discrepancy rather than discarded. The two are not necessarily contradictory in substance — a named consultancy and a prime contractor could both be true of the same person at different points — but nothing sourced resolves it, and the difference should not be smoothed over.

Beyond the list entry itself, no verified biography, institutional page or publication record has been located for him, and the released DIRD does not help: the author line on the cover page is redacted under (b)(6). What is firmly established is the document. 'Pulsed High-Power Microwave Source Technology' carries DIA document number DIA-08-0912-005, published 28 January 2010 with an Intelligence Cut-Off Date of 1 December 2009, in the 'Acquisition Threat Support' series. It runs 37 pages and was released by DIA in redacted form. Its subject — directed-energy source hardware — is among the most conventionally military topics in the entire series.

people.label: Paul A. Czysz
people.sub: Hypersonics engineer; President, HyperTech Concepts LLC; Professor Emeritus of Aerospace Engineering, Saint Louis University
people.narrative:
Paul Czysz is the author the DIA list names for "Space Access," the AAWSAP survey of how the United States has reached orbit and how it might do so differently. He is the least exotic figure in the DIRD author set and that is precisely what makes him useful. Czysz was a McDonnell Douglas hypersonics man, named a McDonnell Douglas Fellow in 1986 for work on hypersonic aircraft concepts, and served as chief scientist on the National Aerospace Plane effort. He left industry for Saint Louis University, held the Oliver L. Parks Endowed Chair in the Department of Aerospace and Mechanical Engineering at Parks College, and ran his own consultancy, HyperTech Concepts LLC, which is the affiliation the DIA letter records against his name.

His DIRD, DIA-08-1001-006, is dated March 2010 with an Intelligence Cut-Off Date of 1 December 2009, and it sits in the Acquisition Threat Support series. Its contents are conventional aerospace engineering: hypersonic configuration concepts, thermodynamics and materials, rocket propulsion, launch options, operational cost of transatmospheric vehicles, landing ellipses for hypersonic gliders. There is no metric engineering in it and no anomalous physics. Its presence in the set matters for that reason. The thirty-eight DIRDs are routinely described as a wormhole-and-warp-drive catalogue; roughly half of them are ordinary technology forecasting of the kind a defence warning office commissions every year, and Czysz's paper is the clearest example. He is a control on the claim that AAWSAP was uniformly speculative.

Czysz died in 2013, before the December 2017 disclosure of AATIP and well before the DIRDs surfaced in bulk in the 2022 FOIA release. He therefore never commented publicly on the programme, was never interviewed about it, and left no account of who commissioned the paper or what the tasking said. His custody proximity is nil and his access level was that of an unclassified subject-matter subcontractor. He is on the board as an author node, not as a witness.

people.sub: Professor Emeritus of Physics, University of Washington; author of the transactional interpretation of quantum mechanics
people.narrative:
The DIA list credits "Space-Communication Implications of Quantum Entanglement and Nonlocality" to Dr J Cramer, University of Washington. Cramer is a mainstream experimental nuclear physicist at the University of Washington who is known outside his field for the transactional interpretation of quantum mechanics, an advanced-and-retarded-wave reading of the quantum formalism that he has developed since the 1980s, and for a long-running attempt to test whether nonlocal correlations could be made to carry a signal.

That is exactly the question AAWSAP bought. The DIRD, DIA-08-1003-016, is dated 30 March 2010 with an Intelligence Cut-Off Date of 1 December 2009, in the Acquisition Threat Support series. The KLAS-TV version of the list titles it "Quantum Entanglement Communication," which states the tasking plainly: could entanglement be used as a communications channel, and if so what would that mean for space communication. The orthodox answer is that it cannot, because the no-communication theorem forbids it, and a defence warning office commissioning a survey on the point from the physicist most publicly associated with probing that boundary is a legible act rather than a strange one.

Cramer is the cleanest example in this batch of an AAWSAP author with an entirely conventional academic standing and no involvement in the UAP question before or after. He holds no documented special access, has no proximity to any custody claim, and has not to date been drawn into the disclosure argument that the DIRDs became the paper trail for. His node exists to hold the document to a real person and to record that the quantum-communications strand of AAWSAP was contracted to a named university physicist rather than to the programme's inner circle of consultants.

people.label: Richard K. Obousy
people.sub: Theoretical physicist; principal, Obousy Consultants; president and founder, Icarus Interstellar
people.narrative:
Richard Obousy is the correction this batch exists to make. "Warp Drive, Dark Energy, and the Manipulation of Extra Dimensions" is the most cited and most reproduced of the thirty-eight DIRDs and is almost universally attributed in press coverage to Eric Davis. The DIA letter of 9 January 2018 does not say that. It lists item 19 as "Warp Drive, Dark Energy and the Manipulation of Extra Dimensions, Dr R Obousy, Obousy Consultants." Obousy is the author of record on the government's own list. EarthTech International's published citation list gives the paper as Obousy, R. K. and Davis, E. W. (2010), with Obousy first named, which resolves the two records rather than contradicting them: it is a co-authored paper on which DIA recorded the lead author and the popular account recorded the famous one.

The distinction is not cosmetic. The warp-drive DIRD is routinely used to argue that a small circle of consultants wrote the programme's most exotic output for itself. On the DIA record the lead author is an outside theorist trading as a one-man consultancy, and the paper's substance, a Casimir-energy and extra-dimensional treatment of the Alcubierre metric, tracks Obousy's own published work on dark energy and compactified extra dimensions rather than Davis's.

Obousy went on to found and lead Icarus Interstellar, the volunteer successor organisation to Project Daedalus that pursued interstellar flight study, where he appears on the team alongside Eric Davis and Friedwardt Winterberg, the DIA-listed author of the negative-mass and advanced-nuclear-propulsion DIRDs. That overlap is itself a finding: the exotic-propulsion half of the DIRD author set was drawn from an existing interstellar-studies community that predates AAWSAP and outlived it.

The document is DIA-08-1004-001, dated 2 April 2010 with an Intelligence Cut-Off Date of 1 December 2009, in the Acquisition Threat Support series. It was one of the first two DIRDs to reach the public internet, appearing in December 2017 and later confirmed genuine by Davis in correspondence with the researcher Isaac Koi.

people.label: J. Albertine
people.sub: Directed Technologies; high-energy laser physicist, M.S.; probably John R. Albertine, formerly of the US Navy High Energy Laser Program Office
people.narrative:
The DIA list names "J Albertine, M.S., Directed Technologies" as the author of the high-energy laser weapons DIRD, and it names him twice. Items 37 and 38 of the January 2018 attachment are the same paper in two versions, one unclassified and one formerly classified SECRET//NOFORN. That resolves what had been an open question in the public record: the thirty-eighth DIRD was not a missing exotic paper, it was the classified twin of the laser survey. Albertine is therefore the only author in the thirty-eight known to have produced a classified deliverable under AAWSAP, which is why his access score sits above the rest of the subject-matter author set.

The identification of "J Albertine" with John R. Albertine is a reasoned inference rather than a documented match and is recorded here as such. John R. Albertine holds a BS in physics from Rose Polytechnic Institute and a master's degree in applied physics from Johns Hopkins, which matches the "M.S." the DIA list appends to the name. He was a senior staff physicist in the Space Division of the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, then from 1976 to 1997 worked in the US Navy's High Energy Laser Program Office directing Navy HEL programmes, retiring from civil service in 1997 and consulting thereafter for OSD, the Air Force, ONR, the Navy HEL programme office and Penn State in the directed-energy field. He guest-edited the high-energy laser systems and components special section of Optical Engineering in 2012. No public source consulted here links him by name to Directed Technologies or to AAWSAP, and that gap is recorded in unresolved[].

The unclassified version, DIA-08-1003-019, is dated 31 March 2010 with an Intelligence Cut-Off Date of 1 December 2009, in the Acquisition Threat Support series. It is the one straightforwardly operational weapons paper in the set, and it is the one the programme classified.

people.label: J. Golightly
people.sub: Lockheed Martin; author of record for the AAWSAP ultracapacitors DIRD. Given name not established in any source consulted.
people.narrative:
The DIA letter of 9 January 2018 gives item 35 as "Ultracapacitors as Energy and Power Storage Devices, Dr J Golightly, Lockheed Martin." That is the entirety of what the government record says about this author, and nothing further was established here. No public biography, publication list or institutional page consulted resolves the initial to a given name. The node is deliberately labelled with the initial rather than a guess, because the whole point of this exercise is that a wrong attribution is worse than an unwired document.

What the affiliation does establish is worth recording. Lockheed Martin is the DIA-listed employer for three of the thirty-eight DIRDs: this ultracapacitors paper, "Aneutronic Fusion Propulsion" by Dr V Teofilo, and "Magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) Air Breathing Propulsion and Power for Aerospace Applications" by Dr S Macheret. Eric Davis said in a June 2018 interview that the advanced nuclear fusion for aerospace propulsion work was undertaken by colleagues at Lockheed Martin, which matches the list. AAWSAP did not only buy papers from universities and one-man consultancies; it bought three from a prime contractor, and Lockheed Martin is a board node on other grounds entirely. The ultracapacitors DIRD is one of the concrete threads between the DIRD series and the contractor-custody cluster.

The document is DIA-08-1011-005, dated 1 November 2010 with an Intelligence Cut-Off Date of 20 July 2010. It is a late DIRD, from the second wave rather than the FY2009 batch, and its Intelligence Cut-Off Date is correspondingly later than the 1 December 2009 that most of the earlier papers carry. Its subject is unglamorous energy-storage engineering with obvious conventional military application and no anomalous content.

people.narrative: Collins occupies the Senate Appropriations chair, one of the six chairmanships that generate a 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) entitlement. Her presence in the group illustrates why the Gang of Eight comparison misleads: appropriators are inside the waived-SAP circle and outside the covert-action circle, while the party leaders are the reverse. Collins is the money side of the entitlement. A waived special access program still has to be paid for, and the appropriations leadership sees the classified annex material that the authorising committees do not necessarily see in the same form. In 2023 Collins held two of the twelve seats simultaneously - ranking member of the full Appropriations Committee and ranking member of its Defense Subcommittee - which is a recurring feature of the group worth flagging: because the same senator often occupies both the full-committee and subcommittee seat, the twelve statutory seats are frequently filled by fewer than twelve distinct people. In the 118th Congress the Senate side of the 119(e)(2) group comprised only five individuals rather than six for exactly this reason. Collins has no publicly documented UAP-specific record. As with the other holders, the absence is notable rather than exculpatory: the statute gives her sight of waived programme material and gives her no mechanism to disclose it.

people.label: Christopher A. Coons
people.sub: Ranking Member, Defense Subcommittee of the Senate Appropriations Committee (119th Congress, serving August 2026)
people.narrative: Coons is the ranking minority member of the Senate Appropriations Defense Subcommittee and therefore the twelfth-listed of the twelve statutory recipients on the Senate side. His entitlement under 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) is identical in scope to the chairman's: the withheld report information and the Secretary of Defense's justification for the waiver go to chair and ranking jointly, not to the chair alone. The joint character of the notification is a deliberate anti-capture feature of the statute and should be represented on the board as such - a waived-SAP notification cannot lawfully be given to one party's leadership only. What Coons does not have is any statutory right to widen the circle. Nothing in section 119 permits him to brief the rest of his subcommittee, and unlike his counterparts on the intelligence committees under 50 U.S.C. 3093(g), he has no assurance that his non-leadership colleagues will even be told that a limited notification occurred. Coons has no publicly documented UAP-specific record. His subcommittee's jurisdiction, as published by the Senate Appropriations Committee, extends across the Central Intelligence Agency, the National Reconnaissance Office, the National Security Agency, the Defense Intelligence Agency and the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency in addition to the military departments, which makes the Defense Subcommittee seats unusually broad in practice relative to their narrow statutory description.

entities.label: AARO Report on the Historical Record of U.S. Government Involvement with UAP, Volume I
entities.sub: report
entities.desc: Volume I is the government's principal attempt to close the historical question by assertion. Dated February 2024 and released on 8 March 2024 under DOPSR case 2024-0263, it was prepared under Sean Kirkpatrick and rolled out by Acting Director Tim Phillips after Kirkpatrick had left. Its headline finding is that AARO found no empirical evidence for claims that the US government and private companies have been reverse-engineering extraterrestrial technology, and no verifiable evidence of off-world technology in US possession. Its method is the weakness: approximately 30 interviewees, no subpoena power, no compulsion of contractor records, and repeated recourse to the argument that witnesses had misidentified authentic classified programmes unrelated to UAP. It analysed an alleged extraterrestrial spacecraft sample and concluded it was a manufactured terrestrial alloy of magnesium, zinc and bismuth with trace elements. It disclosed Kona Blue. It covered Projects Saucer, Sign, Grudge, Twinkle and Blue Book, AAWSAP, AATIP and the UAPTF. On page 30 it addressed nuclear-adjacent allegations - five former Air Force officers who served at Malmstrom, Ellsworth, Vandenberg and Minot between 1966 and 1977, some reporting UAP near silos and ICBM disruptions, one describing a UAP destroying a dummy-warhead ICBM in flight - and it stated that AARO found 'no NDAs that contain information related to UAP.' That sentence is now the report's most damaging line, because in June 2025 the Department confirmed the Air Force had for decades made personnel sign NDAs over a fake alien-technology programme. Deputy Secretary Hicks never publicly endorsed the report's central findings, and Christopher Mellon noted at the time that its assertions were made at the AARO level and never ratified above it. It explicitly deferred unresolved allegations to Volume II.

entities.label: AARO Historical Record Report, Volume II (unpublished)
entities.sub: report
entities.desc: Volume II is the most consequential unpublished document in this domain. Volume I explicitly deferred to it: it was to cover AARO's interviews and research from 1 November 2023 to 15 April 2024 plus every allegation Volume I left unresolved. In August 2024, Pentagon spokesman Maj. Gen. Pat Ryder said officials continued to conduct their review but had nothing further to announce on timing. In November 2024 the incoming director, Jon Kosloski, told reporters the office would release it 'within months.' In June 2025, when the Wall Street Journal published the Yankee Blue investigation, a DoD spokeswoman said the discovery had not been complete when Volume I went out and that the findings would appear in Volume II, then scheduled for late 2025. It did not appear in late 2025. It has not appeared as of 12 August 2026 - after the FY2025 annual report, after five PURSUE tranches, after the standing up of a UAP Governance Board and a science advisory council. The Department has therefore committed, on the record and through a named spokesperson, to publishing an official finding that the Air Force ran a fictitious alien-technology programme on its own personnel for decades, and has then not published it for over two years. Nothing else in the modern record more cleanly demonstrates what the office is for.

entities.label: All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO)
entities.sub: DoD office established 2022; author of the official AAWSAP history
entities.desc: AARO is the Department of Defense's authoritative office for UAP, established by memorandum of Deputy Secretary of Defense Kathleen Hicks on 15 July 2022 and announced 20 July 2022. The memorandum disestablished the Airborne Object Identification and Management Synchronization Group, directed the Secretary of the Navy to disestablish the UAP Task Force and transfer its data and materials to AARO, and placed AARO under the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security. Congress then codified it in the James M. Inhofe National Defense Authorization Act for FY2023, signed 23 December 2022, with statutory authority and reporting obligations now at 50 U.S.C. 3373 and 3373a. In summer 2023, weeks after David Grusch testified, Hicks pulled the office out of the USD(I&S) chain and made its director report directly to her. Read as containment, AARO's design is the point: a single office with department-wide UAP cognizance, staffed at 'several dozen' personnel, without subpoena authority, without an independent press function, reporting to the deputy head of the department whose special access programmes it would have to penetrate to answer the question it exists to answer. Its outputs are consistent across three directors: annual reports whose resolved cases are always prosaic, whose unresolved cases are always attributed to insufficient sensor data, and whose central sentence never varies - no verifiable evidence of extraterrestrial beings, activity, or technology. Its holdings reached 1,870 total UAP reports as of 30 May 2025. Its one genuine investigative product on the historical question, the Historical Record Report, stopped after Volume I; Volume II - the volume the Department told the Wall Street Journal would contain the Yankee Blue findings - remains unpublished as of August 2026. By 2026 the office had been overtaken by its own department: the PURSUE releases at war.gov/UFO put more primary UAP material into the public record in three months than AARO had in four years.

entities.label: ODNI Preliminary Assessment: Unidentified Aerial Phenomena (25 June 2021)
entities.sub: report
entities.desc: The Preliminary Assessment delivered to Congress on 25 June 2021 under Director of National Intelligence Avril Haines is the founding public document of the modern era. It was mandated by the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence's directive accompanying the FY2021 intelligence authorisation and was drafted on the UAP Task Force's dataset: 144 reports from US government sources between 2004 and 2021, of which the assessment could explain exactly one. It declined to attribute the remainder, sorting possible explanations into airborne clutter, natural atmospheric phenomena, US industry developmental programmes, foreign adversary systems, and a catch-all 'other' bin that it said would require additional scientific advances to characterise. It conceded that in 18 incidents, observers reported unusual movement patterns or flight characteristics, and that some UAP appeared to remain stationary in winds aloft, move against the wind, manoeuvre abruptly, or move at considerable speed without discernible means of propulsion. Its analytic move - that limited and inconsistent data prevents conclusions - became the permanent template for every AARO annual report that followed. Read as containment, the assessment is a masterpiece of bounded honesty: it conceded everything about the phenomenon and nothing about the government's history with it, and it said nothing whatever about recovery, materials or reverse engineering, which were outside its stated scope.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded A on a global pass (rank 102 of 1170, score 62). 14 connections, 1 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C0/A2/D3.

entities.label: AARO FY2023 Consolidated Annual Report on UAP
entities.sub: Published 25 October 2023; 291 new reports; 801 total holdings
entities.desc: The first statutory annual report, published 25 October 2023 covering 31 August 2022 to 30 April 2023. It logged 291 new reports - 274 from the period and 17 from 2019-2022 not previously submitted - bringing AARO's total holdings to 801 as of 30 April 2023. Its analytic posture set the template every subsequent report has followed: only a very small percentage of UAP reports display interesting signatures such as high-speed travel and unknown morphologies, the majority demonstrate ordinary characteristics of readily explainable sources, and a large number of cases remain technically unresolved because of a lack of data. Note what the FY2023 report does not contain: any finding, positive or negative, on extraterrestrial technology. That sentence - the 'no evidence of extraterrestrial beings, activity, or technology' formula - enters the annual reports only with FY2024, in the year after David Grusch testified. The negative finding is not a baseline of the reporting series; it is a response inserted into it.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded B on a global pass (rank 319 of 1170, score 38). 4 connections, 1 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C0/A2/D2.

entities.label: AARO FY2024 Consolidated Annual Report on UAP
entities.sub: Published 14 November 2024; 757 new reports; 1,652 total
entities.desc: The FY2024 report covers 1 May 2023 through 1 June 2024 and was released on 14 November 2024, the day after the House Oversight hearing at which Luis Elizondo and Tim Gallaudet testified and five days before Kosloski appeared before the Senate. It records 757 reports - 485 in-period and 272 backfilled from 2021-2022 - with 118 resolved in-period and 174 more finalised by publication, all to prosaic objects: balloons, birds, unmanned aerial systems. Twenty-one cases were flagged as warranting continued investigation by intelligence and science and technology partners on the basis of reported anomalous characteristics or behaviours. It contains the explicit denial: to date, AARO has discovered no evidence of extraterrestrial beings, activity, or technology. It documents the secure reporting mechanism launched at aaro.mil in October 2023 for current or former USG employees, service members and contractors claiming direct knowledge of purported USG UAP programmes dating back to 1945, with confidentiality protections. It cites 50 U.S.C. 3373(k). The report's own numbers are the argument against its conclusion: 21 cases with anomalous characteristics and roughly 900 reports parked in an active archive for want of scientific data is not a null result, it is an unfunded one.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded A on a global pass (rank 85 of 1170, score 68). 8 connections, 1 of them custody/funding/programmatic, 2 official denials recorded against it. Axes C0/A2/D2.

entities.label: AARO FY2025 Consolidated Annual Report on UAP
entities.sub: Released 21 July 2026, months after the statutory cycle
entities.desc: The FY2025 report covers 2 June 2024 to 30 May 2025 and reached the public on 21 July 2026 - months past the annual cycle required by 50 U.S.C. 3373(k), a statutory compliance failure that drew no visible consequence. Document reference 26-P-0880. It records 319 new reports (284 current, 35 historical), 114 of them resolved, plus 256 previously reported cases resolved in-period for a total of 370 resolutions, all attributed to prosaic causes; nine reports were identified for further analysis and 191 transferred to the active archive. Total AARO holdings: 1,870. It reports 50 unmanned aerial system notifications near nuclear infrastructure, up from 18 in the prior period - a near-tripling of drone activity over nuclear sites that the report does not resolve. It reports 262 individuals contacting AARO through the secure mechanism, of whom 255 were deemed out of scope and 7 identified for follow-up interviews. It states that no evidence suggests a USG or private entity has ever captured or exploited UAP-derived materials. And it carries the single most striking unresolved case AARO has published: approximately 100 airborne UAP and two likely uncrewed surface systems observed by US Navy assets off the coast of Virginia - the report's only maritime-domain case - still under active investigation, with AARO stating that a lack of timely and actionable sensor data continues to constrain its ability to resolve cases. The report also touts an expanded capability to identify satellite flares: 42 of 44 space-domain reports came from FAA pilot reports and were modelled as reflected sunlight.

entities.label: DoD OIG - Evaluation of the DoD's Actions Regarding Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (DODIG-2023-109)
entities.sub: Classified report 15 Aug 2023; unclassified summary released 25 Jan 2024
entities.desc: The Inspector General's evaluation of how the Department handles UAP, completed 15 August 2023 and released in unclassified summary on 25 January 2024. The full report is classified; the public has the summary only. Its findings are structural and damning in an undramatic way: the Department has no overarching UAP policy; different DoD components each developed their own separate processes for collecting, analysing and identifying UAP incidents; and as a result the Department cannot ensure that national security and flight safety threats from UAP have been identified and addressed. It made eleven recommendations to the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security, the service secretaries and the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs, including development of a department-wide policy to integrate UAP roles, responsibilities, requirements and coordination procedures into existing intelligence, counterintelligence and force protection policies. For this board the finding that matters is the fragmentation one. An office that formally reviews only what it can reach, inside a department the IG says has no unified UAP process and component-level stovepipes, cannot produce a negative finding of departmental scope - and every AARO negative finding since has been phrased as 'AARO has discovered no evidence', which is a statement about AARO's reach, not the Department's contents. The classification of the full report means the IG's own account of where the stovepipes are remains unavailable, including through PURSUE.

entities.label: YANKEE BLUE (alleged AFOSI indoctrination program)
entities.sub: Alleged USAF/AFOSI program
entities.desc: YANKEE BLUE is the allegation that the US Air Force ran a fake UFO reverse-engineering programme on its own personnel — briefing officers in classified units into believing they had been read on to a recovery effort, using fabricated material, as a counterintelligence or hazing exercise. If documented it would be the strongest single item in the coverup strand, because it is the government generating false UAP belief inside its own ranks. It is not documented. A full-text search of the released AARO Historical Record Report Volume I (63 pp., March 2024) finds no occurrence of the term, and it appears in none of the FY2023, FY2024 or FY2025 consolidated annual reports — which corrects a widely repeated claim, including one this board previously made, that AARO conceded the programme in Volume I. Two FOIA cases have returned negative: OSD case 25-F-3514 (September 2025) reported no responsive records after searches of the electronic and paper holdings, and AFOSI case 2025-06002-F reported no investigative reports, summaries or closure memoranda. On 1 October 2025 Pentagon spokesperson Susan Gough stated she could not confirm the alleged memorandum. The Department reportedly reopened the search in December 2025 with no published result. The programme is retained on the board at Tier B with the allegation graded Tier 3 and the negative FOIA findings graded Tier 1. A negative primary finding is itself a documented fact and belongs on a board about concealment — but it is a finding about the absence of a record, not a record.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded A on a global pass (rank 38 of 1170, score 88). 13 connections, 1 of them custody/funding/programmatic, 4 official denials recorded against it. Axes C1/A3/D3.

entities.label: Sec. 6802, James M. Inhofe NDAA for FY2023 (Pub. L. 117-263) - AARO establishment, Historical Record Report and annual reports
entities.sub: statute
entities.desc: Section 6802 of Pub. L. 117-263 (enacted 23 Dec 2022) rewrote 50 U.S.C. 3373 to establish AARO, and added subsection (j) requiring a Historical Record Report within 540 days of enactment and subsection (k) requiring joint DNI/SECDEF annual reports. This is the statute AARO cites as the authority for both the Historical Record Report and the Consolidated Annual Reports.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded A on a global pass (rank 75 of 1170, score 70). 7 connections, 6 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C0/A0/D0.

claims.text: Pub. L. 117-263 was enacted 23 December 2022 (header NOTE: 'Dec. 23, 2022 - [H.R. 7776]') and is cited as the 'James M. Inhofe National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2023'.
claims.source: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-117publ263/html/PLAW-117publ263.htm

claims.text: Sec. 6802 is titled 'MODIFICATION OF REQUIREMENT FOR OFFICE TO ADDRESS UNIDENTIFIED ANOMALOUS PHENOMENA' and amends 'Section 1683 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2022 (50 U.S.C. 3373)' to read 'SEC. 1683. ESTABLISHMENT OF ALL-DOMAIN ANOMALY RESOLUTION OFFICE.'
claims.source: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-117publ263/html/PLAW-117publ263.htm

claims.text: Sec. 6802(j)(1)(A) sets the Historical Record Report deadline: 'Not later than 540 days after the date of the enactment of the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2023, the Director of the Office shall submit to the congressional defense committees, the congressional intelligence committees, and congressional leadership a written report detailing the historical record of the United States Government relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena.' 540 days from 23 Dec 2022 is 15 June 2024.
claims.source: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-117publ263/html/PLAW-117publ263.htm

claims.text: Sec. 6802(j)(1)(B)(i) fixes the period of inquiry: the report shall 'focus on the period beginning on January 1, 1945, and ending on the date on which the Director of the Office completes activities under this subsection'.
claims.source: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-117publ263/html/PLAW-117publ263.htm

claims.text: Sec. 6802(j)(1)(B)(ii) requires itemisation of, among other things, '(I) any program or activity that was protected by restricted access that has not been explicitly and clearly reported to Congress; (II) successful or unsuccessful efforts to identify and track unidentified anomalous phenomena; and (III) any efforts to obfuscate, manipulate public opinion, hide, or otherwise provide incorrect unclassified or classified information about unidentified anomalous phenomena or related activities.'
claims.source: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-117publ263/html/PLAW-117publ263.htm

claims.text: Sec. 6802(j)(2) compels archival access: 'The Archivist of the United States shall make available to the Office such information maintained by the National Archives and Records Administration, including classified information, as the Director of the Office considers necessary to carry out paragraph (1).'
claims.source: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-117publ263/html/PLAW-117publ263.htm

claims.text: Sec. 6802(k)(1)(A) sets the annual-report requirement: 'Not later than 180 days after the date of the enactment of the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2023, and annually thereafter for four years, the Director of National Intelligence and the Secretary of Defense shall jointly submit to the appropriate congressional committees a report on unidentified anomalous phenomena.'
claims.source: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-117publ263/html/PLAW-117publ263.htm

claims.text: Sec. 6802(b)(3)(A) sets AARO's reporting chain: 'The Director of the Office shall report directly to the Deputy Secretary of Defense and the Principal Deputy Director of National Intelligence,' with administrative matters reporting to USD(I&S).
claims.source: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-117publ263/html/PLAW-117publ263.htm

claims.text: Sec. 6802(i) authorises detailees to AARO from 'the Central Intelligence Agency, the Defense Intelligence Agency, the National Security Agency, the Department of Energy, the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency, the intelligence elements of the Army, the Navy, the Air Force, the Marine Corps, and the Coast Guard, the Department of Homeland Security'.
claims.source: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-117publ263/html/PLAW-117publ263.htm

claims.text: The statute requires ONE Historical Record Report, not a series. The division into 'Volume I' and 'Volume II' is AARO's own construction, and AARO tied Volume II to 'the date established in Section 6802' - which is the same 540-day date, 15 June 2024. On the statute's own terms the Historical Record Report requirement has been only partially discharged since 15 June 2024. Reasoning: Sec. 6802(j)(1)(A) text compared against HRR Vol I pp. 6 and 45.
claims.source: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-117publ263/html/PLAW-117publ263.htm ; phrase quoted is AARO's, from HRR Volume I pp. 6 and 45 — https://media.defense.gov/2024/Mar/08/2003409233/-1/-1/0/DOPSR-2024-0263-AARO-HISTORICAL-RECORD-REPORT-VOLUME-1-2024.PDF

claims.text: Sec. 6802(j)(1)(B)(ii)(III) obliges AARO to itemise 'any efforts to obfuscate, manipulate public opinion, hide, or otherwise provide incorrect... information' about UAP. An Air Force practice of falsely reading personnel into a non-existent UAP program would fall squarely inside that clause, yet no such account appears in Volume I. Reasoning: statutory text compared against the verified absence of any Yankee Blue / AFOSI / Kirtland passage in Volume I.
claims.source: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-117publ263/html/PLAW-117publ263.htm

claims.text: Sec. 6802 is titled 'MODIFICATION OF REQUIREMENT FOR OFFICE TO ADDRESS UNIDENTIFIED ANOMALOUS PHENOMENA' and operates by amending section 1683 of the FY2022 NDAA (50 U.S.C. 3373) 'to read as follows', replacing it with 'SEC. 1683. ESTABLISHMENT OF ALL-DOMAIN ANOMALY RESOLUTION OFFICE'.
claims.source: Pub. L. 117-263 sec. 6802, govinfo enacted text, read 22 August 2026, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-117publ263/html/PLAW-117publ263.htm

claims.text: The office is to carry out 'the duties of the Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force, as in effect on December 26, 2021', which makes AARO the statutory successor to the Task Force rather than a parallel body.
claims.source: Pub. L. 117-263 sec. 6802, new sec. 1683(a)(1), https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-117publ263/html/PLAW-117publ263.htm

claims.text: The Director of the Office 'shall report directly to the Deputy Secretary of Defense and the Principal Deputy Director of National Intelligence', and reports to the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security 'on all administrative matters' only.
claims.source: Pub. L. 117-263 sec. 6802, new sec. 1683(b)(3), https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-117publ263/html/PLAW-117publ263.htm

claims.text: The Historical Record Report required by new sec. 1683(j)(1)(B)(i) must 'focus on the period beginning on January 1, 1945, and ending on the date on which the Director of the Office completes activities under this subsection'.
claims.source: Pub. L. 117-263 sec. 6802, new sec. 1683(j), https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-117publ263/html/PLAW-117publ263.htm

claims.text: The annual reporting obligation at new sec. 1683(k)(1)(A) is joint - 'the Director of National Intelligence and the Secretary of Defense shall jointly submit' - and finite: the first is due 180 days after enactment of the IAA FY2023, 'and annually thereafter for four years'. Five reports, not a standing requirement.
claims.source: Pub. L. 117-263 sec. 6802, new sec. 1683(k)(1)(A), https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-117publ263/html/PLAW-117publ263.htm

claims.text: New sec. 1683(j)(2) obliges the Archivist of the United States to 'make available to the Office such information maintained by the National Archives and Records Administration, including classified information, as the Director of the Office considers necessary'.

entities.label: Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program (AAWSAP)
entities.sub: dia-program
entities.desc: AAWSAP is the official, contract-of-record name of the program the public knows as the Pentagon's secret UFO study, and it is the most completely documented UAP effort in the history of the United States government. It was conceived inside DIA's Defense Warning Office by Dr. James T. Lacatski, funded by roughly $22 million placed in the classified defense appropriation at the direction of Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid with Daniel Inouye and Ted Stevens, solicited publicly on 18 August 2008 as HHM402-08-R-0211 by the DIA Virginia Contracting Activity, and awarded on 22 September 2008 as firm-fixed-price contract HHM402-08-C-0072 to Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies, LLC of Las Vegas at a $10,000,000 base value with four option years running to 30 September 2013. Its stated objective, in DIA's own words, was 'to understand the physics and engineering of these applications as they apply to the foreign threat out to the far term, i.e., from now through the year 2050', across eleven technical areas: lift, propulsion, control, power generation, spatial/temporal translation, materials, configuration and structure, signature reduction, human interface, human effects, and armament. In practice the contractor built a UFO research enterprise: a Las Vegas SCIF, field investigation teams, a case database, a human physiological effects program, a 494-page Ten Month Report delivered in July 2009, and 38 Defense Intelligence Reference Documents surveying every known theoretical route to the observed flight performance. AARO's 2024 official history concedes the drift in one sentence — 'although investigating UFO/UAP was not specifically outlined in the contract's statement of work, the selected private sector organization conducted UFO research with the support of the DIA program manager.' The program was terminated in 2012. What it produced beyond the 38 released papers — Lacatski says more than 100 detailed reports — has never been released.

entities.label: Advanced Aerospace Threat Identification Program (AATIP / AAITP)
entities.sub: dia-program
entities.desc: AATIP is the program at the centre of the 2017 break and the object of the Department's most contorted public statements. The New York Times reported on 16 December 2017 that it ran from late 2008 through 2011 on roughly $22 million, most of it to Robert Bigelow's Bigelow Aerospace, and that Senator Harry Reid initiated it in 2007. Pentagon spokesman Thomas Crosson confirmed its existence and said it was shut down in 2012 because 'there were other, higher priority issues that merit' the funding. On 24 July 2009 Reid wrote to Deputy Secretary of Defense William Lynn III seeking Special Access Program status for it; the request was denied, and the names of Elizondo and Harold Puthoff in that memorandum were originally redacted before later release. Elizondo's position is that AATIP grew out of AAWSAP, that he ran it from roughly 2010, that government funding rather than the program ceased in 2012, and that it morphed into what became the UAP Task Force. The Department's position has moved three times: acknowledged as UAP-related by Christopher Sherwood on 22 May 2019, flatly denied as UAP-related by Susan Gough on 6 December 2019, and partially conceded again on 21 May 2021 when Gough allowed that the contract 'allowed for research drawn from a wide variety of sources, including reports of UAPs' while denying that was its purpose. AARO's 2024 Historical Record Report Volume 1 treats 2009 as the standup year for AAWSAP and AATIP and concludes it found 'no evidence for the USG reverse-engineering narrative provided by interviewees'.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded A on a global pass (rank 20 of 1170, score 108). 16 connections, 6 of them custody/funding/programmatic, 2 official denials recorded against it. Axes C3/A3/D3.

claims.text: DIA Info Memo U-09-2660 (13 Nov 2009) frames the two names as the same thing: it evaluates 'a request from Senator Harry Reid (enclosure 1) to establish a restricted special access program (SAP) for the Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Application Program Contract, referred to in Senator Reid's letter as the Advanced Aerospace Threat and Identification Program (AAITP).'
claims.source: https://www.dia.mil/FOIA/FOIA-Electronic-Reading-Room/FileId/237611/

claims.text: The DIA release consistently spells it 'AAITP' (Advanced Aerospace Threat and Identification Program) in 2009 documents, not the later-familiar 'AATIP'. The USD(I) memorandum subject line reads: 'Senator Harry Reid's Request to Put the Advanced Aerospace Threat and Identification Program (AAITP) under Special Access Protection'.
claims.source: https://www.dia.mil/FOIA/FOIA-Electronic-Reading-Room/FileId/237660/

claims.text: DIA Read Ahead for the 19 Nov 2009 meeting states the DIA position: 'the content of the deliverables from the Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Application Program contract, referred to by Senator Reid as the AATIP, for FY09 and those expected in FY10, do not meet the criteria as specified in DoD 5200.1-R to justify the additional protection provided by a SAP.'
claims.source: https://www.dia.mil/FOIA/FOIA-Electronic-Reading-Room/FileId/237628/

claims.text: AARO Vol. I records that AAWSAP 'was also known [as] AATIP' and that DIA cancelled the program in 2012; supporters then proposed a follow-on program, KONA BLUE, to DHS, which DHS rejected.
claims.source: https://www.aaro.mil/Portals/136/PDFs/AARO_Historical_Record_Report_Vol_1_2024.pdf

claims.text: The concealment-relevant fact is not that AATIP was fake but that it was administratively real and deliberately kept out of SAP channels. DIA's own recommendation against a SAP (Nov 2009) is what later allowed officials to characterise AATIP as low-significance: a program denied special protection leaves no SAP paper trail to point at.
claims.source: https://www.dia.mil/FOIA/FOIA-Electronic-Reading-Room/FileId/237611/

claims.text: AARO Historical Record Report Vol. I states: 'Unlike AAWSAP, AATIP was never an official DoD program. However, after AAWSAP was cancelled, the AATIP moniker was used by some individuals associated with an informal, unofficial UAP community of interest within DoD that researched UAP sightings from military observers as part of their ancillary job duties.'
claims.source: https://www.aaro.mil/Portals/136/PDFs/AARO_Historical_Record_Report_Vol_1_2024.pdf

claims.text: AARO's formulation is the load-bearing denial artifact: it concedes an actual DoD community of interest researching military UAP sightings, then denies it program status on a naming technicality. DIA's own 2009 correspondence uses 'AAITP' and 'AAWSAP' interchangeably for the same contract, so the 'never an official DoD program' line depends entirely on which of the two names is treated as canonical.
claims.source: https://www.aaro.mil/Portals/136/PDFs/AARO_Historical_Record_Report_Vol_1_2024.pdf

claims.text: A single DoD packet records three names for the same effort: official title AAWSAP, Senator Reid's usage AAITP (Advanced Aerospace Threat and Identification Program), and unclassified nickname AATIP.
claims.source: Packet presented to DEPSECDEF, 17 November 2009

entities.label: Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies (BAASS), LLC
entities.sub: contractor
entities.desc: BAASS is the corporate vehicle through which US government money was spent on UFO research between 2008 and 2012, and it is a distinct legal entity from Bigelow Aerospace — registered at 4640 S. Eastern Avenue, Las Vegas NV 89119, DUNS 827037768, CAGE 54JU7. It was stood up to bid and hold the DIA contract, staffed substantially from the alumni of Robert Bigelow's National Institute for Discovery Science, and run day to day by Deputy Administrator Colm Kelleher, a biochemist who had led the NIDS team at Skinwalker Ranch. Its operation was built around a Las Vegas facility with SCIF space, and its work divided into a physics and engineering line — subcontracting the Defense Intelligence Reference Documents out to EarthTech International, Lockheed Martin, and a dozen universities — and a field line that investigated live cases, ran the Utah ranch as a permanently instrumented site, built a case database, and studied the physiological effects of close encounters on witnesses. In 2009 it contracted with the Mutual UFO Network for rapid-response field investigation under the Star Team Impact Project, giving a government-funded contractor a pipeline into the largest civilian UFO reporting network in the United States; the arrangement collapsed in 2010. BAASS delivered a 494-page Ten Month Report to DIA in July 2009. DoD's 2024 history refers to it only as 'the selected private sector organization' and concedes it 'conducted UFO research with the support of the DIA program manager'.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded A on a global pass (rank 16 of 1170, score 113). 21 connections, 11 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C3/A2/D2.

entities.label: Bigelow Aerospace
entities.sub: contractor
entities.desc: Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies was the prime contractor executing the Defense Intelligence Agency's AAWSAP program from 2008, funded by a special appropriation obtained through Senator Harry Reid. AARO's own report concedes that the contractor team, with at least one supportive government program manager, conducted UAP and paranormal research at a property owned by the private sector organisation, and that when DIA cancelled the effort its advocates proposed KONA BLUE to DHS - a program whose explicit purpose was to 'reverse-engineer any recovered off-world spacecraft that they hoped to acquire.' BAASS is the pivot of the custody allegation because it is the entity to which material was allegedly to move. George Knapp testified under oath in 2025 that Bigelow and an AAWSAP colleague negotiated with senior Lockheed Martin executives for material held at a California facility; Luis Elizondo testified in 2024 that an aerospace contractor sought to divest itself of material collected in the 1950s, that the transfer required a Secretary of the Air Force memorandum that never came, and that the transfer was blocked. AARO records, without names, an allegation that an organisation possessed off-world material in 2009-2010 and that a former senior CIA official quashed the proposal to remove it from the corporation. USAspending records roughly $30 million in federal prime obligations to Bigelow Aerospace LLC since FY2008.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded A on a global pass (rank 122 of 1170, score 56). 5 connections, 4 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C3/A2/D1.

entities.desc: Series of ~38 unclassified technical reports produced under AAWSAP by BAASS subcontractors and published by DIA in two series lines: 'Acquisition Threat Support' (FY2009 tranche, published 2009-2010) and 'Defense Futures' (FY2010 tranche, published 2010-2011).
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded A on a global pass (rank 8 of 1170, score 135). 41 connections, 38 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C0/A0/D0.

claims.source: Board maintenance record, notes/L0-IMPLEMENTATION-2026-08-13.md

claims.text: The DIA FOIA Electronic Reading Room posts 37 files whose names begin 'Defense_Intelligence_Reference_Document_'. 32 of those have been retrieved and their cover pages transcribed; DIA document numbers, publication dates and Intelligence Cut-Off Dates are recorded on the individual document nodes.
claims.source: https://www.dia.mil/FOIA/FOIA-Electronic-Reading-Room/

claims.text: The DIRDs fall into two DIA series banners printed on the cover: 'Acquisition Threat Support' (the FY2009 tranche, ICOD 1 December 2009, published Dec 2009 - Apr 2010) and 'Defense Futures' (the FY2010 tranche, ICOD Jul-Dec 2010, published Nov 2010 - Jan 2011).
claims.source: https://www.dia.mil/FOIA/FOIA-Electronic-Reading-Room/FileId/237636/

claims.text: DIA document numbers follow the pattern DIA-08-YYMM-NNN, where 08 ties to the FY2008 program start and YYMM is the production month — e.g. DIA-08-0911-016 (Nov 2009), DIA-08-1003-015 (Mar 2010), DIA-08-1102-007 (Feb 2011 batch). The numbering is sparse in the released set, which indicates the released DIRDs are not the complete numbered series.
claims.source: https://www.dia.mil/FOIA/FOIA-Electronic-Reading-Room/

claims.text: DIA Info Memo U-429-09 Enclosure 1 lists the 26 FY2009 technical reports by working title (not final DIRD title), including several never released as DIRDs under those names: 'Pulse-Power-Based Weaponry', 'Space-Time Modifications for Spaceflight Applications', 'Novel MEMS-Based Biosensors', 'Metamaterials for Aerospace Applications', 'Metallic Glasses', 'Metallic Spintronics', 'Materials for Advanced Aerospace Platforms', 'Wormholes in Space Time', 'Gravity Wave Communication', 'Vacuum Energy Applications', 'Improved Statistical Approach to Drake Equation', 'Maverick vs. Corporate Research Cultures', 'Warp Drives', 'Controlling Devices Without Limb-Operated Interfaces', 'Field Effects on Biological Tissues', 'High-Energy Laser Weapon', 'Quantum Entanglement Communications', 'Space Access: Where Been, Where Go', 'Advanced Nuclear Propulsion for Deep Space', 'Inertial Electrostatic Confinement Fusion', 'Theory and Experiments of Invisibility Cloaking', 'Superconductors in Gravity Research', 'Antigravity for Aerospace Applications', 'Positron Aerospace Propulsion', 'Biosensors and BioMEMS', 'Programmable Matter'.
claims.source: https://www.dia.mil/FOIA/FOIA-Electronic-Reading-Room/FileId/237617/

claims.text: In the DIA-released copies every DIRD author is withheld under FOIA exemption (b)(6) and the 'Prepared by' office under (b)(3) 10 USC 424. Two author surnames survive uncensored inside the review excerpts of Info Memo U-429-09: 'Hathaway' (The Role of Superconductors in Gravity Research) and 'Tsoi' (Metallic Spintronics).
claims.source: https://www.dia.mil/FOIA/FOIA-Electronic-Reading-Room/FileId/237617/

claims.text: That two surnames survive the redaction pass in U-429-09 while every cover page is scrubbed indicates redaction was applied by template rather than by review, and that DIA's own reviewers wrote about these authors by name in internal correspondence. Author identities are therefore recoverable from the released corpus itself, not only from leaks.
claims.source: https://www.dia.mil/FOIA/FOIA-Electronic-Reading-Room/FileId/237617/

claims.text: Confirmed unreachable in this pass: 5 of the 37 DIRD filenames listed by DIA have no resolvable FileId URL — Biomaterials; Materials_For_Advanced_Aerospace_Platforms; Metallic_Glasses_For_Aerospace_Applications; Metallic_Spintronics; Metamaterials_For_Aerospace_Applications. The complete Wayback CDX index for dia.mil FOIA reading-room FileId URLs (3,536 unique FileIds) contains no snapshot of them, and the live page does not expose FileIds to a text fetcher.
claims.source: https://www.dia.mil/FOIA/FOIA-Electronic-Reading-Room/

claims.text: THE MOST CHECKABLE FINDING THE PROPULSION STRAND PRODUCED, AND IT IS ABOUT THIS SERIES. DIRD DIA-08-1003-018, 'Antigravity for Aerospace Applications', cover-dated 30 March 2010 under the 'Acquisition Threat Support' banner, 45 pages as released, attributed on the DIA list of 9 January 2018 to Dr Eric Davis of EarthTech International, DOES NOT MENTION THOMAS TOWNSEND BROWN. Word counts over the whole released PDF, taken 19 September 2026: Biefeld 0, electrogravitics 0, Podkletnov 0. 'Brown' occurs three times and every one of them is the surname of a different author in the reference list: L. S. Brown and Maclay, 'Vacuum Stress between Conducting Plates', Physical Review 184 (1969); H. R. Brown as co-editor of 'The Philosophy of Vacuum' (1991); and J. H. Brownell on Casimir photons (2008). Alcubierre occurs once, as reference [43].
claims.source: Defense Intelligence Reference Document DIA-08-1003-018, 'Antigravity for Aerospace Applications', 30 March 2010, ICOD 1 December 2009, 45 pages as released, https://documents2.theblackvault.com/documents/dia/AAWSAP-DIRDs/DIRD_19-DIRD_Antigravity_for_Aerospace_Applications.pdf , opened 2026-09-19

claims.text: WHAT THE ZERO-COUNTS ARE AND ARE NOT EVIDENCE FOR, stated so no later session overstates them. THEY ARE EVIDENCE that the United States government's own commissioned survey of antigravity for aerospace applications, written under the same programme this board maps, is a review of gravitomagnetic forces, Forward's dipole generator, Felber's effect, negative energy, dark energy, the cosmological constant and quantum vacuum zero-point fluctuation force, and that it never reaches for the figure the electrogravitics literature treats as its origin. THEY ARE NOT EVIDENCE that DIA considered Brown and rejected him: the document shows no sign of having considered him at all, and an absence is not an adjudication. THEY ARE NOT EVIDENCE that Brown's work was suppressed, hidden or classified; nothing opened supports that and nothing here asserts it.
claims.source: Defense Intelligence Reference Document DIA-08-1003-018, 'Antigravity for Aerospace Applications', 30 March 2010, ICOD 1 December 2009, 45 pages as released, https://documents2.theblackvault.com/documents/dia/AAWSAP-DIRDs/DIRD_19-DIRD_Antigravity_for_Aerospace_Applications.pdf , opened 2026-09-19

claims.text: The same survey's own conclusion on what antigravity would require, verbatim: 'Mechanical embodiments that produce antigravity forces require kilometer-sized apparatus, astronomical-sized masses and densities, or extreme mass velocities and accelerations.' And: 'Negative energy has been produced in the lab in very small quantities. The technologies used for producing negative energy are nascent, and so it will be some time before it can be ascertained whether they are capable of producing the astronomical amounts of negative energy required to generate significant antigravity forces.'
claims.source: Defense Intelligence Reference Document DIA-08-1003-018, 'Antigravity for Aerospace Applications', 30 March 2010, ICOD 1 December 2009, 45 pages as released, https://documents2.theblackvault.com/documents/dia/AAWSAP-DIRDs/DIRD_19-DIRD_Antigravity_for_Aerospace_Applications.pdf , opened 2026-09-19

claims.text: Stated inference, and it is about transparency rather than content. Between 1996 and 2002 NASA ran a public, funded, unclassified assessment of exotic propulsion, named the claims it examined, published which of sixteen tasks failed, and closed. Between 2009 and 2011 DIA commissioned thirty-eight reference documents covering overlapping subject matter, released them only under FOIA, and withheld every author under exemption (b)(6). NOTHING OPENED JOINS THE TWO PROGRAMMES TO EACH OTHER and no institutional edge between them is proposed; Marc Millis wrote for both, which is a fact about a person and not a link between the institutions.

entities.desc: Senator Harry Reid's letter to Deputy Secretary of Defense William J. Lynn III asking DoD to place the AAITP under restricted special access protection.
