entities.label: PURSUE Release 05
entities.sub: 7 August 2026; 41 files (16 videos, 22 documents, 3 images); 1950/1953-2026
entities.desc: The fifth and most recent tranche, published 7 August 2026: 41 files comprising 16 videos, 22 documents and 3 images, with a 130MB document bundle and a 513MB video bundle. The portal states the span as 1953 to 2026; the underlying content reaches back to 1950. Its centrepiece is the Gulf of Oman incident of 8 September 2021 - six videos from an AC-130J gunship together with intelligence report DOW-UAP-D101 documenting approximately 25 instances of UAP, described as cold orbs roughly four feet in diameter flying at between 250 and 1,300 mph at low altitude, and reported as reacting to the aircraft's cannon fire. That is a US military gunship engaging unidentified objects and recording their response, released by the Department that engaged them. The tranche also contains DOW-UAP-PR134, a January 2025 video of a small orb over a residential area in the Middle East; FBI-UAP-D031, a black triangular craft with a red light at each corner near a military base at Colorado Springs in October 2023; digital renderings of triangular UAP sightings from 2002, 2011 and 2023; a CIA report on an alleged November 1963 Brazil recovery of a metal sphere containing a deceased occupant in a spacesuit, subsequently deemed unsubstantiated by the American Consulate; and a 1953 US Navy Photographic Interpretation Center analysis of the 1950 Great Falls, Montana and 1952 Tremonton, Utah films. The Navy PIC finding is the most consequential single document in the entire PURSUE corpus: after more than a thousand hours of frame analysis, the Navy's own photo interpreters assessed the Utah objects as bright, silvery reflective disks that were self-luminous and intelligently controlled and inconsistent with natural phenomena or commonly known aerospace technologies. That is an affirmative technical finding by a US Navy analytic unit, released by the Department of War in 2026, and it directly contradicts the disposition the same films received from the Robertson Panel in January 1953.

entities.sub: The publication surface for PURSUE; not an AARO property
entities.desc: The portal itself is a fact worth recording separately from what it contains. PURSUE material is published at war.gov/UFO, on the Secretary's own web estate, with video bundles served from a CloudFront distribution rather than from aaro.mil or from a FOIA reading room. AARO's homepage links out to it. The portal presents five dated releases, each as a paired document ZIP and video ZIP, carries Hegseth's signed transparency statement and a quotation of the President's direction, and offers no assessment, index, manifest, metadata schema or provenance statement for any file. entities.label: Presidential direction to identify and release UAP files (19-20 February 2026)
entities.sub: Truth Social post; no published executive order text
entities.desc: The originating instrument of PURSUE, and a thin one. On 19-20 February 2026 Trump posted on Truth Social that he would direct Secretary of War Hegseth and other relevant departments and agencies to begin the process of identifying and releasing government files related to alien and extraterrestrial life, UAP and UFOs, 'and any and all other information connected to these highly complex, but extremely interesting and important, matters.' Hegseth referred to it five days later as 'that executive order,' but the contemporaneous reporting describes a social-media post and no signed order has surfaced in the public record as of 12 August 2026. Chief Pentagon Spokesman Sean Parnell said the department 'looks forward to working with the interagency to fulfill the president's directive.' The consequence of the missing instrument is that PURSUE has no published scope, no defined universe of covered records, no declassification standard, no review authority named in writing, no compliance deadline and no reporting requirement - every one of which the Burlison FY2027 NDAA amendment would supply by statute. It is a release programme that exists at will.

entities.label: AARO Declassification Information Paper (September 2025)
entities.sub: The office's own account of why it cannot declassify
entities.desc: An information paper published by AARO in September 2025 - one month before its first video releases and eight months before PURSUE - explaining why the office cannot release UAP material. Its argument: AARO cannot declassify anything independently because other government entities originated the classified data; it must request declassification review from originating offices such as the Military Departments; each review determines whether disclosure could cause damage, serious damage or exceptionally grave damage to national security, producing full release, partial release with redactions, or continued classification; and DOPSR reviews redactions before public release. It identifies the obstacles as protection of platform capabilities, locations and collection methods rather than the subject matter itself - noting that even footage of birds and balloons stays classified when derived from sensitive sources - and describes the process as 'deliberate and time-intensive.' Every sentence of that is defensible as a description of the classification system. What it is not is a description of an immovable constraint, and the proof is the eight months that followed: given a cabinet-level direction, the same department cleared and published five tranches containing well over a hundred sensor videos. The paper is the best single artefact of institutional friction masquerading as legal necessity.

entities.label: National Archives UAP Records Collection (Record Group 615)
entities.sub: Created under FY2024 NDAA sections 1841-1843, P.L. 118-31
entities.desc: The statutory records collection, and the quietest failure in this domain. Sections 1841 through 1843 of the FY2024 National Defense Authorization Act, Public Law 118-31, directed the establishment of an Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection at the National Archives. NARA created Record Group 615 to receive it and issued guidance to federal agencies on identifying, preparing and transferring UAP records into that record group. What NARA does not publish is the thing that would make the collection meaningful: which agencies have actually transferred anything, how much, or when. Its public position, verbatim, is that 'NARA will continue to add UAP records to the UAP Records Collection (RG 615) and make them available online through the National Archives Catalog on an ongoing, rolling basis as they are received from federal agencies.' There is no published compliance list, no page or item counts by agency, no transfer dates, and no statement identifying any agency as delinquent. The Department of War asserts progress - AARO 'has made progress in making UAP information available and in transferring those records to the National Archives in accordance with federal law' - but the assertion is unverifiable against NARA's own pages. The Burlison FY2027 NDAA amendment exists precisely to fix this: statutory transfer timelines, a Senate-confirmed review board with subpoena power, and contractor reach. A records collection with no compliance reporting is a collection whose emptiness is indistinguishable from its completeness.

entities.sub: Explanatory products, 2024-2026
entities.desc: The other half of AARO's public output: explanatory papers that teach the reader how to resolve their own sightings. The satellite flaring paper of 22 April 2025, with an accompanying DVIDS animation, explains Starlink flaring - the mechanism AARO used in the FY2024 report to resolve a commercial pilot's white flashing lights against a launch an hour earlier. entities.label: Materials and custody analysis
entities.sub: Cross-cutting domain: physical samples, their analysis and their chain of custody
entities.desc: Materials analysis is the single place where the central claim could be settled by measurement rather than by testimony, which is why both sides of the argument have converged on it. The falsifiable signature is isotopic: terrestrial elements occur in well-characterised isotope ratios set by solar system formation and by known industrial enrichment processes, so a sample whose ratios lie outside that envelope, and outside the known list of processes that can shift them, would be very difficult to explain conventionally. Garry Nolan, Jacques Vallée and colleagues published the methodology for exactly this test in Progress in Aerospace Sciences in 2022, setting out the instrumental techniques - including secondary ion mass spectrometry - applicable to characterising unusual materials for aerospace forensics. The results so far do not support the claim: AARO's January 2026 supplement reports Oak Ridge National Laboratory found a specimen from Ohio to be a conventional aluminium-silicon casting alloy with large grain sizes, interconnected porosity and needle-like silicon precipitates - defects, not exotica. The dual-use route matters here too, because the national laboratories that would perform such analysis are the same ones that perform nuclear forensics under Restricted Data controls. Scoring high on this domain means an entity has held, analysed or controlled physical material.

entities.desc: DoD SAPCO is the exact mechanism at issue on this board. entities.desc: NSA was established on 4 November 1952 by a classified memorandum from President Truman, and like the NRO it spent its early decades as an agency whose name the government preferred not to confirm. Created by the Department of Energy Organization Act of 1977 as successor to the Atomic Energy Commission and the Energy Research and Development Administration, DOE administers the Restricted Data and Formerly Restricted Data categories created by the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 - information that is 'born classified' by statute, outside the Executive Order 13526 framework, and therefore outside any presidential declassification directive that operates only on national security information. A president can order the release of UAP files under EO 13526; he cannot, by executive order alone, release Restricted Data. DOE's semi-autonomous National Nuclear Security Administration, established by Congress in 2000, runs the weapons complex: Los Alamos, Sandia and Lawrence Livermore national laboratories, the Nevada National Security Site, the Pantex Plant, Y-12 at Oak Ridge and the Savannah River Site - a distributed archipelago of guarded, instrumented, contractor-operated facilities with independent security regimes, its own police force, its own clearance system (the Q clearance) and a demonstrated capability to store and analyse anomalous material under a cover story. DOE's documented UAP footprint is old and specific: the 1948-1951 green fireball flap centred on Los Alamos and Sandia, prompting the February 1949 Los Alamos conference attended by Edward Teller, Lincoln LaPaz and AEC and Air Force personnel and the subsequent Project TWINKLE instrumented observation effort; the 1980 Kirtland AFB/Manzano Weapons Storage Area intrusions adjacent to the nuclear stockpile; and the modern materials-analysis work performed for AARO at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. AARO's Historical Record Report records only that 'AARO sent guidance and requests to DoD, IC elements, DOE, and DHS to review and provide any NDAs pertaining to UAP' - a records request, not an inspection. No DOE official has ever testified at a UAP hearing.

AFRL's directorates include the Aerospace Systems Directorate and the Munitions Directorate; it manages a large classified portfolio and a large university and contractor research base. entities.label: Congressional oversight of special access programs
entities.sub: The statutory oversight mechanism, and the hole in it
entities.desc: Congressional oversight of the Department's most sensitive activities is not a general power; it is a specific statutory scheme with a specific, legally sanctioned exception, and the exception is the whole story. Under 10 U.S.C. 119 the Secretary of Defense must report annually by 1 March to the four defense committees on every special access program, giving for each a brief description, major milestones, actual historical costs and estimated costs through the succeeding four fiscal years, and must notify the committees by 1 February of any newly designated SAP, and must notify them thirty days before initiating a new SAP. But subsection (e) permits the Secretary to waive that reporting where he determines disclosure would harm national security; in that case 'the Secretary shall provide the information described in that subsection with respect to the special access program concerned, and the justification for the waiver, jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees.' Eight members of Congress, and no one else. Layered on top of that is DoD Directive 5205.07, which requires any person briefing Congress with SAP material to notify the Director, DoD SAPCO first, and bars contractors from providing SAP material to Congress at all without approval. Layered on top of that is the practical gate described by Chairwoman Luna in September 2025, under which a non-committee member must be approved by the chairman and ranking member of both HASC and HAC-D to see specific material. The result is a structure in which the number of people who can lawfully learn of a waived unacknowledged program is small, fixed, and selected by the department being overseen - and in which a member who suspects a program exists cannot ask for it by name because, as Representative Mace put it, 'if you do not know it, you cannot get the information.' This is the mechanism David Grusch alleges was used, and it is a mechanism that does not require anyone to break the law.

entities.label: Executive Office of the President
entities.sub: The White House staff apparatus; source of classification authority and of the 2026 disclosure directives
entities.desc: The Executive Office of the President was created by Reorganization Act authority in 1939 and is the apparatus through which presidential classification authority is exercised: the National Security Council, established by the National Security Act of 1947, the Office of Management and Budget, which builds and conceals the black budget inside the President's request, and the Office of Science and Technology Policy. The classification system that governs almost all UAP material is a creature of executive order - currently Executive Order 13526 - which means the President can unilaterally declassify it, and the fact that no President did so for seventy-eight years is a datum about the presidency, not about the material. Successive administrations have touched the file: the Truman administration through the 1947-1952 Air Force projects, the Eisenhower administration through the Robertson Panel, the Carter administration through a 1977 White House inquiry, and the Clinton administration through John Podesta's push for declassification. In 2026 the EOP became the principal engine of the record: on 19-20 February 2026 the President directed the Pentagon and federal agencies to identify and release UAP and extraterrestrial files, a separate directive addressed the waiver of UAP-related nondisclosure agreements, and the Department of War stood up the PURSUE release portal at war.gov/UFO, publishing its first tranche on 8 May 2026. Executive Order 14347 of 5 September 2025 - the Department of War renaming order - is a reminder of the same power in a different register: the President can rename the department that holds the files by signature, but he cannot by signature reach Restricted Data held under the Atomic Energy Act.

entities.label: National Archives Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection
entities.sub: Statutory collection under 2024 NDAA secs. 1841-1843
entities.desc: The UAP Records Collection is what survived the Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Disclosure Act. Sections 1841 to 1843 of the FY2024 National Defense Authorization Act, Public Law 118-31, directed the creation at the National Archives of a collection of United States Government records relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, modelled on the JFK Assassination Records Collection - but stripped in conference of the independent review board with subpoena power and of the eminent domain provision that would have compelled private holders of recovered material to surrender it. NARA established the collection as Record Group 615 and announced on 24 April 2025 that it had released records transferred from four agencies - the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, the Office of the Secretary of Defense, the Federal Aviation Administration and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission - and that it 'will continue to add UAP records to the Collection and make them available online through the National Archives Catalog on an ongoing, rolling basis'. The composition of that first transfer is itself evidence: two of the four contributing agencies are civilian regulators. Absent from the transfer are CIA, NSA, NRO, NGA, DIA, DOE, DHS and the military departments - that is, every agency with custody proximity. The collection is nonetheless the correct measurable for this board, because it is the one place where a statutory obligation to produce records collides with the agencies alleged to be holding them, and because any presidential declassification directive must eventually deposit here.

entities.label: DHS Science and Technology Directorate
entities.sub: DHS research and development component; the office that established KONA BLUE as a prospective SAP
entities.desc: The Science and Technology Directorate is the Department of Homeland Security's research and development arm, and it is the specific office inside DHS at which the post-AAWSAP recovery program proposal landed. According to the joint AARO/DHS paper 'History and Origin of KONA BLUE', in 2011 'the DHS Under Secretary for Science and Technology (S&T) established KONA BLUE as a PSAP' - a Prospective Special Access Program - and approximately six months later the DHS Deputy Secretary disapproved it and terminated it, so that KONA BLUE was 'never approved or formally established'. AARO's Historical Record Report adds that the proposal was to 'restart UAP investigations, paranormal research (including alleged human consciousness anomalies) and reverse-engineer any recovered off-world spacecraft', that interviewees described it as 'a sensitive DHS compartment to cover up the retrieval and exploitation of non-human biologics', and that 'Senators Lieberman and Reid asked that the PSAP be established with the promise of additional funding'. S&T is therefore the only office in the United States government for which there is a released government document stating that it created, however briefly and however provisionally, a compartment intended to hold recovered non-human material. The identity of the Under Secretary who signed is not stated in the released paper; the identity of the Deputy Secretary who killed it is not stated either. Those two names are the highest-value outstanding FOIA targets in this domain.

entities.sub: Semi-autonomous DOE agency established by Congress in 2000; operator of the nuclear weapons complex
entities.desc: NNSA is 'a semi-autonomous agency within the U.S. Department of Energy responsible for enhancing national security through the military application of nuclear science', established by Congress in 2000 in the wake of the Wen Ho Lee security failures at Los Alamos. It operates the weapons complex through management and operating contracts: Los Alamos National Laboratory, Sandia National Laboratories, Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, the Nevada National Security Site, the Pantex Plant, the Y-12 National Security Complex, the Kansas City National Security Campus and the Savannah River Site. Every one of those facilities is contractor-operated on government-owned land, carries an armed protective force, operates under DOE's own clearance regime rather than the DoD's, and holds material under Restricted Data authority. NNSA is thus the single most capable custodial architecture in the United States government for material that must be stored, guarded, machined and analysed without appearing in any Department of Defense special access program list. The historical UAP record intersects it repeatedly: the 1948-1951 green fireball events centred on LosAlamos, Sandia and the Kirtland complex; the 1980 Manzano Weapons Storage Area intrusions; the persistent identification of the Nevada Test Site and its S-4 area in retrieval testimony; and the modern use of DOE laboratory analytical capability for AARO's materials work.

entities.label: Department of Defense Office of Inspector General
entities.sub: Statutory independent oversight body within DoD; author of DODIG-2023-109
entities.desc: The DoD Office of Inspector General is the Department's statutory internal watchdog, created by the Inspector General Act, and it is the body that produced the only formal audit of the Department's UAP conduct. On 15 August 2023 - three weeks after David Grusch's testimony - the DoD OIG issued DODIG-2023-109, 'Evaluation of the DoD's Actions Regarding Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena', whose stated objective was to determine 'how the DoD, military services, defense agencies, and military department counterintelligence organizations took intelligence, counterintelligence, and force protection actions to detect, report, collect, analyze, and identify UAP'. The report itself is classified; only an unclassified summary was released, and the OIG issued a press release on 25 January 2024. The OIG is also the office to which Luis Elizondo submitted a complaint in May 2021 alleging reprisal and mishandling. The structural point for this board is that DoD OIG is subject to the same access architecture as everyone else: an inspector general who is not read into a waived unacknowledged special access program cannot audit it, and DODIG-2023-109's classified status means the public cannot determine whether the audit reached the SAP enterprise at all.

entities.label: Waived unacknowledged special access program (waived USAP)
entities.sub: The specific legal category at the centre of every allegation on this board
entities.desc: A waived unacknowledged special access program is the most protected category of activity the United States government operates. Special access programs are activities requiring protection beyond that ordinarily required for information at the same classification level, imposing need-to-know controls, access rosters and separate security architecture; DoD Directive 5205.07 governs them. An unacknowledged SAP is one whose existence is not acknowledged - the response to an inquiry is neither confirmation nor denial. A waived SAP is one for which the Secretary of Defense has exercised the waiver at 10 U.S.C. 119(e), under which the annual report and the justification for the waiver go 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees' instead of to the committees as a whole. Combine the two and the result is an activity whose existence is denied to the public, denied to most of Congress, and known in the legislative branch to eight people. Every serious allegation on this board reduces to a claim about this category: David Grusch's testimony that a multi-decade materials recovery and exploitation effort exists and is unreported; the 2009 Reid request that AAWSAP be granted restricted SAP status, which USD(I) James Clapper opposed; the 2011 DHS attempt to stand up KONA BLUE as a prospective SAP; and the FY2024 NDAA section 1687 limitation on the use of funds for UAP-related programs not reported to the congressional defense committees, which is Congress legislating directly against the possibility that this category has been abused.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded A on a global pass (rank 93 of 1170, score 65). 12 connections, 5 of them custody/funding/programmatic, 1 official denial recorded against it. Axes C3/A3/D3.

claims.text: 10 U.S.C. 119(e) permits the Secretary of Defense to waive SAP reporting requirements and instead provide the information and the waiver justification 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees'.

entities.label: DoD Agency-Wide Financial Statement Audit (FY2018-present)
entities.sub: Annual full-scope audit required by the CFO Act; disclaimer of opinion every year since inception
entities.desc: The Department of Defense was made subject to the Chief Financial Officers Act of 1990 like every other major agency, and for twenty-seven years did not attempt a full-scope audit of its financial statements. The first one covered fiscal year 2018. Every full-scope audit from FY2018 through FY2025 - eight consecutive years - has ended in a disclaimer of opinion: the Inspector General has been unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence to express any opinion at all on whether the Department's financial statements are fairly presented. This is not a qualified opinion or an adverse opinion; it is a statement that the books cannot be audited. The FY2025 audit, reported in DOWIG-2026-081 'The FY 2025 DoW Financial Statement Audit Explained' published 12 May 2026, identified twenty-six material weaknesses across three categories - ten in management responsibility and asset accountability, six in information technology, and ten in accounting. Among the accounting weaknesses is one named 'Unsupported Accounting Adjustments', under which the report states that in the last two quarters of FY2025 the Department's adjustments totalled more than $859 billion, with contributions from the Army, Air Force, Navy and the Defense Logistics Agency across both general and working capital funds. Twenty-two reporting entities received stand-alone audits: eleven clean opinions, one qualified, nine disclaimers, and one (the Navy Working Capital Fund) no opinion under a two-year cycle. Two of the twenty-six weaknesses go directly to the question this board asks - 'Universe of Transactions', meaning the Department cannot establish the complete set of transactions falling within audit scope, and 'Fund Balance with Treasury', an account holding roughly $1 trillion that the Department cannot reconcile. An entity that cannot enumerate its own transactions cannot demonstrate the absence of any particular transaction, and that is the precise structural reason a documented audit failure is evidence in a concealment investigation rather than merely a management scandal.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded B on a global pass (rank 303 of 1170, score 39). 9 connections, 2 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C0/A1/D3.

entities.label: DODIG-2016-113 - Army General Fund Adjustments Not Adequately Documented or Supported
entities.sub: DoD OIG audit report, 26 July 2016; source of the $2.8 trillion and $6.5 trillion figures
entities.desc: This is the report from which the entire '$21 trillion' literature descends, and it must be quoted precisely or it becomes useless. Published 26 July 2016, it found that the Office of the Assistant Secretary of the Army (Financial Management and Comptroller) and the Defense Finance and Accounting Service Indianapolis 'did not adequately support $2.8 trillion in third quarter journal voucher (JV) adjustments and $6.5 trillion in yearend JV adjustments made to AGF data during FY 2015 financial statement compilation.' Footnote 2 of the report states that the amounts are not cumulative and should not be added together. What the figures measure is the gross dollar value of accounting entries made to force the Army General Fund's compiled data into balance, not a sum of money that went missing: the same underlying dollar can be adjusted many times in a compilation cycle, which is why the totals exceed the Army General Fund's annual appropriation by roughly two orders of magnitude. Read correctly, the report is not evidence that $6.5 trillion vanished. It is evidence of something arguably more useful to this board: that the Army's financial records for FY2015 were reconstructed at year end by trillions of dollars of entries for which no supporting documentation could be produced, and that therefore the ledger cannot be used to establish where any given appropriation actually went. entities.label: Reprogramming of DoD Appropriated Funds (DoD FMR Volume 3, Chapter 6; DD Form 1415 series)
entities.sub: The administrative machinery for moving money after appropriation, including below-threshold reprogramming
entities.desc: Below the statutory transfer authorities sits an administrative layer that does most of the actual work. Volume 3, Chapter 6 of the Department of Defense Financial Management Regulation, 'Reprogramming of DoD Appropriated Funds', dated September 2015, establishes four categories of action. Prior Approval Reprogramming, on DD Form 1415-1, requires written approval from the congressional committees before execution and covers major decisions and items of special congressional interest. Letter Notification, DD Form 1415-2, gives Congress thirty days advance notice with an opportunity to object. Internal Reprogramming, DD Form 1415-3, is an audit-trail action processed entirely within the Department for reclassifications between line items where the substance of the programme is unchanged. And Below-Threshold Reprogramming requires no approval and no notification at all: components may realign funds within prescribed cumulative annual limits at their own discretion. The thresholds at which congressional approval becomes necessary are: $10 million for Military Personnel, $15 million for Operation and Maintenance, $20 million or 20 percent of the programme base (whichever is less) for Procurement, and $10 million or 20 percent of the programme base (whichever is less) for Research, Development, Test and Evaluation. Against a Department managing more than $4.7 trillion in assets and executing hundreds of billions of dollars annually, a $10 million RDT&E threshold means that an enormous volume of money moves each year with no external record generated at all. This is the layer at which the audit trail is thinnest and at which the $859 billion of unsupported adjustments reported for the last two quarters of FY2025 lives.

entities.label: Chilean Navy helicopter FLIR case, November 2014 (released January 2017)
entities.sub: CEFAA release of Chilean Navy infrared footage after two years of analysis
entities.desc: In November 2014 a Chilean Navy helicopter on a routine coastal patrol filmed, in daylight and with its infrared camera, an object that the crew tracked from around forty miles away and attempted repeatedly to contact. There was no response. The crew reported it to two nearby radar stations, neither of which could see the object on their screens although both could see the Navy helicopters; air traffic control confirmed that no aircraft had been authorised in the area. The footage shows the object apparently discharging a plume or gas as it moves. CEFAA, then the Chilean civil aviation UAP office, examined the case for two years with a multidisciplinary panel and released the video publicly in January 2017 without an explanation - the first time a Latin American state released military infrared sensor footage of an unresolved object. The release came three years before the US Department of Defense authorised the release of the FLIR1, GIMBAL and GOFAST Navy videos in April 2020, and it establishes the pattern the Canadian government would later identify: the Chilean office publishes what it cannot explain.

entities.label: USS Nimitz Carrier Strike Group Encounters, 10-16 November 2004
entities.sub: Multi-platform radar/visual/infrared UAP encounters, Southern California Operating Area; the 'Tic Tac'
entities.desc: Between roughly 10 and 16 November 2004 the Nimitz Carrier Strike Group, working up off southern California in the W-291 warning area and the Baja approaches, generated the most completely corroborated UAP encounter in the American record: radar, multiple aircrew eyewitnesses, and an infrared recording, on separate platforms, inside a controlled military exercise area. The guided-missile cruiser USS Princeton (CG-59), running a freshly upgraded SPY-1B, had been holding anomalous tracks on its Aegis combat system for approximately two weeks; Senior Chief Operations Specialist Kevin Day ran the air picture. Fravor's sworn statement to House Oversight describes the objects descending from above 80,000 feet 'rapidly down to 20,000ft', loitering for hours, then ascending. On 14 November 2004 Princeton vectored two VFA-41 Black Aces F/A-18Fs off a training event to a contact. Cdr. David Fravor, the squadron's commanding officer, and his weapons systems officer flew the lead; Lt. Cdr. Alex Dietrich and her WSO flew high cover from about 8,000 feet above. Fravor found a small white object, no rotors, no rotor wash, no visible control surfaces, moving erratically over an area of white water in an otherwise calm sea, its long axis initially north-south. Four aircrew watched it for roughly five minutes. As Fravor descended in a spiral to intercept, the object mirrored his turn, then accelerated out of sight; Princeton reacquired it at the CAP point roughly 60 miles away in under a minute. A follow-on sortie that day, flown with a functioning ATFLIR pod and credited to Lt. Cdr. Chad Underwood, produced the infrared footage now known as FLIR1 - the video that leaked in 2007, was published by The New York Times on 16 December 2017, and was formally released by the Department of Defense on 27 April 2020 with the statement that the phenomena 'remain characterized as unidentified.' What happened afterwards is the part that matters institutionally. The Navy's own range fouler report on the incident, released to the Navy FOIA reading room on 12 January 2023, describes the object as 'solid white, smooth, with no edges ... uniformly colored with no nacelles, pylons, or wings ... approximately 46 feet in length', names Fravor and Dietrich, and records the disposition in one sentence: 'Pilots reported the incident through Intelligence Personnel. Reporting terminated at 3rd Fleet, there was no process to share the reporting.' Fravor testified under oath on 26 July 2023 that 'the incident was never investigated, none of my crew were ever questioned, tapes were never taken.' Against that, three USS Princeton crewmen in different divisions - Kevin Day, CEC/Aegis technician Gary Voorhis and Jason Turner - have described in public interviews since 2018 that within roughly 48 hours personnel who did not identify themselves came aboard and removed or ordered wiped the recording media covering the tracks, and that crew were told to stop discussing it. No FOIA release, visit log, deck-log entry or message traffic has ever been produced identifying those personnel or the authority under which they acted, and the Navy has never produced Princeton sensor data for 14 November 2004. The two accounts are not necessarily in conflict - Fravor speaks for the aircrew and the squadron's tapes, the Princeton crew speak for the ship's recorded data - but the confiscation account remains the single most consequential unanchored claim in the modern record, and it is graded here as an inference, not a fact.

entities.label: The Cover-Up
entities.sub: Operational domain - concealment run as a funded programme, not a passive silence
entities.desc: This board treats concealment as a discipline with doctrine, staffing and a budget line, because that is how the surviving record describes it. The 17 January 1953 Robertson Panel, convened by CIA's Office of Scientific Intelligence, did not merely conclude that sightings were harmless - it recommended that the national security agencies 'take immediate steps to strip the Unidentified Flying Objects of the special status they have been given and the aura of mystery they have unfortunately acquired', through a programme of mass-media debunking and the monitoring of civilian UFO groups. That is a covert influence recommendation written by an intelligence agency about its own public. Forty-four years later CIA historian Gerald K. Haines, writing in the agency's own classified-then-declassified journal Studies in Intelligence, admitted that Air Force officers had knowingly issued false explanations - natural phenomena, ice crystals, temperature inversions - to Congress and the public for sightings the Air Force knew were U-2 and OXCART overflights, and called this 'not the full story'. The documented route from ordinary secrecy into active concealment therefore runs through three mechanisms this board tracks separately: false official explanation, record destruction, and the redefinition of a programme so that the honest answer to a congressional question becomes technically 'no such programme exists'. GAO's 1995 search for Roswell records found that outgoing messages from Roswell Army Air Field for 1946-1949 had been destroyed with no disposition authority and no destruction certificate on file - a documented gap where the destruction itself is the evidence. To be scored highly on this domain is to be a producer of concealment rather than merely a person kept in the dark by it: an author of cover stories, a signatory on a destruction order, a briefer who gave a denial he knew to be false.

entities.label: Official Denial
entities.sub: Evidentiary domain - the denial as a dated, attributable artifact
entities.desc: A denial is not the end of an inquiry on this board; it is an entry in it. The editorial rule is that every official denial gets recorded in full, with its author, its date, its precise wording and its scope - because the wording and the scope are the data. AARO's Volume I historical record report of February 2024 states flatly that the office found 'no empirical evidence' that the US government or private companies have reverse-engineered extraterrestrial technology; what the same report also states is the scope of its search, the access it was granted, and which named programmes it did and did not resolve, and those are the parts a hostile audit turns on. The documented pattern that makes this a domain rather than a footnote is the historical one: the National Reconnaissance Office's very existence was an official secret from 1961 until 1992, meaning that for thirty-one years an accurate answer to 'does that organisation exist' was legally required to be no. Denials therefore have a known failure mode - a categorical denial by an official without the relevant read-in is not a statement about the world but a statement about that official's access. Scoring on this domain measures how central official denial has been to an entity's public conduct: an agency spokesman who issues denials, a director who signs them, or a witness whose testimony a denial was written to rebut.

entities.label: Secrecy Law & Classification
entities.sub: Legal domain - the statutory and executive machinery that makes concealment lawful
entities.desc: Everything this board describes is, on its face, legal - and that is the point. Classification authority flows from executive order rather than statute for most national security information, which means the same executive branch that runs a programme also decides whether Congress and the courts may learn of it. entities.label: Secrecy Architecture
entities.sub: Structural domain - how compartments are stacked so that no single person sees the whole
entities.desc: Compartmentation is not a synonym for secrecy; it is a specific engineering choice about who may hold which fragment, and it is the single most important structural fact on this board. The Manhattan Project is the documented ancestor: tens of thousands of workers at Oak Ridge and Hanford who could describe their own task precisely and had no authorised knowledge of the weapon, with compartmentation enforced by physical separation, need-to-know and a security apparatus reporting outside the technical chain. Applied to a recovery and reverse-engineering effort, the same architecture produces the effect witnesses repeatedly describe: a metallurgist who can characterise a sample without being told where it came from, a security officer who moves the container without being told what is in it, a programme manager who signs the contract without the read-in that would let him understand it. The consequence for evidence is severe and must be stated plainly - a compartmented programme generates almost no witness who can testify to the whole, only many witnesses who can each testify to a fragment, which is precisely the evidentiary signature critics cite as weakness. Scoring high here means an entity sits at a junction where fragments were assembled: a control officer, a security review authority, or a person read into more than one compartment at once.

entities.label: Counterintelligence
entities.sub: Operational domain - the security service pointed inward at the programme's own people
entities.desc: Counterintelligence is the function that protects a programme from penetration, and in a compartmented programme it is also the function that protects the programme from its own personnel. entities.label: Legal Doctrine & Liability
entities.sub: Legal domain - non-disclosure agreements, state secrets, amnesty, and the whistleblower's exposure
entities.desc: The law is the terrain on which a witness decides whether to speak, and the terrain is tilted. A person read into a special access programme signs a non-disclosure agreement with criminal exposure attached; the Intelligence Community Whistleblower Protection Act gives a lawful channel to the Inspector General but no protection at all for a disclosure made outside it; and the state secrets privilege can end a civil case before discovery without the court ever seeing the material. The documented cost of the current arrangement is visible in the DoD Inspector General's own product: DODIG-2023-109 exists because personnel used the IG channel, and its unclassified summary is nearly the whole of what the public received. entities.label: Chemistry & Isotopics
entities.sub: Technical domain - elemental composition, isotope ratios and the chain of custody around a sample
entities.desc: Chemistry is the discipline that would deliver the verdict, and it is also the discipline most easily destroyed by a broken chain of custody. Isotope ratio measurement by secondary ion mass spectrometry or thermal ionisation mass spectrometry can distinguish terrestrial from non-terrestrial origin at high confidence for many elements - the technique is routine in cosmochemistry, where meteoritic material is identified by exactly this signature. The Ubatuba magnesium fragments, examined since the 1950s, are the field's oldest test case and remain unresolved because provenance was never established. The strongest modern work runs through Avi Loeb's group, which published elemental and isotopic classification of spherules recovered from the Pacific site of the CNEOS 2014-01-08 bolide in Chemical Geology in December 2024, followed in March 2025 by a study relating the morphology and chemistry of D-type spherules - a demonstration that the analytical approach works and that its conclusions are contestable in the open literature. entities.label: UAP Disclosure Act of 2023 (S.Amdt. 797 to S. 2226; Division G of the Senate-passed FY2024 NDAA)
entities.sub: disclosure-legislation
entities.desc: The UAP Disclosure Act of 2023 is the only text ever passed by a chamber of the United States Congress that legislates on the assumption that recovered non-human technology and biological evidence of non-human intelligence exist and are held, in part, by private entities. It began as S.Amdt. 797, submitted by Senator Schumer on 13 July 2023 for himself and Senators Rounds, Rubio, Gillibrand, Young and Heinrich, and printed in the Congressional Record at 169 Cong. Rec. S2953-S2959. It travelled into the engrossed Senate bill as Division G, Sections 9001 through 9015, and the Senate passed it on 27 July 2023. Section 9002 states the premise in statutory findings: that legislation is necessary 'because credible evidence and testimony indicates that Federal Government unidentified anomalous phenomena records exist that have not been declassified,' in part because of Atomic Energy Act exemptions and an 'over-broad interpretation of transclassified foreign nuclear information.' Section 9003 defines 'non-human intelligence' as 'any sentient intelligent non-human lifeform regardless of nature or ultimate origin,' defines 'legacy program' to reach commercial, academic and private-sector reverse-engineering endeavours predating enactment, and defines 'controlling authority' to include any private entity in physical possession of such material. Sections 9004 through 9006 create a Records Collection at the National Archives with a presumption of immediate disclosure. Sections 9007 through 9009 create a nine-member Review Board appointed by the President with the advice and consent of the Senate, barred from including anyone with previous or current involvement in any legacy program, empowered to order disclosure absent clear and convincing evidence for postponement, and required to produce a Controlled Disclosure Campaign Plan. Section 9010 orders the exercise of eminent domain. Section 9014 authorises $20,000,000 for fiscal year 2024. Sections 9007 through 9011 and 9014 were removed in conference and have never been enacted.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded A on a global pass (rank 9 of 1170, score 134). 26 connections, 8 of them custody/funding/programmatic, 3 official denials recorded against it. Axes C3/A3/D3.

S.Amdt. 797 was submitted on 13 July 2023 by Senator Schumer 'for himself, Mr. Rounds, Mr. Rubio, Mrs. Gillibrand, Mr. Young, and Mr. Heinrich' and ordered to lie on the table; its text was printed in the Congressional Record for that day at pages S2953-S2959, opening 'At the appropriate place, insert the following: TITLE _--UNIDENTIFIED ANOMALOUS PHENOMENA DISCLOSURE' and short-titled the 'Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Disclosure Act of 2023' or the 'UAP Disclosure Act of 2023'. The cosponsor roster is the fact worth holding onto: three Republicans and three Democrats, including the sitting Chairman and Vice Chairman track of the Senate Intelligence Committee's Republican side and two Armed Services members. That procedural fact cuts both ways: it is how the Act got as far as it did, and it is also why it had no committee constituency to defend it in conference.

entities.desc: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2022, Public Law 117-81, approved 27 December 2021. Section 1683, codified at 50 U.S.C. 3373, is the first statute to require a standing DoD/ODNI office for unidentified aerial phenomena, superseding the Navy-led UAP Task Force. It mandates field-investigation line organizations, a science plan to explain performance 'that exceed the known state of the art in science or technology', and an intelligence collection and analysis plan on the 'origins and intentions' of UAP.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded C on a global pass (rank 684 of 1170, score 25). 4 connections, 0 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C0/A0/D0.

claims.text: Sec. 1683 carries the note '50 USC 3373' and is titled 'ESTABLISHMENT OF OFFICE, ORGANIZATIONAL STRUCTURE, AND AUTHORITIES TO ADDRESS UNIDENTIFIED AERIAL PHENOMENA'. Sec. 1683(a) required the Secretary of Defense, in coordination with the DNI, within 180 days of enactment, to establish an office 'to carry out the duties of the Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force, as in effect on the day before the date of enactment of this Act'.

Sec. 1683(c) requires the Secretary and DNI to designate 'one or more line organizations within the Department of Defense and the intelligence community that possess appropriate expertise, authorities, accesses, data, systems, platforms, and capabilities to rapidly respond to, and conduct field investigations of, incidents involving unidentified aerial phenomena' and to ensure those organizations have 'adequate personnel with the requisite expertise, equipment, transportation, and other resources necessary to respond rapidly'.

Sec. 1683(d)(1) directs designation of line organizations 'primarily responsible for scientific, technical, and operational analysis of data gathered by field investigations ... including with respect to the testing of materials, medical studies, and development of theoretical models'. Sec. 1683(d)(2) requires directives ensuring each such organization 'has authority to draw on the special expertise of persons outside the Federal Government with appropriate security clearances.'

Sec. 1683(f) requires a science plan to 'account for characteristics and performance of unidentified aerial phenomena that exceed the known state of the art in science or technology, including in the areas of propulsion, aerodynamic control, signatures, structures, materials, sensors, countermeasures, weapons, electronics, and power generation' and to 'provide the foundation for potential future investments to replicate any such advanced characteristics and performance.'

Sec. 1683(e)(2) requires an intelligence collection and analysis plan 'to gain as much knowledge as possible regarding the technical and operational characteristics, origins, and intentions of unidentified aerial phenomena'.

Sec. 1683(e)(1)(B) requires that DoD and IC military, civilian AND CONTRACTOR personnel 'have access to procedures by which the personnel shall report incidents or information, including adverse physiological effects, involving or associated with unidentified aerial phenomena directly to the Office'.
PL 117-81 was 'Approved December 27, 2021.'

entities.label: FY2023 NDAA, Public Law 117-263 - Sec. 1673 (50 U.S.C. 3373b) UAP reporting/whistleblower protection; Div. F secs. 6802-6803 establishing AARO
entities.sub: authorizing-statutes
entities.desc: The James M. Inhofe National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2023 is Public Law 117-263, enacted from H.R. 7776 and approved 23 December 2022 at 136 Stat. 2395. Buried inside a routine defence authorisation of more than a thousand pages is the single most consequential piece of UAP law on this board: it rewrote 50 U.S.C. 3373 to stand up the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office under the Secretary of Defense in coordination with the Director of National Intelligence, within 120 days of enactment. The statute obliges that office to standardise collection and reporting of unidentified anomalous phenomena across the entire Defense and intelligence enterprise, to coordinate with the FAA, NASA and DHS, to run field investigations, to report to Congress in both classified and unclassified form, and - the provision that matters most here - to compile a historical record of US Government involvement with UAP reaching back to 1 January 1945. Congress does not order a seventy-eight-year retrospective historical record of an agency that has nothing to look back on; the 1945 start date is the year of Trinity and of the earliest incidents alleged in the recovery narrative, and it was chosen by legislators who had by then been briefed in closed session. The Act is therefore both the legal instrument that created AARO and, read as an artifact, a congressional acknowledgement that a concealed institutional history exists and needs to be reconstructed. Section 3373 has been amended repeatedly since - by Pub. L. 118-31 and Pub. L. 119-60 - which is the legislative signature of a fight that did not end when the office was created.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded B on a global pass (rank 177 of 1170, score 48). 3 connections, 0 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C0/A0/D0.

claims.text: Sec. 1673 carries the note '50 USC 3373b' and is titled 'UNIDENTIFIED ANOMALOUS PHENOMENA REPORTING PROCEDURES'. Sec. 1673(a)(1) requires a secure mechanism for authorized reporting of '(A) any event relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena; and (B) any activity or program by a department or agency of the Federal Government or a contractor of such a department or agency relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, including with respect to material retrieval, material analysis, reverse engineering, research and development, detection and tracking, developmental or operational testing, and security protections and enforcement.'

Sec. 1673(b)(1): 'An authorized disclosure-- (A) shall not be subject to a nondisclosure agreement entered into by the individual who makes the disclosure; (B) shall be deemed to comply with any regulation or order issued under the authority of Executive Order 13526 ... or chapter 18 of the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 (42 U.S.C. 2271 et seq.); and (C) is not a violation of section 798 of title 18, United States Code, or other provision of law relating to the disclosure of information.' The express reference to the Atomic Energy Act restricted-data regime is on the face of the statute.

Sec. 1673(b)(2)(A) prohibits reprisal: no official with personnel authority 'shall ... take or fail to take, or threaten to take or fail to take, a personnel action, including the revocation or suspension of security clearances, or termination of employment, with respect to any individual as a reprisal for any authorized disclosure.'

Sec. 1673(a)(4)(B) requires that within 72 hours of determining an authorized disclosure relates to 'a restricted access activity, a special access program, or a compartmented access program that has not been explicitly and clearly reported to the congressional defense committees or the congressional intelligence committees, the Secretary shall report such disclosure to such committees and the congressional leadership.' The statute thereby contemplates the existence of unreported special access programs touching UAP.

Sec. 1673(b)(3) requires the Secretary of Defense, DNI, Secretary of Homeland Security, other agency heads 'that have supported investigations' of UAP events and programs, and FEDERAL CONTRACTORS that have supported such investigations, to identify existing nondisclosure agreements covering that subject matter.

Division F (Intelligence Authorization Act for FY2023), Title LXVIII, sec. 6802(a): 'Section 1683 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2022 (50 U.S.C. 3373), as amended by title XVI of this Act, is amended to read as follows: "SEC. 1683. ESTABLISHMENT OF ALL-DOMAIN ANOMALY RESOLUTION OFFICE."' Sec. 1683(a)(2) as amended: 'The office established under paragraph (1) shall be known as the "All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office"'.

AARO reporting chain fixed by statute, sec. 1683(b)(3) as amended: the Director of AARO 'shall report directly to the Deputy Secretary of Defense and the Principal Deputy Director of National Intelligence', and reports 'to the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security on all administrative matters' and 'to the Deputy Secretary of Defense and the Principal Deputy Director of National Intelligence on all operational and security matters'. The Director is appointed by SecDef in consultation with the DNI; the Deputy Director is appointed by the DNI in coordination with SecDef.

Statutory definition inserted by sec. 6802, new 50 U.S.C. 3373(n)(8): "unidentified anomalous phenomena" means '(A) airborne objects that are not immediately identifiable; (B) transmedium objects or devices; and (C) submerged objects or devices that are not immediately identifiable and that display behavior or performance characteristics suggesting that the objects or devices may be related to the objects described in subparagraph (A).' Sec. 3373(n)(7): 'transmedium objects or devices' means objects or devices that are '(A) observed to transition between space and the atmosphere, or between the atmosphere and bodies of water; and (B) not immediately identifiable.'

Division F sec. 6803, note '50 USC 3373 note', is titled 'COMPTROLLER GENERAL OF THE UNITED STATES AUDITS AND BRIEFINGS ON UNIDENTIFIED ANOMALOUS PHENOMENA HISTORICAL RECORD REPORT' - a GAO audit requirement attached to AARO's Historical Record Report.
PL 117-263 was 'Approved December 23, 2022.'

claims.text: The FY2023 NDAA carries the concealment premise in enacted text: sec. 1673(a)(1)(B) enumerates 'material retrieval, material analysis, reverse engineering' as categories of federal or contractor ACTIVITY OR PROGRAM that a person may need protection to report, and sec. 1673(b)(1)(A)-(B) voids NDAs and Atomic Energy Act restrictions for such disclosures. Congress does not write NDA-voiding and AEA-override language for activities it believes do not exist. Reasoning: the operative nouns are activity/program categories, not hypotheticals, and the remedy structure presupposes existing legal instruments suppressing disclosure.

entities.desc: P.L. 118-31 is the document that records the stripping. The Senate passed S. 2226 on 27 July 2023 carrying two separate UAP regimes: Division G, the fifteen-section UAP Disclosure Act, and Division M Section 1102, Warner's contractor turn-in inside the Intelligence Authorization Act for FY2024. The Act signed on 22 December 2023 contains, in place of Division G, a three-section Subtitle C of Title XVIII: Sec. 1841, the Records Collection at the National Archives; Sec. 1842, review and transmission by heads of Government offices within 300 days; and Sec. 1843, grounds for postponement. There is no Sec. 9007 equivalent, no Sec. 9010 equivalent, no Controlled Disclosure Campaign Plan and no authorization of appropriations. In place of Sec. 1102 it contains Sec. 7343, a bare funding limitation. The Act does retain teeth in two places the House committees controlled: Sec. 1687 cuts off DoD funds for UAP activity 'protected under any form of special access or restricted access limitations' unless the Secretary of Defense has described it to the defence and intelligence committees and congressional leadership, and bars independent research and development funding on UAP from being charged as an indirect expense unless disclosed. Sec. 7343 does the same on the intelligence side. Both are one-year limitations tied to funds authorised by that Act, and neither was renewed in FY2025 or FY2026.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded A on a global pass (rank 41 of 1170, score 87). 12 connections, 1 of them custody/funding/programmatic, 1 official denial recorded against it. Axes C2/A3/D3.

claims.text: Sec. 1841 carries the note '44 USC 2107 note' and is titled 'UNIDENTIFIED ANOMALOUS PHENOMENA RECORDS COLLECTION AT THE NATIONAL ARCHIVES AND RECORDS ADMINISTRATION'. Sec. 1841(a)(1)(A) required the Archivist, within 60 days of enactment, to commence establishment of the 'Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection'.

Sec. 1841(a)(1)(C) defines the scope of the Collection: 'record copies of all Government, Government-provided, or Government-funded records relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence (or equivalent subjects by any other name with the specific and sole exclusion of temporarily non-attributed objects), which shall be transmitted to the National Archives in accordance with section 2107 of title 44, United States Code.' The phrases 'technologies of unknown origin' and 'non-human intelligence' are enacted federal statutory text.

Sec. 1842(a)(2) imposes absolute prohibitions: '(A) Destruction; alteration; mutilation.--No unidentified anomalous phenomena record shall be destroyed, altered, or mutilated in any way. (B) ... No unidentified anomalous phenomena record made available or disclosed to the public prior to the date of the enactment of this Act may be withheld, redacted, postponed for public disclosure, or reclassified. (C) ... No unidentified anomalous phenomena record created by a person or entity outside the Federal Government ... shall be withheld, redacted, postponed for public disclosure, or reclassified.'

Sec. 1842(c)(1) required each head of a Government office, not later than 300 days after enactment (i.e. by approximately 16 October 2024), to 'review, identify, and organize each unidentified anomalous phenomena record in the custody or possession of the office for (A) disclosure to the public; and (B) transmission to the Archivist.'

Sec. 1843(a) sets the postponement standard: disclosure 'may be postponed ... if the original classification authority makes a determination that there is clear and convincing evidence' of one of four harms, including that public disclosure would reveal 'any other matter currently relating to the military defense, intelligence operations, or conduct of foreign relations of the United States, the disclosure of which would demonstrably and substantially impair the national security of the United States'. The determination is made by the agency holding the record; no independent board reviews it.

Sec. 1842(g)(2)(D) sets the outer disclosure deadline: 'Each unidentified anomalous phenomena record shall be publicly disclosed in full, and available in the Collection, not later than the date that is 25 years after the date of the first creation of the record by the originating body, unless the President certifies that-- (i) continued postponement is made necessary by an identifiable harm to the military defense, intelligence operations, law enforcement, or conduct of foreign relations; and (ii) the identifiable harm is of such gravity that it outweighs the public interest in disclosure.'

Sec. 1843(b) allows unilateral withdrawal: 'Senior Agency Officials designated in accordance with Executive Order 13526 or any successor Orders may withdraw records in the Collection that are determined to be both not related to unidentified anomalous phenomena and properly classified', subject only to notification of congressional leadership and the oversight committees named in sec. 1841(e).

Sec. 1841(e) assigns continuing legislative oversight of the Collection to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, Armed Services, and Select Intelligence Committees, and to the House Oversight and Accountability, Armed Services, and Permanent Select Intelligence Committees.

Subtitle C as enacted consists of only three sections: 1841 (Records Collection at NARA), 1842 (review, identification, transmission, public disclosure by Government offices), and 1843 (grounds for postponement). The enacted text contains no 'Review Board' and no 'eminent domain' language.
claims.source: PL 118-31 Div. A, Title XVIII, Subtitle C, table of contents and full text

claims.text: Division G (Intelligence Authorization Act for FY2024), sec. 7343(b): 'None of the funds authorized to be appropriated or otherwise made available by this division may be obligated or expended in support of any activity involving unidentified anomalous phenomena protected under any form of special access or restricted access limitation unless the Director of National Intelligence has provided the details of the activity to the appropriate committees of Congress and congressional leadership, including for any activities described in a report released by the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office in fiscal year 2024.'

Sec. 7343(c): 'Independent research and development funding relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena shall not be allowable as indirect expenses for purposes of contracts covered by such instruction, unless such material and information is made available to the appropriate congressional committees and leadership.' This is a defense-contractor IR&D cost-allowability lever aimed at privately funded UAP work.
Sec. 7341 amends 50 U.S.C. 3373(k)(1) to shift the annual UAP report obligation from the DNI and SecDef jointly to 'the Director of the Office' (AARO).

entities.label: FY2026 NDAA, Public Law 119-60 - secs. 1671-1673, NORAD/NORTHCOM intercept briefings and UAP classification-guide accounting
entities.sub: authorizing-statutes
entities.desc: The FY2026 NDAA shows the disclosure agenda reduced to housekeeping and the oversight machinery beginning to be dismantled. P.L. 119-60, approved 18 December 2025, contains a Subtitle E of Title XVI headed 'Matters Relating to Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena' with three sections. Sec. 1671 amends 50 U.S.C. 3373(l) to require that AARO's briefings include details of any UAP intercepts conducted by NORAD or United States Northern Command, with the first such briefing required to reach back over intercepts 'that occurred during the period beginning on January 1, 2004' — Congress choosing the year of the Nimitz encounters as its retroactive floor. Sec. 1672 repeals Sec. 413 of the IAA FY2022, codified at 50 U.S.C. 3373a, and rewrites the data-availability clause so that intelligence and DoD components must make UAP data available 'immediately' to AARO. Sec. 1673 orders the AARO Director within 180 days to make an accounting of the security classification guides applying to UAP reporting and permits issuance of a consolidated security classification matrix — a direct probe at the classification architecture itself. What the Act does not contain is as important: zero instances of 'eminent domain', 'non-human', 'legacy program' or 'reverse engineer'; no Review Board; and, critically, no renewal of the Sec. 1687 or Sec. 7343 funding limitations. Those were one-year restrictions on funds authorised by the FY2024 Act. They were not renewed in FY2025 and were not renewed here, so the statutory bar on funding undisclosed UAP special access programmes has now lapsed for two consecutive authorisation cycles. The Intelligence Authorization Act for FY2026 that rides in Division F contains no UAP provisions at all.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded A on a global pass (rank 91 of 1170, score 66). 9 connections, 1 of them custody/funding/programmatic, 1 official denial recorded against it. Axes C1/A2/D1.

claims.text: Sec. 1671(a) adds 50 U.S.C. 3373(l)(5): 'Each briefing under this subsection shall include, for the period covered by the briefing, details on any unidentified anomalous phenomena intercepts conducted by the North American Aerospace Defense Command or the United States Northern Command', with summaries of 'the number, location, and nature of such intercepts' and 'a description of the procedures and protocols followed during the intercepts, including any data collected or analyzed during such intercepts.'

Sec. 1671(a) new subparagraph (C) requires the Director of AARO to 'inform the appropriate congressional committees of any failure by the North American Aerospace Defense Command or the United States Northern Command to provide timely information on unidentified anomalous phenomena intercepts' - an anti-stonewalling clause written against two combatant commands by name.

Sec. 1671(b), note '50 USC 3373 note', imposes a retrospective look-back: the first briefing after enactment 'shall include details on any unidentified anomalous phenomena intercepts conducted by the North American Aerospace Defense Command or the United States Northern Command not previously provided that occurred during the period beginning on January 1, 2004, and ending on the last day of the period otherwise covered by the briefing.'

Sec. 1672(a) repeals sec. 413 of the IAA for FY2022 (50 U.S.C. 3373a). Sec. 1672(b) rewrites 50 U.S.C. 3373(f)(1)(A) to read: 'The Director of National Intelligence and the Secretary of Defense shall jointly require that each element of the intelligence community and component of the Department of Defense with data relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena makes such data available immediately to the Office in a manner that protects intelligence sources and methods.' The added qualifier 'in a manner that protects intelligence sources and methods' is new and was not in the repealed provision.

Sec. 1673(a), note '50 USC 3373 note', requires the Director of AARO within 180 days of enactment to 'make an accounting of security classification guides that apply to information used for reports and investigations of unidentified anomalous phenomena' and permits issuance of 'a consolidated security classification matrix for programs relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena to provide a resource for programs that support or may be affected by investigations relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena.' Sec. 1673(b) requires the results to be included in the 2026 annual report under 50 U.S.C. 3373(k).
PL 119-60 was 'Approved December 18, 2025.'
claims.source: PLAW-119publ60 enactment line

claims.text: Sec. 1673's premise is that no one currently has a map of which classification guides control UAP information across the government - four years after AARO was created by statute. The authorisation of a 'consolidated security classification matrix' for 'programs relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena' is an admission in enacted law that a plurality of such programs exists and that their classification authorities are not centrally known. Reasoning: Congress does not order an accounting of guides that are already inventoried.

The 1 January 2004 look-back date in sec. 1671(b) is the month of the USS Nimitz / 'Tic Tac' encounters. Congress selected a start date that reaches back to the earliest incident in the modern public record rather than to AARO's creation, indicating the committees believe intercept records from that period exist and have not been briefed. Reasoning: no other event anchors that specific date in UAP legislative history.
P.L. 119-60 was approved 18 December 2025 and originated as S. 1071; its Subtitle E consists of Secs. 1671, 1672 and 1673.
Sec. 1671(b) requires the first NORAD/NORTHCOM intercept briefing to cover intercepts 'during the period beginning on January 1, 2004.'
Sec. 1673 requires an accounting of security classification guides applying to UAP reports and investigations within 180 days, and permits a consolidated security classification matrix.
P.L. 119-60 contains zero instances of 'eminent domain', 'non-human', 'legacy program' or 'reverse engineer'.

entities.label: House Oversight hearing, 26 July 2023 - 'Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena: Implications on National Security, Public Safety, and Government Transparency'
entities.sub: congressional-hearings
entities.desc: On 26 July 2023 at 10:00 am in 2154 Rayburn, the House Committee on Oversight and Accountability's Subcommittee on National Security, the Border, and Foreign Affairs held the first congressional hearing at which a former intelligence officer testified under oath that the United States possesses craft of non-human origin. The witnesses were Ryan Graves, formerly of VFA-11 and now executive director of Americans for Safe Aerospace; retired Cdr. David Fravor, former commanding officer of VFA-41 and the lead aircrew on the 14 November 2004 Nimitz intercept; and David Grusch, former National Reconnaissance Office representative to the Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Task Force. Rep. Tim Burchett and Rep. Anna Paulina Luna drove the hearing; James Comer chaired the full committee. Three things came out of it that the board treats as permanent. Fravor placed on the record, in writing and under oath, that after the most corroborated encounter in the modern record 'the incident was never investigated, none of my crew were ever questioned, tapes were never taken.' Grusch testified that he had been informed of a multi-decade crash retrieval and reverse-engineering programme, that he had provided the information to the Intelligence Community Inspector General and to Congress, that he knew the exact locations and had provided them to the ICIG and the Intelligence committees in classified session, and that he had witnessed and reported administrative terrorism against colleagues. Graves testified to the operational reporting problem in the Atlantic operating areas. What did not come out of it is equally important: no contractor was called, no document production was compelled, and the 'specific cooperative and hostile witness list' Grusch offered Rep. Nancy Mace under oath has never been produced publicly. The hearing established the subject as legitimate congressional business and simultaneously demonstrated the limits of a committee without jurisdiction over the compartments it is asking about.

entities.label: House Oversight Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets hearing, 9 September 2025 - 'Restoring Public Trust Through UAP Transparency and Whistleblower Protection'
entities.sub: congressional-hearings
entities.desc: On 9 September 2025 at 10:00 am in HVC-210 the House Oversight Committee's Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets, chaired by Rep. Anna Paulina Luna with Rep. Jasmine Crockett as ranking member, held 'Restoring Public Trust Through UAP Transparency and Whistleblower Protection'. The witnesses were Jeffrey Nuccetelli, a sixteen-year Air Force veteran who served in security forces at Vandenberg; Senior Chief Petty Officer Alexandro C. Wiggins, an operations specialist aboard USS Jackson (LCS-6); the journalist George Knapp; Dylan Borland, a former Air Force geospatial intelligence specialist; and, as minority witness, Joe Spielberger, senior policy counsel at the Project On Government Oversight. This is the hinge hearing of the modern era because it moved the enquiry from the phenomenon to the machinery. Nuccetelli testified to the 14 October 2003 Vandenberg incidents over missile defence sites, said each incident was 'witnessed by multiple personnel, documented, investigated and reported up the chain of command', stated that 'official Air Force records documenting it are now held by AARO and the FBI', and reported that a witness was threatened and told to keep quiet. Wiggins testified to 15 February 2023, approximately 7:15 pm PST, aboard USS Jackson: four self-luminous Tic-Tac-shaped objects, one emerging from the ocean, holding formation and departing with near-instantaneous acceleration and no propulsion signature or sonic boom, recorded on the ship's Star SAFIRE multi-spectral EO/IR system with timestamped data and reported to the tactical action officer. Knapp gave the most detailed public account yet of AAWSAP and BAASS: prime contractor status, roughly fifty investigators with top secret clearances, 27 months of operation, three dozen preliminary reports, over a hundred research papers, a 240,000-case data warehouse designed by Jacques Vallee that reportedly remains in agency use, and the fact that most of the papers remain unreleased by DIA. He also described James Lacatski's 2023 statement to DHS that the United States possesses a craft of unknown origin whose interior had been accessed, and the incomplete Bigelow-Lockheed material negotiation. Borland described a summer 2012 triangular craft observation at Langley AFB, alleged more than a decade of retaliation including blacklisting and clearance-record manipulation, and stated he had filed complaints with AARO in March 2023 and the Intelligence Community Inspector General in August 2023. The committee's two findings are the ones that matter: agencies withheld information from the Task Force, and UAP-related spending flows to entities outside the reach of the Freedom of Information Act. That second finding is the direct antecedent of Rep. Burlison's FY2027 NDAA amendment adopted on 23 July 2026, which extends disclosure obligations to government contractors. As of 12 August 2026 this remains the most recent congressional hearing devoted to UAP.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded A on a global pass (rank 13 of 1170, score 117). 33 connections, 6 of them custody/funding/programmatic, 1 official denial recorded against it. Axes C2/A1/D3.

entities.desc: The only open Senate hearing on AARO under its first director, held 19 April 2023 before the Senate Armed Services Subcommittee on Emerging Threats and Capabilities chaired by Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, published as S.Hrg. 118-648. Sean Kirkpatrick testified that AARO was investigating more than 650 cases and that spherical objects made up nearly half of all UAP reports the office had received. His testimony that AARO had found no credible evidence of extraterrestrial activity or of objects defying known physics generated immediate controversy over what the office had actually examined versus what it had asserted. The hearing occurred three months before David Grusch testified in the House, and it is the last moment at which the Department's account went unchallenged in a congressional venue.

entities.label: FY2022 NDAA Sec. 1683 (P.L. 117-81; 50 U.S.C. 3373)
entities.sub: Gillibrand's founding authority for AARO
entities.desc: Section 1683 of the FY2022 NDAA, signed 27 December 2021, is the statutory root of the entire modern apparatus. It directed the Secretary of Defense, in coordination with the DNI, to establish within 180 days an office inside the Office of the Secretary of Defense or a joint DoD/ODNI organisation to carry out the duties of the Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force. Its enumerated duties reach beyond analysis into governance: synchronising and standardising collection and reporting 'including adverse physiological effects' across DoD and the intelligence community, forcing incident reports into a centralised repository, evaluating links to adversary and non-state actors, and coordinating with the FAA, NASA, DHS, NOAA and the Department of Energy. It is codified at 50 U.S.C. 3373, and every subsequent UAP provision — Sec. 1673 of the FY2023 NDAA, Sec. 1687 and Sec. 7343 of the FY2024 NDAA, Sec. 6801 of the IAA FY2025, and Secs. 1671-1673 of the FY2026 NDAA — cross-references it. It was restated in full by Sec. 6802 of the IAA FY2023, which named the office the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office, set the Director reporting to the Deputy Secretary of Defense and the Principal Deputy DNI, entitled ten named intelligence elements to place detailees inside it, and added subsection (j), the Historical Record Report on the United States Government's dealings with UAP built from intelligence community records, oral histories and interviews of current and former officials.
