entities.label: FY2023 NDAA Sec. 1673 (P.L. 117-263; 50 U.S.C. 3373b)
entities.sub: Authorized reporting mechanism and whistleblower protection
entities.desc: Section 1673 is the provision that makes the legacy programme a matter of enacted federal law rather than allegation, and it is routinely underrated. It orders the Secretary of Defense, through the head of AARO, to establish a secure mechanism for authorized reporting of 'any activity or program by a department or agency of the Federal Government or a contractor of such a department or agency relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, including with respect to material retrieval, material analysis, reverse engineering, research and development, detection and tracking, developmental or operational testing, and security protections and enforcement.' Congress does not legislate reporting channels for categories of programme it believes do not exist. The protections are unusually strong: an authorized disclosure 'shall not be subject to a nondisclosure agreement entered into by the individual who makes the disclosure,' is deemed to comply with Executive Order 13526 and with chapter 18 of the Atomic Energy Act, and 'is not a violation of section 798 of title 18' or any other disclosure statute. Reprisal — including 'the revocation or suspension of security clearances, or termination of employment' — is prohibited. Subsection (b)(3) then orders DoD, ODNI, DHS, other supporting agencies and Federal contractors that 'have supported or are supporting such activities and programs' to conduct comprehensive searches of all records relating to nondisclosure orders on these subjects and deliver copies to AARO, which must make them accessible to the defence and intelligence committees and congressional leadership. This is a statutory census of the gag orders. It has never been reported as completed.

claims.text: Sec. 1673(a)(1)(B) covers 'any activity or program by a department or agency of the Federal Government or a contractor of such a department or agency relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, including with respect to material retrieval, material analysis, reverse engineering, research and development, detection and tracking, developmental or operational testing, and security protections and enforcement.'

Sec. 1673(b)(1)(A)-(C): an authorized disclosure 'shall not be subject to a nondisclosure agreement', 'shall be deemed to comply with any regulation or order issued under the authority of Executive Order 13526 ... or chapter 18 of the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 (42 U.S.C. 2271 et seq.)', and 'is not a violation of section 798 of title 18, United States Code'.

Sec. 1673(a)(4)(A) requires sharing of an authorized disclosure with AARO personnel 'regardless of the classification of information contained in the disclosure or any nondisclosure agreements', unless the disclosure likely relates to a SAP or compartmented access program already 'explicitly and clearly reported to the congressional defense committees or the congressional intelligence committees, and is documented as meeting those criteria.'

Sec. 1673(a)(1)(B) legislates a reporting channel for programmes involving 'material retrieval, material analysis, reverse engineering, research and development' relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena.
Sec. 1673(b)(1)(A) provides that an authorized disclosure 'shall not be subject to a nondisclosure agreement entered into by the individual who makes the disclosure.'
Sec. 1673(b)(2)(A) prohibits reprisal including revocation or suspension of security clearances or termination of employment.

Sec. 1673(b)(3)(A) requires agencies and contractors to conduct comprehensive searches of all records relating to nondisclosure orders on these subjects and to provide copies to AARO for congressional access.

entities.label: P.L. 118-31 Subtitle C — Secs. 1841-1843 (what survived)
entities.sub: Enacted UAP records regime, 22 December 2023
entities.desc: What Congress actually enacted is a records-transfer statute with the enforcement removed. Sec. 1841 orders the Archivist to establish the Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection, requires physical integrity and original provenance to be preserved, requires public availability within 30 days of transmission and online within 180 days thereafter, and assigns continuing oversight to six committees. Sec. 1842 bars destruction, alteration or mutilation of any UAP record, bars withholding or reclassification of anything already public, bars withholding of records created outside the Federal Government, and gives agency heads 300 days to review and organise. Sec. 1843 is where it fails. Postponement may be ordered where 'the original classification authority makes a determination that there is clear and convincing evidence' of harm — the clear and convincing standard survives, but the person applying it is the classifier rather than an independent board, which converts a check into a self-certification. Senior Agency Officials may unilaterally withdraw records from the Collection on a determination that they are both unrelated to UAP and properly classified, needing only to notify Congress 60 days beforehand. Where disclosure is postponed the agency head must notify congressional leadership within 15 days with a reason. There is no appeal, no de novo review, no subpoena and no mechanism reaching material rather than paper.

claims.text: Sec. 1841(a)(1)(C) puts the phrases 'technologies of unknown origin' and 'non-human intelligence' into enacted federal law as categories of record the Archivist must collect, '(or equivalent subjects by any other name with the specific and sole exclusion of temporarily non-attributed objects)'.

Sec. 1842(g)(2)(D) requires full public disclosure of each UAP record within 25 years of its first creation unless the President personally certifies identifiable harm outweighing the public interest.
Sec. 1843(a) vests the postponement determination in 'the original classification authority' rather than in any independent reviewer.

Sec. 1843(b) permits Senior Agency Officials to withdraw records from the Collection, with 60 days' notice to Congress, on their own determination that the records are unrelated and properly classified.
Sec. 1842(a)(2) prohibits destruction, alteration or mutilation of any UAP record and bars reclassification of anything already publicly disclosed before enactment.

Retaining the 'clear and convincing evidence' standard while transferring its application from an independent board to the original classifier preserves the appearance of the Senate's regime while removing its effect.

entities.label: Section 9010(a) — Exercise of Eminent Domain
entities.sub: Statutory text passed by the Senate, 27 July 2023
entities.desc: The single most important sentence in the modern disclosure record, and a Tier 1 documented fact whose existence does not depend on believing any witness. Section 9010 of Division G of S. 2226, headed 'Disclosure of Recovered Technologies of Unknown Origin and Biological Evidence of Non-Human Intelligence,' opens: 'The Federal Government shall exercise eminent domain over any and all recovered technologies of unknown origin and biological evidence of non-human intelligence that may be controlled by private persons or entities in the interests of the public good.' Subsection (b) requires that 'any and all such material, should it exist, shall be made available to the Review Board for personal examination and subsequent disclosure determination at a location suitable to the controlling authority of said material.' Subsection (c) directs the Board to decide 'whether the material examined constitutes technologies of unknown origin or biological evidence of non-human intelligence beyond a reasonable doubt.' The drafting is careful and revealing in both directions: the hedge 'should it exist' preserves deniability, while 'shall exercise' is mandatory and the taking is aimed exclusively at private holders, not at Government agencies — the Government does not need eminent domain against itself. A chamber of Congress passed this. It was then deleted, and the deletion is the fact that organises this entire domain.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded A on a global pass (rank 97 of 1170, score 64). 4 connections, 2 of them custody/funding/programmatic, 2 official denials recorded against it. Axes C3/A2/D3.

entities.label: IAA FY2024 Sec. 1102 — contractor turn-in of 'non-earth origin or exotic' UAP material
entities.sub: Division M (Intelligence Authorization Act for FY2024) of S. 2226 as passed by the Senate, 27 Jul 2023; the same text is Sec. 1104 of S. 2103 as reported by SSCI, 22 Jun 2023. Turn-in mandate STRIPPED in conference; enacted as Sec. 7343, Div. G, P.L. 118-31 — a funding limitation only.
entities.desc: Warner's Section 1102 is the most direct legislative assault on contractor-held material ever passed by a chamber of Congress, and it is far less well known than the eminent domain clause. It opens with a sense of Congress that the Federal Government 'must expand awareness about any historical exotic technology antecedents previously provided by the Federal Government for research and development purposes' — a statement that the Government has previously handed exotic technology to industry. It then cuts off all funds for UAP activity under special or restricted access not 'formally, officially, explicitly, and specifically described, explained, and justified' to Congress and the AARO Director, enumerating six categories including personnel whose mission is 'capturing, recovering, and securing unidentified anomalous phenomena craft or pieces and components of such craft,' analysis to determine 'material composition, method of manufacture, origin,' 'reverse engineering or replicating unidentified anomalous phenomena technology,' and 'any aerospace craft that uses propulsion technology other than chemical propellants, solar power, or electric ion thrust.' Subsection (d) then requires any current or former Federal contractor holding such material to notify the AARO Director within 60 days and, within 180 days, to make available all of it plus 'a comprehensive list of all non-earth origin or exotic unidentified anomalous phenomena material.' Subsection (e) grants full civil and criminal immunity to those who comply. Subsection (f) disallows independent research and development funding on such material as an indirect expense unless it is surrendered, effective 60 days after enactment and applicable to money appropriated before as well as after. The Senate passed all of this on 27 July 2023.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded A on a global pass (rank 34 of 1170, score 91). 10 connections, 3 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C3/A3/D3.

claims.text: RENUMBERING AND ATTRITION BETWEEN COMMITTEE AND FLOOR. In S. 2103 as reported by the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence on 22 June 2023, Title XI--Other Matters contained four sections: 'Sec. 1101. Modification of reporting requirement for All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office.'; 'Sec. 1102. Modifications to notification on the provision of defense sensitive [support]'; 'Sec. 1103. Modification of congressional oversight of special access programs.'; and 'Sec. 1104. Funding limitations relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena.' The engrossed Division M carries only the first and the last of these, renumbered 1101 and 1102. Two provisions were therefore dropped between committee and the Senate-passed text, and one of the two dropped provisions was a direct amendment to the congressional oversight regime for special access programs. That is a soft joint the board did not previously have: the same intelligence committee that wrote the UAP funding limitation also wrote a special access program oversight amendment alongside it, and only the funding limitation survived to the floor text.

claims.text: Because the engrossed body was never read, the specific elements the board attributes to Sec. 1102 - a 60-day contractor notification deadline running to the Director of AARO, a 180-day deadline to make material available, the phrase 'non-earth origin or exotic', and the phrase 'assessment, analysis, and inspection' - remain corroborated ONLY by DefenseScoop's 27 June 2023 report, and that report is describing Sec. 1104 of S. 2103 as reported, not Sec. 1102 of Division M as engrossed. The reporter quotes the following fragments inside quotation marks: a mandate on any person currently or formerly under contract with the federal government that 'has in their possession material or information provided by or derived from the' government relating to UAP 'that formerly or currently is protected by any form of special access or restricted access' to notify the AARO Director within 60 days of enactment; and, no later than 180 days after passage, to make 'all such material and information' and 'a comprehensive list of all non-earth origin or exotic [UAP] material' available to AARO for 'assessment, analysis, and inspection'. The bracketed [UAP] is the reporter's insertion, which is itself a sign that the quoted string is being edited. Treat these as reported fragments of the REPORTED text, not as verified text of the ENGROSSED section.
claims.source: Brandi Vincent, 'Senate's intelligence authorization bill questions reverse engineering of government-recovered UAPs', DefenseScoop, 27 June 2023 - https://defensescoop.com/2023/06/27/senates-intelligence-authorization-bill-questions-reverse-engineering-of-government-recovered-uaps/

claims.text: ENACTED SUCCESSOR IDENTIFIED AND CONFIRMED FROM A PRIMARY SOURCE. The provision was enacted as Section 7343 of Division G of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024, Pub. L. 118-31. The Explanatory Statement to accompany the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024, printed in the Congressional Record by Sen. Warner on 14 December 2023 and given the same effect as a joint explanatory statement of a conference committee, states verbatim: 'Section 7343 of the Act provides for funding limitations relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena because of perceptions of insufficient transparency in this area. Section 7343 is also intended to avoid technology and security stovepipes and expand awareness regarding any historical exotic technology antecedents previously provided by the Federal Government for research and development purposes if they are shown to exist. Section 7343 further provides a limitation regarding independent research and development funding to ensure that certain indirect expenses are prohibited.' The explanatory statement says nothing whatever about a 60-day contractor turn-in, a list of non-earth origin material, or a make-available mandate to AARO.
claims.source: Explanatory Statement on the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024, printed by Sen. Warner, Congressional Record, Vol. 169, No. 206 (14 December 2023), pp. S5990-S5991 - https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CREC-2023-12-14/html/CREC-2023-12-14-pt1-PgS5990.htm

claims.text: A SECOND, PARALLEL ENACTED PROVISION EXISTS IN DIVISION A. The table of contents of the statute compilation of Pub. L. 118-31 shows 'Sec. 1687. Limitation on use of funds for certain unreported programs.' in Division A, Title XVI, distinct from and in addition to Sec. 7343 in Division G. The board should carry both: the FY2024 NDAA enacted two separate UAP funding-limitation provisions, one in the defence division and one in the intelligence division.

claims.text: THE ONLY PART OF THE ENACTED FAMILY THAT COULD BE READ VERBATIM CONTAINS NONE OF THE THREE DISPUTED ELEMENTS. The Office of the Law Revision Counsel sets out subsections (b) and (c) of Pub. L. 118-31, div. A, title XVI, Sec. 1687 as a statutory note under 50 U.S.C. 3373, under the heading 'Limitation Regarding Independent Research and Development'. The full text of subsection (b) as set out reads: 'Consistent with Department of Defense Instruction Number 3204.01 (dated August 20, 2014, incorporating change 2, dated July 9, 2020; relating to Department policy for oversight of independent research and development), independent research and development funding relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena shall not be allowable as indirect expenses for purposes of contracts covered by such instruction, unless such material and information is made available the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership.' Subsection (c) then defines 'appropriate congressional committees' as the congressional defense committees plus the two intelligence committees, and 'congressional leadership' as the Senate majority and minority leaders and the Speaker and House minority leader. There is no 60-day deadline, no 180-day deadline, no 'non-earth origin or exotic' language, and no reference to AARO anywhere in the enacted text that OLRC chose to print. The sentence also carries a drafting error that survived into law - 'is made available the appropriate congressional committees', with the preposition 'to' missing - which is itself evidence that this is the enacted text and not a paraphrase. NOTE THE LIMIT OF THIS FINDING: it establishes what is in Sec. 1687(b)-(c), not what is in Sec. 7343, whose body was not retrieved. OLRC set out only subsections (b) and (c) of Sec. 1687 and set out no part of Sec. 7343 as a note anywhere the board has checked.
claims.source: Office of the Law Revision Counsel, 50 U.S.C. 3373, statutory notes (text in effect on 20 August 2026) - https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title50-section3373&num=0&edition=prelim

entities.label: P.L. 118-31 Sec. 7343 — the truncated funding limitation
entities.sub: Enacted remnant of IAA FY2024 Sec. 1102
entities.desc: Section 7343 is the scar tissue left by the excision, and it can be read as evidence of haste. The enacted section keeps a bare prohibition on obligating intelligence funds for UAP activity under special or restricted access limitations unless the DNI has described it to the intelligence, armed services and appropriations committees and congressional leadership. It then keeps subsection (c): 'Independent research and development funding relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena shall not be allowable as indirect expenses for purposes of contracts covered by such instruction, unless such material and information is made available to the appropriate congressional committees and leadership.' There is no antecedent for 'such instruction' anywhere in Section 7343. In the Senate original the phrase referred to Department of Defense Instruction 3204.01, cited in full in Section 1102(f)(1); when the drafters cut Section 1102 down they deleted the citation and left the pronoun stranded. The enacted United States Statutes at Large therefore contains a UAP provision that refers to an instruction it never identifies. The same subsection also loses its point: in the Senate text the disallowance was lifted only if the material was surrendered to the AARO Director under the turn-in subsection; in the enacted text it is lifted if the material is 'made available to the appropriate congressional committees and leadership,' with no turn-in subsection left to make it available under.

entities.sub: The intelligence-side twin of Section 1687, running through the DNI
entities.desc: Division F of Public Law 118-31, the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024, contains at section 7343 the mirror image of section 1687. Subsection (b) bars obligation or expenditure of funds authorised by that division 'in support of any activity involving unidentified anomalous phenomena protected under any form of special access or restricted access limitation unless the Director of National Intelligence has provided the details of the activity to the appropriate committees of Congress and congressional leadership, including for any activities described in a report released by the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office in fiscal year 2024.' The 'appropriate committees' are defined more broadly than in section 1687: the Select and Permanent Select Committees on Intelligence, the Armed Services Committees and, notably, the Appropriations Committees of both chambers. entities.sub: statute
entities.desc: Division G of Public Law 118-31 is the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024, and its section 7343 mirrors section 1687 on the intelligence side with a different addressee and a wider committee list. Subsection (b): 'None of the funds authorized to be appropriated or otherwise made available by this division may be obligated or expended in support of any activity involving unidentified anomalous phenomena protected under any form of special access or restricted access limitation unless the Director of National Intelligence has provided the details of the activity to the appropriate committees of Congress and congressional leadership, including for any activities described in a report released by the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office in fiscal year 2024.' Its 'appropriate committees of Congress' are the Select Committee on Intelligence, the Committee on Armed Services and the Committee on Appropriations of the Senate, and the Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, the Committee on Armed Services and the Committee on Appropriations of the House - six committees, plus the four congressional leaders. Subsection (c) carries the same independent research and development prohibition. Read together, sections 1687 and 7343 mean that as of 22 December 2023 both the Secretary of Defense and the Director of National Intelligence are under a statutory funding prohibition for unreported UAP special access activity, and both prohibitions run to a combined audience far wider than the 10 U.S.C. 119(e) waiver group. Congress did not repeal the waiver; it built a subject-matter carve-out around it.

entities.label: P.L. 118-31 Sec. 1687 — limitation on funds for unreported programs
entities.sub: The surviving teeth, lapsed after FY2024
entities.desc: Section 1687 is the one enacted provision that reaches at the concealment itself rather than at the paperwork. It bars any funds authorised by the FY2024 NDAA from being obligated or expended 'in support of any activities involving unidentified anomalous phenomena protected under any form of special access or restricted access limitations unless the Secretary of Defense has provided the details of the activity to the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership, including for any activities described in a report released by the All-Domain Anomaly Resolution Office in fiscal year 2024.' Subsection (b), noted as 50 U.S.C. 3373 note, then bars UAP-related independent research and development from being allowable as an indirect expense on covered contracts unless the material and information is made available to those same committees — a direct strike at the mechanism by which contractor-held work can be paid for out of overhead without appearing as a Government programme. Its limitation is structural: it restricts funds 'authorized to be appropriated or otherwise made available by this Act,' meaning the FY2024 Act only. It was not re-enacted in the FY2025 NDAA or the FY2026 NDAA, neither of which contains the phrase 'special access or restricted access'. The statutory bar therefore covered one fiscal year and has now been absent for two.

entities.label: FY2024 NDAA sec. 1687 — Limitation on Use of Funds for Certain Unreported Programs
entities.sub: statute
entities.desc: Section 1687 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024 is the moment the SAP architecture and the UAP question meet in enacted law. Subsection (a): 'None of the funds authorized to be appropriated or otherwise made available by this Act may be obligated or expended in support of any activities involving unidentified anomalous phenomena protected under any form of special access or restricted access limitations unless the Secretary of Defense has provided the details of the activity to the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership, including for any activities described in a report released by the All-Domain Anomaly Resolution Office in fiscal year 2024.' Subsection (b) closes the industry-funded route: consistent with DoD Instruction 3204.01, 'independent research and development funding relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena shall not be allowable as indirect expenses for purposes of contracts covered by such instruction, unless such material and information is made available the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership'. The definitions widen the audience well past 10 U.S.C. 119(g): 'appropriate congressional committees' means the congressional defense committees plus both intelligence committees, and 'congressional leadership' means the majority and minority leaders of the Senate and the Speaker and minority leader of the House. Three things follow. First, Congress enacted, on 22 December 2023, a funding prohibition premised on the possibility that UAP activity was being run under special access or restricted access limitations without being reported - a premise it would not have legislated against had it been satisfied no such activity existed. Second, subsection (b) targets precisely the mechanism by which a contractor can fund work internally and recover it as overhead, which is the route that does not appear in any appropriation line. Third, by naming the AARO fiscal year 2024 report, Congress tied the prohibition to a specific document rather than leaving it abstract.

entities.label: IAA FY2025 Title LXVIII — Secs. 6801-6802 (P.L. 118-159)
entities.sub: GAO review of AARO; sunset of Historical Record audit
entities.desc: Title LXVIII of the Intelligence Authorization Act for FY2025, enacted inside P.L. 118-159 on 23 December 2024, is what UAP oversight looked like in the year the disclosure bill got no vote. Sec. 6801 directs the Comptroller General to review AARO's implementation of its duties under 50 U.S.C. 3373, including its operational reporting process and its coordination with DoD, the intelligence community, other agencies and non-Government entities, and to report to the intelligence and defence committees and congressional leadership 'in a timeframe mutually agreed upon' — a deadline with no date in it. Sec. 6802 does the opposite of oversight: it amends Sec. 6803 of the IAA FY2023 to terminate the Comptroller General's quarterly information-sharing on Historical Record Report audits 90 days after the final volume is delivered, and the semiannual verbal briefings to Congress 180 days after. The FY2025 cycle therefore both commissions a new GAO look and puts an expiry on the existing one, while the disclosure regime the Senate had passed twice went unconsidered.

entities.label: NDAA FY2026 UAP provisions (Secs. 1671-1673)
entities.sub: December 2025: reporting requirements repealed, classification guides to be inventoried
entities.desc: The National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026 was approved on 18 December 2025. Its UAP provisions run in two opposite directions at once and both matter to the money question. Section 1672, 'Elimination of Duplicative Reporting Requirements Relating to Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena', repeals section 413 of the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2022 (50 U.S.C. 3373a) outright, and rewrites section 1683(f)(1)(A) of the FY2022 NDAA so that the DNI and the Secretary of Defense 'shall jointly require that each element of the intelligence community and component of the Department of Defense with data relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena makes such data available immediately to the Office in a manner that protects intelligence sources and methods.' Section 1673, 'Accounting of Security Classification Guides Relating to Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena', directs the Director of AARO within 180 days of enactment - by roughly 16 June 2026 - to make an accounting of the security classification guides that apply to information used for UAP reports and investigations, and permits issuance of a consolidated security classification matrix. Section 1671 requires briefings on intercepts of UAP by NORAD and USNORTHCOM. What is absent is as important as what is present: neither the FY2025 nor the FY2026 NDAA re-enacted the section 1687(a) bar on funds for unreported UAP special access activity, which by its terms applied only to funds authorised by the FY2024 Act. The permanent piece - the IR&D indirect-cost prohibition at section 1687(b), codified as a 50 U.S.C. 3373 note - survives; the annual funding bar did not.

entities.label: 10 U.S.C. 119 — Special Access Programs: Congressional Oversight
entities.sub: statute
entities.desc: Section 119 of title 10 is the only statute that tells the Secretary of Defense what he must tell Congress about special access programs, and it is therefore the exact place to look for how a program escapes oversight. It was added by section 1132(a)(1) of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Years 1988 and 1989, Public Law 100-180, signed 4 December 1987, and amended five times since (Pub. L. 101-510 in 1990, Pub. L. 104-106 in 1996, Pub. L. 106-65 in 1999, Pub. L. 107-107 in 2001). The architecture is four affirmative duties and one hole. Subsection (a)(1) requires the Secretary, 'not later than March 1 of each year', to submit to the defense committees 'a report on special access programs' setting forth the total amount requested for DoD SAPs in the President's budget and, for each program, a brief description, major milestones, actual cost for each prior fiscal year, and estimated cost for the current year, the budget year and the four succeeding years. Subsection (b)(1) requires, 'not later than February 1 of each year', notice of the designation of each 'new special access program' and 'justification for such designation', with the current total program cost estimate and 'an identification of existing programs or technologies that are similar to the technology, or that have a mission similar to the mission, of the program'. Subsection (c) requires a report at least 14 days before any planned change in the classification of a SAP or any declassification and public release, with an exceptional-circumstances escape hatch. Subsection (d) requires prompt notice of any modification or termination of the policy and criteria used to designate programs as SAPs. Subsection (f) provides that 'A special access program may not be initiated until - (1) the defense committees are notified of the program; and (2) a period of 30 days elapses after such notification is received.' Subsection (g) defines 'defense committees' as the Armed Services and Appropriations Committees of both chambers plus the defense subcommittees of both Appropriations Committees. Then subsection (e) removes all of it. Nothing in section 119 defines 'special access program', creates a penalty for non-reporting, or gives any committee an enforcement remedy. The duty runs to the Secretary of Defense personally, which means a program concealed from the Secretary of Defense - which is what David Grusch and others allege - produces no statutory violation at all by anyone the statute names.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded A on a global pass (rank 33 of 1170, score 92). 19 connections, 3 of them custody/funding/programmatic, 1 official denial recorded against it. Axes C0/A3/D3.

(b)(2) adds current total program cost estimate and 'an identification of existing programs or technologies that are similar to the technology, or that have a mission similar to the mission, of the program that is the subject of the notice.'

claims.text: WAIVER / 'WAIVED SAP' MECHANISM. 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(1): 'The Secretary of Defense may waive any requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c) that certain information be included in a report under that subsection if the Secretary determines that inclusion of that information in the report would adversely affect the national security. Any such waiver shall be made on a case-by-case basis.' (e)(2): 'If the Secretary exercises the authority provided under paragraph (1), the Secretary shall provide the information described in that subsection with respect to the special access program concerned, and the justification for the waiver, jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees.'
claims.source: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2023-title10/html/USCODE-2023-title10-subtitleA-partI-chap2-sec119.htm

claims.text: The statutory waiver in 119(e)(2) collapses the notified audience from the full defense committees to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the six named defense committee/subcommittee units -- i.e. a maximum of eight members plus the committee chairs' cleared staff, and the delivery is a briefing 'jointly' rather than a written report to the committees. This is the legal definition of a 'waived' SAP.
claims.source: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2023-title10/html/USCODE-2023-title10-subtitleA-partI-chap2-sec119.htm

claims.text: 10 U.S.C. 119(f): 'A special access program may not be initiated until--(1) the defense committees are notified of the program; and (2) a period of 30 days elapses after such notification is received.' Note that (f) is NOT among the subsections waivable under (e)(1), which reaches only subsections (a), (b), and (c).
claims.source: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2023-title10/html/USCODE-2023-title10-subtitleA-partI-chap2-sec119.htm

claims.text: 10 U.S.C. 119(d): 'Whenever there is a modification or termination of the policy and criteria used for designating a program of the Department of Defense as a special access program, the Secretary of Defense shall promptly notify the defense committees of such modification or termination.' This is the hook that makes each reissuance of DoDD 5205.07 a reportable event.

(a) and (b) of this section requiring submittal of annual report to Congress, see section 1061 of Pub. L. 114-328, set out as a note under section 111 of this title.' The FY2017 NDAA's blanket report-sunset provision thus terminated the statutory annual SAP report and the annual new-SAP notice as of 31 December 2021.

Reasoning: (e) waives only (a),(b),(c); the sunset note names only (a) and (b). Whether DoD continued the report voluntarily is not established by any record located here.

claims.text: '10 U.S. Code Section 119 discusses congressional oversight of SAPs, discusses the DEP/SecDef's ability to waive congressional reporting. However, the Gang of 8 is at least supposed to be notified if a... waived bigoted unacknowledged SAP is created and that is public law.'
claims.source: David Grusch, sworn testimony, House Oversight Committee, 26 July 2023

claims.text: The waiver authority reads verbatim, as in effect on 20 August 2026: '(e)(1) The Secretary of Defense may waive any requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c) that certain information be included in a report under that subsection if the Secretary determines that inclusion of that information in the report would adversely affect the national security. Any such waiver shall be made on a case-by-case basis. (2) If the Secretary exercises the authority provided under paragraph (1), the Secretary shall provide the information described in that subsection with respect to the special access program concerned, and the justification for the waiver, jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees.' The waiver is a waiver of INCLUSION IN A REPORT, not a waiver of disclosure - the withheld information and a written justification must still travel to twelve named seats.
claims.source: Office of the Law Revision Counsel, 10 U.S.C. 119, 'Special access programs: congressional oversight' (text in effect on 20 August 2026) - https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title10-section119&num=0&edition=prelim

claims.text: The recipient set is fixed by subsection (g) verbatim: 'In this section, the term "defense committees" means- (1) the Committee on Armed Services and the Committee on Appropriations, and the Defense Subcommittee of the Committee on Appropriations, of the Senate; and (2) the Committee on Armed Services and the Committee on Appropriations, and the Subcommittee on Defense of the Committee on Appropriations, of the House of Representatives.' Six committee entities, each contributing a chairman and a ranking minority member, gives the twelve-seat notification group the board already tracks.
claims.source: Office of the Law Revision Counsel, 10 U.S.C. 119, 'Special access programs: congressional oversight' (text in effect on 20 August 2026) - https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title10-section119&num=0&edition=prelim

claims.text: MATERIAL NEW FINDING - THE REPORTS THE WAIVER ATTACHES TO HAVE LARGELY SUNSET. The Office of the Law Revision Counsel carries a statutory note under 10 U.S.C. 119 headed 'Termination of Reporting Requirements' which reads verbatim: 'For termination, effective Dec. 31, 2021, of provisions in subsecs. (a) and (b) of this section requiring submittal of annual report to Congress, see section 1061 of Pub. L. 114-328, set out as a note under section 111 of this title.' The annual special access program report under 119(a) and the new-program notice and justification report under 119(b) therefore terminated as statutory requirements on 31 December 2021. After that date the only report to which the 119(e)(1) waiver can attach is the 119(c) report on a planned classification change or public declassification announcement. This reshapes the board's question: for activity after 31 December 2021 there may be no 119(a) or 119(b) report in existence to waive information out of, which would make the absence of any 119(e)(2) delivery unsurprising rather than suspicious for that window - while for the period 1988 through 2021 the reports were mandatory and the waiver machinery was live.

entities.label: 10 U.S.C. 119(e) — Waiver of SAP Reporting (the 'waived SAP' authority)
entities.sub: statute-subsection
entities.desc: Subsection (e) is the hinge of this entire board. In two paragraphs it converts the full committee reporting regime of section 119 into a briefing for a handful of individuals. Paragraph (1): 'The Secretary of Defense may waive any requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c) that certain information be included in a report under that subsection if the Secretary determines that inclusion of that information in the report would adversely affect the national security. Any such waiver shall be made on a case-by-case basis.' Paragraph (2): 'If the Secretary exercises the authority provided under paragraph (1), the Secretary shall provide the information described in that subsection with respect to the special access program concerned, and the justification for the waiver, jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees.' Four features matter. First, the waiver is unilateral - no committee concurrence, no ISOO review, no judicial test; the sole standard is the Secretary's own determination. Second, the waiver reaches subsections (a), (b) and (c) - the annual report, the new-program notice and the declassification notice - but not subsection (f), so the 30-day pre-initiation notice to the committees survives on paper. Third, the information does not vanish: it goes to named leaders, which is why programs run under a section 119(e) waiver are called 'waived' programs and are informally said to be briefed to a 'Gang of Eight'. Fourth, and decisively, section 119(e) contains no audit trail requirement - no register of waivers exercised, no annual accounting of how many waivers are outstanding, no requirement that the waived program appear anywhere in an unclassified count. The number of waived DoD special access programs currently in existence has never been published.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded B on a global pass (rank 194 of 1170, score 46). 5 connections, 1 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C0/A3/D3.

claims.text: Verbatim: '(e)(1) The Secretary of Defense may waive any requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c) that certain information be included in a report under that subsection if the Secretary determines that inclusion of that information in the report would adversely affect the national security. Any such waiver shall be made on a case-by-case basis. (2) If the Secretary exercises the authority provided under paragraph (1), the Secretary shall provide the information described in that subsection with respect to the special access program concerned, and the justification for the waiver, jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees.'
claims.source: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2023-title10/html/USCODE-2023-title10-subtitleA-partI-chap2-sec119.htm

claims.text: The waiver authority is vested in the Secretary of Defense personally and is conditioned only on the Secretary's own determination of adverse national security effect; the statute prescribes no finding of fact, no time limit, no periodic re-justification, and no congressional ability to disapprove.
claims.source: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2023-title10/html/USCODE-2023-title10-subtitleA-partI-chap2-sec119.htm

claims.text: Subsection (e) was in the section as originally enacted by Pub. L. 100-180 sec. 1132(a)(1) (4 Dec 1987) and has never been amended: the 2001, 1999, 1996 and 1990 amendment notes in the GPO text touch only subsecs. (a)(1), (c), (f) and (g). The waiver language of 1987 is the language in force today.
claims.source: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2023-title10/html/USCODE-2023-title10-subtitleA-partI-chap2-sec119.htm

claims.text: Because (e)(1) reaches only 'any requirement ... that certain information be included in a report,' a plain reading is that the Secretary may strip content out of the reports but may not skip the (f) 30-day pre-initiation notification of the program's existence. A program whose existence was never notified to the defense committees at all would therefore not be a lawfully 'waived' SAP under section 119 but an unreported one. Reasoning stated from the text of (e)(1) and (f).
claims.source: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2023-title10/html/USCODE-2023-title10-subtitleA-partI-chap2-sec119.htm

claims.text: 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(1): 'The Secretary of Defense may waive any requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c) that certain information be included in a report under that subsection if the Secretary determines that inclusion of that information in the report would adversely affect the national security. Any such waiver shall be made on a case-by-case basis.'

10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2): the Secretary 'shall provide the information described in that subsection with respect to the special access program concerned, and the justification for the waiver, jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees.'
The waiver authority extends only to subsections (a), (b) and (c); the 30-day pre-initiation notice requirement of subsection (f) is not waivable on the face of the statute.
claims.source: Text of 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(1) compared with 119(f)

claims.text: Section 119(e) imposes no requirement to maintain, publish or report a register of waivers exercised.
claims.source: Full text of 10 U.S.C. 119(e)

claims.text: Read literally, 119(g) names six bodies - Senate Armed Services, Senate Appropriations, the Defense Subcommittee of Senate Appropriations, and the three House counterparts - so 'the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees' is up to twelve members, not eight. The conventional 'Gang of Eight' framing for defense waived programs counts only the four parent committees. Reasoning: statutory text versus practice convention.
claims.source: 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) read with 119(g)

entities.label: Waived Unacknowledged SAP (waived USAP) — the mechanism
entities.sub: mechanism
entities.desc: Stack the three documented mechanisms and the result is a program with the following properties, every one of which is sourced to a statute or a DoD issuance rather than to any allegation. Its existence is not acknowledged, affirmed or made known to any person not authorised (DoDI 5205.11 glossary). Its reporting to the defense committees under 10 U.S.C. 119(a), (b) and (c) has been waived by the Secretary of Defense on a case-by-case national-security determination, with the information going instead 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees' (10 U.S.C. 119(e)). Within those committees, DoD policy limits access further: members generally 'shall be authorized access to DoD SAPs ... except for waived programs', and for waived programs 'only the chair, the ranking minority member, and the staff directors' unless the Secretary or Deputy Secretary approves otherwise (DoDD 5205.07 (2010) para 4.f). Whatever paper the committee is shown stays in the building: 'All waived SAP material submitted to Congress, to include annual reports and other products, shall remain in DoD custody' (para 4.h). If the program is executed at a contractor facility, a carve-out approved by the Secretary or Deputy Secretary removes DCSA inspection, DCSA information-system accreditation and the DCSA counterintelligence feed (32 CFR 117.6(b)(3); DoDM 5205.07-V1 Enclosure 2). Fraud, waste, abuse and corruption complaints must be reported 'through SAP channels' and not through collateral channels (DoDM 5205.07-V1 Enclosure 4). The Senior Review Group 'Reviews all waived DoD SAPs annually' and recommends to the SAPOC on continued waived status (DoDI 5205.11 Enclosure 3), so a record of every waived program exists and is reviewed once a year by a body chaired at Principal Deputy Under Secretary level. Nothing in this paragraph is contested. The contested question is only what is inside one of them.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded A on a global pass (rank 22 of 1170, score 104). 13 connections, 5 of them custody/funding/programmatic, 1 official denial recorded against it. Axes C3/A3/D3.

claims.text: 'Waived' is a statutory term of art traceable to a single sentence: 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) substitutes, for the ordinary committee report, delivery of the information and the waiver justification 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees.' Nothing in section 119 requires that this delivery be written, recorded, retained, or shared with other members.
claims.source: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2023-title10/html/USCODE-2023-title10-subtitleA-partI-chap2-sec119.htm

claims.text: The parallel non-DoD, non-IC statute 50 U.S.C. 3348(e) contains the same waiver test ('would adversely affect the national security', 'case-by-case basis') but a materially WEAKER carve-down: 3348(e)(2) still requires the information to go 'to the congressional oversight committees', not merely to chairs and ranking members. The eight-member floor is therefore unique to the DoD statute.
claims.source: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2023-title50/html/USCODE-2023-title50-chap45-subchapIII-sec3348.htm

claims.text: The combination that produces a genuinely invisible program is not one provision but three stacked: 119(e) removes the content from the written record; the sec. 1061 Pub. L. 114-328 sunset (eff. 31 Dec 2021) removed the annual census that would otherwise show a count; and the DoDD 5205.07 carve-out provision (see 32 CFR 117.6) removes DCSA from the contractor facility where the work is performed. Each layer is individually lawful and documented; the stack is what defeats discovery. Reasoning stated.
claims.source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-32/subtitle-A/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-117/section-117.6

claims.text: VERDICT ON THE BOARD'S QUESTION: the waiver has been exercised, and the Department of Defense says so in a currently effective, publicly released instruction - but no public document identifies a single specific instance, a count, a date, a program, or any connection to unidentified anomalous phenomena. DoD Instruction 5205.11, effective 12 September 2024, paragraph 1.2.f, states verbatim: 'The Secretary of Defense may designate select unacknowledged SAPs as "waived" when it is determined that using standard procedures for reporting to Congress would adversely affect national security, pursuant to Section 119 of Title 10, United States Code. Waived SAPs remain subject to congressional oversight.' This is not a hypothetical authority described in the abstract; the rest of the instruction is written around an existing population of such programs.
claims.source: DoD Instruction 5205.11, 'Management, Administration, and Oversight of DoD Special Access Programs', 12 September 2024, cleared for public release - https://www.esd.whs.mil/Portals/54/Documents/DD/issuances/dodi/520511p.pdf

claims.text: THE STRONGEST SINGLE PIECE OF EVIDENCE THAT THE POPULATION IS NON-EMPTY IS A RECURRING REVIEW REQUIREMENT. DoDI 5205.11 requires that in its annual review the Special Access Program Oversight Committee - chaired by the Deputy Secretary of Defense - shall assess, among four listed items, '(d) All waived DoD SAPs to determine the need for continued waived status.' A standing annual agenda item to decide whether waived programs should REMAIN waived is only drafted if waived programs exist. This is a 2024 document, so the finding is current, not historical.
claims.source: DoD Instruction 5205.11, 'Management, Administration, and Oversight of DoD Special Access Programs', 12 September 2024, cleared for public release - https://www.esd.whs.mil/Portals/54/Documents/DD/issuances/dodi/520511p.pdf

claims.text: The Department's own definition, from the DoDI 5205.11 glossary, verbatim: 'waived SAP - A SAP for which the Secretary of Defense has waived applicable reporting following a determination of adverse effect to national security. An unacknowledged SAP that has more restrictive reporting and access controls than other unacknowledged SAPs.' And, adjacent to it: 'unacknowledged SAP - A SAP having enhanced security measures, ensuring the existence of the program is not acknowledged, affirmed, or made known to any person not authorized for such information.' A waived SAP is therefore a proper subset of the unacknowledged SAPs, distinguished precisely by the exercise of the Section 119(e)(1) waiver.
claims.source: DoD Instruction 5205.11, 'Management, Administration, and Oversight of DoD Special Access Programs', 12 September 2024, cleared for public release - https://www.esd.whs.mil/Portals/54/Documents/DD/issuances/dodi/520511p.pdf

claims.text: Administrative plumbing specific to waived programs exists in the same instruction, which again indicates live use rather than dormant authority. Footnote 5 reads verbatim: 'CA and OA SAPCO Directors may delegate AAA for non-waived SAPs to the DoD Component's SAPCO staff. AAA for waived SAPs may be delegated to the SAPCO Deputy Director or alternate designee.' Footnote 6 reads verbatim: 'DoD SAPCO will coordinate on PARs for judicial and other federal agency personnel for waived programs.' A department does not write delegation rules and a judicial-access coordination rule for an empty set.
claims.source: DoD Instruction 5205.11, 'Management, Administration, and Oversight of DoD Special Access Programs', 12 September 2024, cleared for public release - https://www.esd.whs.mil/Portals/54/Documents/DD/issuances/dodi/520511p.pdf

claims.text: THE PUBLIC TAXONOMY HAS BEEN NARROWING. DoD Directive 5205.07, 'Special Access Program Policy', was reissued effective 12 September 2024 and cancels the 1 July 2010 version. The full public text of the 2024 directive - purpose, applicability, policy, all thirteen responsibility assignments, the governance section, the complete glossary and the reference list - contains no occurrence of the words 'waived' or 'unacknowledged' at all. The directive that used to define the waived category no longer mentions it; the taxonomy now survives publicly only in the subordinate instruction, DoDI 5205.11. Anyone checking only the directive would conclude the category no longer exists.
claims.source: DoD Directive 5205.07, 'Special Access Program Policy', effective 12 September 2024, cleared for public release - https://www.esd.whs.mil/portals/54/documents/dd/issuances/dodd/520507p.pdf

claims.text: HISTORICAL CORROBORATION FROM A CONGRESSIONALLY CHARTERED COMMISSION. The Report of the Commission on Protecting and Reducing Government Secrecy (1997), Chapter II, states verbatim: 'Among black programs, further distinction is made for "waived" programs, considered to be so sensitive that they are exempt from standard reporting requirements to the Congress. The chairperson, ranking member, and, on occasion, other members and staff of relevant Congressional committees are notified only orally of the existence of these programs.' The same passage gives the surrounding population: 'There are approximately 150 DoD-approved SAPs (the exact number is classified and others have been created but not yet formally approved), down from 200 in the late 1980s, and roughly 300 SCI compartments, compared with an estimated 800 in the late 1980s.' The Commission gives no number for the waived subset. The phrase 'notified only orally' is the operationally important one: it describes a practice under which the 119(e)(2) delivery leaves no paper.
claims.source: Report of the Commission on Protecting and Reducing Government Secrecy (the Moynihan Commission), S. Doc. 105-2, 1997, Chapter II, as mirrored by the Federation of American Scientists - https://sgp.fas.org/library/moynihan/chap2.html

claims.text: GAO HAS DESCRIBED THE WAIVER MECHANISM BUT HAS NEVER PUBLICLY REPORTED AN INSTANCE OF ITS USE. GAO/NSIAD-93-78, the unclassified summary of a classified report, describes the mechanism verbatim: 'Section 119, 10 U.S. Code, enacted in 1987, requires DOD to submit annual reports to the congressional defense committees on special access programs. Under the law, the Secretary of Defense may waive the requirement that certain information on special access programs be included in the annual report if he determines that the inclusion would adversely affect national security. However, he must provide the excluded information to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the congressional defense committees.' The report then never returns to the subject. Its findings on waivers are about a different thing entirely - 'DOD used waivers and exemptions to limit review, documentation, and reporting requirements' refers to Defense Acquisition Board reviews, competition requirements and Selected Acquisition Reports, not to Section 119(e). Do not let these two senses of 'waiver' be conflated on the board.
claims.source: GAO/NSIAD-93-78, 'Defense Acquisition: Oversight of Special Access Programs Has Increased', 21 December 1992 - https://www.gao.gov/assets/nsiad-93-78.pdf

claims.text: The earlier GAO report in the same series, GAO/NSIAD-89-133, covering the period immediately after Section 119 took effect and prepared at the request of Rep. Barbara Boxer, examines DoD compliance with special access program oversight requirements in detail and does not mention the Section 119(e) waiver authority at all. Its only reference to waived requirements is to DoD Directive 5205.7's January 1989 revision requiring 'listings by the responsible program officer of all DOD regulations for which compliance has been waived' - again a different mechanism.
claims.source: GAO/NSIAD-89-133, 'Special Access Programs: DOD Is Strengthening Compliance With Oversight Requirements', 4 May 1989 - https://www.gao.gov/assets/nsiad-89-133.pdf

claims.text: WHAT SHOULD EXIST IF THE WAIVER WERE BEING USED, AND WHY NONE OF IT IS PUBLIC. Four artefacts are implied by the statute and the DoD instruction: (i) the underlying 119(a), (b) or (c) report itself, which is classified and, for (a) and (b), no longer statutorily required after 31 December 2021; (ii) the Secretary's case-by-case determination that inclusion would adversely affect national security, which 119(e)(1) requires to be made but does not require to be recorded in any publicly indexed form; (iii) the withheld information plus a written justification delivered jointly to twelve named members, which by the Moynihan Commission's account has historically been delivered orally; and (iv) the SAPOC annual review record of whether each waived program should retain that status, which is internal to the Department. None of the four is a public document class. There is no statutory requirement anywhere in Section 119 to report the NUMBER of waivers exercised, the fact that any waiver was exercised, or an aggregate count, to anyone outside those twelve seats. The absence of a public instance is therefore fully explained by the design of the mechanism and is NOT evidence of concealment beyond what the statute itself authorises.
claims.source: Office of the Law Revision Counsel, 10 U.S.C. 119, 'Special access programs: congressional oversight' (text in effect on 20 August 2026) - https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title10-section119&num=0&edition=prelim ; DoD Instruction 5205.11, 'Management, Administration, and Oversight of DoD Special Access Programs', 12 September 2024, cleared for public release - https://www.esd.whs.mil/Portals/54/Documents/DD/issuances/dodi/520511p.pdf ; Report of the Commission on Protecting and Reducing Government Secrecy (the Moynihan Commission), S. Doc. 105-2, 1997, Chapter II, as mirrored by the Federation of American Scientists - https://sgp.fas.org/library/moynihan/chap2.html

claims.text: NO UAP-SPECIFIC EXERCISE OF THE 119(e)(1) WAIVER WAS FOUND IN ANY PUBLIC DOCUMENT. Searches across GAO's special access program series, DoD Inspector General audits and evaluations, Congressional Research Service products, and the Senate and House Armed Services Committee document sets returned no document in which a waived special access program is linked to unidentified anomalous phenomena, and no document in which any specific exercise of the Section 119(e)(1) waiver - UAP or otherwise - is identified, dated, counted or described. The DoD Inspector General's public catalogue for special access programs consists of external peer reviews and quality control reviews of the service audit agencies' SAP audit work, plus a series of entries titled only 'CLASSIFIED REPORT (Classified)'; none addresses congressional reporting under Section 119.
claims.source: Negative result of searches restricted to gao.gov, dodig.mil, crsreports.congress.gov, armed-services.senate.gov, armedservices.house.gov and govinfo.gov during this pass

claims.text: DoDI 5205.11 Enclosure 3 provides that the Senior Review Group 'Reviews all waived DoD SAPs annually. Provides recommendations to the SAPOC concerning continued waived status.'
claims.source: DoDI 5205.11, Enclosure 3, para 3.b(4)

claims.text: DoDI 5205.11 Enclosure 3 provides that the SRG 'Ensures the accuracy of the SAP list submitted to Congress prior to submission of the SAP annual report.'
claims.source: DoDI 5205.11, Enclosure 3, para 3.b(5)

claims.text: DoDI 5205.11 Enclosure 2 requires DoD SAPCO to establish 'the criteria for annual reviews of waived DoD SAPs by the SSWG and SRG.'
claims.source: DoDI 5205.11, Enclosure 2, para 2.m

claims.text: DoDD 5205.07 (2010) para 4.f limits access to waived SAPs, absent SecDef or DepSecDef approval, to 'the chair, the ranking minority member, and the staff directors of the defense and intelligence committees'.

A complete list of waived DoD SAPs demonstrably exists in documentary form, is reviewed at least annually by the Senior Review Group, and is validated by the SAPOC - which means the answer to 'how many waived programs are there' is a retrievable agency record and not an unknowable. Reasoning: DoDI 5205.11 Enclosure 3 assigns the annual review of all waived SAPs and the accuracy of the congressional SAP list to a named standing body.
claims.source: DoDI 5205.11, Enclosure 3

entities.label: 50 U.S.C. 3348 — Reports Relating to Certain SAPs and Similar Programs
entities.sub: statute
entities.desc: Section 1152 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 1994, Public Law 103-160 of 30 November 1993, now codified at 50 U.S.C. 3348, is the sleeper statute of this whole architecture and it is almost never cited in UAP reporting. It imposes on the head of every 'covered department or agency' the same February 1 annual report, new-program notice, 14-day declassification notice and 30-day report-and-wait that 10 U.S.C. 119 imposes on the Secretary of Defense - and it defines 'covered department or agency' as 'any department or agency of the Federal Government that carries out a special access program', excluding only DoD (covered by 10 U.S.C. 119), the National Nuclear Security Administration (covered by 50 U.S.C. 2426) and 'an agency in the Intelligence Community'. Two provisions make it invaluable. First, it supplies the statutory definition of a special access program: 'any program that, under the authority of Executive Order 12356 (or any successor Executive order), is established by the head of a department or agency whom the President has designated in the Federal Register as an original "secret" or "top secret" classification authority that imposes "need-to-know" controls or access controls beyond those controls normally required ... for access to information classified as "confidential", "secret", or "top secret".' Second, as amended by section 103 of Public Law 115-390 on 21 December 2018, 'congressional oversight committees' means 'congressional leadership and authorizing and appropriations congressional committees with jurisdiction or shared jurisdiction over a department or agency', the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, AND the Committee on Oversight and Government Reform of the House of Representatives. The House Oversight Committee - the committee that has run the public UAP hearings since July 2023 - is a named statutory recipient of special access program reports from every covered agency. And its waiver provision, subsection (e)(2), does not narrow the audience: the waived information still goes 'to the congressional oversight committees', not to a chair and ranking member. The non-defense SAP reporting regime is materially stronger than DoD's.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded A on a global pass (rank 98 of 1170, score 64). 6 connections, 2 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C0/A2/D3.

claims.text: Section title and scope: 50 U.S.C. 3348, 'Reports relating to certain special access programs and similar programs'. Codified from Pub. L. 103-160, div. A, title XI, sec. 1152, Nov. 30, 1993, 107 Stat. 1758; formerly classified as a note under 50 U.S.C. 435 before editorial reclassification.
claims.source: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2023-title50/html/USCODE-2023-title50-chap45-subchapIII-sec3348.htm

claims.text: THE COVERAGE HOLE. 3348(g)(2)(B): the term 'covered department or agency' 'does not include-- (i) the Department of Defense (which is required to submit reports on special access programs under section 119 of title 10); (ii) the National Nuclear Security Administration (which is required to submit reports on special access programs under section 2426 of this title); or (iii) an agency in the Intelligence Community (as defined in section 3003(4) of this title).' The government-wide SAP reporting statute therefore reaches none of the three communities where a legacy recovery program would plausibly sit.
claims.source: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2023-title50/html/USCODE-2023-title50-chap45-subchapIII-sec3348.htm

claims.text: 3348(e)(1): 'The head of a covered department or agency may waive any requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c) that certain information be included in a report ... if the head of the department or agency determines that inclusion of that information in the report would adversely affect the national security. Any such waiver shall be made on a case-by-case basis.' (e)(2) requires the withheld information and the waiver justification to be provided 'to the congressional oversight committees' -- with no reduction to chairs and ranking members.
claims.source: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2023-title50/html/USCODE-2023-title50-chap45-subchapIII-sec3348.htm

claims.text: 3348(f): 'A special access program may not be initiated by a covered department or agency until-- (1) the congressional oversight committees are notified of the program; and (2) a period of 30 days elapses after such notification is received.'
claims.source: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2023-title50/html/USCODE-2023-title50-chap45-subchapIII-sec3348.htm

claims.text: 3348(g)(1) defines 'congressional oversight committees' as congressional leadership and the authorizing and appropriations committees with jurisdiction or shared jurisdiction over the department or agency, plus the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs and the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform (now Oversight and Accountability). This definition was ADDED by Pub. L. 115-390 sec. 103(3) in December 2018; before that the statute said only 'Congress'.
claims.source: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2023-title50/html/USCODE-2023-title50-chap45-subchapIII-sec3348.htm

claims.text: 3348(g)(3) still defines 'special access program' by reference to 'Executive Order 12356 (or any successor Executive order)' — an order revoked in 1995 by E.O. 12958 sec. 6.1(d), as the GPO 'References in Text' note states. The operative definition today runs through the successor chain to E.O. 13526.
claims.source: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2023-title50/html/USCODE-2023-title50-chap45-subchapIII-sec3348.htm

claims.text: 50 U.S.C. 3348(g)(2)(B) excludes from its own SAP-reporting regime exactly the three bodies this board is about: 'Such term does not include - (i) the Department of Defense (which is required to submit reports on special access programs under section 119 of title 10); (ii) the National Nuclear Security Administration (which is required to submit reports on special access programs under section 2426 of this title); or (iii) an agency in the Intelligence Community (as defined in section 3003(4) of this title).'
claims.source: 50 U.S.C. 3348(g)(2)(B), OLRC prelim text, read 22 August 2026, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title50-section3348&num=0&edition=prelim

claims.text: The section heading is 'Reports relating to certain special access programs and similar programs'. The word doing the work is 'certain': DoD, NNSA and the Intelligence Community are routed out of it by subsection (g)(2)(B) to their own regimes, and the DoD regime it routes to, 10 U.S.C. 119, is the one carrying a waiver.
claims.source: 50 U.S.C. 3348 heading and (g)(2)(B), OLRC prelim text, read 22 August 2026, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title50-section3348&num=0&edition=prelim

claims.text: 50 U.S.C. 3348(g)(3) defines 'special access program' as 'any program that, under the authority of Executive Order 12356 (or any successor Executive order), is established by the head of a department or agency whom the President has designated in the Federal Register as an original "secret" or "top secret" classification authority that imposes "need-to-know" controls or access controls beyond those controls normally required ... for access to information classified as "confidential", "secret", or "top secret".'

50 U.S.C. 3348(g)(1) defines 'congressional oversight committees' to include 'the Committee on Oversight and Government Reform of the House of Representatives' and the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, as well as congressional leadership and the authorizing and appropriations committees with jurisdiction.

50 U.S.C. 3348(e)(2): where the waiver is exercised, the agency head 'shall provide the information described in that subsection with respect to the special access program concerned, and the justification for the waiver, to the congressional oversight committees' - the full committees, not a chair and ranking member.
50 U.S.C. 3348(g)(2)(B) excludes from 'covered department or agency' only the Department of Defense, the National Nuclear Security Administration and agencies in the Intelligence Community.

entities.label: Executive Order 13526 — Classified National Security Information
entities.sub: executive-order
entities.desc: Executive Order 13526, signed by President Obama on 29 December 2009 and still the operative classification order in August 2026, is where special access programs actually come from. Section 4.3 provides that 'Unless otherwise authorized by the President, only the Secretaries of State, Defense, Energy, and Homeland Security, the Attorney General, and the Director of National Intelligence, or the principal deputy of each, may create a special access program' - and that for programs pertaining to intelligence activities, sources or methods, 'this function shall be exercised by the Director of National Intelligence'. The order requires that a SAP be created only on a specific finding that the vulnerability of, or threat to, the information is exceptional and that normal classification and safeguarding criteria are insufficient; that the number of programs be kept 'at an absolute minimum'; that each program be reviewed annually to determine whether it continues to meet the criteria; and, critically, that special access programs 'shall be subject to the oversight program established under section 5.4(d)' with the Director of the Information Security Oversight Office 'afforded access to these programs, consistent with the policies and procedures directed by the President'. Two structural facts follow. First, SAP creation authority is a delegated executive power that Congress has never legislated over, so the six creating officials can stand a program up without any statutory basis and 10 U.S.C. 119 only tells them what to report afterward. Second, the ISOO access right in section 4.3 is qualified by 'consistent with the policies and procedures directed by the President' - a clause that has been read to permit the President to withhold ISOO access to specific programs, which is the single most important limitation on independent oversight of the SAP enterprise.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded A on a global pass (rank 62 of 1170, score 74). 8 connections, 2 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C0/A3/D3.

claims.text: Sec. 4.3(a) verbatim: 'Unless otherwise authorized by the President, only the Secretaries of State, Defense, Energy, and Homeland Security, the Attorney General, and the Director of National Intelligence, or the principal deputy of each, may create a special access program. For special access programs pertaining to intelligence sources, methods, and activities (but not including military operational, strategic, and tactical programs), this function shall be exercised by the Director of National Intelligence. These officials shall keep the number of these programs at an absolute minimum, and shall establish them only when the program is required by statute or upon a specific finding that: (1) the vulnerability of, or threat to, specific information is exceptional; and (2) the normal criteria for determining eligibility for access applicable to information classified at the same level are not deemed sufficient to protect the information from unauthorized disclosure.'
claims.source: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2010-01-05/html/E9-31418.htm

claims.text: Sec. 4.3(b)(1)-(2) verbatim: 'Special access programs shall be limited to programs in which the number of persons who ordinarily will have access will be reasonably small and commensurate with the objective of providing enhanced protection for the information involved. ... Each agency head shall establish and maintain a system of accounting for special access programs consistent with directives issued pursuant to this order.'
claims.source: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2010-01-05/html/E9-31418.htm

claims.text: THE ISOO ACCESS CAP. Sec. 4.3(b)(3) verbatim: 'Special access programs shall be subject to the oversight program established under section 5.4(d) of this order. In addition, the Director of the Information Security Oversight Office shall be afforded access to these programs, in accordance with the security requirements of each program, in order to perform the functions assigned to the Information Security Oversight Office under this order. An agency head may limit access to a special access program to the Director of the Information Security Oversight Office and no more than one other employee of the Information Security Oversight Office or, for special access programs that are extraordinarily sensitive and vulnerable, to the Director only.' The executive-branch oversight body for the entire classification system can lawfully be reduced to a single individual for the most sensitive SAPs.
claims.source: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2010-01-05/html/E9-31418.htm

claims.text: Sec. 4.3(b)(4)-(5) verbatim: 'The agency head or principal deputy shall review annually each special access program to determine whether it continues to meet the requirements of this order. ... Upon request, an agency head shall brief the National Security Advisor, or a designee, on any or all of the agency's special access programs.' Note the National Security Advisor briefing is on request only, not automatic.
claims.source: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2010-01-05/html/E9-31418.htm

claims.text: Sec. 4.3(b)(6) verbatim: "For the purposes of this section, the term ``agency head'' refers only to the Secretaries of State, Defense, Energy, and Homeland Security, the Attorney General, and the Director of National Intelligence, or the principal deputy of each." SAP creation authority cannot be delegated below the deputy-secretary level.
claims.source: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2010-01-05/html/E9-31418.htm

claims.text: Sec. 4.3(c) verbatim, in its entirety: 'Nothing in this order shall supersede any requirement made by or under 10 U.S.C. 119.' The executive order expressly subordinates itself to the statutory SAP oversight scheme, including the section 119(e) waiver.
claims.source: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2010-01-05/html/E9-31418.htm

claims.text: Sec. 6.1(oo) verbatim: "``Special access program'' means a program established for a specific class of classified information that imposes safeguarding and access requirements that exceed those normally required for information at the same classification level."
claims.source: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2010-01-05/html/E9-31418.htm

claims.text: Sec. 1.7(a) verbatim: 'In no case shall information be classified, continue to be maintained as classified, or fail to be declassified in order to: (1) conceal violations of law, inefficiency, or administrative error; (2) prevent embarrassment to a person, organization, or agency; (3) restrain competition; or (4) prevent or delay the release of information that does not require protection in the interest of the national security.' Sec. 1.7(b): 'Basic scientific research information not clearly related to the national security shall not be classified.'
claims.source: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2010-01-05/html/E9-31418.htm

claims.text: Sec. 1.7(a)(1) and 1.7(b) are the two provisions a whistleblower alleging an illegally concealed recovery program would invoke: (a)(1) makes classification to conceal a violation of law impermissible on its face, and (b) makes classification of basic scientific research not clearly related to national security impermissible. Neither carries an enforcement mechanism inside the order; the only remedy channel is the sec. 5.3 ISCAP / agency appeal process or the intelligence-community whistleblower statutes. Reasoning stated from the text.
claims.source: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2010-01-05/html/E9-31418.htm

claims.text: EO 13526 sec. 4.3(a): 'Unless otherwise authorized by the President, only the Secretaries of State, Defense, Energy, and Homeland Security, the Attorney General, and the Director of National Intelligence, or the principal deputy of each, may create a special access program.' claims.source: EO 13526 sec. 4.3(a), 75 FR 707, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2010-01-05/html/E9-31418.htm

claims.text: THE EXECUTIVE-SIDE NARROWING. Sec. 4.3(b)(3): 'An agency head may limit access to a special access program to the Director of the Information Security Oversight Office and no more than one other employee of the Information Security Oversight Office or, for special access programs that are extraordinarily sensitive and vulnerable, to the Director only.' The oversight body's access to an extraordinarily sensitive SAP can therefore be reduced to a single person, at the agency head's discretion.

claims.text: Sec. 4.3(b)(4) requires that 'The agency head or principal deputy shall review annually each special access program to determine whether it continues to meet the requirements of this order', and (b)(5) that 'Upon request, an agency head shall brief the National Security Advisor, or a designee, on any or all of the agency's special access programs.'
claims.source: EO 13526 sec. 4.3(b)(4)-(5), 75 FR 707, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2010-01-05/html/E9-31418.htm

claims.text: Three separate instruments each narrow oversight of the same object, and none of them depends on the others. 10 U.S.C. 119(e) reduces the congressional readership of a waived SAP to twelve members. EO 13526 sec. 4.3(b)(3) can reduce ISOO's access to one person. 32 CFR 117.6(b)(3) relieves the Director, DCSA of NISP industrial-security oversight entirely on a carve-out. Congressional, executive and industrial-security oversight are narrowed by three different authorities, so closing any one of them would leave the other two intact.
