entities.label: 32 CFR Part 117 — NISPOM Rule
entities.sub: regulation
entities.desc: The NISPOM ceased to be a DoD manual and became a federal regulation with the codification of 32 CFR Part 117, which now carries the rules binding every cleared contractor in the United States. For this board its value is threefold. First, it supplies the operative regulatory definition of a SAP: 'SAP means any program that is established to control access and distribution and to provide protection for particularly sensitive classified information beyond that normally required for TOP SECRET, SECRET, or CONFIDENTIAL information. A SAP can be created or continued only as authorized by a senior agency official delegated such authority pursuant to E.O. 13526.' Second, it contains the carve-out at 117.6(b)(3). Third, section 117.23 is the supplement for ACCM, SAPs, SCI, Restricted Data, Formerly Restricted Data, Transclassified Foreign Nuclear Information and Naval Nuclear Propulsion Information, and its paragraph (d)(1) provides that for DoD SAP contracts 'Contractors will implement the security requirements for SAPs codified in SAP-related policy, when established by contract' - a formulation that pushes the actual security rules out of the regulation and into contract documents that are not public. Part 117 also treats SAP information as 'proscribed information' alongside TOP SECRET, COMSEC, Restricted Data and SCI, which triggers the National Interest Determination process for entities under foreign ownership, control or influence. The whole rule is issued under the authority of section 201 of Executive Order 12829.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded A on a global pass (rank 68 of 1170, score 73). 6 connections, 2 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C2/A2/D2.

claims.text: THE CONTRACTOR CARVE-OUT, in regulation. 32 CFR 117.6(b) (responsibilities of the Director, DCSA) verbatim: 'The Director, DCSA, will be relieved of this oversight function for DoD special access programs (SAPs) when the Secretary of Defense or the Deputy Secretary of Defense approves a carve-out provision in accordance with DoDD 5205.07, "DoD SAP Policy".' The preceding sentence establishes what is being relieved: DCSA 'Provides security oversight of the NISP as the DoD CSO on behalf of DoD components and those non-DoD executive branch agencies who enter into agreements with DoD.'
claims.source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-32/subtitle-A/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-117/section-117.6

claims.text: The carve-out is therefore not a classification device but an INSPECTION device: it removes the one federal agency that would otherwise physically visit, inspect, and record a cleared contractor facility performing the classified work. Nothing else in Part 117 substitutes an alternative external inspector; oversight reverts inside the SAP's own chain.
claims.source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-32/subtitle-A/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-117/section-117.6

claims.text: 32 CFR 117.3(b) defines ACCM verbatim: 'ACCM are security measures used by USG agencies to safeguard classified intelligence or operations when normal measures are insufficient to achieve strict need-to-know controls and where SAP controls are not required.' ACCM is thus a SAP-like access control that by definition sits outside the SAP reporting statutes.
claims.source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-32/subtitle-A/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-117/section-117.3

claims.text: 32 CFR 117.3(b) defines SAP verbatim: 'SAP means any program that is established to control access and distribution and to provide protection for particularly sensitive classified information beyond that normally required for TOP SECRET, SECRET, or CONFIDENTIAL information.'

claims.text: 32 CFR 117.23 is titled 'Supplement to this rule: Security Requirements for Alternative Compensatory Control Measures (ACCM), Special Access Programs (SAPs), Sensitive Compartmented Information (SCI), Restricted Data (RD), Formerly Restricted Data (FRD), Transclassified Foreign Nuclear Information (TFNI), and Naval Nuclear Propulsion Information (NNPI).' 117.23(a)(1) verbatim: 'The contractor will comply with the security measures reflected in this section and other documents specifically referenced, when applied by the GCA or designee as part of a contract. Acceptance of the contract security measures is a prerequisite to any negotiations leading to program participation and an area accreditation (e.g., an SCI facility or SAP facility accreditation).'

A SAP can be created or continued only as authorized by a senior agency official delegated such authority pursuant to E.O. 13526.'
32 CFR 117.3(b) lists SAP information as 'proscribed information' together with TOP SECRET information, COMSEC information, Restricted Data and SCI.

claims.text: 32 CFR 117.23(d)(1): 'DoD SAP contracts. Contractors will implement the security requirements for SAPs codified in SAP-related policy, when established by contract. These documents include, but are not limited to, statutes, E.O.s, CSA directives, instructions, manuals, regulations, standards, memorandums, and other SAP security related policy documents.'

32 CFR 117.23(a)(2) provides that where a CSA-created program requires measures exceeding the rule's standards, 'the CSA-imposed higher standards specifically detailed in the contract or conveyed through other applicable directives will be binding on USG and contractor participants.'

32 CFR 117.3(b) defines ACCM as 'security measures used by USG agencies to safeguard classified intelligence or operations when normal measures are insufficient to achieve strict need-to-know controls and where SAP controls are not required.'
claims.source: 32 CFR 117.3(b), definition of ACCM

claims.text: Because 117.23(d)(1) exports the substantive SAP security requirements into contract documents, the actual rules governing a contractor holding SAP material are not published anywhere in the Code of Federal Regulations and are not obtainable without the contract. Reasoning: the regulation defers to unspecified 'SAP security related policy documents' established by contract.

entities.label: DoDD 5205.07, Special Access Program (SAP) Policy (1 Jul 2010, Chg 2 of 4 Feb 2020)
entities.sub: dod-issuance
entities.desc: This is the version of DoD's SAP charter that governed for the entire period covered by the Elizondo, Grusch and Kirkpatrick record, and it is the version cross-referenced by the NISPOM rule at 32 CFR 117.6(b)(3). It reissued the 5 January 2006 directive, established the Special Access Program Oversight Committee, established the DoD SAP Central Office under the authority, direction and control of the Deputy Secretary of Defense, and set out in plain language the three things this board most needs documented. First, the taxonomy: its glossary defines an acknowledged SAP as one 'whose existence is acknowledged but its specific details (technologies, materials, techniques, etc.) are classified'; an unacknowledged SAP as one 'having protective controls ensuring the existence of the program is not acknowledged, affirmed, or made known to any person not authorized for such information'; and a waived SAP as 'A SAP for which the Secretary of Defense has waived applicable reporting in accordance with Reference (c) following a determination of adverse effect to national security. An unacknowledged SAP that has more restrictive reporting and access controls.' Reference (c) is section 119 of title 10. Second, the congressional access rule: members of the defense and intelligence committees are authorised access to DoD SAPs 'except for waived programs', and for waived SAPs 'only the chair, the ranking minority member, and the staff directors' are authorised access unless the Secretary or Deputy Secretary approves otherwise. Third, the custody rule: 'All waived SAP material submitted to Congress, to include annual reports and other products, shall remain in DoD custody. No copies shall be stored outside DoD repositories or control without the approval of the Secretary or Deputy Secretary of Defense.' A committee briefed on a waived program is not permitted to keep the paper.

claims.text: THE CARVE-OUT REQUEST PATH. Enclosure 2, para 7: 'A CA may seek DepSecDef approval to relieve the Defense Security Service (DSS) of its SAP security oversight role and use DoD Component procedures instead for oversight, security review, and SAP automated information system (IS) accreditation for designated SAPs. DoD Component-designated procedures shall, at a minimum, meet the standards and frequency authorized by DoD 5220.22-M.' entities.label: DoDM 5205.07 Volume 1 — DoD SAP Security Manual: General Procedures
entities.sub: dod-issuance
entities.desc: Volume 1 of the four-volume DoD SAP Security Manual assigns responsibilities and describes the general procedures for the administration of DoD SAP security, implementing the policy of DoDI 5205.11, and it incorporates and cancels the Revision 1 Department of Defense Overprint to the National Industrial Security Program Operating Manual Supplement. Its Enclosure 2 contains the operative statement of what a carve-out removes. The Director, DSS - the office now called the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency - administers the NISP and issues facility clearances for defense contractors 'to include contractors performing on DoD SAPs'; but then, 'Unless a carve-out provision is approved by the Secretary of Defense or the Deputy Secretary of Defense', the Director performs SAP security inspections at cleared defense contractor locations, authorises classified contractor SAP information systems and the introduction of guest systems in contractor SAP facilities, and coordinates with the designated counterintelligence component to cross-share threat and incident information. Read the sentence backwards and it is an inventory of what disappears when a carve-out is signed: the independent physical inspection, the independent accreditation of the computers, and the independent counterintelligence feed. Its glossary supplies the definition in eleven words of substance: 'carve-out. A provision approved by the Secretary or Deputy Secretary of Defense that relieves DSS of its NISP obligation to perform industrial security oversight functions for a DoD SAP.' Volume 1 also documents two cover mechanisms - HANDLE VIA SPECIAL ACCESS CHANNELS ONLY (HVSACO), an unclassified handling caveat used among other things 'When using a SAP nickname for an unacknowledged SAP', and the rule that 'Federal Government-affiliated identification cards will not be used for positive identification in unacknowledged locations'.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded A on a global pass (rank 110 of 1170, score 60). 5 connections, 2 of them custody/funding/programmatic, 1 official denial recorded against it. Axes C1/A3/D2.

entities.label: ICD 906 — Controlled Access Programs (ODNI)
entities.sub: ic-directive
entities.desc: ICD 906 is the directive that governs what the intelligence community calls its special access programs. Its authority is 'The National Security Act of 1947, as amended; Executive Order (EO) 12333, as amended; and other applicable provisions of law', and it 'establishes the oversight and management of Intelligence Community (IC) special access programs pursuant to EO 13526, Section 4.3, or any successor document, referred to within the IC as Controlled Access Programs (CAPs)'. The reissued version obtained for this board supersedes the ICD 906 signed 17 October 2015; the released PDF was generated on 19 December 2024 and its signature block is an image that does not resolve to text, so the exact reissue date is not machine-readable in the public copy. The substance is unambiguous and, for this board, extraordinary. Only the DNI or the Principal Deputy DNI may establish, validate, modify or terminate a CAP. CAPs are defined as 'a top-level control system (such as Special Intelligence, Talent Keyhole, Human Intelligence Control System), and any compartment or sub-compartment under a control system'. Unacknowledged CAPs exist and 'may be established only where knowledge of the existence of a program would reveal aspects of its protected information ... Unacknowledged CAPs may be established only with the approval of the DNI or PDDNI'. Governance mirrors DoD: a CAP Oversight Committee chaired by the PDDNI or designee, and a Senior Review Group. All CAPs are to be recorded in Scattered Castles, the IC personnel security database - 'Any exemption from this requirement shall be approved only by the DNI or PDDNI'. Access may be limited by billet or 'by name or position (BYNOP)'. Critically, ICD 906 assigns the ODNI Controlled Access Program Central Office responsibility for 'the coordination of CAP-related engagements, to include, but not limited to, congressional briefings, requests from the Information Security Oversight Office, and the National Security Council' - and nowhere in the directive is there any counterpart to 10 U.S.C. 119: no annual report deadline, no 30-day pre-initiation notice, no statutory list. The IC side of the architecture has less congressional reporting machinery than the DoD side, not more. ICD 906 also expressly does not apply to SAPs established by the Secretaries of State, Defense, Energy or Homeland Security or the Attorney General, 'Nor does this Directive apply to special access programs under the purview of the National Security Council, such as covert action' - identifying, in one sentence, a third category of program governed by neither regime.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded A on a global pass (rank 50 of 1170, score 81). 7 connections, 2 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C2/A3/D3.

claims.text: Purpose, verbatim: 'This Intelligence Community Directive (ICD) establishes the oversight and management of Intelligence Community (IC) special access programs pursuant to EO 13526, Section 4.3, or any successor document, referred to within the IC as Controlled Access Programs (CAPs). 2. This ICD supersedes ICD 906, Controlled Access Programs, signed 17 October 2015.'
claims.source: https://web.archive.org/web/20250112183207/https://www.dni.gov/files/documents/ICD/ICD-906-Controlled-Access-Programs.pdf

claims.text: JURISDICTIONAL FENCE. Applicability C.3, verbatim: 'This Directive does not apply to special access programs established pursuant to EO 13526, Section 4.3, or any successor document by the Secretaries of State, Defense, Energy, or Homeland Security or by the Attorney General, or their principal deputies. Nor does this Directive apply to special access programs under the purview of the National Security Council, such as covert action.' C.2 adds that the DNI 'may establish CAPs pertaining to intelligence sources, methods, and activities but does not have authority to establish military operational, strategic, or tactical programs.'
claims.source: https://web.archive.org/web/20250112183207/https://www.dni.gov/files/documents/ICD/ICD-906-Controlled-Access-Programs.pdf

claims.text: IC UNACKNOWLEDGED PROGRAMS. Policy D.3, verbatim: 'unacknowledged CAPs may be established only where knowledge of the existence of a program would reveal aspects of its protected information, and when there is no other means to protect information about programs at the collateral classification level, or when required by statute. Unacknowledged CAPs may be established only with the approval of the DNI or PDDNI.'
claims.source: https://web.archive.org/web/20250112183207/https://www.dni.gov/files/documents/ICD/ICD-906-Controlled-Access-Programs.pdf

claims.text: Policy D.2: 'Only the DNI or the Principal Deputy Director of National Intelligence (PDDNI) have the authority to establish, validate, modify, or terminate CAPs. For the purpose of this Directive, CAPs are defined as a top-level control system (such as Special Intelligence, Talent Keyhole, Human Intelligence Control System), and any compartment or sub-compartment under a control system within the IC.' D.2.a: 'There shall not be any levels beyond the sub-compartment levels, unless the DNI or PDDNI determine or approve otherwise.'
claims.source: https://web.archive.org/web/20250112183207/https://www.dni.gov/files/documents/ICD/ICD-906-Controlled-Access-Programs.pdf

claims.text: THE DISCOVERABILITY EXEMPTION. Policy D.5: 'Intelligence and intelligence-related information within all CAPs shall be discoverable or exempted from discovery consistent with the processes outlined in ICD 501 ... Any exemption from this requirement shall be approved only by the DNI or PDDNI, and reviewed and validated at least annually.' E.1.b lets the DNI or PDDNI 'Establish unacknowledged CAPs and/or approve non-discoverability of CAPs if a compelling case can be made that any agreed upon approach to discoverability would reveal a capability, a decision, or a fragile source, and the information contained in the compartment is so narrowly tailored, it is unlikely to be of use to officers who do not already have access to the compartment.' A CAP can thus be made invisible to the IC's own internal information-discovery system.
claims.source: https://web.archive.org/web/20250112183207/https://www.dni.gov/files/documents/ICD/ICD-906-Controlled-Access-Programs.pdf

claims.text: SCATTERED CASTLES IS THE REGISTRY -- AND HAS AN EXEMPTION. Policy D.6: 'All CAPs shall be recorded, and individual accesses to those CAPs shall be included, in the authoritative repository, Scattered Castles, or its successor system ... Any exemption from this requirement shall be approved only by the DNI or PDDNI, and reviewed and validated at least annually.' D.6.a permits access to be 'further limited by billets ... or by name or position (BYNOP).'
claims.source: https://web.archive.org/web/20250112183207/https://www.dni.gov/files/documents/ICD/ICD-906-Controlled-Access-Programs.pdf

claims.text: Policy D.7 establishes the CAP Oversight Committee (CAPOC), chaired by the PDDNI or designee, whose Chair 'shall be responsible for CAP oversight and the management of CAPs, to include all unacknowledged CAPs.' D.8 establishes a Senior Review Group (SRG) that reviews 'all CAPs, including unacknowledged CAPs' at least annually.
claims.source: https://web.archive.org/web/20250112183207/https://www.dni.gov/files/documents/ICD/ICD-906-Controlled-Access-Programs.pdf

claims.text: Policy D.9 makes the Director of the ODNI Controlled Access Program Central Office (CAPCO) 'the accountable official responsible for the implementation of this policy'; CAPCO shall 'Manage a CAP Registry that maintains a list of all control systems, including all compartments and sub-compartments ... and manage all compartment and sub compartment names, codenames, and any other pertinent information' and 'Be responsible for the coordination of CAP-related engagements, to include, but not limited to, congressional briefings, requests from the Information Security Oversight Office, and the National Security Council.' ISOO's access to IC CAPs is routed through CAPCO.
claims.source: https://web.archive.org/web/20250112183207/https://www.dni.gov/files/documents/ICD/ICD-906-Controlled-Access-Programs.pdf

claims.text: ANNUAL RE-JUSTIFICATION OF UNACKNOWLEDGED STATUS. Policy D.10.e.(1): 'For unacknowledged CAPs, IC elements shall include in their annual review submission, a justification for why each such CAP still meets the requirements to be unacknowledged.' D.10.b: 'Any new CAPs not submitted, and approved, will be terminated.' D.10.e: 'CAPs not re-validated shall be terminated and the protected information shall be de-compartmented or protected by a validated CAP.'
claims.source: https://web.archive.org/web/20250112183207/https://www.dni.gov/files/documents/ICD/ICD-906-Controlled-Access-Programs.pdf

claims.text: RECORDS OFFICER REQUIREMENT. D.9.d and D.10.g: IC elements and CAPCO must 'Ensure all records pertaining to CAPs are maintained, and ensure that at least one records official is cleared to all CAP information in accordance with EO 13526.' There must exist at least one cleared records official with visibility into every CAP.
claims.source: https://web.archive.org/web/20250112183207/https://www.dni.gov/files/documents/ICD/ICD-906-Controlled-Access-Programs.pdf

claims.text: The ICD 906 architecture is materially tighter than the DoD SAP architecture on exactly the axis that matters for concealment: unacknowledged CAPs must be re-justified in writing every year, non-discoverability requires an annually re-validated DNI exemption, and unsubmitted programs are terminated by default. The DoD side has an annual SAPOC review of waived status (DoDI 5205.11 3.5.a.(3)(d)) but no default-termination rule and no equivalent single authoritative access registry. Reasoning stated by comparison of the two texts.
claims.source: https://web.archive.org/web/20250112183207/https://www.dni.gov/files/documents/ICD/ICD-906-Controlled-Access-Programs.pdf

claims.text: ICD 906 contains no annual congressional reporting deadline, no pre-initiation notification period and no statutory reporting clock equivalent to 10 U.S.C. 119.

claims.text: ICD 906 section C.3 identifies a third population of special access programs - those 'under the purview of the National Security Council, such as covert action' - which are governed neither by 10 U.S.C. 119 nor by ICD 906, and whose reporting runs instead through 50 U.S.C. 3093. entities.label: ODNI Controlled Access Program Coordination Office (CAPCO)
entities.sub: oversight-body
entities.desc: CAPCO is the intelligence community's counterpart to DoD SAPCO and does two distinct jobs. Under ICD 906 the Director of the ODNI Controlled Access Program Central Office is 'the accountable official responsible for the implementation of this policy', serves as central point of contact for all CAP requirements, and must 'Manage a CAP Registry that maintains a list of all control systems, including all compartments and sub-compartments', deconflict all IC CAPs against all other programs, and 'manage all compartment and sub compartment names, codenames, and any other pertinent information'. It is also 'responsible for the coordination of CAP-related engagements, to include, but not limited to, congressional briefings, requests from the Information Security Oversight Office, and the National Security Council' - the same choke-point design as DoD SAPCO, with ISOO's access routed through the office whose programs ISOO would be examining. Separately, CAPCO publishes the Intelligence Community Authorized Classification and Control Markings Register and Manual, the document that defines the entire marking syntax used across the U.S. classification system, including the Special Access Program marking category. For this board the CAP Registry is the single most valuable unreleased document in the intelligence community: a complete list of every control system, compartment and sub-compartment, maintained by name, in one office, by directive.

entities.label: CAP Registry / CAPCO Register of control systems, compartments and sub-compartments
entities.sub: registry
entities.desc: The CAPCO Register is the rulebook for how classified material is marked across the United States government, and reading it tells you how a special access program looks on paper. The publicly released Volume 5, Edition 1 (Version 5.1), effective 30 December 2011 with an administrative update of 30 March 2012, establishes a distinct Special Access Program Markings category - moved in that edition out of the Non-Intelligence Community Dissemination Control Markings category - which follows the SCI control markings in the banner line. 'The first value in the SAP category is the SAP category indicator either "SPECIAL ACCESS REQUIRED-" or "SAR-" (the authorized abbreviation) ... Following the SAP category indicator shall be the SAP program indicator which is the program's nickname or authorized digraph or trigraph.' Compartments follow the program identifier separated by hyphens; sub-compartments follow the compartment. That syntax is why the sample DoD action memo in DoDI 5205.11 is marked '(S//SAR-GTE)'. The Register was produced by CAPCO with the IC Classification Markings Implementation Working Group, whose members include the Air Force, Army, CIA, Coast Guard, DEA, DHS, DIA, DOE, State, FBI, Marine Corps, Navy, NGA, NRO, NSA, ODNI, OUSD(I) and Treasury, advised by NARA's Information Security Oversight Office. And the title page of the public version carries the note that settles a recurring argument: 'Certain security markings were removed due to classified content. These markings have been compiled in separate classified addenda.' The public register is therefore known, on its own face, to be incomplete - there exist compartment markings whose very existence is classified, listed in addenda that have never been released.

entities.label: 50 U.S.C. 3091a — Congressional Oversight of Controlled Access Programs
entities.sub: statute
entities.desc: Section 501A of the National Security Act of 1947 was added by section 504 of the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2022, Public Law 117-103 of 15 March 2022, and is codified at 50 U.S.C. 3091a. It is the statutory counterpart to ICD 906, and it defines 'controlled access program' by direct reference: 'a program created or managed pursuant to Intelligence Community Directive 906, or successor directive' - the United States Code citing an ODNI directive by URL. As enacted it required the DNI to brief the intelligence committees and congressional leadership on every controlled access program in effect not less than semiannually or on request, prohibited the head of an IC element from establishing a CAP or any compartment or subcompartment within one until the appropriate committees and leadership are notified, and required annual reports listing all active and all terminated compartments and subcompartments, with a DNI certification for each that its creation, validation or substantial modification is 'substantiated and justified', the identification of a control officer for each program, and a statement of protection requirements. Then, on 23 December 2024, sections 6602 and 6603 of the FY2025 NDAA, Public Law 118-159, added two teeth. Section 6602 inserted a new subsection (c): National Intelligence Program funds 'may not be obligated or expended for any controlled access program, or a compartment or subcompartment therein' until the required notification is submitted. Section 6603 added subsection (b)(2), prohibiting the head of an IC element from transferring 'a capability from a controlled access program, including from a compartment or subcompartment therein to a compartment or subcompartment of another controlled access program, to a special access program (as defined in section 3348(g) of this title), or to anything else outside the controlled access program' without prior notice - subject to exceptions for 'an urgent counterintelligence issue' or 'an organizational restructuring'. That second provision is Congress legislating directly against the mechanism at the centre of this board: moving a capability out of one compartment regime and into another to break the audit trail. Congress does not write a statute against a manoeuvre nobody has performed.

claims.text: (b) verbatim: 'A head of an element of the intelligence community may not establish a controlled access program, or a compartment or subcompartment therein, until the head notifies the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership of such controlled access program, compartment, or subcompartment, as the case may be.' L. 118-159 sec. 6603 (23 December 2024): a head of an IC element 'may not transfer a capability from a controlled access program, including from a compartment or subcompartment therein to a compartment or subcompartment of another controlled access program, to a special access program (as defined in section 3348(g) of this title), or to anything else outside the controlled access program, until the head submits to the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership notice of the intent of the head to make such transfer.'

entities.label: 50 U.S.C. 3091 — General Congressional Oversight Provisions (NSA 1947 sec. 501)
entities.sub: statute
entities.desc: Section 501 of the National Security Act, at 50 U.S.C. 3091, is the general obligation against which every claim of concealment from Congress in the intelligence sphere must be measured. Subsection (a)(1) requires the President to 'ensure that the congressional intelligence committees are kept fully and currently informed of the intelligence activities of the United States, including any significant anticipated intelligence activity'. Subsection (b) requires that 'any illegal intelligence activity is reported promptly to the congressional intelligence committees, as well as any corrective action that has been taken or is planned'. And subsection (e) closes the classification defence completely: 'Nothing in this chapter shall be construed as authority to withhold information from the congressional intelligence committees on the grounds that providing the information to the congressional intelligence committees would constitute the unauthorized disclosure of classified information or information relating to intelligence sources and methods.' That sentence is the most useful single line of statute for anyone arguing that a compartment cannot lawfully be used to keep the intelligence committees out of an intelligence activity. Its limits are equally important: it binds only as to intelligence activities and only as to the intelligence committees, so it does not reach a DoD acquisition or operations and support special access program, and it does not reach the defense committees at all.

50 U.S.C. 3091(e): 'Nothing in this chapter shall be construed as authority to withhold information from the congressional intelligence committees on the grounds that providing the information to the congressional intelligence committees would constitute the unauthorized disclosure of classified information or information relating to intelligence sources and methods.'
50 U.S.C. 3091(b) requires that any illegal intelligence activity be reported promptly to the congressional intelligence committees together with corrective action taken or planned.
50 U.S.C. 3091(f) provides that 'intelligence activities' includes covert actions as defined in section 3093(e) and financial intelligence activities.

Section 3091(e) forbids using classification as a reason to withhold from the intelligence committees, but it operates only on 'intelligence activities' and only for those committees, so a DoD operations and support or acquisition special access program is outside its reach entirely. Reasoning: the duty is defined by the subject matter 'intelligence activities' and the audience 'congressional intelligence committees'.

entities.label: 50 U.S.C. 2426 — Congressional Oversight of DOE/NNSA Special Access Programs
entities.sub: statute
entities.desc: Section 3236 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2000, Public Law 106-65, created a separate SAP reporting regime for the National Nuclear Security Administration, now at 50 U.S.C. 2426. Structurally it is a copy of 10 U.S.C. 119: a February 1 annual report to the congressional defense committees, a February 1 new-program notice with justification, a 14-day notice before a classification change or public declassification, prompt notice of changes to designation criteria, and a 30-day report-and-wait before initiation. But subsection (e)(1) is materially broader than the DoD waiver. It gives the Administrator the same power to waive the reporting requirements of subsections (a), (b) and (c), and then adds a sentence that has no counterpart in title 10: 'The Administrator may waive the report-and-wait requirement in subsection (f) if the Administrator determines that compliance with such requirement would adversely affect the national security.' Under 10 U.S.C. 119 the Secretary of Defense may waive what he tells the committees but not the requirement to notify them thirty days before starting a program. Under 50 U.S.C. 2426 the Administrator of the NNSA may waive both. That is the single most permissive SAP provision in the United States Code, and it sits in the statute governing the agency that runs the weapons laboratories - Los Alamos, Sandia, Lawrence Livermore - and holds Restricted Data under the Atomic Energy Act. The waived information goes 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the congressional defense committees'.

claims.text: The waiver mirrors 10 U.S.C. 119(e) exactly: 'The Administrator may waive any requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c)' on a case-by-case adverse-national-security determination, after which the information and justification go 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the congressional defense committees.' A program may not be initiated until the defense committees are notified and 30 days elapse.

claims.text: Two of the three SAP reporting statutes (10 U.S.C. 119 for DoD, 50 U.S.C. 2426 for NNSA) contain the eight-member waiver; the third (50 U.S.C. 3348) does not reduce the audience, and the newest (50 U.S.C. 3091a, IC) has no waiver at all. The waiver-to-four-committee-pairs mechanism therefore exists precisely and only where physical hardware programs and nuclear-adjacent research live. claims.text: 50 U.S.C. 2426(e)(1): 'The Administrator may waive any requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c) ... The Administrator may waive the report-and-wait requirement in subsection (f) if the Administrator determines that compliance with such requirement would adversely affect the national security. Any waiver under this paragraph shall be made on a case-by-case basis.'
50 U.S.C. 2426(e)(2) directs the waived information and justification 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the congressional defense committees.'

50 U.S.C. 2426(f) otherwise imposes the same 30-day report-and-wait as 10 U.S.C. 119(f): 'A special access program may not be initiated until - (1) the congressional defense committees are notified of the program; and (2) a period of 30 days elapses after such notification is received.'

entities.label: Executive Order 12829 — National Industrial Security Program (6 Jan 1993)
entities.sub: executive-order
entities.desc: Executive Order 12829 established the National Industrial Security Program to provide a single, government-wide industrial security regime for contractors handling classified information. Section 201 of the order directs the Secretary of Defense, in consultation with all affected agencies and with the concurrence of the Secretary of Energy, the Chairman of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, the Director of National Intelligence and the Secretary of Homeland Security, to issue and maintain the NISP Operating Manual - the document now codified as 32 CFR Part 117. The order is the ancestor of the carve-out: because it designates the Secretary of Defense as the issuing authority for the manual and DCSA (formerly the Defense Security Service) as the DoD Cognizant Security Office, it also creates the office from which a special access program can be exempted. Its practical importance to this board is that the NISP is the only routine, recurring, adversarial physical inspection of a contractor facility holding classified material. Where the NISP applies, a government inspector who is not part of the program walks the facility. Where it has been carved out, no such person exists.

entities.desc: Requested in response to a Senate report accompanying the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2004, GAO-04-332 assessed the Defense Security Service's oversight of more than 11,000 cleared contractor facilities under the National Industrial Security Program and DSS's actions after possible compromises of classified information. Its title is its finding. For this board the most important sentence is a footnote: 'As agreed with committee staff, our review was limited to DSS's oversight of contractor facilities' protection of Confidential, Secret, and Top Secret information as defined in Executive Order no. 12958, as amended, and did not include DSS's oversight of special access programs at contractor facilities.' entities.label: The defense committees (10 U.S.C. 119(g))
entities.sub: congressional
entities.desc: Section 119(g) defines the term that governs who gets told. As amended by Public Law 104-106 in 1996, Public Law 106-65 in 1999 and Public Law 107-107 in 2001, it means '(1) the Committee on Armed Services and the Committee on Appropriations, and the Defense Subcommittee of the Committee on Appropriations, of the Senate; and (2) the Committee on Armed Services and the Committee on Appropriations, and the Subcommittee on Defense of the Committee on Appropriations, of the House of Representatives.' The definition is the reason the SAP record is structurally invisible to the rest of Congress: the House Oversight Committee, which has held every public UAP hearing since 26 July 2023, is not a defense committee and has no statutory entitlement to the section 119 reports. Neither are the intelligence committees; they sit under a wholly separate regime in title 50. Before 1996 the definition was broader in one respect and narrower in another - the prior text referred simply to 'the Committees on Armed Services and Appropriations of the Senate and House' and 'the Defense Subcommittees of the Committees on Appropriations'. The 1996 amendment made the enumeration explicit. The practical consequence for this board: a member of Congress who is not on one of these six bodies and not on an intelligence committee has no lawful route to a SAP list at all, which is precisely the wall the 2023-2026 UAP oversight effort has repeatedly hit.

entities.label: Public Law 100-180 sec. 1132 — creation of SAP congressional oversight (4 Dec 1987)
entities.sub: statute
entities.desc: Until 4 December 1987 there was no statute at all requiring the Department of Defense to tell Congress that a special access program existed. Section 1132(a)(1) of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Years 1988 and 1989 added section 119 to title 10, at 101 Stat. 1151. The date is load-bearing for this board's chronology: every alleged legacy recovery and reverse-engineering activity from the 1940s through 1987 - the entire period covering Roswell, Project SIGN, Project BLUE BOOK's termination, the 1970s nuclear-site overflights and the origins of the alleged retrieval effort - ran in a legal environment in which no SAP reporting obligation to Congress existed whatsoever. A program stood up before December 1987 and never re-baselined was never a 'new special access program' within the meaning of subsection (b)(3), because that term is defined as one 'that has not previously been covered in a notice and justification under this subsection' - a definition that, on its face, does not reach back before the subsection existed.

entities.label: The annual DoD special access program report to Congress
entities.sub: report
entities.desc: The annual SAP report is the single document that would settle the central question of this board, and everything about how it is produced is documented. It is required by 10 U.S.C. 119(a)(1) by 1 March each year to the six defense committees, and must set out the total requested for DoD SAPs and, for each program in the budget, a brief description, major milestones, actual prior cost, and estimated cost across six fiscal years. DoDI 5205.11 assigns its production: the cognizant authorities 'shall prepare and submit annual reports and other required SAP information through the Director, DoD SAPCO, and the governance structure in order to report the state of DoD SAPs to congressional committees'; the Senior Review Group 'Ensures the accuracy of the SAP list submitted to Congress prior to submission of the SAP annual report'; and the SAPOC conducts 'an annual review and validation of SAP reports sent to the Congressional defense and intelligence committees'. The report is coordinated with the Assistant Secretary of Defense for Legislative Affairs under DoDI 5545.02. Programs identified in it are identified by unclassified nickname. Waived programs are, by definition, the ones removed from it under 10 U.S.C. 119(e), with their information going instead to eight to twelve named members; and under DoDD 5205.07 (2010) para 4.h the waived material 'shall remain in DoD custody' with no copies stored outside DoD repositories. The report has never been released, in whole or in redacted part, under FOIA. It is the highest value single target on the board: one document, produced annually since 1988, whose table of contents is the answer.

entities.label: Alternative Compensatory Control Measures (ACCM)
entities.sub: mechanism
entities.desc: ACCM is the layer below a special access program, and it is the layer with no statute attached to it at all. The NISPOM rule defines it: 'ACCM are security measures used by USG agencies to safeguard classified intelligence or operations when normal measures are insufficient to achieve strict need-to-know controls and where SAP controls are not required.' The rule then requires contractors to implement ACCM protection requirements 'when established by contract, in accordance with applicable statutes, E.O.s, CSA directives, instructions, manuals, regulations, standards, and memorandums', and covers ACCM in the same supplement, section 117.23, as SAPs, SCI and Restricted Data. The importance for this board is precise and narrow: ACCM produces access lists, nicknames and compartmented handling that look and function like a special access program, but because it is by definition the case 'where SAP controls are not required', an ACCM is not a SAP, and therefore nothing in 10 U.S.C. 119 applies to it. There is no annual ACCM report to the defense committees, no new-ACCM notice, no 30-day report-and-wait and no waiver to exercise, because there is nothing to waive. An activity that needs compartmentation but does not want a line in the annual SAP report has a documented, lawful place to sit.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded B on a global pass (rank 236 of 1170, score 43). 2 connections, 1 of them custody/funding/programmatic, 1 official denial recorded against it. Axes C2/A2/D3.

claims.text: 32 CFR 117.3(b), verbatim: 'ACCM are security measures used by USG agencies to safeguard classified intelligence or operations when normal measures are insufficient to achieve strict need-to-know controls and where SAP controls are not required.'
claims.source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-32/subtitle-A/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-117/section-117.3

claims.text: 32 CFR 117.23 places ACCM in the same 'Supplement to this rule' as SAPs, SCI, RD, FRD, TFNI and NNPI, and its heading names ACCM first. 117.23(a): 'Given the sensitive nature of Alternative Compensatory Control Measures (ACCM), SAPs, SCI, RD, FRD, TFNI, and NNPI, the security requirements prescribed in this section exceed baseline standards for this rule and must be applied, as applicable, through specific contract requirements.'
claims.source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-32/subtitle-A/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-117/section-117.23

claims.text: ACCM is the only member of that regulated set with no reporting statute attached: 10 U.S.C. 119, 50 U.S.C. 2426, 3348 and 3091a each key on the term 'special access program' or 'controlled access program', and the NISPOM rule's own definition places ACCM expressly 'where SAP controls are not required.' A capability protected by ACCM rather than SAP controls therefore triggers no congressional notice under any of the four statutes. Reasoning stated from the definition and the four statutes.

claims.text: 32 CFR 117.3(b): 'ACCM are security measures used by USG agencies to safeguard classified intelligence or operations when normal measures are insufficient to achieve strict need-to-know controls and where SAP controls are not required.'
32 CFR 117.23 addresses ACCM in the same supplement as SAPs, SCI, RD, FRD, TFNI and NNPI, requiring contractors to implement ACCM protection requirements 'when established by contract'.

Because ACCM is defined as the case where SAP controls are not required, an ACCM is outside the definition of 'special access program' in 10 U.S.C. 119 and 50 U.S.C. 3348(g)(3), and therefore outside every SAP congressional reporting statute. Reasoning: all four reporting statutes are triggered by the term 'special access program', which ACCM expressly is not.

entities.label: The four SAP reporting regimes and the seams between them
entities.sub: analysis
entities.desc: There is no single United States statute on special access programs. There are four parallel regimes plus covert action, and the differences between them are where a program can live. (1) DoD - 10 U.S.C. 119: annual report by 1 March, new-program notice by 1 February, 14-day declassification notice, 30-day report-and-wait, all to six defense committees; the Secretary may waive the reports on a national-security determination, in which case the information goes only to the chairman and ranking minority member of each. (2) NNSA - 50 U.S.C. 2426: identical structure to the defense committees, but the Administrator may additionally waive the 30-day report-and-wait itself. (3) Every other agency - 50 U.S.C. 3348: identical structure, but reporting runs to 'congressional oversight committees' expressly including House Oversight and Senate Homeland Security, and the waiver does not narrow the audience. (4) The Intelligence Community - 50 U.S.C. 3091a and ICD 906: no annual statutory deadline and no waiver at all, but semiannual briefings on every program, a prohibition on establishment before notification, a funding cutoff since December 2024, and a prohibition on transferring capabilities out of a CAP into a SAP without notice since December 2024. Set beside each other, the ranking is unambiguous: the weakest reporting regime in the United States government belongs to the Department of Defense, and it is weakest precisely at the point where the Secretary decides how much to tell the committees. Two structural seams follow. The first is between regimes: a capability transferred from an IC controlled access program to a DoD special access program changes which statute governs it and which committees see it - the manoeuvre Congress prohibited prospectively in December 2024, three decades after the alleged conduct. The second is around all four: ICD 906 section C.3 records that none of them applies to 'special access programs under the purview of the National Security Council, such as covert action', which are governed only by 50 U.S.C. 3093 and its Gang of Eight.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded B on a global pass (rank 204 of 1170, score 45). 6 connections, 1 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C1/A3/D3.

claims.text: Four statutes, each with a different addressee. DoD: 10 U.S.C. 119 (defense committees; annual 1 Mar; waiver in (e) collapsing to chairman + ranking member). NNSA: 50 U.S.C. 2426 (congressional defense committees; annual 1 Feb; identical waiver). All other non-IC agencies: 50 U.S.C. 3348 (congressional oversight committees; annual 1 Feb; waiver that does NOT reduce the audience). IC: 50 U.S.C. 3091a (intelligence committees + both Appropriations + the four congressional leaders; semiannual briefings; no waiver at all).
claims.source: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2023-title50/html/USCODE-2023-title50-chap45-subchapIII-sec3348.htm

claims.text: The seams are written into the statutes. 50 U.S.C. 3348(g)(2)(B) removes DoD, NNSA and every IC element from its own coverage. 50 U.S.C. 3091a(d)(3) defines its subject by reference to ICD 906. ICD 906 section C.3 in turn removes from its own coverage every SAP created by the Secretaries of State, Defense, Energy or Homeland Security or the Attorney General, and 'special access programs under the purview of the National Security Council, such as covert action.'
claims.source: https://web.archive.org/web/20250112183207/https://www.dni.gov/files/documents/ICD/ICD-906-Controlled-Access-Programs.pdf

claims.text: Composed, the four regimes leave two seams with no annual census obligation running to a full committee: (i) a DoD program under a 119(e) waiver, whose content goes only to chairs and ranking members and whose annual report requirement additionally sunset on 31 Dec 2021 under Pub. L. 114-328 sec. 1061; and (ii) anything protected by ACCM rather than SAP controls, which no statute names. Covert action under 50 U.S.C. 3093 is a third, separately governed channel. Reasoning stated from the four statutes plus 32 CFR 117.3.
claims.source: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2023-title10/html/USCODE-2023-title10-subtitleA-partI-chap2-sec119.htm

claims.text: Four separate statutes govern SAP-type reporting: 10 U.S.C. 119 (DoD), 50 U.S.C. 2426 (NNSA), 50 U.S.C. 3348 (all other non-IC agencies) and 50 U.S.C. 3091a (IC controlled access programs).

Of the four regimes, only 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) and 50 U.S.C. 2426(e)(2) narrow the recipient of waived information to the chairman and ranking minority member; 50 U.S.C. 3348(e)(2) keeps the full oversight committees, and 50 U.S.C. 3091a has no waiver provision at all.

claims.text: Only 50 U.S.C. 3091a carries a funding prohibition tied to notification, added by section 6602 of Public Law 118-159 on 23 December 2024.

A program moved between the DoD and IC regimes changes both its governing statute and its reporting audience, and before 23 December 2024 no statute required notice of the move. That is a documented, lawful, unnotified route by which a program's oversight history can be broken. Reasoning: the prohibition added by Pub. L. 118-159 sec. 6603 did not exist before that date and operates prospectively.

entities.label: 50 U.S.C. 3093 — Presidential Approval and Reporting of Covert Actions
entities.sub: statute
entities.desc: Section 503 of the National Security Act of 1947, added by the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 1991, Public Law 102-88 of 14 August 1991, governs the one category of activity that sits outside every special access program reporting regime. ICD 906 section C.3 states in terms that neither it nor the DoD SAP regime applies to 'special access programs under the purview of the National Security Council, such as covert action'. Section 3093 requires a written presidential finding before any covert action, reported in writing to the intelligence committees 'as soon as possible after such approval and before the initiation of the covert action'. Subsection (c)(2) is the exception the press calls the Gang of Eight: where the President determines it essential to limit access 'to meet extraordinary circumstances affecting vital interests of the United States', the finding may go to the chairmen and ranking minority members of the intelligence committees, the Speaker and minority leader of the House, the majority and minority leaders of the Senate, and any other leadership members the President chooses to include. Subsection (c)(3) permits no prior notice at all, requiring only that the President afterwards 'fully inform the congressional intelligence committees in a timely fashion' with a statement of reasons. Subsection (c)(5), added in 2010, requires a written statement of reasons for limiting access and forces a reconsideration within 180 days - a protection with no counterpart in the SAP statutes. Subsection (d) extends the same notification rules to 'any significant change in a previously approved covert action' and lists the factors that make an undertaking significant, including whether it 'requires an expansion of existing authorities, including authorities relating to research, development, or operations' and whether it 'results in the expenditure of significant funds or other resources'. For this board the importance is structural: an activity characterised as covert action under NSC purview is reportable only under section 3093, is invisible to the defense committees entirely, and can lawfully be known to as few as eight members of Congress - or, under (c)(3), to none in advance.

50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(3) permits a finding not to be reported in advance at all, requiring only that the President thereafter 'fully inform the congressional intelligence committees in a timely fashion' with 'a statement of the reasons for not giving prior notice'.

50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(5)(B) requires that within 180 days of a statement of reasons for limited access the President ensure that all members of the intelligence committees get access, or submit a further statement of reasons.

50 U.S.C. 3093(d)(2) lists among the factors making an undertaking significant whether it 'requires an expansion of existing authorities, including authorities relating to research, development, or operations' and whether it 'results in the expenditure of significant funds or other resources'.

entities.label: The Gang of Eight and the limited-notification convention
entities.sub: congressional
entities.desc: The phrase 'Gang of Eight' has a precise statutory origin that is routinely misapplied to special access programs, and getting it right matters. Under 50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(1) a presidential finding authorising covert action must be reported in writing to the congressional intelligence committees as soon as possible after approval and before initiation. Paragraph (2) is the exception: 'If the President determines that it is essential to limit access to the finding to meet extraordinary circumstances affecting vital interests of the United States, the finding may be reported to the chairmen and ranking minority members of the congressional intelligence committees, the Speaker and minority leader of the House of Representatives, the majority and minority leaders of the Senate, and such other member or members of the congressional leadership as may be included by the President.' Four committee leaders plus four chamber leaders: eight. Since the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2010, paragraph (5)(A) requires a written statement of the reasons for limiting access, and (5)(B) requires that within 180 days either all members of the intelligence committees get access or a further written statement of reasons is submitted. Paragraph (3) preserves the option of no prior notice at all, requiring only that the President 'fully inform the congressional intelligence committees in a timely fashion' afterwards with a statement of reasons. The DoD waived-SAP convention is a different animal that behaves the same way: 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) sends waived information to 'the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees', and DoD Directive 5205.07 (2010) restricted access for waived programs to 'the chair, the ranking minority member, and the staff directors of the defense and intelligence committees'. The DoD version has no 180-day sunset, no requirement to widen access ever, and no statutory statement-of-reasons requirement beyond the waiver justification itself. On paper, covert action is better supervised than a waived special access program.

claims.text: The Gang of Eight is a creature of 50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(2) governing COVERT ACTION findings, not special access programs. The parallel narrowing for DoD SAPs is a different provision with a different membership: 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) sends waived-SAP information to 'the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees' -- the six units defined in 119(g), not the intelligence committees and not congressional leadership.

claims.text: By contrast 50 U.S.C. 3091a(d)(2) writes an eight-person leadership set INTO the mandatory audience for every controlled access program: 'the majority leader of the Senate; the minority leader of the Senate; the Speaker of the House of Representatives; and the minority leader of the House of Representatives,' alongside the intelligence and appropriations committees. claims.text: 50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(2): 'If the President determines that it is essential to limit access to the finding to meet extraordinary circumstances affecting vital interests of the United States, the finding may be reported to the chairmen and ranking minority members of the congressional intelligence committees, the Speaker and minority leader of the House of Representatives, the majority and minority leaders of the Senate, and such other member or members of the congressional leadership as may be included by the President.'

50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(5)(B) requires that not later than 180 days after a statement of reasons for limited access, the President ensure either that all members of the intelligence committees are provided access to the finding or notification, or that a further statement of reasons is submitted to the Gang of Eight.

50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(3) permits a finding not to be reported under paragraph (1) or (2) at all, requiring only that the President thereafter 'fully inform the congressional intelligence committees in a timely fashion' with 'a statement of the reasons for not giving prior notice.'

50 U.S.C. 3091(e): 'Nothing in this chapter shall be construed as authority to withhold information from the congressional intelligence committees on the grounds that providing the information to the congressional intelligence committees would constitute the unauthorized disclosure of classified information or information relating to intelligence sources and methods.'

The covert action regime contains a mandatory 180-day review of continued limited access; the DoD waived-SAP regime contains no equivalent, so a waived DoD program can remain restricted to a handful of members indefinitely with no statutory event ever forcing reconsideration. Reasoning: 50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(5)(B) has no counterpart in 10 U.S.C. 119(e).

entities.desc: The Office of the Chief Science Advisor of Canada (OCSA) is the federal science-advice body that reports into the Government of Canada's science portfolio and advises the Prime Minister and the Minister of Innovation, Science and Industry. entities.desc: The Dirección General de Aeronáutica Civil is Chile's civil aviation authority, and it is the only such body in the hemisphere to have operated a permanent, publicly acknowledged office for the study of anomalous aerial phenomena for nearly three decades. entities.label: 509th Bomb Group
entities.sub: USAAF unit
entities.desc: The 509th was constituted as the 509th Composite Group in December 1944 as the delivery unit for the atomic bomb, flew the August 1945 atomic missions, and was redesignated the 509th Bomb Group and based at Roswell Army Air Field in New Mexico - in 1947 the only atomic-capable combat unit in the world. That is the most important fact about the Roswell episode and the one most often dropped from it: the press release announcing that the 509th had recovered a 'flying disc' came from the public information office of the unit holding the nuclear mission, staffed by officers with the highest clearances then in existence, and it was retracted within hours. The GAO's 1995 audit found the group's own July 1947 unit history recording that the RAAF public information office 'was kept quite busy ... answering inquiries on the flying disc' and stating that the object 'turned out to be a radar tracking balloon'. The same audit produced the finding that anchors this node: the RAAF administrative records for March 1945 to December 1949 and its outgoing messages for October 1946 to December 1949 were destroyed, and the disposition form does not indicate what organisation or person destroyed them, when, or under what authority. A base's entire administrative and message traffic for the period bracketing the incident is gone, with no accountable destruction authority recorded, at the one installation where records discipline was most rigorous. The 509th is therefore not merely the unit at the centre of the founding incident; it is the point at which the documentary record was removed.

entities.label: SAF/AAZ — Air Force Declassification & Special Programs
entities.sub: USAF secretariat office
entities.desc: SAF/AAZ is the Secretary of the Air Force's Director of Security, Counterintelligence and Special Program Oversight, an office of the Air Force Secretariat sitting under the Administrative Assistant to the Secretary (SAF/AA). Air Force Instruction 16-701, 'Management, Administration and Oversight of Special Access Programs' (18 February 2014, OPR SAF/AAZE, certified by SAF/AAZ), assigns it the controlling role over every Air Force special access programme: SAF/AAZ is principal advisor to SAF/AA for SAPs, serves as Director of the Air Force SAP Central Office (AF SAPCO), develops SAP policy, directs and oversees the SAP security programme, serves as Designated Accreditation Authority for all SAP information systems, and serves as the access approval authority for all SAPs with power to approve waivers for SAP access. The same instruction directs SAF/AAZ to 'establish a declassification program' and to ensure information is neither classified longer than necessary nor declassified prematurely - meaning that the office that grants access to Air Force black programmes is also the office that decides when their contents may be released. Any Air Force-hosted programme of the kind alleged on this board would be waived or unacknowledged under SAF/AAZ's oversight, its read-on list would be approved there, and any declassification would have to pass the same desk; it is simultaneously the gatekeeper of the secret and the arbiter of its disclosure, which is the structural conflict at the centre of the whole concealment argument.

entities.desc: Sheffield Hallam University is a large applied university in Sheffield, England, with a City Campus on Howard Street, roughly 31,000 students and 4,000 staff, and a Gold rating in the Teaching Excellence Framework. entities.label: IZMIRAN — Pushkov Institute of Terrestrial Magnetism
entities.sub: Russian research institute
entities.desc: IZMIRAN is the N.V. Pushkov Institute of Terrestrial Magnetism, Ionosphere and Radio Wave Propagation of the Russian Academy of Sciences, founded in 1939 and based at Troitsk outside Moscow, with a branch in St Petersburg. Its published work covers geomagnetism, the ionosphere, solar-terrestrial physics, space weather forecasting and radio propagation - the exact disciplines a state would draw on to explain, or to investigate, unexplained atmospheric optical and radar phenomena. That is why it appears on this board: IZMIRAN is the institutional home of the physicist Yury Platov, identified in the secondary literature as chief executive of SETKA-AN, the USSR Academy of Sciences half of the 1978-1990 Soviet state programme on anomalous phenomena that ran alongside the Ministry of Defence's SETKA-MO, and as co-author of the official history of that programme. No primary Russian archival document establishing IZMIRAN's SETKA role was obtained in this pass, and that is recorded as a gap.

entities.desc: In 2009 BAASS, executing a Defense Intelligence Agency contract, entered a funding arrangement with the Mutual UFO Network — the largest civilian UFO reporting organisation in the United States — to stand up the Star Team Impact Project, a rapid-response field investigation capability that would deploy trained investigators to significant cases within 24 hours and route the resulting data back to BAASS. entities.label: Institute of Field Physics (UNC Chapel Hill)
entities.sub: Privately endowed gravitation-research institute inside the UNC physics department, incorporated 7 September 1955
entities.desc: The Institute of Field Physics received its certificate of incorporation on 7 September 1955 and was placed inside the physics department at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, directed by Bryce and Cecile DeWitt and funded principally by the Winston-Salem industrialist Agnew Bahnson. Its inaugural event was the Conference on the Role of Gravitation in Physics at Chapel Hill in January 1957, now known as GR1. It sits on the same money as the board's existing Martin thread: George Trimble and the Glenn L. Martin Company bought a Founder's Membership for $5,000 while the company was separately standing up RIAS, whose first researcher was Louis Witten. The thing a node must carry is what the Institute wrote about itself. On John Wheeler's insistence a 'Protection Clause' was attached to every IOFP publicity statement declaring that the work 'has no connection with so-called "anti-gravity research" of whatever kind and for whatever purposes', and the department's own history says the instruction to avoid anti-gravity connotations runs through the founding correspondence like a mantra.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded A on a global pass (rank 154 of 1170, score 52). 7 connections, 1 of them custody/funding/programmatic, 1 official denial recorded against it. Axes C2/A1/D1.

claims.text: The January 1957 Chapel Hill conference had one sponsor and four funders, and the Air Force was not the sponsor. The report's title page reads: 'UNDER THE SPONSORSHIP OF THE International Union of Pure and Applied Physics, with financial support from UNESCO / National Science Foundation / Wright Air Development Center, U.S. Air Force / Office of Ordnance Research, U.S. Army'. The Foreword gives the reason the report exists at all: 'The present report was undertaken as a necessary requirement to obtain conference funds.' WADC's imprint is on the cover because the report was the condition of the money, not because the Air Force convened the meeting.

claims.text: Two different acts are recorded for the Institute and a node should not collapse them. The certificate of incorporation this node carries is dated 7 September 1955; the establishment inside the department is dated 1956 by the conference's own paper.

entities.label: Deep Submergence Systems Project (DSSP)
entities.sub: US Navy project for deep-ocean rescue, search, salvage and recovery, established 1964 in the Special Projects Office
entities.desc: DSSP is the documented Navy organisation behind the deep-ocean recovery capability the Area 52 corpus talks about, and the board's undersea thread currently has no office at all. The Deep-Submergence Systems Review Group was established in April 1963, after the loss of USS Thresher, to review Navy plans for the location, identification, rescue from and recovery of deep-submerged large objects from the ocean floor. It reported in February 1964, and the Secretary of the Navy assigned implementation of the resulting programme, renamed the Deep-Submergence Systems Project, to the Navy's Special Projects Office; by 1967 it was a separate project within the Naval Material Command. Its two primary objectives were rescue of personnel from distressed submarines and locating and recovering small objects from the ocean depths, pursued through a rescue vehicle rated for 6,000 feet and a separate search vehicle intended to search the sea floor to 20,000 feet. The project office carried the designator PM-11.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded B on a global pass (rank 459 of 1170, score 32). 1 connections, 0 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C2/A2/D1.

claims.text: The programme has a dated origin and a named parent. 'The Deep-Submergence Systems Review Group (DSSRG) was established in April 1963 to (1) review the Navy's plans for the development and procurement of components and systems related to location, identification, rescue from and recovery of deep-submerged large objects from the ocean floor.' Then: 'In February 1964 the Group reported its findings and recommendations. After review of the report, the Secretary of the Navy assigned the responsibility for implementation of the program, which was renamed the Deep-Submergence Systems Project (DSSP), to the Navy's Special Projects Office.'
claims.source: M. Krenzke, K. Horn and J. Proffitt, Potential Hull Structures for Rescue and Search Vehicles of the Deep-Submergence Systems Project, David Taylor Model Basin Report 1985, March 1965, DTIC AD-614632, https://archive.org/details/DTIC_AD0614632

claims.text: Its stated objectives are rescue and recovery: 'Two primary objectives of the DSSP are to develop the capability of rescuing personnel from distressed submarines and to locate and recover small objects from the ocean depths.' Planned force in 1965 was six rescue vehicles and four search vehicles operational by 1970.
claims.source: David Taylor Model Basin Report 1985, March 1965, DTIC AD-614632, https://archive.org/details/DTIC_AD0614632

claims.text: The 20,000 foot capability belongs to the search vehicle, not the rescue vehicle. The search vehicle's primary missions are 'to search the ocean bottom to depths of 20,000 ft for either large or small objects and to recover small objects either by actually lifting them or by making an attachment to the object so that a surface lift, or buoyancy lift, can be accomplished', while the study states of the rescue vehicle that 'Only operating depths of 6000 ft are considered in this study.'
claims.source: David Taylor Model Basin Report 1985, March 1965, DTIC AD-614632, https://archive.org/details/DTIC_AD0614632

claims.text: The Navy's own 1967 account gives the launch year and the organisational home: 'The Deep Submergence Systems Project (DSSP) was established as a separate Project within the Naval Material Command. The DSSP was launched in 1964 to develop and deliver to the fleet new underwater capabilities: a new rescue system, a large object salvage system, diver tools, the techniques of saturated diving for extended operations on the continental shelf, and new submersible vehicles capable of searching the ocean floors.' The same report describes a planned Deep Submergence Search Vehicle 'whose mission is ultimately to conduct sea floor search to a depth of 20,000 ft, providing coverage of 98 percent of the worlds oceans.'
claims.source: The Ocean Engineering Program of the U.S. Navy: Accomplishments and Prospects, Office of the Oceanographer of the Navy, September 1967, DTIC AD-665974, https://archive.org/details/DTIC_AD0665974

claims.text: Two real recoveries frame the programme in the Navy's own telling: the loss of USS Thresher in 1963, whose hull was located in 8,500 ft of water after the casualty 'focused national attention on Navy capabilities underwater', and the 1966 loss of an unarmed nuclear weapon off the Mediterranean coast, located on the sea floor by ALVIN and recovered by the unmanned vehicle CURV.
claims.source: The Ocean Engineering Program of the U.S. Navy, September 1967, DTIC AD-665974, https://archive.org/details/DTIC_AD0665974

entities.label: Scientific and Technical Intelligence Committee (USIB)
entities.sub: Standing USIB committee, renamed from the Scientific Intelligence Committee in 1974; chartered to form a community position on unidentified foreign activities and anomalies
entities.desc: STIC was the United States Intelligence Board's standing committee on scientific and technical intelligence, renamed from the Scientific Intelligence Committee by a charter of 23 October 1974 to reflect a shift of emphasis toward technology. Its operating precept was early warning of foreign scientific or technical advances affecting national security, and it advised, and coordinated collection and production for, the USIB in those areas. Its charter lists among its Priority Group II objectives the assessment and establishment of an Intelligence Community position regarding certain unidentified foreign activities and anomalies in the science and technology area, which places a standing community mechanism for exactly that question inside the intelligence structure of the 1970s. A Letter of Instruction of 3 August 1975 shows the committee still operating under the Deputy to the DCI for the Intelligence Community and reorganising its subgroups.

entities.label: The Monroe Institute
entities.sub: Private institute at Faber, Virginia; source of the Gateway Experience and Hemi-Sync, assessed in writing by INSCOM in 1983
entities.desc: The Monroe Institute is a private body at Faber, Virginia, founded around Robert A. Monroe's out-of-body work and the brain hemisphere synchronization technique it markets as Hemi-Sync. It matters to this board because a United States Army intelligence command put a written assessment of its method on the record. On 9 June 1983 the commander of Detachment O, US Army Operational Group, US Army Intelligence and Security Command at Fort George G. Meade, wrote a twenty-nine page memorandum analysing the Gateway Experience, on tasking from his own commander, and said explicitly that it was intended as a guide for other USAINSCOM personnel who were required to take the Gateway training. The memorandum concluded that Gateway is plausible in physical science terms and set out a six-step phased programme for bringing personnel to conscious control of the out-of-body state. The date places it inside CENTER LANE, INSCOM's remote-viewing special access programme of 1983 to 1986.

entities.label: Belgian Air Force F-16 intercept and the 1989-90 Belgian wave
entities.sub: NATO air force scrambled, recorded and reported; the MoD was not told at the time
entities.desc: In March 1990 the Belgian Air Force scrambled F-16 fighters against objects reported by police officers and others during a wave of sightings running through 1989 and 1990. The Belgian Air Force sent the UK Ministry of Defence an official statement about it in November 1993, and a four-page account by General Wilfried de Brouwer, Chief of Operations of the Belgian Air Staff, sits in a released MoD file: it says the F-16 pilots obtained radar lock-ons and could not explain the phenomena, and that the events remain unexplained. The Secretary of State for Defence later told Lord Hill-Norton that the MoD had not been informed at the time and that there was no threat to the UK. This node rests on The National Archives' own guide to the August 2009 release and on Project Condign Volume 2; neither Belgian file nor either MoD file has been opened, and the node's date is the date the records give for the imagery and the scramble, not a date taken from a broadcast.

entities.label: Cosford incident, 30-31 March 1993
entities.sub: More than 30 sightings in six hours; ACAS briefed on an evasion, then attributed to a rocket re-entry
entities.desc: On the night of 30 to 31 March 1993 more than thirty reports of bright lights over central England reached the Ministry of Defence within about six hours, from police officers and military witnesses including a police patrol at RAF Cosford. The MoD's UFO desk had the RAF replay radar tapes and nothing unusual had been detected. The Assistant Chief of the Air Staff, Sir Anthony Bagnall, was nonetheless briefed that there was evidence a UFO had evaded UK defences, and The National Archives' own guide to the release then records that the majority of the sightings turned out to have been caused by the re-entry of the Russian rocket that launched the Cosmos 2238 satellite. The node carries both halves because the second is the finding: the internal alarm and the mundane resolution are in the same paragraph of the same official guide. The file is DEFE 24/2086; the paper piece is closed until 2078 and only a redacted digital copy is open.

entities.label: US Army Intelligence and Security Command (INSCOM)
entities.sub: Army intelligence major command; ran the psychoenergetics effort as a special access programme, 1977-1985
entities.desc: INSCOM is the United States Army's intelligence and security major command, headquartered in this period at Arlington Hall Station, Arlington, Virginia, with subordinate elements at Fort George G. Meade. Its own documents date its exploitation of psychoenergetics to Project GRILL FLAME in 1977, undertaken after the Army Assistant Chief of Staff for Intelligence and the commanding general agreed that INSCOM would check out the phenomenon and that Army Intelligence would obligate seventy-five thousand dollars for an SRI International selection and training programme. The successor project, CENTER LANE, was run from the Security Support Detachment of the 902d Military Intelligence Group at Fort George G. Meade under a special access programme designated by the Secretary of the Army, with a category-three access caveat on every page. INSCOM's commanding general recommended ending the Army's involvement in July 1984 and, on 2 March 1985, notified the Department of the Army of the project's deactivation and of the attachment of its assets and resources to the Defense Intelligence Agency under operational control. The command's 1977 establishment order has not been opened; the dateStart above is the year INSCOM's own memorandum gives for the start of the work, not for the command.

entities.label: DoD special access programme governance change, 5 January 1994
entities.sub: SAPOC, Senior Review Group and SAPCO stood up under the Deputy Secretary of Defense
entities.desc: On 5 January 1994 the Deputy Secretary of Defense changed the Department's special access programme management and control structures, standardising the approval, termination, revalidation and restructuring of SAPs through a Special Access Program Oversight Committee chaired by the Deputy Secretary, with a Senior Review Group established to support the SAPOC principals and a Special Access Program Coordinating Office staffing both. By November 1994 the committee was chaired by Deputy Secretary John Deutch with the Under Secretary for Acquisition and Technology, the Under Secretary for Policy, the Vice Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and the Assistant Secretary for C3I as permanent, non-delegable members. The Joint Security Commission, reporting to the Secretary of Defense and the Director of Central Intelligence on 28 February 1994, described the committee as recently formed and supported it. This node exists because the board's sapoc node dates the committee to a 2010 directive, and the 2010 issuance re-established rather than created it.

The same report states that in 1988 'The Deputy Under Secretary of Defense for Policy is required to maintain a listing of all special access programs, but does not do so because of security concerns', and that 'the Secretary's Office has no centralized office with cognizance of all special access programs'.
