entities.label: Armed Forces Special Weapons Project
entities.sub: Joint Army-Navy atomic energy organisation, 1946-1959; military successor to the Manhattan Engineer District
entities.desc: The Armed Forces Special Weapons Project was established by joint directive of the Secretaries of War and the Navy, effective midnight 31 December 1946, to carry on the military service functions of the Manhattan Project that were retained under armed forces control when the Atomic Energy Commission took the civil ones. It reported directly to the Army Chief of Staff and the Chief of Naval Operations, its Chief and Deputy Chief sat on the Military Liaison Committee to the AEC, and its funds came by working fund advances from the AEC out of money formerly available to the Manhattan Project. Major General Leslie R. Groves became its first Chief on 28 February 1947. It was redesignated the Defense Atomic Support Agency in 1959 and, through DNA and DSWA, is the ancestor of the Defense Threat Reduction Agency.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded B on a global pass (rank 183 of 1170, score 47). 5 connections, 1 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C2/A3/D1.

claims.text: Groves held the command for one year to the day. The Defense Threat Reduction Agency's chronology of its own lineage reads: 'Feb. 28, 1947. Maj Gen Groves becomes first Chief AFSWP, serving for one year, until his retirement on February 29, 1948; he is promoted to Lt. General on January 24, 1948.' The same history records that the command stood empty when it was created: 'between the beginning of January and the end of February 1947, there was no officially appointed chief of AFSWP. During this period, Groves' aide, Colonel Hasbrouck, assumed Headquarters command in Washington as the senior officer of the organization.'
claims.source: Defense's Nuclear Agency 1947-1997, Defense Threat Reduction Agency, 2002, Appendix C: Chronology, DTIC ADA412977, https://archive.org/download/DTIC_ADA412977/DTIC_ADA412977_djvu.txt

claims.text: The charter is reproduced in the Department of Defense's own agency history: 'The Armed Forces Special Weapons Project established by joint directive of the Secretaries of War and Navy, effective as of midnight 31 December 1946, will operate directly under the Chief of Staff and the Chief of Naval Operations.'
claims.source: War Department Memorandum No. 850-25-8, 18 March 1947, reproduced in Appendix D of Defense's Nuclear Agency 1947-1997, Defense Threat Reduction Agency, 2002, DTIC ADA412977, https://archive.org/download/DTIC_ADA412977/DTIC_ADA412977_djvu.txt

claims.text: AFSWP took the military half of the Manhattan Project. The charter makes it 'responsible for carrying on the military service functions of the Manhattan Project retained under control of the armed forces', including military participation in the development of atomic weapons of all types in coordination with the Atomic Energy Commission, and assigns to it as of 31 December 1946 the Army units that had been assigned to the Manhattan Engineer District.
claims.source: War Department Memorandum No. 850-25-8, paras. 2, 3 and 5, in Defense's Nuclear Agency 1947-1997, Appendix D, https://archive.org/download/DTIC_ADA412977/DTIC_ADA412977_djvu.txt

claims.text: The Atomic Energy Commission funded the military organisation. Paragraph 6 of the charter: funds for AFSWP other than military pay 'have been made available by working fund advances to War Department from the Atomic Energy Commission, utilizing funds formerly available to the Manhattan Project.'
claims.source: War Department Memorandum No. 850-25-8, para. 6, in Defense's Nuclear Agency 1947-1997, Appendix D, https://archive.org/download/DTIC_ADA412977/DTIC_ADA412977_djvu.txt

claims.text: The founding memorandum was signed by Secretary of War Robert P. Patterson and Secretary of the Navy James V. Groves became first Chief on 28 February 1947 and served one year to his retirement on 29 February 1948.
claims.source: Defense's Nuclear Agency 1947-1997, ch. 'The Post-War Transition, 1946 to 1948', p. 30, and Appendix C chronology, https://archive.org/download/DTIC_ADA412977/DTIC_ADA412977_djvu.txt

claims.text: The National Archives states the same establishment independently: 'AFSWP established as an interservice agency, effective December 31, 1946, by a joint letter of the Secretaries of War and the Navy, January 29, 1947, with responsibility for discharging all military functions relating to atomic energy in coordination with the Atomic Energy Commission'.

entities.label: Defense Threat Reduction Agency
entities.sub: DoD combat support agency, 1998 to present; heir of AFSWP, DASA, DNA and DSWA
entities.desc: The Defense Threat Reduction Agency was established in the Department of Defense as a combat support agency effective 1 October 1998 by DoD Directive 5105.62 of 30 September 1998, consolidating the Defense Special Weapons Agency, the On-Site Inspection Agency, the Defense Technology Security Administration and elements of the Office of the Secretary of Defense concerned with arms control. Its own agency history traces an unbroken line from the Manhattan Engineer District through AFSWP, DASA, DNA and DSWA, and calls it the nation's oldest defense agency. Its published Privacy Act inventory records that it holds nuclear test participation and exposure records reaching back to 1945 and human radiation experimentation records reaching back to 1944. The National Archives holds the AFSWP, DASA and DNA era textual records as Record Group 374 and names the Atomic Energy Commission's own records, Record Group 326, as a separate related group.

entities.label: Office of Naval Research
entities.sub: Created 1 August 1946 in the Office of the Secretary of the Navy; the Navy's research contracting authority
entities.desc: The Office of Naval Research was created by Act of Congress on 1 August 1946, the same day as the Atomic Energy Act of 1946, inside the Office of the Secretary of the Navy. It is headed by a Chief of Naval Research appointed by the President with the advice and consent of the Senate, advised by a civilian Naval Research Advisory Committee of up to fifteen preeminent scientists, and it holds the Navy's authority over patents, inventions and royalties. The Act frees its research contracting from five named sections of the Revised Statutes and from performance bonds, lets appropriated research funds stay available for four further years, and authorises the transfer to it of the Naval Research Laboratory and the Special Devices Division.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded B on a global pass (rank 560 of 1170, score 29). 2 connections, 0 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C1/A3/D0.

claims.text: The Act creates the office inside the Secretary's own office: 'there is hereby created and established in the Office of the Secretary of the Navy an Office of Naval Research', charged with the encouragement, promotion, planning, initiation and coordination of naval research, and with the supervision, administration and control of Navy activities relating to patents, inventions, trade-marks, copyrights and royalty payments.
claims.source: An Act to establish an Office of Naval Research in the Department of the Navy, Public Law 79-588, ch. 727, H.R. 5911, 60 Stat. 779, sec. 1, approved 1 August 1946, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-60/pdf/STATUTE-60-Pg779.pdf

claims.text: Its head is a presidential appointee confirmed by the Senate. Section 2 provides for a Chief of Naval Research 'appointed by the President, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, for a term of not to exceed three years, from among officers not below the grade of commander on the active list of the Navy.'
claims.source: Public Law 79-588, 60 Stat. 779, sec. 2, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-60/pdf/STATUTE-60-Pg779.pdf

claims.text: The Act exempts ONR research contracting from ordinary law. Section 6 permits contracts for research 'without performance or other bonds' and without regard to five named sections of the Revised Statutes, and advance and progress payments without regard to another, while expressly barring cost-plus-a-percentage-of-cost contracting. Section 5(b) keeps obligated research appropriations available for expenditure for four years after the fiscal year for which they were appropriated.
claims.source: Public Law 79-588, 60 Stat. 779-780, secs. 5(b) and 6, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-60/pdf/STATUTE-60-Pg779.pdf

claims.text: Section 7 authorises the Secretary of the Navy to transfer research and development functions from the bureaus to ONR together with personnel, buildings, facilities and other property, 'including without limitation the Special Devices Division and the Naval Research Laboratory.'
claims.source: Public Law 79-588, 60 Stat. 780, sec. 7, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-60/pdf/STATUTE-60-Pg779.pdf

claims.text: On Debriefed, episode 78, 6 March 2026, the guest Gerb named the Office of Naval Intelligence and the Office of Naval Research and their 'historically special projects' as elements he says are deliberately left out of the four-element structure shown in The Age of Disclosure. entities.label: British-U.S. Communication Intelligence Agreement (UKUSA), 5 March 1946
entities.sub: STANCIB and the London SIGINT Board; twelve paragraphs; the clause forbidding disclosure of its own existence
entities.desc: The agreement signed on 5 March 1946 between the State-Army-Navy Communication Intelligence Board and the London Signal Intelligence Board is the founding instrument of what became the Five Eyes arrangement. In twelve paragraphs it commits the two sides to unrestricted exchange of the products of collection, traffic analysis, cryptanalysis, decryption and translation of foreign communications, and of the methods and techniques behind them, with withholdings to be notified and kept to a minimum. It defines third parties as everyone outside the United States, the British Empire and the Dominions, forbids either party from acting toward a third party without the other's agreement, and makes it contrary to the agreement to reveal that the agreement exists at all. It supersedes all previous British and United States agreements in the field and is terminable by either party on notice. Nothing in it concerns anomalous objects or their recovery.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded B on a global pass (rank 356 of 1170, score 36). 1 connections, 0 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C1/A3/D2.

claims.text: The agreement is between the State-Army-Navy Communication Intelligence Board, representing the U.S. State, Navy and War Departments and all other U.S. Communication Intelligence authorities which may function, and the London Signal Intelligence Board, representing the Foreign Office, Admiralty, War Office, Air Ministry and all other British Empire Communication Intelligence authorities which may function.
claims.source: Outline of British-U.S. Communication Intelligence Agreement, 5 March 1946, para. 1, NSA UKUSA release copy, https://documents.theblackvault.com/documents/ukusa/agreement_outline_5mar46.pdf

claims.text: The agreement forbids disclosure of itself: 'It will be contrary to this agreement to reveal its existence to any third party whatsoever.' Third parties are defined as all individuals or authorities other than those of the United States, the British Empire and the British Dominions.
claims.source: Outline of British-U.S. Communication Intelligence Agreement, 5 March 1946, para. 5(a) and its footnote, https://documents.theblackvault.com/documents/ukusa/agreement_outline_5mar46.pdf

claims.text: The exchange is defined by operation, not by target. Paragraph 3(a) commits both parties to exchange the products of collection of traffic, acquisition of communication documents and equipment, traffic analysis, cryptanalysis, decryption and translation, and acquisition of information regarding communication organisations, practices, procedures and equipment. Paragraph 4 extends the exchange to the methods and techniques involved, in both cases unrestricted except on notified withholding.
claims.source: Outline of British-U.S. Communication Intelligence Agreement, 5 March 1946, paras. 3 and 4, https://documents.theblackvault.com/documents/ukusa/agreement_outline_5mar46.pdf

claims.text: The Dominions are held between the parties and the excluded world: 'While the Dominions are not parties to this agreement, they will not be regarded as third parties.' The London SIGINT Board is to keep the United States informed of arrangements with Dominion agencies, and STANCIB is to complete no arrangement with any Canadian agency without first obtaining the London Board's views.
claims.source: Outline of British-U.S. Communication Intelligence Agreement, 5 March 1946, para. 6, https://documents.theblackvault.com/documents/ukusa/agreement_outline_5mar46.pdf

claims.text: The document is signed for the London Signal Intelligence Board by an officer described as Colonel, British Army General Staff, whose name the scan does not render legibly, and for the State-Army-Navy Communication Intelligence Board by Hoyt S. Vandenberg, Lieutenant General, GSC, as Senior Member. It is dated 5 March 1946 and its pages carry the NSA declassification exemption marking NSA25X6 with EO 1.4.(d).
claims.source: Outline of British-U.S. Communication Intelligence Agreement, 5 March 1946, signature page and page markings, https://documents.theblackvault.com/documents/ukusa/agreement_outline_5mar46.pdf

claims.text: The agreement contains nothing about anomalous objects. A search of the extracted text of all six numbered pages for 'flying', 'saucer', 'unidentified', 'aerial phenomen' and 'anomalous' returns no occurrence of any of them. The instrument is a communications intelligence sharing agreement and its secrecy clause covers its own existence, not any subject matter beyond communications.
claims.source: Outline of British-U.S. Communication Intelligence Agreement, 5 March 1946, full text, https://documents.theblackvault.com/documents/ukusa/agreement_outline_5mar46.pdf

entities.label: Norton AFB air show, 12 November 1988, and the alleged classified exhibit
entities.sub: Documented Air Force open house at which an SR-71A flew; the hangar exhibit alleged on the same date rests on one second-hand chain
entities.desc: One date carries two very different things. That an air show was held at Norton Air Force Base on 12 November 1988 is documented independently of the ARV account by a private photographic collection of Blackbird aircraft, whose captions place SR-71A 61-7962 at the base on that day. What is alleged to have happened inside a closed hangar on the same date rests on a single claimed eyewitness, and it is the load-bearing claim of the entire thread: three saucer-shaped craft of the same proportions in different sizes, a second unmanned diamond-shaped craft with 121 ports said to be cylindrical nuclear weapons, black cloth on metal rods dividing the space 'just like a car showroom', and a stated purpose of raising appropriations. The earliest document, taken about two years later, places the account only 'in early Nov. 88'; the exact date and the day of the week come from the 2001 testimony of the man who was not there. The same document records the witness saying he missed the introductions, saw no general officers, and did not know who was running the event.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded B on a global pass (rank 304 of 1170, score 39). 4 connections, 0 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C1/A1/D2.

claims.text: An air show was held at Norton Air Force Base on 12 November 1988, and an SR-71A flew at it. A private photographic collection of Blackbird aircraft carries a section headed 'Norton Air Force Base Airshow, November 12, 1988' with captions including 'SR-71A 61-7962 at Norton AFB on November 12, 1988' and 'The crew of SR-71A 61-7962 shake hands before departing the November 12, 1988 Norton Air Force Base airshow'. This is the only opened record that dates the air show independently of the ARV account.
claims.source: air-and-space.com, Lockheed A-12 / YF-12 / SR-71 Blackbirds collection, https://www.air-and-space.com/Lockheed%20A-12%20YF-12%20SR-71%20Blackbirds.htm , read 2026-09-18, event date 1988-11-12

claims.text: The primary interview document places the account only 'in early Nov. 88': 'His account: Was invited to airshow at Norton AFB, Calif., in early Nov. 88; before B-2 rollout, and around pres. election time.' claims.text: McCandlish's 2001 testimony dates the alleged exhibit precisely and gives the day of the week: Sorensen 'told me how he had seen these three flying saucers in this hangar at Norton Air Force Base on November 12, 1988 - it was a Saturday.'

claims.text: The 1990 document records the alleged exhibit's claimed purpose in the witness's own words: 'And that's what the whole [meeting] was for--appropriations of billions of dollars to develop new craft.' Asked whether he read it as a fundraising exercise: 'Yes; it was showing prototypes...or just vehicles of all different kinds that they wanted money for. So they were trying to impress us. Needless to say we were impressed!...[group had about 30 or so people who were invited].'

claims.text: The same document records the staging: 'They sort of staged it in several different rooms. Was one big hangar, but everything was parked so close that the wings would ...be above the others in the hangar', with 'metal rods as separators and hung black cloth on them', and 'It was like a showroom--just like a car showroom--good analogy!'
claims.source: William B. Scott, interview notes on 'Brad', https://www.arvp.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/SORENSEN-1990-INTERVIEW.pdf , transcript p 4, 1990-12-03

claims.text: The witness's own judgement of build quality, in the same passage that gives the sizes: 'They looked poorly built, compared to the other ones. They had been built by scientists who didn't know a hell of a lot about laying up composite materials or whatever' and 'the whole thing was just coated with thick, heavy lead paint. claims.text: The claimed provenance of the design, in the witness's own words on the same tape: 'They just said that they had come across some hardware ...tried to make contact with these....The [others] didn't want to make contact; they just wanted to deliver the news and leave, OK? He continues: 'Also said they couldn't really make those things that they found work. That they had to build their own...that this was built for our consumption, not theirs.' Asked 'so we just looked at theirs and built our own?' he answers 'uh-huh. Based on what was seen. claims.text: On the claimed performance: 'the guy said that with this group of craft that, uh....they'd been everywhere in the universe, and there's no life', and 'Just take it for granted, we've already tested this thing. entities.label: William B. Scott's interview notes on 'Brad', 3 December 1990
entities.sub: 31 scanned pages: handwritten notes on Aviation Week & Space Technology letterhead plus a 16 page typed transcript; never published
entities.desc: This is the strongest artefact in the whole thread and it cuts both ways. It is a contemporaneous working file authored by a named trade-press editor within two years of the claimed event: thirty-one scanned pages, opening with handwritten notes on Aviation Week & Space Technology letterhead over the name block 'William B. Scott / Senior Engineering Editor', followed by a sixteen page typed transcript headed 'NOTES FROM INTERVIEW ON 12-3-90 WITH BRAD' and 'COMPILED 12-11-90; SCOTT/AVWK LANCASTER'. It carries the claim in the witness's own words, and it carries the interviewer's own doubts in the same pages: a bracketed note that the witness 'continued to confuse' frequency and wavelength, and a note written while driving away that the witness had twice mentioned his $200 an hour rate and had offered a rendering for 'a couple thousand dollars'. Nothing in the thirty-one pages is a published article. Aviation Week printed McCandlish's artwork, not this interview. The scan reached the public through an anonymously operated website in December 2024 and its custody before that date is not established by anything in it.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded B on a global pass (rank 534 of 1170, score 30). 4 connections, 1 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C0/A0/D2.

claims.text: The document is 31 scanned pages in one PDF. Its first pages are handwritten notes printed on Aviation Week & Space Technology letterhead over the name block 'William B. Scott / Senior Engineering Editor', with a McGraw-Hill logo in the lower right. One such sheet is headed, circled, 'Mark - 8/13/90'.
claims.source: https://www.arvp.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/SORENSEN-1990-INTERVIEW.pdf , pages 1 to 2 of the scan, 1990-08-13

claims.text: Its core is a 16 page typed transcript, hand-numbered 1 to 16 at the top right, headed 'NOTES FROM INTERVIEW ON 12-3-90 WITH BRAD' and 'COMPILED 12-11-90; SCOTT/AVWK LANCASTER'. Internal markers show it was taped: '[end side A of tape 1]', 'Side B/tape 1', '[end of tape 1, side b]', '[tape 2,side a]'.
claims.source: https://www.arvp.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/SORENSEN-1990-INTERVIEW.pdf , transcript pp 1 and 5, 1990-12-11

claims.text: Page 16 carries a handwritten addendum in the same hand: 'As of 12/10/90 - additional info from Brad', followed by notes on a diamond-shaped aircraft slowing to subsonic speeds to dispense weapons. The interview was therefore followed up before the notes were compiled.
claims.source: https://www.arvp.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/SORENSEN-1990-INTERVIEW.pdf , transcript p 16, 1990-12-10

claims.text: The interviewer records his own reservations inside the document. Of the propulsion explanation: '[note: think he's talking frequency here, not wavelength, but he continued to confuse the two; also, long antenna hardly consistent with detecting extremely hi freq, if that's really what he meant.]' Of the witness's terms, in notes written 'after leaving meeting, while driving': 'He reminded me a couple of times that he gets $200/hr. as a designer. So, who knows--he may charge us. he also said if we wanted a good rendering of the base burning vehicle, he could provide that for a couple thousand dollars.'
claims.source: https://www.arvp.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/SORENSEN-1990-INTERVIEW.pdf , transcript pp 11 and 16, 1990-12-11

claims.text: The document contains the witness disowning part of McCandlish's drawing. Shown the sketches, Sorensen says of the manned vehicle: 'this is probably the farthest from what I saw, and no, I didn't see anything with an intake up above the windows like this', and 'mark extrapolates a bit too much'. Of the saucer drawing he says the opposite: 'you've got a drawing, as accurate as I could get [the round, saucer-looking thing]. This dwg is so GD..accurate that I can't be much more specific than this.'
claims.source: https://www.arvp.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/SORENSEN-1990-INTERVIEW.pdf , transcript p 10, 1990-12-03

claims.text: The document is a working file, not a publication. Nothing in the 31 pages is a published article, and the notes state that the witness had previously refused to talk and that the artwork, not the interview, was what Aviation Week printed.
claims.source: https://www.arvp.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/SORENSEN-1990-INTERVIEW.pdf , transcript p 1, 1990-12-11

claims.text: The scan's provenance before December 2024 is not established by anything in it. The PDF's own metadata gives /CreationDate 'D:20241017132510' and /Producer and /Creator both 'PDFium'; the file is 9,172,025 bytes over 31 pages with 31 embedded JPEG page images and zero embedded fonts, so it is a scan with no text layer; and it sits under /wp-content/uploads/2024/12/ on a site whose operator is not named. Who held the notes between 1990 and 2024, and how they reached that site, is not in the opened record.

entities.label: USS Princeton (CG-59)
entities.sub: Ticonderoga-class Aegis cruiser, Carrier Strike Group 11
entities.desc: The Aegis cruiser that generated the machine record of the November 2004 encounter and, on the accounts of two of its crew, then lost it. Princeton was operating with Carrier Strike Group 11 off Baja California in the weeks before 14 November 2004 with a freshly upgraded SPY-1B radar and Cooperative Engagement Capability suite. Fravor's sworn statement to House Oversight confirms Princeton had been watching the objects 'on their Aegis combat system for the previous 2 weeks,' descending 'from above 80,000ft ... rapidly down to 20,000ft' and loitering for hours. Princeton's air warfare team, led by Senior Chief Operations Specialist Kevin Day, vectored the VFA-41 section onto the contact that became the Tic Tac intercept. Two Princeton crewmen - Day and CEC/Aegis technician Gary Voorhis - have said publicly that recording media were collected by personnel who did not identify themselves within about 48 hours. No document corroborating that collection has surfaced. Princeton is therefore the board's cleanest example of a custody hole: the single richest sensor record of the founding modern case, held by a US warship, and absent from every release since.

This is the case that most directly prefigures the 2023-2026 incursion pattern: persistent, coordinated, unattributed platforms operating against high-value US assets with impunity.

entities.label: February 2023 Alaska, Yukon and Lake Huron Shootdowns
entities.sub: Three unidentified objects destroyed by US fighters in four days
entities.desc: Between 10 and 12 February 2023, US fighters shot down three unidentified objects over Alaska, the Yukon and Lake Huron, in the days after the Chinese surveillance balloon was destroyed off South Carolina. A Secret memorandum dated 14 February 2023 from Janice Charette, Clerk of the Privy Council, to Prime Minister Justin Trudeau and National Security Advisor Jody Thomas records that 'The full exploitation of UAP #20, which was engaged by the U.S. on February 10, 2023, has not yet been completed,' describing an object roughly the size of a small car at 40,000 feet, 'cylindrical and silver-ish gray' with no apparent propulsion system, which broke apart on sea ice near Prudhoe Bay. The Yukon object, tracked as UAP #23, 'remains unverified' as to 'function, method of propulsion, or affiliation to any nation-state.' entities.label: USS Jackson (LCS-6) Encounter, 15 February 2023
entities.sub: Four transmedium objects recorded on Star SAFIRE EO/IR

entities.label: USS Ronald Reagan Encounter and Logbook Tampering (2003-2004)
entities.sub: Multi-witness flight-deck sighting; deck log pages removed
entities.desc: Between December 2003 and May 2004, while USS Ronald Reagan (CVN-76) operated in the Atlantic, multiple watchstanders observed a round, orange, self-luminous object hovering roughly 100 to 200 feet above the flight deck, pacing the ship at about 22 knots and performing half-circle manoeuvres before departing rapidly. Named witnesses include Quartermaster Karol Olesiak on the bridge navigation table, Seaman Derek Smith on the starboard forward catwalk, and Seaman Patrick Gokey, who observed it twice from different stations; two further witnesses remain anonymous. entities.label: The HASC/HAC-D special access program read-in gate
entities.sub: Access-control mechanism blocking Oversight
entities.desc: The specific bureaucratic mechanism by which the committee with subpoena power is kept away from the material it is investigating, stated on the record by the chair of the House body investigating it. On 9 September 2025 Anna Paulina Luna told the hearing that in preparation for previous UAP hearings the committee repeatedly asked the Department of Defense to allow members to view UAP videos and files, and that DoD notified committee staff that under the Department's special access program rules only members of the House Armed Services Committee and the Defense Subcommittee of House Appropriations could be read in on such programmes; for any non-committee member to view the documents and videos, individual members must be approved by the chairman AND ranking member of BOTH HASC and HAC-D. Luna added that independent staff oversight is a consistent problem because programme budgets are classified and oversight reporting to Congress goes only to the authorising and appropriating committees of jurisdiction. This is the operative architecture: it is not a refusal, it is a jurisdictional routing that makes refusal unnecessary. Eric Burlison supplied two further instances of the same pattern in the same hearing - an NDAA UAP disclosure amendment ruled non-germane 'mostly deemed by staff, not even an elected official,' and members blocked in 2024 from a full AARO briefing by 'someone in House administration.' The Holman Rule threat Ogles made in 2023 and the subpoena Gaetz asked for in 2023 and Luna raised in 2026 are the only instruments that route around this gate, and none has been used.

entities.label: Immaculate Constellation 12-page report entered into the Congressional Record
entities.sub: Whistleblower report, entered 13 Nov 2024
entities.desc: The twelve-page document Michael Shellenberger delivered to Congress on the morning of 13 November 2024 and that Chairwoman Nancy Mace moved into the Congressional Record from the dais, describing it in the hearing's Index of Documents as 'Report, Pentagon, Immaculate Constellation; submitted by Rep. Mace.' Its first section describes an unacknowledged special access program named Immaculate Constellation; its second concerns US Government imagery intelligence. Shellenberger characterised it in his testimony as describing a strategic intelligence programme within a family of longstanding, highly sensitive programmes dealing with the UAP problem, functioning as a central or parent USAP consolidating observations of UAP from both tasked and untasked collection platforms, holding high-quality IMINT and MASINT drawn from low Earth orbit, the upper atmosphere, military and civilian aviation altitudes and maritime environments. It catalogues morphologies - spheres and orbs, discs and saucers, ovals, triangles, boomerang and arrowhead, irregular and organic - and specific incidents including orbs forcing an F-22 out of its patrol area and an orange-red sphere descending to within 100 to 200 yards above a carrier flight deck. Under questioning from Higgins, Shellenberger confirmed he knows the author and the sources, has confidence in them, and declined to say whether they sit inside DoD. Elizondo, asked directly by Mace whether he had been read in to Immaculate Constellation, replied that he would not be authorised to confirm or deny the existence of any special access program by name or trigraph - which is not a denial. The Pentagon says it has no record of the programme.

entities.label: Rep. Burlison records demand to MITRE, 22 May 2026
entities.sub: 10-page letter; 40+ production requests; records back to 1930
entities.desc: The most consequential document in this domain and the first time Congress has formally interrogated an FFRDC operator about UAP holdings. It contains more than forty production requests, including work involving Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, Raytheon, Boeing, General Dynamics, SAIC and Leidos, and covers UAP detection and tracking across air, space, maritime, cyber and electromagnetic domains. MITRE must also account for records created, handled, transferred, withheld or destroyed by the corporation, its FFRDCs or its subcontractors. The rationale is stated in FFRDC terms: 'FFRDCs often receive special access to government facilities, data, sponsor requirements, and sensitive technical information that ordinary private contractors may not receive', and 'They cannot become private vaults for federal records - especially records Congress has directed to be identified, preserved, reviewed, and transferred for public release.' Burlison also states the standard of proof he is applying: 'This inquiry does not require MITRE to accept any particular conclusion about the origin or nature of UAP. It requires MITRE to tell Congress what it knows, what it holds, what it has held, what it has transferred, what it has destroyed or was directed to destroy, and which federal sponsors or classification authorities control any responsive records.' MITRE's answer, that it would coordinate with the federal agencies responsible for the work, is the FFRDC structure asserting itself.

entities.label: Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Review Board
entities.sub: Independent agency, authorised by the Senate, never constituted
entities.desc: The Review Board is the JFK Records Act transplant at the centre of the UAPDA and the thing the conference was most determined to prevent. Section 9007 establishes it 'as an independent agency' — outside the Department of Defense, outside the intelligence community, outside the armed services and intelligence committees. The President appoints nine citizens 'by and with the advice and consent of the Senate,' with nominations due within 90 days of enactment and a replacement nomination required within 30 days of any Senate rejection. Nominees are drawn from recommendations by the four congressional leaders, the Secretary of Defense, the National Academy of Sciences, 'established nonprofit research organizations relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena,' and the American Historical Association. The disqualification in Section 9007(b)(4)(A) is the operative clause: members 'shall be impartial citizens, none of whom shall have had any previous or current involvement with any legacy program or controlling authority relating to the collection, exploitation, or reverse engineering of technologies of unknown origin or the examination of biological evidence of living or deceased non-human intelligence.' The composition is mandated to include a national security official, a foreign service official, a scientist or engineer, an economist, a professional historian and a sociologist. Under Section 9009(c)(1) the Board must order disclosure 'in the absence of clear and convincing evidence' for postponement — reversing the ordinary classification presumption. Under Section 9010(b) recovered material must be made available to it for personal examination. The Board was removed in conference and does not exist. Nothing in enacted law performs its function: under Section 1843 of P.L. 118-31 the postponement decision is made by 'the original classification authority.'

entities.label: Controlled Disclosure Campaign Plan
entities.sub: Sec. 9009(c)(3) — mandated managed-release schedule, never produced
entities.desc: The Controlled Disclosure Campaign Plan is the UAPDA's answer to the objection that disclosure must be managed rather than instantaneous, and it is the concept the disclosure movement has since adopted as its central demand. Under Section 9009(c)(3) the Review Board would have been required to create and transmit to the President, the Archivist, the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee and the House Oversight and Accountability Committee a plan with a classified appendix covering every record, every piece of information, and every item of 'recovered technologies of unknown origin, and biological evidence for non-human intelligence' whose disclosure was postponed. The plan had to contain a justification of each postponement and 'a benchmark-driven plan... recommending precise requirements for periodic review, downgrading, and declassification as well as the exact time or specified occurrence following which each postponed item may be appropriately disclosed to the public.' All of it was removed. No Controlled Disclosure Campaign Plan exists, and no enacted provision requires one.

entities.sub: National Archives collection created under Secs. 1841-1843
entities.desc: RG 615 is the only thing the UAPDA fight actually built. entities.label: Project MKULTRA
entities.sub: CIA umbrella project for research and development of materials to control human behavior; authorized by DCI Dulles 13 April 1953, records destroyed January 1973
entities.desc: MKULTRA is the documented American precedent for everything this board argues about compartmented programmes and their records. It was authorized by the Director of Central Intelligence in April 1953 as a funding mechanism whose normal procedures for project approval, funding and accounting were waived, and it ran through 149 numbered subprojects at universities, foundations, hospitals and prisons that were in most cases not told whose money it was. Its own Inspector General wrote in 1963 that the practice was to keep no records of the planning and approval of test programmes. In January 1973 the surviving files were destroyed on a verbal order. What defeated the destruction was an administrative accident: one branch's Budget and Fiscal Section had sent its finance folders to the Retired Records Center in 1970 in a departure from normal procedure that the Agency itself could not later explain, and those seven boxes were found in 1977 by an employee working a Freedom of Information Act request. The board's own MKULTRA hearing node argues from this programme without carrying it.

entities.sub: CIA interrogation-team programme using polygraph, drugs and hypnotism; proposed to the DCI 5 April 1950 outside the Projects Review Committee; renamed ARTICHOKE August 1951
entities.desc: BLUEBIRD is the documented origin of the CIA's behavioural-control work and the earliest instance on this board of a compartment created by deliberately going round the body that reviews compartments. On 5 April 1950 the Chief of the Inspection and Security Staff submitted it directly to the Director of Central Intelligence rather than through the Projects Review Committee, in writing, on the stated ground of the project's sensitivity and covert nature, and asked that knowledge of it be held to the absolute minimum number of persons. What it bought was two interrogation teams of a psychiatrist, a hypnotist and a technician, working under polygraph cover, with a Washington doctor's office as cover for training and experimentation in drugs and hypnotism, for $65,515 a year. It was renamed ARTICHOKE in August 1951 and passed in 1952 from an intelligence unit to an operating one. By July 1952 the Security Office was reporting to the Director that two suspected Russian double agents had been interrogated under a psychiatric-medical cover using narcosis and hypnosis, one of them left with a total amnesia produced by post-hypnotic suggestion.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded B on a global pass (rank 537 of 1170, score 30). 4 connections, 1 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C0/A2/D0.

claims.text: The founding proposal names its own irregularity: 'In view of the extreme sensitivity of this project and its covert nature, it is deemed advisable to submit this project directly to you, rather than through the channel of the Projects Review Committee. Knowledge of this project should be restricted to the absolute minimum number of persons.'

claims.text: Its purpose, in the document: 'The purpose of this project is to provide for the immediate establishment of interrogation teams for the operational support of OSO and OPC activities. The teams will utilize the polygraph, drugs, and hypnotism to attain the greatest results in interrogation techniques.' A team is a doctor-psychiatrist, a polygraph-hypnotist and a technician, and the doctors' Washington office is to 'serve as a cover for training, experimentation, and indoctrination purposes in the use of drugs and hypnotism'.
claims.source: Project Bluebird, 5 April 1950, https://nsarchive.gwu.edu/sites/default/files/documents/1950-04-05%20JM%20Box%209%20F5%20Replacement%20CIA%20FOIA-ocr.pdf

claims.text: The one-year budget in the attachment totals $65,515.00: $40,800 personnel, $1,025 supplies, $3,190 equipment, $18,000 transportation and $2,500 rent, itemised down to a Keeler polygraph machine and its spare part kit.

claims.text: By July 1952 the Security Office was reporting operational use to the Director: '(a) Subjects were Russian agents suspected of being doubled. (b) Cover was psychiatric-medical. entities.label: John Marks FOIA request F-76-374 and the recovery of the MKULTRA finance file
entities.sub: The FOIA request and litigation that caused CIA to search the Retired Records Center in 1977 and find seven boxes the 1973 destruction order had missed
entities.desc: This is the board's own argument about custody, documented, in another programme. A destruction order given inside CIA in January 1973 removed the MKULTRA files; two Senate committees investigating in 1975 could not recover them; and what defeated the order was a single Freedom of Information Act request and the litigation behind it. The Agency's own memorandum of 22 June 1977 says so in one sentence: as a result of John Marks's FOIA request F-76-374, the Office of Technical Service reviewed its holdings and then searched the Retired Records Center, and it was in that second search that the subproject files were found among the retired records of the Budget and Fiscal Section. Among them was the original memorandum setting up MKULTRA over Allen Dulles's signature. The record also corrects the popular account of the sequence: the finding was done by CIA staff, the Agency was advised to tell the Senate Select Committee before it told the requester's attorneys, and the material reached the public through a Senate hearing six weeks later. The collection those documents sit in today carries his name.

entities.label: Death of Frank R. Olson, 1953, and the compensation and litigation that followed
entities.sub: Army civilian dosed with LSD without his knowledge at a CIA meeting on 19 November 1953; died in New York days later; compensated by Private Law 94-126 in 1976; the family's 2012 suit dismissed in D.D.C. in 2013
entities.desc: This is the one death inside a compartmented American programme that the government conceded, compensated by statute, and then litigated over sixty years later, and it belongs on this board because the paper trail exists on both sides. Frank R. Olson, a civilian employee of the Army at Fort Detrick, was given LSD without his knowledge in a bottle of Cointreau at a CIA and Army meeting on 19 November 1953 and died in New York within about a week. The Rockefeller Commission disclosed the connection in June 1975 without naming him, and attached to its own account a footnote saying the few remaining Agency records indicate he may have had a history of emotional instability. Congress paid his widow and three children $187,500 each in 1976 in exchange for a full waiver, and President Ford signed it saying his administration had wanted twice that. In 2012 two of the children sued the United States alleging the death was a murder concealed for sixty years; the District of Columbia dismissed the suit in 2013 on timeliness, the 1976 waiver and sovereign immunity, while recording that the public record supports many of the allegations. Four opened records disagree about which floor he fell from, what day he died and whether anyone was reprimanded.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded B on a global pass (rank 221 of 1170, score 44). 5 connections, 2 of them custody/funding/programmatic, 1 official denial recorded against it. Axes C0/A1/D3.

claims.text: The Rockefeller Commission's June 1975 report disclosed the death without naming him: 'on one occasion during the early phases of this program (in 1953), LSD was administered to an employee of the Department of the Army without his knowledge ... Several days later, he jumped from a tenth floor window of his room and died as a result.' Its footnote to that passage reads: 'There are indications in the few remaining Agency records that this individual may have had a history of emotional instability.'
claims.source: Report to the President by the Commission on CIA Activities within the United States, June 1975, chapter 16, pp. 227-228, https://documents2.theblackvault.com/documents/rockefellercommissionreport-full.pdf

claims.text: The same report records the ruling that produced death benefits and the discipline that followed: 'The General Counsel ruled that the death resulted from "circumstances arising out of an experiment undertaken in the course of his official duties for the United States Government," thus ensuring his survivors of receiving certain death benefits. Reprimands were issued by the Director of Central Intelligence to two CIA employees responsible for the incident.' The 2012 complaint states the opposite on the second point, that the internal investigation issued no formal reprimands.
claims.source: Report to the President by the Commission on CIA Activities within the United States, June 1975, p. 227, https://documents2.theblackvault.com/documents/rockefellercommissionreport-full.pdf

claims.text: Congress compensated the family by private statute. Private Law 94-126, 90 Stat. 3006 (1976), directs payment of 'the sum of $187,500 each to Alice W. Olson in November 1953, if all of them waive any and all rights arising out of such death.'
claims.source: Private Law 94-126, 90 Stat. 3006 (1976), quoted in full in Olson v. United States, No. 12-1924 (JEB), D.D.C., memorandum opinion of 17 July 2013, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCOURTS-dcd-1_12-cv-01924/pdf/USCOURTS-dcd-1_12-cv-01924-0.pdf

claims.text: President Ford signed the bill on 12 October 1976 and stated the administration's own position on the amount: 'Legislation to appropriate $1,250,000 to compensate the wife and three children of Dr. Olson for his death was supported by this administration. However, the Congress approved a measure calling for the payment of a total of $750,000 to these survivors.'
claims.source: Gerald R. Ford, Statement on Signing the Bill Providing for the Relief of the Survivors of Dr. Frank R. Olson, 12 October 1976, https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/documents/statement-signing-the-bill-providing-for-the-relief-the-survivors-dr-frank-r-olson

entities.label: CIA Office of Policy Coordination
entities.sub: Covert action office chartered by NSC 10/2 as the Office of Special Projects, 18 June 1948; operating from 1 September 1948
entities.desc: The office the Danny Jones corpus keeps invoking has a charter, and the charter is openable. NSC 10/2 of 18 June 1948 created it inside the Central Intelligence Agency under the residual authority of section 102(d)(5) of the National Security Act of 1947, to plan and conduct covert operations, with its Chief nominated by the Secretary of State, reporting directly to the Director of Central Intelligence, and operating 'independently of other components of Central Intelligence Agency'. Two things a node must say and the transcript does not. The directive names the office the Office of Special Projects; the name Office of Policy Coordination appears only from September 1948, when Frank G. Wisner became Assistant Director for Policy Coordination. And the directive's own definition of covert operations is a definition of deniability rather than of psychological warfare: operations 'so planned and executed that any US Government responsibility for them is not evident to unauthorized persons and that if uncovered the US Government can plausibly disclaim any responsibility for them'.

Espionage, counter-espionage and 'cover and deception for military operations' are expressly excluded.

entities.label: U.S. Naval Ordnance Laboratory (White Oak, Silver Spring)
entities.sub: Navy laboratory at White Oak, Silver Spring, where Buehler and Wiley developed the 55-Nitinol shape-memory alloys
entities.desc: The U.S. Naval Ordnance Laboratory at Silver Spring, Maryland is where William J. Buehler and Raymond C. Wiley developed the nickel-titanium shape-memory alloys named 55-Nitinol, the acronym standing for Nickel Titanium Naval Ordnance Laboratory. It reaches this board because the board's strongest materials claim runs the other way: an allegation, carried at Tier 2 on the Battelle node, that the alloy's research lineage is a set of missing 1948-49 Wright-Patterson-sponsored Battelle reports. Two federal reports opened for this pass, one of them written by Battelle for NASA, place the discovery at NOL around 1959 to 1962, cite no NOL nitinol report before August 1961, and cite no Battelle nickel-titanium work before 1968. The Danny Jones corpus dates the NOL discovery to 1954; the record does not support that either.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded C on a global pass (rank 660 of 1170, score 26). 3 connections, 0 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C1/A1/D1.

claims.text: NASA SP-5110, prepared for NASA by Battelle Memorial Institute in 1972, opens: 'Some 10 years ago, Buehler and Wiley of the U.S. Naval Ordnance Laboratory developed a series of engineering alloys that possess a unique mechanical (shape) memory. The generic name of the series of alloys is 55-Nitinol, where Nitinol stands for Nickel Titanium Naval Ordnance Laboratory.'
claims.source: NASA SP-5110, 55-Nitinol: The Alloy With a Memory, C. M. Jackson, H. J. Wagner and R. J. Wasilewski, Battelle Memorial Institute for the NASA Technology Utilization Office, 1972, Chapter 1, p. 1. https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19720022818/downloads/19720022818.pdf

claims.text: The earliest Naval Ordnance Laboratory nitinol report cited anywhere in SP-5110's reference list is NOLTR 61-75 (AD 266607), Buehler and Wiley, 'The Properties of TiNi and Associated Phases', U.S. Naval Ordnance Laboratory, 3 August 1961. The report's own acknowledgments state that 'All the information in the report covers the period from 1955 to March 31, 1970.'
claims.source: NASA SP-5110, references 12 and 74, and Acknowledgments, p. iv. https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19720022818/downloads/19720022818.pdf

claims.text: US Patent 3,174,851, 'Nickel-base alloys', by William J. Buehler and Raymond C. Wiley, assigned to the United States as represented by the Secretary of the Navy, was filed on 1 December 1961 and granted on 23 March 1965.
claims.source: US Patent 3,174,851. https://patents.google.com/patent/US3174851A/en

claims.text: Battelle's documented role in the alloy is late and contractual. NASA CR-1433 of September 1969 records that the nitinol was 'supplied by Mr. William J. Buehler of the Magnetism and Metallurgy Division of the U.S. Naval Ordnance Laboratory (NOL), Silver Spring, Maryland', and that 'As subcontractor to GAC, Battelle Memorial Institute (BMI), Columbus, Ohio, processed the basic Nitinol rod'. The same report calls the NOL work 'the recent discovery'.

entities.sub: Two Imperial Iranian Air Force F-4 intercepts over Tehran, 19 and 20 September 1976, documented in DIA IR 6 846 0139 76

DIA told a FOIA requester in 1996 that a search of its systems of records located one responsive document. That report names one Iranian officer, Brigadier General Yousefi of the command post, and identifies the aircrew only as an unnamed IIAF pilot who was one of its own sources. entities.label: Japan Air Lines flight 1628, Alaska, 17 November 1986
entities.sub: A civil-aviation incident with a 1,500-page federal file at the National Archives, an FAA investigation, an agency press release concluding against a second aircraft, and a documented seventeen-year FOIA recovery
entities.desc: THIS IS THE NODE IN THIS CLUSTER WITH A REAL AGENCY RECORD, AND IT SHOULD CARRY MORE WEIGHT THAN THE WITNESS BESIDE IT. On the evening of 17 November 1986 a Japan Air Lines 747 crossing Alaskan airspace reported an object accompanying it; the FAA investigated, and the paper it generated survives in volume. The Black Vault asked for it in May 2001 and was told in a letter of 27 June 2001 that everything would be destroyed within thirty days; asked again in 2009 and was told it had been destroyed; and then found over 1,500 pages of it at the National Archives in Record Group 237, local identifier 1203, archival identifier 733667. entities.label: Big Sur missile-test filming, September 1964
entities.sub: An Air Force image-orthicon telescope deployment above Big Sur covering Vandenberg launches from August to November 1964, and the subject of two published first-person accounts that agree on who was there and disagree on what was filmed
entities.desc: THE RAREST EVIDENTIARY SHAPE IN THIS CLUSTER: TWO PARTICIPANTS, BOTH PUBLISHED UNDER THEIR OWN NAMES, AGREEING ABOUT THE FACTS OF THE DEPLOYMENT AND DISAGREEING ABOUT ITS PRODUCT. The Air Force placed a borrowed 24-inch Boston University telescope, mounted on a modified five-inch gun mount and fitted with an image orthicon television camera tube, at about 4,000 feet in the Los Padres National Forest above Big Sur, and covered nine of eleven Vandenberg launches between August and November 1964. Robert Jacobs, named on-site commander by the 1369th Photographic Squadron, published in January 1989 that the resulting film showed a saucer-shaped object circling an Atlas warhead and firing a beam at it. entities.label: The Disclosure Project
entities.sub: Private witness-aggregation and congressional-hearing campaign, 1993-
entities.desc: Founded by Steven Greer in 1993 as an offshoot of his Center for the Study of Extraterrestrial Intelligence, the Disclosure Project's method was to locate former military, intelligence, contractor and air traffic personnel with first-hand UFO experience, record their testimony on video, and use the aggregate to demand congressional hearings with subpoena power and witness amnesty. It briefed members of Congress and officials in Washington in April 1997 - the same week the Wilson-Davis notes later record as the trigger for Admiral Wilson's inquiries - and staged its major public event at the National Press Club on 9 May 2001 with roughly twenty witnesses and a stated corpus of more than four hundred. No hearing followed. The project's structural contribution is the demonstration that witness aggregation without documents does not move institutions: the 2001 event produced global coverage and zero congressional action, whereas the 2023 Grusch testimony - one witness with an Inspector General complaint, a security clearance and a statutory whistleblower channel - produced a hearing. The lesson the modern movement learned from Greer is that the paperwork is the lever.

entities.label: National Aeronautics and Space Administration
entities.sub: Civil space agency; host of the 2023 UAP Independent Study Team
entities.desc: NASA was created by the National Aeronautics and Space Act of 1958 as an explicitly civilian agency, and for six decades its institutional answer on UFOs was that the subject belonged to the Air Force. That changed on 9 June 2022, when NASA announced an independent study of unidentified anomalous phenomena, and on 14 September 2023, when it published the 'Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Independent Study Team Report'. The 16-member panel was chaired by Dr David Spergel of the Simons Foundation and included Dr Anamaria Berea, Dr Federica Bianco, Dr David Grinspoon and the retired NASA astronaut Captain Scott Kelly. The report's findings are notable less for what they concluded about UAP than for what they conceded about the data problem: that 'much of the data collected by military sensors or intelligence satellites are classified', that structured data curation 'plays a pivotal role' and is largely absent, and that NASA's Earth-observing fleet and the U.S. commercial remote-sensing industry have 'the collective potential to directly resolve UAP events'. In the foreword, Associate Administrator for the Science Mission Directorate Dr Nicola Fox announced that 'NASA is appointing a Director of UAP Research to centralize communications'. NASA's leverage on this board is that it is the one agency with world-class sensing capability, a statutory public mission and no SAP equity in the alleged recovery enterprise - which makes it the most plausible venue for an unclassified evidentiary standard, and the agency most conspicuously kept at arm's length from the classified holdings.

entities.label: Rendlesham Forest Incident, RAF Woodbridge/Bentwaters
entities.sub: 26-28 December 1980; USAF-occupied NATO base, Suffolk, England
entities.desc: Over three nights at the end of December 1980, US Air Force personnel at the twin bases of RAF Woodbridge and RAF Bentwaters in Suffolk - then a nuclear-capable USAF installation under NATO command - reported an object in the adjacent forest and lights in the sky. The deputy base commander documented it in an official memorandum two weeks later. Three distinct evidentiary layers exist: Lt Col Charles Halt's 13 January 1981 memorandum with its physical-trace and radiation readings; Halt's own live audio recording made during the 28 December patrol; and the signed witness statements of the airmen, including SSgt James Penniston and A1C John Burroughs. The UK Ministry of Defence's contemporaneous position was that the events were of no defence significance, a conclusion reached without interviewing the American witnesses. The incident's later history is the more important part for this board: the memo was released under US FOIA in 1983 before the MoD acknowledged its own file; John Burroughs' US Department of Veterans Affairs claim in the 2010s ran into the unavailability of his service medical records for the relevant period and was ultimately granted; and Halt executed a notarized affidavit in 2010 asserting suppression. Rendlesham is the best-documented case in the world of a physical-trace event at a nuclear-capable NATO installation, and the official position remains that nothing of defence significance occurred.

entities.label: Vandenberg Space Force Base, California
entities.sub: Space Force installation near Lompoc, Santa Barbara County; polar-orbit launch, NRO missions, missile defence sites
entities.desc: Vandenberg, on the Santa Barbara County coast near Lompoc, is the United States' west coast space launch installation: it is where polar and sun-synchronous orbits are reached, where National Reconnaissance Office payloads have long gone up, where ICBM test launches down the Western Range originate, and where ground-based missile defence infrastructure sits. It was an Air Force base until it was redesignated a Space Force base in May 2021. Its place on this board comes from sworn congressional testimony rather than from folklore. Jeffrey Nuccetelli, a sixteen-year Air Force veteran who served in security forces at Vandenberg between roughly 2003 and 2005, testified in writing to the House Oversight Task Force on 9 September 2025 that on 14 October 2003 Boeing contractors reported 'a massive, glowing red square silently hovering over two missile defense sites'; that the same night security personnel described 'a massive rectangular craft, larger than a football field' that hovered silently for about 45 seconds before departing at high speed; that a week later a patrol tracked an object inbound from the ocean that descended and vanished, after which the witness 'was threatened and told to kept quiet about the incident'; and that in 2005 a patrol reported a massive triangular craft hovering low over the main base. Two elements make this the most FOIA-actionable location claim in the modern record: Nuccetelli states that 'Official Air Force records documenting it are now held by AARO and the FBI', naming custodians for specific dated incidents at a named installation, and he states that each incident was 'witnessed by multiple personnel, documented, investigated and reported up the chain of command.' Those records have not been produced.

entities.label: Dulce Base (alleged facility, Archuleta Mesa, New Mexico)
entities.sub: THE HUB. A claimed multi-level joint human and alien facility under Archuleta Mesa, for which no documented facility exists and whose central witness was confessed as an invention
entities.desc: THIS NODE RECORDS A CLAIM. It does not record a facility, and nothing opened by this board places any facility under Archuleta Mesa. What attaches to the mesa is a set of assertions made by named people on datable occasions, and this node is the point at which they converge. Paul Bennewitz is the origin point from about 1979. Myrna Hansen's 1980 abduction account was connected to Dulce by Bennewitz after he had begun to suspect a facility. Tom Adams arrived in the early 1980s by way of cattle-mutilation work. John Lear developed his Dulce hypothesis in 1988, having heard of it from a woman named as Ann West. Tal Levesque wrote the two original Dulce Base articles. Phil Schneider arrived only in 1995 and supplied the specification the modern claim uses: seven levels, over two and a half miles deep, and an alleged 1979 firefight in which he says he shot two aliens and roughly seventy people died. Bill Cooper carried a related frame to a mass audience from 1989, and the precise limit of what he carried is recorded on his own node: his 1989 paper names alien bases under Indian reservations in the Four Corners area and the string 'Dulce' occurs in it zero times. What distinguishes this hub from every other claimant hub on the board is that its central witness has an author who confessed. In November 2015 Tal Levesque told Adam Gorightly by email that Thomas Edwin Castello was 'a creation. A MYTH', described composing the original articles from an account by Ann West mixed with his own research, and described mailing a hundred large packets of supporting material to authors and lecturers who folded it into their own work. That last part is the manufacture of apparent corroboration, and it is why this cluster is the board's cleanest worked example of many sources agreeing because they share one origin. Against the claim sit four independent checks, none of them each other's method: Levesque's confession; Adam Gorightly, who obtained and published it; John Greenewald, who on 1 April 2016 traced the most-circulated photographic 'evidence' to the 2000 film The 6th Day and stated he had found no evidence Castello exists; Norio Hayakawa, who has worked the question since 1988 and concludes 'it does not seem to exist'; and Brian Dunning, whose 3 December 2013 episode calls the imagery case trivially checkable and classifies the base as fictional. And one documentary counterweight that is not scepticism at all but a fact about the ground: on 10 December 1967 the Atomic Energy Commission detonated a 29-kiloton device at 4,227 feet twelve miles southwest of Dulce, and the site remained under federal management, with liquid radioactive waste injected into the cavity and contaminated soil hauled away as late as 2004. A rumour of a secret federal installation in the ground near Dulce is, in the flattest sense, a rumour about something that happened. What the record does not support is the facility, the levels, the depth, the firefight, or the man.

Dulce is a town in Rio Arriba County, New Mexico, on the lands of the Jicarilla Apache Nation, beside Archuleta Mesa. Three documented things attach to it. First, Project Gasbuggy: twelve miles southwest of the town, in the Carson National Forest and just west of the reservation, the Atomic Energy Commission detonated a 29-kiloton device at 4,227 feet on 10 December 1967, and the 640-acre site has been under federal stewardship ever since, with liquid radioactive waste injected into the former cavity and final surface remediation completed in September 2004. Second, Gabe Valdez, a New Mexico State Police officer stationed at Dulce from 1976, who ran the livestock-mutilation investigations of that decade and is the only official investigator in this whole story. Third, a sovereign nation whose position on the claim could not be established: the only Jicarilla Apache Nation official whose words were opened is Legislative Council President Ty Vicenti, quoted in a 2016 newspaper feature issuing a tourism welcome and neither asserting nor denying anything about a base. That is the honest state of the record and it is recorded as a gap rather than papered over. The node is named l-dulce and carries the mesa in its label on purpose: a separate archuleta-mesa node would split one place in two and hand the claimant's framing a second entry on the board.

entities.label: Project Gasbuggy, 10 December 1967
entities.sub: A 29-kiloton AEC detonation at 4,227 feet, twelve miles southwest of Dulce; the documented federal underground operation next to the rumour, twelve years before it
entities.desc: Project Gasbuggy is the best counter-explanation artefact in the Dulce cluster, and it is a government fact sheet rather than an argument. The Kirtland file is where the anomalous-object record, the nuclear weapons complex and the disinformation apparatus visibly overlap.

entities.label: Kirtland Air Force Base and Albuquerque, New Mexico
entities.sub: 51,558-acre USAF installation, southeast Albuquerque; AFRL Directed Energy, AFNWC, Manzano, KUMMSC, Sandia
entities.desc: Kirtland Air Force Base occupies 51,558 acres in the southeast quadrant of Albuquerque, sharing runways with the Albuquerque International Sunport. It began as three private airfields, was taken over as Albuquerque Army Air Base in 1941, renamed Kirtland Army Air Field on 24 February 1942 for Col. Roy C. Kirtland, and became Kirtland Air Force Base on 13 January 1948 - the same day as Wright-Patterson. Its relevance is that it is the single densest concentration of nuclear-weapons and directed-energy infrastructure in the United States sitting inside a city: Sandia National Laboratories, descended from the Manhattan Project's Z Division, is adjacent; the Air Force Nuclear Weapons Center and the 377th Air Base Wing are hosted here; the Air Force Research Laboratory Directed Energy Directorate runs the laser and high-power microwave portfolio here; the Manzano Base weapons storage complex, tunnelled into the Manzano Mountains on the base's eastern edge, merged administratively with Kirtland on 1 July 1971; and the Kirtland Underground Munitions Maintenance and Storage Complex, activated in 1992, is described in the base's own literature as the largest nuclear weapons storage facility in the world, with more than 300,000 square feet underground. Kirtland is also the operational address of the best-documented domestic UAP-adjacent counterintelligence operation on the record. Albuquerque businessman Paul Bennewitz, whose company Thunder Scientific sat on the base perimeter and sold humidity sensors licensed from Sandia in 1966, began a self-funded study in July 1979, filmed lights over the Manzano storage area and recorded anomalous signals, contacted the base on 24 October 1980 and briefed Kirtland officials on 10 November 1980. What followed was a sustained feed of fabricated material through the Air Force Office of Special Investigations detachment here, later admitted in public by AFOSI special agent Richard C. Doty and by UFO researcher William Moore, who stated on 1 July 1989 that he had participated in an effort to push Bennewitz toward a breakdown by feeding him false information. Bennewitz was hospitalised in August 1988 and died on 23 June 2003. The Bennewitz operation is the board's clearest evidence that counterintelligence resources were deployed against a private citizen over UAP-adjacent observations at a nuclear site, and Kirtland is where it happened.

entities.label: The FFRDC Seam
entities.sub: Structural domain - the legal space between government and industry
entities.desc: This is the mechanism the whole board turns on, and it is not a theory - it is written into the Federal Acquisition Regulation. A federally funded research and development center is a research organisation operated under contract by a private entity - a nonprofit, a university, or an industrial consortium - to meet a special long-term research need that, in the FAR's language, cannot be met as effectively by existing in-house or contractor resources. As of February 2026 there were 41 FFRDCs sponsored or co-sponsored by 12 federal agencies. Three features of FAR 35.017 create the seam. First, sponsors are directed to build long-term strategic relationships: initial contracts may run five years and are renewable in similar increments, expressly to give the FFRDC stability, continuity and the ability to attract high-quality personnel. Second, and decisively, the FFRDC 'has access to government and supplier data, including sensitive and proprietary information, and to employees and facilities beyond that common in a normal contractual relationship.' That single clause creates an entity that can legally see both the government's compartmented information and the prime contractor's proprietary information - a vantage no ordinary contractor and no ordinary civil servant has. Third, in exchange for that access, the FFRDC is barred from competing with the private sector for federal R&D work and is required to operate in the public interest with objectivity, free from organisational conflicts of interest, and to fully disclose its activities to its sponsoring agency - to the sponsor, note, not to Congress and not to the public. The consequence is the concealment architecture in miniature. Records held by an FFRDC are contractor records, not agency records, and therefore outside the Freedom of Information Act. Disclosure runs to the sponsoring agency, which is also the classification authority. Sole-source awards mean no competitor ever audits the work. Personnel move continuously between the sponsor and the operator. If a programme wanted to be technically vested outside the government while the government retained absolute control of materials, breakthroughs and data - and while remaining invisible to FOIA, to GAO, and to committee staff without the sponsor's consent - it would be built exactly here. Rep. Eric Burlison made this the explicit basis of his May 2026 inquiry: FFRDCs, he wrote, 'often receive special access to government facilities, data, sponsor requirements, and sensitive technical information that ordinary private contractors may not receive,' and 'cannot become private vaults for federal records.'

entities.label: FAR 35.017 - Federally Funded Research and Development Centers
entities.sub: Federal Acquisition Regulation subpart; 48 CFR 35.017
entities.desc: The regulatory instrument that creates the seam. FAR 35.017 defines what an FFRDC is, requires a sponsoring agency to justify its existence, sets the terms of the sponsoring agreement, and grants the operator its extraordinary access. The operative language for this board is the access clause - an FFRDC 'has access to government and supplier data, including sensitive and proprietary information, and to employees and facilities beyond that common in a normal contractual relationship' - and the disclosure clause, which requires the FFRDC to fully disclose its activities to its sponsoring agency. Nothing in FAR 35.017 requires disclosure to Congress, to the public, to GAO, or to any other agency. The sponsor is simultaneously the customer, the classification authority, and the only body entitled to a full account of what the FFRDC does. Contracts may be awarded for up to five years and renewed indefinitely in like increments, and are routinely awarded sole-source: the government's own notices for MITRE's aviation FFRDC in 2025 were posted as notices of intent to award a sole source contract. In return the FFRDC is forbidden to compete for federal R&D work against industry and must operate free of organisational conflicts of interest. Read as a whole, the subpart constructs an entity with the government's access, the private sector's records status, and no independent auditor. It is the legal chassis on which every entity in this domain sits.

entities.label: The MITRE Corporation

entities.desc: MITRE is the priority institution of this domain and, on the board's premise, the structural heart of the concealment architecture. It was incorporated as a nonprofit on 21 July 1958, spun out of MIT Lincoln Laboratory's Division 6 to carry the systems engineering of the Semi-Automatic Ground Environment continental air defence system - Robert Everett and 485 other Lincoln Laboratory staff walked across at founding. It was created by the Air Force, explicitly on the RAND model, to be a permanent nonprofit answerable to a military customer rather than to a university. It now operates six FFRDCs: the National Security Engineering Center for the Department of Defense under the Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering; the Center for Advanced Aviation System Development for the FAA; the Center for Enterprise Modernization for Treasury and IRS with VA, SSA and Commerce as co-sponsors; the Homeland Security Systems Engineering and Development Institute for DHS S&T, created 5 March 2009; the Health FFRDC for HHS; and the National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence for NIST, created 19 September 2014. NSEC alone was funded at roughly 1.43 billion dollars in FY2024. MITRE also administers JASON, the government's most sensitive standing scientific advisory panel. Its revenue passed 2.37 billion dollars in 2023. The reason MITRE, and not Lockheed or Northrop, is the load-bearing node is the combination in one organisation of: sponsorship by both the defence and intelligence establishment and the civil aviation regulator that owns the radar picture of American airspace; FAR-granted access to both government compartmented data and prime contractor proprietary data; contractor records status that puts its files outside FOIA; a governing board repeatedly chaired or vice-chaired by former Principal Deputy Directors of National Intelligence; and a chief executive imported directly from Battelle. On 22 May 2026 Rep. Eric Burlison sent MITRE a 10-page legislative production request demanding an accounting of UAP records, anomalous aerospace or undersea events, recovered materials and technologies of unknown origin, legacy crash-retrieval or reverse-engineering programmes, Special and Controlled Access Programs, sensor data, materials analysis and classification guides, reaching back to 1930. MITRE's response was that it was reviewing its archives and that 'if any relevant material is found, we will coordinate with the federal agencies responsible for the work' - which restates the exact problem: an FFRDC's disclosure obligation runs to its sponsor, not to Congress.

entities.label: JASON
entities.sub: Independent standing scientific advisory group, est. 1960; administered successively by IDA, SRI International and MITRE
entities.desc: JASON is the government's standing panel of elite scientists convened to answer its hardest and most sensitive technical questions, and it has never once in its 66-year existence been housed inside the government. Established in 1960, it was administered by the Institute for Defense Analyses from 1960 to 1973, then by SRI International, and since 2002 by MITRE. Membership runs between roughly 30 and 60 physicists, mathematicians and engineers holding clearances well above their academic station. In April 2019 the Office of the Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering declined to renew MITRE's JASON contract, which would have terminated the group; within two weeks the Department of Energy's National Nuclear Security Administration posted a notice of intent to award a short-term sole source contract to MITRE to provide management and logistics support for JASON, and the group survived. Bloomberg Government reported MITRE received 34.4 million dollars in obligations for the work as the earlier contract was ending. A JASON recompete was again in the market in 2026 with MITRE as the confirmed incumbent. The significance for this board is that the mechanism by which the United States obtains independent scientific judgement on its most classified problems is itself a contractor-administered instrument whose continuity depends on sole-source awards to MITRE. If a government body ever commissioned a genuinely independent technical assessment of recovered material, JASON is the body it would go to - and the corporation that would convene, clear, house and archive that assessment is the same corporation now under congressional records demand.

entities.desc: A two-page memorandum dated 9 January 1953, reference G-1579-4, classified SECRET and unsigned, written by Battelle Memorial Institute's H. C. Cross to Miles E. Goll at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base under Project Stork. Jacques Vallee found it in 1967 among J. The memorandum recommends establishing controlled experiments in selected areas of the United States with high concentrations of UFO reports, using observation posts equipped for visual skywatch, radar and photography, and states that 'many different types of aerial activity should be secretly and purposefully scheduled within the area.' It was written five days before the CIA-convened Robertson Panel met on 14-16 January 1953 - the panel whose recommendations set the government's public debunking posture for the next fifteen years. Vallee's judgement, which this board records as the significant one, is that the Robertson Panel was never briefed on the Pentacle proposals, and that a separate body had already determined the boundaries of what the panel could consider. The memorandum is the founding document of the contractor-side manipulation thesis: it shows a private institute proposing, to its Air Force customer, to manufacture the stimulus that the official investigation would then be asked to explain. No signed original has ever been produced by the Air Force or by Battelle.

entities.label: Burlison UAP Records Disclosure Amendment, FY2027 NDAA
entities.sub: House-adopted amendment, July 2026; revised text designated Version 2, 15 July 2026, made in order by the House Rules Committee
entities.desc: The legislative instrument that would close the FFRDC seam, and the reason the MITRE inquiry matters beyond one letter. Rep. Eric Burlison's revised UAP Disclosure Amendment was designated 'Version 2' on 15 July 2026, made in order by the House Rules Committee, and adopted by the House as part of the Fiscal Year 2027 National Defense Authorization Act in late July 2026. It would require federal agencies to identify, preserve and transfer UAP records to the National Archives on a statutory timeline, establish a permanent UAP records collection there, and create an independent UAP Records Review Board with Senate-confirmed members and subpoena authority to determine what is released and what stays classified. Critically for this domain, its disclosure requirements extend to certain government contractors that possess covered records - the provision that would convert FFRDC holdings from contractor records outside FOIA into covered federal records subject to a statutory review board. Burlison's stated rationale: 'The government belongs to the American people. For too long, UAP records have remained scattered.' The bill still has to survive the Senate and conference. Whether the contractor-records provision survives intact is the single most important open question on this board, because it is the only mechanism anyone has proposed that would reach inside an FFRDC without the sponsoring agency's consent.
