claims.text: The federal literature on nitinol, one report of it written by Battelle itself, does not support a Battelle 1948-49 lineage for the alloy. NASA SP-5110, prepared for NASA by Battelle Memorial Institute in 1972, opens: 'Some 10 years ago, Buehler and Wiley of the U.S. Naval Ordnance Laboratory developed a series of engineering alloys that possess a unique mechanical (shape) memory. The generic name of the series of alloys is 55-Nitinol, where Nitinol stands for Nickel Titanium Naval Ordnance Laboratory.' The earliest Naval Ordnance Laboratory nitinol report cited anywhere in its reference list is NOLTR 61-75 of 3 August 1961; US Patent 3,174,851 was filed on 1 December 1961; and NASA CR-1433 of September 1969 records Battelle's own role as a subcontractor to Goodyear Aerospace which 'processed the basic Nitinol rod'. entities.label: Los Alamos, New Mexico
entities.sub: Los Alamos National Laboratory; site of the 16 February 1949 green fireballs conference
entities.desc: Los Alamos sits on the Pajarito Plateau in Los Alamos County, New Mexico, and is the site of the laboratory established in 1943 as Project Y of the Manhattan Project, now Los Alamos National Laboratory. Its place on this board rests on two things. First, it is one of the two nuclear design laboratories and therefore one of the small number of American institutions with both the compartmentation architecture and the materials-science capability that a concealed exploitation programme would require; whistleblower accounts collected by AAWSAP and by David Grusch describe materials work distributed across the Department of Energy laboratory complex and its industrial partners, and no document has been produced placing any specific laboratory inside such a programme. Second, and documented, Los Alamos hosted the conference of 16 February 1949 on the green fireballs - the anomalous luminous objects observed repeatedly over northern New Mexico's nuclear installations from December 1948 - attended by Edward Teller and by the University of New Mexico meteoriticist Lincoln LaPaz, whom the Air Force had retained to investigate. LANL's own published account records that the phenomenon was ultimately dismissed as a national security threat, a conclusion that did not prevent the Air Force from standing up Project Twinkle ten months later to instrument it. Los Alamos is thus the first place where American nuclear scientists formally met to discuss unexplained objects over their own facilities, and the meeting is on the laboratory's own record.

entities.label: The five observables (UAP performance taxonomy)
entities.sub: Performance taxonomy attributed to Luis Elizondo from his AATIP work; published from 2019, no government original located
entities.desc:
The five observables are the most widely used frame for what a UAP is alleged to do, and almost every popular account of the subject is organised around them. They matter to this board for one reason and it is not the phenomenology: four of the five are itemised as design goals in a United States Navy invention-disclosure briefing that was released under FOIA. That mapping is documentary and it does not depend on anyone's view of whether the effects are real.

What the list is NOT is a government product. No released government document located for this board states them as a set, and the earliest published statements of them are journalism and material from To The Stars, the company Elizondo joined after leaving the Pentagon. The board therefore carries the list at Tier 2, attributed to Elizondo rather than to the Department of Defense, with the provenance gap stated on the node rather than smoothed over. Presented that way the absence is a strength: the claim being made is about what one named former official formulated, which is defensible, rather than about what the Pentagon concluded, which is not.

The wording is also not fixed, which is itself worth knowing before anyone quotes the list as though it were a definition.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded B on a global pass (rank 495 of 1170, score 31). 3 connections, 1 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C1/A1/D1.

claims.text: The five observables are attributed to Luis Elizondo, who compiled them while running the Defense Department's Advanced Aerospace Threat Identification Program. As listed in History's account of the Navy videos, they are: 'Anti-gravity lift', 'Sudden and instantaneous acceleration', 'Hypersonic velocities without signatures', 'Low observability, or cloaking', and 'Trans-medium travel'. The article says he 'compiled a list of extraordinary, logic-defying capabilities most commonly associated with unidentified aerial phenomena sightings' and 'calls those traits the "five observables"'.
claims.source: Greg Daugherty and Missy Sullivan, 'These 5 UFO Traits, Captured on Video by Navy Fighters, Defy Explanation', History, 20 May 2019, updated 28 May 2025, https://www.history.com/articles/ufo-sightings-speed-appearance-movement

claims.text: To The Stars, the company Elizondo joined after leaving the Pentagon, publishes the same five under the heading 'Five Characteristics Unique to UAP's', worded: 'Sudden and instantaneous acceleration', 'Hypersonic velocities without signatures', 'Low observability', 'Trans-medium travel' and 'Positive lift'. The page carries no author, no date and no attribution to Elizondo or to AATIP.
claims.source: 'Five Characteristics Unique to UAP's', To The Stars, https://tothestars.media/blogs/press-and-news/five-characteristics-unique-to-uaps, read 28 August 2026

claims.text: The list has no fixed text, which matters before anyone quotes it as a definition. The first observable appears as 'Anti-gravity lift' in the History account and as 'Positive lift' on To The Stars, and is elsewhere given as 'positive lift without flight surfaces'. The two published sources located for this board therefore differ on the wording of one of the five and on whether cloaking is named alongside low observability. No canonical text has been located.
claims.source: History, 20 May 2019, compared against the To The Stars page, both read 28 August 2026

claims.text: Four of the five are itemised as design goals in a United States Navy invention-disclosure briefing released under FOIA. The PAX 205 briefing describes a 'hybrid aerospace / undersea craft (HAUC)' that 'would move with great ease through the air / space / water mediums' (trans-medium travel), enclosed in a 'Vacuum plasma bubble/sheath' giving extreme speed without skin friction (hypersonic velocity), with non-linear scattering of radio frequency and sonar signals (low observability), by means of an inertial mass reduction device (lift without flight surfaces). This is the whole reason the taxonomy is on this board.
claims.source: NAVAIR FOIA release 2021-003244, 'PAX 205 - INERTIAL MASS REDUCTION DEVICE', slides 4-5, https://www.navair.navy.mil/foia/sites/g/files/jejdrs566/files/document/%5Bfilename%5D/2021-003244%20FINAL%20VERSION%20PAX%20205%20-%20INERTIAL%20MASS%20REDUCTION%20DEVICE.pdf

claims.text: The fifth observable, sudden and instantaneous acceleration, is NOT itemised as a design goal in the PAX 205 briefing. The briefing speaks of operating the device 'under rapid acceleration transients' as a means of generating the field, which is a statement about how the machine is driven rather than a claimed flight characteristic of the craft. Recorded because four out of five is the accurate figure and five would be the easy overclaim.
claims.source: NAVAIR FOIA release 2021-003244, PAX 205 briefing, slides 4-5, read against the five as published

claims.text: The mapping is better read as convergence on a shared description than as evidence that either side knew of the other. Pais filed from NAWCAD between 2015 and 2018 and the observables were published from 2019, so the briefing predates the published list; both are drawn from the same body of reported Navy encounters, and a designer asked to build to those reports would arrive at broadly these goals. What the mapping does establish, without inference, is that a Navy technical organisation wrote four of the five down as things it wanted to build.
claims.source: Stated inference from the dates of the PAX 205 briefing and the earliest located publication of the observables

claims.text: Elizondo does not state the five observables in his sworn written testimony. His written statement to the House Committee on Oversight and Accountability for the hearing 'Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena: Exposing the Truth', 13 November 2024, contains none of the words 'observable', 'acceleration', 'trans-medium', 'lift', 'hypersonic', 'signature', 'cloak' or 'AATIP'. The full text was retrieved from oversight.house.gov and is transcribed at research/testimony/elizondo-house-oversight-2024-11-13.txt. This is a searchable negative on the most likely government-record source for the set, and it is why the taxonomy stays at Tier 2 attributed to him rather than moving to the congressional record.

entities.label: David C. Grusch v. Michael Chapman et al.
entities.sub: Loudoun County Circuit Court, filed 15 July 2024; dismissed with prejudice 6 August 2025
entities.desc: Grusch's civil action against Loudoun County Sheriff Michael Chapman and a Sheriff's Office employee over the release of records describing his 2014 and 2018 emergency custody episodes, including an October 2018 incident report referencing evaluation at Inova's Loudoun Adult Psychiatric Services where he was evaluated but not committed. The records were obtained under Virginia FOIA and published by Ken Klippenstein in The Intercept on 9 August 2023, two weeks after Grusch's sworn testimony. The suit, filed in Loudoun County Circuit Court on 15 July 2024, alleged the defendants lacked authority to release involuntary commitment material and that the disclosure caused him to suffer personally and professionally. It was dismissed with prejudice on 6 August 2025, on the reasoning that Virginia's mental health confidentiality statute reaches court files rather than police records and that the redacted release complied with FOIA. The case matters to the board not for its legal outcome but for what it establishes: that a UAP whistleblower's most sensitive personal records were lawfully obtainable by anyone who filed a request, and that no protection existed. That gap is exactly what the whistleblower-protection provisions being litigated in Congress since 2023 are aimed at.

entities.label: Air Force Regulation 200-2
entities.sub: USAF regulation on UFO reporting; 26 Aug 1953 and 12 Aug 1954 editions
entities.desc: AFR 200-2, 'Unidentified Flying Objects Reporting', is the internal Air Force regulation that operationalised the Robertson Panel's recommendations seven months after the panel reported. Its release policy states that for objects which are not explainable, 'only the fact that ATIC will analyze the data is worthy of release, due to many unknowns involved', and protects names of principals, intercept and investigation procedures, and classified radar data. entities.label: Low Memorandum ("the trick would be...")
entities.sub: Robert J. Low to University of Colorado administrators, 9 August 1966
entities.desc: A two-page internal memorandum written by Robert J. Low, assistant dean of the University of Colorado graduate school, on 9 August 1966 — two months before the Air Force contract for the UFO study was signed — advising two senior administrators on how the university could take the money without damaging its scientific reputation. It is the clearest surviving evidence that the terminal official study of the legacy era was designed with a predetermined public posture.

entities.label: Roswell Incident
entities.sub: Recovery and retraction, 7-9 July 1947
entities.desc: In late June 1947 rancher W. W. 'Mac' Brazel found debris scattered on the Foster Ranch near Corona, in Lincoln County, New Mexico, roughly seventy-five miles northwest of Roswell. On 6 July he reported it to Chaves County Sheriff George Wilcox, who called Roswell Army Air Field. RAAF dispatched Maj. Jesse A. Marcel Sr., intelligence officer of the 509th Bomb Group - at that date the only nuclear-capable bomb group in existence - and Capt. Sheridan Cavitt of the Counter Intelligence Corps. On 8 July 1947 the base public information officer, 1st Lt. Walter Haut, issued a press release stating that 'the intelligence office of the 509th Bomb group of the Eighth Air Force, Roswell Army Air Field, was fortunate enough to gain possession of a disc.' The story went out on the wires within hours. That same day Brig. Gen. Roger M. Ramey, commanding Eighth Air Force at Fort Worth Army Air Field, staged a press conference with weather officer Warrant Officer Irving Newton and presented the material as a weather balloon and a radar target reflector. The Air Force's own subsequent reports concede the essential structure: the 1994 report identified the debris as a Project Mogul balloon train, specifically Flight No. 4 launched 4 June 1947 from Alamogordo Army Air Field, and explicitly acknowledged that the weather balloon statement had been a cover story to divert attention from a classified programme; 'The Roswell Report: Case Closed', published 24 June 1997 and authored in part by declassification officer 1st Lt. James McAndrew, attributed accounts of recovered bodies to anthropomorphic parachute test dummies dropped in 1950s high-altitude programmes. Roswell's evidentiary value to this board does not depend on adjudicating what the debris was. It rests on two documented facts. First, the United States has conceded in writing that it issued a false public explanation for a materiel recovery in 1947. Second, when Rep. Steven H. Schiff asked GAO to audit the paper trail after the Defense Department declined to answer him, GAO/NSIAD-95-187 reported that RAAF outgoing messages from October 1946 through December 1949 had been destroyed and that no disposition authority for the destruction could be located. The unit's message traffic for the period covering the recovery no longer exists, and nobody has ever produced the authority that ordered it destroyed. That finding has never been rebutted by any agency.

entities.label: The Roswell Reports (USAF, 1994-1997)
entities.sub: Two USAF volumes: 'Fact vs. Fiction' (1995) and 'Case Closed' (1997)
entities.desc: The Air Force's two-volume answer to Rep. Schiff, and a first-class artifact of the concealment effort precisely because it is thorough. 'The Roswell Report: Fact vs. Fiction in the New Mexico Desert', by Col. Richard L. Weaver and 1st Lt. James McAndrew, runs to roughly 881 pages and was published in 1995 (following the Air Force's September 1994 report); it concedes that the weather balloon statement of 8 July 1947 was false and attributes the debris to the then-classified Project MOGUL. 'The Roswell Report: Case Closed', by McAndrew, was released 24 June 1997 and attributes reports of bodies to anthropomorphic test dummies dropped in high-altitude parachute tests — tests which mostly occurred between 1953 and 1959, six to twelve years after the event. The Air Force's position is therefore that the government lied in 1947 for legitimate reasons, told the truth in 1994, and that witnesses compressed a decade of unrelated events into one week. Both volumes are catalogued at the Defense Technical Information Center as ADA326148 and ADA326147. They are the official record and are treated here as such: authoritative on what the Air Force will say, and silent on the question GAO opened, which is who destroyed the base's records and under what authority.

entities.label: 1952 Washington DC Sightings
entities.sub: Radar-visual events over the capital, 19-20 and 26-27 July 1952
entities.desc: On consecutive weekends in July 1952 unidentified targets were tracked on radar at Washington National Airport, at Andrews Air Force Base and by the Air Route Traffic Control Center, with visual corroboration from airline crews and interceptors scrambled from Newcastle. It was the largest concentration of radar-visual events in American airspace over the seat of government, it ran on the front pages for weeks, and it produced the largest Air Force press conference since the Second World War, at which the events were attributed to temperature inversion. The flap is the pivot of the legacy era for one reason: it moved the problem from the Air Force to the intelligence community. Within eight weeks H. Marshall Chadwell of the CIA Office of Scientific Intelligence was writing to the Director of Central Intelligence that official reports had totalled 250 in July 1952 alone and that the situation contained 'two elements of danger which... have national security implications' — the danger being psychological warfare exposure and the saturation of air defence channels, not the objects. Six months later the Robertson Panel met. Everything that follows in the American handling of this subject descends from the government's decision, in the autumn of 1952, that the reporting was the threat.

entities.desc: The CIA's own official history of its involvement with unidentified flying objects, written by NRO historian Gerald K. The dispute is not about whether the government lies about this subject. It is about what else it was covering.

entities.label: House Armed Services Committee UFO Hearing
entities.sub: 89th Congress, Hearing No. 55, 5 April 1966
entities.desc: The first congressional hearing on unidentified flying objects, held on 5 April 1966 by the House Committee on Armed Services after House Minority Leader Gerald Ford demanded an inquiry in response to the March 1966 Michigan sightings and the swamp gas explanation offered by the Air Force's own consultant. It lasted a single day. Secretary of the Air Force Harold Brown, Blue Book director Maj. Hector Quintanilla and J. Allen Hynek appeared. Nineteen years of official investigation received one day of legislative attention, and the concrete result was not oversight but outsourcing: within six months the Air Force had contracted the University of Colorado study, whose coordinator had already written in August 1966 that the trick would be to appear objective to the public while presenting the image of nonbelievers to scientists. Two years later a second and more substantial hearing — the House Committee on Science and Astronautics symposium of 29 July 1968, with McDonald, Hynek, Sagan and others — produced a serious scientific record and no legislative consequence at all. The 1966 hearing is the template: pressure in, study out, closure follows.

entities.label: NARA Record Group 615 — UAP Records Collection
entities.sub: National Archives collection established under PL 118-31 §§1841-1843
entities.desc: Record Group 615, the Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection at the National Archives, is the first statutory records mechanism ever created for this subject and the direct descendant of the legacy-era destruction problem. It was established under sections 1841 to 1843 of the FY2024 National Defense Authorization Act, Public Law 118-31 — the surviving remnant of the far broader UAP Disclosure Act, which would have created an independent review board with eminent-domain authority over recovered materials before it was stripped in conference. Federal agencies are required to identify and transfer UAP records to NARA, which accessions them into RG 615 on a rolling basis, and NARA has been digitising its existing legacy holdings in parallel. For this domain the collection is a test: the 1940s-1960s records that matter are the ones Bolender said went up the JANAP 146 channel and the ones GAO found destroyed at Roswell Army Air Field. Whether RG 615 ever contains an Air Materiel Command T-2 series, a CIRVIS report series, or a disposition record for the destroyed RAAF traffic is the measurable question this board will track. As of the topic page's last update in April 2025 the collection was being populated incrementally.

entities.label: RAAF Press Release, 8 July 1947
entities.sub: Roswell Army Air Field public information office
entities.desc: The only uncontested primary artifact of the Roswell event, issued by the public information office of Roswell Army Air Field on 8 July 1947 over the name of 1st Lt. Walter Haut and carried immediately by the wire services. Its text states that 'the many rumors regarding the flying disc became a reality yesterday when the intelligence office of the 509th Bomb group of the Eighth Air Force, Roswell Army Air Field, was fortunate enough to gain possession of a disc through the cooperation of one of the local ranchers and the sheriff's office of Chaves County'. The announcement was made by the intelligence office of the world's only atomic bomb group, an organisation with the most restrictive information discipline in the United States military, which does not issue accidental press releases about recovered aircraft. And it was retracted the same day, from a higher headquarters, by a general officer. The Air Force's position since 1994 is that base personnel misidentified a classified MOGUL balloon train; that position requires the 509th's intelligence staff to have failed to recognise balloon and radar target material, which is the same material Gen. Ramey used hours later to prove they had.

entities.label: Project MOON DUST
entities.sub: USAF/State Dept recovery and exploitation program
entities.desc: MOON DUST was the US Air Force codeword for the collection and exploitation of objects and debris of unknown origin that survived re-entry - nominally Soviet and other foreign space hardware, in practice an all-source recovery capability with a standing tasking to acquire material that fell from the sky. It ran from the early 1960s under Air Force Intelligence, with State Department reporting channels supporting the overseas collection, and it is documented in released Department of State cable traffic, one file of which was declassified by CIA. Its significance for this board is jurisdictional rather than evidential: MOON DUST establishes that from at least 1961 the United States maintained a named, funded, worldwide programme whose purpose was to go and get whatever came down, with a chain of custody that ran into Air Force technical intelligence at Wright-Patterson - the same institutional address that the Twining memorandum used in 1947. The Air Force told Congress and researchers for years that MOON DUST had nothing to do with unidentified objects; the programme's own charter language on unidentified fallen material is why that answer never held. MOON DUST and its air-transport twin BLUE FLY are the connective tissue between the Blue Book era and everything that follows: Blue Book was the public-facing sighting file; MOON DUST was the retrieval function, and it did not close in 1969.

entities.label: Operation BLUE FLY
entities.sub: USAF quick-reaction airlift for MOON DUST recoveries
entities.desc: BLUE FLY was the airlift and quick-reaction arm attached to MOON DUST: the standing arrangement by which recovered material of unknown origin was moved, on priority, to Air Force technical intelligence at Foreign Technology Division, Wright-Patterson AFB. Where MOON DUST was the collection authority, BLUE FLY was the transport and custody mechanism. The two names appear together in Air Force intelligence correspondence and in congressional correspondence generated when members of Congress - including New Mexico's delegation in the 1990s - asked the Air Force to explain them. The Air Force's answers shifted over time from denying the programmes existed to conceding they existed but concerned only foreign space debris. For a board tracking custody, BLUE FLY is the most important single word in the 1960s-1980s record: it names the pipeline. Any recovered material entering US custody in that period had a designated route, and that route terminated at Wright-Patterson, which is precisely where the 1947-era chain also terminated and where the Air Force's own 1985 public fact sheet felt it necessary to state that 'there are not now nor ever have been, any extraterrestrial visitors or equipment on Wright-Patterson Air Force Base.'

entities.label: 1975 SAC Nuclear-Base Overflights (Loring, Wurtsmith, Malmstrom, Minot)
entities.sub: Documented unidentified incursions over nuclear weapons and missile installations, Oct-Nov 1975
entities.desc: The best-documented episode in the entire UFO-nuclear record, because the paper is the government's own and it was released. Over roughly a fortnight in late October and early November 1975, unidentified objects were reported over Strategic Air Command weapons storage and alert areas and over Minuteman missile fields at Loring AFB, Maine (27, 28 and 31 October), Wurtsmith AFB, Michigan (30 October), Malmstrom AFB, Montana (7-8 November), Minot AFB, North Dakota, and Canadian Forces Station Falconbridge, Ontario. A NORAD document dated 11 November 1975 records that reliable military personnel at all five installations had visually sighted suspicious objects. A Loring AFB teletype states that an unidentified object 'demonstrated a clear intent in the weapons storage area' - the phrase from which Fawcett and Greenwood took the title of their 1984 book. The 24th NORAD Region Senior Director's log for 7 November 1975 records the 341st SAC Command Post reporting sightings from missile sites M-1, L-3, LIMA and L-6 near Moore and Buffalo, Montana at 1035Z; the Harlow launch control facility observing an object illuminating the site driveway at 1203Z; site K-1 tracking a bright object through 10x50 binoculars at 1319Z; and L-1 at 1327Z reporting the object issuing a tubular black object, with surveillance unable to establish any track. The National Military Command Center's Memorandum for the Record of 8 November 1975, subject 'Unidentified Sightings', records that at 0253 EST Malmstrom received seven radar cuts on the height-finder radar between 9,500 and 15,500 feet with simultaneous ground witnesses reporting lights and jet engine noise, that cross-tell with the FAA revealed no jet aircraft within 100 nautical miles, that two F-106 interceptors from the 24th NORAD Region were scrambled at 0254 and airborne at 0257, and that at 0344 EST the objects could not be intercepted because the fighters had to stay above 12,000 feet over mountainous terrain. These documents reached the public because Citizens Against UFO Secrecy filed a FOIA request on 26 December 1977; the Office of the Assistant Secretary of Defense replied on 6 February 1978 identifying twenty-four documents held by the Office of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, and after an internal argument over exempting raw unevaluated reporting, Assistant Secretary of Defense Thomas Ross determined no useful purpose would be served by withholding them.

entities.label: MJ-12 / Operation Majestic-12 Documents
entities.sub: Purported 1952 Eisenhower briefing document and associated papers, surfaced 1984-1987
entities.desc: The MJ-12 corpus originates in a roll of undeveloped 35mm film that arrived anonymously, postmarked Albuquerque, at the Los Angeles home of television producer Jaime Shandera on 11 December 1984. Developed, it produced an eight-page 'Briefing Document: Operation Majestic 12' dated 18 November 1952, prepared for President-elect Eisenhower, naming twelve officials and describing the recovery of a crashed disc and four bodies near Roswell. Shandera, Bill Moore and Stanton Friedman released it publicly in May 1987. The National Archives searched Air Force, Joint Chiefs, NSC, Truman Library and Eisenhower Library holdings and found nothing except a single document in Record Group 341: the Cutler-Twining memorandum of 14 July 1954, whose problems NARA itself enumerated - no Top Secret register number, no letterhead or watermark, a security marking that NSC's FOIA office says post-dates the Eisenhower administration, and a paper stock ('diction onionskin') inconsistent with the Eisenhower Library's sample. The FBI investigated and states an Air Force investigation determined the document to be a fake. The board's position is that the MJ-12 documents are best understood not as evidence of a 1947 committee but as evidence of a 1980s operation: the Albuquerque postmark, the Doty and Moore connections, and the discovery of a planted-looking document inside a federal record group all point at the same place at the same time as the Bennewitz campaign.

entities.label: Citizens Against UFO Secrecy (CAUS)
entities.sub: Private FOIA litigation organisation, 1977-2000s
entities.desc: CAUS was the first organisation to treat UFO secrecy as a litigable question rather than a belief question. Founded in 1977 and directed by the attorney Peter Gersten, it used the Freedom of Information Act and federal litigation against the CIA, NSA and Department of Defense, forcing the release of several hundred pages of CIA UFO records in the late 1970s and then bringing Civil Action No. 80-1562 against the National Security Agency. That case established the fact this board cares about: NSA located UFO-related records, withheld them under national-security exemptions, and defended the withholding with a classified affidavit reviewed only by the judge. CAUS lost every merits ruling and won the only thing that mattered - a judicial record that the material exists. The organisation was still in the federal appellate courts against DoD as late as November 2001. Its body of FOIA correspondence became sufficiently substantial that GAO listed 'National Security Agency, Fort Meade, Md. - FOIA records, Citizens Against UFO Secrecy' among the record sets it searched for the 1995 Roswell report.

entities.label: Citizens Against UFO Secrecy v. National Security Agency (Civil Action No. 80-1562)
entities.sub: FOIA litigation, D.D.C. 1980 - D.C. Cir. 1981 - cert. denied 1982
entities.desc: The case in which the United States told a federal judge, in secret, why it could not release its UFO signals intelligence - and the judge agreed. CAUS sued NSA in 1980. NSA located UFO-related records, withheld them, and supported the withholding with a classified affidavit executed by its Chief of Policy, Eugene Yeates. The district court reviewed the affidavit in camera and granted summary judgment for NSA; the D.C. Circuit affirmed on 3 November 1981; the Supreme Court denied certiorari on 8 March 1982. NSA subsequently released a redacted version of the Yeates affidavit, and released the underlying UFO records themselves with most pages carrying only a few visible words - redaction executed in white-out rather than black ink, which had the effect of making the excisions less visually obvious. A Mandatory Declassification Review filed in July 2013 was required to force further release. The case is the cleanest judicial confirmation in the American record that UFO-related intelligence material exists, is held, and is withheld on national-security grounds. It has never been overturned or superseded.

entities.label: CENTER LANE

entities.desc: CENTER LANE was the Army Intelligence and Security Command's designation for the operational remote-viewing unit from 1983, succeeding GRILL FLAME after the codename was compromised. entities.label: S-4 / Papoose Lake, Nevada
entities.sub: THE HUB. A claimed nine-hangar facility said to be built into a mountain about fifteen miles south of Groom Lake, at a real dry lake on which aerial photography shows no installation
entities.desc: THIS NODE RECORDS A CLAIM AND NOT A PLACE WHOSE CONTENTS ARE ESTABLISHED. Papoose Lake is a real dry lake bed in Lincoln County, Nevada, a few miles southwest of the Groom Lake facility and adjacent to the Papoose Range. Nothing documented attaches any facility to it. What attaches to it is an assertion: from 1989 Bob Lazar has said that between December 1988 and April 1989 he worked at a site he calls S-4, about fifteen miles south of Groom Lake on the Nellis range, built into a mountainside behind nine hangar doors angled at about sixty degrees, holding nine disc-shaped craft whose propulsion he was hired to back-engineer. The node exists because that assertion is the convergence point of an entire cluster: Lazar, John Lear, Gene Huff, George Knapp, the 1989 KLAS broadcasts, the 1991 videotape and the 2018 Corbell documentary all run into it, and so do the people who say it is wrong. The documented half of the surrounding geography is real and should not be blurred into the claim: the Groom Lake facility was officially acknowledged when the CIA history of the U-2 and OXCART programmes by Gregory Pedlow and Donald Welzenbach was declassified in summer 2013. That is a statement about Groom Lake. It is not a statement about Papoose Lake. The node is named s-4-papoose-lake rather than s-4 deliberately, because the two strongest sceptical accounts both say the designator S-4 is real and attaches to a radar facility elsewhere on the range; a node called s-4 would silently adopt the claimant's referent as the board's own.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded A on a global pass (rank 175 of 1170, score 49). 16 connections, 2 of them custody/funding/programmatic, 2 official denials recorded against it. Axes C0/A0/D3.

claims.text: THE SECOND-BEST FINDING IN THIS CLUSTER: TWO PEOPLE REACH THE SAME COUNTER-EXPLANATION BY UNRELATED ROUTES. Tom Mahood, a physics graduate who spent years on the documentary record, concludes in his 2018 retrospective that there is 'nothing at Papoose Lake' and that S-4 actually refers to a radar facility at the Tonopah Test Range. Separately, T.D. Barnes, a former CIA and NASA engineer who worked at Groom Lake, says the real Site 4 is a remote radar site north of the main facility that held captured Soviet equipment, that this and not an underground base is what Lazar referred to, and that a named retired Area 51 security chief confirmed to him that Lazar appears on no manifest. Neither route depends on the other: one is documentary and civilian, the other is recollection by a former range engineer. Shared conclusions from a shared method are not corroboration; these two do not share a method.

entities.label: Element 115: the Lazar claim and moscovium
entities.sub: The claimed stable, machinable superheavy fuel of the S-4 propulsion account, set beside the real element 115 synthesised in 2003, assigned in 2015 and named moscovium in 2016
entities.desc: THIS NODE RECORDS A CLAIM AND A SEPARATE PHYSICAL FACT THAT HAPPEN TO SHARE A NUMBER, AND IT IS NOT AN ASSERTION THAT THEY ARE THE SAME THING. The claim is Lazar's: that a stable isotope of element 115 was the fuel of the reactor he says he worked on, that it could be machined into triangular wedges and stored, that 223 grams would run for twenty to thirty years, and that its nuclear binding field, which he calls gravity A and identifies with the strong nuclear force, extends past the perimeter of the atom so that it can be accessed and amplified. The fact is that element 115 was synthesised in a Dubna and Lawrence Livermore experiment published in Physical Review C on 2 February 2004, that the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry assigned discovery priority on 30 December 2015, and that the name moscovium was approved on 28 November 2016. The two do not meet. Lazar's claim is not that element 115 exists, which was never controversial and was predicted popular physics from 1969; it is that a stable isotope of it exists and that he handled half a pound of it. Nothing in the 2004 paper, the 2015 priority decision or the 2016 naming touches that. Equally, the hostile version, that he invented a number and got lucky, is also wrong: the island of stability near element 114 was in Scientific American in April 1969 and in undergraduate textbooks by 1970. The correct finding is neither prescient nor fabricated from nothing. It is available prior art, used. The board carries the claim as a claim and the element as an element, on one node so that the collision is visible in one place.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded B on a global pass (rank 363 of 1170, score 36). 4 connections, 1 of them custody/funding/programmatic, 1 official denial recorded against it. Axes C0/A0/D2.

claims.text: WHAT LAZAR CLAIMED, in his own 1991 narration. That stable superheavy elements exist 'in the 114 115 range which don't appear on a periodic chart' and that 'Beyond Element 115 the elements become unstable again and in fact element 116 decays in fractions of a second'. That 'the power source is a reactor which uses this element 115 as its fuel', with 115 'used as a Target and is bombarded with protons', a proton entering a 115 nucleus producing 'an atom of element 116 which remember decays instantly', radiating antimatter which is then annihilated for power. That 'only 223 grams of 115 which is just under half a pound can be utilized for a period of 20 to 30 years', that 'element 115's melting point is 1740 degrees Celsius', and that 'the element 115 is machined into triangles like this and is then inserted into the reactor'. Auto-generated captions at 18:42, 19:01, 23:31 and 25:34, so wording is approximate.
claims.source: The Lazar Tape and Excerpts from the Government Bible, Tri-Dot Productions, 1991, captions via YouTube video kc10m6HFbDE, https://archive.org/details/antigravity , opened 2026-09-18

claims.text: THE LOAD-BEARING PHYSICAL CLAIM, which is the one the physics objections attack: 'The most important attribute of these heavier stable elements is that the gravity a wave is so abundant that it actually extends past the perimeter of the atom', and separately 'gravity a is what is currently being labeled as the strong nuclear force in mainstream physics'.
claims.source: The Lazar Tape, Tri-Dot Productions, 1991, captions at 10:43 and 14:14 to 14:26, https://archive.org/details/antigravity , opened 2026-09-18

claims.text: WHAT THE CLAIM WOULD REQUIRE, STATED PRECISELY. An isotope of atomic number 115 with a half-life long enough to be produced in bulk, turned on a lathe into triangular wedges, stored, and consumed at a few grams a year across twenty to thirty years, which is a half-life of years at an absolute minimum and in practice geological. And a strong nuclear force whose range grows with nuclear mass until it reaches outside the atom. This is a stated inference from the claim's own terms and is marked Tier 3 as such.
claims.source: research/leads/verified-lazar-s4-2026-09-18.md section 3.1, reasoning from the 1991 tape's own content, 2026-09-18

claims.text: WHAT WAS ACTUALLY SYNTHESISED. Element 115 was first reported in Oganessian et al., 'Experiments on the synthesis of element 115 in the reaction 243Am(48Ca,xn)291-x115', Physical Review C volume 69, article 021601(R), published 2 February 2004, a Dubna and Lawrence Livermore collaboration. The abstract reads: 'With a beam dose of 4.3x10^18 248-MeV Ca48 projectiles, we observed three similar decay chains consisting of five consecutive alpha decays, all detected in time intervals of about 20s and terminated at a later time by a spontaneous fission with a high-energy release (total kinetic energy ~220MeV). At a higher bombarding energy of 253MeV, with an equal Ca48 beam dose, we registered a different decay chain of four consecutive alpha decays detected in a time interval of about 0.5s, also terminated by spontaneous fission.' The isotopes are 288 and 287, at cross sections of roughly 3 picobarn and 1 picobarn.
claims.source: Oganessian et al., Physical Review C 69, 021601(R), 2 February 2004, https://journals.aps.org/prc/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevC.69.021601 , opened 2026-09-18

claims.text: A PRECISION POINT USUALLY GOT WRONG IN BOTH DIRECTIONS. The International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry assigned discovery priority for element 115 on 30 December 2015 to 'the Dubna-Livermore-Oak Ridge collaborations', and the basis given is work 'starting in 2010, and subsequently confirmed in 2012 and 2013, have met the criteria for discovery'. The priority statement therefore rests on the 2010 to 2013 work and not on the 2003 experiment. The Joint Working Party report is Karol, Barber, Sherrill, Vardaci and Yamazaki, Pure and Applied Chemistry 88 (2016) 155.
claims.source: IUPAC, 'Discovery and assignment of elements with atomic numbers 113, 115, 117 and 118', 30 December 2015, https://iupac.org/discovery-and-assignment-of-elements-with-atomic-numbers-113-115-117-and-118/ , opened 2026-09-18

claims.text: The name moscovium, symbol Mc, was formally approved on 28 November 2016 and announced on 30 November 2016: 'Moscovium with the symbol Mc for element 115... proposed by the discoverers at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research, Dubna (Russia), Oak Ridge National Laboratory (USA), Vanderbilt University (USA) and Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (USA)', in recognition of the Moscow region.
claims.source: IUPAC, 'IUPAC announces the names of the elements 113, 115, 117 and 118', 30 November 2016, https://iupac.org/iupac-announces-the-names-of-the-elements-113-115-117-and-118/ , opened 2026-09-18

claims.text: THE COLLISION, STATED WITHOUT OVERSTATEMENT AND WITHOUT SOFTENING. Nothing about moscovium is stable, machinable, storable or available in gram quantities: it is produced one atom at a time at cross sections of about one picobarn and its decay chains run to completion within seconds. That is a direct contradiction of the claim's central requirement. It is NOT a refutation of the existence of element 115, which was never in dispute and was predicted long before 1989. Skeptic magazine's April 2026 treatment states the position correctly: IUPAC recognition 'does not validate Lazar's specific claims about a stable isotope or gravity propulsion'.
claims.source: Physical Review C 69, 021601(R), 2 February 2004; and Emile Kinley-Gauthier, 'The Strange Case of Bob Lazar', Skeptic, 23 April 2026, https://www.skeptic.com/article/the-strange-case-of-bob-lazar/ , opened 2026-09-18

claims.text: THE PRIOR ART, WHICH CUTS AGAINST THE HOSTILE READING AS WELL AS THE CREDULOUS ONE. The island of stability near element 114 was mainstream, popularised physics well before 1989. Glenn Seaborg's article in Scientific American of April 1969, pages 57 to 67, carried graphics of expected half-lives for superheavy elements, and a 1970 chemistry textbook described element 114, with 114 protons and 184 neutrons, as 'an island of stability in a sea of instability'. A reader of popular science in the 1970s and 1980s had 114 and 115 available. The Seaborg article itself was not opened and is cited here only as Mahood cites it.
claims.source: Tom Mahood, 'Element 115 tidbits', citing Seaborg, Scientific American, April 1969, pp 57-67, https://otherhand.org/home-page/area-51-and-other-strange-places/bluefire-main/bluefire/the-bob-lazar-corner/element-115-tidbits/ , opened 2026-09-18

claims.text: THE PHYSICS OBJECTIONS, NAMED AND DATED. Dr David L. Morgan, a particle physicist, in 'A Physicist's Critique' of 26 August 1996, revised April 2001, makes three. First, on identifying gravity with the strong force: 'The strong nuclear force has NOTHING TO DO WITH GRAVITY... The equations and coupling strengths which describe the two forces are totally different and unrelated.' Second, on the force reaching outside the atom: 'The nuclear force extends out to about the same distance away from a nucleus NO MATTER HOW MASSIVE THE NUCLEUS IS. This fact is fundamental to the science of nuclear physics.' Third, and the one that does not depend on any model of gravity, an energy-conservation objection: if the antimatter must be manufactured on board by bombarding 115 with protons, the energy required equals the energy released on annihilation, so 'If you have to MAKE your own antimatter on board, your system produces NO NET ENERGY AT ALL!!'
claims.source: Dr David L. Morgan, 'A Physicist's Critique', 26 August 1996, revised April 2001, https://otherhand.org/home-page/area-51-and-other-strange-places/bluefire-main/bluefire/the-bob-lazar-corner/a-physicists-critique/ , opened 2026-09-18

entities.sub: Forty-minute videotape written and produced by Gene Huff with Bob Lazar for Tri-Dot Productions, in which Lazar narrates the S-4, element 115 and gravity-wave account in his own words
entities.desc: This is the strongest artefact in the Lazar cluster and it is the one that was actually opened. It is a forty-minute videotape published by Tri-Dot Productions in 1991, created by Gene Huff and Bob Lazar, archived on the Internet Archive since 6 April 2007 and mirrored on YouTube, whose English auto-generated captions run to 38:39 and were read in full by this board's research pass on 18 September 2026. Its value is that it fixes the entire claim in datable, complete, citable form in the claimant's own voice, two years after the 1989 broadcasts and long before the modern podcast circuit. Every element-115 claim, every S-4 description and the Edward Teller anecdote carry timestamps in it. The board should anchor the cluster's claims here rather than on any later interview, because a 1991 videotape cannot be revised in response to later objections and a 2019 interview can. Two cautions belong on the node. The captions are machine-generated, so all quotation from it is approximate and is marked as such wherever it is used. And a videotape in which a claimant narrates his own claim is evidence of the claim, never of its content.

entities.desc: THIS NODE IS DELIBERATELY INCOMPLETE AND SAYS SO, on the precedent already set on this board by ronald-moultrie, scott-bray and brad-steiger, which were built the same way on 18 September 2026. The broadcasts are the custody point for the entire S-4 claim and the most consequential media artefact in the cluster: they are what put Area 51 into worldwide public consciousness. Not one of them was opened by this board's research pass. KLAS's own site at 8newsnow.com, which carries George Knapp's retrospectives on the story, returned HTTP 403 to three separate requests on 18 September 2026, and no 1989-dated listing, recording or transcript was reached by any other route. What the node therefore rests on is one contemporaneous newspaper line: the Las Vegas Review-Journal of 19 June 1990 recording that Lazar 'was the focal point for much of KLAS-TV, Channel 8 reporter George Knapp's award winning series'. That is a Tier 1 anchor for the existence and consequence of the broadcasts. The air dates are not: the May 1989 'Dennis' interview and the 10 or 11 November 1989 named interview are carried at Tier 3 from Tom Mahood's timeline. The node is built thin and honest rather than padded, and a later session should replace the Tier 3 dates with an opened artefact.

entities.label: Los Alamos Monitor, 27 June 1982, 'LA Man Joins The Jet Set - At 200 Miles An Hour'
entities.sub: Terry England's front-page story on Lazar's jet-powered Honda, which describes him in the newspaper's own voice as a physicist at the Los Alamos Meson Physics Facility
entities.desc: This is the strongest documentary thread in Bob Lazar's favour and the node must carry its qualification in the same breath, or it will misrepresent the record in the direction the credulous literature already pulls. The artefact is real: a front-page story with a byline, a date and page numbers, in a daily newspaper published in Los Alamos on Sunday 27 June 1982, about a jet-powered Honda Lazar had built, which describes him in the paper's own voice as 'a physicist at the Los Alamos Meson Physics Facility'. It was printed seven years before the UFO claim and cannot have been manufactured for it. What it is not is an employment record. The description is what Lazar told the reporter, and two independent strands of the opened record place him as a contract electronics technician instead: the Los Alamos telephone directory page that also lists his name states on its face that it covers Department of Energy employees and the outside contractor Kirk-Mayer, and an anonymised Los Alamos colleague interviewed on tape in 1996 said that Lazar 'was a contractor' under Kirk Mayer. The article also matters as a date peg for the Edward Teller anecdote, and there it creates a problem rather than solving one, because Lazar's own 1991 narration places the newspaper story and Teller's Los Alamos speech on the same day while the article's date is fixed at 27 June and Teller's lecture falls on the following day.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded C on a global pass (rank 1009 of 1170, score 15). 3 connections, 1 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C0/A0/D1.

claims.text: The artefact and its load-bearing sentence. Headline 'LA Man Joins The Jet Set - At 200 Miles An Hour', by Terry England, Monitor Staff Writer, Sunday 27 June 1982, Los Alamos Monitor, pages A1 and A8. The sentence, verbatim: 'To Lazar, a physicist at the Los Alamos Meson Physics Facility, the important thing is the jet engine.'
claims.source: Los Alamos Monitor, 27 June 1982, A1 and A8, reprinted at https://otherhand.org/home-page/area-51-and-other-strange-places/bluefire-main/bluefire/the-bob-lazar-corner/bobs-jetcar-article/ , opened 2026-09-18

claims.text: THE QUALIFICATION, WHICH TRAVELS WITH THE ARTICLE AND IS ROUTINELY DROPPED. The description is what Lazar told the reporter, not an employment record. Stanton Friedman, who obtained the Los Alamos telephone directory page carrying Lazar's name, records that the page 'clearly states that it includes employees of the DOE and outside contractor, Kirk Meyer'. A Los Alamos colleague interviewed on tape by Mark Farmer on 25 May 1996 said Lazar 'was a contractor' under 'Kirk Mayer' and that he 'claimed to be' a physicist. Tom Mahood's 2018 conclusion is that Lazar worked as an electronic technician for Kirk-Mayer and that the Monitor article misrepresented his position on the basis of what he told the reporter.

Friedman, 'The Bob Lazar Fraud', https://www.theblackvault.com/casefiles/the-bob-lazar-fraud-2/ ; Mark Farmer interview, 25 May 1996, https://otherhand.org/home-page/area-51-and-other-strange-places/bluefire-main/bluefire/the-bob-lazar-corner/los-alamos-interview/ ; Tom Mahood, 2018 retrospective, https://otherhand.org/home-page/area-51-and-other-strange-places/looking-at-the-bob-lazar-story-from-the-perspective-of-2018/ , all opened 2026-09-18

entities.label: Groom Lake, Nevada
entities.sub: Dry lakebed and USAF/CIA flight test facility, Lincoln County, Nevada; R-4808N; 83 mi NNW of Las Vegas
entities.desc: Groom Lake is a salt flat roughly 3.75 miles north-south by 3 miles east-west at about 4,409 feet elevation in the Groom Lake Valley of Lincoln County, Nevada, 83 miles north-northwest of Las Vegas and 25 miles south of Rachel. The flight test facility on its southwest shore sits inside Restricted Area 4808 North, the 'Groom box' - a 23-by-25-mile block of restricted airspace enclosing the original 6-by-10-mile rectangular withdrawal - and abuts Yucca Flat, where 739 of the 928 Nevada Test Site nuclear detonations occurred. Its acknowledgement history is the reason it belongs on this board as a case study in how the United States conceals a physical installation for decades and then concedes it in fragments. The CIA established the site in April 1955 for Project AQUATONE, the U-2; the first U-2 arrived on 24 July 1955. Project OXCART, the A-12, was established in August 1959, construction of the 8,500-foot runway began in September 1960, the first A-12 arrived 28 February 1962 and flew on 26 April 1962. HAVE BLUE, the Lockheed stealth demonstrator, first flew here in December 1977; the YF-117A first flew on 18 June 1981 with Lockheed test pilot Hal Farley; Northrop's TACIT BLUE first flew 5 February 1982 with Richard G. Thomas. Exploited foreign aircraft were flown here from the late 1960s under HAVE DOUGHNUT, HAVE DRILL, HAVE IDEA and HAVE GLIB. Against that record, the government's disclosure posture is instructive: no acknowledgement of any kind until 1995, when President Clinton issued a presidential determination exempting 'the Air Force's operating location near Groom Lake, Nevada' from environmental disclosure laws - a determination reissued annually since - which arose out of Kasza v. Browner and Frost v. Perry, the 1994 suits by contractors and by the widows of Walter Kasza and Robert Frost alleging exposure to chemicals burned in open pits, in which Rutgers biochemists found elevated dioxin, dibenzofuran and trichloroethylene in claimants' body fat. District Judge Philip Pro rejected the state secrets claim; the suits were dismissed for lack of evidence; the Ninth Circuit affirmed; the Supreme Court declined review. The Air Force acknowledged the site's existence in 1998. Only on 25 June 2013, answering a 2005 FOIA request by Jeffrey T. Richelson of the National Security Archive, did the CIA release the U-2 and OXCART history naming Area 51 and admitting specific activity there. That is fifty-eight years from establishment to specific acknowledgement, achieved by FOIA litigation rather than by voluntary disclosure - the template against which every current UAP disclosure claim should be measured. The cover story function matters too: Groom's own historians note the U-2's high-altitude operations generated a wave of civilian UFO reports in the late 1950s that the Air Force did not correct, meaning a real black programme was knowingly allowed to be absorbed into the UFO explanation space.

entities.label: Area 51 (Homey Airport / Groom Lake operating location)
entities.sub: Named USAF/CIA facility at Groom Lake; KXTA / Homey Airport; part of the Nevada Test and Training Range
entities.desc: 'Area 51' is the name attached to the operating facility on the southwest shore of Groom Lake, carried on aeronautical charts as Homey Airport (KXTA) and administratively part of the Nevada Test and Training Range. It is treated here as a distinct node from the lakebed itself because the name, rather than the geography, is what carries the evidentiary weight: it is the name the CIA finally used in the 25 June 2013 release, the name in the 1995 presidential environmental determination's careful circumlocution ('the Air Force's operating location near Groom Lake, Nevada'), and the name around which the entire modern reverse-engineering claim structure was built. In May 1989 Robert Lazar told KLAS-TV reporter George Knapp in Las Vegas that he had been contracted to work on craft of non-human origin at 'S-4', a facility he placed underground in the Papoose Range near Papoose Lake, about 8.5 miles south of the main base. Lazar's account is the origin point of the public reverse-engineering narrative and remains uncorroborated by any primary record; it is also the reason that, for thirty-seven years, the phrase 'Area 51' has functioned as a container that absorbs and discredits serious custody claims. The board's position is that the two things are separable. The documented reality of Area 51 - a facility whose existence the government refused to concede for four decades while flying AQUATONE, OXCART, HAVE BLUE, TACIT BLUE and exploited Soviet airframes out of it - is itself proof of the state's capacity and willingness to run large, physically substantial, contractor-staffed programmes entirely outside the acknowledged record. That capacity is the load-bearing claim. Lazar's specific allegations are not required to support it and are recorded separately at their own evidentiary grade.

entities.label: GAO accession 130581 - Controls Over Classified Documents for a Special Access Program at Lockheed Corporation
entities.sub: GAO testimony, 24 July 1986, House Energy and Commerce, Subcommittee on Oversight and Investigations
entities.desc:
On 24 July 1986 the General Accounting Office told a congressional subcommittee that a prime contractor's special-access document control had failed, and in the same statement explained that the body which would ordinarily have inspected it had been excluded from doing so since 1965. That conjunction is this board's structural argument, documented and dated. The cover page reads: 'STATEMENT OF MARTIN M FERBER, ASSOCIATE DIRECTOR, NATIONAL SECURITY AND INTERNATIONAL AFFAIRS DIVISION, BEFORE THE SUBCOMMITTEE ON OVERSIGHT AND INVESTIGATIONS, HOUSE COMMITTEE ON ENERGY AND COMMERCE, ON CONTROLS OVER CLASSIFIED DOCUMENTS FOR A SPECIAL ACCESS PROGRAM AT LOCKHEED CORPORATION'. The venue is worth noting: not a defence committee.

The numbers are exact and the popular version of them is wrong. Lockheed reported 1,460 discrepancies in an inventory of about 40,000 secret and top-secret items. As of 19 July 1986 it had completed investigation on 235 of them; 224 were 'later accounted for' and 11 were unresolved -- 7 inadvertently destroyed and 4 not located. The 46 destroyed and the 17 transferred out of the company sit inside the 224 that were accounted for, not outside them. The genuinely unaccounted-for total is 11.

GAO explains the carve-out in its own words: special access contracts are 'carved out of the Defense Investigative Service's periodic inspection program', a 1965 decision, and by 1983 GAO estimated 'there probably were several thousand such contracts'. Its closing sentence is the finding: 'it appears inconsistent to us to establish a special access program because of security considerations and then afford it less document protection than normal classified programs.' The companion letter report to the Secretary of Defense, GAO/NSIAD-86-191 of 7 August 1986, goes further and names the plant the testimony would not.

entities.label: Defense Investigative Service
entities.sub: DoD industrial security inspectorate; excluded from special access programs by a 1965 decision
entities.desc:
The Defense Investigative Service is the body whose absence the board keeps having to explain. It conducted the periodic industrial security inspections of cleared contractor facilities -- including, GAO says in terms, other contracts at Lockheed -- and it was excluded from special access programs by a Department of Defense decision in 1965. GAO's own vocabulary preserves the mechanism: special access contracts are called carve-out contracts 'because they are carved out of the Defense Investigative Service's periodic inspection program'.

Two GAO findings bracket what that exclusion cost. In February 1983, GAO/GGD-83-43 recommended improvements in DoD oversight of carve-out contracts and DoD refused, on stated grounds including that 'access by Service inspectors would proliferate access beyond the minimum number of persons necessary'. In August 1986, after the Lockheed document-control failure, GAO told the Secretary of Defense that the failure 'may not have occurred if the Defense Investigative Service had been permitted to conduct semiannual inspections of the contract, as it does with other contracts at Lockheed.' The board carries DIS because the argument it makes about custody is not that oversight failed but that oversight was structurally absent, and this is the office that was absent from it.

entities.label: 1127th USAF Field Activities Group
entities.sub: Air Force intelligence unit running Project BLUE FLY and Project MOON DUST under its Foreign Materiel Program
entities.desc:
This is the custody chain stated by the unit that ran it, about itself, in a document classified SECRET at the time. The 1127th USAF Field Activities Group's own semiannual history for 1 January to 30 June 1967, document number AFNIABA 014-67, prepared by Anita H. Beasey and approved by Colonel Rudolph C. Koller, Jr., lists on its contents page, under FOREIGN MATERIEL PROGRAM: 'Project BLUE FLY' (p.29), 'MIG-17 Exploitation' (p.29), 'Project MOON DUST' (p.30). The board has carried the Moon Dust and Blue Fly relationship as an inference; here it is an organisational fact, printed in a table of contents.

The BLUE FLY entry describes the mechanism end to end. After the air battle of 7 April 1967, three MIG-21s downed over Jordan were exploited by Detachment 3 of the Foreign Technology Division, and the Staff Operations Branch 'coordinated requirements necessary to deploy the FTD exploitation personnel and to airlift personnel and parts from site of acquisition to Wright-Patterson AFB. The take consisted of approximately three tons of aircraft parts and armament.' The Joint Chiefs had approved a one-year extension of Force/Activity Designator I priority for short-notice BLUE FLY airlift. That is recovery, transport priority and a named terminus, in one paragraph.

The MOON DUST entry, and the companion history of the Assistant Chief of Staff, Intelligence for July to December 1967, carry the figures usually quoted as recoveries. They are not recoveries. Both documents say the unit was NOTIFIED by SPADATS of DEORBITS -- 37 Soviet objects in the first half of 1967, and 49 Soviet plus 17 US objects in the second. Deorbit notification is the tasking trigger; recovery is a separate act neither document counts.

entities.label: Research and Development Board
entities.sub: Statutory coordinating body for defence research, 26 July 1947 to 30 June 1953
entities.desc:
The Research and Development Board sat at the top of the American defence research structure for the exact six years in which the legacy programme is alleged to have been established, and its statutory life is fully documented. The National Archives' finding aid for Record Group 330 states it was 'Established as the Research and Development Board by the National Security Act of 1947 (61 Stat. 495), July 26, 1947. Abolished by Reorganization Plan No. 6 of 1953, effective June 30, 1953, and superseded by Office of the Assistant Secretary of Defense (Research and Development).' The same aid lists its surviving records, including 'Minutes of meetings of the Executive Council, 1946-50' and 'Records of the Committee on Technical Information, 1946-53'.

Truman's published letter to Vannevar Bush of 25 September 1947 gives the predecessor relationship in the President's own words: 'I am happy to know that you are willing to continue in the public service as Chairman of the Research and Development Board created by the National Security Act of 1947 ... Since V-J Day you have continued to render valuable service as chairman of the Joint Research and Development Board set up by the Secretaries of War and Navy.' The RDB is a 1947 statutory body and its predecessor the JRDB is a post-V-J Day creation of the two service secretaries -- so no earlier than September 1945.

What this node does NOT carry is the Sarbacher consultancy. It is the destination every MJ-12 and Wilbert Smith thread points at, and no primary record for it was found. It is carried at Tier 3 on the Sarbacher node, where it belongs, and no edge is drawn from here.

entities.label: RIAS, Inc. (Research Institute for Advanced Studies)
entities.sub: The Glenn L. Martin Company's industrial research institute, Baltimore; gravitation was explicitly its subject
entities.desc:
RIAS is the cleanest documented instance on this board of an aerospace prime setting up a research institute to study gravitation, and the documentation is a participants list and a dated letter rather than an allegation. The 1957 Chapel Hill conference on the role of gravitation in physics prints two of its staff among the attendees -- 'Witten, L. | RIAS, Inc., Baltimore' and 'Bass, R.W. | RIAS , Inc., Baltimore' -- and the institutional style there is corporate: RIAS, Inc., a company in Baltimore, in a room otherwise full of universities.

Its purpose is stated by the executive who proposed it. George S. Trimble wrote to Bryce DeWitt on 10 June 1955 that 'our industry was vitally concerned with gravity' and that 'At least one category of the things one must study, when he desires to bring space flight to reality, is the laws of nature surrounding the force of gravity', describing the proposed body as an 'industrial version of the Institute for Advanced Study'. The conference report that names RIAS is itself WADC Technical Report 57-216, produced under a funding agreement with the Wright Air Development Center.

Grade it honestly. This is a corporate research institute that studied gravitation, and nothing read shows it producing gravity-control results -- the Chapel Hill participants recorded their own concern about 'the absolute necessity to avoid identification with so-called anti-gravity research', and Louis Witten's documented output is classical general relativity. Its value here is the chain and the date, not a result.

entities.label: Aurora (FY1986-FY1987 procurement line)

Aurora belongs on this board as budget mechanics and nothing else. The Washington Post of 8 February 1985, preserved in the CIA's reading room as CIA-RDP90-00965R000807470050-4, reports: 'The Pentagon has said in a public document that it wants $2.3 billion for an Air Force plane called Aurora but responded yesterday that the plane -- if it really is a plane -- is classified.' The denial is in the same paragraph: 'Reminded that Aurora has been put in the public domain by the Pentagon, an Air Force spokesman said his orders still were to say only: It's a classified program.' This is five years before the Aviation Week story that usually gets the credit. No craft claim and no recovery claim attaches here: the article's own sources point at Stealth.

This is the public, distribution-unlimited Department of Defense document that defines the term 'fastwalker' in its own words, and it is on this board because the term reaches the popular literature stripped of that definition. Section 1.1 gives the definition: 'Satellite based sensors looking down at the Earth's surface occasionally observe reflected light from an object passing through the image which is moving too fast relative to the background of the image to be located within the atmosphere. The research conducted by Wong is no longer available.' Bibliography entry 9 is 'OSEDACZ, R. Orbit determination of sunlight illuminated objects detected by overhead platforms (M. S. Thesis). 1989.' claims.text: The federal literature on nitinol, one report of it written by Battelle itself, does not support a Battelle 1948-49 lineage for the alloy. NASA SP-5110, prepared for NASA by Battelle Memorial Institute in 1972, opens: 'Some 10 years ago, Buehler and Wiley of the U.S. Naval Ordnance Laboratory developed a series of engineering alloys that possess a unique mechanical (shape) memory. The generic name of the series of alloys is 55-Nitinol, where Nitinol stands for Nickel Titanium Naval Ordnance Laboratory.' The earliest Naval Ordnance Laboratory nitinol report cited anywhere in its reference list is NOLTR 61-75 of 3 August 1961; US Patent 3,174,851 was filed on 1 December 1961; and NASA CR-1433 of September 1969 records Battelle's own role as a subcontractor to Goodyear Aerospace which 'processed the basic Nitinol rod'. entities.label: Atomic Energy Commission
entities.sub: Civilian atomic authority, 1946-1974; statutory custodian of fissionable material and atomic weapons
entities.desc: The Atomic Energy Commission was created by the Atomic Energy Act of 1946 and took statutory title to everything the Manhattan Engineer District had held: all fissionable material, all atomic weapons and parts, and all processes and technical information behind them. It ran the born-secret information regime, under which data in defined categories is classified by operation of statute and declassified only by an affirmative act of the Commission, and it gated every contractor employee's access behind an FBI investigation and a Commission determination. Its Division of Military Application was established in the founding statute and directed by a serving officer of the armed forces. The Energy Reorganization Act of 1974 abolished it and vested its functions in ERDA, from which they passed to the Department of Energy. Four guests across four Michels lead maps place the Commission at a custody point for recovered material; nothing in either statute or in the National Archives record group description says anything about recovered material, and the node carries the statute rather than the testimony.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded A on a global pass (rank 123 of 1170, score 56). 10 connections, 3 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C2/A3/D1.

claims.text: The Commission gains its first named chairman on this board. The CIA's own declassified chronology records under January 1961: '16 JAN. Dr. Glenn T. Seaborg named AEC chairman, succeeding John A. McCone (confirmed by Senate 24 Feb).' McCone went from the Commission to the Directorship of Central Intelligence, and two years later Seaborg was writing to him there on Commission letterhead. claims.text: The Commission took statutory custody of the Manhattan Engineer District's holdings. entities.label: Bluegill Triple Prime
entities.sub: FISHBOWL high-altitude shot, Operation DOMINIC I, Johnston Island, 25 October 1962
entities.desc: Bluegill Triple Prime was the fourth attempt to detonate the BLUEGILL device above Johnston Island, and the first that worked. Three earlier attempts failed: the 2 June 1962 launch was destroyed in flight after tracking was lost, BLUEGILL Prime burned on the pad, and BLUEGILL Double Prime failed on 15 October. The successful shot is recorded by the Defense Nuclear Agency at 25 October 1962, 2359 local, submegaton, tens of kilometres over Johnston Island, with 22 Air Force aircraft arrayed and nine Navy ships positioned to gather data. Four guests across four Michels lead maps attach a recovery story to it, and the record contradicts them in three places at once. The date is 25 October in the report's narrative and in its own Table 1, not 26 October, which is the GMT rendering of the same instant. DNA 6039F, cited for the shot in the candidates row, is Operation ARGUS 1958 and not the FISHBOWL report at all. And the report contains no unidentified object, no recovery, no debris, no RC-135 and no Cobra Ball: what it does carry is the call sign KETTLE, assigned to three KC-135 photographic aircraft, which is the documented origin of the Kettle film names the corpus uses. The node exists to hold the documented event so that the testimony has something dated to hang from.

entities.label: Invention Secrecy Act of 1951 (Pub. L. 82-256, 66 Stat. 3), codified at 35 U.S.C. 181-188
entities.sub: Act of 1 February 1952, ch. 4; renumbered by the Patent Act of 19 July 1952, ch. 950, 66 Stat. 805
entities.desc: The statute that lets the United States order an invention kept secret and withhold the patent, including an invention the government does not own and did not fund. It is the instrument the board's PATENTS tab is arguing around, and until now the board named it once in prose and carried no node for it. Its short title, printed in the margin of the Statutes at Large, is the Invention Secrecy Act of 1951, although the Act was approved on 1 February 1952; the familiar 35 U.S.C. 181-188 numbering comes from a different statute five months later, the Patent Act of 19 July 1952. Section 181's second paragraph routes a privately owned application to the Atomic Energy Commission and the Secretary of Defense for inspection before any order issues, which is the point at which the patent record and the weapons establishment touch. Orders run one year and renew annually without limit; the Patent and Trademark Office reported 6,543 in force at the end of fiscal 2025.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded B on a global pass (rank 541 of 1170, score 30). 4 connections, 1 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C0/A2/D1.

claims.text: The Act's own short title and date: the Statutes at Large prints the marginal note 'Invention Secrecy Act of 1951.' beside section 1 of 'Public Law 256', 'CHAPTER 4', an Act 'To provide for the withholding of certain patents that might be detrimental to the national security, and for other purposes', approved 'February 1, 1952 [H.R.4687]'.
claims.source: 66 Stat. 3, Statutes at Large volume 66, govinfo, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-66/pdf/STATUTE-66-Pg3.pdf

claims.text: The current codification descends from that Act by way of a second one. The Historical and Revision Notes to 35 U.S.C. 181 read: 'Based on Title 35, U.S.C., 1946 ed., 151 (Feb. 1, 1952, ch. 4, 1, 66 Stat. 3, 4).' The section's source credit is 'July 19, 1952, ch. 950, 66 Stat. 805'.

claims.text: The Act reaches inventions the government does not own. Section 181 second paragraph: where the Commissioner of Patents believes disclosure of an invention 'in which the Government does not have a property interest' might be detrimental to the national security, 'he shall make the application for patent in which such invention is disclosed available for inspection to the Atomic Energy Commission, the Secretary of Defense, and the chief officer of any other department or agency of the Government designated by the President as a defense agency of the United States.'
claims.source: 35 U.S.C. 181, Office of the Law Revision Counsel, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title35-section181&num=0&edition=prelim

claims.text: An order is indefinite by renewal, and wartime orders outlast the war. Section 181: 'An invention shall not be ordered kept secret and the publication of the application or the grant of a patent withheld for a period of more than one year', renewable annually on an affirmative determination that 'the national interest continues so to require'; an order in effect during a time when the United States is at war 'shall remain in effect for the duration of hostilities and one year following cessation of hostilities.'

entities.label: DoD Nuclear Weapon Personnel Reliability Program (DoD Directive 5210.42)
entities.sub: DoDD 5210.42, 25 May 1993, ASD(C3I); reissues the directive of 6 December 1985
entities.desc: The published rule that decides whether a person on a nuclear weapons site keeps his access, and the reason the board can treat 'they were afraid to report' as something other than an anecdote. The directive opened here is the 25 May 1993 edition, distribution unlimited, which reissues an edition of 6 December 1985; the current manual could not be reached from this environment and nothing here should be read as describing it. Its force for this board is not what it says about UFOs, which is nothing, but what it says about who may find a person unreliable and on what evidence: a non-medical certifying official, with access to the individual's medical record without his consent, may act on 'aberrant behavior' or on mood described as unusual happiness, sadness or agitation. Every witness at a nuclear site whose testimony this board carries was subject to a rule of that shape. Two things the corpus attaches to the programme are not in the directive: the duty to report an over-the-counter analgesic, and the figure 167, which is Robert Hastings's count of nuclear-base witnesses rather than a count of PRP personnel.

claims.text: Scope and purpose: the directive applies to 'DoD military and civilian personnel and contractor employees assigned to PRP positions or in training leading to assignment to PRP positions', and exists to 'ensure the highest possible standards of individual reliability in personnel performing duties associated with nuclear weapons and critical components.'

claims.text: Disqualification reaches demeanour, not only conduct. entities.label: Manned Orbiting Laboratory and the DORIAN / KH-10 reconnaissance payload
entities.sub: USAF programme with an NRO black mission; announced December 1963, cancelled 10 June 1969, declassified October 2015
entities.desc: A fully documented case of a real programme carrying a second, classified programme inside it, closed by the government and then released by the agency that ran it. Publicly MOL was an Air Force laboratory to determine the military usefulness of men in space; inside it sat DORIAN, an NRO reconnaissance system handled in the BYEMAN control system and designated KH-10 in 1969. Seventeen officers were astronaut-trained between 1965 and 1969, on a modified Gemini-B with a hatch through the heat shield, for polar launches from Vandenberg on the Titan-IIIM. None of them flew. The programme was cancelled on 10 June 1969 with 13,187 cleared contractor personnel on it, and the NRO declassified almost the entire DORIAN collection in October 2015. It is the strongest available answer to a question this board is repeatedly asked, which is what a secret space programme actually looks like on the record. Two opened sources disagree on one number and the disagreement is recorded rather than resolved: the NRO volume gives a 70-inch aperture and NASA gives a 72-inch diameter primary mirror.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded B on a global pass (rank 238 of 1170, score 43). 5 connections, 2 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C1/A3/D2.

claims.text: The cover and the mission are described by the agency itself. The NRO's volume says MOL was 'open "white" world, but maintained a highly-classified "black" mission', with the reconnaissance mission 'codenamed Dorian in the BYEMAN security system', and its foreword calls Dorian 'a deeply classified program managed by the then darkly hidden agency of the Intelligence Community, the National Reconnaissance Office'.
claims.source: Spies in Space: Reflections on National Reconnaissance and the Manned Orbiting Laboratory, NRO Center for the Study of National Reconnaissance, May 2019, foreword and chapter 3, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GOVPUB-D-PURL-gpo123652/pdf/GOVPUB-D-PURL-gpo123652.pdf

claims.text: The declassification is dated and quantified in the NRO's own words: on 22 October 2015 the CSNR held a panel at the National Museum of the United States Air Force 'on the occasion of the NRO declassifying almost its entire collection of records on the Dorian program. There were over 850 documents with some 22,000 pages and 280 photographs.'
claims.source: Spies in Space, NRO CSNR, May 2019, foreword, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GOVPUB-D-PURL-gpo123652/pdf/GOVPUB-D-PURL-gpo123652.pdf

claims.text: Seventeen officers were trained and none flew: 'Between 1965 and 1969, quietly and without fanfare, 17 non-NASA individuals were astronaut-trained in order to meet the reconnaissance needs of the United States.' The camera is dated and designated: 'In 1969, the Dorian camera system was designated KH-10 within the Talent-Keyhole community.'
claims.source: Spies in Space, NRO CSNR, May 2019, introduction and chapter 3, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GOVPUB-D-PURL-gpo123652/pdf/GOVPUB-D-PURL-gpo123652.pdf

claims.text: The scale of the clearance at termination: 'On 10 June 1969, 13,187 contractor personnel were cleared on MOL and faced reassignment.'
claims.source: Spies in Space, NRO CSNR, May 2019, chapter 4, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GOVPUB-D-PURL-gpo123652/pdf/GOVPUB-D-PURL-gpo123652.pdf
