entities.label: Defense Support Program (DSP) missile early warning satellites
entities.sub: USAF and later US Space Force strategic surveillance constellation; programme commenced 1967, first operational satellite 1971
entities.desc: The infrared early-warning constellation that the board's fastwalker material comes off, and which the board did not carry. GAO describes DSP as a strategic surveillance and warning satellite system with an infrared capability to detect ballistic missile launches, feeding the integrated tactical warning and attack assessment mission, begun in 1967 with the first operational satellite in 1971 and now being replaced by SBIRS-High. Its place here is documentary rather than anomalous: the board already carries the AFIT thesis that defines 'fastwalker' as ordinary space-surveillance vocabulary and cites a 1972-onward observation database drawn from ballistic missile early warning satellites in geosynchronous orbit, which is this constellation. What the popular literature adds, that DSP is the system that sees UFOs, is not stated by any government document opened for this node; that equation is The Black Vault's own gloss. What the record does carry is a refusal: USNORTHCOM found two responsive documents on the fastwalker and slowwalker designations in 2013, withheld both, and declined to search NORAD's holdings at all on the ground that NORAD is a bi-national organisation outside FOIA.

entities.label: TR-AC-47, Joint ATIC-WADC Report on Project Silver Bug, 15 February 1955
entities.sub: Air Technical Intelligence Center, Wright-Patterson AFB; Project No. 9961; declassified 29 March 1995
entities.desc: A joint report of the Air Technical Intelligence Center and the Wright Air Development Center on a Canadian contractor's proposal for a supersonic circular-planform aircraft with vertical take-off. It is the cleanest documented instance on this board of the Air Force funding a disc-shaped aircraft at Wright-Patterson, and its own stated purpose is to stop the intelligence community from believing the exaggerated accounts already circulating about it. It is the control case any Wright-Patterson recovery claim has to clear, and it is cited in the Michels corpus for the opposite of what it says: the transcript frames the project as a funnel and cover for deeper theoretical physics, while the report exists 'to correct the distorted picture presented in previous releases, both classified and unclassified' and says the project 'should in no way be associated with any science fiction or "Flying Saucer" stories because of its external appearance'. John Frost is named nowhere in it, the report names no individual designer at all, and the contractor is A. V. Roe, Canada, Limited, of the Hawker-Siddley Group, not the British Aircraft Corporation, which did not exist in 1955.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded B on a global pass (rank 187 of 1170, score 47). 4 connections, 1 of them custody/funding/programmatic, 1 official denial recorded against it. Axes C2/A1/D2.

claims.text: The title page reads 'TR-AC-47 / (Unclassified) / JOINT ATIC-WADC REPORT ON / PROJECT SILVER BUG / PROJECT NO. 9961 / 15 FEBRUARY 1955', issued by the 'AIR TECHNICAL INTELLIGENCE CENTER, WRIGHT-PATTERSON AIR FORCE BASE, OHIO', and carries a handwritten declassification stamp reading 'Declassified 29 MAR 95', 'Auth: DoD 5200.1.R', 'SAF/AAZD'.

entities.label: AFSWC TR-59-39 Vol I, A Study of Lunar Research Flights, 19 June 1959
entities.sub: Air Force Special Weapons Center, Kirtland AFB; L. Reiffel, Armour Research Foundation; contributor C. E. Sagan; DDC AD 425380

Its distribution list also documents who in the nuclear weapons complex received it. Two corrections the record forces on the corpus: the report is dated 19 June 1959, not 1958 and not May 1959, and the string A119 appears nowhere in it. C. E. entities.label: Senate Select Committee to Study Governmental Operations with Respect to Intelligence Activities (Church Committee)
entities.sub: Established by S. Res. 21, 27 January 1975; final report S. Rept. 94-755, six books, 1976
entities.desc: The only thorough congressional investigation ever made of the United States intelligence system, and the benchmark this board's oversight view has lacked. Eleven senators, a hundred staff, more than eight hundred interviews and over a hundred and ten thousand pages of documents. It is carried here for what its own final report concedes rather than for what it achieved: that it never once examined an agency's files on its own, that the CIA and other executive agencies limited its access to the record, and that three chapters of its published findings, including the chapter on budgetary oversight, were deleted at the request of the agencies it was investigating. Two Michels-corpus speakers who agree on almost nothing else, Michael Shellenberger and Mick West, each name the committee as the template for a successful congressional penetration of a compartmented programme. The committee's own report says the penetration was mediated throughout, and that is the finding.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded B on a global pass (rank 212 of 1170, score 45). 7 connections, 0 of them custody/funding/programmatic, 1 official denial recorded against it. Axes C2/A1/D3.

claims.text: 'On January 27, 1975, Senate Resolution 21 established a select committee "to conduct an investigation and study of governmental operations with respect to intelligence activities and of the extent, if any, to which illegal, improper, or unethical activities were engaged in by any agency of the Federal Government."' Book I of the final report, Senate Report 94-755, was filed on 'APRIL 26 (legislative day, APRIL 14), 1976'.
claims.source: S. Rept. 94-755, Book I, title page and Part I section A, https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/sites-default-files-94755-i.pdf

claims.text: The committee's own account of the obstacles it met: 'Despite its legal Senate mandate, and the issuance of subpoenas, in no instance has the Committee been able to examine the agencies' files on its own. In all the agencies, whether CIA, FBI, NSA, INR, DIA, or the NSC, documents and evidence have been presented through the filter of the agency itself.' It adds that 'the Central Intelligence Agency and other agencies of the executive branch have limited the Committee's access to the full record.'
claims.source: S. Rept. 94-755, Book I, Part I section C, 'The Focus and Scope of the Committee's Inquiry and Obstacles Encountered', https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/sites-default-files-94755-i.pdf

claims.text: The report's own publication note records that it 'has been reviewed and declassified by the appropriate executive agencies' and that 'At the request of the agencies, the Committee deleted three chapters from this report: "Cover," "Espionage," and "Budgetary Oversight."' Two sections of the covert-action chapter and one section of the State Department chapter were also deleted at agency request.
claims.source: S. Rept. 94-755, Book I, NOTE following the Letter of Transmittal, https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/sites-default-files-94755-i.pdf

claims.text: The committee was chaired by Frank Church of Idaho with John G. Tower of Texas as Vice Chairman, and had eleven members, six from the majority and five from the minority. 'The Committee staff of 100, including 60 professionals, has assisted the 11 members of the Committee in this indepth inquiry which involved more than 800 interviews, over 250 executive hearings, and documentation in excess of 110,000 pages.'

claims.text: Among its findings: 'The Committee finds that Congress has failed to provide the necessary statutory guidelines to ensure that intelligence agencies carry out their missions in accord with constitutional processes. entities.label: Atomic Energy Act of 1946 (McMahon Act)
entities.sub: Public Law 79-585, 60 Stat. 755, 1 August 1946; the origin of born-secret classification
entities.desc: The Atomic Energy Act of 1946 is where classification by category enters United States law. It defines restricted data as an entire class of fact rather than as a set of documents somebody decided to mark, makes publication conditional on an affirmative determination by the Atomic Energy Commission, and backs the rule with a capital penalty that reaches concealment and destruction as well as disclosure. It gates every contractor employee's access behind an FBI investigation and a Commission finding, gives the FBI exclusive jurisdiction over violations, and gives the War and Navy Departments a standing consultative claim over the control of weapons information through the Military Liaison Committee, with an appeal that ends at the President. The board argues the 1954 Act's Restricted Data regime is the statutory shield; this is the instrument that built it, a year before the programme's own 1947 start. The popular name McMahon Act appears in no federal record opened for this node; what is documented is Brien McMahon's chairmanship of the Senate Special Committee on Atomic Energy and of the Joint Committee on Atomic Energy in the 79th Congress.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded B on a global pass (rank 213 of 1170, score 45). 5 connections, 1 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C2/A3/D1.

claims.text: The Act's own short title is narrow: 'This Act may be cited as the "Atomic Energy Act of 1946".' The chapter head gives it as Chapter 724, S. 1717, Public Law 585, 79th Congress, 'AN ACT For the development and control of atomic energy', approved August 1, 1946. The popular name 'McMahon Act' appears nowhere in the statute.
claims.source: Atomic Energy Act of 1946, Public Law 79-585, 60 Stat. 755, sec. 21 and chapter head, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-60/pdf/STATUTE-60-Pg755.pdf

claims.text: Classification runs by category, and publication is the exception. Section 10(b)(1): restricted data 'means all data concerning the manufacture or utilization of atomic weapons, the production of fissionable material, or the use of fissionable material in the production of power, but shall not include any data which the Commission from time to time determines may be published without adversely affecting the common defense and security.' Section 10(a) makes it 'the policy of the Commission to control the dissemination of restricted data in such a manner as to assure the common defense and security.'
claims.source: Atomic Energy Act of 1946, sec. 10(a) and 10(b)(1), https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-60/pdf/STATUTE-60-Pg755.pdf

claims.text: The penalty reaches concealment and destruction, not only disclosure, and it is capital. Section 10(b)(4) provides that whoever 'removes, conceals, tampers with, alters, mutilates, or destroys' a document incorporating restricted data with intent to injure the United States 'shall be punished by death or imprisonment for life (but the penalty of death or imprisonment for life may be imposed only upon recommendation of the jury and only in cases where the offense was committed with intent to injure the United States); or by a fine of not more than $20,000 or imprisonment for not more than twenty years, or both.'
claims.source: Atomic Energy Act of 1946, sec. 10(b)(4), and identically at 10(b)(2)(A) and 10(b)(3), https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-60/pdf/STATUTE-60-Pg755.pdf

claims.text: The FBI is both the gate and the investigator. Section 10(b)(5)(B)(i) bars any arrangement, contract or licence unless the contractor 'agrees in writing not to permit any individual to have access to restricted data until the Federal Bureau of Investigation shall have made an investigation and report to the Commission on the character, associations, and loyalty of such individual.' Section 10(b)(5)(C): 'All violations of this Act shall be investigated by the Federal Bureau of Investigation of the Department of Justice.'
claims.source: Atomic Energy Act of 1946, sec. 10(b)(5)(B)(i) and 10(b)(5)(C), https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-60/pdf/STATUTE-60-Pg755.pdf

claims.text: The military keeps a standing claim over the control of weapons information, with an appeal that ends at the President. Section 2(c) directs that the Commission 'shall advise and consult with the Committee on all atomic energy matters which the Committee deems to relate to military applications, including the development, manufacture, use, and storage of bombs, the allocation of fissionable material for military research, and the control of information relating to the manufacture or utilization of atomic weapons', and provides that where either Secretary concurs in a Military Liaison Committee objection he 'may refer the matter to the President, whose decision shall be final.'
claims.source: Atomic Energy Act of 1946, sec. 2(c), https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-60/pdf/STATUTE-60-Pg755.pdf

claims.text: Where McMahon actually is in the record: the 1962 Joint Committee print lists under 'MEMBERSHIP OF THE JOINT COMMITTEE, 1945-61' the 'SENATE SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON ATOMIC ENERGY, Seventy-ninth Congress (1945-46), BRIEN McMAHON, Connecticut, Chairman', and then the 'JOINT COMMITTEE ON ATOMIC ENERGY, Seventy-ninth Congress (1946), BRIEN McMAHON, Connecticut, Chairman'. None of the federal documents opened for this node calls the Act the McMahon Act.

entities.label: National Investigations Committee on Aerial Phenomena (NICAP)
entities.sub: Civilian UFO body incorporated in the District of Columbia, 1956; 1536 Connecticut Avenue NW
entities.desc: NICAP is the civilian organisation the board narrates constantly and has never named as an entity. It was forming at 1536 Connecticut Avenue NW in October 1956 under Thomas Townsend Brown, who told a Scripps-Howard reporter he was executive vice chairman pro tempore and that the group would elect its nine-man board of governors on 1 November; the clipping is in the FBI's own file on the organisation. By 1964 it was directed by Maj. Donald E. Keyhoe with Richard H. Hall as acting director and editor, carried a former Director of Central Intelligence and a former Blue Book headquarters monitor on its board, and published The UFO Evidence, which it sent to every Member of Congress and which the CIA filed. It is the exact official-and-civilian boundary the board argues about: a private body, staffed at the top by people who had held the government's own positions, campaigning for the hearings the government did not hold. The District of Columbia corporate register itself was not opened, so the incorporation rests on NICAP's own statement of it.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded B on a global pass (rank 325 of 1170, score 38). 7 connections, 1 of them custody/funding/programmatic, 1 official denial recorded against it. Axes C1/A1/D1.

claims.text: NICAP states its own legal form and year: 'NICAP is a non-profit organization incorporated in the District of Columbia (1956).' The same paragraph gives its purpose as 'scientific investigation and research of reported unidentified flying objects, and encouragement of full reporting to the public by responsible authorities of all information which the government has accumulated on this subject.'
claims.source: The UFO Evidence, National Investigations Committee on Aerial Phenomena, Washington DC, May 1964, Richard H. Hall ed., section 'NICAP and its Policies', in the CIA's filed copy CIA-RDP81R00560R000100010001-0, https://archive.org/details/cia-readingroom-document-cia-rdp81r00560r000100010001-0

claims.text: Thomas Townsend Brown ran the organisation at its formation. A Washington Daily News report of Tuesday 23 October 1956, filed in the FBI's NICAP file: 'The brass plate at 1536 Connecticut-av nw reads "National Investigations Committee on Aerial Phenomena." Inside they refer to it as Project Skylight. T. Townsend Brown of Leesburg, Va., who runs it, identified himself as executive vice chairman pro tempore. He formerly was a consulting physicist for the Clevite-Brush Electronics Co. of Cleveland, O.' The same report says the committee 'is just now forming. On Nov. 1 it meets to elect a nine-man board of governors.'
claims.source: Jim G. Lucas, 'Project Skylight: New Group Setting Sights on Saucers', The Washington Daily News, 23 October 1956, in FBI file 100-35992 on the National Investigations Committee on Aerial Phenomena, part 1, https://archive.org/details/NICAP

claims.text: A former Director of Central Intelligence sat on its board and joined its campaign for hearings. The 1964 volume: 'Vice Admiral R. H. Hillenkoetter joined with a majority of the NICAP Board in urging a Congressional investigation of the UFO problem.'

claims.text: The volume was addressed to Congress and says so: 'Copies of this report have been sent to all Members of Congress.' Former Air Force Headquarters Monitor of AF Project Blue Book UFO investigation, prepared analyses of UFO data for AF, liaison officer between Dayton project and Pentagon.'

entities.label: National Security Council
entities.sub: Statutory body, 1947; the approving authority for covert action and the issuer of the NSC directive series
entities.desc: The council created by section 101 of the National Security Act of 1947 to advise the President on the integration of domestic, foreign and military policy. It matters to this board as the body that issued NSC 10/2, NSC 5412 and the directive series that governs covert action, and as the place where classification oversight was lodged by EO 11652.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded C on a global pass (rank 667 of 1170, score 26). 6 connections, 0 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C0/A2/D1.

claims.text: The statutory purpose has not changed since 1947. 50 U.S.C. 3021(b)(1) still states the Council's function as being 'to advise the President with respect to the integration of domestic, foreign, and military policies relating to the national security'.
claims.source: 50 U.S.C. 3021(b)(1), https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title50-section3021&num=0&edition=prelim

claims.text: The source credit on the codified section traces the Council to 'July 26, 1947, ch. 343, title I, Sec. 101, 61 Stat. 496', with the first amendment at 'Aug. 10, 1949, ch. 412, Sec. 3, 63 Stat. 579'.
claims.source: 50 U.S.C. 3021 source credit, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title50-section3021&num=0&edition=prelim

claims.text: THE DIRECTOR OF CENTRAL INTELLIGENCE WAS NEVER A STATUTORY MEMBER, AND THE INTELLIGENCE CHIEF STILL IS NOT. The 1947 membership was the President, the Secretaries of State and Defense, the Secretaries of the Army, Navy and Air Force, and the Chairman of the National Security Resources Board. Today subsection (c)(2) makes the Director of National Intelligence and the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff attendees the President MAY designate, not members. A body that approves covert action has never been required by statute to seat the person running intelligence.
claims.source: 50 U.S.C. 3021(a) and (c)(2), https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title50-section3021&num=0&edition=prelim

claims.text: Subsection (e)(3) caps the Council's professional staff at 200.

entities.label: National Security Act of 1947 (Pub. L. 80-253, 61 Stat. 495)
entities.sub: Statute; the source of the NSC, the CIA, and the residual intelligence clause every early covert-action directive is written under
entities.desc: The Act that created the National Security Council and the Central Intelligence Agency. Its section 102(d)(5), the residual clause permitting the Agency to perform 'such other functions and duties related to intelligence' as the Council directs, is the authority both NSC 10/2 and NSC 5412 invoke, which makes it the statutory root of United States covert action.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded C on a global pass (rank 606 of 1170, score 28). 4 connections, 0 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C0/A2/D1.

claims.text: The enrolled text carries the sidenote 'July 26,1947 [S. 758] [Public Law 253]' and closes 'Approved July 26, 1947.' Its short title clause reads 'That this Act may be cited as the National Security Act of 1947.'
claims.source: 61 Stat. 495, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-61/pdf/STATUTE-61-Pg495.pdf

claims.text: Section 102(a): 'There is hereby established under the National Security Council a Central Intelligence Agency with a Director of Central Intelligence'. The Agency is created UNDER the Council, not beside it.
claims.source: National Security Act of 1947 sec. 102(a), 61 Stat. 497, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-61/pdf/STATUTE-61-Pg495.pdf

claims.text: SECTION 102(d)(5) IS THE CLAUSE THAT MATTERS. It permits the Agency to perform such other functions and duties related to intelligence as the National Security Council may from time to time direct, and it is the authority expressly invoked by NSC 10/2 of 18 June 1948 and again by NSC 5412 of 15 March 1954. The United States covert-action programme rests on a residual clause in a reorganisation statute, not on a grant of authority written for it.
claims.source: National Security Act of 1947 sec. 102(d)(5), 61 Stat. 498, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-61/pdf/STATUTE-61-Pg495.pdf

claims.text: THE ACT DID NOT CREATE THE DEPARTMENT OF DEFENSE, and the common claim that it did is wrong on the text. Section 201(a) reads 'There is hereby established the National Military Establishment, and the Secretary of Defense shall be the head thereof'. The renaming to Department of Defense came with the amendments of 10 August 1949, ch. 412, 63 Stat. 579.
claims.source: National Security Act of 1947 sec. 201(a), 61 Stat. 499, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-61/pdf/STATUTE-61-Pg495.pdf

claims.text: The Act also creates the National Security Resources Board (sec. 103), the Departments of the Army, Navy and Air Force and the United States Air Force (secs. 205 to 208), the Joint Chiefs of Staff (sec. 211) and the Munitions Board (sec. 213).
claims.source: National Security Act of 1947, 61 Stat. 495, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-61/pdf/STATUTE-61-Pg495.pdf

claims.text: NOT VERIFIED, AND RECORDED AS UNVERIFIED RATHER THAN ASSUMED: the Statutes at Large prints only 'Approved July 26, 1947' and names no President. Truman's signature is universally reported and no primary signing document was opened for it in this pass.
claims.source: 61 Stat. 495, absence of a signature line, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-61/pdf/STATUTE-61-Pg495.pdf

entities.label: NSC 5412, National Security Council Directive on Covert Operations (15 March 1954)
entities.sub: Top Secret NSC directive; supersedes NSC 10/2 and moves covert-action coordination to the Operations Coordinating Board
entities.desc: The directive that replaced NSC 10/2 as the charter for United States covert operations. It restates the plausible-deniability definition almost word for word, keeps the authority in section 102(d)(5) of the 1947 Act, and makes the Operations Coordinating Board the normal channel for interagency support.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded C on a global pass (rank 692 of 1170, score 25). 4 connections, 0 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C0/A2/D0.

claims.text: The transmittal is signed by James S. Lay, Jr. and states 'The President has this date approved the enclosed National Security Council directive.' Washington, 15 March 1954. Top Secret. The source note places the copy in the Eisenhower Library, Special Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs Records.
claims.source: NSC 5412, FRUS 1950-55 Intelligence, Doc. 171, https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1950-55Intel/d171

claims.text: Paragraph 6 carries the deniability test in substantially the words NSC 10/2 used six years earlier: covert operations are to be so planned and executed that 'any U.S. Government responsibility for them is not evident to unauthorized persons and that if uncovered the U.S. Government can plausibly disclaim any responsibility.'
claims.source: NSC 5412 para. 6, FRUS 1950-55 Intelligence, Doc. 171, https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1950-55Intel/d171

claims.text: Paragraph 4 invokes section 102(d)(5) of the National Security Act of 1947 and makes the Director of Central Intelligence responsible for keeping covert operations consistent with United States foreign and military policy, through designated representatives of the Secretaries of State and Defense.
claims.source: NSC 5412 para. 4, FRUS 1950-55 Intelligence, Doc. 171, https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1950-55Intel/d171

claims.text: Paragraph 7 supersedes and rescinds NSC 10/2 and NSC 10/5, and paragraph 7(c) makes the Operations Coordinating Board the normal channel for coordinating support among State, Defense and CIA.
claims.source: NSC 5412 para. 7, FRUS 1950-55 Intelligence, Doc. 171, https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1950-55Intel/d171

claims.text: NSC 5412 DOES NOT CREATE THE 5412 COMMITTEE, and the widely repeated claim that it does is not supported by the document. No Special Group and no committee of that name appears anywhere in the text. The State Department's own editorial note attributes the Special Group to NSC 5412/2 of 28 December 1955, and says the body became known as the 'NSC 5412/2 Special Group'.

entities.label: NSDD 159, Covert Action Policy Approval and Coordination Procedures (18 January 1985)
entities.sub: Presidential directive creating a separate compartmented access system for covert-action POLICY, with one designated focal point per agency
entities.desc: A National Security Decision Directive signed by Reagan which orders the national security adviser to stand up a separate, specially compartmented control and access system at the Top Secret level covering all policy matters concerning covert action, restricts each agency to a single designated focal point, and directs that the minimum possible number of documents be created. It is the clearest openable statement of the compartmentation architecture this board spends most of its time describing, and it predates the special access programme governance the board otherwise starts from by nearly a decade.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded B on a global pass (rank 239 of 1170, score 43). 4 connections, 2 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C0/A3/D1.

claims.text: THE COMPARTMENT IS ORDERED IN TERMS. The Security Procedures section directs the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs to 'establish a separate, specially compartmented control and access system at the Top Secret classification level for all policy matters concerning covert action.' The compartment is over the POLICY, not only over the operations.
claims.source: NSDD 159, Security Procedures para. 1, https://www.reaganlibrary.gov/public/archives/reference/scanned-nsdds/nsdd159.pdf

claims.text: Access is narrowed to one person per agency: 'Each NSPG member shall designate one senior member of his component as the sole focal point for all matters related to covert action.'
claims.source: NSDD 159, Security Procedures para. 2, https://www.reaganlibrary.gov/public/archives/reference/scanned-nsdds/nsdd159.pdf

claims.text: The stated design goal on page 2 is that knowledge of policy, knowledge of operations and knowledge of supporting activity 'will be strictly compartmented from each other', and paragraph 3 orders that the minimum possible number of documents be created.
claims.source: NSDD 159 pp. 2 and Security Procedures para. 3, https://www.reaganlibrary.gov/public/archives/reference/scanned-nsdds/nsdd159.pdf

claims.text: THE PAPER TRAIL IS DELIBERATELY SINGULAR. The NSC Senior Director for Intelligence Programs holds the only record copies of approved Findings and Memoranda of Notification: 'No other copies of approved Findings or MONs are authorized.' The same officer is tasked to administer the special access security compartment protecting covert action policies.
claims.source: NSDD 159, https://www.reaganlibrary.gov/public/archives/reference/scanned-nsdds/nsdd159.pdf

claims.text: It requires written Presidential Findings for all covert action and Memoranda of Notification for modifications, makes the NSPG the committee that recommends on every covert action, and creates a senior Planning and Coordination Group which 'replaces all ad hoc interagency groups'.
claims.source: NSDD 159, https://www.reaganlibrary.gov/public/archives/reference/scanned-nsdds/nsdd159.pdf

claims.text: The document is marked SENSITIVE, SYSTEM II: 90030, NSC/ICS-400030, Copy 1 of 8, and is signed in ink by Ronald Reagan on page 7. Its original declassification instruction is 'Declassify on: Presidential Approval Only', and its struck-through control line reads TOP SECRET/VEIL.
claims.source: NSDD 159 pp. 1 and 7, https://www.reaganlibrary.gov/public/archives/reference/scanned-nsdds/nsdd159.pdf

claims.text: TWO DIFFERENT RELEASES CIRCULATE AND THEY ARE NOT THE SAME DOCUMENT. The Federation of American Scientists copy is stamped 'EXTRACT FROM NSDD 159' and was partially declassified on 5 June 1987 under EO 12356. The Reagan Library copy is the fuller release, stamped 'Authority Leary to Weinstein ltr 4/20/05 / BY RW NARA DATE 1/30/12'. Anyone citing NSDD 159 should say which one they read.
claims.source: NSDD 159, both releases compared, https://www.reaganlibrary.gov/public/archives/reference/scanned-nsdds/nsdd159.pdf and https://irp.fas.org/offdocs/nsdd/nsdd-159.htm

claims.text: THE COMPARTMENT'S OWN RULES ARE NOT IN THIS RELEASE. The directive states that the special access procedures are to be promulgated under separate cover, and that separate document was not located. VEIL appears only as a struck-through marking and never in the body, so it cannot be said from this text that VEIL is the name of the compartment NSDD 159 creates rather than a pre-existing handling caveat on the paper.
claims.source: NSDD 159, absence of the implementing procedures, https://www.reaganlibrary.gov/public/archives/reference/scanned-nsdds/nsdd159.pdf

entities.label: Executive Order 10501 - Safeguarding Official Information in the Interests of the Defense of the United States (5 November 1953)
entities.sub: Executive order; the head of the modern classification lineage, and the order that puts Restricted Data outside its own reach
entities.desc: Eisenhower's classification order, which fixed the three-category system, stripped original classification authority from dozens of agencies that had acquired it, and expressly left Atomic Energy Act Restricted Data outside the executive classification system. It governed for nineteen years until EO 11652 superseded it.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded B on a global pass (rank 470 of 1170, score 32). 3 connections, 1 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C0/A2/D2.

claims.text: Signed 'DWIGHT D. EISENHOWER / THE WHITE HOUSE / November 5, 1953', effective 15 December 1953 under section 20.
claims.source: EO 10501 secs. 1 and 20, https://irp.fas.org/offdocs/eo10501.htm

claims.text: Section 19: 'Executive Order No. 10290 of September 24, 1951 is revoked as of the effective date of this order.'
claims.source: EO 10501 sec. 19, https://irp.fas.org/offdocs/eo10501.htm

claims.text: Section 1 fixes exactly three categories, Top Secret, Secret and Confidential, and bars any other designation for defense information 'except as expressly provided by statute.'
claims.source: EO 10501 sec. 1, https://irp.fas.org/offdocs/eo10501.htm

claims.text: IT TOOK CLASSIFICATION AUTHORITY AWAY, WHICH IS THE OPPOSITE OF THE DIRECTION THE SYSTEM LATER TRAVELLED. Section 2, 'Limitation of Authority to Classify', provides that for agencies with no direct national-defense responsibility 'there shall be no authority for original classification of information or material under this order', and limits agencies with partial responsibility to the agency head without delegation. The attached memorandum names 28 agencies stripped of the authority, including the Federal Trade Commission, the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Veterans Administration, and 17 more limited to the agency head alone.
claims.source: EO 10501 sec. 2 and attached memorandum, https://irp.fas.org/offdocs/eo10501.htm

claims.text: THE JOIN TO THE NUCLEAR REGIME. Section 13 expressly leaves Atomic Energy Act Restricted Data outside the order's reach. The executive classification system and the statutory Restricted Data system are two systems, and the executive one says so.
claims.source: EO 10501 sec. 13, https://irp.fas.org/offdocs/eo10501.htm

entities.label: Executive Order 11652 - Classification and Declassification of National Security Information and Material (8 March 1972)
entities.sub: Executive order; the General Declassification Schedule, the thirty-year rule, and the first standing classification oversight committee
entities.desc: Nixon's classification order, which superseded EO 10501 and for the first time put classified material on an automatic downgrading and declassification timetable, added a thirty-year rule, and created a standing interagency committee that could take complaints from outside the government.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded B on a global pass (rank 412 of 1170, score 34). 3 connections, 0 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C0/A2/D3.

claims.text: Signed by Richard Nixon on 8 March 1972, published at 37 FR 5209 on 10 March 1972, effective 1 June 1972 under section 15.
claims.source: EO 11652 signature block and sec. 15, and the NARA disposition table, https://www.archives.gov/federal-register/executive-orders/1972.html

claims.text: Section 14, headed 'Revocation of Executive Order No. 10501', SUPERSEDES rather than revokes: it supersedes EO 10501 as amended by EOs 10816, 10901, 10964, 10985, 11097 and section 1(a) of 11382, as of the effective date. The heading and the operative verb do not match, which matters to anyone tracing the chain.
claims.source: EO 11652 sec. 14, https://irp.fas.org/offdocs/eo/eo-11652.htm

claims.text: Section 5(A) creates the General Declassification Schedule. Top Secret downgrades to Secret after 2 full calendar years, to Confidential after 4, and is declassified after 10. Secret downgrades to Confidential after 2 and is declassified after 8. Confidential is declassified after 6.
claims.source: EO 11652 sec. 5(A), https://irp.fas.org/offdocs/eo/eo-11652.htm

claims.text: Section 5(E)(1) is a thirty-year rule: material classified after the effective date is automatically declassified at 30 full calendar years unless the head of the originating Department personally determines in writing that continued protection is essential. Section 5(E)(2) puts pre-existing material over 30 years old under systematic review by the Archivist of the United States.
claims.source: EO 11652 sec. 5(E), https://irp.fas.org/offdocs/eo/eo-11652.htm

claims.text: Section 7(A) lodges monitoring in the National Security Council and establishes an Interagency Classification Review Committee of representatives of State, Defense, Justice, the Atomic Energy Commission, CIA and the NSC Staff, chaired by a presidential designee. Under 7(A)(2) it receives and acts on complaints 'from persons within or without the government.'
claims.source: EO 11652 sec. 7(A), https://irp.fas.org/offdocs/eo/eo-11652.htm

claims.text: Section 1(A), on Top Secret: 'This classification shall be used with the utmost restraint.'
claims.source: EO 11652 sec. 1(A), https://irp.fas.org/offdocs/eo/eo-11652.htm

claims.text: The common description of this order as the first major overhaul of classification since 1953 is a historians' framing and is not a claim the order makes. It is consistent with section 14, which supersedes EO 10501 and six amending orders, but the text does not say it.
claims.source: EO 11652 full text, absence of any such statement, https://irp.fas.org/offdocs/eo/eo-11652.htm

entities.label: Atomic Energy Act of 1954 (Pub. L. 83-703, 68 Stat. 919)

claims.text: The Statutes at Large header reads 'Public Law 703 / CHAPTER 1073 / August 30, 1954 / [H. R. 9757]', at 68 Stat. 919. claims.text: The definition, codified at 42 U.S.C. 2014(y) and enacted as section 11 r.: 'The term Restricted Data means all data concerning (1) design, manufacture, or utilization of atomic weapons; (2) the production of special nuclear material; or (3) the use of special nuclear material in the production of energy, but shall not include data declassified or removed from the Restricted Data category pursuant to section 2162 of this title.' The 1954 enrolled text is identical except that the cross-reference reads 'pursuant to section 142'.

claims.text: WHAT CHANGED FROM 1946, FROM THE TWO TEXTS SIDE BY SIDE. The 1946 Act defined 'restricted data' only 'as used in this section', at section 10; the 1954 Act makes 'Restricted Data' a capitalised, Act-wide definition in the definitions chapter. 1954 ADDS the word 'design'. 'Fissionable material' and 'production of power' become 'special nuclear material' and 'production of energy'. And the 1946 carve-out was open-ended Commission discretion, where 1954 ties removal to a formal declassification procedure at section 142, including the transclassification of weapons-utilisation data into 'defense information' under section 142 d.

claims.text: The 1946 definition it replaced, at section 10(b)(1), covered 'all data concerning the manufacture or utilization of atomic weapons, the production of fissionable material, or the use of fissionable material in the production of power'.

entities.label: Strategic Air Command (SAC)
entities.sub: The USAF major command that owned every installation in this cluster; the institutional spine of the nuclear-incursion record, 1946 to 1992
entities.desc: THE MISSING SPINE. Every incident in this cluster happened inside Strategic Air Command, and until now the board had United States Air Force above and nothing between it and the bases. SAC owned Loring, Wurtsmith, Malmstrom, Minot, Grand Forks, F. E. Warren, Ellsworth and Walker; it ran the alert postures the 1975 documents invoke; and it is SAC command posts that appear as the reporting node in almost every primary record opened for this pass. The 24th NORAD Region Senior Director's Log for November 1975 reads almost entirely as a record of calls from 'SAC CP' and the 341st Strategic Air Command Post. The National Military Command Center's Loring memorandum of 29 October 1975 records that NORAD was informed of the incident by SAC and that the SAC Command Center reported back on the failure of the Army National Guard helicopter to locate the intruder, citing SAC CP OPS CONTROL 291954Z OCT 75. When Echo Flight went off alert at Malmstrom on 16 March 1967 it was SAC Headquarters that called in Ogden Air Materiel Area support for a complete engineering analysis within hours. The node exists so that a reader can see that these are not scattered base-level anomalies but a run of reports moving up one chain of command, and so that the base hubs have something to attach to.

entities.label: Loring AFB, Maine
entities.sub: SAC installation at Limestone, Maine; 42nd Bombardment Wing and its nuclear weapons storage area; the first base in the October 1975 penetration sequence
entities.desc: THE HUB WHERE THE BEST DOCUMENT IN THE SUBJECT WAS GENERATED. Loring Air Force Base at Limestone, Maine was a Strategic Air Command installation home to the 42nd Bombardment Wing and a nuclear weapons storage area, and on the nights of 27, 28 and 29 to 30 October 1975 that storage area was overflown at low level by something the United States military tracked, pursued and failed to identify. What makes Loring the strongest node in this cluster is not the sighting reports but the paper trail above them. The National Military Command Center produced a Memorandum for Record over the signature of a serving brigadier general with a subject line reading 'AFB Penetration', distributed to the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs, the Director of the Joint Staff, the J-30 through J-38 directorates, the service chiefs, and the DIA, NSA and CIA representatives. A Major General of the Army Staff personally approved rules of engagement for a National Guard helicopter: track and identify, no apprehension, no border crossing. The State Department's Canadian desk officer was kept informed. Nothing in this record says what the object was, and the traffic calls it an unidentified helicopter throughout rather than a UFO. What it documents is a three-day command-level flap over an unidentified rotary-wing intruder at a nuclear weapons storage area, escalated to the Joint Staff and to a foreign government, which is a nuclear security record before it is anything else.

entities.label: Wurtsmith AFB, Michigan
entities.sub: SAC installation at Oscoda, Michigan; 379th Bombardment Wing; site of the 30 October 1975 weapons storage area incursion and the KC-135 pursuit over Lake Huron
entities.desc: THE HUB THAT CARRIES THE MOST METHODOLOGICALLY IMPORTANT DOCUMENT IN THE CLUSTER, AND IT IS NOT FROM 1975. Wurtsmith Air Force Base at Oscoda, Michigan was a Strategic Air Command installation home to the 379th Bombardment Wing, and on the night of 30 to 31 October 1975 an unidentified low-flying object was reported over its weapons storage area and pursued by a KC-135 tanker out over Lake Huron. The NORAD Command Director's Log entry of 31 Oct 75/0445Z reports an incident at 0355Z, and the NORAD Senior Director's Log records that a tanker sighted the same object and pursued it thirty-five miles southeast over the lake. A Joint Chiefs of Staff operational report of 30 October 1975 records the prosaic-explanation check that was run and did not fit, contacting the Department of Natural Resources about aircraft searching for hunters spotting deer. But the document that matters most to this board's method is dated January 1979. SSgt Paul J. Cahill, the 379th Bombardment Wing historian, wrote a Research Record of Events on 17 January 1979 stating that he had checked the October to December 1975 Wing History and found no references to the incident, and the following day Capt. Myron Taylor wrote him a Memo for the Record giving the KC-135 crew's account. THAT IS A DOCUMENTED INSTANCE OF A UNIT HISTORY OMITTING AN EVENT THAT OTHER AIR FORCE PAPER RECORDS, DISCOVERED AND WRITTEN DOWN BY THE WING HISTORIAN HIMSELF. It is the correct caution to attach to any argument from a unit history's silence anywhere on this board, including the sceptical argument about Echo Flight.

entities.label: Minot AFB, North Dakota
entities.sub: SAC installation; 91st Strategic Missile Wing and 5th Bomb Wing; 1966 incursions, the 24 October 1968 B-52 case, and a named appearance in the CINCNORAD message of 11 November 1975
entities.desc: THE HUB WITH THE MOST INDEPENDENT DETECTION CHANNELS AND ONE UNRESOLVED NAMING PROBLEM. Minot Air Force Base, North Dakota, home of the 91st Strategic Missile Wing and the 5th Bomb Wing, is the convergence point for three separate episodes this board already carries in pieces without a place to hang them on: the 1966 incursions over its Minuteman launch facilities, the 24 October 1968 B-52 case, which is the best-instrumented nuclear-site incursion in the American record, and its named appearance in the CINCNORAD four-part message of 11 November 1975. THE NAMING PROBLEM IS REAL AND MUST NOT BE SILENTLY RESOLVED. For 10 November 1975 the 24th NORAD Region Senior Director's Log records a sighting at 'Minot Air Force Station', a radar site, and its own next clause says the object 'passed over the radar station'. Nine days later CINCNORAD's summary message lists 'Minot AFB, ND' among the installations where reliable military personnel had visually sighted suspicious objects. Two NORAD documents from the same period name two different Minot installations, and nothing opened by this board resolves which is meant. That matters for this hub specifically, because a degree count on l-minot that silently absorbs a radar-station entry is a degree count that lies.

claims.text: THE NAMING DISCREPANCY, STATED RATHER THAN RESOLVED. The 24th NORAD Region Senior Director's Log for 10 November 1975 reads: 'UFO sighting reported by Minot Air Force Station, a bright star-like object in the West, moving east, about the size of a car. First seen approximately 1015Z. Approximately 1120Z the object passed over the radar station, 1,000 feet to 2,000 feet high, no noise heard. Three people from the site or local area saw the object.' entities.label: Malmstrom missile-field overflights, 7 to 19 November 1975

entities.desc: THE STRONGEST SINGLE ARTEFACT IN THE NUCLEAR STRAND, BECAUSE IT IS A WORKING LOG RATHER THAN A REPORT WRITTEN FOR ANYBODY. entities.label: NMCC Memorandum for Record, 'AFB Penetration', 29 October 1975
entities.sub: National Military Command Center memorandum and four DDO updates on the Loring AFB penetrations, signed by a serving brigadier general
entities.desc: THE BEST SINGLE DOCUMENT IN THE NUCLEAR STRAND AND IT IS NOT A UFO DOCUMENT. It is a National Military Command Center Memorandum for Record, dated 29 October 1975 at 0605 EST, subject line 'AFB Penetration', signed C. D. Roberts, Jr., Brigadier General, USMC, Deputy Director for Operations. Five numbered paragraphs record that an unidentified helicopter, possibly two, was sighted flying low over Loring AFB in proximity to a weapons storage area; that an Army National Guard helicopter was called in and failed to locate it; that NORAD requested and received authority from Canadian officials to cross into Canadian airspace in pursuit; and that a similar incident had occurred the previous evening. Four DDO updates follow, each citing its source message. The distribution list is what makes the document remarkable: CJCS in five copies, DJS in three, J-30 through J-38, the Chief of Staff of the Army, the Chief of Naval Operations, the Chief of Staff of the Air Force, the Commandant of the Marine Corps, the Chief of WWMCCS Operations and Evaluation Division, the DIA representative for the National Military Intelligence Center, the NSA representative, the CIA representative and the Western Hemisphere desk. This is what a nuclear security incident looks like on paper when nobody has decided what it is.

entities.desc: A WORKING OPERATIONAL LOG, WHICH IS WHY IT IS WORTH MORE THAN ANY REPORT. The 24th NORAD Region Senior Director's Log at Malmstrom AFB records thirteen days of reports from the 341st Strategic Missile Wing's field in the controllers' own shorthand, timed in Zulu, with site designators, radar track numbers, height-finder readings and aircraft call-outs. The log is not an advocate's document and does not read like one: alongside the sightings it records that surveillance could detect no track except known traffic, that an airline crew reported a meteor, and that on 12 November the controllers never had any contact on radar at all. It also contains the 10 November entry naming Minot Air Force Station rather than Minot AFB, which is the one unresolved naming problem in the 1975 sequence. NOTE THE ARCHIVE ITEM IS MISTITLED: it is filed as 'Malmstrom Air Force Base Incident - March 16, 1967 NORAD logs' and its contents are the November 1975 log.

entities.desc: THE MESSAGE THAT TIES THE 1975 SEQUENCE TOGETHER IN THE COMMAND'S OWN VOICE. On 11 November 1975 the Commander-in-Chief of North American Air Defense Command sent a four-part message to NORAD units summarising the events of the preceding fortnight. Its opening is the single most quoted sentence in the 1975 material and it is worth quoting in full because of the adjective it uses about its own witnesses. The message names five installations across two countries and, unlike the Loring traffic, it does not call the objects helicopters. It calls them suspicious objects, and it says its sources were reliable military personnel. It also names Minot AFB, where the 24th NORAD Region's own log nine days earlier had named Minot Air Force Station, which is the one internal inconsistency in the 1975 record that this board has found and cannot resolve.

entities.label: Malmstrom AFB missile shutdowns, March 1967
entities.sub: Echo Flight Minuteman off-alert event, 16 March 1967, 341st Strategic Missile Wing
entities.desc: On 16 March 1967 at 0845 all ten Minuteman I missiles of Echo Flight, 341st Strategic Missile Wing, Malmstrom Air Force Base, Montana, went off strategic alert nearly simultaneously. That the shutdown happened is a matter of Air Force paper and is not in dispute: the wing's own history records it, and Robert Hastings publishes in facsimile an Air Force teletype dated 17 March 1967 concerning loss of strategic alert. What is contested is why, and the decisive document is now open. Excerpts of five quarterly 341st SMW histories were released to John Greenewald Jr on 14 June 2001, and in all 88 pages the words 'Unidentified Flying Object' occur exactly once, in a negative: rumours around Echo Flight during the time of fault 'were disproven', on evidence from a Mobile Strike Team that had been at November Flight rather than Echo Flight. The same release is equally hard on the debunk. The engineering investigation of 23 March 1967 reported that the teams at Malmstrom 'were unable to determine a logical cause for the incident'; the electromagnetic pulse conclusion arrived three months later and arrived by elimination, after Boeing's Sensitive Information Network theory was tested at Malmstrom and 'proved this analysis wrong' and the transformer-failure simulation showed no significant noise propagation. Boeing bench tests did reproduce the fault signature in 60 per cent of twenty applications of a 30 microsecond pulse, and the Air Force then bought the fix, in Boeing ECPs 1221, 1141-1 and 1141-2. THE OSCAR FLIGHT CLAIM IS A SEPARATE EVENT AND IS CARRIED SEPARATELY. Robert Salas places his own experience at Oscar Flight, and Robert Hastings now dates it to 24 March 1967 on Capt. Robert Jamison's information; the string 'Oscar' occurs zero times in the release. Against the UFO reading stand the engineering account above and a sustained public challenge from James Carlson, son of the Echo Flight crew commander. This board grades the occurrence at tier 1 and every causal attribution at tier 2.

It also records that the 801st Radar Squadron, Malmstrom AFB, 'gave a negative report on any radar or atmospheric interference problems related to Echo Flight', and that a comparable multi-facility shutdown had occurred at Alpha Flight on 19 December 1966 with the same capsule crew, adverse weather and a commercial power failure.

entities.label: Minot AFB B-52 incident, 24 October 1968
entities.sub: Ground radar, airborne radar, visual and Minuteman site security events, 91st SMW
entities.desc: The best-instrumented nuclear-site incursion case in the American record, and the one where the number of independent detection channels is the argument. In the early hours of 24 October 1968, about thirty miles northwest of Minot AFB, North Dakota, USAF ground radar tracked an unidentified object correlated with an orange glow and passed it to the crew of a B-52H, call sign JAG 31, at 2,000 feet on a 290-degree heading: a target at the one o'clock position at 24 miles at about 3:30 a.m. CDT, 15 miles by 3:35 a.m., and by 3:52 a.m. also being tracked by base weather radar at 3 miles. At 3:58 a.m. Minot requested IFF transponder identification and the B-52H's radio transmitter failed for four minutes. The bomber's own radar tracked a bright red-orange object, and the object was reported down at a location logged as 'AA-43' for some forty-five minutes. Simultaneously, Minuteman ICBM launch facilities of the 91st Strategic Missile Wing designated N, O, J and M Flights reported sightings and electromagnetic effects including security alarms triggered at both the outer and inner rings of a silo, an outer door opened and the combination lock of an inner door moved. Named witnesses include Maj. Bradford Runyon, S/Sgt Bond and S/Sgt Smith. Dan Wilson located 108 documents on the case and NARCAP found 141. Project Blue Book did not send field investigators, and Jan Aldrich's assessment of the Blue Book file is that the Air Force obfuscated the case badly enough that the obfuscation itself is visible in the paper. Richard Haines analysed the B-52H radar imagery. Minot 1968 is the case where the phrase 'threat to a primary nuclear offense system' is not rhetoric: radio failure, radar correlation and physical security breaches at a nuclear launch facility on the same night.

entities.sub: Prime defense contractor; largest single recipient of DoD prime contract obligations
entities.desc: Lockheed Martin is the company named more often than any other in the custody allegation, and the only one named on the floor of a congressional hearing by a sworn witness. Its documented government relationship is total: USAspending records show prime contract obligations to Lockheed Martin recipient entities running to the hundreds of billions of dollars since FY2008, spanning the F-35, Trident II D5, missile defense, national security space and classified aeronautics. It operates cleared facilities under DoD special access program accreditation, including Air Force Plant 42 at Palmdale and the Advanced Development Programs organisation that AARO's own historical report describes by name. The custody allegation attaches at three separate points. First, George Knapp testified under oath on 9 September 2025 that Robert Bigelow and an AAWSAP colleague negotiated with senior Lockheed Martin executives for a quantity of material 'stashed away and protected at a facility in California,' adding 'that material was not made here'; asked to name corporations holding material, he answered 'one of them is Lockheed,' and named a Lockheed executive as a gatekeeper. Second, Luis Elizondo testified on 13 November 2024 that an aerospace contractor sought to divest itself of material collected in the 1950s, confirmed the reported Lockheed-Bigelow transfer was blocked, and described a Secretary of the Air Force memorandum that never came. Third, AARO's Historical Record Report records - without naming companies - an interviewee claim that an organisation possessed off-world material in 2009 and 2010 and that a former senior CIA official quashed the proposal to remove it from the corporation. Lockheed Martin has issued no public rebuttal of the sworn testimony. AARO states that the executives and chief technology officers of the named companies met its Director and denied the allegations on the record.

entities.desc: Skunk Works is the physical and cultural template for how an unacknowledged program is run inside a private corporation. Founded by Clarence 'Kelly' Johnson in 1943 and led by Ben Rich from 1975 to 1991, it produced the U-2, the A-12/SR-71, the F-117, Sea Shadow, DarkStar and the RQ-170 Sentinel - the last of which existed operationally for years before Lockheed acknowledged it, which is the point. AARO's Historical Record Report itself uses Skunk Works aircraft as the explanation for a class of UAP reports, conceding in the process that the organisation routinely fields flying hardware whose existence the government denies while it is flying. Its home is Air Force Plant 42 at Palmdale, a government-owned contractor-operated facility whose accreditation architecture supports program-level compartmentation. For this domain Skunk Works matters in two ways. It is the operational proof that a prime contractor can hold, fly and conceal an object of unknown provenance from everyone without a need to know, including senior officers in the chain of command. And it is the organisation Ben Rich ran, whose post-retirement remarks about technologies 'locked up in black projects' are the most quoted and least documented artifact in the entire field.

entities.label: EG&G (Edgerton, Germeshausen and Grier)
entities.sub: Nuclear test instrumentation and classified site services; Groom Lake support
entities.desc: EG&G is the company that made the secret sites work. Founded by MIT's Harold Edgerton with Kenneth Germeshausen and Herbert Grier, it instrumented and fired US nuclear tests from the Manhattan Project onward and became the classified services contractor for the Nevada complex - the Nevada Test Site and the Air Force operating location near Groom Lake. entities.sub: A privately filed 1964 patent for MHD propulsion, granted 1967, with no assignee and no government interest, which is cited in the ARV literature as evidence for a mechanism it never mentions
entities.desc: THE STRAND'S CONTROL CASE, AND IT IS INFORMATIVE PRECISELY BECAUSE IT IS ORDINARY. US 3,322,374 was filed on 30 September 1964 by James F. King, Jr. of Winston-Salem, North Carolina, at a home address, and granted on 30 May 1967 with 9 claims in Class 244-62. It has NO ASSIGNEE, NO GOVERNMENT INTEREST STATEMENT AND NO SECRECY ORDER. What it claims is a linear induction motor that uses the surrounding ionised atmosphere as its armature: coils arranged serially along the craft's axis, driven by polyphase alternating current, produce a collective magnetic field whose point of maximum flux density travels repeatedly from the leading end to the trailing end of the craft, and that travelling field induces eddy currents in the ionised fluid, driving the fluid backwards and the craft forwards. That is classical electromagnetism and it is the same physics as a seagoing magnetohydrodynamic thruster. The patent is on this board because of what was claimed FOR it rather than because of what is in it: it was offered in a discussion thread as 'ample evidence' that the 'Scalar Physics' callout on Mark McCandlish's ARV drawing refers to spin-zero scalar particles. WORD COUNTS ACROSS ALL SEVEN PAGES: scalar 0, spin 0, gravity 0, anti-gravity 0, zero point 0. The single hit for 'air force' is the phrase 'the ionized air force vector' and is a false positive. This node therefore records a FAILED CITATION, which is a different object from a disputed one: the document is real, openable and mundane, and the assertion made about it is checkable and wrong.

entities.label: Alcubierre, 'The warp drive: hyper-fast travel within general relativity' (1994)
entities.sub: The five-page Classical and Quantum Gravity letter that is the origin of every warp-drive claim in the field, and which states in its own abstract that exotic matter will be needed
entities.desc: THE PAPER STATES A REQUIREMENT AND NOT A CAPABILITY, AND IT SAYS SO IN ITS OWN ABSTRACT. Miguel Alcubierre, then at the Department of Physics and Astronomy, University of Wales, College of Cardiff, showed that a spacetime metric can be written which expands space behind a spaceship and contracts it in front, allowing arbitrarily large apparent speed to outside observers while the ship stays on a timelike trajectory inside its own light cone. He then computed what would be required to source that metric and reported the answer against himself: the metric 'violates all three energy conditions (weak, dominant and strong)', the energy density seen by Eulerian observers 'is everywhere negative', and 'one needs exotic matter to travel faster than the speed of light'. THE WORD 'DEVICE' APPEARS ZERO TIMES IN THE PAPER. The word 'propulsion' appears once, in the sentence naming the idea after science fiction. There is no apparatus, no engine, no method of construction and no experiment. The node exists because the paper is cited throughout the UAP literature as though it described an engineering programme, and because DIA paid for a Defense Intelligence Reference Document built on it. Citing this paper as evidence that a craft could do this is citing a requirement as though it were a capability, which is this strand's pattern in its purest form: unlike the other instances, it is not even a misreading, because the abstract says plainly that exotic matter will be needed.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded C on a global pass (rank 856 of 1170, score 20). 4 connections, 0 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C0/A0/D0.

claims.text: THE ABSTRACT, VERBATIM AND IN FULL: 'It is shown how, within the framework of general relativity and without the introduction of wormholes, it is possible to modify a spacetime in a way that allows a spaceship to travel with an arbitrarily large speed. By a purely local expansion of spacetime behind the spaceship and an opposite contraction in front of it, motion faster than the speed of light as seen by observers outside the disturbed region is possible. The resulting distortion is reminiscent of the "warp drive" of science fiction. However, just as it happens with wormholes, exotic matter will be needed in order to generate a distortion of spacetime like the one discussed here.'
claims.source: Miguel Alcubierre, 'The warp drive: hyper-fast travel within general relativity', Classical and Quantum Gravity 11-5, L73-L77 (1994), DOI 10.1088/0264-9381/11/5/001, read in full from the author's arXiv posting of 5 September 2000, https://arxiv.org/abs/gr-qc/0009013 , opened 2026-09-19

claims.text: THE REQUIREMENT, IN ALCUBIERRE'S OWN WORDS: 'The metric I have just described has one important drawback, however: it violates all three energy conditions (weak, dominant and strong). Both the weak and the dominant energy conditions require the energy density to be positive for all observers.' Having given the expression for the energy density the Eulerian observers see, he writes: 'The fact that this expression is everywhere negative implies that the weak and dominant energy conditions are violated. In a similar way one can show that the strong energy condition is also violated.'
claims.source: Miguel Alcubierre, 'The warp drive: hyper-fast travel within general relativity', Classical and Quantum Gravity 11-5, L73-L77 (1994), DOI 10.1088/0264-9381/11/5/001, read in full from the author's arXiv posting of 5 September 2000, https://arxiv.org/abs/gr-qc/0009013 , opened 2026-09-19

claims.text: His own conclusion, verbatim: 'We see then that, just as it happens with wormholes, one needs exotic matter to travel faster than the speed of light. However, even if one believes that exotic matter is forbidden classically, it is well known that quantum field theory permits the existence of regions with negative energy densities in some special circumstances (as, for example, in the Casimir effect). The need of exotic matter therefore doesn't necessarily eliminate the possibility of using a spacetime distortion like the one described above for hyper-fast interstellar travel.'

entities.label: NASA/TM-2004-213082, 'Prospects for Breakthrough Propulsion from Physics' (2004)
entities.sub: Marc G. Millis's summary of NASA's Breakthrough Propulsion Physics Project, which adjudicates Biefeld-Brown, lifters, asymmetrical capacitors, Podkletnov, metric engineering and high frequency gravitational waves by name
entities.desc: ONE OPENED, UNCLASSIFIED, OFFICIAL DOCUMENT ADJUDICATES THREE OF THIS STRAND'S SIX MECHANISMS BY NAME, AND THE BOARD ALREADY CARRIES ITS AUTHOR. Marc G. Millis of NASA Glenn Research Center wrote this 19-page technical memorandum for a NASA/DoD-cosponsored conference held in Seattle from 24 to 26 June 2004, summarising the methods and findings of the Breakthrough Propulsion Physics Project he had managed since 1996. Its abstract states the project's three grand challenges and its result: 'Of 16 incremental research tasks completed by the project and from other sponsors, about a third were found not to be viable, a quarter have clear opportunities for sequels, and the rest remain unresolved.' Section 3.2.7 disposes of the Biefeld-Brown effect, Lifters and Asymmetrical Capacitors. Section 3.3.1 disposes of metric engineering and records, usefully for this board, that the term itself 'has emerged at aerospace conferences' and that 'The origin of this term is unknown'. Section 3.3.2 treats high frequency gravitational waves as a detection problem. WHAT MAKES THIS THE STRAND'S MOST REUSABLE CITATION is that it is a named author writing under a NASA report number about exactly the claims this board tracks, six years before AAWSAP commissioned its own reports on the same subjects, and it is openable by anyone.

claims.text: THE BIEFELD-BROWN ADJUDICATION, section 3.2.7, verbatim and in full: 'In 1928 a device was patented for creating thrust using high-voltage capacitors. Since then, a wide variety of variants of this "Biefeld-Brown" effect, such as "Lifters" and "Asymmetrical Capacitors" have claimed that such devices operate on an "electrostatic antigravity" or "electrogravitic" effect. One of the most recent variants was patented by NASA-MSFC. To date, all rigorous experimental tests indicate that the observed thrust is attributable to ion wind. Vacuum tests currently underway, sponsored through an additional Congressional earmark to the West Virginia Institute for Scientific Research, also indicate that this effect is not indicative of new propulsion physics. These tests are now assessing the more conventional performance of such devices. These "Biefeld-Brown," "Lifter" and "Asymmetrical Capacitor Thrusters" are not viable candidates for breakthrough physics propulsion.'

entities.label: NASA/CR-2004-213312, 'Asymmetrical Capacitors for Propulsion' (2004)
entities.sub: The NASA contractor report that tested asymmetrical capacitor thrusters at atmospheric and reduced pressures and concluded their operation is fully explained by electrostatic forces and momentum transfer
entities.desc: THE EXPERIMENT BEHIND THE FINDING, AS DISTINCT FROM THE SURVEY THAT REPORTS IT. Francis X. Canning, Cory Melcher and Edwin Winet of the Institute for Scientific Research in Fairmont, West Virginia, measured the thrust of several Asymmetrical Capacitor Thrusters at various voltages, polarities and ground configurations, at atmospheric pressure and at reduced pressures, and in nitrogen and argon as well as air. They built a model of ions drifting between electrodes under electrostatic forces and imparting momentum to air through multiple collisions, and reported that it predicted the measured magnitude of the thrust, the way the direction changed when the ground wire moved, and the independence of the thrust direction from the polarity of the applied voltage. THE NODE IS ON THIS BOARD BECAUSE ITS REFERENCE LIST CITES THOMAS TOWNSEND BROWN'S PATENTS BY NUMBER: US 2,949,550, US 3,187,206 and GB 300,311, which are exactly the three Brown documents the board already carries. That makes the join documentary rather than topical. The report also preserves the only vacuum measurement its authors could find from the previous half-century, Robert Talley's Air Force-contract test, which it quotes directly.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded C on a global pass (rank 857 of 1170, score 20). 3 connections, 1 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C0/A0/D0.

claims.text: THE CONCLUSION, verbatim in the passage that matters: 'A simple model was developed of ions drifting from one electrode to the other under electrostatic forces, and imparting momentum to air as they underwent multiple collisions. This model was found to be consistent with all of our observations. It predicted the magnitude of the force (thrust) that was measured. It also predicted how the direction of the thrust changed when the location of the ground wire changed. Furthermore, it also predicted that the direction of the thrust was independent of the polarity of the applied voltage... In spite of decades of speculation about possible new physical principles being responsible for the thrust produced by ACTs and lifters, we find no evidence to support such a conclusion. On the contrary, we find that their operation is fully explained by a very simple theory that uses only electrostatic forces and the transfer of momentum by multiple collisions.'
claims.source: NASA/CR-2004-213312, Francis X. Canning, Cory Melcher and Edwin Winet, 'Asymmetrical Capacitors for Propulsion', Institute for Scientific Research Inc, Fairmont, West Virginia, October 2004, 23 pages, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20040171929/downloads/20040171929.pdf , opened 2026-09-19

claims.text: THE VACUUM RESULT, which is what answers the question US 3,187,206 raises in its own text about behaviour in a vacuum. The report quotes Robert Talley's Air Force-contract measurement directly: 'Talley wrote, "Direct experimental results show that under high vacuum conditions... no detectable propulsive force was electrostatically induced by applying a static potential difference... between test device electrodes..." Talley concluded (page 91 of his report), "If such a force still exists and lies below the threshold of measurements in this program, then the force may be too small to be attractive for many, if not most, space propulsion applications."' The report adds of Talley's work: 'His report is the only written report we have found from the last half-century that describes a measurement of a force while in a vacuum chamber.' THE TALLEY REPORT ITSELF WAS NOT OPENED BY THIS SESSION.

entities.label: NASA Breakthrough Propulsion Physics Project (1996-2002)
entities.sub: NASA's own six-year project to assess whether propulsion breakthroughs were achievable, which completed sixteen incremental research tasks and found about a third of them not viable
entities.desc: THE REAL, FUNDED, GOVERNMENT ASSESSMENT OF EXACTLY THE MECHANISMS THIS BOARD TRACKS, AND IT IS UNCLASSIFIED AND PUBLISHED. NASA supported the Breakthrough Propulsion Physics Project from 1996 through 2002 under three grand challenges, stated in its own summary document: discover propulsion that eliminates the need for propellant; discover methods to achieve hyper-fast travel; and discover breakthrough methods to power spacecraft. It was managed at NASA Glenn Research Center by Marc G. Millis, who is already a board node and who later wrote an AAWSAP Defense Intelligence Reference Document. The project's approach was deliberately incremental: rather than attempting a breakthrough it funded small tasks aimed at the critical issues behind each challenge, and then reported which ones failed. Of sixteen such tasks, about a third were found not to be viable. WHAT MAKES THE PROJECT BOARD MATERIAL is that its published findings adjudicate, by name and under a government report number, three of the six propulsion mechanisms the UAP literature invokes: the Biefeld-Brown effect and its lifter and asymmetrical-capacitor variants, Alcubierre-style metric engineering, and high frequency gravitational waves. It is the control against which AAWSAP's own Defense Intelligence Reference Documents of 2009 to 2011 can be read, and the board had nothing like it before this pass.

entities.desc: The TR-3B is a CLAIMED craft for whose existence no record has been opened, and the board carries it as a claim and not as an object: every substantive description of it descends from a single named man's speaking script, which he copyrighted himself in August 1998 and which attributes the sighting itself to an unnamed friend. Everything on this node is therefore a description of a claim. One artefact carries that description and is why the node exists: the 62 page transcript headed 'Presentation to IUFOR by Edgar Rothshild Fouche / Copyright Aug. 1998 / Fouche Media Associates', in which slides 69 to 72 give the craft its designation and code name Astra, place it at Papoose, attribute it to 'the Top Secret, Aurora Program with SDI and black budget monies', name the National Reconnaissance Office, the NSA and the CIA as its funders and taskers, name Sandia and Livermore as developers of its propulsion, and specify 'a circular, plasma filled accelerator ring called the Magnetic Field Disrupter' running a 'mercury based' plasma 'pressurized at 250,000 atmospheres at a temperature of 150 degrees Kelvin and accelerated to 50,000 rpm'. THE DOCUMENT CONTRADICTS ITSELF ABOUT THE SIZE OF THE CRAFT TWO SLIDES APART: slide 69 says 'The operational model is 600 feet across' and slide 70 says 'The 200 feet Prototype & the 300 feet Operational TR-3Bs are Code named Astra'. Both sentences are in the same document, in sequence, and nobody outside it has to adjudicate that. Three further things constrain this node. The presentation was given in the same summer as, and in order to promote, a book the Library of Congress catalogues as science fiction, LCCN 98002961, genre heading 'Science fiction.', subject 'Alien abduction - Fiction'. The propulsion specification is refuted by the freezing point of its own stated working fluid: NIST gives mercury a melting point of 234.31 K, and 150 K is 84 K below that. And the presentation's companion craft, the 'SR-75 Penetrator', is the name of a Testors plastic model kit of a speculative aircraft sold from 1993, five years earlier, about which the Air Force told the Baltimore Sun 'such a plane does not exist'.

claims.text: Stated inference, and it is a short one. 150 K is 84 K below mercury's melting point of 234.31 K at one atmosphere. Mercury's melting curve has a positive slope, so a pressure of 250,000 atmospheres raises the melting point rather than lowering it, putting the material further into the solid region and not closer to a gas. A plasma is an ionised gas. The specification therefore describes a solid and calls it a plasma, and it does so before any question of superconductivity, rotation or gravity is reached.

entities.desc: The most tractable question in this whole field is not whether exotic physics is real but who was paid to study it, and that question has a documented answer. Davis of EarthTech International, and 'Antigravity for Aerospace Applications'. Those are real government contract deliverables on precisely the physics a recovered craft would require, written by named authors, with document control numbers. Two readings are available and this board records both: either the topics were selected because someone had a reason to believe they were relevant, or a sympathetic programme manager funded a literature survey of fringe physics. The strength of the domain is that it does not depend on resolving that - the tasking itself is the tier-1 fact. entities.sub: 38 technical reference products produced FY2008-FY2010 for the DIA Defense Warning Office
entities.desc: The DIRD series is the paper trail the programme left behind. Between roughly 2008 and 2010 the Defense Intelligence Agency's Defense Warning Office, through its Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications (AAWSA/AAWSAP) programme and its programme manager James T. Lacatski, D.Eng., commissioned 38 technical reference products from outside performers. On 16 January 2019 the DIA released the list of titles to Steven Aftergood of the Federation of American Scientists in response to a FOIA request; the same list had been provided to Congress in January 2018. The titles are exactly what a reverse-engineering effort would commission if it had hardware it could not explain: 'Advanced Space Propulsion Based on Vacuum (Spacetime Metric) Engineering' (Puthoff), 'Traversable Wormholes, Stargates, and Negative Energy' (Davis), 'Warp Drive, Dark Energy, and the Manipulation of Extra Dimensions' (Obousy and Davis), 'Metamaterials for Aerospace Applications' (G. Shvets), 'Materials for Advanced Aerospace Platforms' (J. Williams), 'Metallic Glasses: Status and Prospects for Aerospace Applications' (T. Hufnagel), 'Metallic Spintronics' (M. Tsoi), 'Biomaterials' (Bruce Towe), 'Invisibility Cloaking: Theory and Experiments' (Ulf Leonhardt), 'Negative Mass Propulsion' (F. Winterberg), 'Detection and High Resolution Tracking of Vehicles at Hypersonic Velocities' (W. Culbreth), 'Aerospace Applications of Programmable Matter', 'Concepts for Extracting Energy from the Quantum Vacuum', 'The Role of Superconductors in Gravity Research', 'Quantum Tomography of Negative Energy States in the Vacuum', and the Green medical study. Read as a set, the series is a systematic literature survey of every physical mechanism you would need to understand if you were holding a vehicle whose performance violated your propulsion assumptions - plus a clinical study of the injuries it inflicts on bystanders. The DIA's own FOIA reading room now hosts the released documents alongside the AAWSAP statement of work, contract status briefs and the Reid correspondence on special access programme status.

entities.desc: Garry Nolan's laboratory in Stanford's Department of Pathology is an unlikely but decisive node in the custody chain. entities.label: Nolan, Vallee, Jiang & Lemke (2022), Progress in Aerospace Sciences 128:100788
entities.sub: 'Improved instrumental techniques, including isotopic analysis, applicable to the characterization of unusual materials with potential relevance to aerospace forensics'
entities.desc: The first peer-reviewed instrumental analysis of physical material associated with a multi-witness UAP event to appear in a mainstream aerospace journal. Published in Progress in Aerospace Sciences volume 128, article 100788 (2022), DOI 10.1016/j.paerosci.2021.100788, by Garry P. Nolan, Jacques F. Vallee, Sizun Jiang and Larry G. Lemke. The subject is the Council Bluffs, Iowa mass of 17 December 1977. The methods are secondary ion mass spectrometry and multiplexed ion beam imaging. The results are deliberately unhelpful to both camps: the isotopic ratios contain no anomalies, so the material could have originated on Earth; but the metals within the once-molten mass are mixed incompletely, indicating an industrial process of unknown origin. The paper then works through the alternatives - meteorite (no cratering, wrong elemental composition, would not arrive molten, iron meteorites contain 5-40% nickel while the sample had only traces), satellite or spacecraft debris (cools and solidifies before impact, no structure, carbon steel is not a spacecraft material), aircraft debris (no incident reported at any regional airport or military facility), dumped molten metal (no foundries operating in the region that day, and the logistics of transporting metal above 2,500 degrees Fahrenheit undetected are formidable), and thermite (the necessary aluminium-oxide byproduct is absent from the SIMS diatomic analysis) - and rejects each. What survives is a residual: a terrestrial-isotope sample formed by an unknown industrial process, observed descending from a structured object by five independent witness groups and photographed by police.
