entities.label: Council Bluffs, Iowa molten metal fall, 17 December 1977
entities.sub: Five independent witness groups; police photographs; ~four-by-six-foot molten mass
entities.desc: On the evening of 17 December 1977, five independent groups of witnesses in the vicinity of Big Lake Park in Council Bluffs, Iowa observed a red luminous mass descending from approximately 500-600 feet to the ground. One witness described 'a big round thing hovering in the sky below the tree tops', 'hovering, it wasn't moving', with 'red lights around the perimeter... blinking in sequence'. One of the first people to reach the site described a pool of molten metal that 'looked like a great big sparkler at first', then 'it cooled down, and it seemed like lava, glowing and bubbling'. The city's assistant fire chief arrived about twenty minutes later and described a roughly four-by-six-foot mass 'running, boiling down the edges of the levee'. Police photographed the scene and interviewed witnesses; one of those photographs is reproduced in the 2022 peer-reviewed study. Contemporaneous newspaper coverage appeared in the Daily Nonpareil on 18 December 1977 and in the Des Moines Register on 26 January 1978, and analyses conducted within weeks identified the material as high-carbon steel and slag. The case is the anchor of the entire modern materials literature precisely because it has what almost nothing else in the field has: multiple independent civilian witnesses, an immediate official response, contemporaneous press documentation, police photography, and a preserved physical sample - a civil chain of custody, complete, from 1977 to a Stanford mass spectrometer.

entities.label: The Galileo Project
entities.sub: Harvard-based unclassified UAP and interstellar-object instrumentation programme, founded July 2021
entities.desc: Founded by Avi Loeb on 26 July 2021, four weeks after the ODNI preliminary assessment and following NASA administrator Bill Nelson's June 2021 call for scientific analysis, the Galileo Project is the largest unclassified instrumentation effort ever directed at this problem. Its founding logic is the board's own logic inverted: if the classified system will not release what it holds, build instruments that acquire an independent record nobody can classify. It raised roughly $1.8 million in its first year from donors including Frank Laukien of Bruker Corporation and William A. Linton of Promega, and involves over 100 researchers across Harvard, Caltech, Cambridge, Princeton, Stockholm University, Wellesley and the University of Tokyo. It operates in three branches: high-resolution multimodal observation of UAP, the search for interstellar objects resembling 'Oumuamua under Amir Siraj, and the search for possible extraterrestrial satellites. Its first observatory was installed at Harvard College Observatory in 2022. Unusually for this field, it published its instrumentation and software architecture before its observations - the Journal of Astronomical Instrumentation special issue of 2023, including Loeb and Laukien's project overview and Cloete et al.'s integrated computing platform for detection and tracking - and it continues to publish auxiliary instrumentation in mainstream venues, such as the 2025 Copernicus paper on deploying a geomagnetic variometer station. Its most contested undertaking was the June-July 2023 Pacific Ocean expedition to recover fragments of CNEOS 2014-01-08.

entities.label: Galileo Project Pacific Ocean expedition to the CNEOS 2014-01-08 (IM1) site, June-July 2023
entities.sub: $1.6m magnetic-sled recovery of sub-millimetre spherules off Papua New Guinea
entities.desc: In June and July 2023 the Galileo Project conducted a fully funded expedition, budgeted at approximately $1.6 million, to the Pacific Ocean site of CNEOS 2014-01-08 - a 0.45-metre bolide that entered the atmosphere near the northeast coast of Papua New Guinea on 8 January 2014 and which Amir Siraj and Avi Loeb had argued, in The Astrophysical Journal in November 2022, had an apparently interstellar velocity. The team dragged a magnetic sled across the seabed at a location determined from seismometer data and recovered several hundred sub-millimetre spherules, which Loeb's group classified in Research Notes of the AAS (31 January 2024) and Chemical Geology (December 2024) as including a distinct composition they labelled 'BeLaU' - enriched in beryllium, lanthanum and uranium - which they argued was inconsistent with solar-system materials. The counter-argument arrived quickly and in the ordinary way. Patricio Gallardo argued in Research Notes of the AAS in October 2023 that anthropogenic coal ash could contaminate a micro-meteoritic underwater search. Steve Desch posted critiques in November 2023 and March 2024. Fernando et al. published in Geophysical Journal International in March 2024 showing that the seismic signal used to localise the search was more consistent with truck traffic than with an ocean impact - meaning the sled may have been dragged in the wrong place entirely. Rudraswami, Singh and Pandey published a re-evaluation of the spherules' proposed origin in Chemical Geology in March 2025. This expedition matters to the board as the control case: it is what a genuine, funded, public physical-recovery attempt looks like, including its failure modes, and every part of the argument - claim, rebuttal, re-analysis - happened in the peer-reviewed literature within eighteen months. That is the standard against which seventy years of unpublished government custody should be measured.

entities.label: Edgar Fouche's Military, and DOD contractors reference Documents
entities.sub: Fifteen page self-published compilation of Fouche's decorations, training certificates, performance reports and one 1984 personnel letter, with his own redactions and his own captions
entities.desc: This is the artefact both sides of the Fouche dispute argue over, and it deserves a node so that the arguments attach to a document rather than to a vague 'his documents'. It is a print of an HTML page, produced on 15 June 2014 with PDF-XChange, fifteen pages carrying 23 embedded images. Its text layer is caption and commentary rather than record, and the commentary is mixed-voice: some of it is a compiler's and some is Fouche's own, one passage being signed inside the text 'My guess is he was a Staff Sergeant judging by his skills. - Ed Fouche'. It is legible. WHAT IT CONTAINS is a 1967 basic training photograph, a Department of the Air Force letter of 10 July 1984, an AF Form 77a of 24 August 1979, a 1968 on-the-job training certificate, a 1970 Field Training Detachment certificate in solid state devices, a February 1974 McDonnell Aircraft Corporation certificate, a 1985 Strategic Air Command liaison performance report, a 1993 contractor performance evaluation, five decoration certificates and citations, and two education certificates. WHAT IT DOES NOT CONTAIN is a discharge certificate, a DD Form 214, a security clearance record, an SF 86, a contract, a programme document, or a drawing. It documents an avionics maintenance career and it supports no aerospace, propulsion or reverse-engineering claim whatever. Its final pages are not about Fouche at all: they are an attack on Bob Lazar's documentation, arguing that his W-2 is suspect, that 'MAJ' on his badge 'could also stand for MAJ COM- MAJOR COMMAND', and closing 'I am still scanning the MIT archives for proof that Bob Lazar was a student there... Haven't found anything as of yet.'
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded B on a global pass (rank 226 of 1170, score 44). 4 connections, 2 of them custody/funding/programmatic, 1 official denial recorded against it. Axes C0/A1/D2.

entities.label: AF Form 77a, Letter of Evaluation, 24 August 1979
entities.sub: The one document connecting Fouche to Groom Lake: a temporary duty assignment to AFFTC Detachment 3, Nellis AF Range, 1 June to 14 August 1979
entities.desc: THIS IS THE COUNTERWEIGHT AND IT MUST BE READ AS ONE. It is the strongest artefact in the entire Fouche thread, it is the only document that connects him to Groom Lake, and it should not be buried inside the compilation node. It is an AF Form 77a, a Supplemental Sheet to AF Forms 707, 909, 910, 911 and 475, stamped AUG 20 1979 and dated 24 August 1979, covering a period of observation from 10 June to 14 August 1979. The ratee is Fouche, Edgar A, active duty grade TSGT; the duty title is NCOIC F-15 AIS; the evaluator is Brewer, MSgt, USAF, 57 CRS, Nellis AFB Nevada. Its closing paragraph is the reason the node exists: 'OTHER COMMENTS: This out of cycle report is generated because TSgt Fouche was assigned TDY to the AFFTC-DET 3, Nellis AF Range from 1 June 79 to 14 August 79. His duties and responsibilities for this period have been verified via a separate report. RECOMMENDATION: Promote at the earliest opportunity.' Peter Merlin's own published reference work is what makes that mean anything: 'Since the late 1970s, the Groom Lake facility has been operated by Detachment 3 of the Air Force Flight Test Center.' AND THE FORM STATES ITS OWN LIMIT OUT LOUD. It does not say what he did while there; it refers that out to a separate report, and that separate report is not in the file. Everything else on the form describes conventional work: 'one of TACs best R&D team builders in areas of ECM, ATS, and cryptological support... the implementation of the TEWS-TITE bed-down, which was lauded by TAC Hq LGM... his MAJCOM involvement in cryptological asset training and provisioning'. A documented ten weeks of temporary duty at a documented secret airfield, doing F-15 avionics intermediate shop work, is a real and non-trivial fact. It is not a claim about a craft, and the claims about craft post-date it by a decade in the claimant's own telling.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded C on a global pass (rank 611 of 1170, score 28). 3 connections, 1 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C0/A1/D2.

entities.desc: This is the custody node for three of the artefacts in this cluster, in the same role the board already gives the-black-vault and arvp-fluxliner-project. entities.label: Testor Corp. SR-75 Penetrator and XR-7 Thunderdart model kits, 1993
entities.sub: Commercially published speculative model kits designed by John Andrews whose designations reappear in Fouche's 1998 presentation as inside knowledge
entities.desc: This node exists because it is the only documented prior-art channel found for any part of the Fouche account, and because it is documented on both ends. On 25 December 1993 the Baltimore Sun reported that Testor Corp. was selling 'the SR-75 Penetrator and XR-7 Thunderdart, the latest in a series of highly speculative military miniature models', designed by 'John Andrews, an aviation historian in San Diego who designed the new models, as well as the F-19', and said to have been developed by analysing sonic boom patterns over Southern California, jet exhaust patterns over Nevada, published stealth and high-speed literature and industry speculation. The same article carries the Air Force on the record through its spokeswoman Capt. Mary Dillon: 'We're not saying no comment, we're saying such a plane does not exist.' Four and a half years later Fouche's presentation devotes slides 62 onward to an 'SR-75' called the 'Penetrator' that is also 'a mothership', and elsewhere to an 'SR-74 Scramp'. The designation and the mothership architecture are the same, the priority is documented and one-directional, and the direction of influence is not established. The node is here so that a build session cannot accidentally let the TR-3B cluster imply the reverse.

It is a real black programme of the right era, run by the right agencies, and its published record is precisely what the claim is not. The U.S. Air Force's own fact sheet states that 'The USAF, the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, and the Northrop Corp. worked together from 1978 to 1985 to demonstrate that curved surfaces on an aircraft result in a low radar return signal from ground radar.' The aircraft made its first flight in February 1982 and had flown 135 times by the conclusion of the programme in 1985. It was placed on museum display in May 1996. Its span is 48 feet 2 inches, its length 55 feet 10 inches, its height 10 feet 7 inches, its weight 30,000 pounds, its powerplant two Garrett ATF3-6 high-bypass turbofans, and its armament none. THE POINT OF THE NODE: it is not triangular, its defining feature is curved surfaces, it is 48 feet across rather than 200 to 600, and it was retired before the TR-3B is claimed to have flown. The brief that produced this build asked for the widely reported analysis that the TR-3B narrative derives from or is confused with TACIT BLUE; that analysis was searched for and NOT FOUND, and the primary record argues against it. The documented aircraft that is close to triangular in planform and that did fly out of Groom Lake in the period is the F-117, which is the airframe Peter Merlin identifies in Fouche's own misattributed photograph.

entities.sub: Introduced 6 April 2026 by Rep. Tim Burchett
entities.desc: A four-page bill introduced by Rep. entities.label: Kirkpatrick, 'Here's What I Learned as the U.S. Government's UFO Hunter' (Scientific American)
entities.sub: Op-ed, 19 January 2024, seven weeks after leaving AARO
entities.desc: Published 19 January 2024, seven weeks after Kirkpatrick left AARO and seven weeks before the office published the Historical Record Report Volume I he had authored. It is the clearest single statement of the containment thesis in the former director's own voice. Its arguments: the investigation found no evidence of aliens, only allegations circulated repeatedly by UFO claim advocates; the public whistleblowers never provided evidence to AARO despite invitations and are therefore 'suspect' for preferring to be 'sensationalist in the public eye'; the narrative is 'a textbook example of circular reporting, with each person relaying what they heard, but the information often ultimately being sourced to the same small group of individuals'; the claims derive from 'a small group of interconnected believers' influenced by Robert Bigelow and originating in the defunct AATIP; and belief in a statement is proportional to the volume and repetition of its transmission rather than to the facts. The document matters for three reasons. It is a former officeholder attacking named living witnesses in a scientific journal within weeks of departure. It previews the conclusions of an official report not yet published, which is a rollout technique rather than an analysis. And its central mechanism - circular reporting from a small group - is precisely the mechanism the Department would confirm eighteen months later in the Yankee Blue disclosure, except that the small group seeding the belief was the United States Air Force.

entities.desc: Peru is one of a small group of states that has maintained an official military office for investigating anomalous aerial phenomena. The Fuerza Aérea del Perú office was reopened in 2013-2014 after a period of dormancy, a development the BBC covered on 5 February 2014 under the headline 'Por qué Perú reabrió la oficina de búsqueda de ovnis'. entities.label: Arquivo Nacional (Brazil) - UFO/UAP collection
entities.sub: Arquivo Nacional (Brazil), Fundo Objeto Voador Não Identificado – OVNI, reference BR DFANBSB ARX, 743 registros, produced by the Comando da Aeronáutica
entities.desc: From 2009 the Brazilian Air Force transferred its UAP holdings to the Arquivo Nacional, the Brazilian National Archives, where they are served through the SIAN online image system with full archival references and downloadable page images - a materially more open arrangement than the paid-download model The National Archives at Kew used for the equivalent British files. The release began with the September 2009 declassification of the 1986 Air Defence Command report and continued through 2010, when O Estado de S. Paulo reported on 14 August 2010 that the Aeronáutica had released documents on UFO appearances and the news agency EFE reported on 10 August 2010 that the Air Force had created rules for pilots in case of contact with UFOs. The Air Force's own position, given to BBC Brasil, is that all material available on UFOs has already been sent to the Arquivo Nacional and that it 'does not have specialised professionals to carry out scientific investigations or to issue an opinion about this type of aerial phenomenon' - a denial that also functions as a permanent transfer of the question out of the military and into the archive. As of January 2022 the UFO collection was the second most consulted holding in the Arquivo Nacional, behind only the records of the military dictatorship, and spanned sixty-four years, from the 1952 Barra da Tijuca photographs published by O Cruzeiro to a 2016 Brazilian Air Force pilot sighting report.

entities.label: Operação Prato (Operation Saucer)
entities.sub: Brazilian Air Force I COMAR (Belem/PA) intelligence-section operation, Colares, Para, 1977-1978; documents held in the Arquivo Nacional Fundo OVNI, BR DFANBSB ARX
entities.desc: Operação Prato was the first Brazilian Air Force operation mounted solely to investigate UAP. It followed a wave of reports on the island of Colares in Pará in 1977 in which residents said descending lights - which they called the Chupa-Chupa - had burned and punctured them; villagers held night vigils, lit fires and set off fireworks, and the mayor, José Ildone Favacho Soeiro, formally requested Air Force help. The operation was commanded by Captain Uyrangê Hollanda and executed by the Brazilian Air Force together with the National Information Service, the intelligence service of the military dictatorship. It ran in two documented phases, 20 October to 11 November 1977 and 25 November to 5 December 1977, produced photographs of lights, and was terminated after about four months with the official finding that no unusual phenomena had been found. The files are held by the Arquivo Nacional and were opened from the late 1990s onward; Folha de S. Paulo reported in January 2009 under the headline 'SNI investigou óvnis durante a ditadura' that the dictatorship's intelligence service had been running UFO investigations. The operation's importance to this board is that it is a documented case of a military intelligence apparatus mounting a field collection effort against the phenomenon and then publishing a negative finding, with the commanding officer contradicting that finding twenty years later and dying three months afterwards.

entities.label: Noite Oficial dos OVNIs - the Brazilian 'Night of the UFOs', 19 May 1986
entities.sub: 19-20 May 1986; 21 radar plots, five FAB fighters scrambled from Santa Cruz (RJ) and Anápolis (GO) across four Brazilian states; ministerial press conference 23 May 1986; report released 25 September 2009
entities.desc: On the night of 19 May 1986 Brazilian air traffic control, the CINDACTA integrated air defence and traffic control network and the Brazilian Air Force engaged twenty-one unidentified radar plots over São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Minas Gerais and Goiás. The sequence, as reconstructed by the Air Defence Command's own report and by BBC Brasil, begins at about 20:00 when air traffic controller Sérgio Mota da Silva at São José dos Campos airport saw stationary multicoloured lights; when he dimmed the runway lights the objects approached, and when he raised them they withdrew. At 21:08 an Embraer Xingu, registration PT-MBZ, flown by Colonel Ozires Silva - the founder of Embraer, returning from a meeting with President José Sarney and due to take office as president of Petrobras the following day - reported large red lights and attempted an unsuccessful approach. Santa Cruz Air Base went to alert at 21:39 and Anápolis shortly afterwards. Five fighters were launched: F-5E FAB-4848 flown by Lieutenant Kleber Caldas Marinho at 22:34 and F-5E FAB-4849 flown by Captain Márcio Brisolla Jordão at 22:50 from Santa Cruz; Mirage IIIEs of the 1st Air Defence Group 'Jaguar' from Anápolis including one flown by Captain Armindo Sousa Viriato de Freitas, plus FAB-4918 (Captain Rodolfo Silva e Souza, 23:17) and FAB-4917 (Captain Júlio Cézar Rozemberg, 23:46). The mission ordered was non-aggressive interception. One F-5 pilot tracked a light that climbed to 33,000 feet while changing from white to red to green, held 10 to 12 miles off, and was followed 180 miles out to sea until bingo fuel. Thirteen radar plots appeared behind the second F-5, which turned 180 degrees and saw nothing. A Mirage closed to two miles of a contact that zigzagged and then accelerated away while the interceptor was already supersonic; in a 1993 TV Globo interview the pilot estimated the object's speed at Mach 15. The objects overflew the National Institute for Space Research and the Aerospace Technical Centre at São José dos Campos and the Air Force Academy at Pirassununga.

entities.sub: Brazilian Air Force; ran Operação Prato and the 1986 intercepts; transfers UAP records to the Arquivo Nacional under Portaria 551/GC3 of 9 August 2010
entities.desc: The Brazilian Air Force is the only major air arm that has (a) mounted a dedicated field operation against the phenomenon with its intelligence service, (b) scrambled fighters against it on a national scale and recorded in a classified internal report that the objects were solid and behaved intelligently, (c) had its minister say publicly with the pilots present that it had no explanation, and (d) then transferred its entire holding to a civil national archive and disclaimed further competence. Operação Prato ran on Colares in 1977-78 with the National Information Service. On 19 May 1986 it launched five fighters across four states; the Air Defence Command's report of 2 June 1986 recorded the finding of solid, intelligent behaviour. In 2009-2010 it began transferring documents to the Arquivo Nacional and issued rules for pilots on contact with UFOs. Its standing public position, as given to BBC Brasil, is that everything has gone to the archive and that it has no specialists qualified to investigate the subject scientifically or to give an opinion on it.

entities.label: Knuth et al. (2025), 'The New Science of Unidentified Aerospace-Undersea Phenomena (UAP)', Progress in Aerospace Sciences
entities.sub: 34-author review of UAP studies 1933-present; Knuth lead author, Szydagis co-author
entities.desc: The companion piece to the UAPx field-expedition paper in the same Progress in Aerospace Sciences special edition, and the larger of the two. UAlbany's news office describes it as 'a comprehensive review of studies conducted on UAPs from 1933 to the present, including more than 20 historical government and privately funded projects as well as recent scientific research efforts in Ireland, France, Germany, Norway, Sweden and the United States', with Knuth as lead author 'co-written by Szydagis and more than 30 other researchers from around the world'. SCU's June 2025 press release puts the author count at thirty-four and gives the DOI as 10.1016/j.paerosci.2025.101097. Its stated aims, per the University, are to clarify the historical scientific narrative, to establish that UAP have been observed and recorded for well over 150 years and studied by astronomers, scientists and engineers, and to show that several serious academic efforts in multiple countries are currently collecting instrumented data. Its significance for this board is structural rather than evidentiary: a thirty-four-author review in a high-impact aerospace engineering journal, led from a state university physics department, is the closest thing the subject has to a conventional field-defining literature review, and it exists because two faculty members at a mid-sized SUNY campus were willing to put their names on it.

entities.label: SOYUZUFOTSENTR - USSR Inter-Industry Ufology Research Centre
entities.sub: 1990 Soviet ufology centre with USSR Academy of Sciences institute rights, headed by V. G. Azhazha; named in UK Project Condign
entities.desc: CORRECTED NODE - previously a bookkeeping stub with a null description and no sources. SOYUZUFOTSENTR is on this board because a UK Defence Intelligence Staff report classified SECRET UK EYES ONLY thought it worth naming. Project Condign Volume 3, Chapter 4 records that a 'UFO' Commission was created under the USSR Union of Scientific and Engineering Societies in 1989, and that in 1990 an Inter-Industry Ufology Research Centre - Condign transliterates it SOYUZUFOSENTR - was created to co-ordinate records; that the centre held the rights of an Institute under the USSR Academy of Sciences; and that it was headed by V. G. Azhazha, 'an eminent researcher and former naval submariner'. Condign records a ten-week school with terms of reference to study 'ufology as a science of unidentified flying objects and their interrelations with the universe and, in particular, with the biotechnosphere of the earth'; that the Institute developed light filters, instrumentation and IR and UV photography; and that claimed imagery of 'peculiar spheres, humanoid figures' was reported but, in Condign's dry formulation, 'if the imagery exists, it has never been published'. The centre sits at the hinge between the closed Soviet state effort and the open Russian ufology of the 1990s: it was founded in 1990, the year the SETKA programmes ended, and it was the first Soviet UFO organisation to operate publicly. It should NOT be confused with the KLAS-TV / George Knapp document story. Knapp's 1993 Moscow acquisition came from the Ministry of Defence via Colonel Boris Sokolov; the KGB 'Blue Folder' associated with Popovich and Azhazha is a separate collection. That distinction is why the obvious media edge from this node cannot be written.

entities.label: Waived SAP Notification Group
entities.sub: The persons entitled to notice of, and access to, a waived DoD special access program
entities.desc: The group that receives notification of a WAIVED Department of Defense special access program is not the Gang of Eight, and conflating the two is the single most common error in public argument about how a legacy programme could be hidden. The waived-SAP channel is created by 10 U.S.C. 119(e). Subsection (e)(1) provides: 'The Secretary of Defense may waive any requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c) that certain information be included in a report under that subsection if the Secretary determines that inclusion of that information in the report would adversely affect the national security. Any such waiver shall be made on a case-by-case basis.' Subsection (e)(2) then specifies where the withheld material goes instead: 'If the Secretary exercises the authority provided under paragraph (1), the Secretary shall provide the information described in that subsection with respect to the special access program concerned, and the justification for the waiver, jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees.' The term 'defense committees' is defined not by the general Title 10 definition but by section 119's own subsection (g): 'the Committee on Armed Services and the Committee on Appropriations, and the Defense Subcommittee of the Committee on Appropriations, of the Senate' and 'the Committee on Armed Services and the Committee on Appropriations, and the Subcommittee on Defense of the Committee on Appropriations, of the House of Representatives.' Six bodies, each contributing a chairman and a ranking minority member: twelve members of Congress. This is deliberately narrower than a full committee and deliberately wider than eight. Note that 10 U.S.C. 101(a)(16) defines a different, similar-sounding term, 'congressional defense committees,' as only the Armed Services and Appropriations Committees of the two chambers - four bodies, eight chairs and rankings. Section 119 does not use that definition; it uses its own, which adds the two Defense Appropriations Subcommittees. A board that cites 101(a)(16) for the waived-SAP group would be naming the wrong set. The Gang of Eight is a separate creature governing covert action, not DoD SAPs. Under 50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(2), where the President determines that it is essential to limit access to a covert action finding to meet extraordinary circumstances affecting vital interests of the United States, 'the finding may be reported to the chairmen and ranking minority members of the congressional intelligence committees, the Speaker and minority leader of the House of Representatives, the majority and minority leaders of the Senate, and such other member or members of the congressional leadership as may be included by the President.' Different committees (intelligence, not armed services or appropriations), different people (the four party leaders sit in the Gang of Eight and are absent from the 119(e) group; the appropriators sit in the 119(e) group and are absent from the Gang of Eight), and different subject matter. The structural comparison is where the argument actually lives, and it cuts against the covert-action statute being the tighter one. Title 50 contains two escape valves that Title 10 does not. First, 50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(5)(B) imposes a 180-day clock: within 180 days of a statement of reasons for limiting access, the President must either give all members of the intelligence committees access to the finding or submit a fresh statement of reasons for continuing to withhold. Section 119(e) contains no sunset, no periodic re-justification, and no mechanism that ever widens the circle. A waiver, once made, is permanent as to that report. Second, 50 U.S.C. 3093(g)(1)-(2) requires the President to tell all members of the intelligence committee that a limited notification occurred and to give them a general description of it. Section 119 has no analogue: the members of the Armed Services and Appropriations Committees who are not chair or ranking are never told that a waiver happened at all. They cannot ask about what they do not know exists. That asymmetry - no sunset, no notice of bypass - is the load-bearing limit on congressional oversight of a waived programme, and it is a limit written into the statute rather than an abuse of it. What the twelve can see is also bounded. They receive the withheld report content and the Secretary's justification. They do not thereby acquire subpoena power over the programme, staff who can read the material, or any statutory right to share it with colleagues. What they cannot see is anything the Department declines to characterise as a DoD special access program at all - the recurring allegation in the UAP context being that recovery and reverse-engineering activity was moved into contractor-held or non-DoD structures where section 119 does not reach. Finally, the mechanism's present scope is narrower than it was. Pub. L. 114-328 section 1061(c)(4) lists 'Section 119(a) and (b)' among the reporting requirements it terminates, and section 1061(b)(1) provides that each such report still required as of December 31, 2021 'shall no longer be required to be submitted to Congress after that date.' The Office of the Law Revision Counsel carries this as a Termination of Reporting Requirements note under section 119. The annual SAP budget report and the annual new-SAP designation-and-justification report are therefore gone. Because 119(e)(1) can only waive a requirement 'under subsection (a), (b), or (c),' the waiver authority now has live operation only as to subsection (c), the report on a planned change in classification or a planned declassification and public announcement. Subsections (d), (f) and (g) survive and are not waivable at all - notably 119(f), which bars initiating any SAP until the defense committees are notified and thirty days elapse.

claims.text: THE STATUTORY GROUP AND THE DEPARTMENT'S GROUP ARE NOT THE SAME, AND THE DEPARTMENT'S IS WIDER. The statute, 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2), names only 'the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees' - twelve seats across six committee entities, and no staff. DoD Instruction 5205.11, paragraph 7.2.a.(3), states verbatim: 'Only the chair, the ranking member, the staff directors, and one designated security manager of the defense and intelligence committees will be authorized access to waived DoD SAPs within their committee's respective oversight jurisdiction. Requests to access additional members of Congress or professional staff must be approved by the Secretary of Defense or Deputy Secretary of Defense.' The Department therefore adds two staff categories the statute does not name, and extends the group to the two intelligence committees, which Section 119(g) does not include. Whether that is a lawful gloss or an administrative expansion is a live question the board can put on the record.

The intelligence committees are authorized access only to those DoD SAPs designated by the Secretary of Defense or Deputy Secretary of Defense as intelligence or intelligence related.'

entities.label: Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Disclosure Act - Burlison amendment to the FY2027 NDAA
entities.sub: Adopted by the House 22-23 July 2026; pending in the Senate
entities.desc: The successor to the 2023 Schumer-Rounds UAP Disclosure Act, and the first time such a framework has cleared a chamber. Adopted by the House on 22 July 2026 as an amendment to the Fiscal Year 2027 National Defense Authorization Act - the first year Burlison's UAP disclosure amendment advanced to a House floor vote, after a similar proposal failed to advance in the previous defence-bill cycle. As adopted it establishes a statutory framework for preserving, reviewing and publicly disclosing UAP records; creates a permanent UAP Records Collection at the National Archives; establishes an independent, Senate-confirmed UAP Records Review Board with subpoena authority to determine what is released and what stays classified; requires federal agencies to identify, organise, preserve and transmit UAP records to the National Archives on a statutory timeline; and - the provision with no precedent in existing authority - extends disclosure requirements to covered government contractors. Burlison's own framing places it in support of the executive programme rather than against it: the press release states the amendment supports President Trump's Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters. Read structurally, it is the exact remedy for each defect PURSUE has: PURSUE has no statutory timeline, so the amendment supplies one; PURSUE has no subpoena power, so the amendment creates a board that has one; PURSUE cannot reach Lockheed, Battelle or MITRE, so the amendment extends to contractors; PURSUE's decisions are made by an unchartered task force, so the amendment's board is Senate-confirmed. It is not law. It must survive the Senate's own version and conference later in 2026 and be signed. The 2023 precedent is the reason for pessimism: the original UAP Disclosure Act's eminent-domain and review-board provisions were stripped in conference by House Intelligence and Armed Services leadership before the FY2024 NDAA was signed.

entities.label: Aztec, New Mexico claim, March 1948
entities.sub: Claimed 99-foot disc recovery, Hart Canyon; sourced to convicted fraudsters
entities.desc:
Aztec is on this board for one reason, and it is not that a saucer came down in Hart Canyon. It is the earliest fully traceable example of a crash-retrieval narrative whose entire provenance can be reconstructed end to end - source, motive, transmission, monetisation, exposure, conviction, and revival - and that makes it the control case against which every other retrieval claim on this board has to be measured. Everything the story needed to survive it had: named military witnesses, a specific canyon, a specific craft diameter, a specific body count, a bestselling book, a metal sample, and a federal-sounding cover-up. What it did not have was a crash.

The chain begins with Silas Mason Newton, a Denver oil promoter whose name first reached the FBI on 24 September 1938 on a suspected wire-fraud referral, and Leo (Leonard) A. GeBauer, a Phoenix electronics merchant who appears in the literature under the pseudonym 'Dr. Gee', the 'magnetologist'. On 8 March 1950 Newton, billed only as 'Mr. X' or 'Scientist X', lectured a room of science students at the University of Denver. He told them he had seen two recovered flying saucers held in a secret government facility; one had come down near Aztec, New Mexico, brought down by a 'magnetic fault line', the other near Durango, Colorado. The occupants of the first had been burned dark brown when a porthole blew out; the crew of the second had suffocated from a change in atmosphere. He described the beings as between 38 and 42 inches tall, dressed in cloth that could not be torn, probably from Venus, flying on magnetic propulsion at twice the speed of light.

Frank Scully, a Variety columnist, had already begun retailing the story in his 1949 columns. In 1950 Henry Holt published 'Behind the Flying Saucers', which turned Newton's lecture into a bestseller and into the template. Scully's version put the event in March 1948, a 99-foot craft - the largest UFO reported to that date - containing sixteen humanoid bodies, recovered by the military after a controlled landing in Hart Canyon roughly twelve miles northeast of Aztec, and hauled away for secret research. Scully added that the craft ran on 'magnetic principles', that the crew carried concentrated food wafers and heavy water, and that every dimension of the vehicle was divisible by nine. Martin Gardner, in 'Fads and Fallacies in the Name of Science', took the book apart as 'wild imaginings' and 'scientific howlers'.

The monetisation is the part that matters. Through the late 1940s and early 1950s Newton and GeBauer were travelling the Four Corners selling 'doodlebugs' - devices that in the oil business claim to locate deposits by remote sensing - and their sales pitch was that the doodlebug was built from, or reverse-engineered out of, the alien technology recovered at Aztec. Herman A. Flader, a Denver industrialist, put in $50,000 for a partnership in GeBauer's Colorado Geophysics & Development company, on the represented understanding that each unit cost around $800,000 to build. Dr. Alfred D. Kleyhauer, a Denver optometrist, lost $15,000. When investigators opened the devices they found surplus military radio parts; the estimated build cost was about $3.50 each. When J. P. Cahn of the San Francisco Chronicle demanded a sample of the miracle metal, the sample tested as ordinary aluminium. Cahn published the exposure in True magazine in September 1952 and returned in August 1956 with a second piece cataloguing further victims. Flader pressed charges. Newton and GeBauer were convicted of fraud in 1953 and also faced federal charges for moving the proceeds across state lines. Neither did jail time; the Denver Public Library's account records Newton still on probation and in violation of its terms by June 1955, and on 30 April 1969 he pleaded guilty again, this time to salting the Buckhorn Mine at Silver City, New Mexico. He died in 1972, probably still on probation.

The story should have died in 1956 and did, for about fifteen years - through the mid-1950s to the early 1970s most ufologists treated it as radioactive. It came back because the surrounding mythology gave it somewhere to live. In 1974 Robert Spencer Carr publicly claimed alien bodies recovered near Aztec were held at 'Hangar 18' at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, drawing official Air Force denials. Leonard Stringfield in the late 1970s went further, arguing the craft was one of many the US military had captured and stored. From there the Aztec details - the small burned bodies, the intact hull, the fast military sanitisation of the site - migrated wholesale into later allegedly first-hand accounts of Roswell, which is the single most important structural fact in this dossier: a documented hoax became a donor of detail to the case that the modern disclosure argument rests on.

It also acquired a paper artefact that will not go away. On 22 March 1950, two weeks after Newton's Denver lecture, Guy Hottel, special agent in charge of the FBI's Washington Field Office, filed a one-page memo relaying a third-party account of three recovered circular craft in New Mexico, 'approximately 50 feet in diameter', each holding three bodies 'only three feet tall' in 'metallic cloth', allegedly downed by high-powered radar. The memo ends 'No further evaluation was attempted'. When the FBI launched The Vault in April 2011 the Hottel memo became its most-viewed document, and in March 2013 the Bureau published a statement that it 'does not prove the existence of UFOs; it is simply a second- or third-hand claim that we never investigated', adding that some believe it simply repeats a hoax then in circulation.

Revisionism continues. Aztec's public library ran an annual UFO Symposium as a library fundraiser from 1997 to 2011. Scott and Suzanne Ramsey, with journalism professor Frank Thayer, spent three decades on the case and published 'The Aztec Incident: Recovery at Hart Canyon' (2012) and 'The Aztec UFO Incident' (2016), arguing the crash was real and independently witnessed; Ramsey placed a commemorative plaque at the canyon site in 2007. Nothing in that body of work has displaced the trial record. Tier it accordingly: the fraud is documented, the retrieval is not.

entities.label: UAP Governance Board
entities.sub: Interagency board above AARO; receives the Science Advisory Council
entities.desc: An interagency governance body sitting above AARO whose stated mission includes optimising interagency processes to ensure more effective support to the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office, and to which the UAP Science Advisory Council announced on 17 June 2026 reports. Its existence matters to this board because it is the layer where the question of who actually controls the UAP portfolio is settled, and because AARO's own statutory position - an OSD office under 50 U.S.C. 3373 with a director reporting through USD(I&S) - does not by itself explain a board 'supporting' it. As of 12 August 2026 no charter, membership roster or meeting record for the Governance Board has been published on aaro.mil or war.gov, and its relationship to the PURSUE release programme is undocumented in the public record: PURSUE is run from the Secretary of War's web estate, the Governance Board is described as supporting AARO, and no published instrument connects the two. This is a first-order research target - a named interagency board with no published charter is precisely the object the Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Disclosure Act's records-review machinery would be able to reach.

entities.desc: The standing House Oversight and Government Reform panel that carries the UAP file in the 119th Congress. Chaired by Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (FL-13) with Rep. Jasmine Crockett (TX-30) as ranking member, its Republican membership is Nancy Mace (SC-01), Tim Burchett (TN-02), Lauren Boebert (CO-04), Eric Burlison (MO-07), Eli Crane (AZ-02) and Brandon Gill (TX-26), and its Democratic membership Raja Krishnamoorthi (IL-08), Summer Lee (PA-12), Dave Min (CA-47), Stephen Lynch (MA-08) and Maxwell Frost (FL-10). The roster is the point: Mace chaired the November 2024 UAP hearing, Burchett and Luna convened the July 2023 Grusch hearing, and Burlison employs David Grusch as a Special Advisor. The task force is not a UAP body - its declared remit spans the JFK, RFK and MLK assassination files, Epstein records, MKULTRA and UAP - and that breadth is exactly what allows it to treat UAP as a declassification problem rather than an aerospace one. It held 'Restoring Public Trust Through UAP Transparency and Whistleblower Protection' on 9 September 2025 in HVC-210, and on 30 June 2026 held 'Mind Control and Accountability: Uncovering the Truth of the CIA's MKULTRA Project.' Its instrument of choice in 2026 has been the document demand rather than the hearing: Luna's April 2026 letter that Release 02 was said to answer, and Burlison's 22 May 2026 ten-page, forty-plus-request production demand to MITRE.

entities.label: National Archives Record Group 615 - UAP Records Collection
entities.sub: Statutory collection under FY2024 NDAA sections 1841-1843; transfer deadline 30 September 2025
entities.desc: The statutory destination for federal UAP records, established by the National Archives under sections 1841-1843 of the FY2024 National Defense Authorization Act. The statute requires NARA to establish the Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection and requires each federal agency to review, identify and organise each UAP record, defined to include copies of all Government, Government-provided or Government-funded records relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence. NARA's guidance directed agencies holding releasable UAP records to contact it to initiate transfers before 30 September 2025, in digital form with proper metadata. As of 12 August 2026 seven agencies appeared as contributors in RG 615: the Federal Aviation Administration, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, the Office of the Secretary of Defense, the National Security Agency, the Department of State and the Federal Bureau of Investigation. On 28 August 2026 the Department of the Air Force became the eighth, and the first military department to appear in its own right rather than inside OSD: catalog series 656595571, accession TR-0615-2026-0003, thirty PDF files dated 25 October 1945 to 31 December 1969, accessioned unrestricted. The absences are still most of the story. There is no CIA series. No Defense Intelligence Agency series. No Department of Energy, no NASA, no National Reconnaissance Office, no National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency, no Department of Homeland Security, and no Army or Navy series. What the Air Force transfer establishes is that a military department can comply, which removes the last structural excuse available to the ones that have not. Nor is there any contractor material, because no statute reaches contractor holdings. NARA publishes no compliance list, no roster of agencies determined to hold covered records, and no statement identifying non-compliant agencies; its FAQ describes the framework and is silent on implementation status. The volumetric picture in the bulk-download inventory as last updated 24 April 2025 is equally telling: the electronic-records contributions are tiny - NRC 11.74MB, ODNI 1.29MB, FAA 63.10MB, OSD 103.37MB - against tens of terabytes of legacy Project BLUE BOOK and Roswell material, including a sanitized Blue Book case-file series of roughly 379GB split across ten files and 36.48GB of BLUE BOOK still pictures. In other words, the collection created to receive the modern record has so far received about 180MB of modern electronic records, and is otherwise a digitisation of the Air Force material that was already public.

entities.label: ODNI Memorandum ES 2026-00818 - Preliminary Guidance for Implementation of NDA Waiver
entities.sub: Signed by Aaron Lukas, Principal Deputy DNI; released by Rep. Burlison 1 August 2026
entities.desc: The single most important primary document of the current cycle, and the first paper instrument to name PURSUE as an entity rather than a website. An unclassified ODNI memorandum, control number ES 2026-00818, headed MEMORANDUM FOR DISTRIBUTION and signed by Aaron Lukas, Principal Deputy Director of National Intelligence, subject 'Preliminary Guidance for Implementation of NDA Waiver'. Rep. Eric Burlison obtained it and published it on 1 August 2026. Its opening sentence establishes the architecture: the memorandum 'provides preliminary guidance for the release of all Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (UAP) information to the Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters (PURSUE) Task Force for review and declassification.' PURSUE is therefore a task force with a declassification review function, not merely a publication portal - and it is a task force to which 'all' UAP information across the Intelligence Community is to be released. The operative direction: consistent with Presidential Direction, the Department of War and the Intelligence Community will implement a process ensuring that current and former government employees and contractors with relevant UAP information 'shall have prior non-disclosure agreements (NDA), agreements, oaths, or commitments waived when speaking with authorized government representatives of the All-Domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO) or PURSUE.' The word 'oaths' is doing heavy work: it reaches beyond signed NDAs to the oral secrecy commitments characteristic of unacknowledged special access programmes. All IC members are directed, within 30 days of receipt, to coordinate with ODNI to establish a PURSUE designee and to inform their workforce of the President's order; to ensure the workforce knows that 'any previous or existing NDAs prohibiting disclosure to the President, or designees like PURSUE, are no longer in force'; and that anyone with knowledge of UAP information 'should report all such information to AARO, or to an authorized PURSUE representative.' Detailed reporting procedures were to be disseminated to IC components within a further 30 days, and DoW and ODNI were to issue departments and agencies detailed implementation guidance 'for the broader PURSUE transparency project.' The distribution list is the IC in full: the Directors of CIA, DIA, NGA, NRO, NSA and FBI; the Under Secretary for Intelligence and Security, Department of War; the Under Secretary for Intelligence and Analysis, DHS; the Assistant Secretary for Intelligence and Research, State; the Assistant Secretary for Intelligence and Analysis, Treasury; the Chief of Intelligence, DEA; the Director of the Office of Intelligence and Counterintelligence, Department of Energy; the Deputy Chief of Staff for Intelligence, US Army; the Director of Intelligence, US Marine Corps; the Director of Naval Intelligence; the Deputy Chief of Staff for Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance, US Air Force; the Deputy Chief of Space Operations for Intelligence, US Space Force; and the Assistant Commandant for Intelligence, US Coast Guard. Read against Record Group 615, the list is an indictment: CIA, DIA, NRO, NGA, DOE and the military departments are all addressees of an ODNI memorandum on UAP information and none of them has a series in the statutory National Archives UAP collection.

entities.label: PURSUE Task Force
entities.sub: Presidential task force with declassification review function; named in ODNI ES 2026-00818
entities.desc: An entity whose existence is established by a single primary document and whose composition, charter, chair and location are unknown. ODNI Memorandum ES 2026-00818 of 2026 directs the release of all UAP information across the Intelligence Community to the 'Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters (PURSUE) Task Force for review and declassification', treats PURSUE as a presidential designee capable of receiving information that existing NDAs would otherwise bar, requires every IC element to name a PURSUE designee within 30 days, and refers to 'authorized PURSUE representative[s]' who may take witness reports in the same breath as AARO. That is a body with three powers: it receives compartmented information, it conducts declassification review, and it can waive secrecy obligations by virtue of being a presidential designee. No charter, executive order, membership roster, chair, staff, budget line or physical location for it has been published as of 12 August 2026. The public evidence of its output is the war.gov/UFO portal and its five tranches. The gap between those two facts - a body with declassification authority over the whole IC UAP holdings, and a website with no manifest - is the central structural finding of this domain in 2026. It also creates a new and unexamined risk that Burlison identified in his 29 July 2026 statement: a witness who tells a PURSUE representative what he knows may have satisfied the waiver while placing his account inside an executive-branch channel, and it is not established that the abrogation extends to testimony given to Congress before referral to the executive branch.

entities.label: Hegseth's UAP disclosure statements, Louisville, 23 February 2026
entities.sub: 'Arsenal of Freedom' tour; 'full compliance with that executive order'
entities.desc: On 23 February 2026, at a stop on his 'Arsenal of Freedom' tour in Louisville, Colorado - four days after the President's Truth Social direction - Secretary of War Pete Hegseth committed the Department to UAP disclosure in terms that have shaped everything since. He said the Department would 'be in full compliance with that executive order, [and we're] eager to provide that for the president. So, there'll be more coming on that,' and that 'We've got our people working on it right now...we're digging in.' He characterised the President as 'just committed to disclosure on lots of levels' and warned that 'It'll be a deliberative process' and 'I don't want to over-promise and under-deliver. So, we're going to take a little time.' The phrase 'that executive order' is the crux: no signed executive order on UAP declassification has appeared in the public record, and the contemporaneous reporting describes a social-media post. Either the Secretary of War mischaracterised a Truth Social post as an executive order in public, or an unpublished order exists. In the same reporting Pentagon spokesperson Sue Gough confirmed AARO had examined over 2,000 UAP cases, with approximately 1,000 reports lacking sufficient data held in an Active Archive - growth of at least 400 cases since late 2024. Jordan Flowers of the Disclosure Foundation urged expedited release of unclassified material and warned against 'misleadingly partial or incomplete disclosures.'

entities.desc: The Air Force is the origin point of the entire American UFO record and of the entire American denial record. entities.desc: The CIA was created by the National Security Act of 1947 - signed on 26 July 1947, seventeen days after the Roswell debris story was killed by the Fort Worth weather-balloon photographs - and it is the agency whose documented conduct most nearly matches the pattern this board is built to test. The Agency's own historian, Gerald K. Haines, published 'CIA's Role in the Study of UFOs, 1947-1990' in Studies in Intelligence in 1997; the article is an eighteen-page institutional admission that the Agency ran a UFO effort out of the Office of Scientific Intelligence, convened the Robertson Panel in January 1953 under H. P. Robertson, and adopted a policy of public debunking coupled with the surveillance of civilian UFO organisations. Haines additionally records the Agency's later position that U-2 and OXCART overflights accounted for a large share of the UFO reports of the late 1950s and 1960s, a claim that simultaneously excuses the deception and concedes that the Agency knowingly allowed false explanations to stand. The CIA maintains a public FOIA collection, 'UFOs: Fact or Fiction?', which it characterises as containing 'CIA information on this subject from the 1940s through the early 1990s', consisting mostly of 'cables reporting unsubstantiated UFO sightings in the foreign press and intra-Agency memos about how the Agency handled public inquiries'. That framing is itself a claim: it asserts that the Agency's UFO holdings are administrative rather than substantive, and it is the assertion that every subsequent FOIA fight has contested.

entities.label: SFFAS 56 - Classified Activities (FASAB, 4 October 2018)
entities.sub: Federal accounting standard authorising modification of public financial reports to protect classified information
entities.desc: Statement of Federal Financial Accounting Standards 56, 'Classified Activities', is the single most consequential documented change to the mechanics of federal financial concealment in the modern era, and it is entirely public, dated and citable. Issued by the Federal Accounting Standards Advisory Board on 4 October 2018 and effective for reporting periods beginning after 30 September 2018, it does for accounting what a special access program does for information: it creates a lawful, standards-blessed route by which the numbers a citizen reads in a government financial statement need not be the numbers in the books. Paragraph 8 permits an entity to 'modify information required by other standards if the effect of the modification does not change the net results of operations or net position', to have a component reporting entity 'excluded from one reporting entity and consolidated into another reporting entity', and to apply Board Interpretations allowing further modifications. Paragraph 9 defines 'modify' with unusual candour: 'Presenting amounts associated with one financial statement line item in another financial statement line item but not presenting narrative explaining the modification', and 'Omitting required disclosures, RSI, or RSSI that would otherwise reveal classified information.' Paragraph 12 requires component entities to disclose that the standards permit such modifications while expressly forbidding them to disclose whether they applied the Statement; paragraph 13 applies the same rule government-wide, requiring only the statement that 'modifications may have been made to certain presentations' and prohibiting identification of which Interpretations were used. The Board's Basis for Conclusions explains the reasoning: identifying which entities applied the standard 'would reveal classified information' and would let users track changes over time. The Department of Defense identified the need for the standard in August 2016 - two months after the DoD Inspector General published the Army General Fund adjustments report - citing the conflict between generally accepted accounting principles and classification obligations under Executive Order 13526. The standard does not authorise misstatement of net position at the consolidated level except through the consolidation route in paragraph 8(b), and it does not restrict cleared auditors, who continue to see the unmodified figures in appropriate environments. What it authorises is precisely the thing this board is about: a published number that is deliberately in the wrong place, with no note telling the reader that it has been moved.
entities.tierRationale: Re-graded B on a global pass (rank 227 of 1170, score 44). 4 connections, 2 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C0/A2/D3.

entities.sub: Standard-setting body for US federal financial reporting; author of SFFAS 56
entities.desc: FASAB was created in October 1990 by the Secretary of the Treasury, the Director of the Office of Management and Budget and the Comptroller General to set generally accepted accounting principles for the federal government. It is a nine-member board sponsored by the three principals, and its pronouncements are recognised as GAAP for federal entities by the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants. entities.label: Summary Report on 'Unsupported Journal Voucher Adjustments' (Skidmore and Fitts, 2017)
entities.sub: Compilation of OIG/GAO-reported unsupported adjustments at DoD and HUD, FY1998-FY2015
entities.desc: Mark Skidmore, an economist at Michigan State University, and Catherine Austin Fitts, a former Assistant Secretary of Housing at HUD and former managing director at Dillon Read, compiled the unsupported journal voucher adjustment figures reported in publicly available Inspector General and Government Accountability Office documents for the Department of Defense and the Department of Housing and Urban Development across fiscal years 1998 to 2015. Their summary report, dated September 2017, arrives at approximately $21 trillion for DoD and approximately $350 billion for HUD. The figure is a sum of gross adjustment amounts drawn from summary tables in OIG reports; the authors state explicitly that 'The Inspector General's reports that are available to the public only provide summary information; thus it is impossible for us to conduct a detailed assessment of the nature of these unsupported adjustments and errors', and that data could not be recovered for a number of years. The number is therefore not a measure of money that went missing, was stolen, or was spent off-book, and the authors do not claim that it is. What it is, and what makes it usable, is an aggregate index of the scale at which two cabinet departments made accounting entries they could not document, sustained over eighteen years and across administrations of both parties. The figure has been repeatedly and damagingly overstated in secondary coverage as '$21 trillion missing'; that formulation is indefensible and should never be used on this board. The defensible formulation is: over eighteen fiscal years, DoD and HUD made publicly reported unsupported adjustments whose gross value totalled roughly $21 trillion, and neither department can say what those entries were for.

entities.label: National Intelligence Program (NIP)
entities.sub: The non-DoD-controlled half of the US intelligence budget; funded across many agencies, controlled by the DNI
entities.desc: The National Intelligence Program is the intelligence budget that the Director of National Intelligence controls, as distinct from the Military Intelligence Program which the Secretary of Defense controls. Its aggregate appropriated total has been published annually since FY2007 under section 601 of the Implementing Recommendations of the 9/11 Commission Act of 2007 (Public Law 110-53), which requires the DNI to disclose the aggregate amount appropriated within thirty days of the end of each fiscal year; since February 2011 the aggregate request has also been published, under section 364 of the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2010. The NIP is not itself an appropriation - it is a cross-cutting programme construct whose money is appropriated inside other bills and other departments' accounts, chiefly the Department of Defense, which is the structural fact that makes the intelligence budget a concealment mechanism rather than merely a secret. A dollar appropriated in a Department of Defense account, scored to the NIP, controlled by the DNI, and executed by a contractor is a dollar with four different institutional owners and one public number.

entities.label: The Classified Annex (NDAA and Defense Appropriations)
entities.sub: Unpublished companion document carrying the force of law over classified programme funding
entities.desc: Every year Congress enacts two sets of numbers for the Department of Defense. One is printed in the United States Statutes at Large and can be read by anyone. The other is the classified annex, and it has been given, by express statutory text, exactly the same legal force. Section 8006(a) of the Department of Defense Appropriations Act for fiscal year 2026 (division of Public Law 119-75, approved 3 February 2026) provides that with regard to the programme, project and activity tables in the explanatory statement 'and the tables contained in the classified annex accompanying this Act, the obligation and expenditure of amounts appropriated or otherwise made available by this Act for those programs, projects, and activities are hereby required by law to be carried out in the manner provided by such tables to the same extent as if the tables were included in the text of this Act.' The authorisation side does the same thing: section 4001(d) of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026 (Public Law 119-60, approved 18 December 2025) states simply 'Applicability to Classified Annex.--This section applies to any classified annex that accompanies this Act', section 4001(a) having just provided that a dollar amount in a funding table is thereby authorised for obligation and expenditure. The annex is prepared by the four defense committees, is not printed in the Congressional Record, is not available to members who are not on the relevant committees without arrangement, and is never published. Its contents are the programme-element-level detail for classified activity: the actual line items, the actual dollar figures, the actual programme names. Section 8059 of the FY2026 appropriations act directs the Secretary of Defense to continue providing 'a classified quarterly report ... on certain matters as directed in the classified annex accompanying this Act' - the annex is thus itself the source of reporting requirements whose subject matter is unknown to the public. This is the structure that answers the question posed at the top of this board: money reaches a programme that does not appear as a budget line because the budget line exists, is legally binding, and is in a document nobody outside a small circle has read.

entities.label: Section 8005 Transfer Authority (annual DoD Appropriations Act)
entities.sub: $6 billion per year of Secretary-level authority to move appropriated funds between accounts
entities.desc: Section 8005 is the standing provision of every Department of Defense Appropriations Act by which the Secretary of Defense, with the approval of the Director of the Office of Management and Budget, may move money that Congress appropriated for one purpose to a different purpose. In the FY2026 Act the ceiling is $6,000,000,000; the FY2024 Act carried the same figure. The conditions are that the transfer be to 'higher priority items, based on unforeseen military requirements', that it not be used for an item Congress has denied, and that the Secretary 'notify the Congress promptly of all transfers'. Two features make it structurally important here. First, notification is after the fact - the statute requires prompt notice of transfers made, not prior approval. Second, section 8006(b) of the FY2026 Act provides that amounts specified in the explanatory-statement and classified-annex tables 'shall not be treated as subdivisions of appropriations for purposes of section 8005', with section 8005 applying only when the movement crosses appropriation accounts; the identical carve-out appears at section 4001(c) of the NDAA, which states that transfer or reprogramming of an amount in a funding table 'shall not count against a ceiling on such transfers or reprogrammings under section 1001 of this Act or any other provision of law, unless such transfer or reprogramming would move funds between appropriation accounts.' In plain terms: movement of money among the specific programmes and projects listed in the classified annex, so long as it stays inside a single appropriation account, is neither counted against the transfer ceiling nor separately reported. Section 8005 was the authority the Department used in 2019 to move $2.5 billion to border wall construction, litigation over which produced a substantial body of case law on the meaning of 'unforeseen military requirements' and 'denied by the Congress' - the only sustained judicial examination of the mechanism.

There is no more precisely fitted mechanism in the federal financial system for the specific allegation this board exists to test: money reaching a private contractor's custody, funding work of the contractor's own definition, on material the contractor holds, without a congressionally identified programme line and without government ownership of the product. It is not a loophole in the sense of an oversight failure - it is a designed feature, intended to keep an industrial research base alive. What makes it evidentiary rather than merely structural is that Congress legislated against it by name in the UAP context: section 1687(b) of the FY2024 NDAA and section 7343(c) of the FY2024 Intelligence Authorization Act both provide that IR&D funding relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena shall not be allowable as an indirect expense unless the material and information is made available to the intelligence and defense committees and to congressional leadership. That is the named mechanism, in statute, dated 22 December 2023.

entities.label: 50 U.S.C. 3510 - CIA unvouchered funds (CIA Act of 1949, sec. 8)
entities.sub: Statutory authority to spend appropriated money outside all normal accounting law
entities.desc: Enacted as section 8 of the Central Intelligence Agency Act of 1949 on 20 June 1949, this is the oldest and bluntest black-budget instrument in American law, and it has never been repealed or narrowed. The operative text: 'The sums made available to the Agency may be expended without regard to the provisions of law and regulations relating to the expenditure of Government funds; and for objects of a confidential, extraordinary, or emergency nature, such expenditures to be accounted for solely on the certificate of the Director and every such certificate shall be deemed a sufficient voucher for the amount therein certified.' Two clauses, two different powers. The first disapplies the whole body of federal expenditure law to Agency spending. The second provides that for confidential, extraordinary or emergency objects the Director's own signature is the entire accounting record - no receipt, no contract file, no audit trail, and by statute nothing further may be demanded. The provision dates from 1949, which places it squarely inside the period in which the alleged recovery programme is said to have been established and in which the institutional architecture of concealment was being built. Any account of how a programme could be financed for decades without appearing in any auditable record must begin here, because Congress wrote the answer in 1949 and has left it on the books ever since.

entities.label: 50 U.S.C. 3306 - Public disclosure of NIP aggregate amounts
entities.sub: The entire statutory transparency regime for the intelligence budget: two numbers a year, waivable
entities.desc: This section, enacted as section 601 of the Implementing Recommendations of the 9/11 Commission Act of 2007 and later supplemented for the request side by section 364 of the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2010, is the sum total of what Congress has required to be told to the public about the intelligence budget. Subsection (a): at the time the President submits the budget, he 'shall disclose to the public the aggregate amount of appropriations requested for that fiscal year for the National Intelligence Program.' Subsection (b): 'Not later than 30 days after the end of each fiscal year, the Director of National Intelligence shall disclose to the public the aggregate amount of funds appropriated by Congress for the National Intelligence Program for such fiscal year.' Subsection (c) permits the President to waive or postpone either disclosure by submitting to the intelligence committees an unclassified statement that disclosure would damage national security together with a statement of reasons that may be classified. The 9/11 Commission had recommended that the overall figure be disclosed precisely so that the public could hold the intelligence enterprise to account; what emerged in statute is the minimum reading of that recommendation.

entities.label: Line item 'CLASSIFIED PROGRAMS' / Program Element 9999999999
entities.sub: The published, legally binding budget lines that state a number and nothing else
entities.desc: The most direct answer to how money reaches a programme that does not appear as a budget line is that it does appear as a budget line - a line whose title is the word 'CLASSIFIED' and whose only other content is a dollar figure. In the funding tables of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026 (Public Law 119-60, division D), twenty-five separate rows are titled 'CLASSIFIED PROGRAMS'. Summed, they carry $95.786 billion requested and $95.907 billion authorized. The largest single one is line 077A, Other Procurement, Air Force: $26,920,092 thousand - $26.92 billion of procurement money in one Air Force appropriation account, described by one word. Immediately above it sits line 077, 'SPECIAL UPDATE PROGRAM', at $1,178,397 thousand, an equally uninformative title with a long history in the Air Force budget. Other Procurement, Air Force is the account in which the intelligence community's aerial and space reconnaissance funding has historically been carried, and this row is what defense-budget analysts call the Air Force 'pass-through': money that appears in the Air Force's total obligational authority, counts against the Air Force topline, and is not spent by or controlled by the Air Force. On the research side the concealment is even more literal: classified research, development, test and evaluation appears under Program Element number 9999999999 - an all-nines placeholder in the Department's own programme element numbering system - with $22,264,031 thousand requested for the Air Force alone at line 293A in FY2026, and further nine-nines rows in the Navy ($2,554,769 thousand at line 259A) and Special Operations ($8,276,313 thousand at line 298A). Operation and Maintenance, Defense-Wide carries $22,750,830 thousand at line 530A; Operation and Maintenance, Army carries $2,385,523 thousand at line 590A. The three-year series computed directly from the enacted funding tables runs: FY2024, twenty-two rows, $86.912 billion authorized; FY2025, twenty-four rows, $88.682 billion; FY2026, twenty-five rows, $95.907 billion. These are the visible edges of the black budget. What they fund is in the classified annex.

entities.label: The misappropriation allegation: Grusch's ICIG complaint and sworn testimony
entities.sub: May 2022 ICIG urgent-concern complaint; 26 July 2023 sworn testimony to House Oversight
entities.desc: The specific allegation that programme funds were moved into private contractor custody outside congressional oversight has a named source, a date, a legal vehicle and an oath. David Charles Grusch, formerly the National Reconnaissance Office's representative to the Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force and a senior technical adviser on UAP analysis at the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency, filed a Disclosure of Urgent Concern and Complaint of Reprisal with the Intelligence Community Inspector General in May 2022, through counsel Charles McCullough III - himself a former Intelligence Community Inspector General. The ICIG found the complaint credible and urgent in July 2022. Grusch then briefed the staffs of the congressional intelligence committees in closed session. On 5 June 2023 he went on the record with Leslie Kean and Ralph Blumenthal in The Debrief, stating: 'Individuals on these UAP programs approached me in my official capacity and disclosed their concerns regarding a multitude of wrongdoings, such as illegal contracting against the Federal Acquisition Regulations and other criminality and the suppression of information across a qualified industrial base and academia.' That sentence is the named mechanism: not a generic accusation of secrecy but a specific claim of procurement fraud - contracting conducted outside the Federal Acquisition Regulation, which is the body of law governing how the government buys things and what the government owns when it has paid. On 26 July 2023 Grusch testified under oath before the Subcommittee on National Security, the Border, and Foreign Affairs of the House Committee on Oversight and Accountability, at a hearing titled 'Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena: Implications on National Security, Public Safety, and Government Transparency', alongside Ryan Graves and Commander David Fravor. His written statement records that he was 'informed in the course of my official duties of a multi-decade UAP crash retrieval and reverse engineering program' to which he was denied access, and refers to 'Non-Human Reverse Engineering Programs'; the specific financial detail he declined to give in open session, offering it in a classified setting. Five months later Congress enacted section 1687 of the FY2024 NDAA, barring funds for unreported UAP special access activity and barring UAP-related contractor independent research and development from being an allowable indirect cost. The sequence - complaint, credible-and-urgent finding, closed briefings, sworn testimony, statute naming IR&D - is the strongest documented chain on this board connecting an allegation about money to legislative action about money.

entities.label: Ministry of Defence UFO Desk (Secretariat (Air Staff) / Directorate of Air Staff)
entities.sub: UK civil-service desk receiving and triaging public UAP reports, c.1950s-2009
entities.desc: The 'UFO desk' was the Ministry of Defence's public-facing single point of entry for unidentified aerial phenomena reports from the British public, police, military and civil aviation. It sat within the Secretariat (Air Staff) and latterly the Directorate of Air Staff, and its defining characteristic - attested by its own last desk officer to hold the post publicly, Nick Pope, and by The National Archives' description of the released files - is that it was deliberately never given a project name of the Project Blue Book kind, because the government wished to play down the extent of its interest. The desk's formal public line for five decades was that UAP reports were of no defence significance. The files released by The National Archives between 2008 and 2013 show that the desk simultaneously routed material to the Defence Intelligence Staff section DI55, briefed ministers, answered parliamentary questions, and in the last years handled the largest volume of sighting reports in thirty years. The National Archives' description of the final June 2013 tranche states plainly that it covers 'the final two years of the Ministry of Defence's UFO Desk (from late 2007 until November 2009)' and invites researchers to 'discover the reasons behind the closure of the UFO desk ... and the disclosure campaign for the truth, which was sparked by the closure of the UFO Desk'. The desk was closed on 1 December 2009, the MoD having, in the broadcaster's later summary, 'deemed it surplus to the UK's defence requirements'. The closure took effect nine years after the Defence Intelligence Staff's own Project Condign study had made exactly that recommendation as its single key recommendation.
