entities.label: Project Condign
entities.sub: UK Defence Intelligence Staff UAP study, 1997-2000
entities.desc: Project Condign is the codename of the secret study run by the UK Defence Intelligence Staff between 1997 and 2000 whose product, 'Unidentified Aerial Phenomena in the UK Air Defence Region', is the most substantive government UAP analysis released by any American ally. The Ministry of Defence's own description of its origin is precise: 'During a policy review in 1996 into the handling of Unidentified Aerial Phenomena sighting reports received by the Ministry of Defence, a study was undertaken to determine the potential value, if any, of such reports to Defence Intelligence. Consistent with Ministry of Defence policy, the available data was studied principally to ascertain whether there is any evidence of a threat to the UK, and secondly, should the opportunity arise, to identify any potential military technologies of interest.' The second of those two objectives is the one that matters to this board: the British government commissioned a classified study explicitly to see whether UAP could be exploited militarily. The report was classified UK SECRET UK EYES ONLY in its sensitive volumes and UK RESTRICTED for the executive summary, ran to four volumes and roughly 400 pages, and drew on about 10,000 reports. Its author was never named; the MoD's publication-scheme record gives only 'DAS'. It was released on 15 May 2006 following a September 2005 FOI request by David Clarke and Gary Anthony.

entities.desc: The Condign report's actual conclusions are consistently misdescribed. entities.desc: The Flying Saucer Working Party was the first British government body constituted to answer the question, set up under the Directorate of Scientific Intelligence and the Joint Technical Intelligence Committee in 1950 at the instigation of Sir Henry Tizard, who reportedly declined to accept that reports should be dismissed without investigation. Its report, delivered in June 1951, concluded against the reality of the phenomenon and recommended that no further investigation be undertaken - the same shape of conclusion, and the same self-terminating recommendation, that Condign would reach half a century later. The report was itself kept classified for decades and only reached The National Archives in the 2000s. The working party's existence establishes that the British state's engagement with the question is continuous from 1950, predating the MoD UFO desk, and that the recommendation to stop looking has been made and then quietly reversed more than once.

entities.label: COMETA - Comité d'Études Approfondies
entities.sub: French 1901-law association of retired general officers and IHEDN auditors, 1996-c.2006
entities.desc:
COMETA is the document that has no American equivalent. A committee of retired French flag officers - an air force general in the chair, a vice-admiral, a weapons engineer general, a chief of police from the Interior Ministry, a research director from ONERA - spent close to three years reviewing UAP case material, wrote ninety pages under the title 'UFOs and Defense: What Should We Prepare For?', concluded that the extraterrestrial hypothesis could not be excluded and was the most credible of the available explanations, and put their names on it. It was not commissioned by the French state, and its authors are careful about that. But it was written by people the French state had trained to think about national defence, using material from the French state's own UAP office, and it reads as a defence staff study rather than a polemic.

The committee's institutional centre of gravity is the Institut des Hautes Études de Défense Nationale. Almost every named member is an IHEDN auditor, identified by promotion number: Michel Algrin, doctor of political science and attorney-at-law (AA 35); Pierre Bescond, Weapons Engineer General, 2nd Section (AA 48); Denis Blancher, Chief of Police, Police Nationale, Ministry of the Interior; Jean Dunglas, honorary engineer general (AR 48); Bruno Le Moine, Air Force General, 2nd Section (AA 41); Françoise Lepine of the Fondation pour les Études de Défense (AA 33); Christian Marchal, research director at ONERA; Marc Merlo, Admiral, 2nd Section (AA 35); and Alain Orszag, Weapons Engineer General, 2nd Section. General Denis Letty, Air Force, 2nd Section (AA 35), chaired it. The report carries a foreword by Professor André Lebeau, former chairman of CNES, and one by General Bernard Norlain, former director of IHEDN, whom Letty visited at IHEDN in March 1995 to explain the project. Letty thanks both, saying that without them 'COMETA would not have been born'.

The report's own account of its lineage matters for this board because it closes a loop back to GEIPAN. COMETA's introduction states that in 1976 an IHEDN committee chaired by General Blanchard of the Gendarmerie Nationale opened the unidentified flying objects file with the objective of making proposals for organising research and data collection, that 'the goal was achieved, because the recommendations of this committee were followed in the creation of' GEPAN, and that twenty years later it seemed useful to take stock again. In other words the same institution produced both the French state's UAP office and, two decades on, the committee that reviewed its output.

The evidentiary base is the French official record. Contributors included Jean-Jacques Velasco, then head of SEPRA at CNES; François Louange, chief executive of the image-analysis firm Fleximage; the pilots Jean-Charles Duboc, Jean-Pierre Fartek and René Giraud; Edmond Campagnac, former technical director of Air France at Antananarivo; Squadron Commander Michel Perrier of the Gendarmerie Nationale; an official of the DGAC; and Air Force General Joseph Domange. Letty specifically thanks the commander of the Air Force Air Operations Command Center for its participation in the investigation into Air France flight AF 3532 of 28 January 1994.

On substance, COMETA reproduces GEPAN/SEPRA's four-category scheme and then states the number that the whole document turns on: 'Category D UAPs represent 4 to 5% of the cases and are called UAP Ds.' Category D means unidentified despite the abundance and quality of the data - not unidentified for want of it. The report's position is that a residue of that size, often attested by consistent testimony and by visual sightings coupled with radar, can no longer be filed as no action: 'if there had only been ten or so UAP D [sightings], this ambiguous file could just have been classified as "no action," but we are no longer at that point and are far beyond that. Thus we are forced to seek plausible explanations.' It records around one hundred GEPAN/SEPRA investigations, several of which 'demonstrated, in the end, the physical presence of a phenomenon the nature and origin of which remain unknown', singling out Trans-en-Provence (8 January 1981) and 'Amaranth' (21 October 1982), documented in GEPAN technical memoranda 16 and 17. On aeronautical cases it records twelve French cases, only three or four of them category D; the first, in 1951, involving Vampire aircraft near Orange; and AF 3532 on 28 January 1994 as the first French case of a visual sighting correlated with radar over fifty seconds. It also draws on Dominique Weinstein's enumeration of 489 well-documented aeronautical UAP D cases worldwide since 1942, most from official sources.

COMETA is structured in three parts - facts and testimonies, the extent of current knowledge, and UFOs and defence - plus a conclusion and seven appendices, among them 'Radar Detection in France', 'Life in the Universe', 'Colonization of Space' and 'The Roswell Affair - Disinformation'. Its recommendations are set out in the introduction: give civilian and military pilots enough information to adopt adapted conduct when faced with these phenomena, and inform the public and decision-makers more generally; develop the actions of SEPRA and promote supplemental scientific monitoring and research; and consider the strategic, political and religious consequences of a possible confirmation of the extraterrestrial hypothesis, 'the bizarre connotation of which it is advisable to eliminate here and now'. Letty's own framing, in the foreword, is the sentence most often quoted from the document and is verbatim: 'The accumulation of well-documented sightings made by credible witnesses forces us to consider from now on all of the hypotheses regarding the origin of unidentified flying objects, or UFOs, and the extraterrestrial hypothesis, in particular.'

COMETA the association was registered under the French law of 1901 on 24 February 1999, having operated informally since 1996, and went dormant around 2006. The report appeared in July 1999 in a special issue of VSD, was reissued by Éditions du Rocher in 2003, and was not widely circulated in its original form because of copyright restrictions. According to Robert Roussel, citing Olivier Schrameck, Prime Minister Lionel Jospin read and annotated it 'to mark his interest'. There was no formal government response beyond that. GEIPAN made an archive of the report public in 2007.

entities.label: Les OVNI et la Défense: à quoi doit-on se préparer? (COMETA report, July 1999)
entities.sub: 90-page report by French retired general officers; delivered to PM Lionel Jospin
entities.desc: The COMETA report is the only document in which a group of senior figures from a NATO state's defence establishment sets out, in their own names, that the extraterrestrial hypothesis is the explanation best supported by the evidence, and then recommends that their government apply diplomatic pressure to the United States to open the subject. It was published in July 1999 as a special issue of the French magazine VSD and delivered to Prime Minister Lionel Jospin. Its conclusion states that CNES's studies with the Gendarmerie Nationale and the Air Force 'tally with other research conducted more or less discretely abroad, mainly in the United States' and that together they 'demonstrate the almost certain physical reality of completely unknown flying objects with remarkable flight performances and noiselessness, apparently operated by intelligent [beings]'. It states that 'secret craft definitely of earthly origin (drones, stealth aircraft, etc.) can only explain a minority of cases'; that 'a single hypothesis sufficiently takes into account the facts and, for the most part, only calls for present-day science. It is the hypothesis of extraterrestrial visitors'; and that this hypothesis 'certainly has not been categorically proven, but strong presumptions exist in its favor and if it is correct, it is loaded with consequences'. The report carries a forward by former CNES chairman André Lebeau and a preface by former IHEDN director General Bernard Norlain, and its opening section records that the whole French official apparatus - GEPAN, then SEPRA - exists because a 1976 IHEDN committee chaired by General Blanchard of the Gendarmerie recommended it.

entities.label: GEPAN - Groupe d'Étude des Phénomènes Aérospatiaux Non-identifiés
entities.sub: CNES UAP study group, Toulouse, 1977-1988
entities.desc: GEPAN was established inside CNES, the French national space agency, in 1977 on the recommendation of a 1976 IHEDN committee chaired by General Blanchard of the Gendarmerie Nationale, with CNES director general Yves Sillard's authority and Claude Poher as inaugural director. It is the first and still the only permanent civilian government UAP office in the world with a published case archive. Its operating model - the Gendarmerie Nationale, the French national police force, teletyping sighting reports directly to the agency, with CNES laboratory resources available for physical-trace analysis - is the single most important institutional difference between the French and Anglo-American approaches. A contemporaneous assessment held in the US National Security Agency's declassified UFO document collection describes GEPAN's June 1978 five-volume, roughly 500-page report to its own scientific council: three special groups (rapid intervention, physical traces, radar alert) had been created; eleven high-credibility, high-strangeness cases were studied in depth, of which only one proved to have a conventional explanation; each case was worked by a four-person team including a psychologist. The NSA-held assessment concludes that 'the care with which distances, angles, and psychological factors were evaluated makes the bulk of the Condon Report seem very poor by comparison', and records that the original French report 'was limited to 120 or 140 copies and was secret'. GEPAN was renamed SEPRA in 1988.

entities.sub: CNES successor to GEPAN, 1988-2004
entities.desc: SEPRA is the name GEPAN carried from 1988 to 2004 and the name under which the French service appears in the COMETA report. The renaming is itself informative: the office was rebadged in 1988 as the Atmospheric Re-entry Phenomena Expertise Department, a title that describes space-debris re-entry rather than UAP, and only in 2000 was the acronym redefined to Service d'Expertise des Phénomènes Rares Aérospatiaux, rare aerospace phenomena. Jean-Jacques Velasco headed it throughout. The Gendarmerie routing arrangement continued, giving SEPRA access to a national database of reports, and CNES technical resources remained available for physical-trace cases such as Trans-en-Provence in 1981. COMETA's second recommendation was directed squarely at this office: boost SEPRA's human and material resources, extend its collection to all of Europe and worldwide, maintain and develop its databases, and raise its foreign-relations status. The service was renamed GEIPAN in 2005 and Velasco was succeeded by Jacques Patenet.

entities.label: GEIPAN - Groupe d'Études et d'Informations sur les Phénomènes Aérospatiaux Non identifiés
entities.sub: CNES unit, Toulouse; the world's only permanent civilian state UAP office with a public case database
entities.desc:
GEIPAN is the answer to the question the US posture keeps deflecting: what does it actually look like when a government decides that unidentified aerospace phenomena are a normal object of public administration. The answer is a two- or three-person office in a space agency, a volunteer investigator corps, a steering committee of police, gendarmes, air force, meteorologists and scientists, a published four-tier classification, and a searchable public archive of every closed case. It has run without interruption since 1977 under three names.

CNES states plainly on its own site that it has studied unidentified aerospace phenomena since 1977, the year GEPAN - the Groupe d'Étude des Phénomènes Aérospatiaux Non identifiés - was created. Its origin was not a scandal or a leak but a recommendation: a 1976 Institut des Hautes Études de Défense Nationale committee, chaired by General Blanchard of the Gendarmerie Nationale, opened the UFO file with the explicit objective of making proposals for organising research and data collection, and GEPAN was created on the back of that committee's recommendations. That lineage is stated in the COMETA report's own introduction. Claude Poher directed GEPAN at its inception. In 1988 GEPAN was replaced by SEPRA, the Service d'Études des Phénomènes de Rentrées Atmosphériques, which absorbed the UAP function into a unit whose principal job was routine monitoring of orbital debris and re-entry risk objects. At the end of 2001 the CNES Direction Générale commissioned an audit to decide the activity's future. The 2005 outcome was restructuring rather than closure: GEIPAN replaced SEPRA, and the audit carried what CNES calls 'une recommandation importante d'informer le public en toute transparence' - an important recommendation to inform the public in complete transparency. That recommendation is embedded in the acronym; the added 'I' stands for Information. It was implemented starting in 2007 with the online publication of GEIPAN's archives and case files.

The structure is worth stating precisely because it is the operational counter-model. GEIPAN sits under the deputy directorate of the Toulouse Space Centre. It is steered by a comité de pilotage (COPEIPAN) chaired by a recognised figure from the aerospace world and composed of representatives of the country's civil and military authorities - Gendarmerie nationale, civil aviation, meteorology, the Air and Space Force, scientific research - plus CNES. That committee's job is to analyse GEIPAN's results and make recommendations to CNES on its direction. Beneath it sits a collège d'experts of roughly thirty multidisciplinary volunteers who take the hardest cases, and a corps of volunteer field investigators across France who are mandated case by case and work to the methods set out in GEIPAN's investigator guide. GEIPAN holds standing conventions with the Gendarmerie, the Air Force, civil aviation, the Navy and Météo France for rapid access to hard data, and works with CNRS and the CEA. The permanent staff, per GEIPAN's own history page, is two full-time CNES agents - the head and an assistant - supported by external contractors for case analysis, statistics, anonymisation and archiving. Canada's Office of the Chief Science Advisor, surveying the office in 2025, counted three full-time employees and over 20 trained volunteer investigators. Funding comes out of the general public-service subsidy CNES receives; there is no separate UAP line item. Frederic Courtade has headed GEIPAN since January 2024.

The classification is what makes the archive usable. Each case is scored on two axes - consistency (C), the product of the quantity and reliability of data, and residual strangeness (E) after comparison against known-phenomenon hypotheses - then filed as A (perfectly identified), B (probably identified), C (unidentified for lack of data) or D (unidentified after investigation). Cases in C and D can be reopened if new information arrives. As of the site statistics dated 11 August 2026, 3,381 published classified cases break down as 950 class A (28.1%), 1,310 class B (38.7%), 1,015 class C (30.0%) and 106 class D (3.1%). Canada's report, working from the 2025 figures, recorded 3,188 cases with 3.2% unidentified after investigation and 31.4% unexplained for insufficient data. The residual is small, it is stable, and it is public.

GEIPAN is also unusually explicit about what it is not. Its FAQ states that it is not an independent structure but a technical department of CNES; that it carries no national-security, space-surveillance or alert mission; and that, 'contrary to popular belief', it is not a research group on UFOs, extraterrestrial life or other paranormal phenomena. It uses only recognised scientific knowledge, 'without speculation or unverified hypotheses'. That disclaimer is not evasion - it is the price of the archive, and it is precisely the trade the US system has refused to make.

The substantive work is on the record. In June 1978 GEPAN presented its scientific council with a five-volume, roughly 500-page report on the first semester of 1978; a contemporaneous English-language summary of that report, held in the NSA's public UFO document collection, records that eleven high-credibility, high-strangeness cases were studied in detail, that only one proved to have a conventional explanation, that in ten of the eleven the conclusion was that witnesses had seen a material phenomenon explicable as neither a natural phenomenon nor a human device, and that the report concluded there was behind the phenomenon a 'flying machine. . . whose modes of sustenance and propulsion are beyond our knowledge'. The same summary judges that the care taken with distances, angles and psychological factors 'makes the bulk of the Condon Report seem very poor by comparison'. GEPAN's most cited physical-trace investigation, the Trans-en-Provence landing of 8 January 1981, was published as Note Technique n° 16, 'Analyse d'une trace', issued by CNES in Toulouse on 1 March 1983 and still hosted on the GEIPAN site.

The office's standing outside France is the argument in compressed form. When Canada's Chief Science Advisor set out to design a national UAP reporting system in 2025, GEIPAN was the model it described in the most detail, the example it explicitly told Canada to consider when establishing a dedicated service, and one of only four international bodies - alongside AARO, NASA and Chile's SEFAA - that it recommended Canada partner with.

entities.sub: French national defence studies institute; source of the 1976 committee and the COMETA auditors
entities.desc: IHEDN is the French state's senior strategic-studies institute, whose auditors are drawn from the armed forces, the civil service, industry and the professions. It appears twice in the UAP record, and both appearances are load-bearing. In 1976 a committee of the Institute chaired by General Blanchard of the Gendarmerie Nationale 'opened the unidentified flying objects file' with the objective of making proposals for organising research and data collection on the phenomena; the recommendations of that committee were adopted and produced GEPAN inside CNES in 1977. entities.desc: The Varginha case is the only Latin American event that alleges the full sequence this board is built around: a crash, a recovery, custody of biological material, and an American removal. In 2010 an official Brazilian military inquiry concluded the young women had seen a mentally disabled man nicknamed 'Mudinho', Luiz Antônio de Paula, and that the military vehicle movements were routine maintenance and Fire Brigade activity misinterpreted. Thirty years later the case reached the United States Congress.

entities.label: Project Magnet (Canada)
entities.sub: Canadian Department of Transport UAP and geomagnetic-propulsion study, 1950-1954 (privately to 1962)
entities.desc: Project Magnet was approved by the Canadian Department of Transport on 2 December 1950 following Wilbert Smith's memorandum of 21 November 1950. Its stated goal was to collect data on UFOs and apply anything recovered to practical engineering - specifically to test whether the Earth's magnetic field could be exploited as a propulsion source, which Smith believed the objects were already doing. It drew on Department of Transport facilities with assistance from the Defence Research Board and the National Research Council; Smith's collaborators included Dr James Watt of the DRB, John Thompson of the DOT, Professor J. T. Wilson of the University of Toronto and Dr G. D. Garland of the Dominion Observatory. Its 1952 report is the document that matters: it concluded that the objects were about a hundred feet or more in diameter, capable of several thousand miles per hour and of altitudes above those supporting conventional aircraft or balloons, that 'we are forced to the conclusion that the vehicles are probably extra-terrestrial, in spite of our prejudices to the contrary', and that the next step should be 'a substantial effort towards the acquisition of as much as possible of this technology, which would without doubt be of great value to us'. That is a government engineer, in writing, in 1952, recommending a reverse-engineering programme. In October 1952 Smith set up an instrumented observatory at Shirley's Bay outside Ottawa with a magnetometer, gamma-ray detector, radio receiver, gravity meter and recorders. The Department terminated funding in 1954; Smith continued privately until his death in 1962.

entities.label: Project Second Storey (Canada)
entities.sub: Canadian Defence Research Board committee on flying saucer reports, 1952-1954
entities.desc: Project Second Storey was established in April 1952 by the Defence Research Board, then Canada's military science agency within the Department of National Defence, to examine flying saucer occurrences over Canadian territory as reported by the armed services. It was chaired by the National Research Council astronomer Dr Peter Millman and drew members from Canadian military intelligence and other government agencies, including Wilbert Smith, who reported Project Magnet's findings to it. Its output was procedural rather than investigative: it built a standardised sighting report form and an interrogator's instruction guide with a weighting system intended to minimise the 'personal equation' - an early attempt at scoring witness reliability that anticipates GEIPAN's consistency-and-strangeness scheme by half a century. The form was never broadly adopted. The committee met six times between 1952 and 1954 and concluded that UFOs 'neither posed a security threat, nor were of scientific interest', recommending the end of all investigations by the Canadian military. Its records are held at Library and Archives Canada under RG 24, acc. 83-84/167, box 7523, file DRBS 3800-10-1, pt. 1.

entities.label: Sky Canada Project - Office of the Chief Science Advisor of Canada
entities.sub: Canadian federal review of public UAP reporting, 2022-2025
entities.desc: The Sky Canada Project is the Government of Canada's first formal engagement with UAP since 1995. Led by the Office of the Chief Science Advisor, it published a preliminary report in January 2025 and its full fifty-nine-page report, 'Management of Public Reporting of Unidentified Aerial Phenomena in Canada', in June 2025. The project was, in its own words, 'spurred by increased public interest and recent developments in other countries, particularly the United States, where formal procedures for addressing UAP sightings are in development' - which makes it a documented downstream effect of the American disclosure wave on an allied government. Its findings are an indictment of fragmentation rather than of concealment: reports are scattered across federal and non-governmental bodies; most departments do not compile what they receive; the RCMP has no UAP classification at all and logs such calls as non-offence incidents under the Aeronautics Act or as 'suspicious vehicle'; witnesses rarely get a follow-up; and there is no official platform for Canadians to report or to obtain explanations, which the report says 'contributes to the proliferation of misinformation and disinformation'. Its international survey concludes that only the United States, France and Chile provide 'interesting examples of coordinated, transparent, and scientifically driven approaches'. Its recommendations amount to building a Canadian GEIPAN.

entities.label: CEFAA / SEFAA - Chilean anomalous aerial phenomena office, Dirección General de Aeronáutica Civil
entities.sub: Chilean civil aviation UAP office, 1997-present (renamed SEFAA 2021)
entities.desc:
Chile's UAP office exists because pilots kept reporting things and a civil aviation authority decided that was an aviation-safety matter rather than an embarrassment. That framing - not disclosure, not exobiology, but the safety of air operations in 32 million square kilometres of airspace - is what has kept it alive for nearly thirty years and what makes it the South American counterweight on this board.

The prehistory runs back to 1968. Anomalous aerial phenomena were first reported officially in Chile at the old Oficina Meteorológica de Chile in the Quinta Normal aeronautical complex in Santiago, where the director, Aviation Colonel Sergio Bravo Flores, began collecting reports and led the Comisión Chilena para Estudios de Fenómenos Espaciales No Identificados, formed with the support of the Sociedad Científica de Chile. Bravo's first act, on 9 July 1968, was to circulate 43 aeronautical installations from Arica to the Chilean Antarctic asking for reports. The commission - a meteorologist from Línea Aérea Nacional, an engineer, a physician, a doctor of physical and mathematical sciences, a Chilean Air Force lieutenant seconded to the aeronautics directorate, and several engineers - stated its object as establishing 'with all seriousness the true causes' of the matter. In seven years it gathered around a dozen reports, some of which were forwarded to the University of Colorado, where the panel later known as the Condon Committee was at work. It wound up in 1975 when Bravo retired.

The modern office was created twenty-two years later. A wave of sightings reported over Arica in the last days of March and first days of April 1997, together with the expressed interest of the former Commander-in-Chief of the Chilean Air Force, General del Aire Ramón Vega Hidalgo, moved the Director General of Civil Aeronautics, Aviation General Gonzalo Miranda Aguirre, to create the Comité de Estudios de Fenómenos Aéreos Anómalos on 3 October 1997, by Resolución Exenta N° 01599. The resolution sited the committee at the Escuela Técnica Aeronáutica in Quinta Normal, Santiago, and on 14 October 1997 the school's director, Colonel Enzo Di Nocera García, set out its organisation and operating basis and named its members: himself as head, air traffic controller Gustavo Rodríguez Navarro, and the heads of the air traffic and meteorology areas as consultants, with ETA specialists and external organisations convened as needed. In practice Rodríguez Navarro carried the office's work through its early years.

The institutional history is not a straight line, and the dossier is stronger for saying so. Di Nocera led the committee until 1998, when Air Brigade General Ricardo Bermúdez Sanhueza took over the ETA and with it CEFAA, running it to February 2002. Air Brigade General Hernán Henríquez Cobaise took the directorship in March 2002 and held it to 31 March 2008, and the DGAC's own account describes the period from March 2002 to March 2008 as 'una etapa de latencia' - a dormancy. On 15 December 2009, by Resolución N° 02/0/01937, Director General José Huepe Pérez ordered the committee to operate from 1 January 2010 reporting directly to the Secretaría General, detaching it from the ETA and putting its members on permanent, exclusively investigative postings. Bermúdez returned to the directorship in 2009 and served to 2016; Hugo Camus Palacios succeeded him. On 18 October 2021, Resolución Exenta N° 04/3/0113/1385 repealed the 1997 resolution and renamed the office the Sección de Estudios de Fenómenos Aéreos Anómalos, moving it under the DGAC's Subdepartamento Comunicacional. It is now based at Av. Pedro Aguirre Cerda 5100, Cerrillos, Santiago.

Its remit is defined by airspace, not by belief. SEFAA's mission is to support the safety of air operations in the national territory and in the airspace of DGAC responsibility, which extends across 32 million square kilometres from Arica in the north, between 120° and 131° west, to the South Pole. Its principal source is pilot reports - military, commercial, private, sport and institutional - supplemented by public reports, and it explicitly reserves the right to select which material is investigable. Investigations are grounded in the scientific method and depend heavily on audiovisual records. A digital case database was created in 2018; by September 2021 the office had received 1,675 cases in total, with 362 arriving in 2020 alone, nearly a 300% jump on prior years, and 300 more by September 2021. Since 2020 investigated and resolved cases have been published on the office's website, with reports made available to the public quarterly, and resolved-case pages remain live by year through 2026. The permanent staff is small - in 2018 the committee comprised its director and two investigators - but it draws on an external research committee of astronomers, geographers, physicists, psychologists, a nuclear chemist, aerospace medicine specialists, air traffic controllers, a meteorologist, aeronautical investigators, inspector pilots, aeronautical engineers, image analysts and armed forces representatives. On its 24th anniversary the DGAC described CEFAA as 'uno de los organismos públicos más antiguos del continente' and as leading a transparency model comparable, allowing for the difference in human and budgetary resources, to a European government body.

Its most visible case is the Chilean Navy footage of 11 November 2014, in which an Airbus Cougar AS-532 helicopter crew recorded roughly ten minutes of infrared video of an object off the coast west of Santiago. CEFAA investigated for over two years and released the footage with an official report in January 2017; Bermúdez, who had directed the investigation, summarised the outcome as knowing what it was not rather than what it was. The case is also the clearest documented instance of European-South American technical cooperation on UAP: photo and video analysts in France, including François Louange, were brought in through GEIPAN, and GEIPAN's analysts proposed a mundane explanation - a medium-haul aircraft venting - that CEFAA rejected. Independent analysts subsequently matched the timestamps and geometry to scheduled flights. The disagreement is the point: two state UAP offices on different continents worked the same tape, reached different conclusions, and both published.

That visibility is now institutional. Canada's Office of the Chief Science Advisor, designing a national UAP reporting system in 2025, described SEFAA as one of only three national models worth examining alongside the United States and France, and recommended that Canada's lead organisation establish partnerships with AARO and NASA, GEIPAN and SEFAA.

entities.label: SETKA-AN / SETKA-MO (later Galaktika, then Gorizont) - Soviet state anomalous phenomena programme
entities.sub: Twin USSR Academy of Sciences and Ministry of Defence programmes, 1978-1990/91
entities.desc: SETKA - 'net' or 'grid' - was the codename for the Soviet Union's twin state programmes on anomalous phenomena, established at the end of 1978 after the sharp increase in reports in 1977-78 and in particular the Petrozavodsk event of 20 September 1977. SETKA-AN ran inside the USSR Academy of Sciences; SETKA-MO ran inside the Ministry of Defence; both were reportedly ordered by the Military-Industrial Commission, which decided to create two research centres that would aid each other and exchange information. A founding meeting took place in the Academy of Sciences on 18 October 1978, attended by Vladimir Migulin and Yury Platov of IZMIRAN (the Institute of Terrestrial Magnetism and Radio Wave Propagation, which became the lead agency), Georgiy Narimanov and Inna Petrovskaya of the Institute for Space Studies, Rem Varlamov of the Moscow Technological Institute, Victor Balashov and Vladimir Volga of secret military unit 67947, A. N. Makarov of the Department of General Physics and Astronomy, Lev Gindilis of the Shternberg State Astronomical Institute, and others including a colonel of the anti-aircraft forces. The programme was renamed Galaktika in 1981 and Gorizont in 1986, and ended around 1990-91, after which a group of experts continued analysing incoming reports in the Department of General Physics and Astronomy of the Russian Academy of Sciences until 1996. Soviet usage substituted 'anomalous phenomenon' for the forbidden term 'UFO'. Guidelines for the Soviet Navy were issued on 7 March 1980 over the signature of the Deputy Commander of the Main Headquarters of the Navy, Vice Admiral Saakyan.

entities.label: Petrozavodsk phenomenon, 20 September 1977
entities.sub: Mass sighting from Copenhagen to Vladivostok; trigger for the Soviet SETKA programmes
entities.desc: On 20 September 1977 a luminous object was reported over an area running from Copenhagen and Helsinki to Vladivostok, and most spectacularly over the Karelian capital of Petrozavodsk, where the TASS correspondent Nikolai Milov described in the mainstream Soviet press - Pravda, Izvestiya, Selskaya Zhizn and Sotsialisticheskaya Industriya - a 'huge star' that flared in the dark sky and spread out 'in the form of a jellyfish, showering the city with a multitude of very fine rays'. Government officials from northern European countries wrote to Anatoly Aleksandrov, president of the USSR Academy of Sciences, asking whether the phenomenon was caused by Soviet weapons testing and whether it threatened the region's environment - which made the event a diplomatic problem as well as a scientific one. A preliminary report to the Academy of Sciences in 1977, assembling visual observations, radiolocation reports, physical measurements and meteorological data, concluded that 'based on the available data, it is unfeasible to satisfactorily understand the observed phenomenon'. By 30 December 1978 Soviet researchers had collected eighty-five reports. The event is the direct trigger for the creation of SETKA-AN and SETKA-MO. It is often attributed to the launch of the satellite Kosmos-955.

Sheridan Cavitt of the Counter Intelligence Corps to retrieve it. On 8 July 1947 the base public information officer, 1st Lt. The report catalogues recurring morphologies observed from 1991 to 2022 - spheres and orbs, discs and saucers, ovals and tic-tacs, triangles, boomerang and arrowhead forms, and irregular or organic shapes - and describes specific incidents: 'orbs surrounding and forcing an F-22 out of its patrol area'; 'the crew of a Navy aircraft carrier watched a small orange/red sphere rapidly descend from a high altitude of 100 to 200 yards directly above the flight deck'; and 'a roughly 13-minute long, high-definition, full-color video of a white orb UAP coming out of the ocean approximately 20 miles off the coast of Kuwait ... joined by another orb that briefly comes into the frame from the left.' Under questioning from Rep. Clay Higgins, Shellenberger confirmed 'I do' know the author, and refused to place his sources: 'I will not say ... I protect my sources, and I am not willing to reduce the potential universe of where my sources might be.' Chairwoman Nancy Mace then moved the document into the record: 'Committee staff asked me to go ahead, and I will do it, to enter into the Congressional Record this 12-page document that Michael Shellenberger brought today that describes the Immaculate Constellation government program.' It appears in the hearing's Index of Documents as 'Report, Pentagon, Immaculate Constellation; submitted by Rep. Mace.' The official response is the important part of this dossier. The Department of Defense says it has no record of such a programme; Pentagon spokesperson Sue Gough has stated the Department has 'no record'; former AARO director Sean Kirkpatrick has denied it exists. No AARO product has ever addressed it: not the FY2024 annual report, not the FY2025 report delivered 21 July 2026, not any statement for the record, and no PURSUE tranche between 8 May and 7 August 2026 released anything under the name. In 2025 a self-identified whistleblower said he had located the material in a folder labelled '2018 Schriever Wargame', and Jason Colavito assessed that the claimant had mistaken fictitious wargame documents for secret UFO revelations - an assessment that, whatever its merits, addresses a later claimant's provenance story and not Shellenberger's source. The board's position is that the load-bearing fact is procedural: a named programme is in the Congressional Record, the Department's answer is a records assertion rather than a denial of existence, and in the twenty-one months since no office has produced a written response, a records search declaration, or a classification review.

entities.label: STAR GATE and predecessor remote viewing programs, 1970-1995
entities.sub: CIA/Army/DIA psychoenergetics effort; SCANATE, GONDOLA WISH, GRILL FLAME, CENTER LANE, SUN STREAK, STAR GATE
entities.desc: STAR GATE is the umbrella name applied in 1991 to a chain of United States government programmes investigating and attempting to operationalise remote viewing, running from 1970 to 1995 across CIA, Army and DIA sponsorship. The CIA initiated SCANATE - 'scan by coordinate' - around 1970 in response to assessments that the Soviet Union was spending heavily on psychotronic research. In 1972 physicists Harold E. Puthoff and Russell Targ began CIA-sponsored work at SRI International's Artificial Intelligence Center in Menlo Park, coining the term 'remote viewing' and working with Ingo Swann, Pat Price, Joseph McMoneagle and Uri Geller. The military side began as GONDOLA WISH in 1977 under the Army Assistant Chief of Staff for Intelligence's Systems Exploitation Detachment, became GRILL FLAME under INSCOM in mid-1978 in Buildings 2560-2561 at Fort Meade, was redesignated CENTER LANE in 1983, moved to DIA's Scientific and Technical Intelligence Directorate as SUN STREAK in late 1985, and was consolidated as STAR GATE in 1991. Maj. Gen. Albert Stubblebine sponsored the Fort Meade effort; Lt. Frederick 'Skip' Atwater oversaw the unit until 1987; James Clapper, later Director of National Intelligence, led the project in the 1990s; Edwin C. May ran the Cognitive Sciences Laboratory as principal investigator. In 1995 CIA commissioned the American Institutes for Research to evaluate the programme; statistician Jessica Utts concluded the laboratory results showed statistically significant effects, psychologist Ray Hyman concluded the opposite - 'the overwhelming amount of data generated by the viewers is vague, general, and way off target' - and the official finding was that remote viewing information 'is vague and ambiguous, making it difficult, if not impossible, for the technique to yield information of sufficient quality and accuracy for actionable intelligence.' CIA terminated the roughly $20 million programme in 1995 and published the records online in January 2017 through the CREST archive; Edwin May's donated 1972-1995 materials are held at the Archives of the Impossible at Rice University. STAR GATE belongs on this board for four reasons and only four. It is a documented case of the United States funding two decades of research into a phenomenon it publicly disparaged. It shows the exact contractor structure a concealed programme uses - a university-adjacent institute holding the science, a compartmented military unit holding the operations, and an intelligence sponsor holding the money. It establishes the personnel bridge that runs through Puthoff from SRI to EarthTech to the AAWSAP Defense Intelligence Reference Documents to To The Stars Academy and the 2019 Army CRADA, and through Christopher 'Kit' Green from the CIA weird desk to NIDS-adjacent biomedical work. And it is the precedent for how such a programme ends: not with a public admission, but with a commissioned evaluation that produces an unusable-for-intelligence finding, followed by termination and, twenty-two years later, bulk declassification.

entities.label: UFO Crash/Retrieval Status Reports I-VII (Stringfield, 1978-1994)
entities.sub: Seven-part self-published monograph series, 1978-1994
entities.desc: The seven UFO Crash/Retrieval Status Reports written by Leonard H. Stringfield between 1978 and 1994 are the founding corpus of the crash-retrieval literature and the reason the subject exists as a research field rather than as folklore. Status Report I is 'Retrievals of the Third Kind: A Case Study of Alleged UFOs and Occupants in Military Custody', delivered as a paper at the ninth annual MUFON Symposium in Dayton, Ohio on 29 July 1978 (revised 20 July 1978) and published in Flying Saucer Review; it grew out of the informant response to Stringfield's 1977 Doubleday book 'Situation Red, The UFO Siege'. Status Report II, 'The UFO Crash/Retrieval Syndrome: New Sources, New Data', is dated January 1980 and was published by MUFON; it introduced the letter-number case coding (Cases A-1 onward, Items B-1 onward) that structures the whole series, and included the first Del Rio and Wright-Patterson entries. Status Report III, 'Amassing the Evidence' (1982), carried endorsements from Dr. Peter Rank, Chief of Radiology at Methodist Hospital, and Richard H. Hall, former Assistant Director of NICAP and editor of the MUFON UFO Journal, and printed a consolidated chronology of every case reported in Status Report II - the field's first tabulated retrieval index. Status Report IV, 'The Fatal Encounter at Ft. Dix-McGuire: A Case Study' (June 1985), is a single-case monograph on an alleged 18 January 1978 incident at McGuire AFB and Fort Dix, developed from a USAF Security Police sergeant who had first appeared as Case A3 in Report III, and opens with a prologue titled 'The Burden of Proof' in which Stringfield states that public research does not possess proof and that affidavits, leaked documents and photographs are not proof. Status Report V, 'Is the Coverup Lid Lifting?' (January 1989), surveys Roswell, Aztec, Kingman, El Yunque and Brown County, Ohio, and argues that confirming any single retrieval would compel eventual sharing of alien propulsion and materials technology. Status Report VI, 'The Inner Sanctum' (July 1991), was self-published from 4412 Grove Avenue, Cincinnati, edited by Richard Hall and typed by Chris Coffey, and opens with the Humpty Dumpty verse from Through the Looking Glass. Status Report VII, 'Search for Proof in a Hall of Mirrors' (February 1994), acknowledges funding from the Fund for UFO Research and cooperation from MUFON, CUFOS and the Mid-Ohio Research Associates, opens with Walter Scott's 'I cannot tell how the truth may be; I say the tale as 'twas told to me', and closes the series ten months before Stringfield's death with a Roswell crash/retrieval update noting a source's placement of the site north of Roswell rather than on the Plains of San Augustin. The series' method - anonymous sources behind letter-number codes - is simultaneously the reason the material exists and the reason almost none of it can be graded above tier 2.

entities.label: The Roswell Report: Fact Versus Fiction in the New Mexico Desert (1995)
entities.sub: Office of the Secretary of the Air Force report to GAO; GPO, 1995
entities.desc: The first of the two official Air Force Roswell reports, written by Col. Richard L. Weaver, Director of Security and Special Program Oversight in the Office of the Secretary of the Air Force, with 1st Lt. James McAndrew. It was produced to answer Rep. Steven H. Schiff's inquiry as routed through the General Accounting Office, delivered to the Secretary of the Air Force and to GAO in July 1994, and published by the Government Printing Office in 1995. Its operative conclusion is that the July 1947 debris came from Project Mogul, the top-priority classified balloon-borne acoustic programme flown from Alamogordo Army Air Field to detect Soviet nuclear tests, described in McAndrew's Attachment 32. The published version duplicates the report delivered to the Secretary and GAO with the addition of a photograph section. The document's evidentiary character is unusual and this board treats it accordingly: it is a denial, and it is also a primary record. It establishes on the government's own signature that a classified programme was flying from Alamogordo in June-July 1947 whose existence had been concealed for forty-seven years, that the Secretary of the Air Force issued a written direction releasing former airmen and contract scientists from nondisclosure obligations so they could speak, and that the inquiry was assigned to the special access programme oversight directorate rather than to a historical office. Every one of those three facts is a fact about the concealment architecture, whatever one concludes about the balloon.

Its four stated conclusions are that Air Force activities spanning many years were consolidated into two or three days in July 1947; that the 'aliens' were probably anthropomorphic test dummies carried aloft by high-altitude balloons; that the 'unusual' military activity in the desert was balloon launch and recovery, with the units that always arrived shortly after a crash being accurate descriptions of dummy-recovery teams; and that the Roswell Army Air Field hospital bodies claims most likely combine a 1956 KC-97 crash killing eleven airmen with a 1959 manned balloon mishap injuring two pilots. The report also asserts flatly that 'the claims of bodies only became part of the Roswell Incident after 1978'. What makes it a first-order artifact rather than a press release is what it printed: anthropomorphic dummy launch and landing locations at Appendix A; sworn witness statements from ten named Air Force personnel at Appendix B including Col. Joseph W. Kittinger Jr., Col. Dan D. Fulgham, Bernard D. Gildenberg and Lt. Col. Raymond A. Madson; and full interview transcripts of five pro-UFO witnesses at Appendix C - Gerald Anderson, Glenn Dennis, Alice Knight, Vern Maltais and James Ragsdale, the Dennis interview supplied by its interviewer Karl T. Pflock. Section 2.1 is the most forensically detailed passage the US government has ever published on a UFO claim: it works the 427th AAF Base Unit Squadron 'M' morning reports and the National Personnel Records Center holdings to establish that Glenn Dennis's 'Naomi Maria Selff' never existed and to identify 1st Lt. Eileen M. Fanton as matching every other particular of his description.

entities.label: Kean v. NASA, No. 1:03-cv-02509 (D.D.C.)
entities.sub: Federal FOIA litigation over the Kecksburg records, 2003-2009
entities.desc: The only federal court case in which a US agency has been held to have failed its search obligations on UFO-related records. Leslie Kean, represented by Lobel, Novins & Lamont (Martin Lobel, Lee Ellen Helfrich), sued the National Aeronautics and Space Administration on 9 December 2003 in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia over NASA's handling of her 31 January 2003 FOIA request for records referring to Kecksburg, the 9 December 1965 incident, the 'Fragology Files' for 1962-1967, Richard M. Schulherr, Project Moon Dust and Cosmos 96. The case was assigned to Judge Emmet G. Sullivan, cause code '05:552 Freedom of Information Act', PACER case ID 106063. NASA ran four searches. The court's 27 March 2007 memorandum opinion records that 'plaintiff contends, and indeed NASA admits, that NASA's first two searches for responsive documents were inadequate', traces how a granted administrative appeal signed by Associate Deputy Administrator James Jennings on 18 June 2003 was simply not acted on because of poor tracking and an office move, and holds that NASA 'has not yet met its burden of demonstrating that the search for documents was adequate.' Summary judgment was granted to NASA only on the withholding of two emails between FOIA officer Stephen McConnell and NASA attorney Bierbower under Exemption 5, which the court reviewed in camera on its own 22 February 2007 order. The court then ordered the parties to propose search and documentation procedures that would create a proper record. A Stipulation of Settlement in Part was signed by Judge Sullivan on 16 October 2007; NASA searched under supervision and filed joint status reports every sixty days from December 2007 to August 2009; the case was dismissed on 24 August 2009 on the parties' joint motion, the court finding NASA had met its settlement obligations. Along the way, NASA public liaison officer Steve McConnell testified that two boxes of papers from the period of the Kecksburg incident were missing.

entities.sub: Federal Tort Claims Act suit over the 1980 Cash-Landrum encounter, 1984-1986
entities.desc: Betty Cash, Vickie Landrum and Colby Landrum sued the United States of America in the US District Court for the Southern District of Texas, Houston Division, over the 29 December 1980 encounter near Huffman, Texas. The original complaint and summonses were filed on 18 January 1984 under the Federal Tort Claims Act, 28 U.S.C. 1346(b) and 2671 et seq., the docket sheet classifying the cause as airplane product liability with damages of $5,000,000 - reported in the press as a $20 million action across the plaintiffs. Peter A. Gersten of Gagliardi, Torpes & Gersten of Tarrytown, New York was designated attorney in charge, with William C. Shead of Houston as local co-counsel; Assistant US Attorney Frank A. Conforti appeared for the government. Sterling entered an Order of Dismissal dismissing the action under Federal Rules of Civil Procedure 12(b)(1), 12(b)(6) and 56. The government's position, and the ground on which the case ended, was that no such vehicle or operation was the United States'. Gersten later said the suit had been a bluff, brought in the hope of a quiet settlement of the medical bills. Two things about this docket matter to this board. First, it is the only time a UFO injury claim has reached a US federal court on the merits. Second, the Defense Department conducted an internal investigation into whether the object was a US military device, and no document from that investigation has ever surfaced.

entities.label: Kecksburg incident, 9 December 1965
entities.sub: Claimed object recovery, Westmoreland County, Pennsylvania
entities.desc: At about 4:44 p.m. EST on 9 December 1965 a brilliant fireball crossed Michigan, Ontario, Ohio, Pennsylvania, New York, Indiana, Idaho and West Virginia; the FAA logged twenty-three pilot reports beginning at 4:44 p.m. and a seismograph twenty-five miles southwest of Detroit recorded the shock wave. Around 4:46 p.m., residents of Kecksburg, thirty miles southeast of Pittsburgh, reported blue smoke, vibration and a thump, and that something had come down in the woods. The Greensburg Tribune-Review reported that the area was 'immediately sealed off on the order of U.S. Army and State Police officials, in anticipation of a close inspection' and that state police had roped it off pending the arrival of Army engineers and possibly civilian scientists; a later edition ran 'Searchers Fail to Find Object'. Local witnesses collected over decades by Stan Gordon describe an acorn-shaped object about the size of a Volkswagen bearing hieroglyph-like markings, removed by flatbed truck. In December 2005 NASA stated that experts had examined metallic fragments from the area and determined they came from a Soviet satellite that had re-entered and broken up, but that the records of those findings had been lost in the 1980s. That statement is why the litigation happened. NASA's own current position undermines the satellite explanation: analysis of the fireball's photographs and sightings indicates a path too steep to be consistent with orbital re-entry, US Air Force tracking data indicate Cosmos 96's orbit decayed earlier than 21:43 UT on 9 December, and other analyses indicate definitively that it could not have been Cosmos 96. The structural fact this board records is that the cordon is documented in the contemporaneous local press, and the disposition of whatever was inside it is documented nowhere.

entities.label: Shag Harbour incident, 4 October 1967
entities.sub: Object impact and Canadian military underwater search, Nova Scotia
entities.desc: At about 11:20 p.m. Atlantic Daylight Time on 4 October 1967 at least eleven people saw a low-flying lit object descend into the water off Shag Harbour, Nova Scotia; witnesses reported a whistling sound, a whoosh and a loud bang. Laurie Wickens and four companions, driving on Highway 3, reported to the RCMP detachment at Barrington Passage that a large aircraft had gone into the water. Two RCMP officers reached the scene within about fifteen minutes and the Rescue Coordination Centre in Halifax was alerted; the object, still lit, sank before any rescue attempt. Local fishing boats and a Canadian Coast Guard cutter from Clark's Harbour searched and found no survivors, bodies or debris. By the next morning RCC Halifax had established that no commercial, private or military aircraft were missing anywhere along the eastern seaboard, in the Atlantic provinces or in New England, and sent a priority telex to the Royal Canadian Air Force 'Air Desk' in Ottawa - the office handling all civilian and military UFO reports - explicitly stating that conventional explanations had been dismissed and labelling it a UFO Report. The head of the Air Desk telexed Royal Canadian Navy headquarters recommending an underwater search, and the Navy tasked Fleet Diving Unit Atlantic, which combed the seafloor of the Gulf of Maine for three days beginning two days after the event. The final report says no trace was found. The Chronicle-Herald of 7 October 1967 ran Ray MacLeod's front-page story 'Could Be Something Concrete in Shag Harbour UFO - RCAF', quoting Squadron Leader Bain of the Air Desk saying the Air Force was 'very interested' and that 'the Shag Harbour incident is one of the few where we may get something concrete on it.' The 9 October follow-up, 'UFO Search Called Off', quoted the Navy: 'Not a trace... not a clue... not a bit of anything.' A summary of the event from Department of National Defence files is held at Library and Archives Canada. Shag Harbour is the strongest case in the whole retrieval literature on the criterion this board cares about most - the response is documented in government paper even though the object is not.

entities.label: Plains of San Agustin claim, July 1947
entities.sub: Claimed second 1947 crash site, 175 miles northwest of Roswell
entities.desc: The claim that a second craft came down in July 1947 on the Plains of San Agustin, a graben basin in Catron and Socorro Counties, New Mexico, about 175 miles northwest of Roswell, best known today as the site of the Very Large Array. It rests on three testimonies: two second-hand accounts from Vern Maltais and Alice Knight relaying what the soil conservation engineer Grady L. 'Barney' Barnett had told them before his death in 1969, and one first-hand account from Gerald Anderson, who came forward in 1990 claiming to have been a five-year-old rockhounding there. The claim entered the literature through Berlitz and Moore's 'The Roswell Incident' (1980), was central to Friedman and Berliner's 'Crash at Corona' (1992), and forced the Roswell literature into two-crash and three-crash constructions to reconcile a debris field near Corona with an intact craft 175 miles away. It was substantially dismantled from inside the field: Mark Rodeghier of CUFOS and Fred Whiting of the Fund for UFO Research published 'The Plains of San Agustin Controversy' in 1992 concluding against Anderson. The Air Force's 1997 report offers a specific alternative reading - that Maltais and Knight, three decades on, may have confused the Plains of San Agustin with San Agustin Pass or San Agustin Peak in the San Agustin Mountains, just outside White Sands Missile Range and the Jornada Test Range, where numerous anthropomorphic dummy balloon flights terminated and were recovered by uniformed teams who told civilians to leave.

entities.label: Kingman, Arizona claim, 1953
entities.sub: Claimed craft and single body recovery; source pseudonym 'Fritz Werner'
entities.desc: The 1953 Kingman, Arizona claim is the retrieval case with the cleanest documented chain of custody for its own testimony, and it is still only tier 2. It was first investigated and reported by the Massachusetts researcher Raymond E. Fowler, working from a source using the pseudonym 'Fritz Werner', an engineer who said he had been flown from an Air Force facility to a desert site under escort and shown a craft and a single small body, with each specialist restricted to his own area of examination and required to sign a secrecy agreement. Stringfield published the case as Abstract 6 in 'Retrievals of the Third Kind' (1978) and referenced it in 'Situation Red, The UFO Siege' (Doubleday, 1977) at pages 178-185. On 11 August 1980 Stringfield wrote to Fowler asking permission to put questions directly to Werner; the answers, dated 2 September 1980, are printed verbatim in Status Report III. Werner's replies are notable for what they concede: asked for facial detail on the deceased entity he answered that after twenty-seven years the details were 'pretty foggy' and that he might 'even be influenced by other descriptions I've seen or heard in the interim' - a witness volunteering, on the record, the exact contamination mechanism this board treats as the central problem of the retrieval corpus. The case is compartment-shaped in a way that fits the domain's premise - specialists shown only their own piece, sworn to secrecy, no one able to describe the whole - and it is unsupported by any document.

The most-cited version in the wider literature is attributed to a retired officer, Robert B. Willingham, who over several decades gave accounts of a disc down near the Texas-Mexico border, with the date, the location and his own claimed rank and role varying materially between tellings and his stated service history contested against his record. entities.label: Majic Eyes Only: Earth's Encounters with Extraterrestrial Technology (2005)
entities.sub: Ryan S. Wood; indexed crash-retrieval catalogue with credibility weightings
entities.desc: Ryan S. Wood's 2005 catalogue is the retrieval literature's attempt to become a database. Where Stringfield produced seven narrative monographs with anonymised letter-number case codes and Kevin Randle produced case-by-case essays in 'A History of UFO Crashes' (1995) and 'Crash: When UFOs Fall From the Sky' (2010), Wood produced rows: each claimed retrieval event given a date, a location, a source trail and a numerical credibility weighting, spanning from the 1940s forward and totalling seventy-plus entries. That structure is the book's contribution and its exposure. It is the fastest way to find out that a claim exists, when it was first made and by whom - which is a genuine research service in a field where the same story recirculates for decades under different names. It is not a way to find out whether a claim is true, because the weighting function is not published in a form a third party can re-run on the same inputs, and because a large share of the source trail terminates in either Stringfield's anonymous informants or the Wood family's own Majestic Documents corpus. This board uses 'Majic Eyes Only' as an index and grades its entries individually against their underlying sources.

entities.desc: Richard Dolan's two volumes - 'Chronology of a Cover-Up, 1941-1973' (2002) and 'The Cover-Up Exposed, 1973-1991' (2009) - are the closest thing this domain has to a standard scholarly history, and they changed the field's centre of gravity. The crash-retrieval literature that preceded them argued from witnesses: someone saw a craft, someone handled a body, and the concealment was inferred backwards from the testimony. Dolan argued forwards from the institutions: the National Security Act of 1947, the creation of the CIA and NSA, the special access programme architecture, the contractor black-programme economy, the classification and compartmentation regime, and the documented behaviour of those bodies on adjacent secrets. On that basis the concealment stops needing an exotic explanation and becomes a predictable output of a system built to produce exactly that result. Dolan also gave the field its most durable formulation, the 'breakaway civilisation' - a technologically and financially self-sustaining compartment operating outside public accountability. The volumes are extensively footnoted to declassified documents, agency histories, contemporaneous press and congressional material, which is why they survived the transition to the post-2017 congressional era while most of the 1990s literature did not: the substrate is documents, and documents keep.

entities.label: Behind the Flying Saucers (Scully, 1950)
entities.sub: Henry Holt and Company, New York, 1950; the first crashed-saucer book
entities.desc: Frank Scully's 1950 bestseller is where the crash-retrieval genre begins, and its provenance is the genre's original sin. Built out of two 1949 Variety columns, it told a mass readership that recovered discs and dead occupants were in US military custody, and it supplied the specific narrative furniture that the field has been reusing ever since: a controlled landing rather than a crash, a small crew of humanoid bodies, an immediate military removal, exotic materials, magnetic propulsion, and complete official silence. entities.label: Guy Hottel memorandum, 22 March 1950

entities.label: Freedom of Information Practice
entities.sub: Procedural domain - the request, the appeal, the Glomar, and what survives the exemptions
entities.desc: The Freedom of Information Act is the only routine instrument by which a private citizen can compel a federal agency to produce a record, and almost every primary document on this board arrived through it. Its limits are as instructive as its yield. Exemption 1 shields properly classified national defence information; Exemption 3 shields information withheld by other statute - including the National Security Agency Act, which NSA has successfully invoked to refuse even to describe its UFO-related holdings; and the Glomar response permits an agency to refuse to confirm or deny that responsive records exist at all. In Citizens Against UFO Secrecy v. The structural gap this board turns on is that FFRDC and prime-contractor records are contractor records, not agency records, and are outside FOIA entirely - so material that moves from a government shelf to a contractor shelf moves out of the statute's reach without ever being classified higher. entities.label: The FFRDC Mechanism
entities.sub: Structural domain - FAR 35.017 access rights as a concealment instrument (see also d-ffrdc)
entities.desc: This is the operative clause rather than the institution: FAR 35.017 provides that a federally funded research and development center 'has access to government and supplier data, including sensitive and proprietary information, and to employees and facilities beyond that common in a normal contractual relationship'. That single sentence creates an entity legally positioned to see both sides of a compartment - the government's classified holdings and the prime contractor's proprietary data - which no ordinary contractor and no ordinary civil servant may do. In exchange the FFRDC is barred from competing for commercial federal R&D work and must disclose its activities fully to its sponsoring agency, which is also its classification authority; disclosure runs to the sponsor, not to Congress. Because FFRDC records are contractor records they are outside FOIA, and because awards are sole-source no competitor ever audits the work. The mechanism therefore permits an activity to be technically vested outside government while the government retains absolute control - which is the concealment architecture in miniature. Scoring high on this domain means an entity operates or sponsors an FFRDC, or moved between the two.

entities.label: Roswell
entities.sub: Case domain - the 1947 event and the four official explanations issued for it
entities.desc: Roswell is not on this board because of what was recovered but because of what the government did afterwards, four times, over forty-eight years. On 8 July 1947 Roswell Army Air Field publicly announced that the 509th Bomb Group had come into possession of a flying disc; the same day the Eighth Air Force at Fort Worth, under Brigadier General Roger M. Ramey, replaced that with a weather balloon. In the mid-1990s the Air Force published 'The Roswell Report: Fact vs. Fiction in the New Mexico Desert', attributing the debris to Project MOGUL, a classified acoustic balloon programme for detecting Soviet nuclear tests; on 24 June 1997 it published 'The Roswell Report: Case Closed', attributing witness accounts of bodies to anthropomorphic crash test dummies dropped in the 1950s. GAO, asked by Congressman Steven Schiff to locate the underlying records, reported in July 1995 that the relevant Roswell AAF outgoing messages for 1946-1949 had been destroyed with no disposition authority and no destruction certificate on file. Four official explanations and one documented records gap is the actual evidentiary situation, and it is the reason the case remains load-bearing. entities.label: Consciousness & Observer Effects
entities.sub: Contested domain - the claim that observation and intention are coupled to the phenomenon
entities.desc: This is the domain where the board is most exposed and must be most disciplined. The claim - that the phenomenon interacts with observers, that experiencer accounts include a cognitive or precognitive component, and that this is a property of the phenomenon rather than of the witness - is not supportable from primary documents, and the board records it as a research direction rather than a finding. What is documented is that the government funded work in this space and kept funding it: the Star Gate anomalous cognition programme ran under federal contract from 1972 to 1995, and the AAWSAP reference documents commissioned by DIA in 2008-2010 include studies of field effects on human neurological tissue by Christopher Green, a former CIA analyst. That continuity is a documented fact about personnel even where the underlying claim is not documented at all. entities.label: International & Allied Programs
entities.sub: Comparative domain - what other states have admitted, and what their disclosures imply about ours
entities.desc: Other governments have made admissions the United States has not, and the comparison is one of the board's most useful instruments because it establishes what an official programme looks like when it is not concealed. France has run GEIPAN, a publicly funded investigative unit inside the national space agency CNES at Toulouse, since 1977 - with a published classification scheme, published statistics and a case archive open to the public, of which the category for cases that remain unexplained after full investigation is the operative one. Brazil transferred its military UFO files to the Arquivo Nacional, making them citizen-accessible, and its 1986 air force incident is documented in that archive. Chile's air force ran CEFAA under named officers who spoke on the record. The comparative point is decisive: none of these disclosures produced the harms the American concealment argument depends on, which shifts the burden onto the party claiming that only the United States cannot afford transparency. The allied-intelligence complication is real too - a programme shared under bilateral arrangements is protected by originator control, giving every partner a veto over release. Scoring high on this domain means an entity ran, opened or is bound by a foreign programme.

entities.label: Moscow, Russia

entities.desc: Moscow is the administrative centre of the Soviet Union's own state study of anomalous aerial phenomena - the programme conducted from 1978 under the Academy of Sciences and the Ministry of Defence, generally known by the codename Setka, whose principal scientific summariser Yuli Platov later published on it openly. edges.label: establishes the office
edges.note: Sec. 6802 does not create AARO alongside anything: it amends section 1683 of the FY2022 NDAA (50 U.S.C. 3373) to read as a new section establishing the office. 'Not later than 120 days after the date of the enactment of the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2023, the Secretary of Defense, in coordination with the Director of National Intelligence, shall establish an office ... to carry out the duties of the Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force, as in effect on December 26, 2021', and 'The office established under paragraph (1) shall be known as the "All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office"'. The reporting chain is set in the same subsection: the Director reports directly to the Deputy Secretary of Defense and the Principal Deputy Director of National Intelligence, and to USD(I&S) on administrative matters only. Read from the enacted text on govinfo, 22 August 2026.

edges.label: the report it requires

edges.label: 119(e) is the waiver that defines a waived SAP
edges.note: 10 U.S.C. 119(e) is the waiver: 'The Secretary of Defense may waive any requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c) that certain information be included in a report under that subsection if the Secretary determines that inclusion of that information in the report would adversely affect the national security.' Where it is exercised, 'the Secretary shall provide the information described in that subsection with respect to the special access program concerned, and the justification for the waiver, jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees.' Read directly from the OLRC text on 22 August 2026.

edges.label: 119(g) defines who must be told
edges.note: 10 U.S.C. 119(g) defines 'defense committees' for this section as six bodies: '(1) the Committee on Armed Services and the Committee on Appropriations, and the Defense Subcommittee of the Committee on Appropriations, of the Senate; and (2) the Committee on Armed Services and the Committee on Appropriations, and the Subcommittee on Defense of the Committee on Appropriations, of the House of Representatives.' Six bodies, chairman and ranking minority member of each, is where the board's twelve seats come from. Read directly from the OLRC text on 22 August 2026, which confirms the count independently of the earlier reading recorded in the L0 notes.

edges.label: Sec. 4.3(c): nothing in the order supersedes any requirement made by or under 10 U.S.C. 119
edges.note: The order creates the object the statute reports on. EO 13526 sec. 4.3(a) is the authority to establish a special access program at all, and restricts it to six officials or their principal deputies: the Secretaries of State, Defense, Energy and Homeland Security, the Attorney General, and the Director of National Intelligence. 10 U.S.C. 119 then obliges the Secretary of Defense to report the DoD ones to Congress. Creation is executive and unilateral; reporting is statutory. Both texts were read on 22 August 2026, and neither cites the other - the relationship is that one supplies the programmes the other counts.

edges.label: 32 CFR 117.6(b) writes the carve-out into regulation
edges.note: The carve-out is in the codified federal regulation, not only in a DoD manual. 32 CFR 117.6(b)(3), 'Responsibilities': "The Director, DCSA, will be relieved of this oversight function for DoD special access programs (SAPs) when the Secretary of Defense or the Deputy Secretary of Defense approves a carve-out provision in accordance with DoDD 5205.07, 'DoD SAP Policy'." The NISPOM Rule was published at 85 FR 83312 on 21 December 2020, so the provision relieving the oversight body has the force of a legislative rule rather than of internal DoD policy. Read from the eCFR renderer API on 22 August 2026.

edges.label: relieves DCSA of NISP industrial security oversight for a DoD SAP
edges.note: The regulation names the office the carve-out acts on. 32 CFR 117.6(b) makes the Director, DCSA responsible for 'security oversight of the NISP as the DoD CSO', and then (b)(3) removes it: "The Director, DCSA, will be relieved of this oversight function for DoD special access programs (SAPs) when the Secretary of Defense or the Deputy Secretary of Defense approves a carve-out provision in accordance with DoDD 5205.07, 'DoD SAP Policy'." So the effect is not that oversight passes to another body but that the cognizant security office's oversight function ceases for that programme, on the written approval of one of two named officials.

edges.label: para 1.2.f designates select unacknowledged SAPs as waived
edges.note: The statute permits the waiver; this Instruction is where the Department operates it. Para 1.2.f. is DoD's own designation authority - the Secretary 'may designate select unacknowledged SAPs as "waived"' - and Enclosure 3 tasks the Senior Review Group with reviewing 'all waived DoD SAPs' annually and advising the SAPOC. Para 7.2.a.(3) then sets who is told, and it is wider than the statute's twelve: the chair, the ranking member, the staff directors and one designated security manager of the defense AND intelligence committees. DIA published Baker's HFGW paper as an official Defense Intelligence Reference Document on 6 April 2010 regardless. This is the sharpest available evidence of AAWSAP's quality-control failure: the programme placed on a JWICS-hosted DIA reference series a topic the government's own senior scientific review body had already assessed as wrong and whose threat premise it had declared not credible. It is also the only case in the 38 where an external government review directly contradicts a published deliverable.

timeline.label: Foo fighters
timeline.text: Allied aircrews over Europe and the Pacific report glowing objects pacing their aircraft. The 415th Night Fighter Squadron files repeated reports; no Axis weapon is ever identified as the cause.

timeline.label: White Sands Proving Ground established
timeline.text: Seven days before Trinity, the Army stands up the proving ground that will become the largest military installation in the United States and the geographic centre of the 1947-1951 New Mexico record.

timeline.label: Truman creates the Central Intelligence Group and the post of Director of Central Intelligence
timeline.text: A Presidential directive on the coordination of foreign intelligence activities provides that personnel assigned from State, War and the Navy 'shall collectively form a Central Intelligence Group and shall, under the direction of a Director of Central Intelligence, assist the National Intelligence Authority', the Director to be designated by the President and to sit as a non-voting member of the Authority. Rear Adm. Sidney W. Souers is the first holder and signs as Director of Central Intelligence within two weeks.
timeline.source: Presidential Directive on Coordination of Foreign Intelligence Activities, 22 January 1946, FRUS 1945-1950, Emergence of the Intelligence Establishment, Document 71, https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1945-50Intel/d71

timeline.label: Project RAND created
timeline.text: The Army Air Forces establish Project RAND inside Douglas Aircraft, inventing the contractor-operated analytical partner form that every institution in this domain would later copy.

timeline.label: The British-U.S. Communication Intelligence Agreement is signed
timeline.text: STANCIB and the London Signal Intelligence Board sign a twelve-paragraph agreement for unrestricted exchange of the products and methods of communications intelligence. It defines third parties as everyone outside the United States, the British Empire and the Dominions, and states that 'It will be contrary to this agreement to reveal its existence to any third party whatsoever.' A search of all six numbered pages returns no occurrence of flying, saucer, unidentified, aerial phenomen or anomalous.
timeline.source: Outline of British-U.S. Communication Intelligence Agreement, 5 March 1946, NSA UKUSA release copy, https://documents.theblackvault.com/documents/ukusa/agreement_outline_5mar46.pdf

timeline.label: Ghost rockets over Scandinavia
timeline.text: Sweden logs hundreds of unexplained rocket-like objects; US and UK intelligence send officers, including Gen. James Doolittle, to assess. No Soviet programme is ever identified.

timeline.label: The Office of Naval Research is created, the same day as the Atomic Energy Act
timeline.text: Public Law 79-588, 60 Stat. 779, establishes an Office of Naval Research in the Office of the Secretary of the Navy, headed by a Chief of Naval Research appointed by the President with the advice and consent of the Senate. Section 6 frees its research contracting from five named sections of the Revised Statutes and from performance bonds; section 5(b) keeps obligated research appropriations available four further years.
