d-ffrdc.desc: How the seam actually works, mechanism by mechanism. (1) RECORDS STATUS. Documents created and held by an FFRDC operator are the contractor's records, not agency records. The Freedom of Information Act reaches agency records. A congressional committee can subpoena a contractor, but it must first know the contractor holds something - which is why Burlison's method of naming a file by its exact designation, as he did with AF-ATIC-FILM 03/52 at MIT Lincoln Laboratory, worked where a general request would not have. (2) DISCLOSURE DIRECTION. FAR 35.017 obliges the FFRDC to fully disclose its activities to its sponsoring agency. The sponsor is simultaneously the customer, the funder and the original classification authority. There is no obligation running to Congress, to GAO, to the public, or to any other agency. MITRE's answer to Burlison - that it would 'coordinate with the federal agencies responsible for the work' - is not evasion in the colloquial sense; it is the regulation operating exactly as written. (3) DUAL ACCESS. The FFRDC sees the government's compartmented information and the prime contractor's proprietary information. No civil servant has the second; no ordinary contractor has the first. That is the informational chokepoint the 2026 UAP Gerb investigation identifies as the 'missing link', and it exists whether or not any of that investigation's specific allegations are true. (4) NON-COMPETITION. Because the FFRDC is barred from competing with industry for federal R&D, no commercial rival ever has cause or standing to audit its work. (5) PERPETUITY. Five-year contracts renewable indefinitely, awarded sole-source, produce institutional relationships measured in decades - MITRE's DoD relationship is 68 years old, Battelle's Pacific Northwest contract dates to 1978, UT-Battelle's Oak Ridge contract runs to 2030. (6) PERSONNEL FLOW. The same executives move between sponsor and operator: a former NRO director chairs MITRE's board, a former PDDNI is its vice chair, a Battelle executive is its CEO, a former STRATCOM commander runs IDA, a former IARPA director runs RAND, and AARO's founding director went to Oak Ridge. Put these six together and you have an entity with the government's access, the private sector's records status, no auditor, no expiry and a shared talent pool with its own overseer. The board's position is not that this proves a concealed programme exists. It is that if one exists, this is where it lives, and that the burden of demonstrating otherwise sits with the institutions that built the structure.

burlison-mitre-letter-2026.desc: The compliance schedule, in full, as reported by MeriTalk and DefenseScoop from the letter text: designate a senior officer responsible for the response within 5 business days; issue a litigation-style preservation hold within 10 business days; coordinate a classified briefing for cleared committee staff within 14 days; deliver written responses and a records-location index within 30 days; produce unclassified materials in native electronic format with complete metadata within 45 days; and separately identify all classified or sponsor-controlled materials with the controlling authority named. MITRE must account for records created, handled, transferred, withheld or destroyed by the corporation, by any of its six FFRDCs, or by its subcontractors. Coverage extends to UAP detection and tracking across air, space, maritime, cyber and electromagnetic domains, and to MITRE work involving Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, Raytheon, Boeing, General Dynamics, SAIC and Leidos. The temporal reach - back to 1930 - is unusual and deliberate: it predates MITRE's own 1958 founding, which means the request captures predecessor and inherited holdings including anything that travelled with the 485 staff who came from MIT Lincoln Laboratory. Counting from 22 May 2026, the 45-day unclassified production deadline fell on approximately 6 July 2026 and the 30-day index deadline on approximately 21 June 2026. As of 12 August 2026 no public production, index, or classified briefing outcome has been reported, and Burlison's office has not announced non-compliance. That silence is the open item on this board.

gao-nsiad-95-187.desc: GAO/NSIAD-95-187 is the only place in the entire legacy-era record where an independent arm of the United States government audited the paper trail and reported what it found. The scope was set by Rep. Steven H. Schiff of New Mexico after the Defense Department declined to answer his inquiries. GAO searched Air Force, Army, Navy, Defense Department, CIA, FBI, NSA, National Security Council and National Archives records, and visited multiple National Archives facilities to review Air Force UFO papers and Army Counterintelligence Corps records for 1947-1949. The report's operative findings are three sentences long and have never been rebutted by any agency: RAAF outgoing messages from October 1946 through December 1949 were destroyed; RAAF administrative records from March 1945 through December 1949 were destroyed; and the document disposition form does not indicate what organization or person destroyed the records and when or under what authority the records were destroyed. The Federal Records Act requires a disposition authority for the destruction of federal records. Its absence here is not a filing irregularity — it is the removal of the entire contemporaneous documentary output of a specific installation across precisely the years in question, with no accountable party. GAO also captured two other facts of standing value: the FBI's 8 July 1947 Dallas teletype recording Eighth Air Force's description of a hexagonal disc suspended from a balloon by cable, and the CIA Executive Director's statement that a search against 'Roswell, New Mexico' in all CIA databases produced no documents. Thirty-one years later, no executive-branch review — including AARO's 2024 historical report — has addressed the destruction finding, and no accountability inquiry has been opened.

robertson-panel.desc: The Robertson Panel is the documentary hinge of this domain because it converts a question of belief into a question of policy. The panel did not conclude that unidentified flying objects were nothing; it concluded that public interest in them was a national security liability, and it recommended action against the interest rather than investigation of the objects. The two stated aims of the recommended education programme were 'training' and 'debunking', with the debunking to be delivered through mass media — television, motion pictures and popular articles — using case histories that had been puzzling at first and were later explained, so as to reduce what the panel called the gullibility of the public. The Walt Disney organisation and the US Navy Special Devices Center were canvassed as production vehicles. The panel further recommended that civilian UFO organisations be watched because of their potentially great influence on mass thinking. The CIA's own official history, published in Studies in Intelligence in 1997, adds the part that makes this a concealment rather than merely a policy: Agency officials required that the panel report be classified and that any mention of CIA sponsorship of the panel be forbidden. Seven months after the panel reported, AFR 200-2 turned its posture into binding internal Air Force law; the following March, JANAP 146(C) put criminal penalties behind unauthorised disclosure. Anyone assessing later official statements on this subject is assessing the output of a system this panel specified.

bolender-memo.desc: The Bolender memorandum is short, administrative, and the most quietly damaging document in the legacy corpus. Its purpose was to justify closing Project Blue Book, and its argument was that closure would cost the Air Force nothing operationally because the reports that mattered had never been in Blue Book to begin with: UFO reports which could affect national security were made in accordance with JANAP 146 or Air Force Manual 55-11, and were not part of the Blue Book system. Read against JANAP 146(C) of 10 March 1954, which made unidentified flying objects a mandatory CIRVIS report and prohibited unauthorised disclosure of report contents under 18 U.S.C. 793 and 794, the memo describes a two-track structure operating for at least fifteen years: a public program that generated 12,618 catalogued sightings and a residue of 701 unknowns, and a classified channel whose output has never been named as a records series, never been accessioned by the National Archives, and never been searched under any disclosure statute — including the FY2024 NDAA provisions that created Record Group 615. Blue Book's records went to College Park. The other channel's records went somewhere that has not been identified in fifty-seven years. That gap is the specific, concrete, documentable thing this board exists to track, and it was opened by a brigadier general writing routine staff correspondence, not by a whistleblower.

cia-haines-1997.desc: The passage that matters, in full, from the section headed 'CIA's U-2 and OXCART as UFOs': 'The early U-2s were silver (they were later painted black) and reflected the rays from the sun, especially at sunrise and sunset. They often appeared as fiery objects to observers below. Air Force BLUE BOOK investigators aware of the secret U-2 flights tried to explain away such sightings by linking them to natural phenomena such as ice crystals and temperature inversions. By checking with the Agency's U-2 Project Staff in Washington, BLUE BOOK investigators were able to attribute many UFO sightings to U-2 flights. They were careful, however, not to reveal the true cause of the sighting to the public. According to later estimates from CIA officials who worked on the U-2 project and the OXCART (SR-71, or Blackbird) project, over half of all UFO reports from the late 1950s through the 1960s were accounted for by manned reconnaissance flights (namely the U-2) over the United States. This led the Air Force to make misleading and deceptive statements to the public in order to allay public fears and to protect an extraordinarily sensitive national security project. While perhaps justified, this deception added fuel to the later conspiracy theories and the coverup controversy of the 1970s.' The article also records that when pressure built for release of the Robertson Panel report, 'Philip Strong, Deputy Assistant Director of OSI, refused to declassify the report and declined to disclose CIA sponsorship of the panel. As an alternative, the Agency prepared a sanitized version of the report which deleted any reference to CIA and avoided mention of any psychological warfare potential in the UFO controversy.' Note what this establishes and what it does not. It establishes, from the Agency's own historian in the Agency's own journal, that the United States Air Force knowingly issued false explanations for UFO sightings to the American public for at least a decade, and that CIA sanitised a scientific panel report to conceal its own sponsorship and its psychological-warfare interest. It does not establish that every sighting was a U-2. The number given is 'over half,' and it is an estimate by the people with the strongest interest in it being high. The residual - the sightings not accounted for by reconnaissance aircraft, in a period when the Air Force was publicly reporting an unexplained rate falling to four percent - is the part CIA did not address.

wilson-davis-memo.desc: What the notes are alleged to contain, and why the board keeps them at claim tier 2 rather than promoting or dismissing them. The document is fifteen pages of handwriting. It is dated 16 October 2002. Its author, Eric W. Davis, is alive, named, and has confirmed authorship. Its subject, Vice Admiral Thomas R. Wilson (ret.), is alive, named, and denies it. The substance recorded is: that in 1997, as Joint Staff J-2, Wilson learned from a colleague of a special access programme concerning recovered non-human material; that he traced it through the SAP oversight apparatus to a programme with an aerospace contractor as the custodian; that he obtained a meeting with the programme's gatekeepers - described as a security officer, a corporate programme manager and a lawyer; and that he was refused the read-on because he had no need to know, notwithstanding his position. Three things make this more than a rumour and less than proof. More: the mechanism it describes - contractor-held custody, access denial to a cleared senior official on need-to-know grounds - was independently described under oath by David Grusch to the House Oversight Committee on 26 July 2023, and Grusch had no access to Wilson. Less: there is no second witness, no corroborating document, and the chain of custody by which the notes reached the public in 2019 has never been established on the record. Neither DoD nor AARO has published anything about the document. Members of the House Intelligence subcommittee put it to Ronald Moultrie and Scott Bray on 17 May 2022 and were told the witnesses were unaware of it. Two men are alive who can settle this, and no institution with subpoena power has attempted to make them.

afosi-kirtland-file.desc: The Bennewitz operation is the only place in this domain where the state's method is documented rather than inferred, and it is worth setting out the sequence precisely. 1979: Paul Bennewitz, a physicist running a USAF-supplying instrumentation company on the eastern edge of Kirtland AFB, begins recording lights and electronic emissions over the Manzano Weapons Storage Area and reports them, in writing, to the Air Force. 10 November 1980: AFOSI generates a record confirming that Kirtland security police have themselves observed unexplained aerial objects in the Coyote Canyon area and noting Bennewitz's activity. That document is the concession. From 1981: rather than investigate its own security police reports, AFOSI - through Special Agent Richard Doty and the civilian researcher Bill Moore - begins supplying Bennewitz with fabricated material about underground alien bases, treaties and biological experimentation, tailored to what he already half-believed. April 1983: Doty runs a parallel operation on a broadcaster, showing Linda Moulton Howe a paper she may read but not copy and promising film that never comes. December 1984: an anonymous film arrives in Los Angeles postmarked Albuquerque, producing the MJ-12 documents. 1988: Bennewitz is hospitalised. July 1989: Moore stands up at a MUFON conference and admits the whole thing. What was protected? Not the truth about aliens; the operation's own content was fiction. The thing protected was whatever was actually generating unexplained objects over a nuclear weapons storage complex - the thing AFOSI's own 10 November 1980 document conceded was happening and which no released record shows anyone ever investigated. Forty-six years later, AARO's historical review does not mention any of it.

caus-v-nsa.desc: The precise posture of the case matters because it is routinely misdescribed in both directions. NSA did not say it had no UFO records; it said it had them and could not release them. The plaintiffs did not lose because their claim was frivolous; they lost because the agency persuaded a judge, in a document the plaintiffs were forbidden to see, that disclosure would damage national security. The affidavit was executed by Eugene F. Yeates as NSA's Chief of Policy. The district court reviewed it in camera and granted summary judgment; the D.C. Circuit affirmed on 3 November 1981; the Supreme Court denied certiorari on 8 March 1982. NSA thereafter released the underlying records in a form that made the point of the litigation vividly: most pages carried only a few visible words, with the excisions made in white-out rather than black ink. A Mandatory Declassification Review filed in July 2013 was required to force further release. The Yeates affidavit itself has since been published in redacted form in NSA's own UFO collection. In 1995, GAO's Roswell records audit listed 'National Security Agency, Fort Meade, Md. - FOIA records, Citizens Against UFO Secrecy' among the record sets it searched, which means a private citizens' FOIA litigation body had become a recognised federal record set. This is the strongest single judicial fact in the American UFO record, and it has never been superseded: the United States holds UFO-related signals intelligence that it has told a federal court it cannot disclose.

yankee-blue.desc: The board's position on YANKEE BLUE is deliberately unresolved, and the reason is instructive. If the Wall Street Journal's June 2025 account is accurate, the Air Force ran, for something on the order of two decades, an institutionalised deception in which personnel were falsely read into a fictitious reverse-engineering programme - which would mean that a substantial share of the insider testimony in this field originates in a disinformation operation, and would simultaneously prove that the US Air Force runs disinformation operations about UFOs on its own people at scale. Either conclusion is damaging to the government. But the paper trail is missing. The Office of the Secretary of Defense searched its Correspondence Management Division and reported no records of the alleged spring 2023 cessation memo (case 25-F-3514, September 2025). It could not locate briefing materials prepared for DNI Avril Haines on the subject (case 25-F-3515, under appeal). AFOSI reported no records of any investigation (case 2025-06002-F). On 1 October 2025 the Pentagon's spokesperson said she could not confirm the memo existed and suggested asking the services. On 15 December 2025 an appellate decision found the CMD-only search inadequate under Oglesby v. U.S. Dep't of Army, 920 F.2d 57 (D.C. Cir. 1990) and remanded. So there are exactly three possibilities and the board holds all three open: the memo exists and the department cannot find its own Secretary-level directives; the memo does not exist and a major newspaper's central sourced claim about Pentagon conduct is unsupported; or the memo exists in a channel FOIA does not reach. The first and third are the concealment thesis. The second is a caution against accepting any account, including a debunking account, without the paper.

gao-roswell-report-1995.desc: GAO's report is the closest thing to a neutral federal referee this subject has ever had, and its findings are narrow, verifiable and damning. It was requested by Rep. Steven Schiff and issued 28 July 1995. GAO searched Air Force, Army, Navy, FBI, CIA, NSA, National Archives and presidential library holdings. It reported: that in 1947 Army regulations required air accident reports to be maintained permanently but that no military service filed a report on the Roswell incident and there was no requirement to report a weather balloon crash; that 'although some of the records concerning Roswell activities had been destroyed, there was no information available regarding when or under what authority the records were destroyed'; that only two government records originating in 1947 were recovered; and, specifically, that 'RAAF administrative records (from Mar. 1945 through Dec. 1949) and RAAF outgoing messages (from Oct. 1946 through Dec. 1949) were destroyed.' The disposition form for that destruction records neither the organisation nor the person responsible, nor the date, nor the authority. In federal records terms that is not an anomaly; it is a defect. Four years and three months of one installation's outgoing message traffic, spanning the exact window in question, eliminated with no accountable authority. GAO also documented that a July 1947 FBI record showed the military had reported an object 'resembling a high-altitude weather balloon' - and that this was one of only two 1947-origin records the entire government could produce.

thesis.desc: The 2026 disclosure episode is real, it is executive, and it is structurally incapable of answering the question the board exists to ask. A Truth Social post produced a task force with declassification authority over the entire Intelligence Community, an IC-wide waiver of nondisclosure agreements, oaths and commitments, and roughly sixteen gigabytes of released material - all without a published executive order, a defined scope, a manifest, a metadata schema, or a single FOIA case number. The one instrument that would change that, the Burlison amendment to the FY2027 NDAA, cleared the House on 22 July 2026 and faces a Senate base text with no UAP provisions in it at all.

dod-sapco.desc: The mechanism, stated plainly. Three documents define the space in which a concealed program could lawfully live. (1) 10 U.S.C. 119: annual SAP report to the four defense committees by 1 March; new-SAP notification by 1 February; 30 days notice before initiation - unless the Secretary waives it, in which case the information and the waiver justification go 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees'. Eight members. (2) DoD Directive 5205.07, reissued 12 September 2024, cancelling the 1 July 2010 version and incorporating the DEPSECDEF SAP Enterprise Reform memorandum of 11 July 2023: DoD SAPCO sits under the authority, direction and control of the Deputy Secretary of Defense; its Director is a GO/FO/SES reporting directly to DEPSECDEF, is executive secretary of the SAP governance committees, and 'coordinates congressional engagement'; and any person briefing Congress or congressional staff with SAP material must notify the Director, DoD SAPCO first, while contractors may not provide such material to Congress without specific approval. (3) The read-in practice described on the record by Chairwoman Anna Paulina Luna on 9 September 2025: a non-committee member must be approved by the chairman and ranking member of both HASC and HAC-D. Composed, these produce a structure in which the office administering a program is notified before the overseer is briefed, the contractor holding it is barred from talking to Congress, and the members entitled to know can be counted on two hands. Nothing in that sequence requires anyone to break the law.

waived-usap.desc: Terms of art, precisely. A special access program imposes protection beyond that required for information at the same classification level - access rosters, separate billets, dedicated security architecture. An ACKNOWLEDGED SAP appears in the budget by name with a classified purpose. An UNACKNOWLEDGED SAP is one whose existence is not confirmed; the correct response to an inquiry is neither confirmation nor denial. A WAIVED unacknowledged SAP adds the 10 U.S.C. 119(e) waiver, which removes the program from the report to the defense committees and substitutes notification to the chairman and ranking member of each. Every substantive allegation on this board resolves into one of exactly two propositions: that a materials acquisition and exploitation activity exists as a waived USAP known to eight members of Congress, or that it exists outside the SAP system entirely and is therefore unlawful. The first is testable by demanding the waived-SAP list. The second is testable by an ISOO NISP audit of cleared facilities. Neither test has been run.

doe.desc: Why DOE is the hardest problem on the board. Restricted Data and Formerly Restricted Data are created by the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 and are classified by operation of statute - 'born classified' - rather than by an original classification authority acting under an executive order. The practical consequences are three. First, a presidential declassification directive that operates on Executive Order 13526 information does not reach RD/FRD; the February 2026 UAP directive is such a directive. Second, RD/FRD is administered jointly by DOE and DoD under a separate procedure requiring DOE concurrence, so DoD cannot unilaterally release it either. Third, DOE's weapons complex - Los Alamos, Sandia, Livermore, the Nevada National Security Site, Pantex, Y-12, Savannah River - is contractor-operated on government land with its own clearance system, its own protective force and a legitimate mission that independently explains every observable security feature. Material held there requires no DoD SAP entry, appears in no 10 U.S.C. 119 report, and would not have been visible to AARO's SAPCO partnership, which AARO describes as covering 'the DoD, IC, and DHS'. DOE is not on that list. AARO's only recorded contact with DOE was a request that it 'review and provide any NDAs pertaining to UAP'.

how-money-reaches-an-invisible-program.desc: The mechanism, end to end, in six steps, each of which is documented in enacted law. (1) AUTHORISATION. Section 4001(a) of the FY2026 NDAA authorises obligation and expenditure of any dollar amount specified in a funding table; section 4001(d) provides that the section 'applies to any classified annex that accompanies this Act'. On the intelligence side, section 6101 of the FY2026 Intelligence Authorization Act authorises appropriations for intelligence activities without stating any amount, and section 6102(a) supplies the amounts by reference to 'the classified Schedule of Authorizations prepared to accompany this division', which section 6102(b)(3) forbids the President to disclose. (2) APPROPRIATION. Section 8006(a) of the FY2026 Defense Appropriations Act provides that the tables in the classified annex are 'hereby required by law to be carried out in the manner provided by such tables to the same extent as if the tables were included in the text of this Act'. (3) PUBLIC EXPRESSION. What appears in the printed law is a row saying 'CLASSIFIED PROGRAMS' and a number - twenty-five of them in FY2026, totalling $95.9 billion authorised, the largest being $26.92 billion in Other Procurement, Air Force - or, for research, the all-nines Program Element 9999999999. (4) MOVEMENT. Section 8005 permits $6 billion of transfer with OMB approval and after-the-fact notice; section 1001 permits $6 billion on the Secretary's own national-interest determination; section 8006(b) and section 4001(c) exempt movements among annex line items inside a single appropriation account from counting against either ceiling; and beneath all of it, DoD FMR Volume 3 Chapter 6 permits Below-Threshold Reprogramming with no approval and no notification, with congressional approval thresholds as low as $10 million. (5) EXECUTION TO A CONTRACTOR. Independent Research and Development, governed by DoD Instruction 3204.01, reimburses contractor-selected, contractor-directed, contractor-owned research as an allowable indirect cost across a contract portfolio - government money, no named programme line, no government title to the result. (6) REPORTING. SFFAS 56 permits the resulting figures to be presented in a different financial statement line item with no narrative explanation, permits omission of disclosures that would reveal classified information, and forbids the entity to disclose that it applied the standard. Every step is public law or public policy. Nothing here is speculative. The only thing missing is the content of the annex.

the-21-trillion-stated-precisely.desc: This must be said once, exactly, and then never loosely. The primary document is DODIG-2016-113, published 26 July 2016, which found that the Army Comptroller's office and DFAS Indianapolis 'did not adequately support $2.8 trillion in third quarter journal voucher (JV) adjustments and $6.5 trillion in yearend JV adjustments made to AGF data during FY 2015 financial statement compilation'. Footnote 2 of the report states that the amounts are not cumulative and should not be added together. A journal voucher adjustment is an accounting entry made during compilation to force data into balance; the same underlying dollar can be adjusted many times in a cycle, which is why $6.5 trillion is roughly fifty times the Army General Fund's annual appropriation. The figure is therefore a measure of entry volume, not of money that went missing. Mark Skidmore and Catherine Austin Fitts, in a summary report dated September 2017, compiled figures of this class from published OIG and GAO documents for fiscal years 1998 through 2015 and arrived at roughly $21 trillion for the Department of Defense and roughly $350 billion for HUD. Their own text states that the public reports 'only provide summary information; thus it is impossible for us to conduct a detailed assessment of the nature of these unsupported adjustments and errors' and that data could not be recovered for several years in the series. Neither the OIG nor Skidmore and Fitts claim that $21 trillion is missing. WHAT YOU MAY SAY: over eighteen fiscal years, two cabinet departments made accounting entries with a gross value of roughly $21 trillion that they could not document, and the government's own auditors said so. WHAT YOU MAY NOT SAY: $21 trillion is missing, unaccounted for in the sense of gone, or was spent on secret programmes. The second formulation is false, is trivially rebutted, and every time it is used it discredits the first, which is true and is devastating. The current equivalent figure, from the FY2025 audit, is more than $859 billion in unsupported adjustments in two quarters - a number that requires no interpretation at all.

sffas-56-what-it-actually-permits.desc: Read the operative words. Paragraph 9(a) of SFFAS 56 defines a permitted modification as 'Presenting amounts associated with one financial statement line item in another financial statement line item but not presenting narrative explaining the modification.' Paragraph 9(b) permits 'Omitting required disclosures, RSI, or RSSI that would otherwise reveal classified information.' Paragraph 8(b) permits a component reporting entity to be 'excluded from one reporting entity and consolidated into another reporting entity' - and the Statement acknowledges that consolidation modifications 'may change the net results of operations and/or net position' of the affected entities. Paragraph 8(c) permits application of Board Interpretations allowing further, unspecified modifications. Paragraph 12 requires a component entity to disclose that the standards permit modifications and simultaneously provides that the entity 'must not disclose application of this Statement'. Paragraph 13 requires the government-wide report to say only that 'modifications may have been made to certain presentations', without identifying which Interpretations were applied. FASAB's basis for conclusions explains that identifying which entities applied the standard 'would reveal classified information' and would allow users to track changes over time. Three things follow. First, the standard is not a licence to fabricate a bottom line: except through the consolidation route, modifications must not change net results of operations or net position. Second, it is a licence to put a true number in a false place with no footnote. Third, and decisively, there is no tripwire: because paragraph 12 forbids disclosure of application, no reader of any federal financial statement can determine whether what they are reading has been modified. The standard was issued 4 October 2018, effective for periods beginning after 30 September 2018, at the request of the Department of Defense which raised the need in August 2016. The exposure draft was issued 14 December 2017 with comments due 16 March 2018; seventeen comment letters were received.

sources.name: SFFAS 56, Classified Activities

the-named-mechanism.desc: The allegation is that programme funds were moved into private contractor custody outside congressional oversight. Its named mechanism, on the record from the witness, is procurement rather than appropriation. David Grusch, quoted in The Debrief on 5 June 2023: 'Individuals on these UAP programs approached me in my official capacity and disclosed their concerns regarding a multitude of wrongdoings, such as illegal contracting against the Federal Acquisition Regulations and other criminality and the suppression of information across a qualified industrial base and academia.' The Federal Acquisition Regulation is the body of rules determining what the government gets when it pays: data rights, technical data, title to property, allowability of costs. Contracting outside it is precisely how the government could pay for something and not own it. Congress then named a specific instrument. Section 1687(b) of the FY2024 NDAA, enacted 22 December 2023 and codified as a 50 U.S.C. 3373 note, provides that 'independent research and development funding relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena shall not be allowable as indirect expenses for purposes of contracts covered by such instruction' - the instruction being DoD Instruction 3204.01 - 'unless such material and information is made available the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership'. Section 7343(c) of the Intelligence Authorization Act for FY2024 repeats it through the Director of National Intelligence. IR&D is contractor-selected, contractor-directed research, owned by the contractor, reimbursed by the government as an overhead cost spread across a contract portfolio, with no appropriated programme line of its own. It is the only standard federal funding instrument that produces, by design, exactly the fact pattern alleged. Congress does not write a subject-specific carve-out to a cost-allowability rule about a subject it believes is absent from the IR&D portfolio. The companion funding bar in section 1687(a) - no funds for UAP activity under special or restricted access limitation absent disclosure to the committees and leadership - applied only to funds authorised by the FY2024 Act and was not re-enacted in the FY2025 or FY2026 NDAAs. The IR&D provision, having no fiscal-year limit, remains law and has never been the subject of a published compliance finding by any Inspector General.

sources.name: The Debrief, Kean and Blumenthal

why-the-failed-audit-is-evidence.desc: A failed audit is normally a management story. Here it is an evidentiary one, and the reason is a single named material weakness. Among the twenty-six weaknesses in the FY2025 audit is 'Universe of Transactions', which the Inspector General defines as 'The complete set of all transactions that fall within the scope of what is audited'. The Department's inability to establish that set is itself the finding. The consequence is precise and inescapable: no one - not the Inspector General, not the Government Accountability Office, not a congressional committee, not the Department itself - can demonstrate that a given payment did not occur, because the population against which such a search would run does not exist in complete form. The same audit finds Fund Balance with Treasury, roughly $1 trillion in spending accounts, unreconcilable, and 'Unsupported Accounting Adjustments' running to more than $859 billion in two quarters. The Department has now received a disclaimer of opinion for eight consecutive years, FY2018 through FY2025. In FY2025 twenty-two entities received stand-alone audits: eleven clean, one qualified, nine disclaimers, one no opinion. From FY2027 those twenty-two become seven, and an independent public accounting firm takes over as group auditor. This does not prove that anything was concealed. It proves that the instrument that would be required to disprove concealment does not exist and, on the Department's own account, has never existed.

sources.name: Statement of Brett A. Mansfield, Deputy Inspector General

the-classified-programs-arithmetic.desc: Computed directly from the enacted funding tables in Division D of each National Defense Authorization Act, counting every row whose title is 'CLASSIFIED PROGRAMS'. FY2024 (P.L. 118-31): 22 rows, $86.574 billion requested, $86.912 billion authorized. FY2025 (P.L. 118-159): 24 rows, $89.566 billion requested, $88.682 billion authorized. FY2026 (P.L. 119-60): 25 rows, $95.786 billion requested, $95.907 billion authorized. The largest single row in each year is the Air Force's Other Procurement classified line - FY2024 line 072A at $25.456 billion, FY2025 line 064A at $25.476 billion requested and $25.048 billion authorized, FY2026 line 077A at $26.920 billion. The next largest are Operation and Maintenance Defense-Wide (FY2026 line 530A, $22.751 billion) and Air Force RDT&E under Program Element 9999999999 (FY2026 line 293A, $22.264 billion requested, $22.385 billion authorized). Immediately above the Air Force procurement classified line sits 'SPECIAL UPDATE PROGRAM' at $1.178 billion in FY2026 - a titled line that discloses nothing. For comparison, the published FY2026 request was $81.9 billion for the National Intelligence Program and $33.6 billion for the Military Intelligence Program, a combined $115.5 billion. No public document maps the $95.9 billion of classified defense line items onto the $115.5 billion of intelligence programme aggregate, and no public document accounts for the difference. That reconciliation, if it exists, is in the classified annex.

throughLine.desc: Every national record on this board contains the same two moves in sequence: a classified assessment that the objects are real and structured, and an official recommendation to stop looking. Britain's Condign said UAP 'regularly appear in the UKADR' and then recommended DI55 stop monitoring them. Canada's Project Magnet said the vehicles were 'probably extra-terrestrial' and recommended acquiring the technology, and was defunded two years later. Brazil's Air Defence Command said the phenomena were 'solid and reflect intelligence' and classified the finding for twenty-three years. The USSR ran two programmes and gave as a reason for their secrecy that the characteristics might be militarily exploitable. Only France and Chile built offices that publish, and in June 2025 the Government of Canada named those two - and the American AARO - as the only models worth copying.

l-groom-lake.desc: Acknowledgement chronology, stated plainly because it is the board's benchmark: facility established April 1955; no acknowledgement of any kind 1955-1995; 1995 presidential determination exempting 'the Air Force's operating location near Groom Lake, Nevada' from environmental disclosure law, issued in the shadow of Kasza v. Browner and reissued annually; 1998 USAF acknowledgement that the site exists; 25 June 2013 CIA release of the U-2/OXCART history naming Area 51 and admitting specific activity, in response to a FOIA request filed in 2005 by Jeffrey T. Richelson of the National Security Archive. Fifty-eight years from establishment to specific acknowledgement, and the concession was compelled by a records request rather than volunteered. Any claim that a programme of this kind 'could not stay secret' has to be measured against this chronology.

immaculate-constellation.desc: The shape of the official response matters more than its content. The Department of Defense has said it has 'no record' of the programme - a records assertion, and the standard formulation used by an office without read-on to an unacknowledged compartment. It has not said the programme does not exist. Former AARO director Sean Kirkpatrick has denied it, but he departed AARO in December 2023, eleven months before the report surfaced. AARO itself has never addressed the name in any published product: not the FY2024 annual report, not the FY2025 report delivered 21 July 2026, not any statement for the record, and not in any of the five PURSUE tranches published between 8 May and 7 August 2026. AARO's own declassification information paper of September 2025 concedes that it cannot declassify independently and must request review from originating offices - which is a structural explanation for why an office chartered to resolve anomalies would have nothing to say about a compartment it is not read into. The result is that a named alleged USAP has sat in the Congressional Record for twenty-one months without a written executive branch response of any kind.

l-kirtland.desc: The Bennewitz operation is the best-documented instance in the American record of counterintelligence resources being deployed against a private citizen over UAP-adjacent observations, and both principal participants have admitted it. William Moore stated publicly on 1 July 1989 that he had attempted to push Bennewitz into a mental breakdown by feeding him false information; AFOSI special agent Richard C. Doty has said he was tasked in the 1980s with hoaxing documents and feeding false information to UFO researchers including Bennewitz; and a 1992 article held in the CIA library names both men. The material fed to Bennewitz - underground bases, alien-government agreements, the Dulce mythos - became load-bearing folklore that has contaminated the field for four decades. The stimulus that started it, the lights and signals Bennewitz recorded over the Manzano nuclear weapons storage area in 1979-1980, has never received an official explanation.

stringfield-status-reports.desc: The seven Status Reports are the domain's founding corpus and its founding problem. Dated and titled precisely: I, 'Retrievals of the Third Kind', MUFON Symposium, Dayton, 29 July 1978 (revised 20 July 1978), also published in Flying Saucer Review; II, 'The UFO Crash/Retrieval Syndrome: New Sources, New Data', January 1980, published by MUFON; III, 'Amassing the Evidence', 1982, endorsed by Dr. Peter Rank of Methodist Hospital and Richard H. Hall, former Assistant Director of NICAP; IV, 'The Fatal Encounter at Ft. Dix-McGuire', June 1985; V, 'Is the Coverup Lid Lifting?', January 1989; VI, 'The Inner Sanctum', July 1991, self-published at 4412 Grove Avenue, Cincinnati, edited by Richard Hall; VII, 'Search for Proof in a Hall of Mirrors', February 1994. Complete scans of all seven are public. The corpus is the reason the crash-retrieval field exists and the reason it cannot be audited: the source-protection coding that made it possible to collect made it impossible to check.

roswell-report-case-closed.desc: The most heavily documented artifact in the Roswell record, on either side. It prints the anthropomorphic dummy launch and landing locations, sworn statements from ten named Air Force personnel including Joseph W. Kittinger Jr., and full interview transcripts of the five principal pro-UFO witnesses. Its Section 2.1 nurse analysis is the only occasion on which the United States government has publicly worked a UFO witness claim down to certified daily personnel accounting records and named the individual it believes the witness actually described. Whatever one concludes about Project Mogul and the dummies, this is the standard of documentation this board holds every claim to, including the ones it finds persuasive.

kean-v-nasa.desc: The only federal court finding in existence that a US agency failed its records-search obligations on a UFO matter. Docket 1:03-cv-02509 (D.D.C.), Judge Emmet G. Sullivan, filed 9 December 2003, dismissed 24 August 2009 after a court-supervised re-search under a stipulated settlement. The opinion's most quotable line for this domain is not about UFOs at all: 'Plaintiff contends, and indeed NASA admits, that NASA's first two searches for responsive documents were inadequate.' The template - request, appeal, sue, obtain a supervised search, litigate status reports for two years - is the only method that has ever forced a US agency to look again.

sac-overflights-1975.desc: The best-documented UFO episode in United States government records, full stop. Five installations in two countries over a fortnight, logged in the NORAD Command Director's log, the 24th NORAD Region Senior Director's log, National Military Command Center memoranda and base teletypes, with F-106 scrambles timed to the minute and FAA cross-tell recorded. It reached the public because two men filed a FOIA request on 26 December 1977 and an Assistant Secretary of Defense decided in February 1978 that no useful purpose would be served by withholding twenty-four Joint Chiefs documents. Nothing in the crash-retrieval literature comes within an order of magnitude of this evidentiary standard, which is precisely the point.

cash-v-united-states.desc: Civil Action No. H-84-348, S.D. Tex., Houston Division. Filed 18 January 1984 under 28 U.S.C. 1346(b) and 2671 et seq. by Betty Cash, Vickie Landrum and Colby Landrum; attorney in charge Peter A. Gersten; dismissed 21 August 1986 by Judge Ross N. Sterling under FRCP 12(b)(1), 12(b)(6) and 56. The docket sheet classifies the cause as 'Airplane Product Liability', which is the United States district court system's best available description of a UFO injury claim. The open thread is the Defense Department's internal investigation into whether the object was a US military device: it happened, and no document from it has ever surfaced.

malmstrom-echo-flight-1967.desc: The domain's cleanest illustration of the difference between an event and its explanation. That ten Minuteman missiles of Echo Flight went off alert on 16 March 1967 is Air Force paper. That an object caused it is testimony from a named officer with a signed affidavit and a corroborating letter from his own commander. That an electromagnetic pulse simulator test caused it is a competing engineering account. One unreleased document - the 341st Strategic Missile Wing unit history and crew rosters for March 1967 - would probably settle both the flight designation and the sequence, and it has not appeared in fifty-nine years.

carve-out.desc: How the carve-out maps onto the allegations, step by step. The central claim on this board is that recovered material is held and worked on by private defence contractors rather than by the government, and that no one outside the program can verify this. The carve-out is the documented mechanism that makes exactly that state of affairs lawful. Sequence: (1) A cognizant authority proposes a prospective SAP and includes, at item 11.d of the SAP Approval Package Checklist, a 'Contract strategy (carve-out justification if applicable)'. (2) The Director of DoD SAPCO sends an action memo to the Deputy Secretary of Defense recommending approval as an unacknowledged SAP and carve-out status - the unclassified template in DoDI 5205.11 Appendix 3 to Enclosure 6 reads, in terms, 'The Defense Security Service will be carved out from its normal industrial security oversight responsibilities.' (3) The Deputy Secretary signs. (4) By operation of 32 CFR 117.6(b)(3) the Director of DCSA is relieved of NISP oversight for that program. (5) By operation of DoDM 5205.07-V1 Enclosure 2 para 2.c, three specific things stop: DCSA no longer performs SAP security inspections at the contractor location; DCSA no longer authorises the classified contractor information systems or guest systems in the contractor SAP facility; DCSA no longer runs the counterintelligence threat and incident cross-sharing for that facility. (6) Oversight passes to a Program Security Officer appointed in writing by the cognizant authority SAPCO and exercising responsibilities 'on behalf of the SAPCO' - inside the program. (7) The signed carve-out approval and the list of carved-out facilities go into the program record file under DoDI 5205.11 Enclosure 7, and DoD SAPCO holds the confirmation of which facilities are carved out under Enclosure 2 para 2.k. Nothing in this chain is disputed, hypothetical or sourced to a witness. The only unknown is the content of two documents that are known by directive to exist: the carve-out approvals signed by Secretaries and Deputy Secretaries of Defense, and the facility list DoD SAPCO maintains.

usc-10-119e.desc: The hinge, stated as plainly as it can be. A witness alleging that Congress was not told about a program is usually assumed to be alleging a crime. Under 10 U.S.C. 119(e) that assumption is wrong. The Secretary of Defense may lawfully decide, case by case, that telling the defense committees something would adversely affect national security, and thereupon tell only the chairman and ranking minority member of each committee instead. There is no committee veto, no ISOO concurrence, no court, no register of waivers, no expiry, no periodic requirement to widen access, and no penalty. Compare the covert action regime, which is normally described as the most secretive corner of American government: under 50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(5)(B), when access to a finding is limited to the Gang of Eight, the President must within 180 days either open it to all members of the intelligence committees or file a further written statement of reasons. A waived special access program has no such clock. That comparison is the single most useful fact this domain contributes to the board: the mechanism at the centre of the Grusch allegations is lawful, is older than the allegation, is weaker than the covert action rule it is usually compared to, and leaves an auditable paper trail in exactly two places - the Secretary's waiver determinations, and the Senior Review Group's annual review of all waived programs.

four-regime-map.desc: Where a program could sit, and what changes when it moves. There are five distinct legal environments, and the practical differences between them are the map of where concealment is easiest. (1) A DoD special access program: reports to six defense committees, waivable to eight to twelve members by the Secretary's own determination. (2) An NNSA special access program: same committees, and the Administrator may additionally waive the 30-day advance notice itself, so a program can begin with no committee ever having been told in advance - and NNSA material is Restricted Data, born classified by operation of the Atomic Energy Act rather than by an original classification authority, so a presidential declassification order operating on E.O. 13526 information does not reach it. (3) A non-DoD, non-NNSA, non-IC agency special access program: reports to House Oversight and Senate Homeland Security among others, and the waiver does not narrow the audience - the strongest of the SAP regimes, and the one covering DHS, NASA, Justice and Commerce. (4) An IC Controlled Access Program: no waiver at all, semiannual briefings, a funding cutoff since December 2024 and, since December 2024, a prohibition on transferring a capability out into a special access program without notice. (5) A National Security Council covert action program: outside all four SAP regimes by the express terms of ICD 906 section C.3, governed only by 50 U.S.C. 3093. The seam that matters is between (4) and (1). Before 23 December 2024 there was no statutory requirement to notify anyone when a capability moved from an IC controlled access program into a DoD special access program, and the move changes both the governing statute and the committees entitled to know. Congress closed that door prospectively in section 6603 of Public Law 118-159 - and left it ajar with an exception for transfers 'necessary to maintain access in the event of an organizational restructuring', a determination the transferring official makes for himself.

sap-annual-report.desc: The single most valuable unreleased document on this board. It exists. It has existed in annual editions since the first one fell due under 10 U.S.C. 119(a)(1). It lists, by unclassified nickname, every DoD special access program in the budget, with a brief description, milestones, historical cost and six years of cost estimates. Its accuracy is certified before submission by the Senior Review Group and validated annually by the Special Access Program Oversight Committee, chaired by the Deputy Secretary of Defense. It is coordinated with the Assistant Secretary of Defense for Legislative Affairs under DoDI 5545.02. Programs whose reporting has been waived under 119(e) are, by definition, absent from it, and the substitute material given to the chairs and ranking members 'shall remain in DoD custody' with no copies stored outside DoD repositories. Three things follow for anyone trying to force the record open. First, the assertion that the government does not know how many special access programs it has is false and is contradicted by DoD's own governance directive. Second, the difference between the count in the annual report and the count on the Senior Review Group's waived list is a single number that would, if produced, tell the public how much of the SAP enterprise is invisible to the committees as a whole. Third, that number has never been requested in public by any member of Congress at any hearing this board has recorded.

sap-taxonomy.desc: Terms of art, precisely, and why each one matters to the allegations. ACKNOWLEDGED: existence admitted, details classified. If a recovery program were acknowledged, its nickname would be in the annual report and the argument would be over. UNACKNOWLEDGED: 'enhanced security measures ensuring the existence of the program is not acknowledged, affirmed, or made known to any person not authorized'. This is the state in which a truthful official can decline to confirm or deny, and in which a denial issued by a press office staffed by people without access is a denial made in good faith by people who genuinely do not know. WAIVED: an unacknowledged SAP whose statutory reporting has been removed by the Secretary. This is the state in which the phrase 'Congress was not informed' can be simultaneously true and lawful. Cross-cutting these are the mission categories - acquisition, intelligence, and operations and support, the last defined to protect 'the planning for, execution of, and support to especially sensitive military operations' and expressly capable of protecting 'organizations, property, operational concepts, plans, or activities'. The word 'property' in an official DoD definition is the closest thing in the public policy corpus to a category designed for custody of a physical object whose existence is itself the secret. And any SAP with subordinate structure is an 'umbrella' with 'compartments, sub-compartments, or projects' - which is why a person read into one compartment can truthfully testify to what he was told about others without ever having seen a document.

dod-sapco-arch.desc: The closed loop, drawn once. Follow the arrows and every one returns to the same office. DoD SAPCO writes the criteria for the annual review of waived programs. DoD SAPCO holds the confirmation of which contractor facilities are carved out of DCSA oversight. DoD SAPCO is the single point of congressional liaison for every DoD special access program. Everyone accessed to a DoD SAP must notify DoD SAPCO when they brief a member of Congress. No contractor may give SAP material to a member of Congress without DoD SAPCO's approval. DoD SAPCO's Director is the Executive Secretary of the SAPOC, the Vice Chair of the Senior Review Group and the Chair of the SAP Senior Working Group, and is appointed by, and reports directly to, the Deputy Secretary of Defense - the same official who signs carve-outs and to whom the Secretary's waiver authority is functionally delegated in practice. There is no external validator anywhere in the loop. That is not an allegation; it is the organisational chart set out in DoDD 5205.07, DoDI 5205.11 and DoDM 5205.07 Volume 1. The Director of DoD SAPCO has never testified in open session and the incumbent's name is not published.

accm.desc: The floor beneath the floor. Every congressional SAP reporting statute - 10 U.S.C. 119, 50 U.S.C. 2426, 50 U.S.C. 3348 - is triggered by the term 'special access program'. Alternative Compensatory Control Measures are defined in the NISPOM rule as the security measures used 'where SAP controls are not required'. An ACCM therefore is not a SAP, and no reporting statute reaches it: no annual report, no new-program notice, no 30-day report-and-wait, no waiver needed because there is nothing to waive. ACCMs carry nicknames, access rosters and compartmented handling, and 32 CFR 117.23 imposes contractor obligations for them in the same supplement as SAPs and SCI. For anyone building a picture of where an activity could be run with the least congressional visibility, ACCM is the answer that requires no waiver, no Deputy Secretary signature and no entry on any list Congress receives. The number of ACCMs in existence has never been reported to Congress because no statute requires it.

sap-cover-mechanisms.desc: What the tradecraft looks like in DoD's own words. Three documented mechanisms convert an unacknowledged program into something that leaves almost no trace in ordinary paperwork. First, nicknames: every DoD SAP gets an unclassified two-word nickname from the Joint Staff NICKA system, and it is the nickname, not the mission, that appears in the annual report to Congress. A member reading the list sees words. Second, HVSACO - HANDLE VIA SPECIAL ACCESS CHANNELS ONLY - which is applied when using a SAP nickname for an unacknowledged program, to protect 'sensitive relationships', and to protect information that does not warrant classification at all, and which the manual states 'is not a classification'. Material marked HVSACO is therefore outside the E.O. 13526 declassification machinery entirely: it cannot be the subject of a mandatory declassification review, automatic declassification at twenty-five years, or a classification challenge, because those remedies operate only on classified national security information. Third, unacknowledged locations: DoDM 5205.07 Volume 1 provides that 'Federal Government-affiliated identification cards will not be used for positive identification in unacknowledged locations' - a rule that exists because there are facilities at which producing a federal badge would itself constitute a disclosure. Together these are the answer to the recurring question of why decades of FOIA requests have produced so little: much of the relevant paper is either inside a compartment or bears a caveat that is not a classification and therefore has no declassification pathway.

icd-906.desc: Why the intelligence side is the harder problem and the softer target at the same time. Harder: ICD 906 has no statutory annual report deadline, no 30-day pre-initiation clock and no publicly reported program list, and unacknowledged CAPs may be created on the signature of two people, the DNI or the Principal Deputy DNI. Softer: since 15 March 2022 the statute at 50 U.S.C. 3091a requires semiannual briefings on every controlled access program in effect to the intelligence and appropriations committees and congressional leadership, requires annual reports listing every active and every terminated compartment and sub-compartment with a DNI certification that each is substantiated and justified and a named control officer for each, contains no waiver authority whatsoever, and since 23 December 2024 cuts off National Intelligence Program funding for any CAP established without notification. On paper the IC has the strongest special-access oversight regime in the United States government and the DoD has the weakest. ICD 906 also does two things of direct forensic value: it requires that all CAPs and all individual accesses be recorded in Scattered Castles, the IC personnel security database, with exemptions approvable only by the DNI or PDDNI and reviewed annually - so a person's access history is a queryable record - and it expressly disclaims application to programs 'under the purview of the National Security Council, such as covert action', identifying the one remaining space that neither SAP regime reaches.

gao-04-332.desc: The audit that was steered. When officials say the special access program system is subject to oversight, the honest test is to ask what the Government Accountability Office has actually examined. GAO-04-332 is the only public GAO product on the security of cleared contractor facilities under the National Industrial Security Program. It was requested by the Senate in the report accompanying the FY2004 NDAA. It found that DoD could not provide adequate assurances that its oversight ensures the protection of classified information, and that DSS had not always followed required procedures after reported compromises. And its second footnote records that, 'As agreed with committee staff', the review deliberately excluded DSS's oversight of special access programs at contractor facilities. The auditor was sent into the building and asked not to open one set of doors - by agreement with the committee that commissioned the audit. Every subsequent assertion that the contractor SAP system has been independently examined has to be measured against that sentence.

_note.desc: Domain and location dossiers carry their full desc, claims[] and sources[] inline on the entity records in entities[], following the convention used by ffrdcs.json and media-structure.json. entityInfo is left empty rather than duplicating that content, so there is one place to correct an error rather than two.

_taxonomy_scope.desc: 50 cls:'domain' entities and 54 cls:'location' entities. The domain set covers every d-* id referenced anywhere in /root/uap-tracker/research plus nine defined forward for wave 2-3 use. The location set covers every l-* id referenced in the corpus that was not already defined by another task, verified by a full re-scan after writing.
